I first played Caves of Qud years ago, and it was in very early development.  I was fascinated by the character customization and the interesting sci-fi world to explore.  Ultimately I put the game down for a while because I wanted to revisit it once it developed further.  That day has come and I couldn't be happier.  If you're looking for an authentic roguelike experience, there are few games that can offer you more.  If you are a lover of science fiction or simply looking for an in-depth, challenging experience, I invite you to join me in Qud.
Live and drink.

Using the keyboard and numpad to manuvre across the land of Qud trying to understand what the Ganglionic teleprojector equiped on your head does you find the entrance to an cave. Its filled with large bats and vicious snapjaws, fighting your way down with your four dubble-muscled arms you find a chest. You are delighted as you find your first musket since that damned qudzu vine rusted you your previous rifle beyond usable condition, now you could show those mean hard-shelled crabs who's the one in charge. Lured by the call of other hidden treasures you press on further down the cave. As you enter the next floor of the dungeon you are terrified as you see the large sleeping slumberling before you. You quickly calm yourself as you recall that slumberlings sleep for all but one day a year, silently you move past the beast to the next room where five snapjaws awaits. two arrows whizzes past your head. Taking cover behind the nearest rock you are once again terrified as you hear a very irritated growl behind you, one arrow hit the slumberling and now it is mad, it is staring right at you, it charges. Within seconds it has struck you down with its huge claws, for a fleeting moment you feel the life leaving you body, you are dead!
Well this is a story that happened to me when playing Caves of Qud, how are you going to meet your end?

Caves of Qud is a fantastically bizarre and alien turn-based roguelike by the developers that made Sproggiwood. This game was originally released years before Sproggiwood, but it was put on hold when the devs began working on other projects. The game is finally here, now with added graphics, new features and mechanics. It's just better in every single way.
This is an open world roguelike and you're able to do pretty much anything and everything you want to at the start of the game, It's one of the few roguelikes out there with a plot and story to follow and actually really works.
Caves of Qud is without a doubt one of the best roguelikes currently available on Steam.

TLDR: The game will draw you in, making you feel something for the characters. By the end, the game rips out your heart. It shows your heart to you. Then it crushes your heart in front of you with just how cruel the reality of the real world can be.
CHARACTERS: 10/10
The characters are actually pretty fun to watch as they interact with each other. There is a shockingly high amount of witty dialogue between most of the characters. Yahiko, the supposedly ever gullible guy who hides his real emotions behind a wall of arrogance and endearing naive attitude. Rui, the witty childhood friend who helped her best friend through a very dark time of his life. Yama, the snarky sarcastic guy with issues who lovingly pokes fun at his friends. Masato, the smart athletic guy who takes most things literally and loves to compete with his friends. Shigure, the independent and intelligent woman who uses her excessively large vocabulary to insult people that♥♥♥♥♥♥her off. This is about half of the cast but I won't spoil this treat for people. The characters are memorable and I will not be forgetting them any time soon. The character personalities and their friendships are fleshed out well enough that I see this aspect being, dare I say, believeable.
MUSIC: 9/10
The accompanying music is actually pretty fitting to the situations that the main character finds himself in. In particular, I really enjoy the title music and the melancholy tracks. When I heard the title music, I suspected that I was in for one hell of a treat when it came to the music. I wasn't fond of the "comedy situation" tracks, hence the 9/10. However, the rest of the tracks made up for that by being very well suited to the themes and situations of the game. Even though there are some parts where there is no music, this doesn't detract from the game at all. The ambient sounds fill the gap rather nicely for almost all of those situations. As for the rest of the situations, the silence works perfectly for driving home specific emotions that are tied directly to the silent scenes.
STORY: 10/10
"Life isn't fair. Deal with it, kid." That sums up the cruelty of this exceedingly well-written story. If you're looking for a lovey-dovey experience that makes your heart feel warm and fuzzy, then you are looking for those things in the wrong game. If you wanna know what the story is about, just read the developer's wall of text in the "About This Game" section. I will say this though: pick your choices wisely or you
.
MYSTERIES: 9/10
Yes, you are actually pushed into solving mysteries in this game. Don't expect Danganronpa murder mysteries here. However, each mystery is well crafted and it can take some time to figure out the correct answers. Still, the answers are always right in front of you. You just need to adjust your way of thinking from time to time. If you don't have the patience for the mysteries, you can always hit up the Lucid9 guides section. There is a guide that only covers the mysteries. Why take the easy way out when you can give your brain a reasonable challenge?
TWISTS: 8/10
About half-way through the game, I narrowed the murderer down to three suspects. To do that, I literally spent about 30 minutes thinking over all the details that had been discovered in the game. However, the murders aren't the only situations with twists. Sometimes, you think you've got a person figured out and then you find that you are dead wrong. Other times, you think you've got some "friend" of the main character figured out. Then, you notice a little context clue that puts an entire fight between two characters into an ugly context all too similar to real life for some people.
I fear for the mental stability of whoever wrote this. That said, 10/10

Awesome, amazing, funny, those are alll great ways to describe this game. The controls are super simple, the gameplay is immense, the jokes are nonstop. If you enjoy humor games then you'll want to pick this one up.
Of course there are some complaints, so lets go ahead and get those out of our way. Super short, yeah it is. you can speed run it in about 45 mins, and can get all achievements in one run through if you take your time and explore resulting in about 3-4 hours of gameplay. I know right. Secondly, the mouse, you will need to adjust your settings when you first start, put them on the lowest setting you can, otherwise you'll spin in circles. Lastly, some people including myself have reported feeling ill while playing this. Turning off the mouse smoothing option will help, however the game also has a 3D element to it, so that might be whats making people get motion sickness. (but if you have a pair of 3d glasses or can make a pair, it makes the game so much more...insane. Yeah thats a good way to put it.
If your young I'll admit you might not get some of the jokes. A lot of the comments and references are from old 70's and 80's films, cartoons and TV shows. Hunter S. Thompson has a nice role in the game, with some great quotes I might add, so that should give you some kind of indication what level of humor we are talking about here. (If you don't know who Hunter S. is, please go watch 2 movies right now, Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and Where the Buffalo Roam. His books and articles from Rolling Stone are better but I can't expect anyone to read a book anymore.)
So yeah I recommend this game, its funny, it looks great, the soundtrack is great, controls are easy and self explanitory. Only issue is that its super short, (makes Protal 2 look like a long game), and it can make some people feel ill after playing for a while.

One of the greatest traditional roguelikes out there, updated and improved immensely from the previous version. Caves of Qud one-ups most of the genre by having fully rebindable keys, a well-crafted UI system, factions, interesting abilities, and very unique areas around its open world. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys turn-based combat, emergent gameplay and a post-apocalyptic setting.

I stood at the entrance to Red Rock, a forbidding stairway leading down into the dark. Taking a deep breath, I prepared to enter, an- OW, CRUD, WHAT THE - BABBOONS? The apes weren't happy. Obviously, Red Rock was their home, and, screeching and throwing rocks, they were making this displeasure obvious. I readied my carbide sword, and attempted to close. But no, their shrieks turned to ape-chortles, and they drew back, still pelting rocks from every side. As consciousness started waning, I flicked open the artefact at my belt, pushed the button on its spherical surface, and threw.
The world went white. My last thought? Screw you, you darn dirty monkeys.
Even a failure in Qud is a story, and it's been an enjoyable romp so far. Want to be a tinker, exploring the secrets of the past, but not being so hot at this "fighting" gig? You're good! Want to be a Mutant, shooting flames from invisibility, but secretly an outcast? Yup, do-able. A no-nonsense gunslinger? Well, needs a bit of working towards, as ammo is rare, but... There's a lot of stories in this game, and while, like many roguelikes, it's permadeath, and at first you aren't going to get very far, you're definitely going to have some stories. Even at this release stage, there's interesting things to do, and places to explore...
Recommended for Roguelike fans, and beware, not everything can be killed by you in the early game, so don't hesitate to run away if things get tough!

Full disclosure: I've been playing the alpha of this game since 2012, and got a free copy from the developer.
Caves of Qud is a roguelike along the lines of ADOM. There's random dungeons, a set storyline, traditional gameplay, sure. But what makes Caves of Qud stand out amongst the crowd is the sheer mystique of the setting - Qud is a dangerous country in a post-apocalyptic era. Most of the humans (potentially including you) are mutants with strange powers that grant interesting tactical choices. The areas feel extremely unique (a rarity in the roguelike genre) - one area has you rushing to the bottom of a pit on conveyor belts while trying to avoid the toxic inhabitants, another area has a strange mix of machine-worshipping humans and armored trolls in a cyrogenic environment with optional frozen bosses... the list goes on.
Character customization is also neat. Beyond mutations, there's also skills, a crafting system, faction relations... It's a bit overwhelming at first. It is fun to eventually grow into a winged psychic with a flamethrower that has a poor relationship with the consortium of plants!
The combat is by far the neatest thing I've seen in a traditional roguelike. Most of the skills and spells have neat effects tied onto them, and most of the enemies have interesting behavior with their abilities. There's a ton of tactics involved, and mashing the basic attack of moving into enemies is a sure way to die past a certain point in the game.
Being a roguelike, there is permadeath, BUT you can turn it off if you wanted to. But hey, what kinda roguelike doesn't have permadeath?
It's also reeeeally difficult. It took me a ton of tries just to get a character past a certain point in the game. Some of it has been rebalanced in the alpha, but you should still prepare to die. And die. And die.
The major gripes I have with this game are its memory issues (which I'm told are being fixed) and that the tiles can make things look really similar (which can be turned off). It's also still unfinished, so there's that too (though it still takes ~5 hours to beat if you don't die. Protip: you will die).
Conclusions:
+ Excellent lore, setting
+ Really cool character customization
+ Interesting combat
+ Togglable permadeath
+/- Pretty difficult
- Memory issues
- Tiles make everything look really similar (togglable)
- It's still in early accessm, so it's unfinished

Alright, time for a seriousness edit:
Caves of Qud is a traditional-style roguelike, set in a fallout-esque world a few thousand years after the end of the world. It's got plenty of procedurally generated caves and ruins to explore scattered across a large overworld, all tied together by a quest line rife with side-quests. At least, that's what it aims to be eventually; currently, the main quest line is not finished, and many side quests remain unimplemented as of the writing of this review. Despite this, there's tons of content to discover and die by.
Even though the quest line is unfinished, you will die many, many times before you reach the end (you'll know when it stops, if you make it that far). The difficulty and frequency of death allows you to explore the rich character creation system the game is packing. This system offers many options, allowing you to choose whether you begin as a mutant (slower skill point gain, but gains useful mutations) or a True Man (higher starting attributes, and increased skill point gain). From there, you've got a number of physical/mental mutations (for mutants) or castes (for True Men) to choose from. Additionally, Qud offers you a skill tree of sorts as you level up, allowing you to gain abilities as you grow more experienced. Oh, and dialogue trees!
Though it may be difficult to get in to, Caves of Qud offers a unique,engaging, and deeply rewarding rpg experience. I wholeheartedly recommend it to people interested in the genre, or to anyone interested in being mauled by a sleepy panther-bear because they spontaneously combusted while sneaking past it.

Disclaimer: I got a Steam key from a developer but these opinions are my own.
This is a classic Rogue-like in mechanics, but innovative in design. It's tough, unforgiving, but there's a lot of depth that will keep you coming back for more and don't let the early access banner fool you: this game has been in development for a long time and is totally playable, with tens of hours of gameplay thanks to the in depth character building systems and epic quest arc. The time played on Steam for me pales to the amount of time I've spent playing the old ASCII graphics version from years ago.
You have the choice of playing a mutant or a "true man", true men have a better time early on but mutant play is where the game really shines, there are a load of different mutations that can completely change how you approach the game. Want to fly over your enemies setting them on fire? Want to spawn multiple copies of yourself and shoot the crap out of something with mind lasers? Want to play a characterr with four arms and legs, each arm wielding a different weapon? Want to play a human beetle with horns and a carapace? You can do all this and more.
The world is rich and interesting too, you have an open world that you're free to explore as you wish (if you can survive), and there are distinct cultures and lore attached to the different places you'll travel to. The lore is so unique, the world being set in a post-apocalyptic age with the remnants of so many societies all layered on top of each other. It's a far cry from the generic mediaeval/fantasy setting you usually get with Rogue-likes.
If you've never played a traditional Rogue-like, the game might seem daunting at first, I know I butted my head against it for quite a wehile before I managed to get anywhere, but if you keep at it you'll find yourself rewarded with a very unique gaming experience.

Survarium is a free to play shooter which aims to reignite the feel and gameplay of the STALKER series. I have heard (unproven) that devs that worked on STALKER are now working on Survarium, which is very cool.
At it’s core the game is a PVP Shooter. PVE is there but I will rant about PVE later.
But let’s get started. I will now talk about my experience in the game
I started as soon as the latest update hit, so I can talk from a newcomer perspective, as to what they changed I can’t tell you – wasn’t there.
It starts you off with 3 days of free premium, which is nice. You have four classes to chose from: Scavengers, Black Market, The Renaissance Army, The Fringe Settlers. Each have different kinds of weapons. The Scavengers, for example, are more of a snipery class. I have only really played the Scavengers, because sniping is just my cup of tea.
The first two tiers are very easy. I went 50-4 or even higher, because I was mainly versing bots with one to three players in the enemy team, the rest got backfilled with bots – I don’t mind. But as soon as I hit T3 the problems for me started.
Problem is, feels like everyone in the game has a scope but me. I see people with 4x, 2x, simple red dot and I have a sniper with Iron Sights. I can still kill people, yes, but I am at a significant disadvantage. An iron sight bolt action sniper versing an Assault Rifle with an 8x scope? Well Good luck hitting his head. I still manage to keep my K/D above 1.0 for the most part, but it is a struggle every time.
1.	Attachments for your guns
You need to kill people with your gun to unlock different spots for upgrades on your weapon. 50 kills for a barrel upgrade slot, 100 kills for an under-barrel attachment (e.g. Laser pointer) and 200 kills for a scope. I got those kills quickly, because, as said before, I am killing loads of people and they all count towards the kills. Thing is: as soon as you unlocked the slot, that doesn’t mean you will unlock an attachment for your gun. If you *WIN* a game you get a random chance to get an attachment. For any gun in the game. Not even the Faction you were playing. For any gun. So now I already have a considerable amount of gear for Assault Rifles, Shotguns, all that good stuff. But I am playing snipers. In 21 hours I got a barrel attachment and a laser sight for my sniper. That’s it. No scopes, no nothing. I am beginning to think that they purposefully don’t drop attachments for the guns you use.
You can buy the attachments for Real-Life currency if you want to but any attachment you buy has the price tag of TWO EUROS!!! I am not paying 2 EUR to get a scope. And with the modifications being pure RNG it is sooooooo frustrating! Because I have no goal to work towards.
If you want to remove the attachment again? Well that’s 100Gold (1$) Unless you want to DESTROY IT!
2.	Damage and Bleeding.
Aka why do I even bother with snipers?
I need two shots to kill others on T3 if they don’t heal up again. Because the game has a powerful healing item which almost instantly gets you back up to full HP With every shot you have a bleed chance. Bleeding means: Heal up or die. But with the enemy shooting me down low with three shots I don’t even get the chance to heal up because the bleed ticks so fast I can’t play the animation to heal myself fast enough. You can Wallbang but my T2 Sniper is only able to shoot through wood while a T3 assault rifle can shoot me through concrete. I want to stick to my T2 sniper though. Because I just want to have a scope on it. Then everything will be so much easier.
3.	Upgrading your gear
You get 4 to 16 scrap for every game you play. Using scrap you have a 50% chance to upgrade your weapon/armour/gas mask. If you spend 10 gold you have a 100% chance. You can pick one of three upgrades for your item and then unlock the 2nd upgrade slot. There is a total of 3 slots per item. The 50% chance is either a lie or I am the unluckiest person on the planet. If you picked an upgrade and later want to change it you can reroll it for a small amount of scrap. BUT you only get 1 of 3 options, the other two options are locked behind the price of 10 gold.
4.	Pve
LOL PVE? You have one map with one mission where you have to find stashes (Loot boxes) and get to the end of the level. There are invisible anomalies you have to throw Nuts and bolts into to find where they are. They almost kill you if you walk into one of them. There are three camps of enemies. Those enemies have wallhack and aimhack So they can one-shot you as soon as you walk into their sights. They are badly programmed and one point in the mission is particularly annoying. They can hide behind a metal door. They can shoot through the door but by the time you find out that one of them is hiding behind said door you are already dead. Imagine this: You walk out and boom – you’re instantly dead. You see the deathcamp and find out that there is a bot hiding behind that door and he, despite not being able to see you, shot your head while you walked out. Nice!
You have those “Access Keys” for the mission. You get two to three for free if you played some PvP You can also buy those keys for real world currency. A key is around 30 gold. 100Gold is a $. So you died because the bot shot you through the door and you already died once before? That’s 30 cents please. There are often jokes that next publishers will make you pay a micro transaction to respawn. Well! SURVARIUM IS LITERALLY DOING THAT.

I was a huge S.T.A.L.K.E.R. fan. Honestly, at the time, who wasn't? When I heard what happened to the dev team and the fiasco that followed with the Russian mob and all that nonsense, I was curious to see how the core would pick up the pieces. We were promised an open-world Stalker with online PVP.
Forward to, what, 10 years later? We have Survarium. I've never played it. Never installed it - until now. What I have done is read the many, many reviews of the game by a lot of people that have very OBVIOUSLY invested a lot of time, effort and even money into the game, and for a long time.
Reading through these reviews, I began to notice comments from a dev involved with the project - joewillburn
You could argue that he is just 'towing the line' and trying to be diplomatic and defend the project he is working on. The problem is clear, he doesn't listen to the comments from his biggest supporters, his long-time users. He is guilty of doing exactly what people say the company is doing - not listening.
This is a huge problem for me and I won't waste time or real money - even though I would GLADLY support a game, and even though I love the lore, universe and everything that the Stalker world offered - I won't bother in this case becauseit sounds like another failing money grab and, as consumers, we have to be smarter about where we spend our money and where we spend our (often limited) time playing a game.
If Vostok stand behind joewillburn, that's great. But he is, in my view, doing a disservice to you and your efforts. If you don't listen to your base, they will abandon you - and it sounds like they have.
It's a shame. Stalker is a classic with incredible potential.

On "ultra" maxed, it looks like a c-class PS3 game. And it's buggy, laggy as hell. Physics? Forget it, bodies just plank flat on top of boxes. What a joke.
There's no hope for this garbage.

Thomas Was Alone is not a particularly long game, it can be completed in about 3-4 hours depending on how bad you are at platforming.  It is also not particularly challenging with most of the levels being fairly easy if you have had any previous experience with platformers.  These can be viewed by some as weaknesses of the title, and I would not argue that they are incorrect.  If you are looking for a challenging platformer with hours of replayability, you will not find it here. The game controls well and I have no complaints about them.
The things that set this game apart from all of the other 2D platformers on Steam are the characters and narration.  The narration is spectacular, which is very important because it is the only way you learn things in the game.  The characters do not talk at any point, but instead, they are described by the narrator.  These non-speaking shapes have more depth and personality than almost every other character I have ever seen in a game.  They blow away every character that I have seen in every triple-A game that comes to mind and they do so without saying a word.
Like I said, if you are looking solely for a ground-breaking platformer, this is not it.  But if you are looking for a spectacular story-driven experience with amazing characters and some of the best narration I have ever heard, combined with a solid platforming experience, this needs to be on your short list of games to buy.

Thomas Was Alone is a captivating and hearwarming platformer. Using nothing more than a charming British narrator and a couple of pixels and light shaders, Thomas Was Alone manages to imbue what at first seem to be nothing more than rectangles and squares with personalities, quirks, and faults. You begin to care about the little red rectangle that is Thomas throughout his journey. The game is long enough to get invested in, but not so much that you still can't beat it in a day. By the time you realize what is happening around Thomas and his friends, your heart will have already been won and cheering them on.
In addition, the Benjamin's Flight missions are a charming addition to the tiny little world of Thomas Was Alone. It even manages a send-up (or sorts) of Flappy Bird which proves that it could have much more depth than it did. The DLC is a bit more challenging than the main game, but it is still worth a shot.

Apogee did the right thing by releasing it using DOSBox, though I can't say the same for the fact they took the approach of stretching the picture rather than presenting in its native aspect ratio. Fortunately, it's something that can easily be fixed with a simple edit of a config file.
Still, if you like vertical-scrolling shooters, it's worth playing and isn't too hard. I played through episode 2 on Easy difficulty with keyboard-only input before writing this review and had 32 lives by the time I got to the end-of-episode boss (and lost three over the course of the fight).

It's a very fun MS-DOS Classic game to play since I was Child.
As for the Storyline, it's painlessly simple: Earth Survives WW3 with most of humanity dead & plauged by a lack of Resources. Then an Alien Race known as the Kretons jump to Earth using a Wormhold and plans to conquer it as if things weren't bad enough. So the call goes out to Major Harrison Stryker, a hero of the Recent World War who takes a Special Attack Starship into the Wormhole to destroy the Kreton Homeworlds on the other side. The Problem is that the Kretons have also taken Human Hostages and you need to free them by ramming into their Holding Cells using your ship since they're immune to Weapon Fire.
With a Total of 24 Levels: 12 Stages & 12 Boss Battles, you'll be blasting the Kretons to Atoms again and again. There's 4 Sectors for each Episode that contains 2 Levels in each Sector & a boss battle for each one:
The Lava Planet contains: The Orbital Station, Water Sector, Land Sector & Lava Sector
The Arctic Planet contains: The Arctic Sector, Land Sector, City Sector & Lava Sector
The Desert Planet contains: The Orbital Station, Desert Sector, Lava Sector & Tech Sector

Quick blurb: It's free, it's short, it's cute as hell, it's a lot of fun. Give it a shot.
As for the lengthier version, this game emulates the ZX Spectrum game visuals of the 80s and early 90s. Empty black backdrop with bright coloured simple sprites, then plays like a zelda-esque shootemup in the combat minigame segments.
Heal the denizens of Hurtworld (both humanoid and not, and both mundane and completely bizarre, in often amusing ways), by shooting representations of their troubles with medical equipment, to progress further until you meet the prince (or was it king?) of Hurtland, and heal them too. Then get married to anybody you like.
I do mean anybody. anyone you've talked to.
anyTHING you've talked to for that matter.
There's very little story here, it's just a silly, fun romp for all of about an hour, and it's completely free, and you absolutely should give it a shot because A) it's free, B) sunglasses, C) it's cute as hell and surprisingly fun and D) it's genuinely charming and funny.
You seriously have nothing to lose, and everything to gain from a daft little gamejam thing that costs you nothing but an hour of your time. Get some healing done.
Also there's a paid for sequel that expands on the game and is also very cheap and you may wanna check that out too.

If you want a rather solid Action based Third Person Shooter to play with a buddy, this is a great game to play
If you are a diehard Resident Evil fan that wants nothing more than a solid Survival horror experience like previous installments, don't buy this
Gameplay is rather fun, might be quite some QTE's but you can turn the bigger ones off if you don't wish for them
Every campaign has something different going for it
Leon's campaign features zombie enemies and a bit more of a horror-ish kind of thing except for the end
Chris' campaign is more like a traditional Military based TPS, focusing on action and firefights with the always mutating J'avo
Jake's campaign also has a focus on action for the most part, also including the J'avo, but switches it up with vehicle segments, exploration segments and an occasional stealth segment
Ada's campaign focuses more on puzzles and stealthy segments for the most part, it was initially designed to be strictly a Single Player experience, but you can play it in co-op, but the Second player will be limited to just shooting and can't interact with any puzzles
If you are done with that, you can always play some Mercenaries, regular or No Mercy
Regular mercenaries is the same as it's always been, No Mercy is pretty much the same but will throw giant waves of enemies at you without stopping, make sure you are capable of surviving or be prepared to die, a lot
TL;DR: Only buy this if you want a solid action game to play with a buddy and don't care if the story's over the top, and specifically don't buy this if you are a Die-hard fan who can't give RE taking a different turn a chance

I absolutely love this game, I recommend it to anyone who enjoys zombie-action games, it is scary in places, but not enough to make it a survival horror game. It is in NO WAY like Resident Evil 1-3, if you're playing just for the scares, look somewhere else. If not, it's definitely worth your money. The next few sections talk about the campaigns you get to play, Leon's, Chris's, Jake's and Ada's. All spoiler free.
One of the best things about Leons campaign is the atmosphere, you'll find you are constantly moving between stunning burning cities and creepy cemeteries all in the dead of night. Personally, I really enjoyed Leon's story, even though the dialogue can be a little cliche sometimes, Leon and Helena are both interesting characters and you'll like watching the cutscenes. Sadly, this is the only campaign where you'll face actually zombies, so enjoy that while it lasts.
Chris's campaign has to be the worst, it feels like a poor, out of place action game than anything else. Mainly because you don't fight ANY zombies, but creatures called J'avo, which are basically smart zombies that have guns and shoot at you, which isn't great considering the cover mechanics are terrible. You'll also find you run out of ammo fast as you don't get a pistol, but an assault rifle as your primary weapon, and meleeing against enemies who are shooting you is not fun, to top that off, Piers (player 2 in Chris's campaign) doesn't get the survival knife that Chris has, so as you're failing to melee with your sniper rifle while the enemies pound you with bullets, you can take time thinking about why the BSAA doesn't give all it's soldiers the same equipment. As for the characters themselves, Piers is a boring stereotypical soldier with every bad action movie line and will soon annoy you and make you cringe, maybe this was why the BSAA thought he wasn't worth giving a survival knife to. Chris is just OK as he actually has some character development mainly building off his experiences from RE5.
Jakes campaign is very good despite you're only fighting the J'avo, his storyline is incredibly interesting and what makes it stand out from Chris's is the characters, Jake and Sherry's chemistry I found brilliant watch and that alone makes this campaign great. The only negative I found on this campaign is a ridiculously unrealistic action scene from Chapter 4. That being said I think Jakes tied with Leons for best campaign, even though they play completely differently.
Ada's campaign is less about shooting enemies and more about wrapping up loose ends from the other 3 stories. Even though Capcom released an update so you didn't have to unlock her campaign by beating the other 3, I would still recommend you save her campaign until last, otherwise you won't get the full benefit from the story. There's a good amount of stealth involved, which is very difficult to pull off on your first attempt so it doesn't really feel like an achievement when you finally manage it, but it does offer some good puzzle solving scenarios, all of which are quite difficult and very satisfying when you figure them out. Also the chemistry between her and Leon is built on from the events of RE4, and as a result produces some gripping scenes.
Overall it's a very good game, and definitely does not feel like a traditional Resident Evil game (which is the reason for majority of the poor reviews the game received). Bear in mind the graphics are amazing, the story is just excellent and game goes as low as £4.99 on a flash sale. This game is well worth picking up.

While maybe not as immersive as games like Outlast, Slender: The Arrival does an exquisite job of setting the mood to the point that the atmosphere alone can be enough to make players hesitate on moving onward through the game, only to super-charge that tension when it becomes apparent that there are very clear and frightening threats to be avoided at all costs in the midst of various isolated and lonely settings, ranging from a simple forest in the dead of night to the dark abyss of an empty mining facility and more.
Throughout the game, there are a number of moments and levels far more scary than the others, with occasionally a little silence in between to let you catch your breath. The enemies you shall be running from are frightening and very well designed, each with their own unique mechanics and characteristics.
Slender: The Arrival has a very simplistic story on the surface, starting with the player character, Lauren, visiting the isolated home of her friend Kate, only to find her missing and sets out in search of her. However, as the game progresses, small and even subliminal clues can reveal the nightmare fuel behind the horrors you witness.
Unfortunately, the game was somewhat short upon release, but a healthy dose of extended and new levels from Blue Isle Studios certainly made up for that problem. It is still not as long as games like Outlast, but the various difficulty settings, achievements and small level of randomisation in the levels will always be alluring for those with the courage to go again.
Slender: The Arrival is a worthy adaptation of the original Slender: The Eight Pages game and does an excellent job of making you feel as if Slenderman could be right behind you at any time. The tension and atmosphere are exquisite, the story is chilling and the scares are unforgettable. After all this time, I can still not get enough of this game, and can certainly recommend it to anyone looking for a good horror experience.

Title is quite self explainatory, William Goldberg, owner of his own and rich arms industry, has been murdered in his estate, His butler, second wife, stepdaugher, son and associate are the only ones present in this isolated mansion and one of them could be the murderer.
Novice detective Clark will assist one of the most famous detectives in the county, Detective Knox, during this investigations. Now the real entertainment of the game (except for the case itself, of course) is given by Detective Knox's interaction with his new assistent Clark and all the witnesses and suspects in the house, as his personality is unusually unique, yet quite predictable if you are used to tv series, animes and movies. The easiest comparison could be with Benedict Cumberbatch's Sherlock, as they both are brilliant detectives, bored by common cases and people, thrilled by complications, disrespectful towards anyone especially their superiors, yet very dedicated to the case they're working on. Oh, and of course their methods are non conventional.
As a graphic novel the game consists of static "portraits" of a fistful locations, with static characters appearing and text lines on screen or below in case of thoughts and narration or dialogues. Visually it is just static and characters' drawings are not exceptional, yet they are decent and work.
Unfortunately there's no voice acting so you'll have to read everything but here comes another pleasant aspect of the game. Most themes are made of bluesey or happy themes, anyways in general soundtrack is unexpectedly nice, pleasant, suiting to various situations such as the funny classic guitar themes during the frequent squabbles between Knox and Clark, or during Knox's unorthodox interrogations. Why such a worthy soundtrack doesn't get an OST pack to be purchased on steam is a mistery that gets quickly solved as all resources for the game, both pictures and sounds, are loose inside the game's own folder.
There's not much to do, you can actually just read everything as the game runs for itself. From time to time you will be prompted to choose the question to ask during interrogations but there's no right or wrong as it will be your responsibility to choose wisely and pay attention to everything said as only one choice will matter and that will be the final choice of the culprit. Unfortunately if you choose the wrong one you will assist to a ridiculous explanation where even Clark will point out all the mistakes following a black screen end game. There won't be a checkpoint, if you didn't save moments before the final choice it means you'll have to start all over again. And let me say that the end is worth the effort. You will feel bantered at first, but there's a reason for everything, and you will realize it was your fault for not paying enough attention.
Besides the cheap trick for the culprit, the art is a bit poor and deserved more attention or effort at least. Most characters have no more than two pictures and they're too few, considering the different situations they will be into. The easiest example is Alex, where while being accused of something horrible has been shown with her happy stance... Nonsense.
The absence of a real gameplay could be considered a bad thing. But if you don't know what a graphic novel is and totally ignore the tag in titles I believe that is your problem, not the developers'.

In a detective's novel you follow the story of a detective called Knox, nicknamed after a famous writer, and his assistant Clarke as they try to solve the murder of the owner of the largest firearms company ever. Though it's visuals are not spectacular it isn't very important to the story; the most important part is done right.

In this Visual novel you as the player follow the story of the two detectives, this is done by clicking and see what each character has to say as well as being able to look back to what has been said. Once in while you can make your own choices which do have effect on the story, which is a lot better than some games with choices out there.
The visual part may have been a bit primitive however the story is well constructed and allows for enough variability to make it feel like your own and not an entirely prescripted one. Although the base setting is a bit cliché this can be ignored by the still interesting style of writing; ignoring the minor grammar and spelling mistakes.
In A detective’s novel you, the player, follow the 2 detective’s to figure out who the murderer of the CEO of a famous firearms company, William Goldberg, was. In a remote mansion high in the mountains the detective’s meet a cast of 5 characters, all of them with their own grudges, ideas and morale. These made the story feel a lot more real and had me enveloped and questioning things that in most detectives; I don’t do. The main detective was quite arrogant throughout the story, although at first this bothered me after a while I began to appreciate this as it made him feel very different from the average “Genius detective” in  most shows or books.
Although some character’s felt a little uneasy as they felt very distant from the story this didn’t ruin my enjoyment of the story.
In order to keep it interesting for players you can along with seeing how the story progresses also ask questions through the mind of the head detective, this makes it a lot more interesting as these choices affect the story which made me as a player think about what I was asking which made me more involved in the story.
Especially in the end where you as a player have to decide who the killer is. Besides from scaring me for doing something I didn’t expect it also made me feel like I was actually in the story; although this was quite late it made all the events that happened before feel much more real. The best part about this decision is that you can totally choose the wrong person and make yourself look like a fool, and with how arrogant the protagonist is; it’s even more hilarious.
The writers of the story have done a few things so that even though there are choices the story still ends up the way they wanted it to. The story takes place in an isolated location and when a place other than the one the story takes place in its quickly dismissed by a character to not get the story tangled with other affairs. Throughout the story there are also many occurrences of rooms only having one access key or other restrictions that guide the players mind along the right path; I say mind because the developers can control where the characters go, that is why the restrictions are there.

Overall the story is quite polished with dialogue that didn’t make me feel like I was watching a bad comedy show. Although there are flaws I do not view them as important enough to ruin my experience of the story. Personally I am not fan of my detectives as they often disregard certain facts or problems while this one mentioned them a lot and made me feel like I was, somewhat, watching an actual detective. Overall I would recommend it to anyone that has a few hours to spare and nothing to do.

A thoroughly enjoyable physics based puzzle game. 100+ official puzzles and a workshop integrated sandbox mode makes sure you'll never run out out of challenges.
Edit: After a few more hours, i've finally found something really irks me.
- The biggest issue is that many levels are not very fun. The appeal of this game, for me, is to visualize a solution, executing it and lastly improve it. The problem is that all those damned loop-de-loops, jumps, and other gimmicks pretty much requires that you painstakingly tweak tiny things for ages to get your budget down, and make sure a random twig somewhere doesn't snap for no apparent reason. This is likely my own fault, partially, since i'm trying to go <budget and <100% stress, yet still, it detracts from my personal enjoyment
- Tied in with this, it's a huge problem that the game sometimes doesn't save your progress. Sometimes i'll spend hours getting blue dots on 3 really complicated puzzles, and then i'll come back another day and find that them unsolved with only an incomplete autosave to help me remake them.
I'd still recommend the game, but be cautious and always save solutions to hard puzzles before moving on to the next level.
Verdict: 7.5/10

It's fun to watch your bridges collapse and cars sploosh into the water. Wait, isn't that what you're supposed to do? Seriously, it's also fun and a matter of pride when you finally get a bridge to stay up and survive (in my case, barely) the crossing of vehicles. And the jumps are awesome (even if they fail. Sploosh!) It can be a significant challenge since only the bare bones are covered in the tutorial. I had a lot of trouble with my first jump level, and sometimes I look at the level and think... Whaaat? But then I do like games that are challenging and require a little creativity. There are 100 levels in the game and many more in the workshop, so if it's your cup of tea there's plenty to do, and you can contribute your own levels. If you don't want to have to think too hard in a game, and you get upset if you can't quickly complete levels, this may not be the game for you. As with all puzzle games, the level of difficulty may be too great for some, too easy for others. For me, it's just about right, challenging but doable. The puzzles are based on physics principles, so are pretty logical (well, apart from the jumps which wouldn't be very practical in the real world!) I would recommend this game if you like a challenge.

This game is a short story about Princess Remedy who has a quest to cure the Prince of Hurtland.
However, in order to reach him along the way you will need to heal other people aswell.
Game itself is very simple, besides traveling through villages, you will have to heal other people in order to unlock the hearts which will let you progress through the story, and which will also increase your healing stats.
Healing is a minigame, very similiar to Undertale the Bullet Storm style, while throwing bandages and painkillers at enemies, you will also have to run away from enemies and dodge their attacks.
Besides that there isnt much, finding secret chests with upgrades and hearing interesting stories and illnesses from other people in Hurtland.
Even though its very simple and short, i did acctualy enjoy the game. It takes around 1-2 hours to finish.
Pros:
- Short, unusual story
- Low system requirements and small download size
- Over 50 different characters, each with unique illness, healing level and story about it
- Customizable difficulty (Normal, Hard, Master)
- Music is pretty nice
- Secret rooms and collectible upgrades
- 3 save files
Neutral:
- Graphics probably wont appeal to everyone, however they do give special charm to game, and it looks and sounds like something you would play on Gameboy
- Short and simple, some people like diversity
- No equipment nor money, only thing you collect are the keys for doors and upgrades from chests and cured characters instead of collecting money/equipment. Every upgrade is direct non customizable upgrade, that means you cant lower your stats if for some reason you want to (f.e if you want harder challenge at some parts of the game)
Cons:
- 30 FPS cap
- No achievements
- It seems like some healing levels are either alot harder or alot easier for the part of the game (town) they are in, it starts somewhere in midgame
- Alot of flashing lights, can cause headache if you play with Fullscreen
- Maybe could use a little bit of customization for character, couple of outfits or something, but its not a big deal

Ludosity games always seem to have one or two issues that ruins their games for me. Whether it was the lack of significant meaningful choice in deckbuilding in Card City Nights or providing not quite enough information to the player in PsyCard* leading to a lot of feeling like success or failure came down to random chance. Luckily, Daniel Remar had his hand in this particular stew so I  dove right in.
First off, I love the graphic style of this game. The 2-color 16x16 tiled canvas has some amazing pixel work to create a vibrant world where everything is nicely readable and with the sort of visual acuity that makes it easy to navigate.
In general, the gameplay is pretty good, you travel the land seeking out people who are suffering from various maladies and 'cure' them by taking part in a single-screen arena shooter match. It plays out sort of like a twin-stick shooter like Robotron or Smash TV, except for the part where there's a second stick, and that's where Princess Remedy sort of falls apart. It's not terrible, you only can shoot in the direction you're facing, but it adds a layer of challenge that's not really needed for this style of gameplay. And it's not that the various stages are really all that difficult outside of Master difficulty doing no-chests up to the secret chest, and then again at the last boss doing 101%.
The point is it just feels bad, even an old game like Robotron knew you needed to be able to control your gun independantly of your character! The hitbox on Remedy also feels off, which again for the vast majority of gameplay isn't really an issue, but she's a chunky sprite and there are times when it seems like she can squeeze between certain bullet patterns and other times when she gets hit. There not a good feeling of how many invincibility frames (if any) you get after being hit too, and sometimes bullets seem to do wildly different amounts of damage, though I suspect there's a bit of either overlapping bullets happening or some bullets are just allowed to hit the player more than once. Whichever it is, it's really too bad because it turns the game from feeling challenging to just feeling arbitrary.
Again, this is really only important at the highest difficulty the game provides. All in all, these issues don't completely spoil the game and I would certainly recommend Princess Remedy to anyone looking for a fun little game with tons of style. And I'm certainly looking forward to trying the sequel.
*While I can't really recommend this game, there's a super fun dungeon crawer style minigame that comes with it that's really fun and it's almost baffling they didn't make that into a full fledged game experience.

A prime example of how you can have all the fancy tools and resources of the industry at your disposal and still produce the video game equivalent of "art for a refrigerator". Particula has a nice graphics engine, local/internet multiplayer, even voice chat, but amidst all these great utility features there's a distinct lack of a good game, or much of a game at all. It has some sort of abstract vector graphics aesthetic going on, which would be alright if this was a fast paced arcade type affair, but it's quite the opposite. It's kind of hard to relate to or get involved over a bunch of 3D colored blobs flashing at other, differently textured blobs.
It's mechanically threadbare as well, with simple maps that are pretty much all the same and 9 towers that can be condensed to only 3 functionally different towers just at varying power levels. Also, there is NO TUTORIAL or any kind of guide to ease you in, not that you really need one if you've played any other tower defense before. Still, you're better off playing that instead. Heck, there are free mobile games that are more entertaining than this personality-devoid cookie cutter project.

This game is deceptive...VERY deceptive.
Much like any civ-builder you start out on an island with some raw materials. You use those to build a nice small starting base of operations. Those guys needs good; which you then supply untill you are ready to advance to the next tier. Thos eguys need other goods; some needing your first goods as a basis. All's fine and well while you use your excess goods to make some cash untill you can advance yet another tier.
Then it starts to hit you; building space. No worries as there are other islands to develop as you progress yet another tier and start to notice that your infrastructure isn't all that great.
Yet another tier and the juggling ensues with you trying to keep all tiers of population happy while still maintaining a proper infrastructure.
Before you know it you've been playing this game for quite some hours, restarted several times to improve on your logistic system, tore some hairs out of your head wondering why you're making a deficit, cursed those researchers for tearing theire homes down because they didn't have their meat for a cycle or two. etc etc etc
Pro's
* Easy to learn, hard to master
* Simplistic graphics so it really doesn't take a monster rig to run and it does have it's charm for people who like Indie's
* VERY interactive; nice to have a management game that requires some modicum of attention to make sure everything
keeps working
Con's
* Early Access; development means it's not shining in it's fullest with some ackwardness in the UI and some bugs (though I, personally, haven't found any yet) but the devs are hard workers so this con will disappear in time
* Unclear tutorial (there's tools for various blueprints that never get explained properly)
* Simplistic graphics (even though this means lesser computers can also join in on the fun you DO have to like the simplistic nature of it...it REALLY IS a pen&paper style game when it comes to graphics)
Most of the con's will disappear with further development, I'm sure, adding more scenario's (even though the first will keep you busy for a while). So being a lover of management and Indie games my verdict:
8/10

uses the production management systems you might find in games like
or
and dials it up to 11 with the addition of a
-style puzzle of instructions that has to be completed in each building in order to produce resources. You are required to engage in both the building placement and building ratio exercises that will be familiar from the initially-mentioned games (or from
, which has been described to me as a 'building placement puzzle game'), while also striving to upgrade your production technology, making sure your buildings are operating in a logically efficient manner, and so on.
Your workers and researchers (as well as other henchmen) require both food and pay; if you continually fail to satisfy their needs, they will abandon you for greener and presumably jollier pastures (i.e. it's quite possible to lose in this game).
In the release version, there is both more content (via additional scenarios) and a much improved playing experience. The launch saw Steam Achievements added as well, which made me replay the content I had previously plowed through, and I'm positively delighted with the changes. Buildings now clearly communicate how much they are producing versus how much they theoretically could be producing. You still need to do the mental gymnastics of figuring out how to solve this (for example, my iron ore mine eventually had a full output queue not because of some transportation problem but simply because I temporarily had no need for iron ore and all my stockpiles were already filled up), and there's still a few minor snags (UI bugs mostly), but overall it's much improved. The tutorial has been split up into separate parts explaining different concepts, while the Steam Workshop provides the potential for endless extra content. The only thing I could still complain about is the rather monotonous music, but you can't expect a varied soundtrack for $3. Hours of fun!
======================
The big problems present in this Early Access release all are of a User Experience (UX) nature. The interface makes it hard to figure out how the building ratios should be to each other and how optimised your production is; often the interface is clumsy when it comes to managing routes and production; when there is a warning message associated to a building, there is no easy shortcut to find the affected building, and buildings that are not producing for one reason or another so far don't communicate clearly why this is so. A lot of manual troubleshooting is required if your production process hits an unexpected snag.
Because of clarity issues with regards to the interface, the "plan" stage of "plan - produce - profit" is moderately unavailable at the moment.
The music and the graphics assets give off a strong placeholder vibe, but the game's very name betrays that that is sure also intended by the developer.
Considering the game has been available to the public for mere days, and the developer's
patching
, I'm confident these points will be addressed in due time. For what it's worth, the game retails for a pretty nice low price.

Better than its predecessor and certainly more compatible with Windows 8 and 64 bit systems, Crysis 2 is proof that a game can never be too finished. The new functions of the HUD, namely the ability to tag objects, use thermal vision and navigate the environment in more inventive ways than before, all add a great new dimension to the Crysis universe. The setting of New York is very well recreated. The crisis of the aliens invasion is masterfully plotted and the introduction in which you and your squad members have to swim to saftey, only to be rendered unconscious by an unknown enemy, sets the stage for a compelling adventure.
The  weapons are as modern, diverse and advanced as ever. They make you think that all soldiers of the future should adopt them. The AI is no pushover and will give you a run for your money. The physics of the various impacts are well researched, impressive and fun to see. You will find at least a handful of ways to take the enemy on and have a good laugh.
Crytek  created a great followup in the form of Crysis 2. The extras also add extra replayability, so, if you have the means and love Crytek games, get this one. You won't be disappointed.

This game started out as a big disappointment with it's dull and boring "intro". I almost quit the game before I was done with the intro, as I thought that was the actual game. Once I started with Leon's campaign, I re-evaluated the game and actually found myself liking it. It captured the horror/survival game we all know and love about the Resident Evil series.
Unfortunatly Leon's campaign is just 1 out of 4. If you play the campaigns in order, the game gets worse and worse. Chris's campaign takes us away from the horror/survival genre and put us in a bizarre 3rd person shooter game that takes place in East Europe. Still the campaign was okay.
Jake's campaign gets even worse. We're still in East Europe, and we spend most of our time running from stuff. With a car, with a motorcycle, with a snowmobile, on a boat and by foot. A lot of the time we are running with a fixed position camera angle, which annoyed the crap out of me.
Dear CapCom running away in an intense situation with a fixed camera position doesn't make the game more intresting, it makes it annoying. No one likes it when you run forward using "W key" just to all of a sudden have to use the "A key" in order to run straight forward. If you got  great scenery you wanna show off, find some other way to do it.
The 4th and final is Ada's campaign. After playing through the first chapter, I really feel I don't want to continue playing this game. Again we find outselves running from everything. We have to stealth and avoid enemies, we have to climb ladders and swim on a timer.
Feel free to throw 100's of brain eating zombies at me. Give me puzzles to solve, make me fight unreasonable big and hard bosses. But don't ask me to stealth and run away from everything. Don't give me mini-cutscenes in the middle of a boss fight. And for the love of God, let me decide from what angle I want the camera!
I'm really sorry to say, but I don't recommend this game. At least not if you like horror/survivor games. I really wish capaign 2, 3 & 4 were more simmilar to the first one. But it seems that CapCom decided to try and please everyone, by making each campaign aimed at different types of players. I'm sorry Capcom, but instead of pleasing a greater audience, you now have people hating 75% of the game. I don't see how it's possible to enjoy all 4 campaigns.
It's as absurd as if you were to make the next Tomb Raider 25% Tomb Raider, 25% Mario-Kart, 25% Silent Hill and 25% Farmville. Chose 1 line and stick to that.

All in all it was a fun/interesting game. I enjoyed Jake Muller's Campaign the most, but Ada's was also up there with his. I didn't care for the creatures that would get back up after being defeated, they were quite annoying! So yeah great game ;D

More of an overhaul of the genre, RE6 is technically, environmentally and atmospherically, the most accomplished of the series so far. The open melee system is a compelling new addition. To punch, kick and whack the zombies and other enemies with the buttstocks of your rifle is a satisfying experience. Each character has his or her own very distinct one click finishing moves that are very satisfying for me to watch.  The counter moves in which the PC uses the zombie´s own weapon to kill it is inventive and impressive. The settings of the game are dark and chilling, both when they are silent and when they become battlegrounds.
Not much new is added, otherwise. The developers of this game improved upon what had come before more than anything else. They have given it more visual flare and a more realistic edge, which RE5 began to do, but then RE6 did to a much higher degree. The creatures have a mixture of original and recycled designs, enough to be different from the previous installments of the series, but many resemble creatures seen in previous games and other well known others, as well as mythical or fairy tales.
The characters are all first rate. They are in fact given  more exposure and dialogue than earlier games. The ingame talk makes them deeper and more introspective than they were in the earlier episodes of the genre. The inclusion of Sherry was an excellent idea. At long last we get to see Birkin´s daughter in action, after so many years of wondering what became of her.
A high end system is needed to flesh out RE6 in all its wonderful detail, but it is worth the extra money. Capcom have made a decent effort with this game, even though they didn´t introduce anything that has not been seen before.

The only downsides I can think of would be some minor bugs here and there, as well as some extremely difficult gameplay during some parts (Died countless times during some specific missions having to do with boats and helicopters).
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 7/10, recommended even if you're not familiar with the Resident Evil series.

Such was the massive success of the 2012 hit Slender The Eight Pages, Blue Isle decided to follow it up with a sequel, Slender The Arrival.
The game begins beside your car, Lauren has arrived to visit her friend Kate who has decided to sell her mother’s house after her passing. You soon find yourself running down a road leading to Kate’s house and by the time you reach the outside walls daylight has transformed into total darkness. You find the front door of the house wide open, inside completely empty. Your first action is to search for a flash light to lift the darkness and then set about investigating Kate’s disappearance. The whole idea of being alone in this game can be pretty daunting especially when you know there is a faceless man stalking you.
Slender doesn’t really appear too much in the Prologue but he makes enough of an appearance to let you know he is there and watching you. You’ll be standing still and hear gravel shifting or footsteps behind you and then my personal favourite, a door shutting by itself!.
You will find clues throughout the house in the form of scrapbook items which you can collect at any point and view via the Book in the main menu, these items give you some insight into what is going on within the game.
In total there are nine stages, eight of these are story related with the extra stage being a revamp of the original Eight Pages and for those not familiar with the previous game, the aim is to collect eight pages scattered around a wooded area but you have to find all eight before Slender kills you. Pages can be found tacked to objects like trees and cars and you can very quickly find yourself running in circles looking for them while praying your flashlight doesn’t run out.
The game also introduces two brand new stages namely Homestead and a secret stage only revealed after finding a secret object while in the stage Flashback which itself has been split into two stages to accommodate Homestead. Now the end of Flashback is called Escape.
There is also a new enemy to deal with, one that does not appear in the original release and you’ll find him on the third stage.
Overall the game is very short and can be easily completed in less than an hour. Maybe what it needed was a longer and stronger storyline, one that wasn’t so repetitive. But seeing as it was already a well known game across the steam community it was to be expected that not much would change coming across to the consoles. Though with new content there is something to look forward to and of course there is the main protagonist Slender who without a doubt will make you jump when he randomly appears throughout the game and trust me, turning around to get a face full of him, turning my screen all distorted and full of static was enough to give me goosebumps or attempting to make my way through a burning forest with his tentacles appearing in front of me trying to grab me, made me wonder why I didn’t just remain in the cave.
The game is a lot of fun to play, especially in a darkened room by yourself or maybe with friends I would also recommend playing it with headphones in or if you have it surround sound because it makes the experience that much scarier. If you are a fan of the games and all things Slender you shouldn’t be too disappointed and if you’re someone who has only ever heard about Slender it’s definitely worth checking out. To sum it up, if you’re looking for a storyline forget it but if you love being scared senseless while wandering around in the darkness then this should suit you down to the ground. Hopefully in the future Slender will get the retail game it surely deserves.

Learning how to connect the game to the guitar is step one. I dont mean plugging in the guitar, I mean mentally attaching the colors on screen to actions in your hands. You must learn to play this game before it is able to teach you.
You also have to want to learn the guitar. This game will not force guitar skill down your throat, not at all. There is a tremendous amount of forgiveness with hitting chords and notes which will make you an obscenely sloppy player if you rely on this game to be your sole source of guitar talent.
This game is a must for any folks with the desire to learn guitar. However, there is soooo much more beyond this game for any enthusiast to learn.
I was one of the lucky ones. Music has been a passion my entire life and this game gave me the excuse to dedicate hours into learning the techniques of guitar. My mind screamed at me to learn the "Whys" of music and I discovered everything this game is missing, which is everything outside of technique.
What this game will teach you:
Technique (the How of every note)
What this game will not teach you:
Music Theory (the Why of every note)
Guess which you need to learn to play Music? Anyone can get good at learning how to "parrot" these songs while the colors are on screen... but how many will walk away from this game with the desire to make their own music? Not nearly enough I imagine... but at least one victory is won here with me.

This is a cute little game with NES / late Atarish graphics that I polished off in under an hour while waiting for my buddy to put together a Pathfinder character.
It's free, which is obviously a plus, and it has a very cute, albeit it not uproariously funny sense of humor about it. Still enough to make me smile. You're healing people by destroying various representations of what's wrong with them, which takes the form of a bullet-helly sort of shooter. Ends with a bizarre multi-stage boss fight.
Other than the very short length, the only real detractor is the control scheme. You can WASD or arrow key around, and escape is the "cancel out of menu" button, and literally every other button is the action button. Pressing these will enter a menu, select things within the menu, and pressing and holding it while pressing one of the directional keys will make you run. This means that often I'd be trying to run, but press the buttons out of sequence by a split second and end up nearly saving and quitting. It's a short game and not a huge deal, but it was a pain, and as feedback for the dev for future titles, I would advise against this hyper-simplified control scheme. My recommendation would be to have one rebindable button for action, one rebindable button for cancel, and one rebindable button for run. In that order I'd recommend x, z, and shift.

**This is a review in progress**
First off, this game is way more in depth than I originally thought. It reminds me a lot of Factorio, which is great! I opened the game, started the tutorial, expected to breeze through it...but it's been 30 minutes and my brain hurts now, not to mention, it's 1 AM. This is one of those games that you can play over and over again to try and achieve the fastest and most efficient "trade" route for your goods. It's damn good already in it's early state and I only expect it to get better.

This game still has a while before Early Access, so there are some bugs and issues, but for the most part, it's a pretty good game. The very low price makes me highly reccommend this game. There is a lot of content considering the price.
This game is pretty similar to Factorio, and if you liked that, then you'd probably like this. (I liked Factorio more than Blueprint Tycoon. Factorio's just a larger game, but it also costs more)
I haven't experienced any gamebreaking bugs, but the game does lack polish. The UI's are (as of writing this) very messed up. After playing for a little bit, the menus become very difficult to use. Some of the menu's items go through the menu, or behind other buttons, making them very difficult to read and use.
I know I haven't played this game very long, but I think it was long enough to write a review, considering the low price of the game.
I can't see myself playing this game for more than about 6 hours in it's current state. It has a lot of cool planned features that will extend the game, but at the moment. it seems like you can do everything the game has to offer in less than 8 hours.
This game is pretty sandboxy, so there's more than one way to solve each situation, however it doesn't really reward creativity. You can optimize your buildings and their placements, but beyond that, there's not really much else you can do. For example, in Factorio, there are tons of moving parts you can change. You can move items by trains, conveyor belts, or inserters, all of which have their benefits and their drawbacks. In Blueprint Factory, there are a few ways to move things, but in most cases, it's very obvious which mode of transportation you should use.
I feel like I've been just pointing out the negatives in this game, but that's mostly because I've been comparing it to more expensive and larger games. This game is much more casual, and forgiving than other games of this genre, and having played some of these other games, this game just seems a little too easy and simple. This is a fun game, especially if you want to play something more casual or are new to this kind of game. Also, I feel like I can't stress the price enough, $3 is really cheap for what the game offers.
Also, it looks like on some other reccommendations, people were complaining about text size. I played on fullscreen with 1920 x 1080 resolution, and I thought it was fine. People also thought the tutorial was pretty bad, and I'd have to agree with that. I felt like it told you what to do and not why you were doing it. I figured it out pretty quickly after leaving the tutorial though.
It's fun and free so go "buy" it.

I don't think a game has ever made me so spiteful with its design decisions.
All menus (including saves) work in real time. There is no pause. There is no remit from this unending nightmare. The inventory is clunky garbage. Progress is only truly saved at the end of chapters (about four to a campaign, and about two hours long each.)
Furthermore, the game is in over-the-shoulder cover-shooter controls most of the time. And then unexpectedly it's in tank controls. And then sometimes the camera decides to decouple from your shoulder, orbits around you, and reverses all your movement inputs while it's doing this. Not as a bug, mind you. As a feature.
I don't think I can adequately describe how awful this is, so instead just imagine Capcom's boot stomping on a human face forever.
EDIT: Died a few more times. Figured out a workaround for the problem. The game gets very confused (bless its little heart) when you try to maneuver while running with the arrow keys. Don't get me wrong, I love Resident Evil REmake/Zero, but it's better this way if they really want to make Resident Evil a action series.
The content in this game is amazing. With 4 long campaigns to play with Rankings, collectibles and Co-op the replay value is very high and with a long play time even if you play alone. The Graphics in the game is AMAZING, and the optimization is silky smooth with even low-end machines being able to run it decently.
And now for some complaints. Some of the deaths in the game are very cheap. The ranking system which implies that you need to play EVERY character on EVERY difficulty is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, what were they thinking? And the last and biggest complaint is of course, it's not scary, at all. Leon's campaign started out good with suspenseful atmosphere and promise of the game being scary, but that quickly shatters when Leon leaves the collage and that atmosphere never returns (except a few intense chases in one of the other campaign) Pity.
But in the end I recommend this game for those who like action fun,  so go get a buddy and play this cheesy pile of cheese. If you want good horror, look somewhere else. Resident Evil Remake (wait for the HD re-release coming soon) and Zero is a good choice, Revelations if you want a modern Resident Evil.

This game is very different compared to your typical shooter. No matter how good your aim is, no matter how fast your reflexes are, when faced against superior "tactics," you will not win. Map knowledge, and how your team abuses that knowledge is what ultimately wins games.
*Bash some holes through walls and shoot that 1 pixel that turns dark indicating someone is walking past and get a kill..* If the enemy doesn't have good map knowledge, they would not even see that coming, and would not even have the chance to fight back. This makes the game a lot more tactical than other shooters, and a breath of fresh air compared to something else like Call of Duty.
Now onto this game's problems.. HIT DETECTION can be PRETTY GARBAGE. Game is nearly 2 years old and the developers have claimed time and time again that the hit detection will be fixed. Well, it hasn't been fixed. This game will cheat you out of kills fairly often because of it.
Renown (the resource used to unlock characters) is a lot more difficult to obtain now since they have nerfed the fastest way to obtain it (solo Terrorist Hunt mode). No matter what Ubisoft comes up with to explain why they did this, the reality is: the harder it is for you to earn this resource, the more likely you will use real money to buy in-game currency or their season passes. This game is a business for them, and they intend to earn as much money from it as they can. This is extremely detrimental to a newcomer of this game and makes the game extremely non noob friendly. Unless you plan on playing day in and day out constantly, don't expect to unlock all the characters any time soon.
In conclusion, this game can be quite fun with friends and you do not need to have very good aim for it. But I hope in your eyes the pros outweigh the cons otherwise this will be a very frustrating game.
