On a more serious topic, this game is really fun. It looks all kiddy and what-not, but it's not as simple as it seems. I mean, woah? You are a mouse, you have one objective... Get the cheese and return it to the mouse hole. But there's much more to it than that.
There's also a lot of cosmetic stuff you can buy with your cheese (currency) or with the fraises which you buy with real-world money. This in absolutely no way affects how good you are in the game, though, it just shows your decorating abilities. The real skill comes from practicing as shaman and helping your fellow mice accomplish their sole objective. There's quite a lot you will learn just by playing each map and watching closely what other shamans do with their skills (you can invest points into several different skill trees) and learning from them. You will make many mistakes and people will probably tell you to kill yourself (as a mouse, to decrease the timer and stop wasting everyone's time if all is lost), but if you can get past the sometimes unhelpful community (they are usually not that bad) you will find a really cool game!

First, if you’d like to see gameplay footage, check out my video here:
If you’d rather do that whole reading thing, well, keep reading.
Cards of Cthulhu is a thoroughly silly game; it’s the hair metal of games, every cheeseball 80’s movie rolled into video game form. You drive along on your tricked out bike, laser shotgun in hand, blasting through various Heavy Metal inspired creatures. Oh, and you play cards to take them down.
That’s all you do really, play cards. The setting and backdrop are really there just for show as the entire game boils down to clicking a card to play when you think it’s an opportune time to play one. You start with only a couple of cards, gain a few more as you play and Thunderdome your way through a series of bosses until you take on big daddy Cthulhu himself.
At first glance there appears to be almost no strategy; click a card and something happens, move on. As you play a bit more the strategy does make itself more apparent as each boss does have their own moveset as well as a strategy they play by, but let’s not pretend here; it’s pretty low strategy. There is definitely some thought and luck of the draw (including what cards you get into your deck) but rarely are you going to feel like you missed out on winning a battle because your strategy was weak.
This game is all cheese, but it’s gloriously ridiculous. The biggest problem is there’s just not a lot here; yes, you unlock some cards through “missions” (which seem to be nothing more than just playing the damn game) but once you’ve unlocked the handful of extra cards, that’s it. Same bosses. Same game. Same cards.
Which isn’t bad; the framework of the game and the mechanics are surprisingly entertaining. I’m not even saying this isn’t a full game. It just feels like…more of a really good framework for a game. With some more cards, a bit more variety, this game would be killer. As it stands, I’d still recommend it for the occasional fun little outing (and its super touchscreen friendly which for some is a huge bonus) but it feels like such wasted potential of what could be something truly entertaining.

The single player campaign attempts to be a story with focus on characters in small segments and world building through exposition, level design and "observables" which can be found throughout the levels. It tries to explore the lore of the land in this way, but they kinda messed it up. Too many inconsistencies.
Examples:
- Conquerors are criminals conscripted as shock troops, yet we see them lead others, even command castles and wardens.
- Lawbringers allegedly uphold the law and god help you if you break it near them, yet Holden Cross allows all sorts of travesties in his presence.
- Lawbringer armour construction is a secret of their order, yet they fight for multiple different factions.
- Wardens are super skilled knights who embody the virtues and ideals of chivalry. Big focus on oaths and vows. But they're all mercenaries?
Those are just some select inconsistencies from the Knight faction. I could probably list more, especially if I kept digging, and I don't doubt that you can find more on your own just by watching cutscenes, visiting the wikia or playing the game.
There's an honest effort here, they really did try to make a decent single player campaign experience. I genuinely do not doubt that. It's just that the result is kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥

Cards of Cthulhu is a casual little game, simple in design but with suprising depth. You pick cards for your deck from a choice of random two. Two cards at the beginning and more are added as you progress through the battles. Then you jump onto your motorcycle, grab your shotgun and ride across the wasteland to face off against Cthulhu himself - who stole your girlfriend, as villains in games have traditionally been fond to do.
Each opponent you meet on your way you fight by playing your cards (and autoattacking with your shotgun).  Simple enough? The depth of the game is knowing when during a combat round to play each card, in battles with consequitive fights of more than one enemy which card to save for the next enemy, which card in a given situation perhaps not to use at all, which cards to deny your enemy from playing, and when to not play cards.
Currently you will possibly have seen everything in the game in a couple of hours. That does not mean you will have beaten it. And it definitely won't mean you will have gotten bored. And with more cards to be added to the game, new strategies will emerge and add to the fun.

Having played the guitar for around 7-9 years (At time of review) I've never really found any way to improve my skill at playing. Until I bought this game. I have previously had someone to teach me to play. But this proved to be rather expensive in the long run. A few years after that, I found Rocksmith. I thought that it would be quite fun. I wasn't wrong. It was extremely entertaining and quite educational at the same time. Then a year later Rocksmith 2014 was released. I made sure to buy it as soon as possible. This one was even more fun than the original, giving you the option to change the difficulty, which is better for more experienced guitarists that don't need to learn the basics and prefer a challenge.
There are plenty of songs included with the game, then thousands more that you can purchase as DLC or find for free online. My personal favourites in the base game are Bat Country, by Avenged Sevenfold, Blitzkrieg Bop by The Ramones and Satch Boogie by Joe Satriani.
It is really easy to pick up the mechanics of the game and how everything works. Which is one of my favourite things about the game. The strings are colour coded, and frets numberd so you know exactly where the note you're supposed to play is. Red for the low E string, Yellow for the A string, Blue for the D string, Orange for the G string, Green for the B string and Purple for the high E string. And for those of you that are colour blind, there's an option for that. There is also an option to switch between left handed and right handed, invert the strings so that the Low E is on the bottom of the screen rather than the top (good for those of you that, like me, play using tab), an option that lets you choose between a 6 in-line and a 3x3 headstock, the help you tune the strings and also an option that lets you turn your electric guitar, into a bass guitar. Useful when you don't own or have the money for a bass guitar.
This game also features an amazing arcade style experience called "Guitarcade" (Get it? Good, huh?) This is a section of the game that involves minigames that assist you in learning certain guitar techniques such as chords, fretting and many more. This is a really useful and fun thing to put into the game. The arcade-esque minigames also give you high scores. So you can compete for 1st place with people worldwide.
There is also local multiplayer in this game that allows you to play with a friend (Duh) You could play lead guitar, while they play bass. Or rhythm and bass, or lead and rhythm etc. Which I haven't tried myself, but im sure is pretty cool.
Side note: as the store page says, in order to play this game. You must buy a Realtone cable. You can pick those up on sites like Amazon, eBay or your local game/ tech retailer for £20/$30 US. If you wish to play multiplayer, you obviously need two.
Overall, this game is an extremely useful learning tool for anybody that dreams of playing the guitar. But as always, it takes time to learn how to play (I have about 3-4 hundred hours on the PS3 version of this game, so ignore the fact that i've been playing RS2014 for just over a day on the steam version), so if you're interested, put the hours into the game and it will help.
In my opinion this game is definitely one of my favourite.

If you have a PC capable of running this game, it is worth getting, especially during a sale (like right now). Running the game on ultra settings it looks absolutely AMAZING, heck even on low settings (which they call "high") the game looks damn good. The story of the game kind of dragged on for a while, but I enjoyed it and the few plot twists that were included, overall a fairly strong narrative. Gameplay wise it is one of the most fun FPS's I have ever played. It is not your typical CoD FPS, and if you play it like one you will die. A lot. It requires strategy and timing, especially on the higher dificulties. If you enjoy single player story driven games with good combat and a good story, then this is a must have, especially since I've played the game for roughly 14 hours in the story mode lifetime and still havent finished (although I did have to start over once and spent a while tinkering in the settings). However most of the good parts of the game end here. The multiplayer partition of the game is nowhere near as poished as the campaign. The multiplayer tries to do what CoD does, and like I said before, this game is not like CoD and shouldn't be played like it. The powers seen in campaign remain here, but are drastically nerfed with quicker draining energy, weaker shields, and easier to spot cloaking. This may be so to balance the game, but this didn't work because I found this multiplayer to be very unbalanced. I would always die from someone I would never see, or even I would get the jump on them and they would still kill me. I would accredit this to the fact that I was awful at the game, but after 2-3 hours of gametime nothing changed, and looking at other reviews it's safe to say that the multiplayer is highly flawed. However even so it is still fun to play. Overall: great single player experience, tacked-on multiplayer, and generally a good game, especially with a powerful PC.

What a precious little game this is! At first glance the graphics are very minimalistic and when you first start the game up you might think this a negative. I think it's a rather well thought through design decision. As the game progresses past the setup of your first few buildings the screen quickly gets filled with information, but the simplicity of the graphics design makes it easy to keep track of it all. There's small visual ques on the buildings that show you the rate of production or if there's a hiccup somewhere and production has stopped. Clever design that quickly becomes second nature to read.
The music adds a soothing backdrop and I quickly find myself in the tycoon game spirit of just wanting to optimize this one thing, just one more supply route to sort and it'll be perfect, but you're never quite done. You keep chasing that next big payoff while trying to manage your resources. Your goal never seems out of grasp and that makes this game rather addicting.
I will say that at first this game bombards you with information. It's not immediately obvious how things connect and what you need to do. But the tutorial is amazing. It shows you the steps without being too long so if you forget and come back to the game later on you can quickly blast through the tutorial to be reminded of the motions.
There's a great depth to how far you can go with the streamlining of your production and the devil is in the details. It's all about the blueprints. You set each building up to produce something and there's generally a blueprint for it. There's default blueprints which you can use to get a basic idea of a setup, but beyond that you'll want to fiddle with them a lot to up production and thus your cash flow. I love the idea of the default blueprints because they let you get on with the game quickly and help you save some 'oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ moments where you've missed a vital part of your production chain. I also love how you can change them and build your own setup using a variety of fun tools for your workers. Who doesn't want to use a jetpack to quicken the process of goods delivery in a supply chain?!
I see some people are having trouble with the text size, but this is because the game launches at a low resolution. Simply bump it up to where you usually play your games and all the text is easily readable.
As I'm writing this there are some issues in the game, as is expected with an early access game. Some menus overlap eachother in an annoying way and some internal workings need a little bit of streamlining, but I've not had any crashes or hiccups or gamebreaking bugs. I'll be keen to watch this game develop and evolve because even though some edges are a little bit rough right now you can really tell there's a true gem at the center of this production.

On first glance, Jazzpunk looks like the larger and grander version of Gravity Bone (Or Thirty Flights of Loving), offering lots to see and do. With advertising as confident as it was, it looked like it would be a pretty solid title, despite the fact that it was never disclosed exactly what you did in it. The trailers showed a few setpieces and environments, the screenshots showed a large world to explore and the key features mentioned "Half a dozen jokes" and an original soundtrack. I was never hyped for the game before release, and only heard of it recently. So when I went into Jazzpunk, with no expectations or knowledge of what it was and came out disappointed, I know something went wrong.
The first ten or so minutes seemed promising. A well done intro set up the tone and feel of the game, but never did anything with them. You spend the mission faffing about in environments with a multitude of things to do, but with none of them interesting. While the tasks themselves resemble point and click adventure games in which there is little logic and a lot of dull things to do, the humour is referencial and circumstantial. Go to a cinema, annoy the patrons while watching a repeated advertisement from the 1950's. Go and spray people with bird pheromones, watch them get covered in birds. Go and contemplate how dull this game is, then listen to the same looped track for the fourth time. In these sections, there is nothing of substance or worth, and these are the main part of the game!
Intersperced between these prolonged sections of bland mediocrity are the occasional part that requires actual skill, like playing Frogger or Space Invaders. That's right, this game is so insubstantial it relies on games that are the best part of two or three decades old. These mini-games also come in the form of Duck Hunt, Quake, Virtual Boy 3D Tennis and more that are either rip-off other (Better) games or just made without any thought put into them. As they try to do a variety of old games, it fails to do any of them well and they all end up being the same (If not lesser) than whatever they were replicating, and as such there's no personality in these mini-games. Quake is thinly disguised as Wedding Qake, which is a watered down version with uninspired designs for everything inside the mini-game. Near the end, there are several of these re-used mini-games in a row which you're supposed to lose for the story to go on, with no prior knowledge that you failing was vital to what little plot there is, and as most of these mini-games control poorly, you end up putting a fair amount of effort into something you inevitably lose, which is always annoying.
This is generally the part where, if you haven't already, you talk about the story and memorable parts, however in this case I'll mention the lack of each. The plot is pushed along by your pre-mission briefings, and the occasional scripted sequence. None of those flashy scripted sequences shown in the trailers mind you, those never really happen. Instead you have these very slow and unexciting sections in which you go from point A to point B, maybe knocking down a few people if you go out of your way for it. There is no sense of pacing whatsoever, and anything interesting it has to offer to shows off as soon as it can shoe-horn in a bad punchline.
In addition to that, the minimal amount of interaction required is plagued by some rather bizarre technical issues. Mouse smoothing and acceleration change from time to time with no reason or indication that it's happened. The artstyle itself can be off-putting from time to time, so having your mouse go completely nuts combined may lead to motion sickness, especially in the penultimate level in where you're inside some sort of technical difficulties area, complete with bluescreens and enough whizzy things to make your head spin. That and the layout of the level may lead to headaches, without factoring in problems with mouse acceleration or smoothing. Using a gamepad works well, thankfully, and I reccomend that if you can play through Jazzpunk with a controller that you do. There's no real challenge here, so anyone can use a controller with ease in Jazzpunk.
Jazzpunk reminds me of Borderlands in a way. The admittedly nifty artstyle and its brand of humour (If you can call it that) are just a cover for an insubstantial game with horrible gameplay and a lack of a plot. Unlike Borderlands however, Jazzpunk doesn't have moments of catharsis or entertaining distractions from the main quest. Despite all of that, Jazzpunk is well intentioned and with a little more thought put into the humour and gameplay, it may even stand up as a game, not just a sightseeing tour.

Gave a bad review, got voted down a lot, went to play other RE games instead.
...Came back some years later, surprisingly Steam forgot my review, tried it again, giving my second review.
...It still sucks.
Maybe it's because I prefer a more atmospheric, forgiving game like Revelations than an Action-focused one like this (believe me, this is way more Action than Horror). But this game more than any other RE game I've tried so far is unbelievably unforgiving and frustrating.
I'll just list them in bullet points.
Good
- your partner AI is competent
- the story is engaging
- atmosphere is good, and very RE
- lots of gameplay mechanics
- Action (if you're into that)
Bad
- too much action: the pace is too fast and involves much more button mashing
- camera + controls: the camera swings wildly alot if you're playing on a mouse. I put the sensitivity to 0 and it still swings around like a drunkard. Also moving backwards makes your character turn around in a small circle (unpredictably clockwise or anti-clockwise) which is realistic but very clumsy, and combined with the camera in tight spaces, that really made me sick.
- darkness: the high dynamic range is excellent and atmospheric, but too much of the game is in pitch darkness, and too many zombies are hiding in it. I kept getting hit by zombies or losing sight of a zombie I knocked down due to the darkness + crazy swinging camera.
- clumsy hit zones: I'd rush to a zombie to deliver a killing blow only for the indicator to not appear as I had to be still closer to trigger it, and sometimes a zombie would jump at me faster than my animation would trigger, which would trigger the infamous -
- QTEs: the single biggest thing that was talked about in all those negative reviews. Too many QTEs, too easy to trigger, difficult to overcome. Do this, QTE. Break free, QTE again. Hit someone, try to hit again and miss. Get grabbed. QTE. Suddenly a train dashes at you. QT-oh you missed it. Die and repeat the last 5 minutes again.
- Cutscenes: a lot of pausing in the action to force a cutscene on you, sometimes allowing enemies to get the jump on you while you're frozen there watching the whole thing. It breaks the flow of the game and often resets the camera making you confused when it ends.
- No pausing to access options: VERY frustrating when you're just trying out controls or settings and got your sensitivity wrong or something and you can't switch.
Overall, it's a frustrating experience. Maybe it might have helped if I had tweaked the controls properly (although I swear I already spent too much time doing so), but the experience as a whole did little to convince me to spend more time to do so.
If you want horror-action, do yourself a favor and get Dead Space or any other RE game instead. There's a reason RE7 took so long to get started.

The Sparkle ZERO is a game about the evolution of different organisms, fighting for their food and fleeing from stronger creatures.
You begin as a very small something with the ability to eat cells. Each time you collect enough pieces of food you will evolve, becoming bigger and getting a random look. And once you reach specific levels a wormhole opens, leading to another stage with more organisms and other types of creatures.
I played the game after a long day at work and I really enjoyed the fact that I can just relax and play this more or less peaceful game.
The graphic style is very beautiful and flashy. As the game title says, everything here consists of sparks or at least looks like them.
The music is also great and I could easily sleep to such music. The game was like a dream, everything is so flashy, such a relaxing music and the game also ended quite unexpectedly.
But it also has some bad aspects. After playing for a while my fps has shrunk to about 5, but I fixed it by leaving to the main menu and starting the game again. Then, in the end, I was shown a white screen. This screen didn’t disappear and I couldn’t leave by pressing keys, so I had to alt+F4.
Positive:
+ beautiful graphics
+ relaxing music
+ random evolution
+ controller support
+ easy 100% achievements
Negative:
- fps sinking after a while
- couldn’t exit in the end
All in all I enjoyed the game, but it lacks some things like other types of evolution (maybe depending if you eat other creatures or just “cells”) or other monsters trying to kill you. I could be better, but it’s a good game to play after a hard day, when you don’t really want anything.

'Sparkle ZERO' is a casual game. A controller is recommended to play this game but not absolutely necessary. You control a sea-dwelling creature called a sparkle. The only thing you need to do is swim around and eat everything you can. The more you eat, the larger your sparkle becomes. When you reach the maximum size (level 50), the game ends.
Your sparkle will look different depending on the type of food you eat the most. Unlike the other Sparkle games, there is no color to differentiate the types of food, and no tutorial or explanation of the mechanics, so I'm not sure how you're supposed to know what to eat to become the type of creature you prefer. I ended up just devouring everything and suppose I became an average sparkle, the 'omnivore' of 'Sparkle 2 Evo'.
'Sparkle ZERO' is not a colorful game like the other Sparkle games. Look at the screenshots. It's practically a game in black & white. The music is rather weird: it came and went as if someone was slowly turning the volume of my speakers all the way down and then back up to where it was, and repeated this the whole time.
Steam tells me I played the game for 87 minutes. In that time, I finished the game and got all the achievements. So it's a very short experience. It didn't need to be any longer, because the last 10 minutes or so I was getting bored with it already and just kept playing until the game ended, to get that last achievement to pop.
I noticed two technical issues, as well:
- when using a controller: after you opened any of the menu options and go back to the main menu, you can't navigate anymore (pressing 'up' or 'down' on the controller does nothing), so you have to use the mouse to navigate the menu;
- when the game ends, the screen becomes white and freezes like that. You need to force a shutdown of the game by using the task bar (or maybe alt + F4 works too, I didn't try).
I don't think I'll be recommending this game. I bought it for only 99 cents and enjoyed it for what is was, but it's way too short for its full price and 'Sparkle 2 Evo' is a better alternative because it's more colorful and more varied. If you like this sort of game and can buy it heavily discounted, it'll bring you about an hour and a half of fun and an easy 100% achievements, but that's it. I see no reason to play this game twice.

Sparkle ZERO is a deviation from the prior Sparkle games, Sparkle 2 Evo & Sparkle 3 Genesis. Though both are casual games, Sparkle ZERO is even more so. Sans changing levels, evolution appears to be completely passive in nature and determined by what one's organism consumes. There is no real goal to the game other than to evolve interesting creatures and store images of them in the gallery.
Gamers looking for a game with a goal like the prior Sparkle releases would certainly be disappointed by this game, which is evident by many of the comments. I, however, love a truly casual/mindless game from time to time where I can just let my mind wander. This is an ideal relaxation/distraction game, no stress, just enjoyable music and creation. My only disappointment is that it is not as colorful as the other games.

A Detective's Novel is a mystery visual novel both developed and published by Amaterasu Software. On a cold November night in a desolate estate deep in the mountains an innocent life has prematurely perished and its up to the player to find out who did it. As the lead man on the investigation, you are Detective Knox, one of the most famous detectives in the entire state who has yet to stumble upon a mystery he is unable to unravel. Teamed up with the Junior Detective Assistant Clark...can you solve William Goldberg's murder and bring to justice the person responsible?
This novel has an interesting story filled with an ensemble of varied characters that you must get to know closely if you are to successfully solve the murder. One has to keep an open mind and pay close attention to the smallest of details in the environment as well as what the suspects tell Knox as you try to piece the clues together in this murder mystery. With that said, Detective Knox the protagonists in this V.N., is a complete jerk yet I still really liked the guy. He's blunt, rude and I found him to be just hilarious even though he says the most obnoxious things to people. He literally just doesn't care. I guess we all know someone like this which is why I assume that this character really appealed to me? In closing, this visual novel's narrative is just really entertaining and quite funny.
Visually, A Detective's Story is mediocre at best in my opinion. I was not really a fan of the artstyle used in this particular V.N. but after some time it sort of grows on you as I do like to see variations from the typical manga inspired style of art used in many visual novels. The sound quality though is excellent as was the musical score filled with peppy upbeat tempos that compliment the narrative quite well. However, one of my biggest gripes with this visual novel is the outrageous amount of typos peppered throughout the dialogue. If you read alot of V.N.'s you are going to notice incorrect spelling but usually they are few and far in between but A Detective's Story is literally brimming with them from start to finish. I actually lost count and if you are even keeping count at all that alone should let you know that there is a problem. Yet despite that I was able to push through the story to the end. To summarize, despite the large amount of immersion breaking typos, I was still able to truly enjoy the entertaining story in this captivating visual novel.
Although I was not able to successfully solve the murder on my first read I still liked the narrative in this story and will definitely re-read in the future. It was a fun and light-hearted read that I really enjoyed even though it was a bit short. There aren't many options available for this V.N. and no Steam Achievements but there are Steam Trading Cards to collect. If you are a fan of visual novels and can withstand the constant barrage of typos in this title then I would RECOMMEND A Detective's Story for a nice if not brief read.

Thomas Was Alone is an example of a simplistic puzzle platformer done right. The game design was, well, minimalistic, but everything was presented geniusely.
In the minimalism field, designers and artists alike often coined the thought "less is more", meaning to use a subject in its most basic elements to convey or produce a message. This game did exactly that: you will find no more than playing as rectangular characters navigating around rectangular platforms. Everything is designed in such a way, that even though an obstacle or a character is presented with basic geometry, you can at least guess its function even before the game tells you in the tutorial. That alone exhibits great game design. Further on, the philosophy behind the game is much beyond all those simple shapes and images: that is the real beauty of the game.
Once I played through half of the game, it's not about plainly navigating through the puzzles anymore, it keeps turning me back to the original question: What is this simplistic world all about? Who is this rectangular guy called Thomas? Will Thomas ever stop feeling alone?
Aside from that, the puzzles are eye-pleasing, the story is intriguing, and the music is well-crafted. Along with a great concept to piece everything together, Thomas Was Alone is a true masterpiece of the minimalistic genre.

Ah Crysis, the fantastic first person shooter which combines amazing graphical fidelity with open world like levels. I really enjoy this game but sadly, there are a few technical issues which hold the game back from a perfect 10.
For this review, I will seperate the review into 4 parts (Similair to my Blacklight: Retribution review).
1st category: Graphics
The graphics in this game are unlike any in the firstperson shooter genre today. Utilizing Crytek's greatest engine; The CryEngine 3, Crysis 2 has gorgeous graphics with very high res textures and other graphical fidelities such as bloom, shadows, particle effects, and more. However with all this in mind, this game (like its predessecors) requieres a hefty gaming PC to run it. Furthermore, this isn't even the best looking Crysis game. That title belongs to Crysis 3, just released last February. That game uses the CryEngine 3 to its full potential. If you have an underpowered machine, such as a slow laptop or a mediocre gaming PC, this game will put a significant load on your system.  I have a Youtube video which shows what the performance will be like on a standard laptop. Now if I was to play this game on my desktop on the same settings, I would get much better performance. So buyer beware, Be prepared to do ALOT of configuring in the "system.cfg" files to get this game to run at a solid 25+ frames. It took me nearly 4 hours to configure this game until it was playable. Besides that, Beautiful graphics!
Link to video:
Category 2: Gameplay
Crysis 2 is not your average shooter. The whole story and gameplay revolves around the Nanosuit 2, a supersuit with different abilities. Each ability drains you suit power to different degrees depending on the intensity of the battle. There are a total of 3 abilities. Cloak, Armour, and Nanovision. Cloak makes you invisible, Armour lets you take more bullets, and Nanovision is a thermal imaging ability which lets you soo where the enemy is. As for shooting, it is standard stuff. Assault Rifles, Shotguns, Snipers, and even Grenade Launchers. The guns feel very meaty and have good recoil, and if a certain gun doesnt fit your playstyle then you can simply tap "X" and adjust the gun to your liking. Other then that, its a standard shooting mechanic.
Category 3: Story
WARNING SPOILERS
Crysis 2's story is a mixed bag between alien invasions and corperate takeovers. During the beginning, you fight soldier called the C.E.L.L and by the middle to the end, you will fight aliens. The main plot is about a Marine called Alcatraz who was attacked by the Ceph (aliens) and nearly died. Then a soldier named Prophet shows up and sames him and grants you the Nanosuit. From there you will travel to different parts of New York, killing aliens  and evacuating civilians. If there is a sniper on the enemy team and he is cloaked, there is no way you will be able to find him. That is really the only issue with multiplayer and this being the Maximum Edition of the game, you also get some exclusive dog tags and camos.
Additional Sub-Category: Cons
Crysis 2 has alot of problems with freezing issues. Sometimes as I reach a checkpoint the game will freeze and drop to 0 FPS and I will have to restart my PC. This is very unfortunate because it happenes so frequently. I hope Crytek will look into this issue, but as for now expect random spontanious game crashes.
Verdict: Crysis 2 is another win for Crytek, even with small issues the game succeeds in both story and multiplayer. Overall 9.5/10

An entertaining game, to say the least. Like card games, you have to defeat a sequence of enemies with your deck. After each boss your deck increases, but so the number of enemies. Unlike regular card games, the battle takes place in real time, so plan your deck and use the cards in the right moment is crucial. I like the concept (card game with real time battles), but I feel variety of cards could be improved for the sake of the strategy. It shouldn't keep you from playing though.
I'd place Cards of Cthulhu in a Casual+Strategy category. It's a good choice if you're looking for something in your library if you have a few minutes spare, but nothing stops you for playing it for a whole hour.
Now for something more detailed:
PROS:
The cards strategy + real time battle thing. I'm not really a RTS guy. I can go through the first wave of enemies easily, but after that things starts to get quite challenging and get your strategy ready is crucial.
The art is amazing. Kudos!
A great pick when you want to give a break of your job (hey, I'm a freelancer, I make my own rules :) )
CONS:
I feel the game could improve on the variety of cards. When you think of card games, big part of the fun is building your deck. More cards >> more strategy thinking >> more fun.
Also, maybe an improved deck building screen could help to expand the game experience and add more value to the gameplay.
The lack of a tutorial or introduction makes you feel a bit lost at first. It won't stop you from playing, but a little more polishing in the intro would be great. Maybe something more about the Cthulhu myhtos.
TL;DR : A good casual game that mixes card strategy and real time battles. Worth the buy.

Started playing this game about 4 years ago, came back to it a couple months ago and I don't remember why I stopped playing. Transformice is an MMO platformer with the main character as a mouse, with the goal to collect the cheese and bring it back to the hole, a concept quite simple on paper but vastly more complicated and agonizing in reality. To help you along your way, each round there will be a dedicated shaman, a mouse with powers to help mice get to the hole. Collecting cheese and saving mice as a shaman helps you unlock new titles and new shop items as you play. A very simple concept that is rewarding and enjoyable to play, with pretty much infinite replay value.
As casual and easy going as the game goes, it also caters well for the competitive side too - different game modes mean the game panders towards casual and competitive players. Competitive players can aim for "firsts" in normal rooms, or play the harder bootcamp or racing game modes, while casual players can enjoy the normal rooms and survivor mode.
The game is constantly being updated, with new shop items available from week to week, to new events periodically to celebrate different holidays, rewarding players with new titles and badges. Not to mention the community constantly creating new maps to help keep the game fresh, it's difficult to imagine someone getting bored of this game.
One of the main problems that free to play MMOs suffer from are play to win in-game microtransactions, but the in-game purchases in Transformice are solely visual.  As a new player, the game is not difficult to pick up at all either, with the controls being extremely simple and the in-game mechanics are easy to understand. It's simply a case of playing enough to understand the map rotation and how to finish each map, and once you've done that you can compete with everyone else.
However there are some things that less this game down, mainly being the community. By and large I've found that the majority of people playing this game are of a young age, and the in-game chat is always filled with slurs and other random♥♥♥♥♥♥ Additionally, veteran players are also not so welcoming of new players, and it becomes very apparent when someone is new to this game, when everyone else is waiting for one person to finish the round.
As far as free to play games go, this game is simply brilliant. It's a game you'll play a couple rounds of when you have some time to kill, and hours later you'll wonder where that time went. Played about 200 hours of the browers version on top of my time played on Steam and it's still a game I look forward to playing. Transformice is the benchmark of user friendly MMOs, and is unique within the genre.

I never quite understood why everybody hates on this game... Being a Resident Evil fan since the beginning, I can say that this is a solid title, regardless of it not being a survival horror game anymore! I can say that with confidence...
PROS:
-The story is fantastic... Still residing in the same RE universe, it brings out many intense moments as well as plot twists that blow my mind!
-Most of the major RE characters you've known and loved are playable in 4 seperate campaigns that intertwine together (Online coop works with this in the fact that, at certain points in the game you will run into people playing different characters that mix into a different characters story... Really innovative!)
-Still keeps some of the thrill of a survival horror through Leon Kennedy's campaign (Low amounts of ammo, health, various jumpscares)
-While the movement and combat is more lenient instead of limited, it plays rather well control-wise and is very easy to get used to.
CONS
-I don't think of it as a con personally but it has lost its essence of survival horror that it used to have and has been placed in a more action adventure type genre.
-The inventory has improved, as switching weapons is as easy as tapping a button on the D-pad but depending on the predicament you are in, you may have trouble navigating the inventory menu while avoiding enemies at the same time.
-There is no pause button... Easily the most annoying flaw to the game, you press the select button which only pulls up an options menu where you can adjust settings or quit the game! HOWEVER, quiting the game puts you in the spot you left off which isnt as useful but its tolerable...
-The cover system can be finnicky... Characters may not always snap to cover like you want them to but it depends on the environment you're in... I personally haven't had much problems with it but I can see how annoying it may be...
-Multiplayer is different compared to other games, as they are more objective based coop type games rather than deathmatch... They are very fun gametypes but I prefered the Operation Raccoon City which was the only amazing thing about that game...
There are many other things I can list, as this is a very in depth and lengthy game (4 campaigns, about 8 hours each), but I only wanted to point out the campaign aspect of it more than anything else... The game, despite reviews from critics and fans, is very enjoyable! Not the best RE game I will admit but definitely one of the better ones... Personal review score: 8/10

Okay, this will not be the most sincere review, but it will give you an idea of what the game is made of.
So, alas, and ergo, I begin.
Imagine a game that played all of the Resident Evil games, yet only cared for 4 and 5, but took a liking some of the words from the others. Words like, "Umbrella", "Zombie", "T-Virus", "Jill Sandwich", and "Wesker." Then the game watched every one of the RE movies, back to back - everyday, for a week. And then wrote a "script" from four different points of view. None of these individual stories make any sense on their own, yet once you've beaten the game(s) and dealt with their UNIQUE playstyles (see: Unfocused, Confused, and Sexually Curious), the story somehow makes 100% LESS sense than when you first had no idea what was going on.
While growing up, this game took the whole "Buddy System" concept entirely too seriously, and decided to tattoo the phrase across its chest when it turned 18. It was also raised to be severely narrowminded concerning all Eastern European/Slavic peoples. It was brought up to believe that, "They're a bunch of dirty, war-mongering, genocidal, tracksuit-wearing, subhuman, walking garbage cans, who only cause trouble and kill each other. Plus they're actually monsters."
Anyway, the amount of action scenes, and scripted, "GO! RUN! STRUGGLE! JUMP! HELP YOUR ***PARTNER*** AND ACT LIKE YOU CARE!" content makes the whole RE "film" series feel like Terms of Enrampagement - No, sorry, I meant Terms of Endearment. I feel a little uncomfortable at the moment, so, in conlusion - Imagine a slippy, slidey, third person Serious Sam game with an almost, possibly, nearly functional, "cover-system," with the narrative tone of The Road, acting equal to that of a six and a half year old Cambodian immigrant, and the rollicking sense of humor of a wet cinderblock with a dead cat on top.

TL;DR Cons outweigh the Pros, while the game is fun for a minute or two it's ultimately bland and not worth the money. Sorry devs.
Time to give this a real review, now that I've beaten the game. I'll start with the pros;
- Simple gameplay
- Nice atmosphere/ beautiful graphics
- Eat ****, get bigger; really fun to watch
Now the cons....so many cons.....
- No tutorial, not even a simple menu to show basic commands. Took me 5 minutes trying to get through my first portal before I gave up and googled it. For those wondering, it's the "R" key or scroll the mouse wheel down.
- Bumpers. F***ing BUMPERS. They exist just to ruin your day. They make you want to strangle whatever idiot thought it would be a good idea to make these.  I don't mind a challenge, but those F******* BUMPERS.  I would suggest the devs balance these so they're not as aggresive, just my opinion.
- Eating speed. Everytime you eat a little cube your sparkle's mouth closes for a second and he can't eat, then it opens and... you get it (except when eating enemy remains, those are how it should be). Now this alone wouldn't be annoying, but the devs made these little lines of cubes everywhere for you to follow that lead to cube fields or enemies. Problem is, your 'sparkle' moves juuuuust fast enough and eats juuuuuust slow enough that you have to hesitate at every cube i.e you can't just swim through the line to your objective and gobble the cubes as you go. It gets old....fast.
- It's bland. While the atmosphere is nice there's really nothing to do but eat cubes and attack the 2 types of enemies. Bland.
- Enemies die too easily, everything is a 2 hit kill. Jellyfish (?), 2 hits. Giant sparkle as big as you, 2 hits. It would be better if the other sparkles got more health the bigger they got, more of a real challenge.
- No replayability. Once you've seen the first level, that IS the whole game. Once you've beaten it you have no reason to play it again.
- It's short. Completed it in roughly 1 hour, I think. (play time is higher because I let it idle for a while)

I'm not usually the type of person who will complain about the length of a game relative to its price; but for Jazzpunk I feel as though I have to make an exception.
I hate to list this as "not recommended"; it's a great game, I'll give it that much. But even at Holiday Sale prices, this just wasn't worth it for me. For $7.49, I got a little over 3 hours of playtime. I wasn't speed-running, and I didn't focus on the main mission; for the most part, I tried my best to explore and find the variety of sidequests, activities, and little jokes scattered throughout the game. Seven bucks for three hours is still better than, say, a movie ticket, but unlike games with similar time-to-price ratios (Gone Home, The Stanley Parable, Thirty Flights of Loving), the quality wasn't *quite* up to snuff. Although it is very funny (and even hilarious at times), some of the gags get old, and I felt as though the latter half of the game doesn't quite live up to the first.
The game itself plays like a more absurd, less thought-provoking version of The Stanley Parable. It even includes some meta moments, though never to TSP's extent. I experienced quite a few bugs (though relatively minor) during my playthrough, though I may have just been unlucky. Once, I had to restart a chapter because I had gotten permanently stuck in an elevator shaft; another glitch caused the game to crash every time I attempted to play a record (thankfully, this was not crucial to the main mission).
I feel almost guilty to list this game as "not recommended"; Necrophone has created a witty, funny, brilliant game, and they should be proud. But I'd suggest you wait until it drops to three or four dollars.

Ingredients
Original recipe makes 12 servings
4 cups milk
5 whole cloves
1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
12 egg yolks
1 1/2 cups sugar
2 1/2 cups light rum
4 cups light cream
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1. Combine milk, cloves, 1/2 teaspoon vanilla, and cinnamon in a saucepan, and heat over lowest setting for 5 minutes. Slowly bring milk mixture to a boil.
2. In a large bowl, combine egg yolks and sugar. Whisk together until fluffy. Whisk hot milk mixture slowly into the eggs. Pour mixture into saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly for 3 minutes, or until thick. Do not allow mixture to boil. Strain to remove cloves, and let cool for about an hour.
3. Stir in rum, cream, 2 teaspoon vanilla, and nutmeg. Refrigerate overnight before serving.

Excellent graphic and very cool concept unfortunately terrible gameplay execution. I really expected to like this title. This game was obviously made to play with a controller and is virtually unplayable with mouse/keyboard. I mean who tries to tie both the attack AND block mechanics to mouselook? I want to look left to see that guy coming my way - now I am blocking left (get hit), but wait - I need to attack this guy in front of me but I have to look right to do it - now I can't see the other guy (get hit) - crap dont look left I was just trying to block that way (get hit). I am trying to turn the camera up there to see those archers not block up - ugh hit again - now I am dead. Just frustrating. Also, after like 30 minutes all this screen jiggling around from moving the mouse back and forth to block and attack has given me vertigo and a headache.
Even doing both tutorials many of the ingame mechanics are not intuitive and/or completely obtuse. The enemy is doing - some attack. Can I block this incoming attack? Maybe? I did the block thing I was shown in the tutorial but got hit anyway? Why? No idea. Was it unblockable? Was I at least close to blocking? No idea. Try to dodge attack - hit while rolling - sometimes. Trying to execute my special attacks. Did it work? No idea. Was I close to executing it? What did I do wrong? No idea. Was I interrupted? Did I push the wrong button? Wait hold on did I just see a blue streak maybe? Was that it? No idea. I just picked up some kind of power up - what does it do? No idea. Battled through 60 trash mobs and two dozen enemy warriors - died - started over at the beginning of the whole level. Where was the checkpoint? No idea. Did I miss something. No idea. Battled through 60 trash mobs and two dozen enemy warriors (again) - doing good - mission failed. What  happened. No idea. Get to some new boss surrounded by wolves. Wait what - the tutorial doesnt mention wolves - how do I fight them? No idea. Wolf attacks from left - move mouse left to block - boss hits you from the right - wait what how do I block both the left and the right with mouselook? No idea.
I have an idea. Uninstall. Great idea.
I don't know. Maybe there is a good game in here somewhere if you spend a few hours surfing youtube on how to "git gud" at For Honor. Maybe there is some better control setup that can be configured to stop the headache inducing attack/defend tied to mouselook problem. For me I found it frustrating and simply not compelling enough to warrant the additional effort.

The game itself is pretty fun for a time killer. At least that's what it looks like at first. The graphics are pretty OK, I suppose, nothing too spectacular, but captivating nonetheless. The music, albeit absent for most of the game, is also very nice done. It adds to the already alienating atmosphere.
You go around eating stuff to get bigger to kill bigger mobs, sure, plenty of games like that, but this one gets the gameplay just right, it makes you feel like you're under a " microscope". The controls are pretty nice, there are not tight or to loose, just right for the type of " vehicle " that you are driving.
Even though the graphics are not too intense, at higher " levels " (or layers since the stages are layered on top and under one another) , they all add up, so the elements/food/mobs from the lower levels are in your field of vision so your FPS take a huge hit the higher up you go. I went from a silky smooth 60fps to a horrible 9fps, though I'm pretty sure this is because I didn't " eat " everything in the lower levels.
Game ran great otherwise on a 980gtx @ 1440p. Superb.
I do see a lot of people claiming that they are unable to get the game running, but its actually quite simple: You create a profile and then hit the " GO " button, that's it.
I do wish the music was more constant since its awesome, though.
I had 0 issues with launching the game,pausing, unpausing, taking screenshots through the in game feature.
I do want to keep going just to see what my little " guy " evolves into, or how it changes. Pretty imaginative game.

Due to the very nature of slower paced interactive narratives, the "jokes" are dwelled on for longer than they should be, long enough for you to realize that they are mostly only half jokes to begin with and lack any real punchline. Why should you buy this game and not other tycoon games of the same genre?
Blueprints! It's a casual, fun game. You can spend hours in the tutorial alone (if you want to find issues.. almost 2hours here and I haven't finished the tutorial.. and not because I am a bad player.. Just focusing on helping and finding issues.)
You can hire workers and in order to keep them happy they need to be fed and paid! (duuuh)
You can create your custom blueprints to maximize efficiency. Same goes for contracts. You can choose what to deliver and how many pieces of each.
You can research new stuff, go to other islands and much more.
The only minus I could find in this game would be time taking to complete it/get bored. But I haven't reached that point yet and I'm sure I will not too soon. There's too much to learn/test/do right now.
EDIT:
Finally completed tutorial (not because I'm dumb but because I test the game more than play it right now)
Gave a shot to the Scenario before finishing the tutorial and I was lost... Really really lost :)
Now that I finished the tutorial I understand more of it and will sure have a fun time with the Scenario.
There's not much to do after a certain point and yeah.. it gets a bit boring, hoping to have some new quests or something to keep you interested in playing, sort of a story mode even though I don't see how one could have a story mode here.
Enjoyable game, Still recommend it. The price is fair. Game is still in development and it will get even better than it is now!

Started playing this game about 4 years ago, came back to it a couple months ago and I don't remember why I stopped playing. Transformice is an MMO platformer with the main character as a mouse, with the goal to collect the cheese and bring it back to the hole, a concept quite simple on paper but vastly more complicated and agonizing in reality. To help you along your way, each round there will be a dedicated shaman, a mouse with powers to help mice get to the hole. Collecting cheese and saving mice as a shaman helps you unlock new titles and new shop items as you play. A very simple concept that is rewarding and enjoyable to play, with pretty much infinite replay value.
As casual and easy going as the game goes, it also caters well for the competitive side too - different game modes mean the game panders towards casual and competitive players. Competitive players can aim for "firsts" in normal rooms, or play the harder bootcamp or racing game modes, while casual players can enjoy the normal rooms and survivor mode.
The game is constantly being updated, with new shop items available from week to week, to new events periodically to celebrate different holidays, rewarding players with new titles and badges. Not to mention the community constantly creating new maps to help keep the game fresh, it's difficult to imagine someone getting bored of this game.
One of the main problems that free to play MMOs suffer from are play to win in-game microtransactions, but the in-game purchases in Transformice are solely visual.  As a new player, the game is not difficult to pick up at all either, with the controls being extremely simple and the in-game mechanics are easy to understand. It's simply a case of playing enough to understand the map rotation and how to finish each map, and once you've done that you can compete with everyone else.
However there are some things that less this game down, mainly being the community. By and large I've found that the majority of people playing this game are of a young age, and the in-game chat is always filled with slurs and other random♥♥♥♥♥♥ Additionally, veteran players are also not so welcoming of new players, and it becomes very apparent when someone is new to this game, when everyone else is waiting for one person to finish the round.
As far as free to play games go, this game is simply brilliant. It's a game you'll play a couple rounds of when you have some time to kill, and hours later you'll wonder where that time went. Played about 200 hours of the browers version on top of my time played on Steam and it's still a game I look forward to playing. Transformice is the benchmark of user friendly MMOs, and is unique within the genre.

Sparkle ZERO is a deviation from the prior Sparkle games, Sparkle 2 Evo & Sparkle 3 Genesis.  Though both are casual games, Sparkle ZERO is even more so.  Sans changing levels, evolution appears to be completely passive in nature and determined by what one's organism consumes.  There is no real goal to the game other than to evolve interesting creatures and store images of them in the gallery.
Gamers looking for a game with a goal like the prior Sparkle releases would certainly be disappointed by this game, which is evident by many of the comments.  I, however, love a truly casual/mindless game from time to time where I can just let my mind wander.  This is an ideal relaxation/distraction game, no stress, just enjoyable music and creation.  My only disappointment is that it is not as colorful as the other games.

I had a really fun time playing Jazzpunk. It's a surreal adventure set in an alternate universe 1950's that is often very funny. The game play is pretty simplistic, but what makes this game really good is all the little interactions with the characters and the environment. There are a lot of little neat touches sprinkled throughout every corner of the game world. Before doing the main objective in any level, I'd just roam around the level and click on everything I could to see if something would happen. The humor is silly, weird, wacky, random, and sometimes just plain bizarre. Kinda like your average Adult Swim show without the sadism and satanism. WARNING: Be prepared for a deluge of puns. There are a TON of pop culture references (not necissarily in joke form).  The developers of this game sure do love Street Fighter 2! Even if the developers do mistake references for jokes sometimes, it was still fun looking for them.  Every level looks fairly unique and is usually visually interesting. The art style of the game is aesthetically pleasing and kind of reminds me a bit of Psychonauts. The game is only about three hours total and that's after getting all the achievements.  The main down sides to the game are that the game play is really basic, there's a fair amount of really corny jokes,  and there's a sequence at the end of the game that just felt like going through the motions, that no matter what I did the outcome was already predetermined. That was only a very small part of a game that's otherwise fantastic. I definitely recommend Jazzpunk!

The average Rainbow Six Siege multiplayer match contains a surprisingly small amount of shooting. Gunplay is, of course, still central to the Siege experience, but there's so much more to it. You'll spend just as much time strategizing with your teammates, carefully laying traps, reinforcing destructible walls, and feeling your heart race as the dull, distant rumble of your enemies' breach charges suddenly gives way to intense and immediate chaos. And that's just on defense.
Few modern shooters can match the heart-pounding exhilaration and immense strategic depth Siege achieves with its asymmetrical PvP. With no respawns, no regenerating health, and only five players per team, every life suddenly feels meaningful and precious (though you can still monitor security cameras and communicate with your team in death). Running-and-gunning will almost certainly land you on the sidelines, so you're much better off using your drivable drone to scout ahead or coordinating with your teammates to ensure all sightlines are covered.
Not only does the intense one-life setup encourage players to approach every encounter thoughtfully and methodically, it also fills a long neglected gap in the FPS genre. While shooters that emphasize twitch shooting over tactics can grow tiresome, Siege's seemingly endless array of viable strategies makes every round memorable and organically begets the kind of brilliant, unpredictable moments you can't wait to tell your friends about.
In any given round, you could repel from a rooftop, smash through a window, and flash the room with a stun grenade, or just lie prone in a dark corner waiting for enemies to wander past. Maybe on defense you'll fortify four team members in a single room but send the fifth out into the wild in hopes of catching the other team off guard. You could also play some mind games by remotely detonating an explosive purely as misdirection before infiltrating through another point of ingress. All these mechanics breed creativity and allow the game to evolve as players develop (and react to) new strategies.
Unfortunately, there is a campaign-sized hole where Siege's single-player should be, and while a carefully crafted, story-driven experience would have further solidified the game's position as one of the year's best shooters, Siege still manages to compensate in other ways. Franchises like Halo and Call of Duty have set the bar for the amount of desirable content you can cram into a game, and Siege clearly falls short of that mark. But consider a game like Rocket League, which has delivered serious longevity with a single game mode. Siege, to me, feels like Rocket League or even Team Fortress 2 in that its pure, competitive nature makes it eminently replayable.
Even outside of its natural competitiveness and deep well of mechanics, Siege's PvP provides enough variables to keep players engaged. There are multiple match types, over a dozen maps, randomized objective locations within those maps, differing times of day for every stage, mixed mode servers that automatically scramble all these options together, and, most importantly, 20 distinct Operators, all of whom open new gameplay avenues. Even characters whose unique gadget seemed useless at first inevitably proved me wrong. I assumed Doc's remote revive dart would never come in handy given that allies are far more often killed than wounded; then I saw someone punch a tiny hole through a wall to revive a fallen teammate pinned by gunfire on the other side.
And while Siege may not contain a campaign, it does offer 11 singleplayer "Situations" that are both legitimately helpful and surprisingly robust, considering they're essentially training missions. Each situation features three difficulty options and three optional objectives--which enhances their replayability--and each one focuses on a different aspect of the game like bomb defusal or destructible cover. They lack the cohesion, polish, and narrative drive of a campaign, but they're at least diverse enough to prove worthwhile.
You can also choose to tackle Siege's Terrorist Hunt mode alone, though it's definitely more approachable as a cooperative experience. As with the competitive multiplayer, each player gets one life and only a finite amount of health, but here you must hunt down a preset number of AI-controlled terrorists or disarm bombs while an infinite number of enemies attempt to interfere. Being so outnumbered while having no way to heal turns every round into an intense war of attrition; even if the first guy doesn't kill you outright, he might shave off enough of your health that the next guy can easily take you out. When you make it to the end of a 20-minute round with only a tiny sliver of health remaining, finishing off that final terrorist provides such an incredible high I found it nearly impossible to hold in my reflexive "Hell yeah!"
Despite all this excess adrenaline, Siege still suffers a few rough edges. The progression system, for example, feels slightly empty and metes out experience too slowly. Thankfully, Casual PvP will be available right out of the gate, but you'll have to accrue enough XP to reach level 20 before you'll unlock Ranked PvP. It makes sense the game would gate Ranked matches given that they remove much of the in-game assistance that makes Casual PvP accessible (a fact the game fails to explain, unfortunately), but grinding all the way to level 20 takes far too long. Why not set the limit lower and let players decide when they're ready?
In addition to XP, players also earn Renown--Siege's version of in-game currency, which can be used to purchase new Operators, weapon attachments, and weapon skins. Again, forcing players to slowly earn new Operators makes some sense: it creates a sense of connection and ownership while encouraging players to really explore and capitalize on each character's unique skills. I was also able to unlock two attackers and two defenders in roughly three hours (thanks in part to some generous boosts early on), and that collection of four Operators proved substantial enough to enable my enjoyment despite limiting my options.
However, I still encountered situations where my operators had already been selected by other players, which forced me to play as the generic "recruit" stand-in. And more importantly, customization options are extremely limited. You can buy custom sights and scopes or equip your guns with various stabilizers and silencers, but these attachments only marginally impact gameplay, and because you're only outfitting one or two Operators at a time, you'll earn every upgrade with very little effort. This undoubtedly preserves the balance of the game, but it's pretty difficult to feel like you're progressing when there's so little to work towards.
Being an always-online game, Siege also comes with it's fair share of minor annoyances that, while mostly unobtrusive, are still worth mentioning. Map rotation could be more consistent. Console players could use more in-game communication tools beyond the temporary marker icon. Matchmaking needs to be just as smooth on PC as it currently is on consoles. Purchasing and equipping new gear shouldn't require players to back out of matches. There needs to be an easier way to kick and report disruptive players.
Everything from the strength of your internet connection to the makeup of your team can impact your enjoyment of Siege, but importantly, Siege itself does everything it can to ensure you're able to enjoy the game in spite of these variables. Across all the hours I spent online, players were consistently cooperative and communicative, and to some degree, I have to credit Siege's tutorials and situations for adequately conveying how the game is meant to be played.

10/10 Best bridge simulator 2015. Would destroy another bridge again and still succeed.
EDIT: An actual Review (As of 7/14/15)
Poly Bridge is one of the best Bridge-building simulators (idk if it's a simulator or not) I've ever played so far. I bought this game in early access and although there's some bugs and whatnot, it's playable from start to finish. The graphics and art style are simple, yet nice. I am a fan of the music. It's so relaxing that I literally slept because of this. The levels, although easy at first, are quite challenging and requires your brain to think further. Pretty much you can build anything! From regular bridges, to ramp jumps or even overly complicated tilting bridges or something like that. Still not fun w/ the existing levels? Try the workshop where over thousands of player-made levels. And finally, the developers of this game are quite responsive to the community fanbase which overall improved the experience of playing this game.
Overall I still gave this game 10/10. Would recommend to friends, family, construction workers, architects, civil engineers, anyone i can think of.

Note : Steam says I have played the game 50+ hours but that's not the case, I am currently closer to 15 to 20 hours, tops.
---------------
As far as bridge building games are concerned, Poly Bridge is just glorious.
It is the same gameplay as in other similar games as the old Bridge It, Bridge Constructor Set and the more recent Bridge Constructors (from the dev ClockStone) :
- you design a bridge with a limited set of money and materials
- then you watch one or several vehicules go accros hoping your bridge will stand
Except that Poly Bridge is superior in most aspects particularly its editor.
You can now use many simple but very usefull tools as
- multiple select of joints/sections !
- copy/paste/delete/flip of the selection !
- move of individual joints !
- trace tool, that allow to easyli create actual arches !
I don't like however that the editor is only 2D, a little perspective is sometimes welcome.
On the graphical side, the low poly, plain colors, "miniature" feels of the game is super nice.
One nice thing too, is to compare oneself with others at the end of each levels + all the options to share a level, save replays and steam workshop.

Is it a good game? -Definitely
Will it teach you how to play guitar/bass? -Yes
What did I like about the game?
-Riff repeater is great for practicing harder parts of songs
-The dynamic diffuculty scales nicely, though sometimes it will be completely unresponsive
-Minigames and session mode are fun, score attack shows just how much the rest of the internet is better than you and always will be
-Tone designer is fun to fiddle with
-Good but somewhat shallow selection of songs (not including DLC)
-They have something for every skill level
What didn't I like about the game?
-The note recognizing is pretty shotty at best, I play using a Epiphone SG and when I play the proper note it will either sometimes or very often give me a miss (It might be a hardware thing)
-ANYTHING TO DO WITH BENDS, the note recognition is attrocious for bends and you need to hit it darn near PERFECTLY for it to register. Very unforgiving
-The dynamic difficulty would sometimes become unresponsive and will stop raising or lowering the difficulty when you need it
-Master mode will hide the notes at the worst possible times
-Riff repeater would sometimes resume the song instead of repeating the specific section
-I never exited the game feeling satisfied, mostly frustrated or feeling like I didn't learn anything new or gotten better
Overall it's a good game and I recommend it wholeheartedly to beginners and amateurs a like, the little problems, while annoying, are rarely game-breaking. Play this on a good computer, this game demands a lot from it.

This might not be the worst RE game in the series, but it's pretty close.    It's like they took a list of everything that fans hated about Capcom games and used that as a design document.
First, the game is like 65% Quicktimed events.   Quicktimed events have to be amongst the most hated console game design tropes ever devised.    The sequences where the player is under direct control are extremely short, linear, and only lead to randomly placed (and longer) periods of scripted sequences, with lots of button mashing.    Only to give the player control again for another random 30 seconds, only to rip that control away again for another scripted, quicktime event.
Then, there's the saves.   They're at the end of the chapters and only at the end of the chapters.    Even the original RE game had typewriters all over the place to let you save the game.     RE6?   They have checkpoints, but that's only a temporary save so if you get killed, you don't repeat the whole chapter.   If you quit before the chapter's end, you will have to replay the whole chapter from the beginning.   I can't blame this on a sloppy port, because even a modern console has memory cards and hard drives.   There's no reason not to include the ability to save whenever you want.
You know how just about every other game (including previous RE games) would pause the game world when you went to the game menu, or at least include a pause option?    There is no pause.     If something crops up in the real world (phone rings, someone at the door, dog needs walking, human needs a bathroom break), you cant pause the game.   I guess they expect you to just play through or quit and restart the chapter later.
Invisible walls.   The game levels are linear, and on the small side, with plenty of invisible walls.    So much for "going back to the series' roots" as was claimed.   They had exploration since the first game, but that's gone too.
Bad controls.  A lot of people complained about the unresponsive controls.   The controls aren't really that bad -- when you actually are in control.   The trouble is, the game tears control away from the player every few minutes and seemingly at random.  You'll then find yourself in a scripted sequence leading to a quicktime event or four, or they'll give you the pointless illusion of control.   There's at least two sequences where you're moving along a corridor and feel like you're in control.   The character stops when you stop pressing a button.   The trouble is, the camera's locked (try to look around and you can only look in a narrow cone, and the camera snaps back), and you can only move forward (press anything and you just move forward).    It may as well be a fully scripted sequence.    Then, as if quicktime sequences aren't bad enough, there's at least 3 places in the game where they suddently change the camera angle and reverse the controls, so that instead of running away from a creature or explosion, you suddenly run INTO it with little margin for error and no warning about the change over.
Then, the game ends with slightly less than 10 minutes of credits -- which you CAN NOT skip without doing a kill-9 on the game (that's where you use the OS to shutdown a rogue program).   To flip the bird at the player one last time, the credits end with 2 minutes staring at a plain Capcom logo in the center of the screen.
They've taken a cue from the Marvel movies and put in a post-credits epilogue sequence, but what they don't get is that what makes those post-credit scenes great is that they're an easter egg for people who CHOOSE to sit through the credits.   You're not given that choice since you can't skip the credits without doing a kill-9 or shutting off the system.
I did like that they brought the setting back to the darkness of RE2.   The graphics are a bit more gritty and the game world objects feel like they belong there rather than something that sticks out and looks green screened in.    The trouble is, once you take out the quicktime events, pseudo interactive sequences, and sequences where the player's not in direct control for long, there's just not much game there, and it's certainly not worth the asking price.
It's embarassing when the handheld companion to this game (RE: Revelations) is more interactive and fun than a game that's supposed to be part of the main series.

I've been a fan o RE since the beginning and unfortunately I can't recommend this game. This would've been fun if it weren't for all the incessant quick time events and chase sequences. The problem is probably with the port, the game is clearly made to be played with a controller. Trying to run with a keyboard during a chase will drive you insane, especially with all the ridiculous fixed camera changes. Seriously, I'm still trying to finish Chris's campaign, that last chase is absurd! And without checkpoints!
Quick time events were the main cause of my deaths. Which is a shame, because when you're going around killing zombies or whatever it get's pretty fun. But before you know it, you're thrust into one those obligatory race, underwater(really?), chase sequences, quick button smashing that all games seem to have nowadays and then everything goes to hell.
The combat gameplay is good, it feels great to be able to take down a zombie with your hands. Every character feels different, the dodging mechanic works (once you get the hang of it) and the weapons, while not the best, definitely doesn't detract from the game.
The story is... fine. Your usual bag of cliches. Although it succeeds in creating a frenetic apocalyptic atmosphere.The characters are great for the most part (though I wish there was a bit more of race and gender diversity). It was nice seeing Leon and Sherry again. But can someone explain to me why the hell does Leon have feelings for Ada? They were together for like, 2 hours, in RE2! Ugh! All his scenes where they mentioned this were groan worthy.
The atmosphere is really where the game succeeds  Especially in Chris and Jake's campaign, the set pieces looked great, from Europe to China, they all had a distinctive feel. Unfortunately, the first half of Leon's was really out of pace. They tried to bring the survival horror aspect back, but it doesn't work anymore, not with the frantic combat style of the game.
Overall I'm disappointed. This game could have been great, but it fails in its execution.
