Friday the 13th is a unique game. I've followed it's progress since the beginning of development when it was just known as Summer Camp. It was made by a group of die-hard fans of the Friday the 13th movie franchise and being a die-hard F13 fan myself, it is easy to see the heart and soul that has been poured into this game. Even if you aren't a fan of Friday the 13th, this horror movie simulator is well worth your time.
The maps are modeled after the environments from the various films and are ridiculously detailed -- to the point where you can even notice the same books on the nightstands or the same plaques on the fireplace mantels. This contributes to a heightened level of immersion and makes you feel like you are actually in the movie.
The different Jasons are modeled in fine detail (you even get to see what's under the masks) and battle music plays for all of the different Jasons from their respective films during battle encounters. Aside from the vast amount of  environmental kills, each Jason even has multiple unique ways of dispatching camp counselors. Every Jason is unique and has stats respective of their film.
Camp counselors are all unique and their attributes reflect that. You have all of your standard horror movie archetypes ranging from the girl next door (who has average stats), the nerd (who is excellent at repairing objectives but not at fighting), the jock (who can run and fight but can't do much else), even the stoner (who can repair, fight, but can't run too long from all the smoking -- haha), just to name a few.
There is a progression system in Friday the 13th. You start off with some basic counselors and Jasons and as you level up, new ones will be unlocked for later player use. Every action you perform as a Jason or as a counselor contributes XP to your profile. As you level up, you can unlock perks to customize your counselor's stats & appearances or unlock kills for your Jasons. This adds lots of replay value to the game.
Gun and Illfonic have done a great job keeping players & fans of the game informed ever since the very beginning of F13's release. They granted front row access to everyone in the development of the game and showcased the different struggles in bringing Friday the 13th to life. They have been active in the forums and constantly been trying to improved the quality of this game.
I must say that in F13's current state, lots of work still needs to be done. The game still contains some demoralizing glitches, whether its getting stuck/frozen while breaking down a cabin door as Jason, or shooting Jason with a shotgun or flare gun as a counselor and receiving credit for it but Jason is still able to blink forward to grab and dispatch you without being stunned from the shot.
There are also some mechanics that need to be corrected to reduce player frustration. There is currently no penalty to players who quit at the beginning of a match when they see they weren't selected to play as Jason - This is frustrating to the player who has played several matches as a counselor and finally gets the opportunity to unleash their inner Jason to find out that there are only 3 players left in a match. A que cool-down for the quitters can easily fix this problem (Like in Dota 2).
Another wasted opportunity is counselor selection. I've played matches as Jason where every single counselor chose play as Vanessa Jones, an athletic character that can sprint and recover her stamina in little time. If you have chosen to play a Jason that can't run and you are against a team of runners, you're going to have a bad time. The fix for that would be to make it so everyone has the chance to choose one unique counselor at the beginning of the match so there are no duplicates, giving a well rounded team and a unique experience (Like in Overwatch).
All of that being said, Friday the 13th is a great game and a very unique experience. You may run into the odd frustration here and there, but the good in this game far outweighs the bad. I have full faith that in due time all of these issues will be addressed. Why you ask? This game has one thing that none of the current games out there have - a driven, passionate design team. Gun and Illfonic, be proud of your accomplishment and please continue to keep up the great work.

To navigate this high-tension environment, players must use skill and craft in order to obtain food, weapons, supplies, and other resources necessary to survive in a desolate and dangerous city.  Players will need to choose whether or not to team up with others or go at it solo against the Nethers, other players, and unpredictable, treacherous world objectives.  In the end, players must decide if they will Prey or Pray.
All in all, Nether is a great time. It’s a highly engaging and realized survival experience; something we need more of.

For many the Resident Evil franchise has seen less and less horror over the last few installments. While some see this as a downfall of a franchise, others like myself see it as an evolution of a franchise.
The Resident Evil series started as a top down horror game. This is where it got its rise to fame. Later down the line, after 3 direct installments and some spin offs, we got the fourth direct installment to the series that changed everything you knew about a Resident Evil games and is now one of the most critically aclaimed games of all time. Resident Evil 4 gave you that 3 person perspective while still keeping the horror aspect. Fast forward to present day and IMO Resident Evil 6 stands as one of the best in the series. While alot of the horror has been taken out, there is still enough to let you know you are playing an RE game. The story can take full credit for the trasformation of the gameplay. You are no longer a lone survivor looking for answers and a way out. You are at war. Bioterrorist seek to take control of all that you know and it is your job to stop this before the entire world becomes what Raccoon City was. You get to play from 4 different perspectives. You get to play as heros from past struggles in the RE series as well as a couple of new comers. After playing through 1 perspective you may seem confused but by the time you have played them all, all loose ends are tied and it feels like one wild ride.
While i may be praiseing the game for almost everything there are still a few set backs. For one, a cover system was poorly implemented into the game. Also some boss fighs seem a little too easy. Other than that the game is a welcome installment into the Resident Evil franchise.
+ Great story
+ Returning cast
+ New cast
+ Third person mechanics
- Poor cover system
- Easy boss fights

This is my first Steam review, so it might be a bit disorganized, and is also a bit lenghty. I apologize for both.
Now honestly, I knew nothing about Lucid9 when I saw it here. I was looking for free games, I saw it, and I downloaded it simply because I had nothing better to do. Visual Novels were a game genre I had never really played much of, and as a result I both didnt know what to expect and didnt expect much, seeing it as "another anime game". I enjoy anime and am a huge hypocrite for saying that, but I digress. Anyway, when I started it up I was initially confused but intrigued, which was enough to draw me in. The characters made me laugh and reminded me of my own friends, and so I began the game thinking it simple, but nothing that could hold me. And then I slowly got more and more engrossed. I met Shigure an actually thought out what I was going to say, I did my best to not cheat on her "test" (besides that horse question, screw that one. Good on you guys though) and I really liked the mystery feel I got from the game. Yama himself was probably what kept me tied, as he reminded me a lot of myself, Sarcastic, believing school to be a waste of time, the "weird kid" with few but close friends. It felt nice to have a character to relate to. Yahiko's optimism and oblivious personality made me laugh, Masato continued to impress and surpise me with, completely betraying the typical "jock" feel I initially got from him. And then it got serious. With the murders, the investigations, this happy game (well, novel) I was once playing (well, reading) turned into a much more serious and thought provoking game, especially when characters like Mr. Ryouta and Airi were involved. Without spoiling it, I went through a LOT of bad ends, looking for my happy ending, before I eventually realized that I wasn't SUPPOSED to get a completely satisfying ending. I repreatedly fought the killer, and a certain someone repeatedly died. It wasn't until I made it past the ordeal that I realized I got my happy ending, just not the way I wanted. And then the ACTUAL ending came, and holy balls. I felt angry, confused, betrayed, wanting more...and I can't wait for the next part of this. Lucid9 impressed me repeatedly with both it's lighthearted moments and the more serious one, its dumb seemingly meaningless questions and phrases a huge part of the plot, the psychological questions and detective games forcing me to think and really immerse myself into this amazing game. Seriously, it might not mean much coming from a guy sitting on his computer, typing on a keyboard, but good on you guys, you have made one of the most unique experiences I've ever,,,experienced (couldnt think of  a better word) in a game (again, well novel). If you're on the fence about buying this game, go for it. Well, its also free, so also nothing to lose...but ignoring that fact, this game will draw you in and really make you think and become attached to its amazing characters and think about its story. Again, sorry about being disorganized and lenghy, but alot to say, might as well say it. Can't wait for the next part guys, this is amazing. To shorten it up: GET THIS GAME/VISUAL NOVEL ITS GREAT.

The general misconception among people is equating low price with low quality. I assure you this far from that, assuming you have the basic cognitive functions I would expect from a chimpanzee. I wouldn't considered myself an expert on VN's but this Visual Novel most definitely has more substance than some of the ones I've played...or is it read?Who cares.
The sprites are exceptional quality and add to the various scenes in here. The characters are unique in their own right, seemingly one dimensional characters abiding by overused stereotypes become diverse characters each with their own quirks and personality. As an aspiring writer I can appreciate the authors tone as well as the imagery choreographed into the intense and immersive dialogue and narrative. And most of all, it gives choice. Of course we will go down the plot but the choices you make allow you to learn about this exciting world brought to life as well as it's characters.
Though my ratings aren't that important it would appeasing to the skim readers out there to see this:
Plot: 10/10
Character sprites: 8/10
Dialogue: 10/10
Character Development: 9/10
Grammar: 10/10 (I have yet to see one mistake)
Audio :10/10(No obnoxious elevator music or static)
Background Music: 10/10(Used effectively to set a certain mood... I got all the OST's on my phone)
Pacing: 10/10( The story doesn't feel rushed in the least and it progresses at a reasonable pace)
Tone: 10/10 ( The character's voice isn't cliche and is rather relaxing in the text. It even feels a bit relatable to be honest)
Choices: 10/10
Character Voice: 10/10 (Each character has a unique way of speaking and thinking and their personalities become prominent within the dialogue.)
Worldbuilding: 10/10 ( Of course it may seem to some that the setting is rather vague but it does so to keep you engaged. The VN tells you what you need to know while leaving you in the dark about a few things. Things which you can learn via the narrative or dialogue,,,and maybe intuition if you actually have the critical thinking skills required to make logical deductions.)
Connection to characters?(Mind you this is a person opinion. I felt fairly connected to each of them. They all had their own unique sides to them. Keep in mind that each of the characters had their own INDIVIDUAL person to create them. It wasn't just one or two goofs who created the whole cast. It was an army of them. Apparently skilled individuals in their own right and it showed in the final product that is Lucid9.)
Am I shamelessly promoting them and do I work for them? Nope, I wish I did, then I'd have something to brag about to my extremely small social circle. Am I promoting them? You're the genius go figure that one out.
One a side note: The person I felt that I would have an easy time hanging out with is Airi. Socially awkward, sure but, she's one hell of a character. Top waifu for sure in my books.
I won't spoil anything so go and enjoy or hate Lucid9. If you have the time to read this whole essay of pretty words and such then you probably have the time to play (or read) Lucid9.

It's not always a bad thing, as the funneling can lead to more intense/concentrated fights where you can't just dart off in any direction when you hurt your knee. And besides, there ARE some pretty open parts where it feels farily open worldish (almost).
The audio and visuals are terricfic - especially the graphics. I played it in DX11 mode on "Extreme" (there's also a "Ultra" setting) as it seemed like a good framerate/eye candy compromise. The blend of scorched city, lush grass/trees and alien tech looks amazing.
The campaign lasted me a little short of 9 hours, which I found appropriate in length, but the story itself is pretty generic alien invasion gibberish with an attempt at a plot twist when someone you thought was your ally was actually plotting against you (oh noes!).
The only really bad thing here is the A.I. Sometimes it's just plain broken. Here are a couple of examples:
I come up on a fight between soldiers and aliens, and decide to let them duke it out, and then kill the hopefully few suvivours. The last 2 NPC's standing is an alien and a soldier, who apparently found friendship while trying to kill eachother and just stood there 2 feet apart facing eachother - doing NOTHING. I put them out of their misery.
Two aliens standing atop a container scouting for enemies (me). The guy nearest me apparently didn't have the keen eyesight of the one behind him, because he just stood there like a statue, while somehow managing to block the path of the alien behind him. Judging by his hyperactive movement he REALLY wanted to run towards me, and climing down the container to either side to circumvent his mime colleague was just not an option. After a giggle I vent into stealth mode and sneaked off.
[SPOILER ALERT]
The final fight with the 4 cloaked super aliens was just a (not funny) joke. They all more or less just got semi stuck in the terrain/invisible wall and figured the best thing to do was to insist on not shooting back, but instead trying to hide by turning on the cloak, which worked 0.02 seconds until my next bullet hit it. Jeez.
[/spoiler alert]
For the most part I really enjoyed the experience though - 80%.

The practice of witchcraft has obviously continued unhindered at Crytek HQ, because Crysis 2 manages to look even better than it's predecessor. However, unlike it's predecessor, Crysis 2 doesn't quite manage to get quite as much right, and not even ridiculously beautiful visuals can patch that up.
Unlike the first Crysis, Crysis 2 sets it's scene in a post-invasion New York City that has been partially infested by the alien Ceph. Players take the role of US Marine, Alcatraz, the only believed survivor of his team. Upon arriving in the city, you soon discover that an alien invasion is upon the planet, and meeting 'Prophet' you quickly set off to put a halt to the invasion equipped with all the wondrous capabilities of the Nanosuit.
Sporting an updated engine, Crysis 2 is a simply beautiful game. While some may disagree, it's quite plain that Crysis 2 is in fact better to look at than the first game, with improved lighting effects, tessellation and rendered models. Light slithers through leaves casting majestic rays to the ground, bricks jut from the walls and shatter on impact while dust kicks up at the vibrations of your firearm. Crytek's second iteration is a spectacular action ride with a phenomenal soundtrack composed by Hans Zimmer himself, and vertigo inducing cityscapes that would put a movie to shame. I don't usually get quite so worked up over something quite so trivial as visuals in a game, but in this instance, you just can't take an achievement such as this lightly. On a different note, the game play has been streamlined from the first game, with the Nanosuit ability interface from Crysis replaced with one that combines strength and speed into a single mode, and binocular and identification vision implemented into the suit, instead of as external tools. Furthermore, a climb and parkour system helps to speed the flow, overall creating a far more slimmed down experience that actually does improve the game in some respects. While some may disagree, I do feel that this far better fits Crysis as whole.
Thanks to the improved engine, Crysis 2 was able to run on last generation's consoles, but because of this the game doesn't quite look as good as it could have been, and does suffer from some limitations that could possibly have been avoided had the game been designed as a PC exclusive like the first game. Environments, while aesthetically pleasing and atmospherically different, are far more linear than in the previous game, which does cause the game to become boring after a while, as we are constantly spoon-fed the next section with little room to breathe. While the sound effects are still of top notch tier, the actual selection of weapons available is in fact far smaller than in the first game, meaning that you feel like less of an overly-equipped bad♥♥♥♥♥ something I'm sure we can agree isn't exactly a selling factor. In addition, while the story does well to justify your marine/ alien kill spree, it simply isn't quite as gripping as the first game, with explosions and falling buildings seeming to happen *just-cus*, eventually numbing you to the action.
The multiplayer is still present, moving from an open Battle-Field-like approach and to one that more resembles Call of Duty. Again, the excellent graphics do wonders to patch up some of the game's more minor flaws, but unlike the previous game, they don't do enough to hide some of the more jarring facts. It would appear that Crytek substituted innovation for convenience in the production of the game play mechanics themselves, and because of that we have received a game that feels like it could have been so much more had the team not been hindered by limitations of the console scene...
+ Yet again phenomenal graphical fidelity
+ Streamlined game engine
- Linear world
- Numbing plot that doesn't quite match Crysis'
7.5/10 ~ Good

Slender: The Arrival is the official expanded version of Slender: The Eight Pages. It meant to have a story behind why the Slender Man is after you, and a few others. What do I think of this game you may ask? Well, this review will cover that.
First off, I will start with the setting and character's. The game take's place in an unspecified state of America. Most of it take's place in park with a radio tower and a mine complex. Now on to the character's. The game's protagonist is Lauren, a woman looking for her missing friend named Kate, who has recently disappeared. A man only known as CR can be read about in the in-game collectibles.He apeared to be somehow involved with Kate and the Slender Man, whom does not need an introduction.
The next thing I want to cover is the overall gameplay. I think it is both good and bad. I will start the good. The atmosphere is probably the best part of the the game. It gave me an unsettling feeling throughout the game. Another great thing about The Arrival is the genuinely creepy music. It gets more and more tense as you complete the objectives. And also, not being able to fight back can also keep some people on edge.
Now for the bad. Unfortunately, there are more bad aspects than you might be thinking. Let's start with the objectives. Pretty much every level involves somehow interacting with a certain amount of objects. It does'nt take very long for the game to start feeling quite repetitive. While a recent update added two new levels to branch off from this, those two levels are'nt very good and may leave quite a bit of gamers feel pretty unsatisfied after completing them. Another thing I will cover is the overall scares. They start out great, but lose their charm less than halfway through the game. The Slendern Man himself begins to dwindle as the as the game progresses. While he seems terrifying at first, he later starts to become less and less scary to the point that you can easily walk past him and not have even the slightest sense of fear. The two new enemies added also begin to have this effect. The hooded person at first seems pretty scary, but it's cheap jump scare attack becomes pretty un-scary and rather just annoying and cheaply animated. The skeletal figure is also pretty unsettling, but soon just apears to be a generic horror cliche. Another thing is the game's incredibly short length. The game can easily be finished in less than two hours, incuding the bonus level.
The Verdict
Slender: The Arrival simply feels rushed. The music and atmosphere are great, but the repetitive gameplay, cheap scare's, and extremely short length just ruins the experience. If you want a cheap and short horror game, buy Slender: The Arrival. If you want quality scares and fun gameplay, look elswhere.

Sparkle ZERO is from the same series as Sparkle, Sparkle 2 and Sparkle 3 are from. It is a simulation game whereby you start off as a small organism and try to become the biggest of them all. Although this game in the series, it does seem a bit out of place compared to the other Sparkle games in the series.
With the game being from the Sparkle series there are some standards that have been set from the previous games that you would expect to be in this game or be better than the previous ones. The game is fun to play, to a certain extent. Playing for about 2 hours I found myself getting fairly bored of just eating other smaller organisms and getting bigger to eat more. It was a endless cycle of trying to be the best of them all. For me this was not a decent enough goal set to keep my entertained enough to motivate me enough to play the game more.
I feel like in my own personal opinion that the game doesn't cover enough mechanics to keep a player interested enough to go back and play the game more. There is little, or no replay value of this game because of just how boring the game is the first time you play through it.
Something good about this game though, is the graphics and some of the sounds that were produced as you play through and grow your organism. The sounds are rather quite nice, with a sort of ambient feel to it which really sets the tone for what this game is, it makes you immersed into the game and pulls you in with the sounds as well as the graphics. The graphics of the game also set the tone for the game and really fits the game well, as the previous Sparkle games have done.
+ The game is fun to play for a hour or so
+ Full controller support
+ Beautiful ambient sounds
+ Nice graphics
+ Steam achievements and Trading cards
- Game gets boring after playing it for over 2 hours
- The game doesn't set a decent goal to want me to go back and play it more
- Doesn't feel like it belongs in the series of the other Sparkle games
- The asking price isn't worth the game
- Little or no replay value
The game for me is split in half, on one hand my first experience of this game was fun. The first hour or so of the gameplay was enjoyable to play, the graphics are really nice as are the ambient sounds. But then again, now that I look back at the  gameplay I feel like it wasn't really worth it. I will definitely not be going back to play more of this game. Final verdict, don't buy this game, waste of your time and your moneys worth.

Lucid9, where to start with this gem?
I really don't know what I was expecting when I installed this game. But what I recieved was more then I've expected.
Honestly after playing this game, like most other people, I agree that I would have payed for this game. The fact that a game that so thought out and hard worked on is free, honestly leaves me slightly upset. In fact I would've rather spent $60 on this game then any other game I've ever bought in my 12 years of gaming, regardless of the fact that it is 'only' a visual novel.
But more about the game:
The first thing that comes to mind is how masterfully fluid the game felt. The first bit everthing was a blur, not paying much attention to the subtle things that all came back when it mattered. But as I played longer and felt myself getting more immersed, it was hard not to remember everthing. I realized everything I did, learned and 'saw' was more important then I possibly could have imagined. But in the end I feel like I did more than play a game.
For Example, meeting multipe indepth characters that not only I could relate to, but could empathize with. I not only meet and felt for these charaters but came to care for them, which is rare to find in games now-a-adays. Just throwing people into a game and telling some background on them doesn't mean there's a connection. How quickly the characters in this game got to me was amazing.
I also personally love the music. The way every scene has a specific piece and how it set the mood for who's talking or what's about to happen. There isn't much else to say about it other that.
But to sum up the game, it's one I won't be forgetting, in a good way. I haven't played my other visual novels but I feel it was that opened me up more to the catagory. And I have this game to thank for the many, many more VNs I see myself playing in the future.

The main character and some of his friends are initially quite hard to like, but you do warm up to them some, after a while.
As far as EVNs go, the writing is definitely a cut above average, with few errors (not none, but there's a lot of wordage), and the mystery is well-developed, and handled competently.
The climax is something of a tricky labyrinth of bad-ends, with little signposting - though the bad ends themselves sometimes give some clues. I feel that area could have been done a bit better, and the hard-to-thread web of choices during it does suck some of the immediacy out of the climax.
Content includes some pretty horrifying material, at times - which is further thrown into contrast by the lighter, more everyday scenes. That contrast serves to increase the impact. If you've a sensitive disposition, you should take care to pace yourself some.
While this is a first part, and not a whole, story progression is solid. Think of it as the first season of a TV series. Arcs are started and completed, but there's still more to carry on with at the end.
All in all, though, an excellent effort that should keep you going for a dozen hours, at minimum.

This is surely god's gift to guitartists..a game that has changed me from a 10 year part time guitar player of mediocre capability to someone who is starting to master some tricky lead licks from bands like Blind Melon, Alice in Chains and Metallica. I have never felt so comfortable with my instrument and it's been only 1 year. If you are on the fence you NEED to buy this game, like now! Just make sure you have a Rocksmith cable. I'd like to address a few criticisms which are not valid about this game.
1. It does teach technique. It has a video library which covers most of the basic and some advanced guitar techniques..and includes play along songs to practice. It is no substute for a teacher, or a self critical approach to your instrument. Those who are disciplined and take the time to use riff repeater and the technique games properly will develop great skills with this game. It has helped me learn the fretboard, I can almost play anything now without looking at the guitar neck, instead I'm reading the note track. I never got to that point with years of Guitar Pro or Tabs.
2. You can do a songlist. There IS a free play mode where you pick whatever songs you want to play and it will put them back to back..there is even an achievement for doing this.
3. Bends are not broken. The main problem with bends is that you are either not starting on the correct note pitch (premature bending) or not pushing the bend far enough (arrows indicate how many notes up you need to bend to). Ensure your guitar is properly tuned and do some slow bends to get up to speed. I was failing most bends, until I learnt I was bending prematurely and once I losened and relaxed my bend start point I became a better player. When you bend right you will see the game highlight the note track as you reach the right spot. If it doesn't highight you are probably starting from the wrong note. It is so effective I have learnt how to play complex bends using it.
4. The difficulty is not broken. Learning how to use the Riff Repeater is essential. I use an xbox 360 pad as it's fast to navigate, but learn the keyboard keys for it. You can select parts of a song, adjust the difficulty and speed and also set how many times you need to play it perfectly before increasing speed/difficulty. This is the secret of this game, building up your speed slowly through repetition of each section is the best way to learn a song. As soon as you start struggling in a song..open riff repeater..
5. Latency is a fixable problem. Out of the box with a decent PC there are no issues with latency for the average guitarist. If you use a USB soundcard it may be more of an issue (especially it it's crap), I am using a FIIO E07K and have reduced the latency using the Rocksmith.ini file. Sometimes it crackles, but alt-tabbing out and back in fixes it. I also use Process Lasso to reduce other system load. The Ubisoft forums have a long guide to reducing latency if it is a concern for you.
But really, when it all comes together and you nail that solo you have been working on..just an amazing feeling I love this game!

I got this game in the summer sale after a recommendation from a friend.  I was not dissapointed.
Though I haven't completed the game yet, I can give my thoughts so far.
The way the story and feelings of the characters are conveyed through simple narration (which, incidentally, is excellent) is masterful, so much so that I found myself caring about coloured squares and rectangles.
On top of that, the game's art style gives it an unmatched charm that is felt for every second played.  The art style is also incredibly simple and minimalistic, yet enticing at the same time.
The soundtrack is beautiful as well.
I was so charmed by this game that when I came across a particularly fiendish platforming section and dies quite a few time, I felt genuinely bad for getting angry at the game and the character who had to make the jumps.
Oh yeah, and the actual game mechanics and gameplay are terrific too.  As of yet, I have only found one problem with this game, and it isn't even major: when a character is jumping in a direction you are holding, when you let go of the key, they stop dead in the air and drop.  This hasn't caused much trouble and could be helpful with precision platforming, but I just found it a little hard to get used to at first, because I'm used to a little momentum.
Overall: 9/10.
I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone.  This game strips everything back to basics and says "This is all you need."

How can I be so emotionally invested in those simple geometric shapes? That is what I've been asking myself again and again as I played Thomas Was Alone. I love my characters with personalities, especially how they move and how they react to the environment. Can a simple rectangle express enough emotion to make me care for it?
Surprisingly, quite enough. As do all the other characters in the game. A big part of that emotion comes from the smart voice-over, fleshing out a plot and character connections that would simply be lost without it. But the other crucial element, and the reason TWA is so effective, is contextual meaning from which it achieves a suspenseful buildup towards a metaphysical resolution.
Scratch that, I'm making the game sound way more pompous than it really is. This is a smart puzzle platformer with great art direction (your eyes will love the contrasts created by light, shadows and colors). It's not taxing, it's actually very relaxing and you'll just want to know what happens next. And you will care for the fates of these little simple shapes. Because we are not solely defined by how we look like, but rather by what we do.
Or something like that. And to be honest, I've written this review to get the Pillar of Community badge. Still, please play this game, it's amazing.

After reading so many comments in the forums and a very helpful and friendly message from the dev himself i want to write a review about this game.
-----------------------------------------------------
Destination sol - what is it?
Destination sol pretty much is a 2D game with a tiny progression system but very small amount of content. I've played it for 2 hours if i'm not mistaken and to be honest, you can't really write a review about this game because there isn't really anything you can give constructive feedback about.
Destination sol - What did i expect?
My expectations were simple: A game that you can play for 10, maybe 20 hours and some replay factor. I actually expected a game which comes with a various amount of content, planet landing was one part of it... well, that's it. You fly around, shot at everything, get stopped by pesky asteroids, you are busy farming a little bit, get the best equipment, kill everything unless you forgot how to fly... That's really it, you don't do more here. No story, no more systems...
Destination sol - Why would you dislike a free game?
This was actually a question i got asked from various players of this game, and the answer is as simple as true. I've played a lot of free games actually besides of MMO(RPG), Star Sword, Star Raid and Star defender 4... all 3 games are great games, star raid is even full 3D, maybe a bit hard to understand but free... I played 20 hours of star raid, 3 days i actually had a game that i could play while destination sol only filled 10% of that.
Yes, i dislike a free game because it lacks on useful content... "planet landing", great, you sit on a planet, search for the shop, look at it's offers, possibly buy a new weapon and done. maybe killing 2 enemies to get a "rare" weapon and that's it. No story missions as mentioned already, not even any missions, lack on enemies, lack on weapons... not even background music. I used the background music of galactic arms race because it fitted most.
Destination sol - Recommend?
No. You can find way better games by simply using google, there are many gaming sites offering some simple flash games which offer way more stuff, Enigmata: Stellar war is one great example.

I was immensely hopeful for this game, as watching the gameplay in the trailer made me think it was exactly what I was looking for. I loved the open sandbox concept and roguelike mechanics, but I'm afraid what ruined it for me was the controls. I guess I never cared much for the Asteroids feel of only being able to accelerate, and then slow down by accelerating in the opposite direction. I felt like a blind man on ice most of the time trying to cruise about. The system does work extremely well when you are battling other ships in the outer atmospheres of planets and close to the other ship's speed. Surprisingly well. But I found the system to be pretty clunky in outer space or when too close to the surface of a planet. In the latter environment, I feel something that would have helped a great deal would have been manual control of the zoom, as the camera often got too close for me be able to navigate the terrain effectively.
But hell, the game is free. If the concept grabs you the way it did me, there's really no reason not to give it a shot. If you can get into Asteroids-style controls, then you'll probably have a blast playing it. I did enjoy most of the game's design (weapons, charges for special ship abilities, switching to different ships, recruiting other ships to join you). It reminded me a lot of the cellular and interstellar phases of Spore. If the control system were more to my liking I'd probably sink many an hour into it.

Did you enjoy that school project where you build a bridge out of popsicle sticks?
Does being an engineer or architect sound appealing to you?
Like solving problems with logic and creativity?
You know the drill, if you answered yes to any of these, this game may very well be for you.
To briefly summarize the gameplay, in each level you have one or more automobiles that must be transported across a gap. You do this by building a bridge. Some of the materials at your disposal are wood, asphalt, steel beams, rope, and hydraulics. You can build draw bridges, suspension bridges, arch bridges, etc. As you progress, the challenges get more difficult. As an example, in one level a car will drive over the bridge, then a ship will travel underneath, and finally a heavier, longer car will travel over the bridge. Here, you must take into consideration the size of the ship when selecting a height for your bridge. Also to be considered is the length of the second car, which may hinder its ability to get up a steep incline. Some sort of draw bridge may be the best option here, which can be very fun and challenging to build.
In my experience so far, each new level brings a new challenge which keeps everything fresh and interesting. It's a game that makes you think in a very fun and relaxing way which is something I value. It's got great graphics and a really cool looking art style. The soundtrack is all wonderfully relaxing acoustic guitar from an artist named Adrien Talens, very Jack Johnson-esque, but purely instramental.  All of this combined with a fairly polished presentation and a decent amount of content make this a recommendation for me.

The main character and some of his friends are initially quite hard to like, but you do warm up to them some, after a while.
As far as EVNs go, the writing is definitely a cut above average, with few errors (not none, but there's a lot of wordage), and the mystery is well-developed, and handled competently.
The climax is something of a tricky labyrinth of bad-ends, with little signposting - though the bad ends themselves sometimes give some clues. I feel that area could have been done a bit better, and the hard-to-thread web of choices during it does suck some of the immediacy out of the climax.
Content includes some pretty horrifying material, at times - which is further thrown into contrast by the lighter, more everyday scenes. That contrast serves to increase the impact. If you've a sensitive disposition, you should take care to pace yourself some.

It’s taken me a while to mull over why I love Jazzpunk, but I think I have a single line that best describes my experience:
Jazzpunk provides me a nostalgia for a past that had never happened.
The game itself is very quick if you just hit all the triggers, but getting to explore the world inside the game is a wild and silly combination of 50’s Spy thriller, parodies of known games in the past lexicon, and the touch of something that I can only describe ”The Naked Gun: Even more Surreal than usual”.  It’s as if everything that happens in this world exists for a reason, but not for the one you think it does.  This alone is why the experience was so amazing, you never knew what to expect once you accepted that weird things was going to happen.
Beyond that, the experience of the game reminded me so much of playing older games Like King’s Quest and Day of the Tentacle.  Jazzpunk is best played as a First Person Point and Click adventure, and as such, there was so many hidden secrets to find.  From weird and enjoyable convo trees to interactions with the world that were unexpected.  By the time I reached the Hotel, I made sure to explore every single room in hopes to find another morsel of content that was stashed away from the “non-believers”. (Much like how secrets were hidden in games like Dark Forces).
Jazzpunk is not going to be for everyone, and your mileage may vary.  If you have time to just explore and experience though, I highly recommend this game to anyone that needs a fun and casual break.

I reviewed Sparkle 2 and Sparkle 3, so I may as well review Sparkle, um, 0.  I'm not sure if this is meant as a reboot or maybe a tribute to Ringu, but for whatever reason, the new Sparkle game has a lower number.  Pedantic musings aside, I really liked Sparkle 2, and reviewed it as the best jellyfish eating simulator available.  The Sparkle games have held that title since Pac-Man, even though when asked if the creatures in Pac-Man were jellyfish, Toru Iwatani replied “I’m surprised that you made the reference to a jellyfish. The assumption must be from the transparency in their design and also their characteristics.”  You notice that he did not deny that the enemies in Pac-Man were jellyfish, so I'll just stick with that theory.
Anyhoo, Sparkle 0.  The game is lovely.  Sparkle games always are.  This time around I get a sort of cyberspace cyberpunk cyberjellyfisheating vibe from the graphics.  It's you against the world, and you gotta bag and tag em chummer.  Sorry.  All that cyber talk brought out the Shadowrun in me.  Yeah, remember when Shadowrun was cool?  Hmm, maybe it never was, but I liked it.  I used to read the books, back when books were a thing.
So, what was I saying?  Right!  Sparkle!  Back on track!  My reviews have been gettings so narrow that maybe like three people will even get the references.  I'm starting to feel like Dennis Miller.  So it goes.
So the graphics are nice, as always.  The gameplay is more like Sparkle 2, very chill, no real danger, just eat jellyfish and pretty much any other creature you meet, with the ultimate goal of evolving your creature to become more bigger and such.  This process has been stripped down to the point that there are no longer evolutionary trees, and you just eat and grow without having any input, as if you were Marlon Brando in Apocalypse Now.  This may be a pretty big step backward in the series, but at least you don't have the spikey tunnels that plagued Sparkle 3.
Overall, I still suggest Sparle 2 Evo as the best in the series, and I hope they return to the variety that game had to offer, but Sparkle 0 is still a good game.  Just a bit less so than fans of the series might have hoped.

Anyone being used to Sparkle knows that you need to eat nutriments so that your little sparkle can grow into a powerful organism that can be herbivore, carnivore or omnivore. So, you were used to the green, blue or red elements floating, with medusaes to eat or any other species wanting to challenge you. Besides, some levels were huge as you needed to use vortex to reach another level.
That's Sparkle 2 Evo and Sparkle 3 Genesis.
Erase everything you've learned because Sparkle ZERO, despite belonging to the same series, just wants you to grow a sparkle, without any tutorial and learning about the commands, that will be the predator of everyone. No more carnivore, herbivore or omnivore, no more faster sparkle or with a better range of absorption or with a better defense. However, everything else is still there: micro-elements that will grow your sparkle, jellyfishes still floating, other species still there to annoy you (bumpers that will send you far away of your food, parasites stealing it, etc.) and vortex to use if you want to evolve.
You don't have missions anymore, you're just eating, growing in a deep blue sea, with white stuff all around. You still have that sixth sense that will guide you to the nutriments but now, your little one can also sense vortex or enemies and show the way to them, which is good because as usual, the minimap on your right corner isn't really clear. I've seen it because I recognize the symbol for a vortex. Now, on the map, you can also see species wandering around.
I don't know how many layers exist because I finished the game before checking if I was at the end or not. I largerly preferred the ancient system of levels and missions, mainly because you can come back to them and keep growing in beautiful landscapes.
I finished the game in 95 minutes, where the others took me more time to do it. I was kinda disappointed that I couldn't control anymore the evolution of my little sparkle thanks to the DNA manipulation and that I couldn't see my level, so that I didn't know if I was nearing level 50 or not. I managed to reach it quickly because I've cleaned every floor - in other words, I've eaten all elements presents and defeated every enemy.
Sparkle ZERO has still a relaxing soundtrack, at least, the new developers didn't remove that good feature.
I was under the impression that Sparkle ZERO was in reality the first game in the series, if I didn't check before if it was the case. Apparenlty, it's not. For me, it's a huge step behind compared to Genesis and Evo and for the new player, without any indication about the commands, it will seem impossible to use a vortex. I only managed to do it because I remembered more or less how it was for the other games.
So, should I recommend it or not? I must say that the game is avoiding a thumb down because I still enjoyed the challenge, despite all the missing features that I liked. But if you want to try one of the Sparkle game, I would point you to Evo and Genesis.

I found Destination Sol while searching for quality 100% free games on Steam. It doesn't have any sort of mission or objective system, so people that need direction to their games might not enjoy it in its current state, but it works very nicely as a sandbox space RPG where you explore the different systems and worlds to find increasingly difficult enemies and higher tier equipment.
There's two ways you can progress. The first is earning money for the shops by destroying enemies or asteroids and picking up cash, and the second is looting weapons and supplies from enemies and either selling or using them. This naturally encourages you to fight more powerful enemies to progress faster, and you can upgrade very quickly this way. You can also gain loot from destroyed allies if you want to scavenge for it, but there's no option to intentionally attack allies as a pirate. There's a pretty sizeable number of playstyles between all of the different weapon types and the different ship abilities and weapon mounts (light auto-targeting and heavy fixed weapons).
A few things I'd fault DS for, there's a lack of player friendliness in some of the mechanics. You drop some weapons and cash when destroyed but aren't given much indication of what you'll drop or why, and respawning also costs you currency. You have to pay to change ships even if you've owned the ship previously, and cannot sell or trade-in your own ship. All but two weapons (blaster and heavy blaster) require some form of priced ammunition, and of those two infinite ammo weapons, the heavy weapon varient only seems accessible by killing and looting a ship carrying it. That means no infinite firing heavy weapon early on. Light weapons can only be used on light weapon slots and heavy weapons only on heavy slots, and only a couple ships carry both types.
Basically, your only two ways to gain money or supplies require a weapon and it's entirely possible to get stuck in a ship with no weapons or ammo and no way to find more, which would force a restart. You can actually damage armor directly and destroy things by ramming them, but this also damages your own ship, and the only way to repair armor damage is with bought repair items. It's especially possible for this issue to happen early game when you don't have much cash to begin with, so I'd recommend first upgrading to a ship with two light weapon slots and grabbing two blasters as a good safe starter setup, and it's a good idea to always keep a few hundred in cash on reserve when shopping.
Some other small gripes and feedback:
· The collision alert system has too low of a range for comfortably maneuvering at full speed, and an option to upgrade the map with detailed proximity asteroid and minor enemy locations would be nice, as would some kind of scanner minimap.
· The presentation is a little rough around the edges. I like the graphic assets a lot, but the menu buttons could use a little styling, and soundtrack implementation would really help tie the experience together.
· I think only forward thrust was a deliberate design choice, but I believe it'd improve planet maneuvering greatly if there were weaker RCS thrusters for sideways and backwards movement too. You could make them stronger on small ships and weaker on large ships to improve the ship variety and further increase playstyle choices.
· AI flying actually seemed really good, but mercenaries had issues with crashing trying to follow you and would occasionally steal your loot.
· As for the expensive/depleted ammo issue, it could be interesting to have another free ammunition weapon type that relied on scrap pickups as ammo rather than being infinite firing.
Overall, this game was a fun few hours. It has more complexity and attention to detail than most free flash games of comparable style I've tried, and it'd be great to see this game grow and develop. It's free, it's open source, and it's a fairly small download, so why not try it out?

Not a bad game, but in general there's not much to do. No quests, nothing that interesting in the universe besides all the asteroids. The controls are a little basic, not ability to strafe or move backward. Also, on my first time playing the game, I managed to get myself into a situation where I had a bigger ship, but nothing to attack with, and I was unable to sell off enough items to buy a big enough gun for the ship.
1. I purchased the 400 token ship, leaving me with 13 tokens, not realizing that the ship <required> a bigger gun to even operate. The small blaster couldn't even be used.
2. I didn't have enough money to switch back to my old ship (an odd notion - you'd think that after I bought my old ship I wouldn't have to pay to get it back).
3. Also, when you buy a ship, there's still an option to buy the EXACT SAME SHIP. This is very confusing for a first time player, as I thought the first ship on the list would obviously be some kind of upgrade. I was wrong, and without warning lost 200 tokens for an item I already had. You get no tokens for "selling" your ship, you just pay to switch.
4. The pirates are boring. The ones that are just stuck around in the system don't even move, they just shoot at you. You can basically sit around and blast them, and no matter how many times they directly hit you, as long as you don't miss, you'll win and won't have to use a repair pack. If you get a better shield, you can basically just sit around farming.
5. I expected more from the promise of "open world" than just no loading screens. There's not much to an open world that just consists of three or four planets, two stars, and "mazes".
6. There's no contiunation value. Once you clear out all the pirates and get the best ship and guns and such, there's nothing left to do.
7. All the information tabs are unclear and confusing to someone new at the game.

Anyway, there's something for everyone in this VN, especially for those who are fans of other VNs, manga, anime, and the like. With the variety of romance routes, cute girls (and boys), self-referential humour, satire, and lots of tearjerking kmoments, I guarantee something will get to you. The music and art is pretty neat, too, and the assets are arranged in a way that definitely maximises the writing's impact.

outdated/clunky menus. Lucid9's everything is so clean and minimal, and I can't thank the devs enough for that, hahaha.

I already knew how to play guitar and bass when I bought this game. I grabbed it while it was on sale mostly because I was curious. I already had the rocksmith tone cable because a friend gave me an extra when I told him I was getting it since he had recommened it. The game is fun and entertaining. The exercise games make warm ups and fretboard familiarity more engaging and not seem so tedious. Playing the songs is fun and takes you at a slow pace to learn the song in the proper key and tuning. Once you've played the song well enough times the visual keys vanish and you are required to play based on memory. I guess the theory is that you learn through repeating. It's not hard but not my favorite way to learn a song. I prefer to actually read the music. But I understand not everyone wants to or can read music and this is a nice middle ground. I noticed no improvements in my playing but have been playing in live bands for years prior to purchase. This is a fun break from playing the usual stuff and allows me to venture out of my musical comfort zone when practicing alone which is a fun change of pace. As a learning tool I'm sure it is very helpful to new and intermediate players. To advanced players this is just a fun escape from your usual routine, and maybe you'll pick up a few new warm up exercises like I did. Overall worth the price I paid and would purchase another Rocksmith title if one is released in the future.

Two thumbs way up! I've seen all the testimonials and 60 day challenges on youtube like most others and I bought the game expecting somewhat of a let down from the videos. I mean, it couldn't be that good could it be? Well, yes and no. I have the game since about xmas and I have logged about 90hrs or so on it. And yes, I have gotten much much better. Pour Some Sugar on me, Satifacation and a few others I am almost playing the entire song already. Notes and chords I looked at in confusion the first week are common place and fairly easy for me now. I had no idea at all how to play anything on the gutar when I started and now I have a clue. I almost exclusivly only do the "learn a song" part of the game so if I were to actually use the other learning parts of it I am sure I would be better than I am.
Some things I am not in love with are
1. Sometimes on some songs you have it mastered to the percentage of the song it lets you play but it just dosn't seem to open up more notes on the song for a long time.
2. Too many songs have LONG periods of no notes to play while you are at the begining stages of the song. There is no need to go 5-15 seconds waiting for your next note. But once you "level up"the song that is corrected.
3. I would prefer if the songs played on normal speed from the first time you play it instead of often starting at a slower speed until you "level"it up. I find I actually play the song better when I don't have time to think about what note to hit. Also, if you play new songs and it plays at the slower speed, it sort of messes you up for a bit for the songs that are playing on the normal speed when you play them. You get use to the slow speed and now have to readjust to the normal speed.
4. My biggest peeve. WTF is up with the tuner? If you play almost ANY song thats not played in the "E" key, it is near impossible to get the top two strings in the first 3 or so frets in tune. Oh, the game says they are but when you go to play the song I am clearly hitting the right notes but the game keeps saying I missed them. Often I have to move a whole fret down to make the note register. That is a royal pain when you are trying to learn a song because you don't know at first if you are missing the note or if the guitar isn't tuned. Then you have to remeber to mpve your hand down a fret lower than is called for each time to hit the note. :( And no amount of tuning will get it to work right. You basically just have to compensate when you play a note.
Finally, there is NO WAY I could play any song without seeing the notes coming down on the screen as I play. So, You would need something else to actually learn how to play the guitar in a real setting. But having said that, I clearly can now somewhat play the guitar and actual songs. I usually play 2 hours at a clip and the time just flys by.

When you are in the last throes of your life, and your body is riddled with cancer, you lay there in bed contemplating all of the things you have ever done in life. All of the wrong doings you regret, all of the relationships you never got to form. Just waiting  for the abyss to take you into nothingness, and the only thing that slips into your mind before you fade away is, why on earth did I let Capcom swindle me out of twelve dollars during the steam sale of 2013 for Resident Evil Six.

Controls infinitely better than its console iterations. The game definitely isn't without its flaws but there are so many gameplay mechanics here that are unique to RE6 that can't really be found elsewhere at the moment. The best parts about the game aren't immediately evident and take some digging, but they are there for people who are willing to give the game a real chance, along with some patience.
If you can look past the fact that this is an action game and not a horror game, then it'll probably be a lot more enjoyable. The controls do have some nuances to learn, and there are mechanics that the game doesn't tell you about, so it's good to learn about those to fully enjoy the gameplay. Also, the game spans across 4 full-length campaigns and is easily at least ~30+ hours, of gameplay, not including the extra content such as Mercenaries (which is the best iteration of RE4-era Mercenaries yet, thanks to the gameplay) or the online versus modes.
The story feels like one of those animated Resident Evil movies like Degeneration, it gets pretty involved at times. If you're easily bothered by corny writing, then prepare because there's a lot of lines that feel like they could be written better. It tends to be the mid-gameplay banter that pushes the corniness and ridiculous one-liners though, with the cutscenes generally being pretty enjoyable. Leon's campaign feels pretty confused all the way through though, with Chris', Jake, and Ada's campaigns having a more compelling story and satisfying ending. Contrary to what people might think before buying the game, Leon's campaign is more than likely the weakest story of all of them.
There are even sections in the story where your story as Leon/Helena will cross paths with Jake/Sherry, and will actually search for other people at that section of the game to make an up to 4 player coop session spanning two different campaigns. It's a shame that this feature doesn't get used much (if at all) since the number of players actually playing campaign at this point isn't the greatest. That, and they're such specific points in the campaign that it's unlikely to cross paths with someone else at that same section of the different characters' stories.
The most fun I've had with the game is with the co-op and overall gun/melee-play. It's so dynamic once you get the swing of things and really offers gameplay that isn't found in a lot of other places. The revamped combat system they made for RE6 is incredible and makes for extremely fluid combat with the right mastery over the controls. Being able to dive roll in any direction, melee at any given time, and loads of ways to dispatch the infected make the game super satisfying- but again- only if you're willing to take the time and learn all the controls (including the ones they don't tell you).
Different characters in both the story and the extra content modes do have different unique traits and equipment to each of them. Some of which put a twist on the game or just suit different tastes better, and it's worth looking up. Especially if you're playing as Jake.
If you know you're dead set on probably hating it, or that you probably won't like it even if you play with a friend and get the hang of the controls- you're better off not buying. And don't come for a super-serious story, and just kind of try to enjoy it almost like a kind-of-bad-but-likeable B action movie, because that's kind of what RE6 is.
P.S. Ada's campaign was originally intended to be a singleplayer-only campaign, but co-op was added some time after release due to popular demand. It's kind of ridiculous how people complain that co-op for Ada's story feels shoehorned in, because it really was- but only because people wanted it when it was never intended. Lucky that it was done at all.
P.P.S. Don't use the cover mechanics. Just don't bother, as you'll often fight with the controls. Unless you're in Chris' campaign on Professional and you know what you're doing, though.

Underrated, unfairly tarred game with lots of value
If you're a Resident Evil purist, look away immediately. This RE is not a survival horror game in the slightest; you'll be better off seeking such thrills in the throwback Resident Evil: Revelations rather than the action movie-themed 6.
There are a number of drawbacks marring this game. The story is a bit convoluted, spread out non-chronologically among four different intersecting campaigns. The narrative itself isn't anything to phone home about, adhering largely to cheesy action movie tropes. The textures and environments are a step-down from the stunning RE5. And the gameplay, which is a departure from 4 and 5's more straightforward "shooting gallery" mechanics, seems a bit unwieldy and clunky at first.
Once you get the hang of the mechanics, though, RE6 turns out to be a surprising bit of cooperative fun. Unlike previous games in the series, 6 is a melee combo shooter hybrid. In most cases, you're encouraged -- though none of this is properly taught to you via in-game tutorials -- to quickshot stun enemies, then run up to them and combo them with your character-specific melee moves. Doing so proficiently provides an unusual flow to the action somewhat reminiscent of the Arkham Asylum series and conserves precious ammo.
The four campaigns, while somewhat disjointed, provide an immense amount of value. You'll easily clock 20+ hours to beat them all; I personally logged over 30. Such game length, and value, is pretty much unheard of in the action game genre.
Those looking for a solidly entertaining action game, particularly in conjunction with a buddy, can't go wrong with RE6, particularly if they can pick it up at a budget price. Survival horror fans should look elsewhere, however.

This is a real improvement from the first Slender game. The first Slender game was very scary. But the objective is just to collect the 8 pages, survive with out Slender ripping your face off and congratulations, you have successfully beaten Slender. But this game brings it to a whole new level.
You start off as some kind of adventurer, seeking in the woods just like normal people would do. But you come across things that you've never seen before like this house and of course the old fashion 8 Pages. And some tall guy with no face chasing you down of course. You get the 8/8 Pages easier on this Slender because there is just so much more to it. You then travel a bit more and then their he is. Not Slender, but some other kid that you have to blink the torch with in order for him to go away. Instead of getting 8/8 pages. You need to turn on the things with out the little kid trying to brake your legs.
But I won't ruin the rest of the game or the ending for you. But there is much more to this game then meets the eye. If you're into scary games and trying to figure out the storyline of a game at the same time. Then this game is for you.

The game remains very true to the youtube series such as Darkharvest00, EMH, marblehornets etc, which I love, as I am a huge fan of the slendy series. The settings are all very similar, and the camera overlay was a nice touch.
It has a good atmosphere, with creepy sound cues and lighting. This could have been improved with more buildup of tension as seen in amnesia and in the slender vlogs, where you anticipate that something will happen around every corner. Still, the environments are well designed, and the graphics are very good, including shadows, hdr and a nice touch of colour distortion from slendy at various points in the game. The game also runs very smoothly, unlike the first game (8 pages) which had serious fps issues.
The jump scares are fantastic, and really make the game. To see slendy in front of you and then turn around to find him behind you is terrifying, and is a good change from other horror games where you can just lock the door and know that you will be alerted to the monsters arrival when he tries to break it down.
The proxy is a questionable addition in my opinion, and not well designed. While its good to have another enemy to run from, there seems to be no way of getting rid of her or to combat her. She will just stand there indefinetley when you point the torch at her, and when you runaway, she will suddenly appear out of nowhere behind you and kill you. Initially she is scary, but after the 5th time she gets you in a few minutes, she becomes more of an annoying obstacle than a terrifying monster.
Overall, while the game does have its faults, it is still a fantastic horror game, and also a must have for any fan of the slenderman mythos and videos.

It’s taken me a while to mull over why I love Jazzpunk, but I think I have a single line that best describes my experience:
Jazzpunk provides me a nostalgia for a past that had never happened.
The game itself is very quick if you just hit all the triggers, but getting to explore the world inside the game is a wild and silly combination of 50’s Spy thriller, parodies of known games in the past lexicon, and the touch of something that I can only describe ”The Naked Gun: Even more Surreal than usual”.  It’s as if everything that happens in this world exists for a reason, but not for the one you think it does.  This alone is why the experience was so amazing, you never knew what to expect once you accepted that weird things was going to happen.
Beyond that, the experience of the game reminded me so much of playing older games Like King’s Quest and Day of the Tentacle.  Jazzpunk is best played as a First Person Point and Click adventure, and as such, there was so many hidden secrets to find.  From weird and enjoyable convo trees to interactions with the world that were unexpected.  By the time I reached the Hotel, I made sure to explore every single room in hopes to find another morsel of content that was stashed away from the “non-believers”. (Much like how secrets were hidden in games like Dark Forces).
Jazzpunk is not going to be for everyone, and your mileage may vary.  If you have time to just explore and experience though, I highly recommend this game to anyone that needs a fun and casual break.

Normally Jazzpunk would be the sort of game that's impossible to properly describe, lucky for us we have had two games in the last couple years come out to summarize just what you'll be experiencing when you Jazzpunk it up: Thirty Floors of Loving and The Stanley Parable.
Jazzpunk borrows the almost incomprehensible unpredictable design/plot, art style, and humor of Thiry Flights, while having a story-driven narrative similar to that of Stanley. Jazzpunk ends up feeling more substancial than Stanley for having actual gameplay away from moving the character around, but ends up being much more linear and easier to figure out while you have to work for the various Stanley endings and think outside the box just a little bit more. That said once you're finished with the game you're likely to run back through it to see just what you may have missed the first time.
Still, Jazzpunk is an experience that is certainly worth it if you pick it up on sale since no two playthroughs will likely be the same or even experience the sheer amount of insanity that lies within. Given the amount of original content, $15 can be worth it but it's also really short (a little under two hours, even if you're interacting with just about everything) so ultimately it's up to you.

This game is the equivalent of eating a single potato chip.
You may like it in the moment, but when you finish you'll find the experience lacking.
Personally, I think that telling stories through games provides an interesting opportunity to allow for the player's input to guide the way the story unfolds; yet that isn't what happens here at all. The only choice the player will make is whether to pad out the time by clicking the optional bits in each scene, which adds a little extra flavor text and personality -- but there's no story defining choice you'll make otherwise.
Linear storytelling is well and fine when there's a satisfying amount of it, where you're able to submerge yourself in the author's world. This is just a marvelously reflective puddle. Lovely pixel art, fitting music, but barely enough there to get your imagination wet.

I've been working on a more comprehensive review, but looking through the ones already available, I feel as though I don't need to go into depth about game mechanics.
To start, here's a short list of my personal Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- The physics are fantastic
- The game gets rather challenging fairly quickly, but never seems to give an unfair challenge
- With the construction system, on most of the levels there's room for an extremely large ammount of Creativity. (Notice I said Most. I'll get to that later.)
- The soundtrack is relaxing, and this is one of the few games I would buy a soundtrack for (Also will mention this later)
- Customer Suport is extremely good.

Cons:
- Like I mentioned previously, most of the levels offer room for Creativity. Unfortunately, there are a handful of levels that ristrict so many of the peices that there's only a few ways to complete the level. These are by far the worst part of the game.
The game itself, despite the small quantity of poor levels, is extremely fun to play. I'd spent over 10 hours playing the game when my save got deleted, but I enjoy the game enough to replay throught the game again.
When I recently started playing the game again, I had some technical issues that were causing my music to create constant popping noises. Long story short, I couldn't fix the audio due to unrelated issues with my PC, and ultimately couldn't play the game with music. When the creator saw my forums post, one of them added me (Christian_Akacro), and gave me a free copy of the sound track to use while playing the game.
Looking through the forums a bit, the creator seem to be extremely active, and seems to respond to any and all messages he can. I really appreciate the effort that's been but into the game and the community, especially considering that it was independantly created.
To sum up everything, the game is extremely well polished, and is pretty much exactly what the trailers make it look like.

Cons:
game structure is very standard, you start with a boring small ship, and then go places and can buy better ships and upgrade stuff. commonly in this kind of game you come across several small upgrades or access options that match your strategies/play style, and help lure you with hints of bigger weapons  to continue. Surprisingly, there is very little accessible for a good while into the game (as an hour into the game i found 4 competent weapons, two of which vagualy matched my preferences), as well as minimal customization options (you can get a ship that has a single slot for one weapon type as opposed to a ship that has a single slot for another weapon type).
the ship is controlled by exactly one thruster, meaning you accelerate in the direction you are facing, which can work in some games and some layouts. however, the turn rate is frustratingly slow and overtorqued, in the way that if you land on a planet (which considering it was highlighted feature is annoying to find it has absolutely no use) and you move your mouse slightly (the turn control and ALSO used to access your menu), you rock and roll around in a ridiculous manner, possibly causing damage to yourself and potentially moving into the line of fire of one of the generated enemies (did i mention that the only way to pause in-game time is to enter the main menu?).
pros (kinda):
i will say the transition between outer-space and planetary space is seamless, although it was very disorienting the first several times as there is NO indication that your frame of reference shifts as you approach a planet and that the compass that sometimes appears is an idiation of 'universal north'.
I have not looked into the open-source aspect of the game, but other than the point on the shop page, there is no indication of it in-game, or anywhere else i saw (i didnt look very hard either).
the game is truly as it claims to be when it says it is free, so i have no complaints about that.
it is also smooth/solid fps, which is cool and enables you too see nice details on the planet surfaces like trees and snow, but it also makes it very easy to see all the things that are not-so-nice.
TLDR:
basic rpg-ish with slow progression, there are no instructions at all, no key binding options, the controls overlap, messed-up motion mechanics, minimal items, interesting physics/inertia, entirely actually free, smooth, interesting graphics.

I wrote a really in-depth and long review which I realized probably would bore people. So now short and sweet.
Story:
Never a dull moment. And I have the attention span of a yogurt bottle (does yogurt have attention?). Don't be fooled by what it appears to be at first- a simple slice-of-life visual novel with plenty of wit and and humor. It's not. Very deep and
Characters:
They may appear stereotypical but they're not. No, not at all. Each are unique and interesting in their own way.
Art:
I don't know anything about art, but to me, it was really high-quality.
Music:
I typically don't notice the music as much as i do the other features. This one I did. They all fit the scenes perfectly and definitely helped raise my stress during the more intense scenes (and of course helped me laugh during the comedic scenes). I wouldn't mind paying some money for future DLC which includes the soundtrack (though the complete OST is on Youtube).
Overall:
Lucid9 definitely could have cost around $10 and it still would have been worth it. You can tell the effort put into this marvelous game in every aspect as you play through it. Even if you're not a fan of visual novels or even anime, I highly recommend playing this. I look forward to the next installment (and the voice acting patch next year; gives me a good excuse to re-read it).

So you purchased Rocksmith 2014 on Steam. You have two options:
- Purchase a $30 DRM cable that is poorly manufactured and will die if you look at it the wrong way. There is nothing special about this cable vs. some other $5 cable, except for the fact that the game is hardcoded to only recognize this one specifically.
- Download a hack exe from some random person's Dropbox or Mediafire to be able to use any audio input, which Windows thinks is malware.
After you've picked your poison, when you run the game you will be greeted by horrible latency that makes it impossible to play along with the songs. You would be better off muting the guitar. So your next step is to scour the internet looking for fixes. After an hour or two you MAY achieve semi-acceptable latency after editing the game's INI file (and repeatedly relaunching the game and waiting through the 30 seconds of intro crap that somehow is still prevalent in 2015), depending on whether the developers decided to test the game with your hardware.
After all of this, you will realize that the guitar tones the game produces sound buzzy and thin, like a tin can. In addition, no amount of calibration in the game (which sets the noise gate threshold) will get rid of the hissing static noise.
Surely the game's tones can't be that bad, right? So you will look through a few gameplay videos on YouTube and see that others are apparently getting pretty decent tones. Unfortunately, these are probably false, edited videos created Ubisoft shills. Slender: The Arrival is good...for an indie game.
It's probably the best Slenderman game to come out of the hoard of other games that tried to capitalize on the success of the original, but that's not saying much.
Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed Slenderman: The Eight Pages, and I even liked the idea of having Slenderman's aggression dependent on the amount of pages you'd collected. It was a fresh idea, but it wasn't exactly compelling or fleshed-out enough to warrant spending any more than 30 minutes to an hour with it.
Slender: The Arrival aims to lenghten, and provide greater context to the original idea, but it hardly manages to do either successfully.
The story is presented to the player through signs and notes that are scattered around each environment in the game, and its your job to collect them and determine what happened in Slenderman Land. Who (or what) is Slenderman? What happened to the family who lived there? Who are they, and why is Slenderman targeting them? The game definitely raises more questions than it answers, so be prepared for dissapointment if you were expecting a decent payoff. Even if you do manage to piece it together, the story is textbook horror, and it doesn't offer any significant surprises or revelations.
The game is dissapointingly short as well, clocking in at 2 hours or less on normal difficulty, depending on how often you need to retry the difficult sections of the game.
If you go into to Slenderman: The Arrival with low expectations, you might find it enjoyable. The visuals look nice, and the audio design is suitably creepy when it needs to be. In all honesty, it's impressive when you consider that this is Blue Isle Stuidio's first game, but at the end of the day though, Slenderman: The Arrival is undone by its cryptic storytelling and ridiculously short length. I'd only recommend that you pick it up when it goes on sale.
