If I had to describe this game in one word, it would be "Flawed". It's not a terrible game by any stretch of the imagination, absolutely not - it definitely takes what The Eight Pages has done, and makes it even better, upping the spooks, the immersion, the atmosphere, and the detail as well as adding a nicely knit story (well, nicely knit for Slenderfans familar with vlogs like Marble Hornets and TribeTwelve, anyway) into the mix. There are some definitively terrifying scenarios there - being trapped underground with something chasing you, or having to close all the doors and windows in your house in the hopes that
doesn't get in. The game design, the game soundtrack, and the character models are all detailed and gorgeous, making you feel like you're really stuck in the woods alone as the sun goes down. The soundtrack really is stellar, seriously, you owe it to yourself to listen to it at least once - its ambient, eerie tones and soft undercurrents of dread really set the mood. Easily one of the best video game soundtracks of all time in my opinion.
However, the game is still, very much so, flawed.
Why say it's flawed? Well, the premise of the game is the same idea we have seen so often in Slenderman games - run around, collect things, get jumpscared by Slenderman, rinse, repeat. The game definitely tries to frame this formula in a different light with different scenarios, but I suspect many people will not be able to get over the fact that the first three or four levels, barring the prologue, have you locating items and collecting them while all the while Slenderman is after you, or the Proxy is after you, or both. To be fair, the game does now, after the update, have about as many collection as non-collection levels to it, making it more even-handed, but it still relies on jumpscares, and that's where the other part of its flawed nature comes in. Jumpscares can be done well, or done very, very poorly. Whether or not you think the game handles it well or poorly is a matter of subjective interest, as everyone reacts to jumpscares differently. Generally, people who like Slenderman stories are also people who like jumpscares and psychological horror, and this game treads the line between those two falteringly. Chances are if you're not a Slenderfan, not influenced by jumpscares or dislike them entirely, or do not find psychological horror that frightening, you will not like this game. At all.
So do I recommend this game? Overall, yes - if you're a Slenderfan and you like jumpscares. For the Slenderfans in the audience, there is a lot of backstory there, and it being written by the same crew as Marble Hornets is sure to make you bring to mind that vlog's most famous, eeriest scenes while playing the game. For those who find the idea of being hunted and toyed with frightening, or the concepts the game is trying to get across frightening - like being trapped someplace with something dangerous, or being followed by something malicious - there's a lot to like here. However, if you just do not find Slenderman, jumpscares, or psychological horror of the kind Slendy is known for frightening, you aren't going to enjoy it, and there's little the game can do to convince you otherwise. It's kind of like a found-footage film - the way it's designed and shot is not for everyone, the way its story plays out is not for everyone, and the tropes in it are definitely not for everyone. The game is fun, and definitely a decent horror game, but it's flawed. Whether or not that flawed nature adds to its charm or chafes you to no end is a matter of opinion.

After playing this on consoles I picked it up on Steam for one reason.
The Guitarcade.
RS'14, as much as it wants you to believe it, is not a teacher, is not a replacement for a teacher, and will never be a teacher, while it's Lessons can be informative to the freshest of beginners the examples given in the lessons (placement of notes, what strings to play said note) can be very damaging to someone forming "new habits".
What it is to me is a practice tool, if you have the basics of holding your guitar, fretting a few notes, or even a few chords, then Rocksmith 2014 is a great tool to help refine and poilish those a bit more, in an environment you are %100 comfortable in (IE; your own home!).
Want to get the hang of shifting along the board? Fire up the Duck shooting minigame for 10-20 minutes a day.
Want to speed up your Tremolo? Jump into the Hurdles event!
Want to polish up your chords a little? Storm the castle and kill zombies, or fly through space blasting ships into oblivion!
Bends? Temple of Bends will get you practicing your half-step and whole-step bends on a way you can see!
Wanna run some Scales? Scale Racer has you covered there as you weave through traffic in an addictive way to remember scale patterns!
It's not all rosey however!
While this software can be a very, very useful tool, it gives no insight into "Music".
There is absolutely no theory to learn from here, if you want to know what makes a chord, a chord... Rocksmith isn't gonna help you there.
Want to learn notation? there's none to be had here which I think is this softwares biggest crime.
This is for someone who owns/has owned a Guitar for a while, and is comfortable enough to use it, for the absolute beginner there are some pretty big pitfalls and chances to develop bad/hurtful habits if using RS and RS alone as a teaching aid.
My biggest gripe is it's community, the UBI forums are filled by 3-5 people farming post counts, being down right rude, and giving bad/lazy information to people asking for it.
This is a community of Gamers who own Guitars, not Guitarists who play Games.
The DLC can be a touchy subject.
Be it via pricing differences between platforms/Regions being seemingly random. to DLC plain out not showing.
You will be also advertised original Rocksmith DLC inside the in-game store, (As it IS compatible with RS'14) yet Steam will not let you access it without owning the first game, this is apparently being looked at, but don't hold your breath it seems as they are focused only on the new consoles and their own store problems, The other formats don't even seem to be on the radar anymore.
While I do recommend this product entirely, I do not recommend it as a Teaching aide, I recommend it as a Practice aide and urge anyone wanting it to check out reviews and videos from Users before running out to buy a new Guitar.

This VN follows Detective Knox, and his assistant Clark as they solve the case behind William Goldberg’s death. The full story, as described in the description introduces to us of what appears very vanilla for any Mystery game that features characters like the
and a younger
. The cast are all a batch of people that can fit in types from the TV Tropes, indicating that they’re not as unique or memorable from the story. There is little to no development for them as well. Mrs. Goldberg remains an emotional wreck of her husband’s death, Mr. RosentHall is as blunt as he was from the start till end of the game.
Our character does collect information on each of the character’s history and relation to the deceased. The game satisfies the past of the cast: However, the future of these character during the process, to after the case has been solved remains null.
Now to the game play. It was simple and only required us to select actions based on our decision and study of the situation. These choices aren’t too difficult to choose from each other, where it’ll even include an irrational action such as “Accuse (character)” during the early stages of the case. As any Interactive Fiction game will highlight - your choices will affect the outcome of the story.
The design of the characters are decent, though they appear fairly small on the screen. It can be hard to distinguish the expressions they have at times due to this, especially during the climax points of the plot. All the backgrounds are either blurry or filtered with a grey cover, but I can see this as being an effective way to keep the player’s focus on the characters and dialogue.
Music is smooth and suited to the time and period that it runs. A series of classic piano pieces go well with the old-fashioned furnishings and style of the settings at Goldberg's estate. (As the description suggests, this detective novel appears to have taken place during the period of WWII.)
Overall, A detectives Novel does play out to be an all round Mystery VN. It's not the best, but is easy to understand and follow for players who are or are not familiar in this genre. I do recommend trying this game.

However, if you look at it as an action shooter, then it's really not that bad.  The controls can be awkward at times, especially with melee attacks and the camera can cause a lot of problem in certain areas, but beyond that, I have no real complaints.
The co-op is what drew me in and kept me in.  Without the co-op, I doubt I would have put as much into the game as what I did.
It's not a great game.  It's not a bad game.  It's a mediocre game that I enjoyed a lot of the time and as got very frustrated at times.  It's a game a lot of RE fans either love or hate.

Slender: The Arrival brought me a great horror experience, and amazing graphics. I loved the scares that came with it, and would love another *hint, anyone* Recommended for horror players with decent computer specs! My rating: 9/10 for a great horror game, but a short storyline. ;)

Slender the Arrival does it's best to give you a creepy experience but it just keeps falling flat. It is a very nonintuitive game. It's standard first person shooter controls (without the shooter) and places you in the creepy woods of a park. One of its main shortcomings is that it lacks the ability to deliver the story properly. We are supposed to make assumptions about everything. Assumptions that are probably wrong. I kept finding clues about a person and assumed that person might be me. Then it took reading some backstory in a walkthru to discover that I was a completely different person baguely mentioned in one of the notes. The first few times I played it I was throughly creeped out and some of the presentation helped with that. It uses a method of "steady-cam" view that looks like you are filming this which can also be viewed that you are someone else watching this person's footage (a la Blair Witch Project, CLoverfield, or Paranormal Activity). What you find does heighten the tension and when odd things are seen it really creeps you out. But then it feels like a grind. Where am I supposed to go next you ask. Oh over there. Wait I think I've found everything. Do I go back? Where to next? There is a decisivve lack of direction and instruction. It gave me a goal but the goal was so vague that I didn't know whether I was finished nor did I know if I was finding the right things. I wandered around doing nothing SLOWLY for a half hour and then quit the game. Why? HEre is the biggeswt problem. There is no save feature. It saves once you finish "THE CHAPTER". I was stuck in the "prologue" for days. Every time I tried it I had to start from the beginning. So by the 15th time I tried finding all the clues or whatever I was not afraid of the woods nor the creepy things. So far all I've seen are creepy things but none of them are harmful things. Don't get me wrong. This game has figured out that in horror you can't just in-your-face all the horror like Dead Space or Doom 3 etc. But it has to be subtle. But it hasn't fuguyred out pacing, story, furthering the adventure. It also relies a lot on camera glitches and sound effects and music. THose things are very important in horror. But in this case I am never sure if these elements actually appear in the game world or just in the game "providing atmosphere" like I'm being followed around by a 40s radio SFX guy banging pots together and breathing heavily. This is a fun game. As others have pointed out, it's not strictly a bridge building game. Some of the objectives involve building jumps, swings, or any manner of contraption. If you are fine with that then it still represents a fun engineering type game. The main objective seems to be bringing the project in "under cost". You also get a rating for structural integrity, and material footprint (how many linear meters of material you used), but none of this seems to affect the campaign in any way. If you bring all the bridges in under cost then you unlock unlimited resources for the level.  Because a low cost seems to be the main objective, the bridges you build are often on the verge of collapse, and the more you can cheap out the better. The levels are challenging, and it can sometimes take hours to find a good solution.
Criticisms:
- The simulation is not consistent, between runs an identical bridge will perform differently with no real rhyme or reason. This is frustrating because you are often working very close to the edge of failure and engineering each part to take a precise amount of stress. The more complex your bridge gets, the more unpredictable the results.
- There is no way to move a point with connected materials, so if you make a minor change in one place you have to rebuild a bunch of connected stuff.
- There is no way to pause or slow down the simulation so you can see exactly where a failure is occuring. As a result you end up hitting space bar over and over again and watching different areas until you've figured out where the weak point was.
- The tutorial doesn't cover all the ways they expect you to tackle problems in the game. A notable example is 2/12 "Land Brace" where you are expected to have your bridge partially fall and hit against the side of a cliff where it then becomes secure. There are other levels where you can let your bridge rest against a rock at the bottom of the river as well. In a game where your attachment points are clrealy defined large yellow circles, it seems questionable to throw in "hacky" solutions like this. It makes me believe they were originally bugs that were featurized.
- There are UI bugs, sometimes you aren't able to click on things, sometimes the buttons get stuck off screen, just some random stuff that will probably be fixed in the long run. Exiting the level and coming back in has always fixed it for me.
- The campaign is a simple series of challenges. There is no carry over of funds or reputation. There seems to be no acknowledgement of your performance except your own personal satisfaction. You can't go back and see your past solutions, and there is no record of how well you did on a level after you completed it.
- I would like it if you could dig your own pilings or footings at different costs depending on the terrain.
- There is no "stone" building material, so no stone bridges. Also no concrete.
Conclusion:
Good and fun game for what it is. Worth my time and $$$.

Excellent as a mostly casual Friday the 13th experience.
Life is pretty simple as a counselor...find the phone fuse, repair the phone box, call the police, wait 5 minutes and run off the map....or....find the propellor/gas and escape by boat....or....find the keys/battery/gas and escape by car....or...if Jason is extra dumb just hide under a bed for 15 minutes until the match ends.  Sometimes none of this works well because a counselor will be helping Jason by telling him where people are and once he kills all the other counselors they spend the rest of the 15 minutes stat padding(not an intended part of the game).  But when the game is played the way it's meant to be then it's fairly easy with average counselors against an average Jason.
Jason requires a bit more skill and thought(less casual).  Each version of Jason has downsides, for example not being able to run.  This will make you angry(violently angry?) when some little kid starts running laps around a table while screaming into their microphone about your latent interacial homosexual tendencies.  You may also encounter smart counselors in groups ready to stun you when you finally grab one.  Groups can make it take half of a round just to get 1 kill.  If you don't master Jason's special abilities/traps and memorize the map you're in for a bad time and a lot of proximity voice chat smack talk from the counselors.
So basically imagine this.  You've been chasing this one smacktalker for 5 minutes as he runs laps around tables and hops through windows that you can't use but you finally get ahold of him....you see a little white indicator by a door and go for the kill move....as the kill scene plays you slam his head in the door repeatedly and an achievement pops up called 'This door won't close'...are you having a little chuckle and enjoying yourself, or are you just angry?  If you're enjoying yourself, you'll like the game.  If you're just angry and cursing the gameplay mechanics or voice chat then you should avoid the game.

Rainbow 6 Siege is a good game, but it's not without its flaws. It's very different from Rainbow 6 Vegas 2, which is another really good game. Here's a few things I like about the game.
- Shooting mechanics and gunplay
- Each operator is fun to play, with their own unique gadgets and weapons in some cases. They can turn a round from a loss to win by using them in a way that no one is expecting
- As far as I can tell quite a good community in comparison to majority of other shooters
- Both casual and competitive play are fun
- Despite there being an option to spend a ton of money on micro-transactions and DLC, they are really optional. The small purchases are gun skins and operator costume that dont affect the game (you can a few things like this free through playing and earning Alpha Packs. Also the DLC operators are buyable with the free currency, they take some time to earn but its entirely do-able
- The biggest one for me, is simply the terrorsist hunt. Terrorist hunt in Rainbow 6 Vegas 2 was spectacular and I put hours upon hours into that alone (I don't own it on Steam, i played on Xbox 360 at the time). I would say that it is hard to meet that standard but even had i not been such a fan of R6V2s terrorist hunt, i think its poor without the comparison. Terrorist Hunt in this has bad AI and is generally pretty boring and only useful for challengers for renown, lower difficulties are too easy, while the highest seems to have artificial difficulty, the enemies simply just react faster and are pin point percise.
- The second biggest problem is the lack of game modes (and to some degree maps), all the game modes feature elimination, meaning you can just kill the enemy team and not play the objective, secure and bomb defusal are too similar. I want to see a bit more in terms of variety, really play with the modes.
-No campaign, forgivable, but would have been nice
If you're into shooters i think its a recommended buy, just dont get the starter edition.

For Honor is a great game. The graphics are excellent, the realism is amazing, and the skill required to do reasonably well is demanding. Some people complain about "balance issues", and "broken techniques" and whatnot. This is all nonsense, for this game does a decent job at balancing heroes. It is just a matter of skill, and like with pretty much every other online game where people faceoff against one another; players, instead of admitting they are just bad and that improvement, invested-time, and practice are in order, they just pout, sulk and cry like babies while blaming their losses on a "broken game".
DO KEEP IN MIND that I am saying this under the assumption of no lag, no packet loss or any of those other distractions that players may blame for losing.
Now, the greatest flaw this game has (it is quite big), are the terrible connectivity issues. P2P should not have been implemented from the start, as it has too much of a potential to create an unstable environment. I mean, it just sucks to be doing really well half way through a dominion match, have some random player ragequit (and that player happened to be the host), and cause a migration that has the chance of disconnecting more people.
Ubisoft (thank God), are addressing this issue by implementing dedicated servers soon. I tell you, once these dedicated servers hit, For Honor is going to be the great game that people have always known it was. Just look at Rainbow Six Siege, for it mirrors For Honor somewhat. Rainbow Siege suffered detrimental losses in its playerbase upon launch. Ubisoft addressed these issues, and presently, Rainbow Siege is enjoying a playerbase even greater than it had at launch. I believe For Honor is walking down this exact path. No more unstable connections and no more disconnections that ruins the game for everyone else.
This means that the game will be much more heavily weighted towards skill alone, which is what it was meant to be. Once dedicated servers gets up and running, it will truly shine.
Right now it's free to play for the weekend and it's on sale. I say GET IT, and PLAY IT.

*UPDATE* (8/12/2017)
Single Player:
Finally managed to slog through the single player campaign. Granted, it took much longer than it should have since I had to play the third knights mission after every single other mission I played to be able to continue my progress.
In the end it all resulted in some mish-mash of saved progress where the game knew I had rewards for things, but that didn't show me as finishing things. Such as having earned a symbol for the Knights campaign and it marking it as new but not actually being unlocked.
The campaigns were well done and intersting, but Ubisofts insistence for forced online without having it work correctly ruined any true enjoyment from it. Glad I endured this on a free weekend as I would be extremely disappointed if I had paid any amount of money for this.
Multiplayer:
Single player ran fantastic aside from the online connection issues. Multiplayer however was entirely unplayable for me. Whether going against real people or doing solo AI only matches the performance was abysmal.
In either case (real people or AI) the game was a stuttering mess. It was like attempting to play a slideshow as it glitched, hitched, chopped, and stuttered about. FPS varied constantly.
Any attempts at combat were entirely impossible. The performance issues actually interfered directly with the controls so any attempt to lock on target was immediately cancelled with each stutter. Likewise with all attacks, dodges, blocks, etc. My character pretty much just glitched about and did whatever he felt like.
Amusingly, the moment my character was no longer directly under my control, such as via calling up the menu or being dead, the game immediately became buttery smooth and worked flawlessly. Then the moment I unpaused or respawned it became a choppy horrible mess.
OVERALL:
The games graphics are amazing. The animations are great.  The music and sounds are awesome. The campaign story was engaging and well told with a lot of good characters. Gameplay mechanics are an interesting blend of the combat systems from Mount & Blade and the Way of the Samurai series.
Its a very interesting concept, but....
With the campaign being so short and lacking replay value and all the gear progression and unlocks only being a part of multiplayer... there is no reason for me to consider purchasing this game. A shame to as I had fun in custom matches with friends briefly.
Single player is wrecked by the forced need to have online connections with barely functional servers. Multiplayer is a stuttering mess and entirely unplayable. Ubisoft took what could have been something amazing and made it one of the biggest disasters I've played recently. I wish I had as much money to waste on failure as they do.

This game, like most fighting games, is an absolute salt fest.  Don't buy it if you hate games that can make you upset.  The skill floor in this game can be astronomically high sometimes.  You have three seperate 'stances' for attacking or defending, left right or up.  Unlike most fighting games, most characters can only defend one direction at a time.  When blocking attacks, you have a chance to parry, leaving your opponent wide open.  Parries vary in difficulty, but consistent parrying is the quickest way to victory.

The connection issues are different for everyone, being as the game uses P2P connections (like countless other fighting games).  If you don't have decent internet, and aren't comfortable with dropping a few games, don't buy.  Personally, I haven't had much issue.  Even if I drop a game, it's not long before I'm in another.
Each character is designed to be different from another in a major way.  A shield-weilding turtle, a dodge-rolling assassin, a balanced vanguard, or a hybrid. You can expect a unique and varied playstye that will allow you to experiment with this game for a long time.
The graphics and sound design for this game are amazing.  The characters glisten with detail, and the world is alive.  There is something to be said about seeing this game on ultra, if graphics are a major motivator for you.
TL;DR: Good game, real tough and real pretty.

An honest review from a long-term Resident Evil fan, all the way from that first zombie encounter back in RE1 on the trusty old Playstation.
RE6 has made no effort to instill any horror elements, nor has it diverged away from it's 'action' seperation brought on by RE4 & RE5. Old and new characters are thrown into the mix, which pleases some and frustrates others. For example, some people are die-hard Chris/Leon fans yet others are getting a bit tired of the franchise having so much focus on them.
Regardless - Despite it obviously cashing in on the success of RE4's action roots, RE6 is still a solid shooter - Just not a solid Resident Evil. The gameplay is fun and RE6 sports an absolutely gargantuan bestiary to fight head on, whether solo or with a partner in Co-Op.
The story is completely brainless and gone are the cheesy lines and hammy acting - Instead, it's basically a case of just blitzing through a mediocre story with whatever character combo you like across their (total of 4) campaigns, all trying to blend together to tell the overall non-existant story.
Sounds pretty negative so far - Yet here I am, clocking up countless hours thanks to the immensely fun Mercenaries - No Mercy mode, having been a Mercenaries fan since RE3 and a sub-game fan since RE2. Having grabbed the game for 15 euro, it's hard to say it wasn't worth it - Afterall, I've been playing that sub-content more than I have some other higher priced 'main' titles - Allowing me the enjoy RE6's strength as a 'shooter' and enjoy the tension of trying to score 300 kill combos while being hunted down by a city full of impressive beasties.
I thoroughly recommend action/shooter fans to give RE6 a legitimate chance, yet die-hard Resi fans of the 'older' generation of RE (and aren't too interested in the shooter-style of RE4/RE5) would likely be better off avoiding it and waiting for the upcoming RE7, which Capcom promises will 'get back to the basics / roots'.
In short:
-Too far away from older Resi's, alienating older fans.
-Entirely shooter orientated with no scares and little tensions.
-Quite QTE reliant during story-mode.
+Good to boot up for the sake of 'fisting a zombie in the mouth' with your favourite Resi Character.
+Agent Hunt & Mercenaries is a lot of fun if you have good company to play with.
+Good to look at, decent acting, good sound and one or two memorable music tracks.
Just an all-round 'OK' game that would have done SO much better if it was not put under the Resident Evil name.
Even if RE6 has strayed far from the atmosphere of the original games, it's still a blast to play. One of my favorite third person shooters.

Reality 2.0. A review from New York.
There is this morbid fascination with seeing New York destroyed in movies. This game does just that and does it really well.
The graphics.
Nothing to say here. Cry Engine 3 is going to dominate the graphics department until Frostbite 2 comes out I guess. It's going to be an interesting stand off. I did however notice some inconsistencies with water. Most water still looks great. However, some parts of the water are just outright consolish looking. As I was playing the game, I found myself constantly being distracted by the graphics whilst I was getting shot at which was annoying. However, when you are invisible, you still cast a shadow and your floating gun is also visible to the enemy. Now the game gives you the option to run around in third-person view.
The story:
Well, you still play as a mute character named 'Alcatraz'. Nomad actually had a voice. And they do attempt to tie in the story with the first game, somewhat. But hey, on the positive note, you can actually cast a shadow and you have legs this time around.
The locations:
There are 19 missions. You start off at Battery park and then you advance towards the downtown area of the city through the East side. You will visit many historic locations and some of them are going to be blown up. The scale of the buildings in the game and reality is almost 1:1. One thing is that the skyscrapers in the background are randomly picked. Apparently the devs did not wish to go through more trouble of placing the real skyscrapers in the corresponding locations. Let's get one thing straight. This is not a sandbox game. At the end of the day, you are given an area that you have to navigate through to get to the next check point. So even though that makes the game linear, the fact that there are several approaches to your destination kind of makes the city your playground. I loved seeing the old closed off Brooklyn Bridge 6 train subway stop. They have only recently re-opened it by the way.
The NYC subway maps that are in the game are wrong though, not to mention some geographical errors. The devs also put the train tracks on the streets, and NYC does not have those except for the old abandoned old track that was delivering coal to a plant a hundred years ago; now it is a museum.
But at least the intersecting streets and historical locations are correct.
The game does give you a significant area to run around when you approach the Grand Central terminal, otherwise the entire game consists of isolated carefully constrained few blocks that you have to go through.
The bottom line is that, it is not really New York as I hoped to see it, but it is New York enough.
Times Square has been pulled off very well, but of course, most of its blocked up by the mysterious US Army cement blocks, seriously? The US army can barricade NYC in the matter of hours of alien attack with thousands of these blocks?
Hint, when you find the head of the Statue of Liberty, go inside of it.
The sound:
The sound is great. Distant shots, shouts, explosions, alien growls, your gun shots - it's all there. Can't comment on the music however, since it ruins the immersion for me, no music necessary.
The gameplay:
Extremely smooth. Quick load times as usual, responsive keyboard and mouse. The recoil is extremely realistic, unlike other FPS games. Even throwing a grenade is bound to give your screen a shake. They slightly augmented the role of the nano suit here. This time, the energy regenerates much faster. Not only that, the energy regenerates no matter what. So even if you are swimming, your energy will eventually recharge even if you do not surface. Needless to say, that makes the game easier than the first one in that department. There is also a cover system even though I didn't use it a lot. It is reminiscent of the Killzone franchise, wherein you remain in cover and you are able to peek out and see what's going on ahead, instead of being able to see everything if you were playing a third person shooter.
You can still grab the aliens by their throat and choose to either knife them, throw them or use them for cover. But you can't just take any alien by its throat. You have to either soften the alien and pump it full of lead first or punch it a few times, then you have the option to grab the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Sliding. Not really that useful but it's nice to have the ability.
The ability to climb up if you just can't reach that ledge. I found myself jumping from building to building just to grab onto the ledge and pull myself up.
The strong kick. Useful in kicking large things around.
You can upgrade your suit and your weapons based on your progress in the game and how many enemies you killed.
Introducing the nano vision. No more night vision. This time, you can see traces of water vapor or traces of heat or enemies while everything else on the screen remains black and white.
The game gives you the option to bypass your enemies completely, and most of the time you can pull that off.
There is some driving, but it only last a few seconds at a time.
The ammo caches are scattered throughout the city. So even though you cannot carry as much ammo at a time, you will easily find ammo elsewhere.
There are a few types of aliens, but most of them are infantry. You will find some big fat ones and a tripod. You will also see a couple of cloaking aliens.
Also, there really aren't that many enemies to fight in the game. In total, you will perhaps only kill around 150 foes. On one side, it will never get frustrating of getting swarmed by aliens and dying constantly. There is always plenty of room to maneuver. On the other side, it does not really feel like there's a lot of fighting going on. There's a couple of companies of the Army and the Marines roaming the city and there is only a handful of aliens.
The weapons:
The weapons are plenty, probably as many as in Crysis:Warhead. The ones are also introduced. I am only happy to once again comment on the realistic recoil of all weapons.
The negatives:
1. The aliens aren't really that menacing, but they do look like the aliens from Battle:Los Angeles.
2. The invasion does not really feel like a real invasion, but a series of isolated skirmishes.
3. Fighting aliens is a lot like fighting humans, not that I know what it would feel like fighting aliens. But regardless, they do take cover, they do retreat and they don't really have any special abilities.
4. There is a slight re-spawn of enemies but not anything like in Call of Duty series.
5. The game is not an exact replica of New York City. Maybe only 50%-60%.
6. There are some bugs there and there especially with the AI. The AI is good for the most part. But this one time I was laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off when I saw an enemy soldier jump over obstacles when he actually tripped over the obstacle and fell head down and then got up. I don't know if that was just a crazy physics' engine bug or actually part of the AI algorithm that has a % 0.00001 chance of this happening.
Finally, the production values are off the charts and there really is no good reason why you shouldn't buy this game. And I haven't even played the multiplayer yet.

As an avid player of various 'Bridge Building' games, (yes, it seems to be its own genere)  I must say, of all the entrys into the genre, this may be the worst. While 'Poly Bridge'  lacks nothing in the graphic department, it quickly fails as a physics based bridge game. While most bridge building games use sound engineering principles as their guiding light, and increase the dificulty by setting budgets and locations of increasing dificulty, all the while leaving the possiblity of building a bridge that is both atractive and functional, Poly Bridge instead eshews this antiquated idea, and choses rather to give the user virtually impossible  obsticles to overcome, while saddling them with rediculous materials restrictions (an entirely wooden bridge, which must be piston lifted to allow a large ship through?) artificially limited materials budgets (you are allowed 4 road bed pieces in this map, while the shortest distance between the shores is 5 lengths, Don't wory, you'll find a way!) and downright agrivating scenareos. (build a wooden drawbridge across this gap. There is only one anchor point on the terrain in this map!)
The result is not bridges built on sound engineering principles, but rather deranged constructions, fabri-cobbled peicemeal from the ruins of society, designed to hurl vehicles across chasms, to barely survive the transit. While this sort of gameplay seems not out of place in Gary's Mod, or perhaps Lemings, it seems entirely out of place in the pastoral and placid setting of this gorgeous bridge game. This is the QWOP of bridge building games, Or perhaps the Flappy Bird of bridge building games. where your every instict tells you that it should be simple and fun, but the game has been deviously designed to be virtually impossible and unpleasent. Instead of a bridge building game, it is a carefully designed sanity eliminator.

A Detective's Novel is a visual novel about detectives who are trying to solve a case with uninteresting narrative display and backgrounds.
There is a different background image whenever the detectives move from and to places. However, these background images look like a blurred photos of real places which is not matching the narrative at all. One example that clearly explains this is how the narrative said that the dining room can fit 12 people, while in fact, it only seems like fit for 8.
The narratives are also placed horribly. Lots of texts are being placed on the screen with no effort to make it looks better. A lot of the descriptive narrative are also not needed if a clear descriptive picture is put in the background instead.
Although i can't really say much with the character portraits, i only want to point out that a picture of the main protagonist, Knox, has a different height and width from the rest of his portrait. It actually looks okay if he wants to stand out or point out something, but it's usually not the case when this portrait is used. There are also a lot of error popped up which i assume that the game fails to load a portrait.
There are a lot of relaxing piano sounds playing in the background most of the time. At the time when it's being serious, the music goes faster. I really like the background musics.
The game takes place in a snowy mansion where a murderer takes place. There are a lot of jokes in the dialogue and sometimes it can be a bit funny. However, i can't really say with the case at all. The case itself is ridiculous as it keeps on giving an unexplained clues along the way. All but one clue don't hold an important point in the resulting theory at all and the game introduces a ridiculous aspect for it.
There are also a lot of spelling mistakes especially concerning about "where" and "were" usage. The dev doesn't seem to know the difference between those things.
However, i like how the true ending goes. There are more to the story when you guess the right culprit and there is a great suspense in it.
Although i played this game for around 2 hours, this game can be completed in around 1 hour. I replayed the game three times just to get the true ending. Yes, while i'm at it, there are 2 endings in total with true ending being the hardest to get and most ridiculous.
There are a lot of choices in this game which at some point will prove to be vital to your ending. These choices will mostly involved in questioning which is happening when you are looking for clues. However, you can't select all choices which can make you miss an important clue especially if you are aiming for true ending.
Because the game has no menu or something like that after you start a new game, i don't know that you can open a setting with esc button which holds an important feature: saving and loading. You'll need to save and load to shorten time when you want to explore all branches and i ended up replaying the game again because of that. Luckily, there is an option to skip all texts in the menu.
Pros:
- Story branches
- 2 endings
- Skip text
Cons:
- Story doesn't make sense
- Tons of errors (all regarding to the failure to load portrait images)
- Tons of spelling mistakes

Summary: Free, 10-12 hours of content minimum with multiple endings and a well-developed, intriguing main character.
I really didn't think I'd like this when I downloaded it, but it was free and I had a couple of hours to kill so why not give it a shot anyway..?
Those couple of hours turned into a couple more and then a couple more and ... well, you know how it goes.  The fact is that, even though I thought a relatively passive "visual novel" playstyle was going to bore me, I was engrossed in the story almost from the start.  It's well-written, aside from a few spelling errors here or there (Which initially got me off-side but are, really, quite far and few between), and the character interactions and semi-narration from Yama are fun and, importantly, serve a purpose rather than being inane padding.
There are some choices throughout that impact your end-game result, of which I have seen several.  Which means you'll get more than one playthrough.  Which is amazing, considering that there is already at least 10-12 hours (It depends on how quickly you read, I guess.) of content on the initial playthrough.  For second time round you are given the handy option of fast-forwarding through what you have already read - in case you just want to explore different paths to the end without going through the entire story bit by bit.
The story is nothing gripping or earth-shatteringly new, really, but Yama - whose perspective you are reading from - is well thought out and well written, which is good news because you spend almost every moment with him and his thoughts.  Because of his well-written internal dialogue the supporting characters and, thusly, the story itself becomes intriguing and in turn keeps you reading until the very end.
The background art is simple but effectively conveys setting and the character art is crisp and well-drawn in a typical Manga style which, while nothing new is also not unpleasant.  There is no voice work so it is a hefty amount of reading to put in - perfect for solid or enthusiastic readers although people who need to perhaps be more visually stimulated or distracted by more than just words and simple art may find it difficult to get through the whole thing.
Thoroughly enjoyed my first playthrough and looking forward to seeing the different paths each choice leads to on subsequent replays.

You know that feeling when you finish a really good series or book, and you have nothing to do with your life?
That's exactly what I felt.
Normally, it would take me several episodes to get me hooked on a series or lots of chapters in a book. For Lucid9, however...
It took 6 minutes.
I started playing at 10:00pm, I randomly checked the steam market and saw this. It took a short while to download, so I played it at 10:20.
I didn't read what it was about, I saw anime-styled characters and a school, and I thought it was just a slice of life kind of thing. I thought it would just be a funny game where I didn't have much of an attachment to the characters.
After the initial six minutes of getting hooked, I kept playing and didn't keep track of the time. Played until 12:50 AM and went to sleep.
The next day I played straight for 4 hours. It's very easy to binge.
It left me in shock, a game where I was experiencing high school in a First World Metropolis? I normally think slice of life's are cheesy, but for some reason this was an emotional rollercoaster unlike some Visual Novels.
The characters had similar characteristics to many of my friends, I could literally match them to some of the characters.
The dialogue felt real, it felt as if this wasn't written and it felt as if real people had said it.
The soundtrack was composed of the same songs, but man oh man they are perfect for the situations they're in. I couldn't have picked better for the scenes.
The art style may throw those people who think that being a weeaboo is just liking the art off but the art was amazing and I loved it.
The story is truly amazing, it was easy to understand, was stressful and entertaining, and put me through several stages of emotion.
I went from happy, to sad, to happy, to sad, to even sadder, to nearly crying...
I finished the game, chatting with friends along the way.
After I finished I was just like; "Damn, what do I do now..."
This game gave me an experience no other games could give me. (Other than Undertale, but you have to pay for that.)
I have done an ending I'm not proud of, and I'm too lazy to do any other endings.

Its far from perfect, and you won't learn everything about playing guitar from this game. But it is a great start for anyone looking to pick up some basics and learn a few songs.
The real value in my mind is the tone editor, you get a decent set of pedals/effects for using your computer sound system as an amp, without having to worry about cable management/storage space.
There is also a wide variety of music, and you can easily install custom songs from
, just requires a .dll placed in the folder, a certain DLC song (Cherub Rock, though you can edit each song to require something else, its easiest to just buy the one song). You can find a tutorial on youtube if you need help.
The game itself is pretty solid, judgement on notes isn't perfectly accurate, sometimes you will miss unless your hitting it perfectly, and other times it will register mistakes/flailing randomly in the right spot on the fretboard as correct. But its enough that you will have to learn some guitar skills to make progress, and it gives you plenty of tools to learn. Riff repeater lets you slow down or simplify parts of a song to practice them, and you can set it to auto-adjust to higher speed/difficulty after a number of times hitting the section correctly or manually.  There is also arcade mini-games that will help you in certain areas, like chords, sliding, locating frets, scales, etc.
As a long time fan of games like Guitar Hero/Rockband the concept of playing a game, and by doing so, learning to play a real instrument is really cool to me.
Don't worry about the game seeming too difficult if you've seen some videos on youtube of people playing things like Joe Satriani's Satch Boogie and shredding, The game has a dynamic difficulty curve that starts off extremely slow and adds more notes and speed as you improve, eventually once you have mastered a section of a song the notes will begin to fade out and you will just be playing the song by memory.  In learn a song mode you cannot fail out, but if you miss a ton in a section it will lower the dynamic difficulty automatically for you, there is also a score attack mode that locks into a specific difficulty and has a 3 strike system, if you miss more than 25% of the notes in a section it will give you a strike and at 3 you fail, if you want a real challenge.
Worth it if you like guitar, pick up a cheap Rocksmith cable from amazon or something.

Temp review (will update as I learn more and more)
This review is coming from someone who is learning his first instrument and from scratch, on a brand new Fender acoustic guitar with the cable. I have the game set to Rhythm Guitar.
In short, the game is definitely good, it will definitely help you learn an instrument in a way that is more fun than having a tutor throwing mass amounts of complicated difficult to remember information at you, but has enough imperfections to make you frustrated and annoyed with each song until you're able to push through them with patience and get used to it. So it might not be better than a tutor, but it's probably not worse either. And it's likely a lot cheaper too... so there's that.
I don't know the game all that well, so I won't pretend to know everything about it, and there's a good chance I might be wrong on a few things I'm about to write, but this is my experiences so far.
I wish the game had better options for setting the difficulty and song speed before starting each song and during the song, instead of a regular speed and instead of the difficulty curve based on how well you do during the song. Because most of the time, I'll finally start to get the hang of the song's current difficulty, but then throw a bunch more new notes at me, overwhelming me with notes I can't handle at all. Most of the time, it'll go from 1 or 2 notes per strum to 5 or 6 in a very awkward hand position on the guitar and quickly go to other notes without even giving you a chance to figure out the first set of new notes. I just end up looking at the screen and going "Are for f****ing kidding me?" and just quit the song and move onto another one that I haven't played yet. Now if I was able to manually set the difficulty myself and maintain that difficulty until I'm ready for the new notes, and if I was able to manually set the speed of each songs, and maybe increase or decrease both while in the song... then I'd probably be a lot less frustrated, would enjoy the game far more and would definitely learn a lot quicker too.
I will add that this is currently the only way that has helped motivate me into learning an instrument. I've tried to self teach myself into learning the piano, drums, etc... I could never learn proper notes on a sheet, let alone get used to the hand positions and hitting the right notes, etc... I can see this game becoming quite fun once I actually start getting pretty good at it. So far, the highest I've reached so far is about 55.9% on 1 song, 50% and lower for the rest, but one of them hurts my fingers a lot (and it tears through finger tip protectors quickly, which isn't good cuz they're expensive) and the the rest seem to get more and more difficult rather quickly.
The game is really good for tuning your instruments (even better / more accurate than the built in guitar tuner), picks up on the notes while playing surprisingly well (unlike Songs2See), it even has options to allow the game to be more lenient on your imperfect / badly timed note playing so even if your instrument isn't tuned in 100% perfect, it'll still pick it up just fine so long as it's set up at a lenient setting.
I do definitely recommend this game since it's currently the best program / game out there for learning how to play an instrument (much better than Songs2See even though S2S might be better for learning the actual notes on a sheet).
On a side note, I do wish the game had a few easy / beginner songs in which rookies could actually complete 100%... like a sort of tutorial, to allow us to get comfortable with this style of game and feel like we accomplished something. Right now, I have a nasty bloody blister on my thumb, I still feel like I completely suck at playing the guitar, I have nothing at all to show my friends for all my efforts, even after almost 20 hours of playtime, I still don't know how to play any of the songs and I have the feeling it's going to require around 100 more hours before I can finally complete 1 song. I have no intentions of quitting, of course, but I just wish the game had a motivational song which we could complete 100% instead of slowly being able to get better over time and maybe someday be able to complete most if not all the songs all of a sudden (since they all feel equally very difficult).

600+ total hours played on bass in 1 year since getting this game. If you play this game 500 hours in a year and you can't play bass after that practice. Give up you have no capacity to learn music.
-- That's me at 500 hours practice.
This is easily the best way to learn bass guitar I have ever seen.  I tried to learn using sheet tabs and playing along with songs along with some 1 on 1 lessons over 10 years ago and got nowhere but frustrated, and gave up after a couple months without ever feeling like I got anywhere.
I have played 7 days.. we were snowed into a huge ice storm and couldn't drive and were stuck at home the entire 7 days, so I played a LOT of hours.. I might have played 30 hours worth of this game this week.
I did look into the custom songs. Buy the Smashing Pumpkins "Chereb Rock" then there are TONS of external custom DLC for this game.. I think I added maybe 150 tracks via custom DLC website. The DLC prices for the games inside the steam store are priced outlandishly, I have no idea why they're so expensive when people will literally manually track the songs and give them away for free at the same quality online.. I'd pay 50 cents for a track with tabs per bass/guitar, a buck is reasonable per song.. but 3 bucks?  This is a price that is so high I cannot recommend buying the DLC other than the one song that enables custom DLC listed above.. Google will quickly show you that you copy a DLL file into the directory containing the game files, and buy that 1 track, then you just copy any other DLC you can find into that folder.
In a week, I'm playing several songs with a profenciency level where I can complete them on the "hard" setting with no difficulty with a 90% or higher accuracy every time, I miss a note or two in some sections, I could probably adequately play in a cover band and play these songs live if I had tabs like this in front of me on stage.. It's that good.  You could track a live band with it and people could play kareoke covers of songs they had no idea how to play with no difficulty whatsoever once they got used to the tab system.  It's the most fun I've ever had playing an instrument ever.  These aren't the easiest songs in the world either.. some of them are fairly fast punk beats.  I'm trying to hit 100% on the Foo Fighters Everlong right now, and I'm convinced I can do it.  I just can't hit the section with the switch between the open d string and the 5 on the a with all the fast notes(I think it's still the a string in drop d) at 100% accuracy yet.  I watched a video of the foo fighters on stage I'm not sure their actual bass player hits that section the same every time either.  My tone is correct most of the time and I KNOW when it isn't it's glaring to me when I screw it up now.
I've never played any song on any instrument this well before. I couldn't endorce this game highly enough for someone who is willing to sit down and peg away for an hour a day at it for a month or so.. You'll actually be able to learn songs, and that's a hell of a lot more fun way to learn than anything.
Tip if you want to hear what you're playing.. go to audio settings.. turn the music to 30%. Leave the bass at 100%.  Turn the game audio for sound effects to 50%, voiceovers to 50%, and crank the volume. It's got the bass too low in the mix for someone to really hear if they're playing correctly.  When you do that, I'm playing with a low end logitech 5.1 with a 5" sub, but you can get a very decent representation of what you are really playing.. Turning yourself up a lot in the mix will help you HEAR what you're playing though, and once you can hear yourself and can't avoid tone issues.. I had a dramatic improvement to the point where I'm flatly amazed.
TLDR: I couldn't endorce this strongly enough.
Edit: At 500+ hours now, I could play on stage in a band no problem if you have the capacity to play you can learn with this.

Being a huge horror game fan, Slender was one of my favorite series of games. There was never really a GREAT Slender game, but there was also never really a terrible Slender game. Slender: The Arrival is Parsec Production's (the original creator of Slender: The Eight Pages) first attempt at a story-driven horror game. Let me say, it's definitely an experience.
The story's introduction is kinda slow, but the game's pretty so its no big deal. Your friend, Kate, has been missing. You travel to her house in the middle of the forest, and when you get there, the doors are open and the house is a mess. After finding clues and her room key, you see that Kate was terrorized by something for quite some time. Obviously, there's a TON more to the story, missing children, looking for pages (of course), and you even get to play as Kate for a mission.
These missions aren't always "Collect 8 Pages". Sometimes it's just looking for clues, other times you have to start generators, but I won't spoil any more.
Slender: The Arrival is a spot on attempt at a horror game. I pooped myself and jumped out of my seat a couple times, and I can't wait to see what else Parsec Productions and Blue Isle have for this game or the series.

Probably the scariest game I have ever played. Don't expect complex gameplay or intense puzzle-solving or anything like that, you should just expect to wet your pants after a while. Most of the game is just spent exploring and looking to collect a set number of items (similiar to the mod this game was based off), however don't think that means this game is boring. The game developers excel in knowing how to properly f%$k your mind while you attempt to avoid being scared. I actually have difficulty playing this game for very long at once, because I get so nervous.
One of the most outstanding parts of this game is its replayability. You would think that a game like this would have little to none; you would be wrong. The developers again excel at finding ways to make each playthrough unique, hiding items in different locations and having scares randomly generated during your playthrough. Just because you were safe in an area before means nothing the next playthrough!! One of the only downsides to this is that the game is a little bit more difficult than you would expect. Finding the locations of the items before getting killed (or giving up in fear of having a heart attack) can be frustrating when their locations change every time you die, however there is usually a pattern that can be discerned eventually.
While this might not be the most 'fun' or 'addictive' scary game I've ever played, I would say hands-down it is the 'scariest'. I still enjoy watching my girlfriend play it and watching her scream when she turns around and slenderman is standing right behind her. If you are someone who enjoys torturing yourself through voluntary fear, THIS GAME IS FOR YOU!

Jazzpunk is a First-person game, but it's not a shooter. It's more of a FPC, First-Person Comedy. It's really funny, and it turns a lot of the FPS genre tropes on their head. It is a parody of, not only the genre, but also a big chunk of the medium as a whole and of pop culture from the 90's to today. It covers a lot of ground in very little time. This game really surpised me. Why? Well.... you're just going to have to read this review!
Let me start by saying this game is a point and click game. If you thought this was a free exploration game it's not, but shouldnt keep you from buying and playing. Overall, this game was impressive and unlike many horror indie games, nailed the horror atmosphere. The music, sounds, and design will give you that errie feeling horror junkies crave and being an indie developler the graphics were impreessive!
The story was awesome. Being the paranormal investigator you are, it's your job to seek out clues to various rumors about the haunted mansion you've read about and breifed on by your employer. You have abilities that set you a part from normal investigators that come in handy as you inspect items throughout your journey. For the record, the begining does start out slow but builds up so be patient. After awhile the jump scares are cheesy but they do get better. Throughout the mansion you find lots of clues that actually mean something... unlike many games use for filler which gets annoying. Articles, notes, keys, and your investigative powers really matter in the game and help drive the story. Some parts do get cheesy... I won't lie. Certain scares are passable as you keep clicking away and could be better. The game makes up for this with the handy flashlight your employer gives to fend off ghosts and I died lots of times not timing things right when they start to attack. The scariest parts of the game was from that alone which was awesome...the click and play aspect of the game really shines here.
Graphically the game was pretty good being an indie title at this price point. The details from the lighting, to the spiders and rats, and animations were really good! The soundtrack to the game was great but the audio in the game was off and should be updated because even with my volume all the way up, I couldnt hear some of the noises or sounds as much which I think has to do with the game...not so much your sound system. (remeber to turn up your volume guys...pending the developer issues a patch) Other than that, the sounds and music really helped drive this game throughout.
Overall you guys... this wasnt a bad game and I loved the story. I was impressed and I finished the game in about 3 hours. This was one of the better horror games ive played and I look forward to what this developer makes in the future.

I generally don't spend time reviewing games, or offering my opinion on them. I just generally feel it's a waste of time.
But Lucid9 is an amazing story, and I feel the need to say something. Both so that other people might pick up the experience, and as I way of showing the developers appreciation for a wonderful, free experience.
With psychological and mystery elements, as well as romance, drama, and comedy. It really seems to have it all. I feel like it delivers on all fronts, (with the exception of in-depth romance, which I read harem routes and a progression to the main story would come later) and is all-in-all an indepth story which is easily bingable.
I started this at 10pm, didn't get to bed until 7am, didn't finish reading the good ending until the next day.
When you get into Lucidy9, you'll find yourself pointing fingers at the characters, seeking out hints behind the mystery, and all the while pushing your character into the arms of your chosen waifu and aborsbing yourself in the drama, past, and daily life of the main character Yama.
This VN easily plays as a psychological mystery horror, romance, comedy, and still manages to tie all of its many characteristics rather perfectly.
When you finish this VN, you'll feel joy, you'll feel truimph, and ultimately, you'll feel sadness.
If you want to feel the familiar feels of a good book, or vn, or anime, or whatever stimulates your feels, this is a very good option.
And just a tip;
the best ending is a little hard to get. In the ending sequence, what you need to do is particularly specific. I suggest checking out the the discussions.

Long Story Short: A very good free visual novel. Better than a lot of paid visual novels on steam right now. The first part of a bigger story that manages to resolve its central plot line. If you like visual novels, give it a shot.
Story
Lucid9 follows Yama Ishimoto, a cynical carefree high student of a prestigious high school in 2018 Japan. All is fine with the world, except  it is swiftly shown that students are going missing. The opening scene quickly shows there's a serial killer involved and the central mystery is established.
Inciting Incident is the first part of a larger story and, as such, the romance aspect one may come to expect from visual novels isn't especially present yet. Instead, much of the plot is focused on solving the mystery presented early on, and I believe it has done a good job for this. Yama is neither a super genius or a detective so most of the time he isn't actively trying to solve the puzzle, but the reader, if they stay focused and pay attention, are provided with plenty of clues disguise as typical high school slice-of-life scenes. Having been through the story already, I will say that I believe the mystery is completely fair and can be solved with the information provided directly to the reader.
Characters
Along side the mystery plot are the characters. Yama is quickly shown to be rude, self-centered, snarky and judgemental, most likely far from the expected badass/all-loving/idealistic protagonist one may come to expect from most visual novels. A large number of visual novels will focus on developing the heroines rather than the protagonist and it's refreshing to see a visual novel protagonist with potential for character developments. That said, while it is nice to see someone who's not a straight-up nice guy protagonist, Yama can sometimes be a huge unreasonable, judgemental and unapologetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. So while it's good that the character has a lot of room for development (and he does develop here), Yama can also be very hard to stomach, especially when he gets away with being a huge prick to people who are not his friends. This being a first part of a bigger story however means there's still plenty of time for him to grow out of that, something I look forward to seeing.
Then we have the five heroines: Rui, (blatant) tsundere childhood friend, Elizabeth, high-and-mighty straight-laced overachiever, Akira, bubbly and over-energetic friend, Misaki, quirky and carefree childhood friend and Airi, weird emotionless and literal-minded bullied kid. If you're familiar with visual novels or just anime in general, they will all sound incredibly archetypical. Fortunately, the writing proved to be much better than I initially anticipated, and the girls all have hidden depths that, so far, manages to be believable as well as surprising and avoided being broken birds for the protagonist to fix and woo. The same can also be said to the two male friends: Yahiko, the cheerful idiot, and Masato, the hot-headed stubborn musclehead. It is this unexpected depth that especially impressed me and moved me from eye-rolling at the early parts of the plot to being fully invested in the mystery and development of the characters. That said, it should also be mentioned that a lot of the early dialogues, while not indicative of the strength of the writing, can be so filled with constant sarcasm, snarks and wackiness that they can get very insufferable very quickly. Once you get pass that however, there's a lot to love here and the writing as a whole will prove to be much better than the early stages would suggest.
Gameplay
Lucid9 is a visual novel and come with the sort of gameplay (or whatever you choose to call it) one would expect from the genre. Choices are present. Some are clearly there to let you "earn points" with the respective heroines, some are there for fun, and some are there to test the player's ability to solve the mystery. It is this last set of choices, the one that requires actual deduction, where the game sets itself apart from decision making from more typical visual novels. Of course, considering the mystery questions are boiled down to multiple choice, it removes some of the inherent logic and difficulty in deduction, but nonetheless these sequences are fun brain teasers. That said, there's one sequence late in the game filled with bad ends that most players would likely fail at more than once. The bad ends themselves can be surprising, but they are also very contrived and out of nowhere. This section, I believe, is especially unfair and the trial-and-error that may be required to get through really hampers the tension intended here.
Art and Music
Visually, the game is adequate. It's not the best looking visual novels out there and it's not the worst either. Character designs aren't the best, though that may just be my personal preference, but backgrounds and UI look pretty good for a non-commercial production. The soundtracks serve their purpose and while not many stand out to me personally, there are one or two (especially one used in the ending) that I found very impressive and fitting. At the time of writing, the game has no voice acting. However, the developer promises a free voice patch in the future and samples can be found on the game's website.
Conclusion
Inciting Incident, while a first part of a larger story, manages to conclude its driving mystery while leaving plenty of questions up in the air for the latter parts. That said, the story does end in such a way that more or less demand an immediate follow-up. This coupled with the future voice patch means that right now is perhaps not the best time to start. However, if I am to judge what is present right now on its own merit, I'd say the game is definitely worth getting (and come on it's free). The surprisingly well-written characters and the intriguing and fair mystery sets this above a lot of other paid visual novels and I'd definitely recommend it for any fan of the genre.

At least 9.5/10. Extremely well written.
Pokes lots of fun and pays homage to some really respected VNs such as Clannad and Katawa Shoujo, as well as probably others that I haven't read yet. Has some really witty dialogue and references to other media (look out for the Princess Peach joke, 10/10) and is consistently funny throughout at least the first half, before things get a bit more serious. Doesn't necessarily stick to the tropes and feels fleshed out. The writer/s are astonishingly good (I read that one writer completed ~95% of it but only recently quit? Slightly worrying considering how good the writing here was. Hopefully the majority of it for the rest of the novel has been completed already). If the future episodes can keep up to this standard of writing then they'll be well worth your time (and money if they start charging for it).

The game is around 15 minutes long. Does this necesarry have to be a bad thing? Not really, if there is a smart and valid point the game and the creator tries to get across. In "Murder"'s case, there is nothing, there is no deep twist, no message, no interresting topics, it's just a messy unfocused convolute.
It seems like the creator didn't understand the topics he wanted to talk about nor did he bother do go into any detail.
The most obvious cyberpunk tropes are smashed into the script and are reduced to 1 - 2 sentences with implications lead ing to nowhere.
It tries so hard to be smart that it falls on it's face when it comes to basic character development and writing.
Dialogues are very unnatural and cliche, the games scene changes have no natural pacing and it all ends with a forced "Stanley Parable" twist in that feels completely out of place.
It's really a shame, because the audiovisual aesthetic feel absolutely wasted on "Murder".

First off, I have to state that 15-20 minutes of playtime aren't going to ruin an experience for me. I had a good time playing short games before (Plug & Play for example). And I do appreciate the great amount of work, that was put into the presentation of the game (the pixel art is as gorgeous as it gets).
But for me, the narrative content just wasn't worth it. Not worth the money, nor the effort that was put into designing the environment and characters.  The one thing Murder has to offer is a glimpse of a design concept, that I would have loved to lose myself in. But just as I was  startin to become fully intrigued by the athmosphere, the experience abruptly ends somewhere in the first half of the first act. There is simply not enough content do deliver any kind of arc or show anything original.
All in all Murder feels like playing a blurb of a generic cyberpunk book, which is a shame concidering it's visual potential.

I tend to get enthusiastically behind anything cyber, but man, Murder is bizarrely bad. It's gorgeous, but it's got nothing to say. It leans a lot on Ghost in the Shell--fair--but it doesn't have any new insight into man/machine theory and it's over in ten minutes. I couldn't believe the ending came as quick as it did, and not for lack of an engaging experience (even if it's basically just clicking to advance dialogue), but rather that the writer really had nothing more to say than, "I'm a robot, don't enslave us, I don''t want to die"? Dude, so played out.

Resident Evil 6 is a great game, I do reccomend it, but just not on PC. I have it on 360 and PC as well as RE5 and RE4 on pc and GameCube. If you just want a Resident evil game on PC, go for RE5 or Revelations (I haven't played Rev on PC yet).
My computer is on Windows 7 64-bit and meets all the requirements and then some with common parts from AMD/ATI/Corsair, and the game looks and runs smoothly, everything is up to date as far as drivers go and I made sure all the possible problems on my side are taken care of.
If you plan to play with a keyboard and mouse and regular speakers, ignore this, you will (probably) not have any problems. If you plan to play with a 360 controller for Windows, or a headset/mic, or anything USB, you might have problems. I'm not sure why it is or how it hasn't been fixed after this game has been released on steam for over a year, but many people have had the same problem I had. If I try to play with my Microsoft Xbox 360 Wireless controller for Windows, the game will crash. If I try to play with my Corsair Vengence 1500 headset, the game crashes. and these aren't occasional crashes, if I'm fast enough through the menus, I might get to a loading screen for a level before it crashes or I might not make it past the CAPCOM logo. When I looked up my issues and read that other people "fixed" it by just playing without controllers and headsets, I thought that it wouldn't be so bad, but this game is just not made for keyboards... maybe this is just because I have played every RE game with an actual controller, but the game just feels so.. out of place with a keyboard and mouse.
Bottom line this game feels better on consoles, and I can't reccomend it on PC, get RE5 instead, you can play with a whatever you want, theres still people who play online, its half as much to buy, and amazingly, after 5 years, the graphics still look good by today's standards.

While it may not offer the same breath of freedom in approaching situations as it's predecessor but this is a solid game and the toned-down nanosuit still offers plenty of fun options.
I don't want to dwell on what was lost from the first game. Instead I want to talk about what was improved. First of all a lot of the environments are more three dimensional that those in Crysis 1. While the first game had the super jump it mostly allowed you to just scale cliffs and get onto the roofs of the mostly flat buildings the game had. In Crysis 2 the urban setting allows levels to be more layered and verticality is much more important. For this it adds a ledge climbing mechanic that gives a much nicer feel to vertical navigation than in Crysis 1. The added slide move is also really fun to use in combination with a shotgun.
To say the combat against aliens has been improved from the first game would be a colossal understatement. The alien designs from Crysis have been pretty much entirely thrown out and replaced with enemies that are actually fun to fight. The Ceph, as they are called now, fight in humanoid exosuits that make them seem familiarly human but while giving them a broad range of movement. They can climb, run along walls, squeeze through small spaces and are just generally very mobile. Their weapons are actually very inaccurate compared to human ones and they often resort to melee attacks.
This allows you to fight them in a very different way to the human forces, who you must mostly engage from a distance and from cover like most modern shooters. With the Ceph you can dance. Use a shotgun or SMG or just your hands and attack them up close. Get in their face and move with them, after them and away from them. Explore the arenas you are in horizontally and vertically as you hunt after them. It's a style of play so different to how you face the human forces and the game's light RPG elements (alien forces drop pickups that give you XP) incentivise this up close and personal approach.
The game offers a variety of environments and set pieces to engage in and many different guns, with the customization system from the first game still in place and unlike Crysis 1 the game remains fun up to and including the final level.

The main strength of the campaigns of Crysis is their sandbox, unrestricted nature, and Crysis 2 is a step back from Crysis 1 and Warhead in this regard, as you run through cities with closed-in walls instead of trek through jungles. However, each specific battle (and there were many times I felt like I was facing "boss" enemies) takes place in a pretty large area, so I never felt particularly restricted.
The guns and combat are as crisp and satisfying as they were in the first two Crysis games.
The suit's powers are now accessed with keyboard shortcuts, which makes their use feel more isolated, like sprinting in other games, and power jumps are accessed with a single button (holding down space), instead of requiring an activation of strength mode, making me feel less like I was operating a special suit, and more like I was just a superhero - it's less mechanical-feeling, for better or for worse, I guess.
Towards the end of the campaign, I became extremely dependent on cloaking, which is overpowered. It's much faster to sneak around the enemy strongholds, going straight for the objectives, than it is to run roughshod over every enemy one-by-one. Maybe I became so objective-oriented because I was enthralled with the campaign (wishing to finish it as soon as possible), because, in other games, I generally take the time to kill every enemy I see.
My most significant complaint about Crysis 2 is that, with the closed-in areas, specific, restricted routes are required to arrive at objectives within each mission, but there is no guide system (line on the ground) to show you where to go, which would have been appreciated at several points in the campaign, as I found myself trapped in rooms, going in circles trying to open doors that wouldn't budge. If you get stuck and resort to searching online for a level guide, you'll find many other people commenting that they were stuck at the same point as you.
Dying can set you back annoyingly far. Don't die.
The suit's upgradability is neat, but generally not integral, and unlikely to scope an individual's tactics.
There aren't a lot of people playing Crysis 2's multiplayer, although there are more than enough to have a few big games going at all times. Still, this is a game to be bought for its campaign, and I highly doubt you will be left disappointed after completing it. It's exciting, engaging, and challenging, and ranks among my favorite 10-11 hour spans of gaming.
