I have to say that overall this game is extremely refreshing. A lot of people have been comparing it to Undertale and I can see why. I can't think of a line that I didn't enjoy, the characters had really cute designs, and while the game has fights where it can be really difficult/annoying it never really gets to the point of the Undyne and Sans genocide fights where some people can just drop the game because they've been trying to beat it for so long and just can't. The story is as cute as the characters and it fits really well with how short the game is. A normal run takes about an hour to complete (at least for me, but I got adjusted to the always shooting mechanic really quickly) and only a little bit longer if you're going for the special normal run. I was listening to my own music for the most part but for the moments when I was listening to the music it really fit the aesthetic of the game.
Misc. good things:
A protagonist that isn't straight but it isn't like a huge deal or anything.
So many endings (none that really affect that much, it just gives certain characters a few extra lines. So no one should really feel that pressured to get every ending like someone that is playing a game like Undertale might be).
Humor that can range from witty to really stupid but is lovable either way.
There was really only one fight that I found annoying but it was clear that it was one that was supposed to be difficult (and no it wasn't the final boss).
I'm not a parent or anything but I can see this being a really good game to play with kids (as far as I can remember there isn't any dirty jokes or anything so if you're someone that worries about that kind of stuff this game is good to go).
Misc. bad things:
I can't really think of that much??
I imagine some people won't enjoy the graphics or music.
I can also see the colors getting a little straining if you're struggling with certain fights or trying to find something.
Some people wouldn't find some things funny or cute or anything (the biggest one I can think of is the character sprite being on just like a black square that moves around. Personally I found it really cute/charming, but I know some people that found it irritating/annoying).
But yeah, overall I would recommend this game. Some people just aren't going to enjoy this game and I totally get that. But as far as I can tell a lot of people are going to love it.

Destination Sol is a very simple game, and I love it for that. it's a 2D space ship games that couldn't have been that hard to make, seeing as one of the very first video games was pretty much the same thing. Yet, despite it's addicting breed of shooting actiony gameplay, there are very few games that truly explore this genre.
This game is about half of what I want. I want to explore space and new planets and interact with a variety of people. I want to have harrowing space battles with pirates or rebels all while customizing my ship.
Really, Destination Sol is good, but it's not great, which isn't a surprise for a free game. There are plenty of unique weapons to experiment with, and the galaxy is large enough to occupy a good four or five hours, but after that, there isn't much to do. There are no people to talk to, and practically everything wants to kill you.
When you do die, which can be easy at times, you start back at the beginning of the game, and getting back to where you were is annoying because asteroids are so abundant you slam into them constantly (at least until you get to the light speed points, which are satisfying to use even if they take forever).
Getting into orbit around a planet is finicky as well. They don't actually have gravity unless you're extremely close to them, and they're so small that your engines just propel you right out of their atmosphere and back into space, which is annoying when you're trying to take down other orbiting ships.
Honestly, though, the game is free, and I suggest it to everyone even slightly interested. I'd be willing to pay money for this for the person to make it even better, even.

Being that I already tried to post this earlier, but failed due to Steam being a butt, I'll keep it short.
Background: Originally, I approached the creative team behind Lucid9 to inquire about potential voice acting, and despite being skeptical at first, I managed to convince the team to allow my team to provide them with such, further bringing the characters to life. We have currently recorded all of day 1 and will resume day 2 sometime this month. Note: I did not read the entirety of the script prior to recording as I wanted the full experience by actually playing the game.
Story: Short and simple. I'm a picky person in regards to storytelling and Lucid9 managed to be one of those stories that did exactly what I wanted and captured me. Smooth writing with clear and concise details and a plot that seems very light-hearted but with a brutal twist as you near the end. Some minor grammar, punctuation etc errors, but that's just a nitpick. Basically, Lucid9's story and storytelling were both captivating and effective.
Characters: Typical anime tropes with tsunderes, quirky comic reliefs, sarcastic know it alls and more, but with heavy background that isn't explicitly described in detail. I presume they are waiting until post common route to get into individual routes which would more then likely have detailed backgrounds of each character. Still. The characters and their interactions with each other were both colorful and dynamic, assuring my growing love for them.
Art: Need I say more then beautiful? It is very Key-esque, and probably even Key inspired. Very detailed and colorful.
Music: Always catchy for me. Music is something that is paramount to a good game, movie, anime, etc. This game had music that kept me humming along whenever one I really liked popped up.
Verdict: 9/10 Frankly, Lucid9 is one of the best OELVN's I've played, which is unfortunately not many and I recommend it to everyone. It even managed to keep me awake a full night with no sleep. That should tell you something. I'm excited to be working on the voice acting for the patch, slated to be released next year and will work extra hard to make sure we give you the performace that really brings these characters to life.

Sigh, okay. I concede. It may be time for all of us smarmy-arsed reviewer types to put our tails between our legs, because somebody just managed to make a genuinely impressive game using Unity Personal Edition.
Sure, they needed to reduce the otherwise "real-time" move mechanics to pointing-and-clicking, but that kinda thing is just "resourceful" in my book. First rule of being indie: don't try to take on the big boys. You ain't gonna make Bioshock: Infinite 2 on a free engine with a staff of less than ten people, boys and girls. Those kinds of production values are BOUGHT, plain and simple.
So how do you compensate for that? Innovation. And while Curse evidently isn't the most jaw-droppingly original game ever made, it certainly does a commendable job of turning its potential shortcomings into assets. That's clever game-making, kids.
So the first people I'm going to recommend this game to is anyone else - especially you lazy ♥♥♥♥ing Europeans - who are contemplating making a game with a small team on crap-all money. This game will do a great job of teaching you all how to make humble pie, while still retaining enough flavour to produce an agreeably tasty little treat.
One group I definitely WOULDN'T recommend this to are the anti-linearity brigade, 'cause, yup, it's pretty darned linear. There are moments where you have a bit of agency as to what order you investigate things in, but beyond that, the tightly-constructed plot pretty much leads you where it wants you to go, and decides in what order you open what door or investigate which piece of furniture. It's up to the individual to decide how much such a storytelling device peeves you. Me, I'm fine with it as long as there's good enough reason for it, and as long as I'm still taken on a journey. This game mostly succeeds on both of those counts, in my opinion. You may not agree.
Oh, and those people who don't like to READ: I'd be tempted to warn you people, too, if it wasn't for the fact that you can actually ignore the longer texts and opt for the short "summary" which the game offers (which you've gotta click through anyway, in order to progress through the game). In other words, those of us who DO like to read can take our sweet time, and the rest of you can just skim past all those "boring" bits. So best of both worlds right there. (Oh, and to the aforementioned Euro indie game developers: this game could also teach you a thing or two about how to WRITE NOTES in a competent and entertaining manner. In English, no less...)
Which brings us to two of the biggest questions you're all liable to ask, namely: can an ostensibly point-and-click game be SCARY? And is there any "action" to speak of, or is it entirely free of danger and/or time pressure?
Answer to the first question: yes, it's pretty scary. Not persistently terrifying, perhaps, but certainly spooky. Oodles of atmosphere, and some perfectly effective jump-scares. Oh, and some real-time do-or-die bits as well. Which brings us to our second question...
Yes, there is real-time action. Every now and then a nasty ghostie comes for you, and you have to destroy them with a concentrated burst of flashlight (why hello there, Mr Alan Wake)! It's no great shakes as action game mechanics go, and regrettably provides the game with some unnecessary "cheap deaths", but provides enough real-time tension to ensure that you'll have your flashlight at the ever-ready for these admirably tense occasions. Minus these moments, this would essentially be a mere "walking simulator", and I know how much you philistines hate THOSE.
Oh the whole, Curse reminded me of a cross between Layers of Fear, a limited-agency interactive novel, and the flawed-yet-interesting point-and-click "classic" Scratches. Don't get me wrong: if I were to compile a list of my all-time Top Forty horror games, this wouldn't even come close to making the grade. If, on the other hand, I was to compile a list of the top ten horror games released on Steam in the past year, I'd fancy its chances.
Is the price a bit steep? Yes. Probably. But Steam sales are a dime a dozen, so just wait for one of those if you're still unsure. If you only play three horror games a decade, DON'T make this one of them. But if, like myself, you play at least a dozen each and every year, this is probably one worth checking out.
Verdict: 8/10.
UPDATE: Since I wrote this review, I see the devs have been wise and dropped the price. Seven bucks? Sold!

You're a paranormal investigator and your task is to investigate a haunted house.

The big plus in this game that its kept me going on just to see what was coming next. Its creepy at times, got some jumpscares and imo its well made in terms of gameplay, story (great ending!), atmosphere, graphics, animations and sounds.

I give it a thumbsup because of that.
However, for people who are interested in buying I have to point out some issues:
- There's no freedom and no free movement. You move from one spot/room to another and you have to finish investigating until everything is covered. Only then you can move to the next spot/room. Rinse & Repeat.

- It´s linear. The only choice I had in is wether to start investigating the library or dining room. I finished the library and went into the Dining Room after I completed the first route. I guess its the same if you would start in the dining. Sometimes you can choose wether to interact with an item or not, but thats it.
- Its a REALLY slow game. Because you have no free movement you'll have to watch a load of movement and door opening animations before you can continue your investigation.
- You'll die. For instance there are scenes where you have to shine your flashlight for some time at an approaching ghost. You never know which direction its coming from as it can change after a reload. I also died because I made a wrong choice in a conversation with a ghost.
The biggest problem with dying is that you have to redo a couple of actions. And because its a slow game its annoying. Especially the last part of the game where its easy to make a small mistake. I think I had to do that part about 20 times before I was succesfull. I almost gave up on it because I was getting really mad. (It took 1.5 minutes to get to the part where I kept dying. You understand having to sit through this 20 times can get your blood boiling...)
- Unplug your controller! At some point I had a conversation with a ghost and could ask some questions. I had to end this in the proper way or I would die. I kept dying because I wasnt able to select the proper response (it just picked the first at hand automatically). After unplugging my controller it all worked fine. That was really annoying because it took some time before I figured it had to do with my controller.
- Its rather short. It took my 3.5h to complete it. You can take off 0.5 if youre a smarter player than I am. The very last part of this game took me way too long.

EDIT: Last update after finishing the game on easy.

The concept of digital novellas is really interesting. This game never claimed to be anything more, and should not be punished for its shortness. But this particular instance of a digital novella is not interesting at all—the story is neither compelling nor original, the characters are underdeveloped, and there is absolutely no sense that anything is at stake.

Despite being a bit shorter than I expected I really enjoyed this title.  It's a wonderful peice of work with a narrative that really fits in well with its cyberpunk setting.  Despite feeling like I should have been able to point-click and walk to an a spot in an area like a classical point and click adventure, the point-of-interest mechanic driving the game really does a good job of guiding the player through the narrative the author wishes to tell, but also provides sufficient non-critical interest points that add a nice touch to the overall experience of the game.

An excellent, scary, and fun ghost hunting game for once with hardness levels you can pick at the beginning! This is not your typical "point and click" adventure. Combining more a mondern style of point and click with first person action scenes throughout, this game surpasses many first person ghost games that are twice as expensive. You find yourself, a psychic ghost hunter, investigating the infamous Atherton Manor. Once there, you cannot leave and have no choice but to discover the secret to the hauntings that definitely can, and will, hurt you. The graphics are excellently creepy; dark enough to give that scary atmosphere with colors like red and dark umber saturating the scenes, but light enough that you can see what the heck is happening..most of the time ;). Every fear I have so far has been addressed, lol, from large spiders to darkness to ...well, won't give away too much; I don't want to ruin the great jump scares. This is not a game for people who do not like to read. Full of notes from a past ghost hunt gone bad in the 1980's (Gnarly dude!), you find yourself following their bread crumbs to the source of evil in the manor. There are also wondferful little additions that true horror movie lovers might recognize from classic horror films such as a recorded message left by Mr. Atherton via a victrola that plays itself when you enter his dark abode, similar to the same event in the classic  movie "Hellhouse" from a Richard Matheson award winning book of the same name.This game ROCKS!
A 10/10 game for playability, graphics, storyline, atmosphere, and originallity. Absolutely was delighted with this and hope Stormgod Studios makes more!

Just in time for Halloween, it's Curse. A point and click adventure you should buy, but for the length, price, and rage inducing, I can't say yes. I feel like saying no isn't right either, but it's not a yes.
The sad thing is, Curse has a lot going for it. While the story is slightly cliched, it starts off strong and it's actually kind of pretty. It's going to remind you of a lot of nostalgic games you played as a kid. It's not too easy, it has a slow creepy and WOW THAT'S DISTURBING WHO CAME UP WITH THIS! factor, and an approach that I do actually like.
I really wish there was an "on the fence" feature because that's what I really am for this game. On the fence.
Really. I should be praising it. There's a minor combat system in a point and click game! But it's actually difficult even on easy mode and severely spanks you for not getting it right the first time, then forces you to replay that slow action that led up to the combat over and over again until you pick route one, two, or three and get lucky to shine the flashlight on the ghost. It's pure luck and if you guess wrong or lift your finger off the spacebar too slowly/quickly, you're dead and it's START AGAIN FROM MUNDANE AND SLOW ACTION. This has led to at least four extra hours of playing time and no, that's not an angry exaggeration. I really wanted to enjoy that because combat, even if minor, in a point and click is pretty awesome and while it's not perfect, that's a pretty nice try. Just punishing me so severely for not getting it right feels like a kick to my stomach. When you get lucky enough to zap the ghost, they are disabled in a brilliant display of green fire and you feel pretty great about yourself.
Again, if you got lucky enough to zap them.
Then there's a bit of a disappointment that we have two "main baddies" to banish. There's a pretty interesting storyline and after you conquer the one in the first half, the one in the second half hardly matches up to the first one. Admittedly, a lot of video games suffer from this. The point is to hook you because you're probably going to stop playing after you get so far in the first half. It starts of amazingly strong and the storyline does keep you clicking around going "BUT WHAT NEXT? TELL ME. TELL ME!" It's not a let down at all that things aren't what they seem in the "Blood Manor". It's more that you're honestly wishing there was more to it and there just isn't as much there as you hoped. Especially since the regular price of the game (even if I got it on sale) makes me think I'm getting a little more. I was hoping for more than two (three-ish) ghosts. If this house is that haunted, I was hoping to make contact with more than just what I made contact with. There's a lot more hinted in story that happens and I was just hoping to see a little more.
Curse also has this ugly illusion of choice. Sometimes you get to investigate on your own...but only what the game illuminates for you to investigate. You get the option to not 'read' certain items and this will keep you from being attacked by the ghosts in the house, but that's not really a choice. Truthfully, the biggest choice I got to make in the game was left or right. And then everything else was YOU MUST CHECK EVERYTHING ONE BY ONE AND ONLY WHAT WE SAY YOU CAN LOOK AT. It felt very, very painful to do that. You can't even make your character go backwards to double check something. It's ridiculous.
There is the minor issue with the options. I can't mess with my mouse options, which is all over the place in this game. Listen, my mouse isn't this sensitive on my regular screen. How come I'm metaphorically sneezing here and it's going bonkers? You need to give me some more options here other than fullscreen/windowed and to change the dimensions. You really need to do a little more here for me. I can't be the only one swearing when a game does this.
There's also an odd imbalance to the "jumpscares" from the first and second half of the game. Second half has some silly skeletons under a sheet that made me giggle and yell spoopy while the first half of the game made me feel very upset and emotionally attached to a ghost trying to rip my face off. The pacing just seems weird. It's almost like someone played half way, got offended, and then they decided to done it down with a silly crawling ghost and "spoopy scary skeletons" and "standard covenant with Satan". It's fine, it's just a horror trope and one many are tired of. While I don't care, it's something people are going to hone in on and start shredding to bits...
Let's look at some strong points here. Say we try to look at Curse as a haunted house simulator without too much key collecting. Mission accomplished if so. You've got a decent sized house to explore, get a few scares, have things peer at you from outside, and then move on to the next room. Not bad. We've got a virtual ouija board without the threat of inviting demons and great aunt Ethel to come haunt us. Awesome. We have pop culture references to classic Ghost Busters and even a slug at Five Nights at Freddy's. The game also seems to be self aware at general paranormal silliness. There's a lot to like here. The character design also is rather nice when it comes to Mary and Eve. You know...when they aren't dripping blood, throwing scissors, or punching you... Oh and the music is lovely. It matches the feelings of the investigation into the manor. From tense violins to sad music while investigating a child's toybox, you'll notice the music is really nice...
It's just all of those nice points are hard to remember when I'm dying and I have to replay parts over and over again while I'm watching a ghost punch me in the face and hearing the little gagging death noises. It really harshes my vibe. There goes my enjoyment just because of my stupid frustration. That wasn't all that got my goat, so to say...
There's also a few game crashing bugs present. If you try to switch your difficulty after dying to a ghost and restarting your game, that ghosts will not show up except for cutscenes. You cannot play the phonograph in the hall and you cannot progress. If you want to switch difficulties after dying, please exit your game. If you die to a ghost and want to fiddle with options in between, just don't do it and wait until you have a ghost-free moment to do that. You will seemingly bug out your game and need to restart everything. I encountered these bugs more than once.
As standard with my reviews, here's your health hazards. Flashing lightning and other bright lights are not appropriate to those suffering from seizures or those sensitive to quick changes of light. While I suffer from severe migraines and this did not trigger a migraine, this is certainly migraine territory gaming. Game with caution.

I'm going to write a long paragraph about this game.  As much as I've played thus far, this Unity-based game is quite unique.  You get to play the role of a ghost hunter sorta like the ones on tv, except you don't see with nightvision goggles and aren't searching for spirit orbs.  You are blessed/cursed with the ability of psychometry at your disposal and you also get to have (take a deep breath) .....a flashlight!  You point and click where it allows you to; to nativigate around the haunted estate with a macabre history.  You also point and click to investigate clues/notes or to pick up keys or cursed items when allowed to.  You have a basic inventory system that allows you to utilize those keys or items when you're prompted to do so.  But (this is the downside), you don't get to do any free exploration and this I have to say, makes this game feel like it on rails.  However, What makes this game FUN is that you'll feel that the manifestations or malevolent paranormal entities could try to appear and also try to kill you at ANY time.  You never know what's going to happen next in terms of WHEN these haunting manifestations will occur as you are playing.  Although this game has sequentialized jumpscares, you'll get to use that SPECIAL flashlight or yours to defend yourself whenever you are attacked, so you aren't completely helpless like most other indie games with jumpscares.  I've encountered many (oH♥♥♥♥♥♥ Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥) instances where I had to quickly turn my flashlight weapon on at a moments notice.  The cool part is that if you get killed you have the option to pick-up right about where you were just before you became the ghost's 81tcH.  Additionally, during the flight or fight encounters with these evil spirits, the paranormal entities do not attack from the same location twice so you're randomly being brutalized.  The devs did a great job of creating a tense atmos-FEAR in regards to that. The music is creepy.  The creeks of doors and drawers opening on their own, the random scatch noises, and the echoing whispers, voices, and giggling sounds of the spirits are astounding.  The story is also fascinating in that you uncover in the beginning that a paranormal investigation team had been dispatched to the same estate in the recent past but their disappearance became an unsolved mystery.  You're tasked at trying to solve the unsolve mystery of their disappearance while trying to excorcise the estate at the same time.  That's just awesome right there.  Try this game out when the free demo gets released.  If you enjoy it like I do, then BUY the game.

Murder is a "game" that features neither gameplay nor story. The entire thing is over in 22 minutes, and most of that will be watching the character walking, waiting for the elevator, or waiting for a train to arrive.
The prologue (the first ten minutes of the game) involves diving into a damaged robot's brain and setting up the second part, then the credits roll once. The credits are interrupted by waking up again and walking through the same three locations as the prologue. This time, the people are replaced with a glitchy man speaking in Matrix Architect technobabble. The experience ends by doing the exact same thing, diving into the damaged robot's brain and hearing the same lines of dialogue. The end. No closure, no development, just hints that a plot might have happened in ten minutes if the second credits roll had not interfered.
The voice acting is serviceable, the pixel art is very evocative of classic cyberpunk movies, and the ambient music fits the scenes. There are no puzzles, just clicking on an object to walk to it or change scenes. This was a big disappointment, all style and no substance.

Though the setting and story initially seems intriguing, the game is just too damn short, the voice-acting too damn poor and to top it all off, there are typos in a game with a script that would fit on half a page.
I have played Thirty Flight of Loving and loved it, the length didn't bother me. But Thirty Flight was probably at least 15 minutes and I guess my lower limit for a game is somewhere above the 7 minutes I spent on this.
Despite my nowadays too common complaint on game-length as a measurement of worth I think that 7 minutes of quality would be enough. But the quality just isn't there.

Murder is a short game.
Murder fails to engage as a game, and though it clearly wants to be seen as a short story told using pixel graphics and several interactive elements it fails on this front also.
As a game Murder is low on content, low on interaction, low on features.
As a story Murder fails to really establish anything like setting or characters, has only a few bits of dialogue and no real core or content, not so much mystery as it is missing.
At first I thought the story was dropping us in at the deep end to let us take everything in but then it just sort of... ended.
All this is rather sad as I genuinely enjoyed the music and style for this game.

I started with Genesis, then Broken World and there is Imperium now. This is game is what HoMaM used to be. In a battle every unit counts. Loss of veteran unit is doubly painful. Finding the right mix of units and skills pays off.
At the beginning of a campaign you are either introduced to a given situation and continue from there with already levelled hero/es or you start from scratch (the sandbox). I was a great fan of the original mega campaign in Genesis and BW. It is sadly not present here in Imperium. But the sandbox  replaces (kind of) the experience of starting with one province, your stronghold, lvl 1 hero and a land to conquer.
The map is divided into provinces. Each province can be upgraded by 3 different buildings (unlocked at the stronghold). Each building can have upgrades offering additional benefits. A province is usually guarded by local population (humans, goblins, orcs, nomads, lizards, etc.). After your hero attack the province and wins the battle / or gets a deal through diplomacy option, you gain access to its resouces.
These are gem income, gold income and special resources (like iron, mithril, black lotus, etc.). Gold is primarily used to buy buildings (province/stronghold), recruit units/heroes, buy items at stores and during random events.
Gems are also needed for units, events and to power your spells and rituals.
Each province can be explored, which can reveal additional dungeons = battles, events or special resources. One can also station units at provinces or hire a guard.
There are also buildings and stores offering quests often in exchange for powerful items. One can also find schematics for special buildings.
Enemy is eliminated once its stronghold is captured.
The number of buildings which can be built in the stronghold is also huge and they are expensive. Better give the planning and your playstyle some thought beforehand!
At some point your hero will become quite strong and it will have no problem to conquer AI oponents. But even then there is plenty to explore and the high level units are challenging to beat. And there is the Arena.
The AI itself depends on brute force. Usually the battles are tipped in favor of AI. Either having better units or simply more units than you in a regular battle with environment. If AI gets their heroes going, they can press you nicely in hero vs. hero battles.
All in all, there is a good attention to detail, the mechanics are well done. Very enjoyable game.

I WANT A MOTORCYCLE CHASE WITH A FRIGGIN HELICOPTER COMING AT THE PLAYERS!  THEN, I WANT A PART IN THE GAME WHERE PLAYERS FIGHT A T-REX, FROM A HANG GLIDER!" The movement and hand-to-hand combat system is fun as hell, but players may find it difficult to use when the game constantly flashes to tedious cut scenes or forces your camera angle to look at some minuet detail going on in the background.  These interruptions or hiccups in gameplay happen far too often; it was as if the developers were concerned that players might not catch the small details they inserted, so they force you to look at them, every time. A short but somewhat challenging game. Fans of
will appreciate the game's sense of humor, and its gameplay is similar. For players familiar with the bullet hell genre,
will be quite easy. A warm up exercise, maybe. But for the casual gamer, this is a fun hour or two. Your time with the game will go by fast regardless.
Despite this, I don't wish the game was any longer. Hidden upgrades to look for and the multitude of short dialogues you can get for the game's ending were a nice addition that could take away some of the monotony from replays.
In addition, this game has more variety and complexity in its types of enemies than some triple-A titles I've played this year, with undoubtedly less code than said big budget titles. Another refreshing difference is that the game barely holds your hand. Only your controls are explained, involving a single button's functions, and the four directions. The player heads out into the world and just starts playing. Despite having not informed the player of what certain enemies do, he or she can figure out their behaviors and easily learn them all, without the game using a character like Megaman X's Alia to instruct the player on what to do. This element of
makes it a charming re-creation of the good side of games from the era of the Commodore vic-20 and 64 to the NES, with less repetition and punishing difficulty, and more variety.
My only problem was that the game was not resizeable, but simply zoomed in. Up close, it seemed less sharp. This was less of a problem and more of a slight annoyance, which disappeared when I sat back on my couch with a controller, further away from the screen.
is a great demonstration of the developer's understanding of game design, and a fine example of what they can do in a very short amount of time.

This game throws you in at the deep end. You have so many more options than in other first person shooters, and as a result every time you die you're immediately thinking about what else you could have done, what other angles you could have taken and what mistakes your opponents were making that you could have capitalised on. The community is a little better than most, which helps. The developers have done a great job fixing bugs and listening to the player base, but they do make a lot of work for themselves by not testing enough, so things do go wrong at times. Oh, and don't get the starter edition, you'll have enough trouble unlocking everything on the regular one.

First of all, who doesn't like slenderman? Just beat this with my friends today. It has a lot of good jumpscares, and is way funner when you play with your friends. This is the first horror survival game that i've ever played. Definitely won't get some sleep tonight. This game is really worth it.

There's a common complaint among fans of horror video games that very few of the titles in the genre have any real subtlety anymore. It's hard not to agree after having played such games as Dead Space or any recent Silent Hill game. Slender: The Arrival at least attemps to reverse that trend by waiting until around the twenty-minute mark to actually show the eponymous character on screen. Even so, The Arrival is little more than an amalgamation of boring horror cliches that do very little to actually frighten the player once they've figured out the game's basic mechanics.
The main premise of Slender is that you are a guy... or a girl... looking for someone named Katie. It's not exactly very big on the details, and I guess the developers wanted to leave those up to the player so that they wouldn't have to go through the trouble of writing an actual plot. The player spends most of the game wandering through a forest that's roughtly the size of an average high school auditorium looking for "clues" that look more like the drawings of a troubled 9-year-old who thinks he's "so hardcore". All the while being pursued by some faceless guy in a suit that was likely ripped off from Agent 47.
Let me step away from the idiotic premise for a moment, so that I can harp on how technically unimpressive the game is. Notwithstanding the fact that it's only $3 on sale (honestly, it's not even worth that much). The Arrival looks like just another generic "indie" game that was developed by a team of college kids in their mothers' basement. The lighting is godawful; the player's flashlight is the only light source that actually illuminates the surrounding area. Aside from the player character's head bobbing back and forth, there is no animation to speak of. Slenderman appears out of view and causes some cheap distortion in the player's view. That's it. Nothing else. Even the game's indie credentials don't absolve it from the fact that it was obviously developed on a shoestring budget by a bunch of people who have no idea what they're doing. The "soundtrack" consists of a handful of boring ambient tracks that try desperately to create a tense and oppressive atmosphere, but manage to fail at both, only serving to exacerbate just how boring the game actually is.
Aside from all of that, between the bad lighting, poor level design, and sparse information, the game's main objective is too difficult, and the game itself too uninteresting to inspire the player to rise to the challenge. If you have a friend or family member who is into Slenderman and also under the age of twelve, this might be a worthwhile purchase. Otherwise, don't even bother, just stick to Marble Hornets.

It's a bit hard to quickly describe Jazzpunk - it is a satirical, humorous and surreal spy game, focused more on exploration than puzzles, though it does have a mini fps game inside and some other goodies.  It is first person.  The game references some movies and games in its humor, but you don't need to be hyper aware of those in order to find the game funny and enjoy your experience.  I intentionally am leaving this review vague, because the discovery aspect of this game is half the fun.
Overall this was the funniest game I played in 2014, and I highly recommend it.  I even plan on replaying it to get some more achievements.

Well it isn't pretty. There can be beauty in simplicity, but this isn't that.
It isn't deep. There's no atmosphere, I'm not even convinced the game has a plot.
And, well, it seems like the game really thinks its funny but it just isn't. I can appreciate some cheap humor but that's all the game has. I chuckled at some opening gags but the charm quickly wore thin. There's no effort put into developing jokes, nor do any gags require even the slightest bit of brain activity. There's no characterization, no charm.
It's like sitting through a comedy show where the humor never gets beyond, "a man steps into a bar -- ouch."
The vision of this bizarre world was perfectly realized. It is so dense with brilliance you won't even care how short it is.
A game composed entirely of the irreverent humor from Lucas Arts' games.  A shorter game, even exploring the world, but its length allows it to not overstay its welcome.

If you like FPS games, you'll like this, because it's every other FPS, all at once.
* You're the only survivor of your team, which is killed off before you're actually briefed on your mission.
* You're special, because you've got this super armor.
* There are soldiers, working for an evil corporation. In a shocking twist, you use their weapons against them.
* Also, aliens.
* Also, there's a horrible disease and the city is quarantined, using extremely brutal yet totally ineffective methods.
* US flags fscking everywhere
* You have to rescue some guy, who keeps giving you orders, and who somehow knows in general everything that's going on within a few miles of his location, but can't explain anything in detail.
* Also, guy who needs rescuing keeps getting angry at you because you're taking so long, despite your near-death with the rest of your team, your having to travel miles on foot through all sorts of absurd side-paths, and your having to single-handedly defeat several hundred soldiers.
* Hey, ammo cache! I wonder if there's a big fight coming up?
* Hey, laser-guided RPG! I wonder if I'm just about to fight a helicopter gunship?
* Occasionally, the game pauses for a bit of tutorial, pointing out that you have tactical options -- which are extremely difficult to actually pull off, and don't offer any advantage over the standard tactic I've used in every computer game I've played in thirty years, which is to work around the edges and pick off enemies in detail, because sneaking through the middle always means you just fight everyone at once.
Uniquely, and perhaps a first for any FPS, CRPG, and for the entire meta-genre of speculative narrative, the horrible disease does NOT turn people into zombie. At least not so far -- I'm only a few hours into this game.
The graphics are quite good. The designers are of the school of thought where there's incredible detail and extent, but you don't feel you can actually explore much. It's almost the opposite approach of Bethesda-style games, in which there's far less fine detail, but lots of time and space to explore.
The game has several glitches. For instance, I often find I'm unable to switch between semi-automatic and full-automatic on my weapons. At least once, I had a scripted event fail to trigger. Both these problems were solved by exiting, and going back to a save-point.
Excellent game with excellent graphics! You should definetely buy this game! :)

TL; DR Highly enjoyed + recommended, and it's free so it can't hurt to try it out anyway.
Aside from an attention-grabbing mysterious prologue about a psychopathic murderer, Lucid9: Inciting Incident starts off as what may seem like a typical high school slice of life RomCom. Set in the near future of 2018, you have your highly intelligent but seemingly lazy, cynical and snarky male protagonist. You also have the female childhood friend love interest who stuck up for him in the past, helped him get through some past trauma and essentially stick to him like glue his entire life, whilst never actually confessing to him. You even have childhood friend number two, the female transfer student, and let's not forget the protagonist's male allies either;  the apparently aloof, warm-hearted and kind womanizing support character number 1, and support character number 2, the jock (although in his defence his grades are superb). Oh and of course the first female childhood friend has a female friend support character trying to match make the protagonist despite also having feel-
Ok, so you get the idea. As one of the characters say, the protagonist's school life seems like the perfect set up for a 'really crap anime'.
Thankfully, it is anything but.
Despite the initial setup that might send warning signs of a 'cliche', 'boring' or 'generic' environment, the witty dialogue, references, memes and humorous character chemistry create a thoroughly entertaining and amusing experience. The dialogue is spectacular, which is probably partially due to the fact this is an original English story, but to the writers' credit, I'm still surprised by how good the dialogue is.  As you can probably tell, I really enjoyed this section of the game; the protagonist's snarky attitude reminded me of Yuuji from Grisaia with his internal dialogues, and the cutesy art and music meshed together pretty well to create a fun slice of life RomCom.
Except, of course, that's not what this VN is about. Or at least that's not the main driving force behind the plot. Even throughout this happy-go-lucky style of plot, there is an undercurrent of a darker, more mysterious and dangerous force at work, just in case you didn't notice from the store page screaming murder and mystery at you. And this is where the story really picks up and becomes more about the mystery, murder and detective aspect rather than the high school life of an ordinary student. We see more about the tragic past of the protagonist and his friends, and more foreboding of the murderer's intentions with the chilling music emphasizing the danger as we attempt to deduce who it is. However,  despite the transition into the faster paced plot driven 2nd half of the VN, the focus of the original story is never lost. That is to say, even with all the events in the plot building up climatically to the final showdown, there is always a focus on the main character, his relationships, his past and how he'll change for the better, which I think is a pretty good thing. Because if I had to pick one aspect of the game as a whole that I like the most I'd have to say the characters. Despite what I said about them coming off as generic and cliche at the start of the game, they develop and become fleshed-out, and they seem, believe it or not, human. Which is actually a big deal. They become relatable and pretty damn loveable, which is why they're my favourite part of Lucid9.
What impresses me the most though is the fact that this is done without any monetary support. To be frank, I was expecting the lack of monetary funding to result in compromises whether it be in the technical elements like the settings/menu options or in the quality of the writing/art/music. But the art style fits the tone, the UI is polished and almost 40 tracks accompany the novel throughout, from the 'nostalgic emotional memory' feel to the 'imminent boss fight' feel, which really does enhance the effect of whatever may be going in the story at that time. For me, I usually place a lot more importance on the writing and art than anything else, but when all the other bits and pieces work, even I can appreciate what a difference they make to the overall quality.
Another technical element worth highlighting is the choice system, and the interactive aspect of the game in general. Some of the choices give access to new comedic scenes, CG arts or achievements but some of the others are more serious, dictating whether you reach the bad or 'true/good' end. I think a nice balance between difficulty and importance is achieved as a result, because it's pretty easy to either create meaningless choices or give options to a problem that is too tedious to solve by mistake. The few logic puzzles are an enjoyable aspect as they change the pace a bit and force you to think, but at the same time they're definitely accessible, and if you choose the wrong answer or the joke answer you're easily forgiven too. I'm eager to see more of them in the future since I suspect they will become more common in the individual heroine routes when the fundamental mystery plot is actually revealed.
I suppose the one gripe I have is that a technical feature that I think could be implemented is missing; a skip to the next choice feature, mostly for replaying + achievement/cg hunting. Personally I've never been that much of an achievement collector but I admit I get curious if I see a bunch of hidden achievements and missing CG art, enough to want to select the choices I didn't choose last time and see what happens. A skip to the next choice feature would help in that regard, rather than just using the ordinary skip function whilst making a lot of save points at all the choices.
Overall though, I'm pretty damn impressed by Lucid9. I'll definitely be looking forward to both the voice patch and the heroine route patch, since this is only the beginning after all. This is easily in my top 6 VNs, and to be honest, if you've gotten this far in the review and still aren't sure whether to try it or not, just do it. It's free after all.

I could not put this down for 9 hours straight immediately after download and installation, and then proceeded to yell about how good it is on Twitter. That alone not enough of an impression as to how recommendable this game is? Very well, keep reading!
THE DIALOGUE IS THE BEST I'VE HEARD IN A LONG TIME. If I were to come out with it thus far, the dialogue is one of the strongest points for this entire visual novel. The balance between comedy and seriousness is very... well, balanced as well as well-written. The dialogue just perhaps IS the strongest point of Lucid9. I have had so many laugh-out-loud moments reading the dialogue as well as shudders of fear because of this dialogue and any and all implications. It's so well-written for each character as well as the protagonist's narration. Even the text messages. Good lord, the text messages.
THE WRITING OVERALL IS SO VERY DETAILED. I do not think I have been as impressed with writing in a visual novel in my whole life. As mentioned, I believe dialogue to be the strongest thing in Lucid9, but the aforementioned narration of the protagonist is just as amazing with how descriptive it can be. May I add that it never overstays its welcome, either. If there's something funny but fast being commented on, then the response in narration is short, snappy, and funny. If it's serious, you bet it'll switch to longer panel/novel sections to describe it. As aforementioned, I feel the balance is on point. It feels like conversation and thoughts in real life.
THE CHARACTERS ARE ALL THREE-DIMENSIONAL... DESPITE WHAT YOU MAY THINK FROM APPEARANCES. You may being seeing these cutesy anime waifus and pretty bishounen anime husbandos being like, "ugh, I bet SHE'S gonna be all uguu kawaii desuuuuUUUU," or, "ugh, I bet the protagonist is gonna be ALL ABOUT that harem lifestyle!" No. Please. Please let me tell you that the characters are some of the most three-dimensional that I've ever seen. I can relate to many of the things the protagonist says, and can honestly feel like he... is human. He feels so human. And others around him feel human, too. Also believe me when I say they know what they're talking about here; these writers have knowledge in the cliches and tropes and popular trends of anime, pop culture, technology, and society when considering their characters and their interests, etc; they parody it frequently. (Or at least, I think so). So far, every single character has beat my original impressions based on appearances or introductions alone. I love everyone.
THE ART IS SOLID AND THE UI IS WELL ORGANIZED, STYLISTIC, AND CONSISTENT. Sprites are very pretty to look at! I prefer the male character art as opposed to the female style in this, but it's definitely right for those who want their cute waifus! The menus already (really, the title) can give off the tone this game wants to set and stays consistent all throughout. These 9 hours I have poored in definitely do stay comedic, but it almost feels like they want you to know what you're getting into. By the time you hit 'start,' you'll have an idea. The in-game menus (save, load, quit, etc.) are also much more effective than your usual visual novel. They are shortened to just icons in the corner of the screen and take up virtually no space so that the writing is put on the spotlight always.
THE MUSIC AND SOUND IS WELL-COMPOSED, CATCHY, AND VERY ATMOSPHERIC. The music the moment I got into the title screen is good, and again, sets a very specific... tone. The tracks are not too repetitve in my opinion unless your patience is short, and some of the more dramatic tracks are still on my brain right now. I'm no sound effects specialist or anything, but the sound effects are also very good. Please play with headphones on! The sounds of passing footsteps going from ear to ear is honestly lovely to hear as a touch.
THIS IS A FREE VISUAL NOVEL, BY THE WAY. IT'S FREE, and it goes FAR beyond my expectations for what a free visual novel usually contains. I have not gazed upon such a beauty of a visual novel in a very long time, especially being free. Have I mentioned that it's free?
IF I HAD ONE CRITICISM, it might be the... setting. All of this feels particularly strange being set in Japan. Not that I am against it at all because it does remind you it's Japanese, but it feels so very westernized. I guess that's me just being nitpicky about Japanese names, honorifics, etc that may give those unfamiliar a hard time later on.
EDIT:
I did not take into consideration at the time of writing that this is supposed to be introductory towards visual novels, meaning good for beginners in the genre, but is as well for seasoned readers. Though my point is still accurate with how westernized it feels, I believe that it is more appropriate that this is westernized for such a cause. IF YOU DISLIKE JAPANESE NAME WESTERNIZATION(?) THEN STEER CLEAR(???).
Still though, please consider trying Lucid9. I have already considered this much beyond a visual novel; I consider Lucid9 an experience.

TL;DR: Long, in depth review. Extremely well executed plot. Deep, flawed, very loveable, human like characters. Nice art (I'm too dumb to tell more than that). Notable BGM and some very polished minor details. FREE. FREE FREE FREE. Go play it.
Warning though: INTENSE.
FULL REVIEW:
I went into this game figuring I'd play it a little bit at a time. It looked ok enough, at least.
I marathoned it pretty much in one sitting. Skipped class to do it, too. It's THAT good. Even if you don't like the whole anime subculture, give it a shot. It dodges or parodies a lot of the cliches and presents a deep, thought provoking, and emotionally powerful story. If you DO like the anime subculture, you'll probably like it even more.
There's so much to be said about it... What a rollercoaster.
Very mild spoilers below; I won't discuss specific events, but I might mention themes and such. Anything I say you can figure out from the description of the game.
PLOT:
It seems like a nice, innocent little setting. High school, cute girls, blah blah slice of life.
It's not.
This is not to take away from the first part of the game; I enjoyed it. It was funny. About one third to half way through the story, though the plot gets more and more intense. It transitions from "cute and enjoyable" to "powerful and meaningful."
The climax is absolute insanity; it's horrifically disturbing yet simultaneously exhilirating, fueled all the more by the sudden influx of decisions you have to make. Everything is connected very logically and coherently, however. It's not some random shift that leaves you scratching your head wondering how you got there. It's an inevitable build up that leaves you both anticipating and dreading your arrival at that point. The contrast between the first and last parts of the game really emphasize a feeling of breakdown.
More generally, the plot is extremely well constructed and paced. It never felt too fast or too slow, which is probably why it managed to retain my horribly short attention span for such a long period. It flows really well too, where one event easily leads into the next. The actual events of the plot are good, but nothing spectacular, but the way it's executed makes it fantastic.
I loved the whole thing. Laughed like an idiot almost nonstop at the copious wit and comedy, raged at the insanity, cried when appropriate. It's an absolute rollercoaster, but so worth the ride.
Fair warning, though. It gets REALLY intense. And it really hurts sometimes. I liked the pain though.
If I have any complaint, it's that there were some plot points that I found disatisfying, as a player. I understand why they were made though. That doesn't mean I have to be happy about it. Lucid 9 unappolgetically proposes some very difficult themes and sticks to them. It's a story that has meaning.
The rest of the game HAS to come or I'll cry for real.
CHARACTERS:
My favorite part of any story. If I don't like the characters, I don't read. Simple as that.
Lucid 9 has really, really good characters.
While they're obviously based on common anime archetypes, Lucid 9's characters transcend the cliches on which they were born. They're nuanced, fleshed out, very flawed, and so, so lovable. They feel very human and complex, in a way that almost no other anime or game I've seen has managed. You won't always agree with them. Actually, a lot of the time, you probably won't. But they're all the better for it. And most of the time, you'll laugh and cry with them anyways. Just don't try to write yourself into the story or expect them to be perfect. This ain't no utopia.
Also, the girls are cute. And the guys. So if you don't care about any of the stuff I just spouted, at least there's that.
WRITING:
The writing is super smooth; this is very clearly a game that was originally written in english, not translated. I'm kind of a prose nerd, and some of the phrases gave me chills. The word-art is every bit as well done as the visual-art.
It's also hilarious and amazingly witty, especially in the beginning. At the end, when everything goes nuts, nothing feels cheesy, which is quite a feat in emotional scenes. I'm a very critical reader, but I had no issues with the writing. 10/10
Oh, and Gover Mecher is genius. Funniest satirical parody.
ART:
It's pretty. I like it. Sorry, I have the artistic talent of a brick. Go look at the pictures. You'll know if you like it or not.
MUSIC:
I don't notice the BGM in most games, but Lucid 9's really stood out to me for some reason. It manages to be catchy and noteworthy without overbearing, enough so that I felt inclined to include it as a seperate section.
OTHER:
There are plenty of little things that make the game feel very polished and add a lot to the atmosphere. Simple things like phone animations, ocassional game-esque overlays, and flashing or faded UI contribute heavily to a scene without being ostentatious. It's not stuff I would have thought of, but there are some scenes that I can't imagine without them.
VERDICT:
Excellent game. Deep, provactive, but fun and enjoyable. I read through it in one sitting and I don't even like VNs. Those of you brave souls that DO will probably like it even more.
Also, it's free. FREE. With far better production value than most commercial stories. You legit have nothing to lose. Except time, I guess. Which most of us will probably waste in worse ways anyways.

6.5/10 - If You Aren't Too Particula; This One May Be For You!
I really love Tower Defense so I tend to have some high expectations; this one definitely doesn't blow my mind but offers some cool elements to make it worth that $1. So our group had a surplus of these free Particula keys (30) so we all launched yesterday at 9:30 to investigate. Verdict = Really Fun. I highly recommend the Multiplayer; you must bring your own friends though which sucks!
The TD takes place within the human mind. Your towers are some sort of brain synapses that must eradicate negative thoughts such as jealousy, greed, self-consciousness and other negative thoughts that would cross one’s mind. Pretty clever on that front; this allowed the minimalist graphics to actually work and make sense. The levels are quite long and almost AFKable with some friends
There are quite a few things that didn't work for me. There was no tutorial; I was super confused at the start. Stick with it because the learning curve is quick. Multiplayer "works" but it’s dead since few play this game on the regular. There are only 3 levels to alternate between which include 6-7 levels of difficulty. This is cool but I'd rather have more variance in the maps instead. Finally, the chat box is MICRO; you can only type and read so much. Communication in multiplayer almost has to be done with voice to be effective.
Overall, not bad for $1! It's short and you need to BYOF (Bring Your Own Friends.) Free at Accidently Reviewed!

Resident Evil series have become long way from atmospheric single player horror games to a quick time events generic Third Person Shooter... but... the question is : Is it bad TPS ?
To answer this question I have to say that Resident Evil 4 in my opinion was the best in the series ( although RE 1 Mansion leaves this nostalgic feeling :). It combined Third person camera ( which I prefer than still camera shots ), good controls ( action oriented ) where you could shoot zombie in different place of the body and then finish with a melee to save ammo ( really fluid combat with doging etc. ) add to that amazing story with plot twist and a "Bit" of tension ( horror )... I couldn't ask for anything else. However that was RE 4. RE 6 is still ok game ( especially Leon campaign with slow moving zombies ) but it falls flat with creating atmosphere later on. It's more action oriented rather than "survival"... which takes the tension out of it and it feels a bit boring at times.
However I really like updated combat it feels fluid, easy melee, dodging takes a bit practise and feels good so you can spend a lot of time playing Merceneries Mode :) Which I would recommend.
Sadly however its hard to find people to play online... so If you buy it make sure you have friends or just enjoy singleplayer :p
For some Resident Evil fans this game might be a dissapointment but it works for me as a Third Person Shooter... not a survival horror...

After seeing this game in my recommended list for several months, I decided screw it and gave it a try. Needless to say, this game was more than I ever could have expected.
The story is incredibly simple, but seeing as this game is only about an hour long, its still very satisfying and enjoyable. This game has a very large number of endings, each determined by whom you decide to marry at the end of the game, it's honestly astounding how many people you can marry, and its clear that a lot of effort and heart was put into the endings, as you can marry just about every NPC in the game, plus some stuff that isn't even NPC's!
The game itself is litered with fun secrets, hidden rooms, secret passages, etc. Plus a short sidequest near the end. The NPC diolouge is quirky and enterntaining, all of these help increase how immersive and captivating this game is.
PR in a World of Hurt is home to some extremley addicting shoot-em-up gameplay. There are three levels of difficulty- Normal, Hard and Master. Normal mode is pretty easy, but the two higher levels provide a real challenge for fans of bullet-hell senarios or people just looking for an excuse to snap their keyboard over their knee. Attempting to get a 101% on master is seriously one of the most painful and frustrating things I've ever done, but it's still loads of fun doing so. Throughout the game, you can collect upgrades by opening chests, which make you more powerful in a variety of ways. This leads into yet another way the game excells, it is paced perfectly. Even though you get stronger as the game progresses, the enemies and situations you are put in still get progressively more difficult, starting at pushover in the begging and get to decently challenging towards the end. You never feel overpowered or that the game is rigged against you (Except in master).
Princess Remedy in a World of Hurt, while it may be very short, it's honestly one of the best experiences I've ever had on Steam, or PC gaming as a whole, and games like this are a shining beacon of the possibilities of Indie games. This game is only about 50MB, installs almost instantly, and best of all, it's absolutley free! Given this, I see no reason why anyone should not try this game out, trust me, you will not be disapointed.

Fan of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.? Then avoid this. The game divides the player base with tiers of classes. (I agree with some sort of progression, but this is terrible). You'll have some higher level players lower their gears tier to play at lower levels. Now, this doesn't sound like a bad thing, but then there's a Skill Tree. These Skills do uneven the odds for newer players, plus the fully modded weapons they have compared to yours. Again, this might not be a problem for I didn't have that MUCH trouble dealing with players with better gear than me. It rewards skillful players.
The main issue is the playerbase being divided. It's so disheartening to wait almost 15 minutes to finally get into a game, with maybe 2 other real players, and the rest are bots. It'll be a slow grind to get to the higher tiers to where, maybe real players are at.
Other issues are waiting for updates. The latest update added CO-OP PvE, and they ruined it by have a restriction on how many times you can play it, by you needing Keys to enter. What a huge slap in the face. Having it where you can run out of ammo during these missions, having stupid invisible anomolies where you have to spam throwing nuts everywhere,  unclear paths, and waitinf 15 minutes to get paired with non-native players that'll quit in 10 ~ 20 minutes.
The pros of the game is, it feels pretty good. Gunplay is very nice, but it's not something you'll feel really rewarded for when all you play against are bots. The guns also sound amazing -- I think one of the best sounding guns I heard in a long time. Definitely immerses you into the world. But even with the goods, it does not outweight the bad.
Just go install S.T.A.L.K.E.R., and have more fun.

Well lets see. 15 hours in. A few bugs here and there but not game breaking. This is a very good strategy game if you ask me. An interesting take on the genre. There is a bit of rng thrown in but not enough to hamper your goals.  There is a lot to do and see in this title. You build up your castle whilst your hero(s) explore the lands around you building up your heros levels. You can recruit an army for each hero as well. There is a lot of variety from little goblins to obsidian golems. Building your castle up is good too. The more you build the better your lands are. If you build certain buildings in your castle, it allows you to build certain buildings in your provinces. Provinces fuel your gold and gems(used for magic). I find it quite enjoyable to build up a scout and work one end of the shard(map) and a sorcerer to work the opposite side. There are hundreds of items to find and craft and hundreds of beasties to fight. I litterally spent hundreds of hours on the first Eador a few years ago on my friends pc. Then the second came out and spent a few hundred more. I fully expect to put a few hundred hours on this gem of a game and hope that the devs continue updating. And if the devs are listening, Consider building a new version. There are plenty of loyal fans and new players that are willing to invest in a well polished game. I might also consider a new way of advertising. Im on steam every day and I just happened to of bumped into this title. I had no idea it was released, let alone a year ago. Say hey to Nestur for me!

One of the few times a game has actually made me care about a rectangle...or rather several rectangles.  Thomas Was Alone is a very simplistic looking game...until you start to play it.
Pros:
-Gameplay: In short, it is a puzzle, platformer, but with an interesting mechanic. Each different square or rectangle is given its own jump ability...or lack thereof in the case of Chris. And some can float on water. No two squares/rectangles are the same and you'll be utilizing them in different ways to solve the puzzle and move on to the next room. It can be a little frustrating at times or a little tricky, but the payoff is a sense of accomplishement and more of the story. The game is always evolving, throwing in new game mechanics, but none are particularly hard to learn. (The upside one can be a little tricky.)
-Voice over: While there are many different characters within the game, there is only one voice actor: the narrator, kind of like Bastion. But this guy doesn't have the cool, slick voice that the guy from Bastion does. Instead, it's a soothing, British accent. (I'm bad at figuring out which accent is which.) He sounds a bit like a calm Wheatley.
-Puzzles: They are entertaining and (at times) a bit challening. The game goes easy on  you when you get a new game mechanic and then slowly ramps up the difficulty with that game mechanic.
-Story: It is a simple one about a bunch of A.I.s (and well...I'll let you find out the rest) that unfolds as you go. While it is simple, it's certainly is entertaining and well presented.

Resident Evil 6: Biohazard was a bit of a... mystery to me. Unlike with Resident Evil 4 and 5, I can't tell if I really hated it or really liked it. Maybe I'll say I feel both ways because - like anything else that's popular in our world - the game had its golden moments - good gameplay, kept me on my toes - as well as its meh moments - never enough ammo, literal dead ends against some enemies, bosses that won't die. Mind, for me, Resident Evil 4 and 5 just kind of got to the point and basically stated at the start of their games, "Resident Evil 4 is going to be old style and be scary while also being the newest third person shooter. Resident Evil 5 is just going to be outright zombie smashing, sharp shooting, partner cooperative excitement".
The least I gathered on Resident Evil 6 was this, "We're going to take everything from the latest games and... What are we going to do with it? Oh, yeah, right, you're going to have a choice over which type of game you want to play. First off, there are four decent or such campaigns in the title. One is Leon's: Classical scary, zombies eating people type of stuff and you trying not to get eaten. Another is Chris's; basically a third person shooter against terrorist zombies. Third is the newest character's, Jake's; a guy with a mysterious past who has to save the world itself. Fourth is Ada's; just a frustrating, overwhelming, annoying storyline filled with puzzles, riddles and drama."
So, seriously, back to my review, sorry for my rambling... God, Resident Evil 4 is still the best third person shooter/scary title that Capcom has come out with since it remodified itself. Resident Evil 5 just kind of dropped the scary and became a action packed thriller. And as for Resident Evil 6, the only real good thing I found that came out of that was the newest character, Jake Muller, along with the Mercenaries Game Mode. If you play R6, you'll know what I'm talking about here. As for my rating: 7/10. The game really should have been worked on a little more.
P.S - If Capcom intends to keep going with their, ugh, zombie horror/action series - I don't know what Resident Evil is anymore these days, blah - they should definitely make the next game based on Jake Muller. That'll save them and their fans a lot of grief I do believe.

My review of resident evil 6:
This game is great but struggling with a few bugs and errors/complications. The graphics are nice mostly. Textures are well made, and effects are very good. Also, the sound is quite good with music that reflects the current scenarion in the game. The developers chose weapons most carefully, which i like. For the AI in the game, it is much better than in RE5. So now you can play Resident Evil in single player mode without getting too frustrated. Many people complained that it was too many QTE:s in the game, but i think you get used to it. The controls are mostly ok, introducing the new free movement for the series. There is sometimes hard as you don't really want to do what the game thinks you want to, e. g. move over a box .. but you'll get more or less used to it.
Going back to the original roots of the game, i would say that playing Leon and Helena Chapter 1-3, and Jake & Sherry Chapter 2, was what took this game mostly to it's roots (RE1,2,3). The Chris campaign was really messy with too many hard enemies/QTE kinda.
I think that the story is pretty well defined (except for the chris campaign maybe). You have good interaction between the different characters of the game.
Overall pros and cons:
+ The Leon and Helena Campaign
+ Nice graphics
+ Nice choice of weapons
+ Good controls for the PC (compared to the previous entries)
- The Chris Campaign
- The controls are a bit messy sometimes
- Too many QTE:s in some chapters

If you like Minesweeper you'll like this game bottom line. There is a dungeon mode that plays out exactly like Minesweeper but what makes this game unique is it lets you get competitive and play against another human or CPU in a battle mode where you compete for who can find the most mana (mines) the fastest. You then use your acquired mana to attack and ultimately defeat the opponent. There's a decent cast of characters to choose from each with their own special ability that'll either make finding mana easier for you or harder for them. I feel the reason why this game has mixed reviews is because its  taking an already complicated game and making things even more complicated. Again if you're a fan of Minesweeper this is game is definitely worth getting otherwise you may be better off passing on this one or waiting for it to go on sale.

The premise is excellent on paper - multiplayer competitive minesweeper. Unfortunately, all of the parts put together fail to come together to create a good game. Moreover, the game is technically poorly done - it's clearly unoptimized, and this causes issues.
In the following, I do not use the game's terminology. This is because this game is clearly multiplayer competitive minesweeper. The core mechanic is the following:
You control a character, you collect mines. Your character moves around a map with hexes. Each hex tells you how many mines are adjacent to it. You see the values on the hexes surrounding your character. You place a marker where there is a mine, and if you're correct, your marker is placed on the mine. Every mine you correctly place adds to your chain, and the higher your chain is the higher your score multiplier is. You can purposefully break your chain, which gives you all of the points. Alternatively, your chain is automatically broken when all of the mines have been found on the level, and a new level begins. If you try to place a marker where there is not a mine, either your chain breaks for you (1P) or you lose all the markers you have placed (2P). You win when you increase the score gap between yourself and your opponent by a certain number.
(Those of you reading who have played will have noticed that I've failed to discuss the attacking mechanic. That is because it is superfluous - all you have to do is realize that your attack score is above a certain threshold to win.)
The secondary mechanic is that each character has a special attack, which they can use after a cooldown. These special attacks usually restrict the opposing character's movement in some fashion, although some are more interesting.
This leads to the question: what is this game really about? The core mechanic suggests that the goal would be "the player who figures out where the mines are first and fastest wins," but the fact that the characters move rather slowly, combined with the fact that the special attacks are designed to make your characters move even slower, suggest that this is not it. It's not a blind game of snatch-em-up either; you have to know where the mines are in order to do well. It's an attempt at a combination of both.
This is the flaw, and it is fundamental. The game has technical problems which often lead to the accidental blowing of chains, but even without that problem, the game is bad. The core mechanic and the secondary mechanic lead to a sort of anti-synergy, which makes the game feel like a disjointed and schizophrenic mess of an idea. There are mechanics that could have been completely stripped away leaving the game fundamentally unchanged, and most importantly, the game fails to correctly target any audience well enough for anyone to particularly enjoy it. Everything this game does well is done better elsewhere.

I remember spending hours playing minesweeper way back. So when I read about this game being based on the concept of minesweeper but more players I was intrigued. Are you curious too? Well, play it, it’ll be a refreshing discovery. You’ll enjoy it (more if you play with a controller, because of diagonal movement).

ManaCollect is competitive minesweeper where two players compete to clear the same board. If you can mark all the bombs by yourself you get a massive bonus, and if you make a mistake, you lose all the correct mines you have identified no the board. Each character also has a special skill that can be used strategically to hinder the opponent's mine finding efforts. When you have found enough mines you can launch attacks on the other player which, after you deal sufficient damage, will win the game.
Overall I found the game somewhat mediocre. It is fun if you have a friend who also loves minesweeper I guess. I own all the Eador titles, Imperium I got early and it had very few features, but they have continued to develop and improve the game.
The best thing is they have NOT lost the good parts from the first two but have tried to add features and items.
Yes some bugs still exist and some things have not been fixed but they are not really game breaking bugs, they annoy me but are able to work around and with a turn by turn auto save are mostly able to do over.
You will need a master save about every hour not so much because of the game but because 5 turns something may have happened had you known say 7 turns past you could have avoided but that is personal preference vs game issues.
End of the review if you like turn based games, you like upgrading units, if you like many choices and no "right" way to finish ,  Then you will enjoy Eador.
Whats the difference between this title and others, different units, different types of game play,
Masters of the broken world you had shards to conqure and gain power.  Imperium you have different storys to play out with chapters vs shards and different options to carry over uints/items.
One game not "better" than the other more each game plays different and allows different options but the basic game play turn by turn is the same.  A good example of if its not broken don't fix it.

This game is a good start but doesn't follow it's best notes to completion. That said, it is FREE, so all you lose is time.
The game art is really good. The tutorial is barebones but gets the job done. You start out with a small, weak ship that can only kill some satellites without too much danger. When you earn more money, you can get better ships. Even the second ship is good enough to fight some enemies with so you can do more. The combat with enemy ships was fun, but it was sometimes too hard to find them.
The game does a good job of communicating when you're near an enemy that will kick your butt too hard. One detail I loved is that if you fly too close to a sun, you start to take damage.
The problems with this game are mostly with the interface, specifically the camera. The only control problem is that you can only go forward and rotate. While it was somewhat cool to build speed and then fly backwards like a real space ship, it makes combat harder. The other problem is that because of the poor view, you have little time to react if an asteroid suddenly appears in your path. This is a big deal because collisions bypass your shields and damage your hull. The problem with this is that if you are stationary, you will automatically repair if you have a repair tool. If you have taken more than 2 or 3 points of damage, it will use up one tool, no matter if you are repairing 4 points of damage or 20. Unless you move or shoot, in which case it will stop, requiring you to use another tool if you want to repair again.
The camera troubles continue when approaching planets. It will swing around so the surface is below you, which is nice, but it gets annoying when you fly around that threshold and the camera keeps moving back and forth. Also, it's far too zoomed again, so you can't see the surface of the planet very well.
I did have some fun with the combat, but ultimately there isn't much to do.  The game is the base of a much better one.
