As a pixel art lover, I loved this game. It's beautiful.
As a point & click adventure fan, I say it has potential.
As a player, I'm frustrated with it. Too short.
ART:
This game art is incredible, great perspective, great animations, great colour palette, great characters. If I had to rate this game into an ART rank it would be between GODS WILL BE WATCHING and SWORD & SORCERY, it still has a bit to evolve, but I'd give it a sweet 8/10 to it's Art & Graphics. Also, the soundtrack is awesome.
GAMEPLAY:
As a Point & Click adventure, this game starts really well giving the players some options to explore the rooms and interact, but as each scene passes there are fewer and fewer options, and there aren't that many scenes. Also the amount of cutscenes and the fact you can't walk around are annoying, the game should be a bit more player-driven. For Gameplay I'd say it's worth a 3/10.
STORYLINE:
The main problem of this game is it's length. It is waaaaaaay too short. As for a first act where you are supposed to present a bit of the world, the character, the antagonist and dive into the fantasy, this game lacks the necessary length. The plot might be very interesting or be obvious as most guessed, but we can't really tell because it ends before we can finish connect with it. And this makes me sad and angry. Such a potential wasted, I almost asked for a refund. The story might or might not have potential we can't even evaluate ??/10.
CONCLUSION:
I know development is expensive, but I really think this game has invested it's resources the wrong way. I believe almost all players will complain that this game should have been longer, because by the time we are diving in it's fantasy... it ends. Also, I believe there wasn't the need for so much voice acting, foley and unnecessary animations like the elevator one. These probably wasted time and resources that could have been used for making a few more scenes and interactions so players could at least have enough game time to create a connection with the game. And since we're talking about resouces, I've seen longer and better games achieved with smaller teams. The game itself is not worth buying, but I'd recommend for those who support good and potential indie developers.

There is no rating system available here.  It's just "Yes" or "No."  I can't say to stay away from this game entirely.  There are merits.  However, for fans of the RE series, this is an utter disappointment. I didn't play the game until it had been out for a year or so.  I read the reviews ahead of time and thought, "They are blowing this out of proportion.  It can't be that bad."  Well, I was wrong.  Compared to the other games in the series, it is pablum.  It is generic.  And I think that is the biggest criticism that I can come up with.  It doesn't allow for a deep, immersive experience because it doesn't provide for an individualized experience.  It takes you by the hand, tells you where to go, and lets you shoot in the meantime.  The story element is intriguing.  I enjoy having the stories overlap to tell a complete one ala the movie "Go."  But this game is as generic as they come.  When will developers learn that we would rather have a little exploration than a big explosion?  If this game was producd by Michael Bay, I wouldn't be surprised.  Let's hope they get this game back to what made it popular in the first place.  Changing that is just dumb.  Make another game if you want to cater to the explosive junkies.  Don't ruin what you have built by catering to the least common denominator.

The game lenght can take good several hours to complete. There are four campaigns, and five chapters each one.
You play as Leon/Helena, Chris/Piers, Jake/Sherry or Ada/Agent.
The story reveals itself properly, and the difficulty scales slightly if you play the campaigns in order, as Ada's campaign throws in some mid-tier monsters pretty early in the game, and her story reveals a lot of mysteries behind the other three campaigns.
The multiplayer mode is alright, though also weak. For the PC, the community is horrendeous small. It might be due to the huge gap between the release dates of consoles and PC.
Now is this game good? I say "yes".

It certainally isn't a perfect game. The progression get's shockingly slower and more grindy once you hit level 3. The balance sometimes feels off. And the graphics, while not bad by any stretch, aren't anything to writ home about. However, it is worth noting that the game is in early access so all of this is subject to change. I also have had a lot of fun despite all of these issues. The game has a nice feel to it (If you like the feel of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series then you'll love the feel of Survarium) and I get a Call of Duty 4 feel from the gunplay. The game also has a tactical, methodical feel to it during matches and you can set your character up to compliment your playstyle. Want to be armoured to the teeth and destroy everything in a hail of bullets at the price of manuverability? Go ahead. Want to zip around with an SMG while taking advantage of the anomolies on the map? Knock yourself out.
In conclusion, I feel like if you want a good, free shooter with solid, if unremarkable mechanics that will soon be introducing PvE then I'd recomend giving Survarium a go.

A beautifully narrated game about a bunch of quadrilateral shapes overcoming the odds and saving the day for other quadrilateral shapes. Solid mechanics and fun puzzles made better through a surprisingly deep and well executed story.

This game just oozes warmth, wit and an aching sense of humanity. That may sound pretentious for a simple game revolving around coloured blocks, platforming their way across small stages. But Danny Wallace's narration, outlining an excellent, deceptively philosophical story with humour and gravitas, adds immense character to the experience, as does an excellent score.
It's a mark of the excellence of the game's characterisation that you start viewing some coloured blocks as characters in themselves, actually caring about them and their story. And their story deals with weighty themes of self-discovery, sacrifice, the human spirit and the capacity for people to work together to accomplish great things.
This game was genuinely affecting, for all its simplicity and short length. Highly recommended.

An Act of Mindslaughter – Murder
Profound,  captivating, mysterious, pretentious – these are all words which could be used to describe Peter Moorhead’s cyberpunk thriller, Murder. Regardless of where you stand however, it is most certainly a thought provoking experience unlike any other.
Murder‘s protagonist, Lieutenant Motomeru Minori, is called out to a crime scene where a man has been violently killed. No biological clues or evidence has been left behind though, making it almost impossible to find the killer. Not that Motomeru’s colleagues are all that concerned, of course. This is just another day at the office for them. Another loss of life is of no real importance, so long as they can still clock out at the end of the day.
Murder‘s various scenes present optional and critical scenery for you to interact with, in a point and click “look at this, now go there” style. Talking to citizens and humanoid robots reveals a world where life is cheap and disposable, possessions are of the utmost importance, and where contentedness seems forever fleeting. There are definitely parallels with today’s world.
Moorhead’s depiction of Neo Tokyo is striking. It’s a world where human life and robots are at an intersection. For every human living life and consuming autonomously, there’s a machine reaching sentience and becoming aware of itself. Aware of its servitude to human kind. The tables have turned, and only the robots have realised The impact of this awakening has potentially far-reaching repercussions for all of mankind, yet most people are too wrapped in themselves to notice.
During its short 20 minute run time, Murder poses numerous uncomfortable questions – many more than it has time to answer. But perhaps that’s the point?
If you enjoyed my review, why not check it out on my website?

Peter Moorehead continues to refine his micro-minimalist approach to adventure games and environmental storytelling. In half an hour Murder packs in a ton of big ideas and folds them neatly into references to important sci fi and cyberpunk settings and characters. You'll find Stanley Kubrick and Isaac Asimov standing by PKD and Ridley Scott, while droids from Shirow Masamune's works scurry about crime scenes. Departing from Stranded's silent approach, Murder introduces a voiced cast of characters, adding a new layer to the environmental story telling. Also the soundtrack is a dead-on collection of glitched out electronic styles that successfully informs the visuals and situations.
If you are interested in concise atmospheric storytelling in a light, minimalist adventure game format this is definitely worth your time. If you are a fan of cyberpunk and the idea of a short, minimally interactive game doesn't bother you then you may find this intriguing as well.

It's hard to feel shortchanged given the $2.50 price tag, but I'm honestly blown away by how short and empty this "game" was.
There is nothing here. There is the start of a potentially interesting story (trust me, it doesn't go anywhere. It's the same tired cyberpunk story you've heard about AI rights and the nature of sentience a million times before,) and then the entire second half (that is to say, the next 5 minutes) is a repeat of the same scenes as before, but with a navelgazing monologue about the relationship between player and creator.
There is simply not enough here to justify a purchase, even at the price offered here. There is no gameplay, which would be fine if there were an interesting story to be told, but there just isn't.
The art was pretty neat, and the music was good, though.

While the game isn't badly made, it's way too short so there is no investment in the story.
There are other games such as The Fall or SOMA that tackle the same issues but those games actually invest you in them enough to care. While it's hard to compare a $2.50 game with these, it's plain to see that this format of game just doesn't work in such a small installment.
I wouldn't really recommend it but it is only $2.50.

Ok... Where to begin...
RE4 is my all time video-game favourite. Like, to me, there is Resident Evil 4, and the video games. I was very disapointed with RE5. I did like it in coop, but the solo, no thanks. I said to myself, well, let's hope they haven't messed up RE6.

The game itself? Is it possible to make it graphically worst than its predecessor? Yes! Do you like QTEs? Do you like them so much that some game sequences can only be played with QTEs? Really? Sometimes, you don't even have to do a thing, just stay at some place, doing nothing, the game will do it for you, the AI, the script will help you for your uselessness, will reward you for doing nothing!

The only good thing that I liked, was the enemy design. That I must say it has surprised me, in a very good and pleasant way. That's it! I spent more than two month to complete the campaigns, I was like, please, it's RE, at least try to finish it man. I did, but I regret that I am not recommending a game from a RE franchise. But I must, developpers must learn why they failed!

Actually a fun game.
I haven't played a resident evil game since re4 and i bought this game simply because of the l4d feature. But after playing a few hours with a buddy of mine in co-op, i think im gonna play the entire game. Heres why
Most re games feature a UI that i have never been a fan off. I dont like the menus, i dont like the layouts, and its always felt like a jrpg was trying to infect the game(pun intended). This has always turned me off of re games but usually i fought through it because of the story and how intense the gameplay felt. This is no different. Many people complain about how fast ou need to react to certain QTE's, but i feel ike that makes it more realistic. In real life, you would NOT have 10 seconds to react to something. You have a split second. And even though they change up the means of breaking the attacks saving yourself, they stick to very few options, and usually you have enough time to react. The times you do not do not take more than one try to figure out what it is you need to do and when, so i dont think this takes away fromt he gameplay at all. If anything, it adds to the immersion.
Speaking of immersion, the cut scenes are incredible. The scene in the beginning of leons campaign with the helicopter? Not going to give anything away, but MAN! As for the ambulance that many people have brought up, well, its sucks, but its a mninor moment and dying only sets you back about 30 seconds, and if you cant figure out where to be after one or two times you should probably start plaing Animal Crossing and leave these kinds of games for the grown ups.
The other thing im looking forward to, even though i havent gotten there yet, is the replay factor. Every RE game i have played i have replayed several times over. I cant wait to start this again with all my OP weapons and just breeze through it. RE games, like the movies, are just about entertainment and NOTHING else. They will not win best game just like the movies wil not win best film. But they are very entertaining and well worth the money, especially if you pck this up on sale.
And on another note, although i havent had the pleasure of playing the L$D crossover yet, this has to be one of the things ive been most excited about in video games. I loved old RE, and i loved both L4D's, and mixing the two seems like a match made in heaven.
I would reccomend this game to anyone but i would also STRONGLY reccomend playing this with a friend. The amount of time you have to react is VERY realistic and a lot of times you wil find yourself needing your partners help.

This game is my favorite Space Simulation since X³ Albion Prelude.
And that's one of the games that are the most similar to Void Destroyer 2.
You start in a little ship, that has almost no firepower, can`t haul stuff, but is agile and fast. You can progress by carrying passengers, racing or by bounty hunting. After you got some credits you can buy a better ship and do whatever you like, cause it's a Sandbox.
You can (right now):
- Fly every ship you see.
- Takeover stations and control them. (Control what they produce, export, import, they can build ships for you)
- Go mining & trading
- Hire Mercs or buy ships to expand your fleet
- Be a pirate and steal cargo or capture ships
- Go bounty hunting
- Takeover the whole sector
- Take a walk inside a base. (Don't expect too much, you can have a look on your ship and go to the remote Terminal when owning the base)
- Change between ships, Strategy Overview & First person whenever you like.
- more
What I like:
- The total freedom, do what you want to do. Be a pirate, a merch, a warlord. Your choice
- Modding -> There aren't many modders here yet, but it is possible to add own ships,factions,weapons&stations
- The style - It is simple but it has its own charm. (And yes you can change the skybox to a more pretty one)
- The roadmap says: ,,Storyline incoming, walking inside big ships & more)
There are games on Steam that have far less Content, but are far more expensive. I totally recommend this game. The Developer tries his best and has an ear for the Community.
This is an alpha, there is much more to come, but even in its current state, you can enjoy it for at least 20+ hours. (It's a Sandbox, so it also depends on your own creativity)

Void Destroyer 2 is a great work in progress of a sandbox combat oriented space sim. Despite being early access, the game is very playable, polished and most of all FUN. There is still alot of content and features planned, such as larger ships and more overworld sandbox events.
Pros-
-Great flight model and dogfighting is fast paced and action packed
- Many different ships to choose from, with different stats... from light fighter up to Frigate (more is planned)
- Ability to form fleets and have AI ships work for you, despite being single player your never truely "alone"
- Overworld sandbox mode similar to mount and blade
- Many Scripted missions to partake in
- Can switch to tactical mode and order your ships RTS style, while also dogfighting in your primary ship. Makes managing large battles easy.
Cons
- Needs more content and depth, ie larger ships are not yet implemented.
This is as one man show, one developer working his tail off to make a great game. Overall I am extremely happy with my purchase and highly recommend to anyone who wants a more combat oriented space sim. Even if you don't buy it, it is a gem to keep your eye on as it moves through early access toward launch.

I have never written a review before about a game but I feel that this one and its prequel MOTBW deserves it for many reasons. It truly is an undiscovered gem; A perfect blend of map exploration, combat, fantasy, rpg mechanics and fun, witty story telling. It blends the best from HOMM, Age of Wonders and Civilization.
The combat in this game is extremely well done. It is  much more satisfying than the kind of combat in Endless Legend, Warlock and the stacks of doom in Heroes of Might and Magic. It is to me on par with Age of Wonders 3 and above Fallen Enchantress/Sorcerer King.  Hero and troop progression is also extremely satisfying throughout the leveling process and scratches the AD&D itch.
The Civ Building side  is better than Age of Wonders because it forces you to make choices on what buildings you want and there are many more building options,  These choices will determine your army composition as well, leading to a multitude of combinations that increase the replay value tremendously.  There are even meaningfull class and skill choices for the heroes that also add to fun in trying out new builds. The province concept adds a nice and refreshing twist from the genre as well. While the game is not without its flaws; the UI a bit clunky that takes a while to get used it, I have yet to encounter any bugs that many have complained about so I imagine most were fixed by now.
There is so much untapped potential in this game and the FANTASY TBS 4X games  as whole I feel that it is our duty  as a community that enjoys these types of games to support the developper and the title.  We all talk about wanting a worthy Master of Magic successor and supporting the right developpers like Snowbird may bring that dream to fruition one day....we have EADOR right now and while amazing already I can see it becoming so much more.....

The Crysis games have always been about graphics and style over substance.  I guess Crytek tried to make some kind of story to go along with the nifty polygons for Crysis 2 but they wound up failing.  The story is quite generic, Aliens invade and blow stuff up and you as a nanosuited soldier have to stop them.  There is also something  about a group of people that wan the nanosuit for themselves so you have to fight humans, too.
While I wouldn't say the game is bad necessarily, it was a just so formulaic that it did not give me a lasting impression after I finished the campaign (about 10 hours or so).  It seemed as if Crytek said "Oh hey, those Halo games are popular and so is Call of Duty so lets just copy them."  Basically if you strip out the (admittedly amazing) graphics you would be left with a generic sci-fi shooter that, while certainly entertaining, won't feel like anything new.  The characters you have interactions with are just plain bland and I really didn't care if they died or not.
The multiplayer was surprisingly fun since you can utilize the nanosuit powers of armor, cloak, and what not but it is not something I will devote a lot of time to.  If I want to jump into a game and play for 30 minutes or so then it works great but I prefer the Battlefield series to Modern Warfare, which is what the multiplayer feels like.
One thing Crysis 2 does very well is give you character a sense of weight, which is sadly missing from most first person games.  Instead of feeling like a gun floating in air, Crytek have made it feel like you are an actual person moving through the environment.
What it boils down to is if you like Call of Duty and Halo then you will probably like Crysis 2.  I would recommend the game if it ever goes on sale again (75% off or more would be ideal) because it is entertaining wile it lasts, just don't expect anything very deep.  It's like a Michael Bay movie put into game form: come for the explosions and eye candy but leave your brain at the door.

This is a very strange game. To give an idea how it start, you're a spy, your headquarters is hidden in a derelict train station and you start your first mission by taking medication (or drugs). Oh, and somewhere inbetween there's a whoopie cushion for good measure.
From there on it's an erratic ride through spy plots, a hurricane of puns (many computer-related), plenty of references throughout (from Street Fighter 2 to a Bananaphone), robots, random events and sidequests.
I've never gone "Wat" so often in such a short time.
This is structured around more or less open-world based levels, with finding all the silly little secrets and the like being the main focus of the game.
Also, the design is more clever than you'd expect from a game like this, as it's easy enough to get used to the game's internal logic, and the weirdness is consistent enough that you can figure out a lot without outside help when you reach that point.
One final word: You'll really want to go for some spoiler-free achievement hunting to get the most out of this, as the actual story is sadly far too short.

The biggest problem that causes so much negativity around the game is the Steam community itself. By that I don't mean the community is trash. I mean that the everybody was expecting way too much. This is an indie game, guys. The F13 franchise is huge, everybody knows at least a little about it. However, that does not mean that you should expect so much from a game, whose devs are not as famous as Ubisoft for example. What I'm saying is that even if they created a masterpiece, there would still be guys that would say that the game is trash, just because the hype for it was unnecessary big. It was not reasonable. Since this is a positive review, I'll start with the cons :
-Indeed, it would be better if the game was stated as an Early Access game. It is just not finished. A lot of elements are missing, it looks like they just did few things in order to earn some cash and that's all.
-The price is more expensive than it should be. It is not a full-priced game, of course, but 36 Euro, (which is doubled in my country, tho it doesn't really matter, it is complex for explaining) is just way too much for the quality of the game.
-Gamebreaking bugs are a thing in the game. However they don't appear that often and most of the time they will not last for long.
-The physics are terrible. The devs could really do a lot better than that. Everything feels clumsy
-If you are reading this and you are like 12, delete your steam immediately, because the game is full of kids that use the mic for their own needs and because of a lot more obvious reasons and it just does not need more immature guys.
Now here are the pros :
-Somehow the devs managed to make this game extremely fun. Even if you only play with strangers. It is probably the most entertaining game I have ever played.
-The game is getting a lot of patches, you can't just say that the devs don't give a damn about the community that plays it.
-DLCs are lit and cost cheap.
-Instead of charging us 10 euros, the devs decided to add some of the biggest update contents for absolutely free.. Something your favourite DbD does not seem to do.
-Bugs are getting fixed a lot.
-Jason's models.
-Tiffany's model.
-Jason's kills are brutal, cool and just very well executed (no pun intended).
-It looks repetetive, but it is not. With all the options you have, every match feels different.
-Underaged are seen often, but most of the time you will be matchmaked with the chilled part of the community (which is the most of it).
-New multuplayer gamemode, story mode and new content incoming.
In conclusion : game is unfinished. However, it does have a lot of potential that is not ruined (so far) and if you are willing to sacrifise some gameplay mechanics, that you have seen in your AAA games, for the fun that these AAA games did not manage to bring on the table, buy it, test it : if you like it - keep it; if you don't - refund it.

This is by far the biggest and the most ambitious RE game to date. Unfortunately it is also, in my honest opinion, the worst one of them all.
Things I didn't like:
There are a lot and I do mean a LOT of QTE's(quick time events) in this game! QTE's are not a bad thing when done properly. But, when you need a QTE for pretty much everything from opening doors, leap over and across obstacles, fending off zombies, fighting bosses, dodging attacks, etc'... Then it becomes a chore and most of the time just frustrating. Some QTE's will get you killed when thrown at you and you were expected to react in a superhuman speed! It felt like the designers just wanted you to fail and die in some parts of the game... speaking of.. look out an ambulance........BAM YOU'RE DEAD!
Bullet sponge enemies will make you beg for ammo and when you actually find some crates you will be disappointed to discover skill points instead of ammo which you desperately needed. Some parts of the game are just 3rd person shooter which is OK, but when it's done with scarce ammunition system from a horror game than it is just a BAD game design!
A lot of the time I felt like the game just doesn't want me there. Constantly striping me of control over my cherector, taking away control over the camera, making me trip over dead bodys(which I found to be the most stupid thing I have ever seen in a game!), knocking me down when bullets hit me(You will spend a lot of time on your back when playing Leon's compaign).
What is it with RE games and the lack of boss health bar?? For once I would have loved to know how am I doing! Am I supposed to be shooting that big♥♥♥♥♥monster or run away? The game does terrible job at telling you when it's time to fight and when it's time to run or what you're supposed to do in that matter.
The cover system is horrible and most of the time just useless because the game spawns monsters behind you as well as in front of you.
Weapons upgrade system is gone and replaced with a useless and not very rewarding skill system in which you can only equipped 3 at a time. You will need to grind a lot to upgrade everything.
Boss fights are terrible, you will be forced to beat the same boss again and again and again and well.. you get the point.
I can't say much about the story because I was playing with a buddy and I wasn't following it that much. But what I do want to say is that fighting the same boss  twice with diffrent characters just because you came across these two other characters you played in a previous campaign is just dumm game design!
Things I like:
- Clever enemy design. I liked the fact that some enemies evolve after you shot them but at the same time it was very annoying because you are very limited with your ammo and you just want them to freaking die already, again that is just poor game design!
Gameplay: 2/10
Graphics: 6/10
Sound design and music: 4/10
Story: 2/10
Final verdict: 3.5/10
Edit: The co-op in Ada wong's compaign is just terrible!!! Your partner has absolutely no intersection with the world what so ever!!! You just stand there and watch your friend play the game!
Resident Evil R.I.P!

Many games boast about a "truly living world" despite the player not being able to see any of it. Where Void Destroyer 2 stands out against all these games is its inclusion of the Overworld. You can actually watch ships travel from one location of the map, pick up cargo, then transport it to another location. Not only that, but you can also watch as they may become intercepted by pirates. And, if you choose, join in the battle and help the ship out.
Another great feature of Void Destroyer 2 is the way it controls. Plenty of space games offer six degrees of freedom and Newtonian physics, but in most games it serves as a burden on the player. Here, all of the ships have adequate forward and breaking thrust, making it so that most of the time you won't slam into somethings unless you're moving far beyong the intended speed limit of your ship (which is nicely bound to a single keypress).
Being in Early Access, I hope that later down the line more activities will be added as profitable playstyles, with others receiving refinements. While this game is combat focused, the living world means that a player can take on any role they so choose, from civilian trader to black market smuggler, bounty hunter to cargo stealing pirate, and debris cleaner to high speed racer.

The Void Destroyer Games represents everything that the gaming industry should aspire to be (Listen up EA & No Man's Sky!)
Created by a single developer, I feel this game has the potential to be one of the best Space-Sandbox games on the Indie market. It combines the action and combat of a flight simulator with the overhead tactical controls of an RTS and it works so well!
You start off with a single shuttle that's as weak as a vegans♥♥♥♥♥♥sample. From there you earn credits by completing contracts, making allies, establishing mining operations and forging trade routes.
You can reinvest your profits into bigger and better ships and even build up fleets to defend your mining/trading operations.
Or, if you fancy a more illegal method of profit, try some piracy! Harrass trade convoys whilst evading the Navy. Extort defenceless civilians and make an infamous name for yourself.
The latest update to appear at the time of this review has introduced an excellent Space Station capture/management system. This allows you to perform large-scale assaults on enemy stations and sieze them for yourself. Once under your control you are able to build your own ships and tighten your grip on the flow of raw materials into your station.
Void Destroyer 2 is the perfect continuation from an already amazing game.
Whilst the flight controls are difficult and can be offputting to new players, I highly recomend that you give this game your time and patience.
I personally look forward to many more updates and the return of the outsiders!

One word to describe it: Beautiful. It is absolutely beautiful. Even on mid end laptops like mine, it looks incredible. The color and lighting makes this game look so realistic, and the intro video to the game is the most epic intro I have ever seen in a game. The graphic quality is on par with the best games TODAY (Despite being almost 2 years old), and easily wins over most FPS. The score is by Hans Zimmer (who also composed the Dark Knight), and is very well done. The gameplay is special - it kind of reminds me of a combo of Battlefield, Blacklight: Retribution, and Halo. Elements from each game polishes this one, and the campaign is a lot of fun. Got it from the Humble Bundle, and very happy that I donated and got this game:)
Overall:
Graphics: 10 out of 10. This game challenges big ones like Planetside 2 and Battlefield 3 in terms of graphics. CryEngine 3 for the win!
Gameplay: 9.5 out of 10. In this game, you are more than just a character... you are a WEAPON. Stealth and strength are your main tools; you can either choose to use stealth elements and make the combat feel like an FPS Metal Gear Solid game, or use "Maximum" elements and go bananas on the enemies using brute force.
Campaign: 9.5 out of 10. Has good replay value, and long story line.
Multiplayer: 8.5 out of 10. The multiplayer is awesome, but you may need to be very patient. My first few matches online were miserable... I was confused on how to set up my classes, and the people online are very competitive. There are lobbies dedicated for "Recruits", but those are always filled up, so good luck on "Standard" or  "Pro" lobbies. Doesn't take long to adapt, however.
Overall score: 9.5 out of 10. All I could say is... I regret not buying this game any sooner. I will buy the entire series (Crysis Maximum Edition and then Crysis 3) very soon. A MUST play.

tl;dr: if you like trying out different builds and strategies and like leveling your favorite units, this game is a treat. And there's also a lot of tactical depth to appreciate.
One of my favorite things in games in trying out different builds and strategies. And this game absolutely excels at that. There's so much room for strategic and tactical freedom. between which hero class(es) you pick, how you build your hero, which units you take, what buildings you focus on, whether you expand your territory or build up existing provinces, etc. Even such choices as investing in hiring and maintaining large expensive force to conquer strong enemy forces and claim valuable resources, or keeping a small army that can level up more quickly and is more mobile, leaving more funds to invest elsewhere.
And that brings me to another of my favorite parts of the game: the fact that all units can level up, not just the heroes. And you have a say in how they grow as well. while most units can't subclass on top directing their stat growth like heroes can (though a handful of them can indeed class change), and they can't be decked out with equipment, they can still grow quite a lot, and learn new abilities, and you can direct their development. For instance, I can grow a fairy from a frail light support unit into a powerful healer that can sustain a small army or a strong mobile ranged attacker that can singlehandedly take down heavily armed and armored mounted knights. Or even a difficult-to-kill evasive distraction. One of my favorite hero builds is an enchanter mage where I pick a couple of favorite units and overcharge them with loads of buffs and level them up quickly. Like taking a basic low mobility footsoldier and turning him into a monstrous unstoppable killing machine by giving him armor buffs and a speed buff and focusing his growth into damage powerups.
Also I have a lot of appreciation for some simple mechanics that enhance the tactical depth. Like stamina. very simple, but most games don't do it, and it adds a lot. Most actions deplete stamina, and being low on stamina reduces attack power and mobility, and dropping to 0 immobilizes the unit for a turn and halves its defenses. Attacking costs a small amount of stamina, and moving and attacking in the same turn costs additional stamina. Agile ranged attackers typically have low stamina, so while they can kite slower melee units, it tires them quickly. Many units have access to special abilities they can use for a hefty stamina cost. And moving through difficult terrain also costs stamina. But my favorite part is that it opens up enitire strategies, revolving around depleting your enemy's stamina before moving in to attack while they lack the energy to fight back. Then of course there are all the usual things you find in tactical games such as terrain bonuses and pentalties, flanking bonuses, etc. I love impactful terrain in general in tactical games. It can make a huge difference whether you mount your assault on an enemy province from, say a neighboring swampy province from the east or from the open plains province from the south, as which you pick will influence what kind of terrain is on your half of the tactical battlefield.
It is not a perfect game, however. It has bugs that can cause crashes. There is risk of randomly crashing every few hours and having to redo your last tactical battle (it autosaves after every strategic turn). I do not know what causes it. You can go dozens of hours without a crash, or crash every 2 hours. Also pacing can get slow at times. But those are the only real flaws.

A strange, fun, and slightly uncomfortable adventure that I wish I could just keep playing... I think. This game is the oddest title I have ever played, and I have played some weird games. Really, I would never have though to try this game had I not gotten it from a humble bundle. Anyways, on to the game itself. As i previously stated, it is really freaky. You go from turning people into flies to fighting a car to being eaten by a crocodile-man who was your director. However, it is a very good kind of freaky. Each oddity makes you laugh, cringe, scratch your head, sometimes all of the above. Yet, these oddities are what keep you coming back for more. The story is just enough to get you intruiged, and the fast, witty humor is wonderfully done. I am not much of a game music/sound person, but this soundtrack was perfect for the game. Anything else would have taken from the immersion tremendously.
I do have two, albeit minor, issues with the game: 1. It is far too short. 2. A couple of the sequences, particularly the after mission ones, are shown, and then never explained or referenced later.    Let's start with number 1. The game was so great, so funny, and so utterly dominating that I wanted so much more. I was incredibly disappointed when I saw the first credits begin in the final level. As I progressed through this stage, I kept hoping it wasn't over. Alas, there was no more. As the game was so great in such a short amount of time, it is difficult to fault the game very much for this. Number 2: This is less of an issue and more of an afterthought. Perhaps the game did explain this more, and I simply missed it. But this bothers me enough for it to stick into my mind.
Final thoughts: This is a magnificent game, full of laughs, plot twists, and strangeness. I am lucky to have gotten it in a humble bundle, but for anyone on the fence, this 1 1/2 hour experience is easily worth anything under $35 dollars. I wish the game was much longer, but it packed so much into such a short amount of time, I am going to go play it again.
Score: 9/10

I'm a massive fan of tactical shooters and military games in general, and some of the funnest gaming I've ever had was on Call of Duty's Search and Destroy game mode because it took intimate map knowledge and team coordination to consistently come out on top. So I figured R6S would be a good pick, especially when it went down to $7.00.
I was shocked, to say the least, at how boring this game is and how clunky it felt for a 2015 game. Not only is it a major deviation from the typical Tom Clancy franchise formula, the fact that multiplayer is confined to virtually a single game mode mechanic is damning (5 v 5). Most of the operators are extremely niche-related whereas others shine in almost any situation - a key balance and variety issue in my opinion. The game mode itself rewards tactical gameplay and coordination but it also rewards map exploitation and those who abuse camping. Attackers spend the first 30 seconds of every game looking for defenders with mini robots, operators have shields on their rifles, some have technology that will likely be invented in another 100 years, and this all just makes the game seem like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of a true tactical shooter and an arcade-like experience with ultra-unrealistic gear and weaponry. The recoil patterns and reload logic is completely ripped out of a page from Call of Duty. There is no advantage of controlled, semi-auto shooting over fully-automatic, Hollywood movie spray and pray. There is no mechanic that makes you waste ammo permanently for dropping a magazine early due to reloading.
It essentially comes down to what you want out of the game and I was expecting a more skill-based game, and not one where all but the best players rely on camping and their operator's 22nd century piece of gear to see through walls or turn invisible. It's a must buy if you want a game that is a step above COD in terms of realism and teamwork, but it's a pass if you are looking for any sense of realism.

People calling this "too easy" I think are missing the point. Particula is pretty clearly not meant to be a super-intense hardcore game that makes your palms sweaty and that you sink days and days into beating. It's casual and soothing, and if you take it for what it is -- something very clearly meant to relax and de-stress -- then it does a pretty good job.
You are literally destroying things such as "Negativity" "Anger" "Sadness" etc with your towers, preventing them from getting inside your "head" (their end point and your base). The visuals are very pretty, and the music is soothing and compliments the ambiance. Even your "attacks" and the explosions of your turrets have sort of an "ooh, ahh" feeling to them. Nothing is overly harsh, grating, loud, or clashing.
If you want some intense tower game that'll challenge every last aspect of your gaming repertoire, then yes, I'd suggest you look elsewhere. There aren't a ton of turrets to choose from and aren't very many stages; the complexity level is pretty low. If you want a game that you can relax with after a stressful day of work or in between frying your brain in study sessions, I'd say Particula could do the job. It's cheap, and it's pretty, and while I may not get hundreds of hours of intense gameplay out of it, I really can't say I dislike the hours I do.

Rocksmith has been a huge help to me as a guitarist. I have been playing for 8 years now and rocksmith has taught me techniques that I struggled with in the past. I had some previous (limited) experience playing guitar, but this game really makes me want to play regularly.
Positive Points:
+ Progressive learning, with automatic tailoring to your skill level
+ Clean and mostly intuitive interface
+ Large assorment of guitar tones that match the tones used in whatever song you're playing
+ Few to no latency issues after fiddling with the settings a bit
+ Large song library with a variety of genres (mostly varieties of rock, to everyone's big surprise)
+ Many additional songs available as DLC (small note: Considering that this game cost me a little more than the price of two albums and the featured artists have to be payed royalties, the 60 or so included songs more than justify the overall price in my opinion. The additional DLC gives the publisher incentive to add more content along the road, increasing the chances of more songs you like being added)
+ Lots of fun arcade-style guitar minigames, such as a game where playing the displayed chord fires your ship's weapons at the ship attacking you)
+ Built-in tuner that actually works and is fast to use
+ Loads and loads of rewarding fun. Play a game and acquire guitar skills at the same time
Negative points:
- Requires expensive proprietary cable (mine cost as much as the game itself)
- Volume control can be a bit off, sometime you can't hear yourself properly
- Any other sound device on the same bus will mess up your guitar signal to the point of it being unplayable. If you're using a USB sound card or headphones, you could very well have the same issues I had.
- Some fiddling around required to get the latency figured out
Although this game has its issues, most revolve around the hardware used. Once everything is set up properly, you shouldn't have any more issues. This is a very enjoyable game, and I can definitely recommend it to anyone who wants to pick up a bit of guitar skills and learn the riffs to some of your favorite songs. After around a month of playing (30h game time), I predict I won't hit the skill ceiling of this game for at least another 300-400 hours.

Fist thing, I would like to say I'm here because the in-game pirate suggested me so. If you don't know already, there is a text event where a developer, under the alias of a 17th century pirate, tells you of the hardship the game and the company went through in the last years. Well, call me soft, but it touched me. Indie developers are often on the razor's edge, and having worked as a game journalist I know my fair share of them, and understand how difficult can be their job.
Now, the game. I own the original Eador on GOG. Played it halfway through the campaign. It's decent, but it can get tedious because, well, there is little persistence and every map is basically a sandbox. No more: in Imperium there is still a sandbox mode, but there are also more traditional campaigns in the style of Heroes of Might and Magic. And, indeed, this game is very similar to HoM&M, and works like a "more-of-the-same" version of the previous Eador.
There is a strategic layer and a tactical one, both quite deep. A lot of units, buildings, spells, heroes. It's basically what a fantasy 4X should be, it doesn't reinvent the wheel. It lacks some of the more outlandish things of Dominions 4 (while being far more accessible, in exchange) and it hasn't the visual quality of the the latest HoM&M. But it's good, solid, with a lot of content for the price. If you are a fan of the genre, there is no reason not to buy it.

This game is something between Disciples and HoMM, a turn-based strategy with a huge RPG element where your heroes lead small parties of units to war. Both heroes and units gain experience and develop over time (if you manage to keep them alive - however, heroes can be resurrected). You can also equip your heroes with items like in a standard RPG.
The key feature of this game is variety. There are 7 hero classes who play quite differently. And then, there is multi-classing, much like in DnD. The number of different units is great, and you choose wich unit dwellings to buld in your capital to make them available for hire. Some units cannot be hired - only summoned using spells or rituals (like undead and demons). You can also ally with non-human races (dwarves, orcs, etc.) to gain acess to their racial units.
Likewise, the magic system includes 6 spell schools, containing combat spells and global rituals, and you can choose wich to develop, and to what extent.
So, this variety leads to many strategies being available. You want a gunlune that shoots you enemies off the field? You want a shieldwall backed up by healers and casters?! You want a necromancer leading an undead squad? You want a lone mighty warrior hero who vanquishes the enemy while his small retinue heals and buffs him? You want a wizard that blasts enemies with damage-dealing spells? You want an army of rampaging monsters and magical creatures?
In Eador, you can do it all (and much else)!
And in Imperium, you can now also worship different gods and gain benefits from it.
Definitely worth trying if you like turn-based strategies, or RPGs, or both.

This is absolutely one of my two favorite turn based strategy games. I've got an embarassing 990 hours eador, masters of the broken world and this game basically is the stand-alone expansion.
What really does it for me in this game is how every unit in your army AND the commander can all level up to level 30 and every single level has a fun choice to make in increasing the units stats. On top of that the amount of completely different units, spells and commanders that you can both control and fight against is staggering, and SOMEHOW they managed to make almost all of them meaningfully different especcially when leveling up.
This won't be your most balanced or least buggy game ever owned, but for me it certainly is that game that even with flaws gets my unconditional love for eternity. It's just so much FUN.
Do not buy if you're not into strategy games, but if you like games such as Heroes of Might and Magic you owe yourself giving this game a chance.

Particula is another game where I'd choose a 'maybe' option for my recommendation: it sits midway between yes and no. But in this case, I'm leaning towards no.
Particula is a very simple tower defense game. It has three levels and that's it. Each level has 25 waves of enemies, which are always the same, and that's it. And it has three different tower types, each with three different levels of effectiveness, and that's it. Upgrades to towers are also simple, with up to 10 speed upgrades (taking each tower from attacking once every three seconds at minimum to once every two seconds at maximum), and a seemingly unlimited number of damage upgrades, adding one point of damage with each upgrade.
The graphics are well done and the music is lovely. The controls are simple enough that the game doesn't need a tutorial. The game supports multiplayer, but I've not been able to find anyone else to play with, so I can't comment on that. From what I can gather from the Steam community discussions, the maps are still the same. And the game is very slow to play.
Particula was an interesting experience, but there's just not enough to it for me to recommend it. It comes with trading cards, which is a nice bonus for those interested in them, and does have in-game achievements to encourage some replayability, at least, but these are not mapped to Steam achievements, which reduces interest in them to many potential players.
With a bit more variation and Steam achievements included, I'd not hesitate to recommend Particula. As it is, however, I'm still stuck leaning towards no.

The game itself is incredibly witty and it never misses a beat of entertaining and wild situations you must play through. It is essentially a walking simulator, but the amount of ways you can interact with the environment were enough to keep it fresh, and the ridiculous tasks that are thrown at you can make you scratch your head at the absurdity of it all. Overall - I loved this game and will probably play it again in the future. My advice? Buy it on sale if you're as cheap as I am.

I was pleasintly surprised with Eador Imperium.
I had liked the game previously but felt it is slightly slugging due to its old engines. While that remains the same, the game offers great replayabilty and value for money. Something I cant say for many games that end after the story campaign.
The hero system and exploration offers a different game each time.
The pros/cons for each hero make the decision of which hero to recruit very critical and can fully change the style of the game.
The Auto Combat AI is one of my biggest fears. I always tend to press it and regret right after. While it is frustrating to see units die in a slam dunk fight, it does make for a challenge of never going for Auto unless its a sure thing and fighting the rest manually.
Between the building aspect, the hero equipment, the skills, unit levels; this game offers a lot of features that are very refined compared to what you see in other games.
Set Items & Artificats do make a difference. Choosing the right skills for your play style makes a huge difference. Most important what buildings you go with first and which units you select can make the biggest difference.
There's no one right combination. What works for a mage character might not work for a scout or warrior.
However, its also important to note that this game is a time sink. It takes a very long time to finish and I find that fantastic!

Cons:

Remember Slender: the Eight Pages?
It basically was a level where you collect 8 spooky pages with child drawings, while being chased by so called Slenderman. And while nothing really special, it was pretty fun, atmospheric and scary.
Now, this game is basically the Eight Pages on steroids, which is both a good and bad thing...
Game is very atmospheric and it gives you feeling of hopelessness. Since you only have a flashlight and a camera, your only options of defence is running away with your tail between your legs.
Sound design is pretty good. Wind blowing through trees, camera static, creepy ambient sounds and echoes sound pretty great.
There is also a new enemy type that you will meet on a few levels, adding some variaty.
If you are easily scared, you'll probably get your heart and adrenaline a nice little workout.
Game got some love with patches and some new (and old) levels completely for free, which is nice
Story is basically non existent. You're there to find some boy or a girl, but why, where and when is never really explained, unless you find and read all the collectibles.
Even then I had to go to on the internet to get my story fix. I know, it's a "scary simulator" but it is such a shame we don't get to know any of the rich lore behind Slenderman or ingame characters.
If you're into horror games, have played a few, or are not so easily scared - you will get bored pretty quickly. This game relies heavily on jump scares and spooky sound effects, which, while scary at first, will get repetitive pretty quickly
Difficulty is way to easy on easy (no pun intended) and medium but WAY to unforgiving on hardcore.
On medium you're pretty much unstoppable, save for a few spots, but on hardcore some levels are so EXTREMELY annoying and unforgiving, you'll be sent to the retry screen so fast, you'll think that the game has crashed and got stuck on the same screen.
Protagonists movement speed is something of the worst I have ever expirienced! Your movement speed is comparable to a turtle and sprint makes no sense at all, since it's completely random... Sometimes when you spot Slenderman, your character will run like a Nascar vehicle on a rampage, but other times (especially when you really need to) you really start to wonder if main protagonist you play as has a death wish or something, since her run speed will be so bad, a toddler would crawl past her while he was asleep...
It also doesn't help that the game is just so dark 90% of the time, which lead to...
This game is so friggin dark... I mean brightness cranked all the way to maximum but still dark - dark!
But don't give me flak about that, I know Slender: the Arrival is supposed to be dark and spooky game, which is the point, but I mean really? This games darkness will give a black hole a run for it's money!
Even with brightness at maximum, you are blind as a bat without you flashlight. You won't see crap and  it is really frustrating, especially on hardcore, because you flashlight have limited battery.
Got 7 out of 8 pages but you flashlight depleted the battery? Might as well restart, since there is no way you'll be seeing anything, except maybe Slendermans buttcheeks rubbed against your face anyways if you're lucky.
Graphics are pretty terrible, even for a indie game. I mean, most of the game is dark and you won't be seeing much anyways. It still isn't good excuse for this game to look like Half Life 1. Textures looks old, muddy and dated, animations are just... basic, and water, trees and grass will probably make a senior pc enthusiast cry.
Game have been out for a year now, and it ran pretty terribly back then. Well, 1 year and 3 days later and it still performs somewhat terrible, even after patches...
While not nearly as bad as before, on some spots however, this game will really live up to it's predecessors name, the Eight Pages since your top notch gaming beast machine will  cry and sweat  proficiently to spit 8 FPS out of this game
For me personally, Slender: the Arrival got repetitive pretty quickly. While game started out really great, jumpscares got old and missions became repetitive and just plain boring. But It's hardly a problem though since Slender: the Arrival is so amazingly short...
Yes, this game is alarmingly short. I mean REALLY, REALLY short. There is even an achivement for completing it in 45 min. Don't worry, it isn't hard since you can easily ace through it in no more than 30 min with some practice.
All in all, Slender: the Arrival is hit & miss. While some people will enjoy it, for me, it got boring really, really quickly.
I was hoping for a really scary game with rich lore and lot's of exploration, but what I got was a boring, short, walking simulator with a lot of jump scares, bad graphics, non existent story which was way to easy on normal and way to frustrating and rage indusing on hardcore.
My honest opinion?
Try it at friends house, get it on sale, or spend your money on something else

First and Only review to anything. So here is what the game is and about.
Void destroyers 2 is an Early Access, Indie, Strategy, Sci-fi Space Sim. Its always nice to start off with pretty much nothing and working your way up into something powerful or a fleet of something powerful. For Void destroyers 2, it does just that. To becoming something powerful you will be needing money, and reputation. Money is the big part, but reputation gives you access to buying bigger ships of different factions.
There are 6 factions of which reputations can be earned from or loosed from: The MU, The reborn (Pirates), TSF (military), Civilians, pirates, the Bounty hunter, and the Black market.
Each faction has:
•	Their bases scattered around the map.
•	Their own types of ships they sell. Except for the pirates, they got 2 separate pirate factions and ships. As well as the Black market, since they sell some of the illegal ships there).
•	An economy. Which you can trade resources with.
•	Each ship is unique in their own way.
•	Enemy’s
•	Different Missions (also except for black market).
Earning Money:
There are different ways to earn money, by mining or commanding Mining ships to mine for you, destroying ships with bounties on them, buying then selling cargo or selling stolen cargo at bases, if you got your own base you can sell what is being produced, doing missions, etc.
Bounties:
If not from doing missions and mining, trading or capturing a ship then selling it. You can destroy and earn money off of destroying ships.
There are 3 different factions you can take bounty’s off of without the use of a mission. Destroying the Bounty hunters and Military ships if your going through the pirate role or just the pirates if you stay with the civilians and bounty hunters. The bigger they are the bigger the reward. As well you can’t “kill steal” you would have to gang the ship with your fleet or destroy it by your self.
A Cheeky and obvious move is to wait near a military repair station (not a civilian or you wont get anything out of it) and to destroy or capture big military ships.
Bounties can also lead to getting an bounty/Wanted on you, where the military and the bounty hunters will come after you. Having a wanted score if you haven’t attack any pirates will allow you to buy a ship from their base and take their mission.
Faction Ships:
The MU has the ships infused with asteroids. a few the bigger ships are just the ship as a gun.
The Reborn Has ships with big cannons. As well as their own capture ship and capture bases ships and a carrier.
The Civilians are not helpless. They are the only faction besides the black market that sells mining ships.
The Military are deadly. Currently you can only buy two vehicles there, because its the military.
The bounty hunters, just have ships that where made to kill every type of ship.
The Black Market currently have no missions but randomly have different illegal ships for sale, from every faction. Like civilian capture bases ships, big military ships. But not all ships, they won’t have the really big ones like the Priam from the bounty hunters, etc.
There are many types of weapons from bullets to rocks, to missiles to lasers. There are nice unique weapons and secondary weapons. Weapons come from the ship you cannot for most change the weapons on that ship.
Upgrading:
After entering a base, you can upgrade it by adding a turret for curtains small ships (like starter ship). Or increasing the ammo and maneuverability. You can also add abilities like a shield to the front of your ship when activated, a repair, a big increase in forward thrust, etc. You can also change what space looks like.
Player own bases:
Other than taken over a base and selling what ever is produced, in the base you can use ore to reduce the cost of building a ship in the base.
Controls:
At first if you didn’t play Void Destroyers, it will feel weird. But if you are determined you can you can deal with it. Personally, I don’t like flying the hornet, too fast for me in turns of turning and looking to the left or right and passing where I wanted to look at.
All in all, I’ve been enjoying the game, and can’t wait to see every new thing that gets added.

Sadly you may have better luck finding a pot o gold at the end of a rainbow than a list of redeeming qualities Nether currently has.
At the games start, I thought to myself "Sure. It looks like a post apoc style game, wthat blends in two of my fave genre's...stealth and shoot-em-up. While the game has both of these qualities, one can never really achieve high skill in either.
Stealth: 3/10
The stealth mechanics are able to be increased with skill levels as the character progresses, however these only work for the creatures hearing and not other players. Other players can still hear you, and when in close proximity can still see your name hover over you no matter how much you are trying to become one with the tall grass. Even with a pegged out "stealth" skill set in the character build, you gear does nothing for visual stealth. I have requested to rename my character to Neon-sign Ninja...but was declined. As a player who rather enjoys stealth based games, this one gave promise, but refused to commit.
Weaponry: 5/10
Some of the weapons are quite unique, and frankly I can appreciate/understand it taking multiple pieces in order to create a gun. However, some melee with very high dmg are easy to find or cheap to buy.   The choice ends up becoming, do you want to try taking out something or someone with a sword, or take a shot, and hope that you do not make enough noise to attract anything in the nearby vicinity. Due to the price of ammo, I have typically chosen the former and gone medieval on anything I can. The high price of ammo and also difficulty to locate/craft all the parts needed for a high end weapon does leave a newer player severly disadvantaged on some servers.
Layout/Mobs: 5/10
The mobs have a limited number of types and once you see them a couple times, you more or less can go through without a single round of combat with them if you really want. The have set patterns or simply stay in place...staring...unmoving...like a cat at a window. If you move calmly and quietly there iss little issue, but make too much noise or disturb them in any way and they will try to take your face off. The city and mob spawn sites start to get ingrained into your memory after multiple times around the sadly small map.  While it would be quite large if you could enter all buildings, only a few per block have that option, leading people to keep running into each other in farming patterns for gear and other loot.
PVP:  3/10
After playing pvp in WoW and other games I had certain expectations on how things should playout.  Gear does factor in to a degree, same with lag, and player skill.  This game however has had a staggering amount of negative pvp. Beyond the usual gamking the safe zones can be repeatedly camped, and gear/character level can truly be the deciding factor. Each server has different rules on what PVP actions are allowed, and if someone breaks one, your character is still dead...your gear lost, any player levels lost, and part of your money.  Your only recourse would be to complain to a server admin. While camping/ganking I fully understand are part of any pvp experience, at least in games such as WoW they do not give any exp or other bonuses for attacking a lvl 1 when you are lvl 30...in Nether they still do. Once you are able to make it to max level, it usually means only another well geared player or two can take you out.  You can solo just about anything else the game may throw at you. That being said a tooltip or something on the neon sign of a character name bar hovering just above our hears would help determine if I am about to take out a level 1, just joined the game player, or fight someone of my level.
All in all, I game the game my best. I tried it multiple times and maxed out multiple characters in different specs on different servers and sadly the story remains the same. The servers are privately run, the server you like may not be on when you want to play, the mechanics are still broken, and the game has no patches or content updates in sight.

Yet another fantastic indy title by this one man game dev.
A TL:DR of this game would be that its Mount and Blade in space.  It still has a few bugs, missing features and is in need of polish, but clearly the developer is clearly putting effort into the continued development of the game.
Void Destroyer 2 is a neat space RPG/RTS that can have you flying everything from the smallest fighters to massive corvettes in both first person and RTS modes.
You can expand your fleet to either aid you in combat, or gather resources for you.  EG: Mining ships will mine asteroids for you, trading ships will trade, ect.  Every ship is pilotable, and you can even hotswap between ships in combat.   (It's good to note that if your main ship dies, its still game over if you are flying a different ship.)
All in all, I am impressed with what is there right now, and looking forward to future updates.

VD2 is a fantastic space sandbox game. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed X3, Elite Dangerous, Mount And Blade or Homeword. At the time of writing, it is far from complete but already a solid and enjoyable title. At $15 I found it a steal! I "beat" it in ~30 hours. More late-game content is planned.
PROS:
- Very well crafted combat system, smoothly going from dogfighting in a single tiny fighter to commanding enormous fleets into battle homeworld-style from a tactical view. Both styles and everything in between are very fun and rewards skills and thinking.
- Large variety of things to do. Buy or build ships, customize themwith passive upgrades and abilities, mine asteroids and trade (or get AI ships you own to do it for you), do a huge number of varied missions, improve relationships with factions (unlocking perks like higher-tier ships, missions or auto-docking option), capture ships and bases and explore the game world.
- Extremely friendly, mature and responsive dev. He's addressed my many bug reports and feedback promptly and gives me the feeling that this game is in very good hands.
- Beatiful art and original ship/base designs
- Fluid gameplay with lots of quality of life features. Huge amounts of keyboard shortcuts available. Ability to try out a ship (or upgrade) before investing your savings into it, lots of automation for trading/mining, time compression for fast travel and dilation for careful battle management, ability to create copies of a heavily customized ship when building a large fleet, etc.
- Great sense of progression/achievement as you go from a tiny, weak fighter to a huge empire.
- Low number of bugs for a space sandbox game (!)
CONS:
- The learning curve is fairly steep. Perhaps a bit lower than the X games, but expect to spend the first hour or two getting used to all the ways to interact with your ship(s) and the world.
- Some of the interface for ship management needs polish when dealing with very large fleets (100+ ships)

One of my favorite titles in the third-person shooter genre.
A good example where the sum of it's parts are greater than the individual pieces.  The controls can be clunky and overcomplicated (use a gamepad), quick-time events are always a point of contention, the graphics (while very good) can be a bit underwhelming in spots, the interface is odd and takes time to familiarize yourself with, the story is completely over the top...
But the way it's all wrapped together just works so well.  It's an immense coop experience.  It's a very long experience by third person shooter standards (roughly 20-25 hours for a complete playthrough of all campaigns) and honestly I loved almost every bit of it.  Heh.  Most of these "flaws" are really just a matter of getting used to change.  This isn't the Resident Evil of old, and convention is regularly defied.  Which isn't always a bad thing, but you'll have to adjust for it.  The tension of tip-toeing and backtracking through a mansion for hours on 10 bullets is replaced with shootouts, explosions and grandeous boss battles.  The "zombies" often have guns.
If you can manage to appreciate that this is an action game first, and Resident Evil second... go in with an open mind, and more importantly, go in with a friend... you'll have a great time.  The little flaws will be almost endearing in the bigger picture.
If you can't appreciate that... odds are the issues I mentioned above could ruin it for you.

Crysis was a commando game, essentially. You were alone, no hand holding you, just go in, do your♥♥♥♥♥♥ You're the Rambo-Predator hybrid.  The dude in the suit was a faceless numbnuts, you were playing as the suit, and the gameplay was about playing as the suit.

Compared to that, Crysis 2 was an utter waste of time.

Well, where to start? This game is a great example of corperate greed. Yeah, that sounds about right.
First off, the storyline is mediocre. I wish I could understand it, I really do, but to me this is like an epilogue to a poorly written spin-off of crysis. That isn't even the beginning.
Gameplay...Basically, it's Call of Duty with a nanosuit. Gun play and other mechanics mostly found in multiplayer are extremely close to CoD style, Crysis was it's own game and didn't rely too much on other games for ideas. That has come to a close with Crysis 2. Oh, and I almost forgot that everything is much more linear in the campaign than the original one was aswell.
Multiplayer, yet again it's CoD with a nanosuit. In Crysis 1 you had tanks, vtols, and helicopters, and you had a CS styled buy menu, everything was bought with points you earned. Now, it's default weapons with class loadouts and unlocking new weapons requires leveling up, sound familiar? Oh, not to mention killstreaks such as Radars and Radar jammers, air strikes, and a ton of other things. Oh, and Mesa, the biggest MP map in the original crysis, is probably bigger than all of the MP maps in this game combined.
"But if it's so bad, why did you get it?" It was part of the EA Humble Bundle, I didn't have to touch the keys for it but here I am, wanting to try and play SP again to see if I can make more sense out of it than I did when I first played and beat it.
TL;DR: Don't get it if you're a huge fan of the first game in the series. If you love Cawadoody but you're looking for a little bit of change in your life, this will take the cake and your wallet.

It's difficult for me not to be slightly biased when it comes to this game, just because there once was a time when I honestly loved it. I've had some great experiences, met awesome people, even made friends, so for that reason alone this game will hold a special place in my heart. That being said, those days are long gone.
The thing that changed the most is the community. It's very rare to get people that actually communicate and want to help each other nowadays, it's either complete silence where literally no one speaks, or a couple of premades chat in their own language and refuse to talk in English, and it obviously ruins the experience for everyone else. Not to mention the toxic trolls or annoying kids who intentionally scream in their mics (which wouldn't really be an issue if the "mute" button worked properly (and sometimes (or should I say a lot of times), it doesn't). In a game where communication is the KEY element, those things certainly make you enjoy the game less.
Another thing is the cost. Let's be honest here, the game is completely overpriced. When I first bought it, I expected there to be a lot of major updates. It's been about 3-4 months since the first time I've played it and not much has changed. They did introduce a new map and new killer, yet, sadly, everything still looks almost the same. And in a game that revolves around 1 specific killer (Jason), what else could be expected? There's only THAT much that can be done. It never had a potential to grow into something bigger. And it probably never will. So the price seems a little bit ridiculous.
Another issue is the never ending in-game bugs. Some of which are completely game-breaking. I can't even count how many times the game completely froze on me. Or how many times I got stuck in weird places and had to leave matches because I couldn't move. That being said, the bugs ARE constantly getting fixed, so now everything is much more stable that it was before. Yet it's still miles away from a smooth gameplay.
And last (but not least) is the game-leavers. There is no ranking system whatsoever, and you don't really get a lot of perks for staying until the very end (except experience points (which, let's be honest, matter only in the beginning)). There is no penalty system for leaving, you don't lose anything if you decide to walk, nothing, you can start a new game instantly, so be prepared to see a lot folks leaving games just when they start for not getting the killer. It's extremely annoying and frustrating when you want to play a game and just enjoy yourself, but it happens ALL the time. Be prepared to face the killer with only a couple of people, and die almost instantly. Chances are pretty high that you will.
Would I recommend it? At this point - no. There are a lot of issues, it gets extremely repetative after some time, and it's not woth the money. At least for now. I only recommend this if you have a solid group of friends that all can play together. Honestly, that's the only way to fully enjoy this.

It is unique,  a gem in its' own right. A mix between Sid Meiers Civilization 5+6, Legends of Callasia, Endless Legend and Age of Wonders 3. A tile is no longer just a bit of plains, its a province on which you can construct fortresses or villages. Every tile (province) has it's own separate locations within it, e.g a Dark Wood may have "Dark caves and Primordial hedges"
You cannot just recklessly invade provinces, the populace has to be taken in regard, for when they are truly unhappy with their new masters they revolt, you gotta keep em happy with you.
The combat happens on a smaller map, much like in Age of Wonders and Endless Legend, and consists of a hex-turn-based unit command sort of thing.
The tutorial is thorough, easy to understand, fun to play, and very helpful.
There are endless possibilities with the game, how to expand your empire, how to manage it, which path to take.
I haven't run into anything detrimental to my gameplay and thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough, even now, im heading over to dominate Eador Imperium.
I fully recommend the game to Civ and AoE fans out there, as well as to fantasy, strategy and (to a lesser extent) RPG fans out there.

The RPG elements of the game are esp. appealing to me for example the different spell casting rules for wizard and sorceress. As for the city building part, as a beginner I am really overwhelmed by the number of buildings in the game. Not sure if you must build nearly so many buildings in a SimCity game. I can only guess at this moment that you get a really profound feeling of achievement after you build everything in your capital city? Maybe I will find out later.
Of course there are some negative impressions you don't need to play the game for 100+ hours to be certain of, such as the lack of combat soundtracks and glitchiness in the performance once in a while. For the time being I will try to ignore them and focus on becoming more familiar with the game.

Absolutely love this game. It's challenging, it's addictive, and looking at the planned features it's shaping up to be in my top 5 space games. It feels like a cross between Freelancer and Homeworld, with a little of the X series games thrown in. The game lets you play either through a first person or top down RTS view, but the best result is achieved through using a bit of both. Control anything from a tiny fighter all the way up to a massive carrier. Build your own fleet, capture bases, destroy all who oppose you.
Being an early acces title there are obviously some issues with the game, friendly fire being one of the most annoying at the moment, especially when you have a lot of big ships defending a station, shots go astray and can hit allied ships.
The story elements aren't in the game yet, so it's really just a pure sandbox at the moment, if that bugs you you might want to wait until a little further into development.
Overall highly reccommend this game, very fun and very addictive. The dev is also very friendly and active on the forums, answering questions and recieving feedback to improve the game.

Pros:
After 90 hours of playing, I still have not run out of things to do.
Unconventional methods of obtaining ships that aren't on any sort of market
There are currently 9 factions including 2 pirate factions that are constantly at each others throats.
A large number of bases and large platforms, like shipyards and defense platforms, as well as radar platforms.

You can get close to any faction without making more than 1 faction hate you.

The game progresses very slowly at first, but once you are able to perform specific tasks you can obtain large sums of money, and become a super power in the system.

Cons:

It will crash eventually, and once it starts it crashes a lot.
I have heard people complain about controls and performance issues. I haven't had trouble with either of these.
I feel that this game is too easy, compared to the first game, but there are still challenges even for players like me.
More to come in this review, and please keep in mind that this is the first serious review that I have written in awhile.

I loved Void Destroyer. And I'm not much of an RTS player, I'm a pilot. That really says something about the "individual unit control" the game provided. Void Destroyer 2 however, takes it to the next level. Rather than starting off with the difficult task of commanding an entire military fleet, you begin in a small utility ship, converted into a sad excuse of a fighter. And from there, you climb your way up, your fighter becomes a gunship, then a corvette, then a heavily armed battleship. And your money grows and grows as you purchase fighter escorts, trading and mining ships, and more. This game is everything I wanted from VD1, and everything I loved from it too. It has a bit of a learning curve if youve never played Void Destroyer, (pro tip, take up courier missions, and eventually you'll see an entire station swarming a single pirate frigate. Wait until its almost dead, then be the last person to hit it.) For an Early Access game, the "To-do" list is pretty well checked off. The only downside imo is that there is no planned multiplayer, and that the ships don't have fleshed-out cockpits and interiors. If the cockpits were more varied, and the ships had basic interiors you could walk around in and walk directly out of into a station, this game would be a 10/10 in my book. For now, I'll say 9/10.
