Resident evil... it has changed quite a lot since that first time we stepped inside that mansion. There are a lot of mixed reviews regarding RE6 - what did I think? I actually liked it, and this comes from an all-time fan of the franchise. I guess you have to look at this game not as a survival horror but as an action game with old characters. The campaign is really fun and very hard due to the new controls but at the end satisfying and isn't that what we look for in a video game? Having fun but getting challenged?
Now I'm not saying that this is the best RE game (I think that title belongs to RE4), but it is a good direction to take, maybe in the future we might get to see these action-based controls in a more suvival horrorish kind of game, who knows, that's all up to capcom. But you know what I would criticize? I think it's time for a change of characters - I liked Sherry and Jake as new protagonists, but seriously it's time for Chris to hang the towel, he's been on RE1, RE: Code Veronica, RE5, RE6 and Revelations (the ones that I know), so there's not much character development left.

This game gets too much hate. I've been playing Resident Evil since the first one on the PS1 and I think 6 is a great game. Just because it's different from the first ones, it gets crap reviews. The series evolved, get over it. People complain about the QTE's. Why, though? Is your timing horrible that it makes you lose? You think instant deaths are "unfair and stupid"? Resident Evil 4 had QTE's and people loved that game. Enemy grabs you? You get a chance to make a comeback with a QTE. Enemy about to make a lethal attack? Time it just right, and you can turn the tides. It adds depth, it not just "get hit and that's it" you have a system that awards your fast reflexes. I can understand why people wouldn't like QTE's in say.. cutscenes, but many games do this as well, it's not just RE6. I didn't mind them, keeps you on your toes.
The story line is crazy, yeah. I enjoyed it, I don't know why people QQ'd over it. Three intersecting story lines? Common, that was great how that played out. Cheesy dialogue? Yeah, every RE has it, nothing different, right? I don't see the big deal.
And even after the story is over, you get to play the amazing mini game, Mercenaries. Gotta keep that combo up! The pressure of needing to keep killing is awesome. Combat system is great, I really feel like this is the most underrated thing in RE6. On PC, shooting the undead is really satisfying. You get great mobility and evade tactics. You have to strategize to get a higher score and a higher combo. Utilizing items that the map gives you, meleeing enemies to gain time. Mercenaries alone is worth it even if you think the main game is garbage (which like I said, I don't think is the case).
Great game Capcom, I loved it and you have a satisified fan eagerly waiting the next Resident Evil.

I hadn't played the prior Eador games, but I was pleasantly surprised by the concepts and mechanics of this game.  Compared to other games, this has the most similarities to the Disciples series (particularly the third game).
This game is very hero-centric.  You typically start with a single hero, and can usually build up a few more as the game progresses.  Like in other hero-centric strategy games, the earlier you hire heroes, the more useful they are, as it takes a significant amount of investment to level them up; and heroes are only useful when they are leveled.  Heroes are also the only units that can move around on the world map.  They are your agents for exploring your territory and conquering new territories.
Outside of heroes, there is a resource management component.  The base of your operations is a territory (a hex) containing your stronghold.  You can spend gold and crystals (the two currencies of the game) to build buildings and hire units.  As you build more buildings, you unlock higher tier units, access to schools of magic, different "rituals" (basically magic cast on the strategic map), and improvements you can construct in your outlying territories.

This is what Heroes of Might and Magic should have been! I'm really enjoying the game and love the whole take over each province strategy. There's so much to do in Eador: Imperium. You can search provinces for special locations, construct buildings (there are a lot of different types), level up your hero and units, rename your hero and units for a more personalized adventure, learn spells, equip items, and much more! Combat is similar to Heroes of Might and Magic but with more complexity and mechanics involved. The music is nice and relaxing and fits the game. There are plenty of different unit types including summons, there is a random map generator, and there are different game types like sandbox mode. Eador: Imperium is probably the best strategy game I've played since the Age of Wonders series and the earlier HOMM games (before HOMM5).
So, as my promise to the mysterious pirate who I met in the game, I have shared my thoughts and I would recommend this game for anyone who likes the Heroes of Might and Magic or Age of Wonders series or for people who like fantasy strategy games in general. Eador: Imprium is worth more than the price tag that it has right now. 10/10!

Imagine it, you're walking down a dirt road in the woods at dusk, it is autumn the leaves are turning orange and red. You come across an abandon vehicle on the road. The sun quickly sets, leaving you in the dark without a flashlight and suddenly, you aren't alone anymore. You are being watched and stalked by something. It feeds off of the power of your video camera, which is the only way to see it (I guess).
When your video camera flickers, it is closing in on you. It is drawing the power from the batteries as it draws near. It is Slenderman. A tall thin humanoid creature that looks over you from afar from hilltops. The creature that opens the doors that you just closed. The creature that your only defense is to not look at it. To wish it away as you cower in fear by looking at the ground. No... just run away until your video recorder stops flickering. How do you run from something that just teleports in front of you? You can always walk backward.
This is Slender: The Arrival, less of a game and more of a first person experience along the lines of Dear Esther and Gone Home. It preys on your fears. It has a great, creepy atmosphere and great sound design. You have little in the way of controls, left stick to move, right stick to look, a sprint button, flashlight button, zoom button, and a use button. There are other buttons, but they feel redundant.
The game dumps you in and never explains why you're there. Not just the first chapter of the game, but over and over again, its the same thing, you start at dusk in the woods and go into the night and then find an abandon building. Each chapter has a different task, such as turn on X generators, find X pages in the woods and close X windows. Simple things, but you're just stuck with something that can be anywhere at anytime that will warn you when its near. The more things you collect, the more intensely you will be harassed.
As you wander in the dark you quickly come across an average house. Depending on where you enter, it looks like there is nothing wrong. Just a normal house for sale with a playground in the back. Soon enough you'll find things scrawled on the walls and rooms in disarray. Eventually, you'll find a flashlight that will help you. The idea of wandering in the woods might seem like an easy way to get lost, but as you roam the darkness, you'll be enticed by audio and visual cues such as paths, lights and dozens of arrows pointing in one direction that will guide your way.
If you think you'll get used to Slenderman, once you progress far enough, eventually you will reach an abandon facility and have a follower. Perhaps it is a follower of the Slenderman, but it follows, chases and strangles you. This isn't a creature like Slenderman, so it doesn't have magical powers other than it is getting closer, running after you. You'll hear its footsteps running up to you. Your only defense is to focus your flashlight and blind it. That adds something different to the game. Getting trapped in a side room means there is no way out and no where to run away from the follower.
It is a toss up if this experience is for you. If finding stuff in the dark isn't for you then skip it. You'll be searching open areas for sometimes tiny things (sheets of paper). Lost in the woods and abandon buildings. Being thrown off your direction from having to run away and forced to figure out where you're going again in an area that is mostly woods. If you can't handle bobbing and weaving cameras, avoid this game. It might be a nitpick but sometimes the camera seems to be at a person's waist. The height of a sink or a doorknob.
I couldn't really recommend Dear Esther or Gone Home. They were both beautiful and immersive, but I didn't feel anything playing those games like I did with Slender: The Arrival. Is it worth $10 for an hour or two of gameplay? I feel like I was engaged and always challenged by a single strange foe with powers to teleport anywhere.

Ember is a simple but charming RPG that is an extremely simplified take on classics such as Baldur's Gate. I particularly liked the art direction; not too cartoony and just enough detail to look cool. I also found the ingame books to be entertaining. Though they were largely informal, they did a decent job of dispensing lore.
The core of the game, the combat, is very simplistic. You have at most 3 characters with at most 3 skills each. This makes for little variety during combat. One notable thing about combat is that there is a combo system that awards increased damage when skills are used consecutively. Beyond that, there is not much to it.
The main quest line runs linearly with very little choices to be made and it will take you through most points of interests in the world which makes the world seem small. Still, there are lot of different environments with plenty of nooks to explore and treasures to find.

Reviewer Game Progress: Game is completed with 100% achievement completion.
TL;DR
Story: 3 out of 5
Gameplay / Mechanics: 2 out of 5
Graphics: 3.5 out of 5
Sound: 3 out of 5
Bugs: 4.5 out of 5 (higher score = less bugs)
Overall Rating: Average
Summary: Short CRPG, with simplistic combat and game mechanics. Game can be completed with 100% achievement completion in about 15 hours which includes doing the majority of the side quests, I think I may have skipped 1. Has a crafting system for those wanting to craft their own gear, but it is not a necessity to complete the game. If you are looking for an rpg that you do not have to invest a lot of time into with an okay story, then give this a go. Or if you are looking to get into CRPGs and would like to be eased into them this should be a decent start.
Story: The story of Ember is somewhat interesting, but not all that engaging. While the lore is interesting enough the pacing and overall progression of the game falls into the realm of 'generic rpg'. What I mean by that is, you run the generic quests of dealing with 4 elements requiring you to go to temples or shrines for each element to restore them and so on.
Gameplay / Mechanics: Combat is real-time with pause, requiring the player to draw lines between party members and the target to attack or use skills. Skills are restricted based on runes attached to the currently equipped gear, think Path of Exile, however you are limited to only 3 possible skills per character, with a party limit of 3. Leveling and character progression are basic and straight forward with player class falling into 3 archetypes; Caster, Melee, or Ranged. Stat allocation is done every level with 2 points being available to be assigned into only 4 stats; Intellect, Stamina, Strength, Dexterity. Stats stick to general RPG format, strength for melee, intellect for caster, etc. My last gripe would have to be with pathing. Pathing in this game is not that great and controlling your additional party members can be a chore. Sometimes, when you move your party members in combat, they will stop attacking all together, other times they take strange routes into AOE damage despite directing them around it. Teleportation or blink abilities get blocked at random times. Sometimes you can teleport past party members other times you can't, etc.
Crafting: There is a crafting system in this game, but it seems like something that was simply added for the sake of having rather than having any real impact in the game. If you like to search and craft things it is there if you want it. If you don't, then there is no need to bother with it as you can simply buy some of the better gear or acquire it through quests and still be powerful enough to complete the game.
Graphics: The overall graphics are about what you would expect of isometric RPGs, but it was nice to be able to zoom in and look at your characters.
Sound: Has some decent music and sound effects, but nothing that really caught. Be warned, the splash screen for N-fusion is insanely loud so quickly click past it.
Bugs: I only encountered game crashes twice. Both times it occurred when transitioning zones, but nothing that was a deal breaker.

The Resident Evil series has not been doing too well lately. Survival horror has changed as a genre to adapt to the new market and new hardware available, Resi however seems to have gone down an entirely different path- a path of something that's no longer survival horror, but an action game that has flayed survival horror and is now shuffling around in its skin, occasionally turning slowly on the spot.
Resident Evil 4 actually sort of worked. I liked it anyway- it struck a balance between dodgy control and the precision needed for action, keeping combat tense without (mostly) leaving you feeling like it was intentionally crippling you.
Resi 5, was a bit of a mess.
Resident Evil 6... what is this I don't even?
It's a kludge of ideas, a mishmash of QTEs, set pieces, corridor shooting, holdouts in a sequence with no rhyme, reason, or flow. A conglomeration of poorly thought out stages and level design built on slip shop concepts and gameplay that quickly falls over into a huge pile of fail. It's hard to point out what exactly is wrong as there's nothing specifically terrible; it's just that nothing is done to the point of satisfaction. Everything is so half arsed, nothing works properly and so you can't single any one element out- none of it is up to scratch. The end result is a game that is frustrating from the moment you're in the start menu to the moment you turn it off.
Resident Evil 6 is a classic example of a game that's trying to please everyone but utterly fails to do so thanks to being totally under developed in all areas. It needed tighter direction and a sharper focus on a more limited concept. This game may well kill the franchise. Leave it alone, it died a long time ago and this is its reanimated husk.

This is a pretty simple game to just pick up and play, and it will probably only eat up about an hour or so of your time.  Your job is simply to heal everyone in the kingdom who has various illnesses and physical ailments.  The chests that you find will increase your hearts (your life force), shooting strength, number of shots fired at once, or the number of flasks you can throw during a single battle.  You'll also earn hearts after each battle.  Your battles consist of dodging enemies and their attacks while you auto-fire at them.  Press your lone action button to throw a flask; it takes some time to adjust to the distance they are thrown, but they are good in some encounters for clearing out multiple enemies.  Gates on the world map block your progress if you either haven't collected a certain key or enough life hearts.  Search everywhere for treasure chests!
For me, the game had sound and slowdown issues.  I received errors with DirectSound initialization, and music rarely ever played.  Also, the game would slow down dramatically during more intense battles, causing my inputs to be eaten and moves or flasks I was trying to execute simply not coming out.  This is my primary gripe; things like this shouldn't happen on a system with a 3.9 GHz hex-core processor with 12 GB of system RAM and a 2 GB video card (Windows 10, by the way).  Still, I was able to play through the entire game and beat it.  The final boss battle is very interesting and a nice test of your skills to that point.  I won't spoil anything, but to me, it's reminiscent of Kefka in
.
Aside from the issues I personally experienced, there's not much to keep me from recommending this game.  If you don't have the issues I encountered on your own system, then add another point to this score.

Sure, Eador MotBW was great, but you could never really go Huge. Now we have Eador Imperium sandbox mode. Where you can go Huge. Because sometimes you want to build an empire _before_ you go to war.
By the simple expedient of making each ring of unowned hexes away from your capital _much_ harder to capture and control than the previous ring, map size determines ( more or less ) how long it will take to reach your opponents, and how powerful you'll be ( or they'll be ) when you arrive ... so ... basically, what game pace you want. A tidy mechanism. It also means the environment itself is always challenging, as you are always surrounded by big-bads, but you take the challenge at the pace you want ( until a doom stack arrives on your border ). This works because each hex territory you hold has to be incrementally explored and subdued before it yields all of its bonus and benefits. This takes time and lots of fighting, so you're always doing stuff within your borders while planning your expansion.
So fire up a big map, with lots of stuff in each hex, recruit your heroes, build your armies, pacify and develop your lands, grow strong, beguile your populace with god, guns and liquor to keep them distracted, then go say hello to the neighbours.
It's quite satisfying.
Or play your own way, which is kind of the point.

Rocksmith 2014. Where to begin?
For those whose primary interest lies in playing videogames, Ubisoft's Rocksmith games are the next step up on the evolutionary ladder from the likes of Guitar Hero and Rock Band; a way for them to unlock their inner rockstar for real by graduating up from the plastic five-button instruments they'd been accustomed to for the better part of a decade.
For the musicians, novices and band stalwarts alike, Rocksmith is Ubisoft's attempt at creating the ultimate accessible instructional package and, despite their recent missteps with the likes of Assassins Creed: Unity, this is an example of what they're capable of when (almost) everything goes right.
Taking a leaf out of Harmonix's book when they introduced "pro guitar" difficulties into Rock Band 3, Rocksmith - both the original and its more polished sequel - went down the route of using its interface to help ease in the novices, gamers and those with absolutely no experience with music theory, which was welcome news for me, meeting all three of these criteria.
With your "controller" this time around having dozens of "buttons", the interface took a lot of Guitar Hero-esque stylistic decisions in order to help those who had ever picked up a six-string (or a bass, they're catered to here as well) get going.
Instead of a horizontal row of buttons at the foot of the screen, you have a transparent representation of your instrument's fretboard, complete with a full set of colour-coded strings. Like its spiritual predecessors, the notes of the songs flow down to you in a familiar stream.
However, where Rocksmith breaks away from Guitar Hero is in its "Dynamic Difficulty" mechanics. Instead of throwing you in at the deep end and expecting you to perfectly hit every single note, it starts you off simply. To begin with, there'll only be one or two notes for you to play in that riff you know so well and, as you get better at hitting that "one or two notes" through repetition, it'll gradually ramp up the difficulty, effectively piecing together a puzzle until, before you know it, you're playing the full riff.
Rocksmith 2014 is the bigger, more polished brother of the original, complete with a wide array of lessons, minigames and challenges tailored to improvement in the arts of rocking out. As one would expect with such a product, the financial barriers are rather more significant than Guitar Hero, requiring you to purchase the Real Tone Cable (connecting your guitar to your PC by way of USB and the amp jack) and, as you would expect, an actual guitar if you don't already have one.
Put simply, If you're interested in learning how to play guitar/bass, whether after years of nailing songs on Expert on Guitar Hero or not, you'd be hard-pressed to find similar products on the market that offer such a varied suite of options for beginners and experts alike for a "videogame" price.
Easy and fast way to learn how to play a guitar... It does not substitute a teacher, but it's a lot easier to do with this game than with a teacher alone!

If I'd have to describe this game in one sentence:
Homeworld x Freespace x Open World sandbox, all this with Borderlands style graphic.
Pros:
- combat is very well ballanced (every ship type is useful)
- AI is actually competent and most of the time don't require micromanagement (I have a fleet of 80+ ships and usually I can just give "attack all" or "form up" commands and the AI just do the rest)
- (some) generic missions have persistence (e.g. I took "repair military ship" mission and once I finished it that ship begun patroling the area and engaging local pirates. In other mission I failed to destroy huuuge pirate group, because it was...well huge - I ran away forgeting about them. some time later I notice that same group terrorizing the area - now my plan is to take lost of "repair military ship" missions so that the military could deal with them)
- freedom - you can be Pirate, Bounty hunter, Trader or Miner.
- Several diffrent factions with their own distinct design and ballance philosophy
- each faction has distinct set of generic mission that player can take
- 80+ ships for these faction, all of them with wide range of upgrades and customizations
- flight mechanic is well balanced between newtonian flight and arcade shooter
- you can build your own fleet of combat ships, trading freighters and mining ships
- ability to quick and easy jump between ship combat and ship command mode (RTS style)
- already good price to content ratio (look and above, look at the Price tag, then take a look on "One Man's Lie" price tag) despite it's still very early access
- game developer is very active and open to feedback
Cons:
- If you was already after years with Homeworld 2, you will notice that the general GUI is still very crude and require a lot of work. However as this was openly admitted by author, the GUI was low-prio for the first release. He already begun GUI tweaks and improvement in last few day. It made a huge leap in good direction.
- There is almost no ships above Frigate size yet due to early access. If you dream about your personal battleship or carrier then you will have to wait.
- The number and variants of generic mission is still limited due to EA, so after several days they become very repetetive.
- the "borderlands" style graphic might look quite ugly at first, so depending on the taste this might be very big issue and this is the only issue not related to early access status.
Now the last paragraph about VD2 Early Access in general.
We all know how "bad" the pernament Early Access games are in these days. Some of them ending up as almost a scam.
Void Destroyer is not like these "bad" EA.
I bought VD1 as Early Access played for a few hours, had some fun...then forgot about the game because it was EA work in Progress. Year later I received steam mail that VD1 is now out of EA and with release status.
I jumped back to the game and had a lot of fun playing the main story (not your average casual game, once aliens appear you need to prepare to discover new meaning for "being screwed" and then they joy when you finally begin to push them back).
What does it mean for VD2 EA? I'm confident that author will deliver what he promised - his roadmap is clear, the core gameplay is ready, feedback from players is well processed.
To me this is best spent 15$ on a game this year.

I just have to say this is the most enjoyable space combat I've experienced. It's hard to really explain why... the flight mechanics, the weapons, the ships themselves... it all feels "just right" to me. If you're not sure, watch some of the videos where Paul (the developer) shows off some combat- that's when I was sold.
You've got thrusters for 6 directions and a newtonian flight model ("auto-thrust" helps compensate and can be toggled on/off any time). I've had many hours of fun dogfighting with enemy fighters and wearing down larger ships and trying to avoid their firing arcs. Learn the controls and/or change them to something that works for you and it will pay off. I went through 2 or 3 setups until I decided to map the up, down, left and right thrusters to my hat switch. Lots of ships have turrets so whatever you do, make use of those thusters!
If you're in a bigger ship, you can press F5 to go into Command Mode which makes it kind of like Bridge Commander. Take control of the ships turrets while trying to bring those big forward guns around. Very cool. I just have not used it much since I apparently like pretending to be an ace pilot.
Once you start having big fleet battles, you may want to use the tactical/RTS mode. You can slow down time while you give orders- and oh boy, can you give orders! There is more going on here than I can really tell you so I will just say tactical mode can be an incredibly powerful tool for the player. You wont be forced to use it but the more ships there are, the more useful it will be. It's a bit like Homeworld or Nexus: the Jupiter Incident, I think.
The ships are all awesome and unique, you can upgrade the heck out of them (even upgrade the amount of upgrades they can have), and they almost all have a cool secondary weapon. I still go back to flying a Brick from time to time. It's slow and weak but it can lay mines that turn into heat-seeking missiles :D
Right now, the biggest ship you can fly is a frigate with cruisers, destroyers and carriers still to come. Ship capturing and base capturing are still to be implemented but the "end game" is that the player will be able to take over the entire sector.
Random info:
The game is meant to be played with mouse and keyboard so joystick is optional
Low system requirements- my GTS 450 is still going strong
It's $15
It's not 4x but it is a sandbox- set up auto trading and mining to get those credits flowing
I would say if you are looking for fun, intense space combat look no further. Even in it's Early Access state you should at least get your money's worth.
P.S. Just be aware that this is not baby's first space game. When you play games like this you usually have to take some time to figure stuff out. Don't hesitate to ask questions on the forums.
P.P.S. As of this writing, I have 2 Steam codes for Void Destroyer 2 and not enough friends who play space games. Send me a message and maybe I can give you one.

Except there is no endless onslaught of baddies to keep you entertained like a mobile game, nor is there the depth of story you would expect from a well-crafted PC game. The world feels empty and alone once you get settled in. The nice touches like deciding to help an animal or person being attacked by baddies or just watching the fight play out just aren't enough to carry the game.  The graphics are dated by at least 10+ years. The music is okay, but the track loop, like the rest of the game, gets repetitive quick.
Pros:
- There is no grind.
- Quests are almost all story based, with very little side quests.
- Very easy to play, not complicated at all.
- Money is balanced in your favor; you are never short on cash.
- You can camp and regain full health/mana at any time while not in a fight which means...
- Cooking/harvesting mats is completely optional and largely just a waste of time.
- A lot of history via reading/collecting books. A lot of thought went into creating the backstory for the main character and many of the NPC's.
Cons:
- Lacks depth of story or sufficient action to hold interest. Slogs along at a dull repetive pace.
- Almost no character development and very little dialogue between the characters you control.
- Decisions have no consequence; even though you are given dialogue choices during an encounter the story progresses along the same track regardless of choices made.
- Crafting is pointless: it is entirely not required, it is just as expensive as purchasing items from vendor, and with regards to crafting armor and weapons, you have no idea what stats the equipment will have until it's made.
- History and backstory is mostly presented through multi-volume books that have to be found and read, often after you meet a questgiver and while on a quest. Who wants to read 5-15 pages of history per quest?

Poly Bridge is a game currently in Early Access and it merges two genres (puzzles and simulation) into one seamless, addictive experience. I’ve seen (and played) plenty of games like this before, starting years ago actually, but somehow there always seems to be room for improvement. So here we have the big question: does Poly Bridge bring anything new to the table? And can it be enjoyed if this is your very first time playing such a game?
I will begin by answering these questions first and will get to the more detailed analysis later.
No, the game doesn’t bring anything *truly* new to the table, but it does manage to improve upon (quite) a few aspects and all of these improvements definitely make the game more fun. The result of this is that anyone, new or experienced, can play this game with relative ease.
Poly Bridge is just one of those games that makes you want to try again and again just to see if you can get better results or to see if you can build something the way you imagine(d). Granted, at first you’ll be limited to the game’s tools and therefore you won’t have access to everything just yet, but even with a limited toolset you can build brilliant bridge constructions.
To be fair: the goal of the game is to build a bridge with as little money as possible (i.e. keep it below the budget) but the game still allows you to continue if you exceed this budget, as long as the vehicles have passed the flag. That, in my opinion, is an excellent way to pull in all kinds of players; you’re free to do whatever you want as long as you’re able to create and finish a solid construction. In fact, you can choose which level you want to play (almost) right from the start. There’s no set ‘story’ to follow.
The downside to this design choice is that the ‘true’ goal of the game (build a bridge with limited resources and money) gets lost somehow; it becomes kind of a secondary, optional, objective and I’m not sure if that’s the intention of the developer.
Sure, the main goal is to get the vehicles across the bridge, but let’s face it; the vehicles need to get across anyway. In order to do that you need to build a solid bridge in the first place. So the way I see it it’s some sort of secondary objective, really.
Still, I like it the way it is currently handled and I’m sure there are many others that share that sentiment, but I just wanted to address it for a bit. Please keep in mind that it’s my point of view and you might feel different about it.
The interface is easy and intuitive: in the top left corner you have your usual menu, in the top center you have your budget and available resources (among other things) and in the top right you have the simulation controls that starts or stops the… em, simulation.
Now, to start building you just middle-click on the screen and you can then select your tools from a radial menu. Right-clicking deletes and item and holding and dragging the right-click button lets you delete multiple objects at the same time. This works extremely well and it’s actually a joy to use, especially if a large part of your construction needs to be revised. Left-clicking obviously places the objects that you selected on the screen. Basically that’s all there is to it. It’s one of the easiest editors I’ve even seen.
Finally, the building part is done from a 2D perspective, seen from the side, and it’s great to see your bridge come to life in 3D when you eventually run the simulation (where you can also move the camera more freely).
As we know the game is still being worked on, so we can expect more levels and features to be added in the future, but for now there’s more than enough content to keep you occupied for hours. Finishing levels will also unlock new vehicles for use in future levels. Actually, once you unlock a vehicle it’s almost always used in the very next level. And while they aren’t true collectibles it’s still a nice way to keep players interested and they add a bit of a challenge for the levels to come (because of the weight, of course).
All-in all I’m very impressed with the build so far. I’m happy to say that it’s also being actively worked on and updates appear regularly.
There’s not much to say about the audio; it’s a bit repetitive, but other than that it’s relaxing and non-obtrusive. It didn’t make me want to turn my volume off, which sometimes happens with other, similar, games. So, for that: bonus points!
The visuals of the game are amazingly beautiful. They’re low polygon and they have just the right amount of detail. It’s a nice combination of cartoony graphics and realistic objects. See it in motion and you’ll understand what I mean.
Sometimes the physics get a bit messed up (mostly because of collision detection) and so far I haven’t encountered any gamebreaking bugs, but do they affect the graphics. Parts of the objects just get relocated to a different position of that same object then, or ‘break off’ altogether. Still, it all worked fine for me personally, but it did detract from the experience. But I guess you have these sort of bugs and glitches in almost every physics system nowadays. It’s nothing noteworthy really, but still should be mentioned in case you expect a bug-free game here (which you should never expect, to be honest).
Overall, nothing to complain here. Nothing but clean and stylish graphics.
The replay value for this game is amazing. You have a GIF creator that lets you save your simulations to GIF format. Also, Steam Workshop has already been implemented so that we can share all of our amazing creations with each other and, of course, this can not be done without the level editor, which is naturally also already included in this Early Access version.
Potentially, you could play this game over and over again, just to beat your previous scores/budgets. In a way it’s endless (but in reality it’s not). Still, damn good value.
Poly Bridge is an amazing game for young and old. It’s still needs a little work: right now it can be seen as a diamond in the rough, but I’m confident it will be fully polished by the time it releases, somewhere later this year.
I have nothing bad to say at all about the gameplay, which is fun and invites you to try out different things. I do have some questions about some of the design choices, though, but fortunately these are kept to a minimum. It’s absolutely worth the current asking price.
Pros:
+ Easy to use editor
+ Stylish graphics
+ Plenty of levels
+ Just plain fun and addictive
+ Relaxing, non-obtrusive music
+ Steam Workshop, level editor and GIF creator add tons of replayability
Mixed:
+/- Budget aspect doesn’t seem all that well integrated
Cons:
- Some physics glitches
- A couple of bugs

Zombies, abominations, and rampant viruses. Many games have touched on those keywords, but CAPCOM's Resident Evil series has set the table for the zombie-killing survival horror genre. Since the first game, the series has strived to capture the struggle of surviving in zombie-infested mansions, cities, and laboratories with nothing but your wits and whatever weapon you manage to get your hands on. With an evil pharmaceutical company's creations running amok, it falls upon you to uncover their secrets and get out alive. Over time, the borders of the series have shifted and parted to suit the changing times, but as I've noted with Resident Evil 6, the newest addition to the series, the core has remained the same.
Resident Evil 6 is the creation of fusing the fourth and fifth game together while keeping aesthetics of the first three games scattered about in select scenarios like trudging through a dying, infested city or escaping from a seemingly invincible foe. Taking place a few years after the events of the previous game, the world is on the brink of another bioterrorism catastrophe, and it's up to a handful of distinguished individuals to put a stop to it, all the while bringing the masterminds to justice. Returning to the fight are four original fan favorites: Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Sherry Birkin, who is a grown woman at this time and Jake Muller's partner, and Ada Wong, who stars in her own campaign as she did in RE4's Separate Ways campaign. All characters are joined by new partners to assist them in their campaigns, of which are four divided into five chapters each.
A few words of warning: the main game's campaign is much longer than 4 and 5's story. Each chapter can take up to an average of an hour and a half of your time, and a campaign can take up about half of your day, even if you're the speedrunner type. It's a good thing that the campaigns are varied, else those hours spent would be unbearable.
Leon's campaign is a callback to the days of Resident Evil 2. Although Leon is joined by Helena Harper, a regretful woman armed two powerful weapons, there is no safety in this. The campaign guides the player through many dark and eerie locations that keep them tense and alert, and the zombies faced by Leon and Helena are soupped up to match the times and advanced controls. It can be easy to be caught off guard and overwhelmed by the varieties of zombies, but they can be quickly dispatched with a calm mind and a quick trigger finger. For those wanting survival horror, Leon's chapter delivers.
That said, the opening sequence can leave the player baffled at the abruptness of the situation. The President is a zombie, the surrounding city is infected, and a cathedral owned by the big bad villain is supposed to hold all the answers. On top of that, the guilty Helena Harper is tight-lipped and doesn't explain herself to Leon until the end of the second chapter. On multiple occasions the agent asks for exposition or reasons to which Helena waves her hand, choosing to jeopardize what little trust there is between each other for the sake of theatrical deliverance at the right moment.
And let's not forget to mention Simmons, the villain whom the players must fight four times before he finally dies. Granted, the boss fights take place in spectacular arenas and there's enough ammunition to force the next sequence, but the sheer tenacity of the villain weighing against the exasperation of both the players and the characters themselves leaves a bad taste. If Leon's campaign was a filling dinner, the ending with Simmons was a sour tart that took too long to finish.
Chris's campaign is more of what RE5 offered, that being survival action rather than survival horror. With the army of BSAA troops at Chris's back and Piers Nivans, a talented sniper, at his side, the campaign transitions into a third-person shooter play style where cover is much more important, especially against enemies who use firearms. There are no zombies for the Arklay Mansion survivor to fight. Instead there are the J'avo, which are humanoid enemies like the Ganado and Majini from the previous games. The difference with the J'avo is that they are able to mutate body parts in response to getting shot, which can result in a variety of enemy types that force the player to change tactics.
CAPCOM had tried to appeal to the Call of Duty fans with the Chris campaign, but in doing so they lost some appeal to the fans of the RE series. The campaign focuses too much on action and throws enemy after enemy at you without giving the ammunition or health needed to tackle them at times. Another gripe with the campaign is the final level and its overuse of the camera. Typically the camera would be over the shoulder of the player, but in the final sequence the camera is unreliable as it focuses on a large BOW that players have no hope of destroying at the moment. To make matters worse, the controls follow the camera just as well as they did when the cameras changed in the first few games. This makes running from a foe or looking where you're going an unsavory challenge.
Jake's campaign is hands-down the most varied of them all. Players are taken for a rollercoaster ride through urban warzones, avalanche-prone mountains, a deadly manor, burning streets and even an undersea research facility. The enemies are the J'avo and BOWs again, but while the player can dispatch them with ease, a new foe inspired by RE3's Nemesis chases the characters through all missions. Layered between the various fight and flight elements is the personality of the campaign's two characters, Jake and Sherry. They're personable enough for players to relate to and they're interesting and determined enough that one can't help but root for them. Not to mention the awkward yet adorable scenes between them... Other than a few unforgiving parts in the levels (snipers on an icy slope, for instance), Jake's campaign is exciting, rousing, and a hell of a lot of fun.
And as per usual, Ada's campaign sets out to provide exposition and tie up loose ends left dangling during the three main campaigns. Her gameplay has many stealth elements, staying true to her character playing games behind the scenes. As she encounters all of the main characters in their campaigns, she also fights the various enemies in each campaign: zombies, J'avo, and BOWs. Beaten only by Jake's campaign, Ada's run is filled with variety and backstory, although trying to decipher a story by CAPCOM is a Herculean effort in itself.
Yes, like most CAPCOM games the story is lacking. Here's a brief summary: It's a one-sided love story that results in a mad clone of Ada, the death of the President, and a Chinese Raccoon City. Given that the series loves to make its characters remark that every city with zombies reminds them of Raccoon, maybe CAPCOM just has a bad case of nostalgia that most fans have gotten over by now.
RE6's controls are a far cry from the tank mechanics of the first few games. The heroes can perform mad dashes, move while aiming, physically attack on whim, and dodge attacks by rolling, ducking, and sliding with minimal effort. Adding to the formula is a new mechanic that allows you to counter an enemy's attack with one of your own, provided you have the reflexes to execute the counter. Cover, which was used in some places in RE4 and 5, can be taken anywhere. By pressing the aim button near a wall or object, a character can snap to the cover and peek out to shoot at hostiles. It's a gimmicky mechanic that needs more refinement, but other than that, the new controls are easy to get a hold of.
If you're not griping about the story, then you must be having difficulty with the camera. In short, not bad, but not the best that CAPCOM has created. If you're going to try RE6 out, I'd recommend renting it before making the decision to buy it.

I almost didn't try this game because of the bad reviews.. Seems like steam is kind of screwing this game by showing all bad reviews on the first page even though if you look at the overall reviews it actually has more good reviews then it does bad. .  The bad reviews almost made me pass the game up, but I been bored with my other games so I decided to give it a try anyway. Glad that I did. I downloaded it this morning, and have spent most of the day playing it.  It's not a bad game. Especially for free. It's basically a russian call of duty with better graphics, and none of the flying jetpack or running on walls stuff. People are saying that it is pay to play but that isn't true. You don't have to pay to do well or get gear. I upgraded to a fully loaded ak in less than an hour, and.... was on top of the leaderboards  a lot of the games I played. Took me about two games to get the feel for it, and then I was dropping people.. It is true that they have a bunch of micro transaction stuff, but the game itself is free so what do you expect? And...  it's not necessary to buy any of it. There is plenty of stuff to unlock in game.  I didn't spend a dime on this game, and so far I have had a good time with it. I like it 10 times more than any of the last 3 call of duty games. It sort of reminds me of the original black ops, or some of the older cod's back when cod was good,.. but with better graphics. Oh.. and none of that killstreak crap. The game is pretty well optimized as it doesn't seem to require a massive pc to run it. I have a decent pc and was able to turn on dsr in my nvidia settings and then change the game resolution to like double my native resolution & still get 80 fps. Game looks awesome in high resolution like that. I also turned off all the hit marker crap in the display settings which made the shooting feel a lot more realistic and more immersive. Once I did that.. the game is pretty sweet for what it is.  Overall I like this game. Rocksmith's greatest flaw is that I want to keep playing well past when my sore fingers will allow me to comfortably.  There are many guitar practice/playing options within Rocksmith and each of them is uniquely devised as basic practice.
The lessons are generally basic, but mastering them can take quite a bit of time.  For instance, the practice of hammering on and pulling off was not entirely difficult but I didn't score perfectly.  So, I'll have an opportunity to come back for later practice and perfection.

Okay first off I need to point out that you will not understand this game in a short time unless you have played Masters of the Broken World for a long time. This is not to say you have to play the previous game - just that you need to have played either one of them for a long time before judging them. Neither game lends itself to being open to criticism from those who have barely scratched the surface of these incredibly deep and detailed games.
Secondly, you have to realise that you are looking at a labour of love and messing with the livelihood of people who placed themselves in a difficult situation for that love and for the core of fans who loved MotBW. Having played MotBW for 130 hours, and fully intending to play it for at least that length of time again, I freely admit that I am one of those fans.
There is a point in the early stages of the game where you will meet a character called "Alexander the Developer" who explains some of this to you. And then you kill him and the symbolism of that is all very sad. Whilst I sympathise with the plight of the original dev team I have to point out that anyone releasing an unfinished game, for whatever reason, deserves what they get. It's time developers realised that the old system of pushing out a game in that state just to meet publisher deadlines with the mindset of "we can patch it later" just isn't going to fly..and bad reviews and/or getting sacked should be the EXPECTED result.
Imperium has all the markers and potential of a world beating game. It is still being updated regularly and continues to improve. It still has MINOR issues and MINOR bugs. It should absolutely not have been released before now. Now it is a fully playable and enjoyable, if unpolished, game. The graphics are an improvement over its predecessors, the artwork is beautiful, the gameplay more complex, and the music is incredible (likely the best I have encountered in any game). At this stage the storylines and setting are not as well developed or as fun as those in MotBW and the English translation is pretty bad in places. The tutorial is now extensive. The absence of a promised multiplayer mode could be a deal breaker for some.
My advice is that if you get it to play it for a long time before rushing to judgement, to go into that process with open eyes and an open mind, to stick with it even if there are things you aren't entirely happy about.
If you can't do all of those things then it is more a case of you not being worthy of the series than the series not being worthy of you.
You always have the other option of waiting until the patching and polishing process is complete.

I've been looking for quite a while for a complex turn-based strategy game (having played Fantasy General and others for quite a bit) and I can say that Eador Imperium comes close enough for me to like it. Haven't yet figured out all the mechanics and tricks to this game but I am truly enjoying it, thus I recommend it to anyone looking for a something similar. The journey of discovery is what this game seems to be about.
My only gripes at the moment are the end of turn mechanics (the fact that I'm seeing all the players' turns on screen twice, due to the two phases - maybe they can be compressed in a nicer SINGLE animation that doesn't cover up the whole screen) and the fact that enemy ranged units seem a little overpowered in the beginning (but that might just be me not knowing the game well enough).
All in all, it's a great time sink, especially on the largest of maps :)
@Developers:  if you plan on doing a similar game in the future, do inspire yourselves more from older games. Starting up seems a bit tedious, there is some lack of information regarding some important stuff (e.g. choosing to construct some recruiting buildings locks you out of others + why do my conquered provinces keep rebelling and how can I prevent those constant fights in the beginning?!), yet the general mood is great; I can see this (future?) game become more like FG/HOMM3:WOG in some aspects (e.g. making some items available for units too, not just heroes).

This is an ambitious space game, so far it delivers.  The art style is simplistic yet consistent and enjoyable.  All the ships and weapons seem pretty well balanced.  The AI is pretty good.  Keyboard and mouse control is very tight, I prefer a joystick but I found those controls too loose and unrefined, and you can't customize axis sensitivity (yet).  Progression is good at this point, you'll be upgrading to better ships in no time after your first few missions.  I have about 12 hours so far and I've gotten a corvette, which is 1 tier below the highest available in the game so far.
There is no speed limit (!).  Most space games don't do this because simulated physics problems, but it's so immersion breaking.  It's exciting to try to outrun an opponent, which you'll have to do if you want to "warp" away to the overworld.  Your weapons have a limited range of around 1km, so you can't attack from super far away, nor can you effectively fly like a bat out of hell so fast and engage in combat and put down more than a few shots.
Speaking of the overworld, this is such a great way to traverse the map.  It's basically a 2D map that you fly on to simulate warp speed, you can see other ships, friend and foe while in this overworld map and get an idea if you want to attack them.  Sometimes they might pursue you too.
Some negatives, but keep in mind these didn't ruin my enjoyment of the game, and it is Early Access:
The game crashed a few times on me, but it autosaves often enough that I never lost any progress.  Loading times are minimal and I was back in no time.
A story is planned, but so far little is present beyond the introduction.  Their are plenty of missions to do to earn credits and get used to game mechanics, I am anxious for the story though.
Most of the time the AI is good, but there are some enemy ships I would find that would just sit there and let me beat them up.  Great source of credits...  Once, a ship I was supposed to protect went to a repair platform, and sat for several minutes before repairing.  AIs that fly with the player need to communicate their status or intentions better, it's not always clear what they're doing.

What an excellent gem!
This is very similar to a few other such games. Rebel Galaxy comes to mind.
Observations:
However, this is a sandbox. The script driving the story has not intruded in my vast hour and a 1/2 experience. ;)
Mouse control is tricky - not necessarily bad, but tricky. Takes practice and settling into a style that suits. A different way to view the action other than the default cockpit view or maybe a change in tactics - strafing runs versus dogfights.
EDIT - there is now a setting for return to dead zone - on 50% I can fly like a pro.
The artwork is different. I like it. It becomes immersive and transparent.
The ships types are many and varied. The ships with turrets are animated as the turrets follow targets et cetera.
A stylized sort of Art - Deco look. A fresh visual rather than the ubiquitous Steam Punk or Homeworld - esque.
The tutorials are accessed in a base via the "Simulator." I heartily suggest playing through them.
The "Overworld" map view is similar to Homeworld although not as detailed. Still it is functional. I have used it to skirt enemy ships I spotted on the way to a mission objective.
EDIT - the dev is working like a madman. Since I first got the game the overworld map and its function has been enhanced & expanded.
The developer is very responsive and seems to be hard at work. Since obtaining the game (9/25) I have seen two updates? (More like 6, now) Also friendly. My first few comments were not flattering and yet I was greeted with suggestions to alleviate my problems in the game. (And they are MY problems)
When I first read the timeline and expected progress I rolled my eyes and figured, "Riiiiiiight." Now, I quite expect things to progress apace.
EDIT -  no crepe. There are so many updates. I am certain the timeline is real and the expected progress is very believable.
And I have yet to plumb the depth of the game.
So far, I have been playing courier and debris wrecker.
EDIT - Now I am a Bounty Hunter. Mostly civilians because the pirates are too difficult for me at the moment. But that is the game. Choose your profession and pursue it any way you like.
Funny point between the two games - in Rebel Galaxy (or Mount and Blade: Warband, Freelancer, Homeworld & X3) the graphics are of the polished, cinematic variety. Explosions are Star Wars style WOWs! In VD2, you blow up a ship or debris etc and you get a momentary white out of the screen - so much for cinema.
EDIT Viewed from a respectable distance the explosions are a bit more cinematic, with debris spinning off etc.
Also there are hints that the reason the skybox appears as it does is because us "stubs" see the Electro-Magnetic Spectrum differently than regular humans.
When the story line is implemented...I can only imagine.
Void Destroyer 2 is reminiscent of cel animations. VD2 (yeah, that makes me giggle) wins big on this one, though.
VD2 bases are 3d objects and not pretty pixels that you "crash" into to hear that female, "Docking" exhalation.
You can fly circles around the bases in VD2.
EDIT - leaving certain bases and you'll see a lot of traffic weaving in and out of the base.
As far as negative issues, I am down to one.
Music - I can name games with good soundtracks on one hand. This one is not memorable.
I would very easily recommend this game if you enjoy RG and the notion of a true sandbox in which to play.

STORY
bio terorisme menyerang dunia, membuat semua orang ketakutan, dan siapapun yang terkena virus pasti berubah menjadi zombie. Sherry, chris dan leon dari BSFAA , kembali jadi tokoh utama untuk mengembalikan kestabilan dunia dengan mencari penyembuh dari virus ini , ditambah dengan tokoh cantik yang misterius si Ada Wong yang suka bermain di air keruh. Di game ini juga disimpulkan siapa sebenarnya ada waong itu , dan siapa si jake itu, yang masih ada hubunganya dengan serial RE sebelumnya.
GAMEPLAY
Campaign dibagi menjadi 4 campaign dengan memainkan 4 karakter berbeda. yaitu Leon dengan sidekicknya Helena, Chris dengan sidekicknya Rick (lupa gan) , Jake dengan Sidekicknya Sherry dan Ada wong dengan sidekicknya petugas neo umbrella .  yang menarik setiap campaign mempunyai benang merah dengan campaign2 lainya. Standard game action horror gan, kalo lagi alurnya lambat , musiknya kalem, kalo lagi tegang2nya , ato perang2, background soundya  pacenya cepat.

I honestly feel so bad for the devs. They work their butts off to make the only amazing Friday the 13th Game this world has ever witnessed, and they get crap for every little thing they do. Bugs can't just be patched out right away. Extensive tests and work needs to be done in order to find what causes these bugs, and how to remedy them. The game isn't perfect. It hasn't even been a year yet, and IllFonic has been working so hard to get awesome new content out, while also simultaneously patching bugs and working on single player mode. Yes, there are setbacks in place, but so far, this game doesn't dissappont. You can't blame the developers for tending to what kind of content we want or the community for that matter. Literally every online game with a competitive nature to an extent, will always have toxic players. Every game has cheaters and exploiters, and the dev team has been doing an outstanding job at patching bugs and exploits so far. Some may think 40 dollars is overpriced for the product, but honestly there's enough free content to be able to be enjoyed that makes this game worth it. New maps, counselors, Jasons, gamemodes, and more to come. What's not to like? People need to understand that this game has a long ways to go still.
In terms of the gameplay, overall it's great. My counselor to jason rate is about 50/50, so I've played each side enough to be able to form an opinion.
On the counselor side, it can be pretty fun. The attention to detail on each map is insane. You feel like you're playing through one of the movies. Having seen each and every movie in the series, the maps that are in the game so far are creepily accurate. The bathhouse from Part 1 on Crystal Lake, The barn from Part 3, The Lodge and surrounding cabins from Part 2, and even the two houses from Part 4. Everything is where it should be. On the counselor side, I feel like you get to explore the maps a little more than Jason can, and you have more time to take everything in. Truly an amazing experience standing where characters from the movie stood. Each map has a set of objectives in order to escape. There are multiple ways to escape, and the items needed to do so are randomly spawned around the map, which is a nice touch. You can fight back at Jason, but it's a lot easier to do with a lot of people and games can be pretty interesting when this happens. The amount of outcomes each game has is endless.
Playing as Jason is just as it should be. Everything looks movie accurate for each version of Jason, right down to the little details, like the strap of Part 3 Jason's hockey mask covering one of his ears. The devs even changed one of the eyes on a Jason for continuity's sake. The animation is good, as it was motion captured with Kane Hodder, the actor for Jason in parts 7,8,9, and X. From his idle animation, to his walking/running animation to every kill in the game, it was all motion captured with Kane, which is so time consuming as there are probably 70 different kill animations or more at this point. Each version of Jason has different abilities and each one plays slightly different from the next. I also like this, because it accomodates every playstyle even though Jason's individual playstyle is the same. You set traps, defend objectives, stalk counselors, and have a damn good time doing it.
This game is truly an amazing feat. The copious amount of time spent working non stop tending to each person's demands with a small team astounds me. Everything is just right. Like I said, the game has it's flaws. But if you are a true fan of the series or horror in general, you will be able to overlook these bugs and have faith that the developers will patch them eventually. I am so excited for the future of Friday the 13th, and so should you. I would definetely reccomend this game to any person who wants to sit down and just have a good time, or any fan of Friday the 13th, casual or serious. Both kinds of fans will appreciate this game.

TLDR: This game is a little rough around the edges, but thats to be expected with an early access beta game. Its still very playable and i can see myself following this game all the way until full release if and when that day comes.

Summary:
The passion put into the game by the authors is evident in every aspect of it. Totally worth the price. Recommended for all rpg fans.
This is a very nice looking, rather simplistic and small-scale (~25 hours to complete on normal), easy to learn rpg game with a catchy little story about our human greediness and selfishness and how these traits could ultimately spell a disaster for the world.
More remarks:
World map is not very large. Can use fast travel to places already visited. Environment is varied (forests, farmlands, swamps, desert, snow, ice, lava, cities, sewers, tombs, caves, ...).
Some quests, including the main quest, offer choices of how to complete them. Number of optional quests is small, but it is enough. Leveling curve seems OK. I was never behind in levels expect in the first large forest area.
Party size is 3. Number of recruitable NPCs throughout the game is 3. Only a small part of the NPC dialogue in the game is voiced.
Lore is huge for such a small game. There are many books to read. The stories in them are actually very interesting, too!
RPG elements are very simple. "Class" is defined by putting points into base stats str, dex or int, when leveling up. There is also vitality to increase HP. Points can be redistributed anytime, for a price.
The palette of active and passive skills is not very large. There are damage, crowd control and healing skills. Skill damage scales with base stats. Healing scales with int. Some skills scale very poorly, doing only slightly more damage than auto-attacks even with high base stat.
Skills are bound to equipment pieces. Max. 3 active and 2 passive skills per character. Can change skills in equipment anytime, for a price.
Itemization is simple. Items come in tiered categories with increasing level and stat requirements (heavy armor = str, medium armor = dex, light armor = int). There are one handed and two handed weapon varieties for melee and ranged characters as well. There are 4 quality tiers: crude, normal, superior, legendary. Crafted items are always superior. Can craft equipment (but not jewelry), potions and food from the ingredients harvested in the world.
Combat is simple. Most of the party damage is done by auto-attacks complemented by occasional skills. Can pause combat at anytime. Combat AI of party members is OK. It always attacks the target of main character unless told otherwise. Most enemies use melee attacks, so I opted for a party composition with one heavily armored tank and 2 ranged dps characters. It worked very well. Many enemies use annoying AoE spells targeted at random party members, preferably ranged characters. Some more difficult fights will require a simple strategy to beat, but it can be figured easily, after 1 or 2 tries.
The game crashed on a few occassions, but luckily there is a frequently saving auto-save feature.
The UI could use some small tweaks, mainly shortcuts, e.g., F1, F2, F3 to select individual party members, SHIFT+click to buy/sell/move to crafting table/move to bag of entire stack, adjustable party window and quickbar position, etc. The crafting UI could also be improved, e.g., display the list of known recipes when opening crafting table.
This is an extra-ordinary RPG game. It's not too short, not too long, and the storyline is great. Buy this game, you won't regret it.

Ember is a charming homage to classic isometric CRPG's, and while it doesn't present the depth of Baulder's Gate or many of the games that emulate it, it is still a title worth the time put in. At just about 25 or so hours of gameplay for a measly $10, I regret none of the time I actually spent playing. (See the ---'s for the CRASHING)
+ Simple live combat with the ability to pause
+ "Open ended" skill point allocation
+ Respec skills easily (for a cost)
+ Simple but decently rewarding crafting
+ Interesting story with a (for my taste) very pleasing ending
+ Tons of background knowledge in books
+ The areas are very pretty, with whispy magical things and... glowing mushrooms? rocks? Who knows.
+ Not difficult, but still satisfying (normal)
- Positiong your characters is a nightmare
- "Open ended" skill point allocation really means you can put 2 skill points per level into one of four stats... so the options are limited, plus all of the items have level AND stat restrictions
- Each of the three characters you get in your party is one of three archetypes... which can make your PC useless if you gain them at a certain time in your development
- Too few "skill check" dialogue options, but then again there are only 4 skills (only the main PC can make these checks)
--- Has the uncanny ability to crash to desktop when transitioning areas for no reason. Probably the most frustrating thing about the game besides the movement of your dumb characters. This happened about 10 time throughtout my experience. The only time I regret buying it was when the game randomly crashes. F5 is quicksave, use it often.
Other than that I liked it.

If you wonder if this game will ever be finished, the dev already completed a huge game - Void Destroyer - that was in early access and, if you're still doubting, go check that one out and how players like it. This dev has been working on Void Destroyer 2 since Void Destroyer was published and has just now put VD2 on Early Access. This dev has a track record of following through and creating great games.

Apart from that, upgrade your ship, buy better ones, bounty hunt, build a fleet, and use RTS controls when you have enough ships to do what you will. There are missions available at every docking station and factions to ally yourself with, or fight against. EVE style wanted timer for pirating neutral vessels, with promises of many more features. My rule of thumb with early access has become to not recommend anything based on "potential" that might or might not be fulfilled, but to look at it from a perspective of what is already there.
Void Destroyer, though in its early stages, has a solid gameplay formula that is quietly satisfying. Dogfighting bandits, collecting bounties and upgrading your ship can be quite fun. What makes this more fun to me than the usual space sandbox sim is the tactical interface which allows you to easily command huge fleets with the same ease as though it were an RTS.
At the moment there are a few non-game-breaking bugs to be sorted out (one of the cargo ships I was escorting trying to dock in a fighter hanger at a repair station for example), and not everything is in the game yet (a number of ship classes and models will be implemented later). Even if none of those things are fixed or added though, the game is very fun as it is right now.
My only complaint is that I liked the graphics of the original void destroyer a bit more. You're able to change the skybox from the weird neon blue but it's an upgrade to your ship you have to pay for, although it only costs a pittance in the game's currency.
This game does have a bit of a learning curve. Don't expect to just pick it up and be good at it. It will take you a few hours to get used to the controls and flight model, but if you are willing to put in the time, Void Destroyer 2 has a lot of fun to offer.

Probably one of the best scenarios of don't count your chickens before you hatch. This game had alot of potential and still does. Sadly the game has been abandoned. This game has been passed down and runned poorly by several devs (1st phosphor, then pure fps which ran several other games to the ground including this one with horrible coding and p2w mechanics, then back to phosphor who at least gave us single player and player hosted servers vs how pure left it which was a ruined game that noone could play since all servers were official servers), and hackers did not help to slow the progression into the downwards spiral. This is truely sad as it was a real potential survival game with an entirely unique atomsphere.
To sum up what this game is, think about the metro franchise. Now imagine that humans started living above ground, and it was in england instead. Also imagine instead of a nuclear holocaust war, it was a sunspot that burned everything and the mutants all evolved from a small % of the humans that didn't get incenerated to a crisp. That is nether, an open world metro with factions and mutants that takes place in england.
It is very sceneric, and atm its $5. The way it is now theres enough content to keep you busy and give you your money's worth. So if you have a couple of spare dollars and you wanna buy it to try it go ahead, but in all honesty theres no more updates coming anytime soon or at all, and the money can better go towards another game or steam items. It is also very buggy and has a ton of glitches and exploits like any other early access game (warning you ahead of time).
to go more in-depth for anyone actually thinking of buying it to try it out or just wants to know more about the game:
nether is an open world survival set in a post-apacolyptic world after the largest recorded sun spot in earth's history happened, wiping most inhabitants that were unlucky enough to be exposed to the solar rays. Most people, animals, and plants died. A small % of exposed humans were mutated by the sun spot's rays into what are known as nether. Few humans did survive that were not exposed to the rays enough to perish or be mutated, which you play as one of. Your one goal: survive
There are several species of nether, including a boss nether that has smaller nether around him for protection. All nether have the ability to teleport and can be alerted by loud noises or if they are attacked by survivors. Each nether can drop nether parts, supplies, weapons, and xp towards your character.
basic nethers:
crawlers=basic nether that have low health, low damage, and are fast. They attack in packs, however, so they can overun you easily if not prepared.
the forgotten=1/2 nether 1/2 human or nether that stopped 1/2 through the mutation process. They explode if they get too near or if you hit them/shoot them. Literal ticking timebombs, however they are slow and hard to come by.
shriekers=loud nether that scream and attract other nether to help if they spot survivors or are damaged. They can also blur vision if they get to close by spitting on survivors.
watchers=red glowing eyed nether that use their eyes as spotlights to catch survivors in their sights, although that alone gives them away sometimes. mid-health and also blur vision by throwing up on survivors.
hunters=fast agile and moderate health nether that hunt in packs, like the crawlers. They use sneak attacks and usually attack by spraying bone shards from their exposed rib-cages. It has a low range, but can deal massive damage in a short time to unaware or surprised survivors.
golems=large elephant feet-like nether that can tank alot of damage. They are slow, but their main usefulness is tanking damage as well as dishing out massive damage that can cripple or even kill survivors in one-hit.
mantids=flying nether that spit fire on survivors. Aside from that, they usually are found mainly on the rooftops of buildings.
boss
reaper=boss nether that appears as an event with its own message. They are fast and agile, can tank massive amounts of damage (more than any nether) can dish out massive damage from their razor sharp blades, and are always surrounded by a mass group of other nether. If defeated, they drop a ton of loot including money, food, health supplies, guns and ammo, and other nether items including exclusive reaper blades (although this is bugged and sometimes they don't drop anything).
Your play as a survivor, who must deal with nether as you explore and survive to obtain supplies such as food, health items, money, and weapons and ammo. Your character lvls up by doing certain tasks such as killing nether, completing objectives, or through other means. You must also deal with other players on servers with pvp active.
There are safezones throughout the map. Each safezone is an outpost that has posts for trading, buying and selling, storing items, and is a general safehaven from nether and other players (players cannot shoot inside active safezones). These safezones, however; are only temporary and they do have their generators and anti-nether devices breakdown as events. If so, pvp is enabled (on pvp servers) and nether invade the outpost. They can be made safezones again by restarting the generators or fixing the anti-nether devices. If successful everyone involved gets xp, the safezone becomes safe again for trading and other tasks, and all the nether inside the safezone despawn. If not repaired during an alotted time, the safezone becomes downed for a given time before they are made back into safezones again.
each player gets bonuses from lvling up including more perks when respawning if you die and skill points. Skill points are used to lvl up your character. They are lost upon death, but theres a small amount before you max them out so its not a big worry. You lvl up your character by doing tasks in-game such as killing nether or objectives. theres a skill tree that unlocks skills based on the branch from sneaking, to more gun/melee damage, sprinting, and more. Theres a character based lvl up that caps at lvl 31 and a global lvl up system that tracks progress as a whole rather than each character. The global system also doesn't reset upon death.

Ever played a puzzle game, and wondered, this could use some gaming commentary.
Well, this is what this game is, it tells a little story while you're solving your puzzles.
The puzzles themselves are platformer puzzles, with jumps and terrain navigation.
After the tutorial levels are over, the puzzles flow became less polished. I found myself trying to edge out a few pixels here and there in a balancing act several times, to only find myself dismayed when my building blocks toppled over.
Other small gripes;
-It would sometimes display inconsistent behaviors for the blocks while on moving platforms.

-There were also a few missed opportunities to place a new hidden items.
Such as the area where the water spills out of in 3.9. I found that you could jump blocks off other blocks while they were in midair. Shame that there wasn’t anything hidden there.
-Weird design choice for the game physics
You'll see this most apparent in 4.8 and 4.10, the way jump works is you stop dead in mid air if you aren't physically controlling the block. Also applies if something else is launching you up. You will lose all forward momentum.
But what makes this game interesting is to see how narration ties in with your gameplay.
Whether if it the narrator pointing out things you might overlook, or just help change your view on your actions when personify the objects.
Though there isn't a lot of dialog in the game, I couldn't help but imagine some while playing.
Claire: ‘Don’t drown little guy, I’ll catch you if you fall!’
Chris: 'I don't need you, I can do this alone.'
A great, simplistic platformer with innovative mechanics and a cool soundtrack.

I currently have Eador: Masters of the Broken World listed as my favourite game in my profile; with well over 100 hours. Funnily enough, I don't think I even approached the end of the massive, massive campaign. Bugs aside, it really was (and is) a fantastic game.

Would it use a brand new shiny engine? Would it contain massive changes and alternations of the original game?
The answer to the above, for the most part, is no. Yet, I still recommend the game.  There really isn't anything exactly like it
