Void Destroyer 2 is a space sandbox game (and the sequel to Void Destroyer) developed by Iteration 11, a one-man dev ‘team’. In Void Destroyer 2 (VD2) you start with nothing, in fact you start as nothing. Confused and disoriented you wake up in a small, fighter class with two men talking you through how to fly your ship, it acts as an introduction to the premise of the game as well as a tutorial. After completing this fairly short but useful tutorial section, you’re free to explore the sandbox doing as you please (within the game’s limitations of course).
Getting around in VD2 requires the use of VD2’s ‘Overworld View’, it’s pretty similar to how the Mount & Blade games work. You have an overview of the whole map and you move around between spaceports and other points of interest using it. The reason you’ll want to use it is because Overworld View has Time Compression, in other words you’ll get around much quicker than just flying there normally. The Overworld View displays everything from ships (different classes of ships have different icons) to asteroid fields and of course it also displays all the different spaceports. The Overview View is only available if you’re a set distance away from certain objects, the distance away you need to be is usually related to the size of the object or how dangerous it is, for example a cleared out mine-field only requires you to be 1000 units away whereas you have to be 10,000 units away from hostile ships before you can enter Overworld View. You’re also pulled out of Overworld View when you get too close to an object.
Outside of Overworld View most of your time will be spent actually controlling your ship (there’s also a tactical view which can be used to control your fleet). VD 2’s controls are good and all the ship handling felt good to me. There’s also a good amount of difference in handling between the different ships I’ve flown so far. How well a ship can maneuver during flight depends on how fast you’re going, your ship’s cruise speed or lower is the optimum speed to turn at as the correction rockets are able to manage your momentum in different directions so you keep going in the direction you’re actually facing. You can of course go faster than your cruise speed (as well as turn off auto-correction) but generally you’ll only want to do that if you’re trying to quickly leave or get to an area.
As with most space sandbox games, there are three main ways of earning money in VD2: trading, mining & completing jobs picked up from spaceports. From what I’ve seen so far, trading is the best way to earn large amounts of reasonably quickly (especially if you have fleet or hired ships, more on those later). Mining is fairly self-explanatory, I’ve never been a fan of mining in space sandboxes so I haven’t messed around with it too much though there are ways of having ships automatically mine for you. As for the jobs, there’s currently a decent variety of jobs available to you, ranging from simple courier jobs to escort missions and bounty hunting. Each spaceport offers different jobs to you, some of the jobs will require that you use a faction ship. Completing jobs (of a certain difficulty, the level of difficulty required depends on what your level already is) will increase your relationship with the faction. Some ships available to buy at spaceports require a certain faction level before you can buy them.
The main idea of the game is that you start with next to nothing and as you progress you become more powerful. You do this in two ways. The first, and most obvious way, is by purchasing increasingly better ships when the money becomes available to you. The other way is to purchase new ships (or use older ships you’ve upgraded out of) to create a personal fleet of ships, as it stands there is no maximum fleet capacity or any upkeep costs. If you can’t afford to buy ships but need some backup or extra cargo capacity, you can also hire ships. Hiring ships is pretty cheap right now and the way it works is that you pay a set fee for each ship you have hired (you can hire a maximum of three) each time you dock at a spaceport. Each spaceport has certain ships which are available for you to hire and you may not be able to find what you’re looking for at each spaceport.
As you’d expect with an Early Access games, there are some bugs. I’ve had a few crashes so far as well as some minor bugs where my ship spins out of control when colliding with something or having my ship change positions randomly when trying to enter Overworld View while targeting a moving object such as debris. There have also been some issues with the way the achievements have been set up but chaosavy (the dev’s Steam name) has been working on fixing that. Speaking of chaosavy, he’s super active in the Steam forums (in fact posting in the forum is the easiest way to get a hold of him) which is great to see, especially with an Early Access game.
My main issue with the game as it stands is that the trading side of things feels a bit unbalanced. When I started trading I had roughly 60,000 credits and through hiring ships and after figuring out a good trade route I was sitting on 600,000 credits. It took me an hour to get to that point. I don’t want it to be like it is in Elite Dangerous where you have to grind for tens of hours to afford what you want but I feel like the game would definitely benefit from it taking a tad longer to get the best ships. Alternatively, trading could be more difficult by having groups of wandering pirates who might attack you while you’re travelling. If this is already in the game, then I didn’t see any of them during said hour so I was able to go without upgrading my very basic ship.
Furthermore, VD 2 felt a little bare to me in some areas. Not necessarily lacking content (though more job variety would be welcome) but it just didn’t feel like a lived in game-world at some points. For example, when travelling close to spaceports I never saw any ships coming in or out of the spaceports. It’s a relatively small detail, and at this stage it’s definitely not a priority, but I would like to see it addressed at some point down the line. Another improvement in this department would be more ships
Void Destroyer 2 is off to a good start, it isn’t without issues and it can feel bare at times but it's still a very enjoyable edition to the space sandbox genre. It has a long way to go but due to how hard chaosavy/Iteration 11 has been working even since release to fix things and improve the game I’m confident that a good final product will be delivered.

This game is a HUGE improvement from Crysis 1. I made a comparison post, but it looked like♥♥♥♥♥♥ But I'll tell ya now, this game is much better. Crysis 1 was more of a copy/paste of Far Cry just with nanosuits and OP Koreans slapped on it. In Crysis 2, the enemies aren't as OP as before, plus they don't come out of nowhere. There are also added stealth elements, as Crysis 1 did have a cloak, but that was more of something used to regen health to get away and such. With the new stealth kills, lower energy consumption and such, gameplay is a huge improvement. Though you aren't allowed to use your fists as a way to preserve ammo anymore, which sucks balls. Also, customization was nerfed as well. Max Speed, Strength, and Armor have been replaced not only controlwise but gameplaywise as well. Your powers are now mapped to certain keys instead of a wonky controlled quick menu. This allows you to switch between powers in real time more quickly. In gameplaywise, for Power mode, you have power jumps,sprinting, and power kicks. Max Armor is the same though, only the energy doesn't go down the drain quickly anymore. Plus, now you can upgrade your powers by stealing points that you absorb from dead alien Ceph bodies.This allows stuff like when you use Max Armor,it doesn't drain as quickly as before.The ammo caps in this sequel kinda makes the whole Crysis 1 ammo draining situation a little more worse. Plus, the CELL gunship fight is freakin hard. SO the diffuculty is somewhat dummed down, but still proves a challenge even on easy. With Cry Engine 3 I can say the graphics are beautiful! All the destroyed NY buildings look amazing! Not as beautiful as the island impressiveness of Crysis 1, but still pretty good.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8/10 Some people believe Crytek can't make awesome games and that what they make is more or less just a way to show off their graphics engine. I somewhat believe this. But Crysis 2 shouldn't be shunned, it should be appreciated a little. Like shooters with challenge that require some mean skills? Then this is for you.

The crafting system seems OK, but since you can always loot or buy lots of good stuff i saw no point in even trying it.
Now, the biggest pro is the story: it really drags you in and keeps you wanting more. That is, if you like to read. A lot. Besides from the dialogues there is quite a number of books, ranging from history books to diaries and musings about the nature of religion. All well written, adding lots of detail to the world. But that is also a big problem: the books describe things you can't actually see ingame. For instance there is a set of diaries belonging to a side quest, which leads you (according to the books) to a quiet town with about 100 persons living there. In reality, this town consists of a single hut in the forest with noone living there. Or the ruins of Darkwood, with the story of their origin, rumours and dangers told in books and dialogue - they are even a fast travel spot on your map: just two simple huts, not fitting the description in about any possible way.
So if you like to read stories: get this game, you'll get good entertainment for about 25 hours. If you would rather like to see the world than read about it: Ember might dissapoint you.

Thomas Was Alone is a sneaky, tricky, deceptive game.  I say that because so much of it is simple.  And yet...
The gameplay is straightforward. Navigate one or more blocks through short and discrete levels with simple obstacles ranging from small pits to moving platforms to spiked ceilings.  Each block has different attributes and abilities: one can jump high, one can float in water, one can act as a trampoline, and so on.  It's not a complex idea, and yet it is executed so well that it is very easy to lose yourself in the pulse of the game, playing level after level well into the night.
Playing the game is a joy, but what brings the game close to transcendence is the storytelling.  Each block has a distinct voice and, more importantly, an immediately relatable personality: one is an observer, one dreams of being a superhero, one is jealous of the others' talents.  Again nothing complex, and yet that very simplicity allows the player to immediately relate with each block - their dreams and fears and hopes and insecurities.
At first this engagement is simply amusing, another minor incentive to keep the player pushing through the game.  But as the plot unfolds and the blocks begin to understand the true nature of their situation, the player becomes truly invested.  And when the blocks individually come to their moments of self-realization, I found them each aspirational.
There are a few minor flaws in Thomas Was Alone - the last chapters feel a bit anti-climatic, and there are some annoying jumping challenges - but nothing that should stop anyone from playing the game.
---------- Elliot Was Alone ------------
Elliot was kicking at the scruffy soccer ball when he heard his sister shout, "Cape cape CAPE!"
They were alone in their aunt's apartment, a stifling small two bedroom in a fading complex. "Better than a foster home," his aunt had shrugged. She was right, of course, and her being right just made everything worse.
The sudden spike of fury was sharp and would not be contained. Elliot set his left foot and used the right to whack the ball against the flaking wall. It bounced off with a sharp
, and something in the bathroom fell to the floor and shattered. Elliot cursed - loudly - and slammed open the door to the bedroom that he shared with his sister.
"You're not supposed to say that word," Abby said without looking up. Being chastised by a sibling four years his junior - or was it five? it was strangely difficult to keep track these days, with time feeling soft like clay - did little to improve his mood. "A cape?" he said, ignoring her comment. "You made your dumb blocks capes?"
Now Abby did look up, but only to smile. "Just one cape," she said, holding up a badly cut paper square. There was a picture on it, drawn in crayon, of something that might have been a mutated two-headed cat. "Claire wants one."
Elliot rolled his eyes. "Claire" was a big wooden cube scribbled through with whorls of blue. Months after the accident Abby had taken six or seven of her blocks and colored them each with its own color. Then she had given them not only names, but distinct personalities as well. "Thomas likes to watch things," she might say as she bounced the red block along the floor. Or,
tossing the purple one up into the air: "Look! How can Sarah even go so high? She must have amazing powers!"
Sometimes it was all Elliot could do to stop himself from throwing the blocks down the garbage chute. He imagined the pleasure he would feel listening to the gong-like sounds the blocks would make as they bounced off the sides.
"Claire's a superhero, you see," Abby continued in a matter-of-fact tone. "She's the only one of them that can float in water. Like a rubber duckie." She put her hand to the side of her mouth; whispering loudly she said, "She can't jump very high though, but. . . look what happens when she jumps on top of Laura!" Laura was a pink block laying horizontally on the ground. Abby took Claire and touched the blue block to Laura; then she made a
ing noise and arced
Claire high over her head.
Elliot could only stare. "Are you kidding me?"
Abby looked puzzled. "Kidding about what?" She set Claire before her and reached for the cape.
"About. . . about all of this!" He squatted down. "It's all so
," he said, picking up a yellow block and shaking it in front of Abby's face. His anger was growing again, like it so often did these days. He didn't want it to. He just couldn't help it. "And this cape, what do you think it - ?"
He snatched at the cape expecting his sister to let go, like she always did when he grabbed at something. But this time her skinny fingers held on tight. And the paper ripped in two.
The silence that ensued rang loudly in Elliot's ears. Time crept like a worm while his face flamed and his stomach roiled, and it was an eternity before he finally stammered, "I. . . I didn't mean. . ." Then he stopped. Because of course what was
didn't matter. Nothing that had happened in the past year had been
. But it
, and why did it always feel like he was the one, the only one, that had to deal with the consequences?
The resentment inside of him was like a stone; it centered him. He took a sullen breath. "It was just a dumb cape. I can -" he began. Then he met Abby's eyes and stopped again, this time out of shock. Her face was stiff and her eyes were burning, and although he had never seen his sister that way, he recognized the look at once - because it was like looking in a mirror. And that was when he realized that he wasn't the only one that had to deal with consequences.
"I'm sorry," he whispered. "I'm sorry. Can I - ?"
"
" she shrieked, and Elliot watched, sick inside, as she half-rose with the force of her word.
"Yes," Abby muttered, sitting back down. She tossed a small orange block at him; he caught it\ out of the air. "You can be Chris."
Elliot kept his mouth shut, swallowing his first response back down his throat. Then he asked in an even voice, "What's Chris like? What can he do?"
"Nothing," snapped his sister. "He's small and mean and he can't even jump very high."
His anger was gone now. It had been replaced by shame, a whole ocean of it, enough to drown him a thousand times over. Was it better to feel like this? He rubbed his eyes. Maybe it was. At least he wouldn't hurt anybody this way.
Abby touched his arm then, softly. "Hey," she said. "But, you know, Chris isn't. . . he isn't really
mean. He's just confused. Confused and. . ." She paused. ". . . and sad." Her face relaxed. "He doesn't know it yet, but he's going to be a hero. Just like the rest of them."
Elliot smiled. "Tell me."
Abby began to talk, and Elliot sat and watched in wonder as his sister's face bloomed once more.

Well, there isn't really anything to complain.
The graphics look simple, but they work surprisingly well in conjunction with the story. And the story really is what kept me hooked, or the narration. Probably both, as one goes with the other.
The soundtrack is excellent as well.
Levels are rather simple to do for the most part; getting 100% achievements is no deal.
This isn't a game meant to challenge or frustrate you -- at least I don't think it is. If that was their intention, they failed horribly. The gameplay merely connects the story pieces, and since most of the narration is at the beginning of a level, you don't really want to spend hours trying to figure out how to complete it.
However, for what it does, the gameplay works very well. I used a XBox-360 controller so I can't judge the keyboard controls, but the game did exactly what I told it to do.
As you progress through levels, Thomas will eventually no longer be alone, but except for a few levels at the end, no two characters are identical. The narration even assigns them personality; in terms of gameplay they have different sizes, jump lengths and possibly other abilities, so you need to combine them appropiately to get everyone to their designated exit point.
All in all, if you're looking to maximize hours/buck, go elsewhere. If you like to try a simple game with an excellent presentation and execution that -- in my opinion -- doesn't fail at anything it attempts to do, go for it.

Void Destroyer 2 is excellent, well optimized, runs smooth, and most importantly is a ton of fun. It more than exceeds the bar for an early access title and I, like others, am super hyped for its continued development. Chaosavy is an awesome, extremely active dev that listens to his playerbase. Example: Some people didn't like the blue skybox, so he added more! So many pretty colors.
Now what's in the game right now? A solid tight sandbox, it's not giant but there's plenty to do. Think M&B Warband overworld style map. You start off as a fighter, can do courier, escort, bounty hunting, piracy, base and platform defense, platform destruction, hire or purchase trading and mining ships, automate ships, purchase and choose from about 30 ships (not including pirates) from light fighters to frigates and upgrade them. You could even technically do noncombat and fly around in a repair ship just helping your own fleets or NPC's. All at a smooth 60 FPS with no jitters and what is really a blast dogfighting.
Really outside of more content, which is planned, like blueprints for cruiser, capital, dreadnought ships, base capturing and management, market events for dynamic trading, more missions, more UI polish, there is at least 30 hours of great content just doing "law-abiding" stuff alone. And perhaps most important, a dev that cares and listens to the community.
Perfect for first day early access, could be at the top of the genre in 6 months.

Jazzpunk is another game that, like Zeno Clash, tries to be held up entirely by weirdness.  It fails just as spectacularly.  Behind the extreme weirdness, there is nothing interesting nor compelling just a bland game full of random occurences and random references.  I would liken it to the recent teenage buzzword "random":  It feels like a desperate cry for attention by being different when in reality it's rather predictable and not the least bit interesting.
Gameplay consists of walking around and interacting with various objects and completing very short side missions while you accomplish your main objective for each level.  There are only a couple missions and they go by quickly.  The game tries really hard to be funny but there's not much humor to be found when nothing makes any sense, barring a couple lines from side characters.
From a technical standpoint, the game is a bit odd.  It has very simple graphics and should run on a toaster due to that but for some reason is limited to 60 fps.  Keyboard movement keys are not set by default so you have to do it yourself and the mouse control is very sluggish and stuttery.  The game also stutters occasionally.  All of these things are extremely strange for a game running on the Unity engine but it doesn't get in the way too much.
So to summarize Jazzpunk is a very weird game held up entirely by weird random references and humor, neither of which work.  How this game has gotten over 90% positive reviews completely baffles me.

A solid RPG! Not amazingly complex but very well put together and quite enjoyable. Control a small party of 3 (out of 4? choices), kill a small variety of enemies, loot and craft. TBH I never bothered with crafting. I do like that not all weapons/armor are generic combinations that you can craft, there are a few unique items. And you do have the opportunity to kill some NPCs like the Goblin King, which is fun. Graphics and art design are excellent.
Special comment about the Lore in the game - it is extensive, well-written, and genuinely interesting. The story is engaging and fairly original. I especially liked the treatment of the Giants and Shepherds. Some of the side quests are worth doing just for the story progress (though some are pointless fetch quests).
The combat system is also very good. I loved the drag-line attack/magic assignment in particular. Though I appreciated the simplicity of the magic system I did miss not having actual spells to cast, instead of just equipment-imbued charms. The lack of click-and-hold for general movement controls was annoying, but quickly got used to it.
Overall, recommended to any RPG fan. Great value for money, a solid 20 hour quest and a very well made game.

The green cube in some levels is a save point.
Most levels do not have save points.
The levels are a mix of easy to hard all the way to the end.
Some levels you can become trapped, though this is pretty rare and if you put your brain on overdrive, you can solve most anything.

I'm a huge puzzler fan and I have been following this game before it's release. Now that I have had a chance to play it, I feel like I must say a few things about this game. I am not going to go deep in explaining game mechanics in this review, but it is a mechanic that I never saw in any game before where you bend the level between two cubes and those cubes converge while the space between them vanishes, rendering us able to progress.
First of all the level designs are great. They teach you the game the Nintendo way: by making you figure it out with placing obstacles along the way, and along the way they make sure you have learned how to use that mechanic, otherwise you can't progress. Along with that there are really challenging levels that intrugues your brain. I had to think a lot in some levels as the game progressed. I also like the simplistic design of the game, as there are very few things that feel out of the line in art design. Another minor side that is good about this game is that it is very lightweight and you never wait between the levels and scenes as it smoothly progresses to the next level even in hard drives.
Moving to the cons of the game, I must say that there are some: The most important one being the color choices, and although I don't especially like the design, I am talking about your eyes. They will get hurt if you play it too much, which is not likely in most games these days, as most of them have figured using color schemes that work well. About game design, the level progression is ridiculous. After you have finished early levels that ought to teach you the game mechanics, you get to see challenging levels as you progress; but after that level there might come a really easy level or a moderately difficult level that uses the same game mechanic or an approach to solve which you have just mastered using in the previous levels, and they appear to be no challenge at all, where you pass them for nothing. One way to solve this problem would be placing those levels before the difficult one. Another thing I have to mension about level design would be the dead end cases. Yes, I can restart the level from checkpoint but reaching a dead end without return is a little inconvenient while you still live. Talking about checkpoints, it was pretty hard to understand the purpose of the checkpoint box, as it had a weird animation where the whole level shrinks in to this box instantly and you just get confused about what is going on all of a sudden. I understood it when I saw the fading Fabric logo on the lower right corner, as it means the game is being saved in most games.
So overall,
Pros:
+Distinct, innovative game mechanic
+Challenging levels
+Great way to teach game mechanics without tutorials
+Simplistic design
+Very Lightweight, no loading screens
Cons:
-Colors, your eyes get hurt
-Inconsistent level progression
-Dead ends that force you to restart level
I would definitely recommend this game as the challenging levels and the distinct game mechanics instantly pulled me in. I don't recall so many puzzle games that intrigued me like this game did. The only big problem here is that the game is tiring for the eyes, and you have to bear with this respect of the game if you want to play it.

*Note: this review was written before the 2.0 update and many issues have now been fixed*
This is one of those odd games to review. You see initially i was having an enjoyable experience and wondering why this game got lower scores but now that i look back i see some of the outstanding issues. At the beginning of the game I was pretty freaked out, you know, taking my time looking around every dark corner. This was good, the opening prologue level was probably my favourite part of the experience. But after the end of this level that's when things start to fall down. Slowly as you progress through each level the fear factor actually decreases. With brighter lit enviroments as you progress the game it took away some of the worry that i had since i no longer needed to worry about what was in the dark.(BTW i love darkness in games but when you make it so dark it's impossible to navigate i have an issue) Not only does the scare factor drop with the lighting system but when i first watched the Chaser from a distance i was more laughing than scared since the animation was jerky and the AI seemed to be in a state of pants-on-head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This strikes me as odd though that an enemy that you will spend a lot of time looking at has crap animation while the Slenderman(the creature you'll want to spend the least time looking at) has proper and well designed animations. The other creature, Charlie, seemed to have near-non existant animations and when he was sitting still it looked more like a something from Doom where it's a 2D images worked into a 3D enviroment.
The sound design feels well done with creature and enviroment noises adding to your already tense state. But i stopped for a minute when I heard the sounds from Slender: The Eight Pages. I guess it's supposed to be a callout to the last game but this is a new game and i'd like to hear improved versions of these sounds.
Speaking of the last game, I did enjoy the Eight Pages remake level, which did a good job of calling out to the last game while still keeping a sense of originality.
Now here's the big one besides the ending, the glitches. Now I only had one real gamebreaking bug but in horror games even if a bug isn't game breaking it can still absolutely ruin the immersion for a player. For example, the first time I played the Eight Pages level I had 7 pages and was freaking out ,worrying about the Slenderman but then I saw him and was baffled when he was about to kill me and then just left. I didn't see him like a retard and walked right into him and ♥♥♥♥ all happened. And I know this isn't supposed to happen since I tested the level other times. Other Slendy bugs were dying from him even though he was nowhere to be seen, him teleporting inside other objects and a weird one where he hovered above the ground. My gamebreaking bug was when I was caught by the Chaser and waited to die but the camera just sat there fixated on the Chaser's face like it had grabbed me. After a few minutes the Chaser started running away with the camera following it's face from the front. This continued for about 7 minutes before i gave up and had to restart the level.
We now come to the ending. Now I feel like I could spoil the ending here and not ruin it for you at all but I won't for the sake of fanboys everywhere. What you should know is the ending is a major cliffhanger with nothing being resolved. It just kinda ends. Maybe I could have overlooked this but with the game being obnoxiously short it makes it un-compensatable. It feels like after the ending was actually once a level just a leading to the next level and they were just like, "♥♥♥♥ it we can sell it like this" and then just folded in.
So all in all,
PROS:
-Nicely designed enviroments
-Atmospheric SFX and music
-Very well directed opening
-Small enclosed enviroments(buildings, etc...)
-Scary and well designed creatures
-Interesting secret level
-Some genuinly scary moments
CONS:
-Embarrasingly short
-Buggy creature animation
-Poor AI
-Massively well lit sections
-Repetitive objectives
-Too much audio taken from S:EP
-Many glitches and bugs
-The door opening mechanics
-Extremely aggravating to get the secret level
-Unsatisfying ending
I wish there was a maybe button on Steam because that would suit this perfectly since there are good sequences but it is overall lacking so I'm afraid I can't recommend this unless it's on a decent sale.

What kind of a strategy game is Eador: Imperium?
For those who do not know Eador: Genesis / Eador : Master of the Broken World:
Turn based strategy, with Turn based combats - that happen only at the end of the turn.
Both tactical and stratetic map is HEX-based.
Source of income are provinces, but that is rarely enough - to build your economy up - you will need to attack neutral places (dungeons) - as there lies the true wealth.
True source of power lies in the starting city (starting province). Losing this province = defeat. Building this province up (selectable choice-based, meaning, that building something may prevent you from building something else. Specialization is applied for units/spells/items)
Other provinces have very limited options for upgrade and any buildings built there either boost your economy, local happiness or provide strategic improvement (forts)
Your main military power lies within your Hero (later you can buy additional heroes)
Heroes gain XP from battles (and some rituals - strategic map spells).
Can equip items (specific for each class: Warrior, Ranger, Mage, Commander)
Can cast spells (tactical = battle map)
And are the only way to capture neutral provinces, as well to siege and defeat enemy players by capturing their main province.
AI of Eador is pretty high and challenging.
Luckilly, this game provices different difficulty options.
Compared to previous games (MotBW) this game adds new spells, units, heroes, maps...
Compared to Genesis, this game is much more visually appealing, even having much better music.
Bugs - I have completed one campaign and did not encounter any bugs so far, but the game is so complex, that I can't say I am certain, there are no bugs at all.
Complexity : number of strategies has limited combinations first 1-10 levels of your main hero, when you have access to basic units, spells, and hence limited tactical advantages (also you can select your enemies very wisely - from narrow list, if you want to win)
But beyond level 10, you can upgrade your hero, restock you army with higher tier units, and find + equip much more powerful items.
Then your tactical options explode and you can nearly double your battle effectiveness - but still avoid 35-40% of neutral enemies.
But if you make it up to level 20+, then you can add even more peculiar strategies, some of them built on pure luck (based on items/spells drops from victories or from random-encounter shops in your provinces) - this is when you realize, the game cannot bore you and each new playthrough can surprsie you. Sometimes ina bad way (non-applicable drops, no  good spells and no powerful merceneries - beating the game becomes much harder), sometimes in a good way (over powered item or spell or unit will be found while exploring and you can start defeating much stronger neutral - reaping the rewards / spoils of war like a BOSS)
Due high randomness, this game just cannot become boring, but it always will be challenging.
If you like to play difficult strategy games, and love good visuals / music. This game is for you!

This game is a weird blend of
and
that seems to blend some of the worse parts of both of those games. The controls are unintuitive if you have played a computer ARPG before, as some of the genre staples don't function properly. While the game doesn't look like a mobile port, it definitely feels like one with drag and drop controls that add a different flavor to the gameplay. The story is pretty basic with a few twists and slaps you with an awakened messiah with amnesia back story out of the gate. Quests are basic fetch and kill quests.
The game looks OK for an indy game with out a big budget. But compared to its peers like Grim Dawn, Titan Quest and Diablo 3, it feels very cartoony and simplified. The lighting effects are not too bad. The graphics aren't bad, but they aren't going to wow anyone either.
This is the worst part of the experience. The controls are clunky and counter-intuitive. To move the main character, you can click anywhere in the environment that has a fairly open path to it, or you can click on any character and drag the cursor to the spot you want them to go. This is the ONLY way to move other characters in your party. It feels like a
. Many ARPG staples for movement and skills are gone. You have exactly 3 hot keys, and no right click or middle click attacks. However, combat is incredibly slow to accommodate your lack of quick action. If it's still too fast, here comes the Baldur's Gate portion: you can pause the game and issue orders then resume. There are 4 stats to increase, at the rate of 2 points per level. This is fine, as Strength, Dexterity, Intellect, and Vitality cover pretty much all the areas that need it. Skills are obtainable through equipped items only, which is kind of meh. There is no character skill development in this one. It's like Path of Exile if that was incredibly dumbed down.
The story is fairly generic, and side quests barely serve to flesh out anything. The backstory of your character is ok, you were once an angel that helped win the war against evil, sleeping for thousands of years and awakened with no memory of your actual past. Most people older than 12 will see where this is going. The path it travels is well trodden, but those old stories are constantly retold because they are good. This is no exception. Nothing original, but it's still enjoyable enough to experience.
The game is enjoyable enough to play once you've learned to wrestle with the controls. It feels like baby's first ARPG with slow combat that isn't deep, and since combat is most of what there is to do in this game, that takes away from it. I recommend it, if just barely because it isn't the worst experience, and brings a few nice ideas to the table. The game is better played on an iPad than the PC, though and is very ambitious for a mobile game. Would have loved to see some changes to the controls for the PC port though.

Slender: The Arrival is a short game where the player takes control of Lauren who is searching for her friend, Kate, in the middle of the forest controlled by the omnipresent Slender Man. With players viewing the action through Lauren's video camera, the game is at first deeply atmospheric but flaws that hinder the experience soon become apparent.
The majority of Slender: The Arrival involves the player walking through dark, open environments where the Slender Man can appear from anywhere. On a first playthrough, Slender: The Arrival is very tense, with each step forward making the player feel uneasy. The overall atmosphere is bleak with finely presented environments, eerie music and collectible notes helping construct an unsettling experience. Players familiar with Slender Man lore will undoubtedly find the experience more unnerving than those who are not.
Despite the rich atmosphere and tangible tension, Slender: The Arrival turns into a trivial, almost dull game once the Slender Man actually appears. The first time a player observes the Slender Man, their inital response is most likely one of fright. However, each time the Slender Man appears on screen, the frightning effect is diminished. Players will soon realise that the game consists of a foe that can teleport around the environment to provide cheap jump scares and little more. It soon becomes tedious and if one were to turn around and see the Slender Man merely floating toward them as if it were on a wire, it all becomes easily managable.
Slender: The Arrival is good during the first hour but it soon becomes a tedious collection of jump scares which fail to fright and interactions with a folkloreish entity that strips away all creditable mystery or menace. Even harder difficulty settings fail to improve the frights in a lacklustre horror experience.

Princess Remedy is a charming & sweet little bullet-hell-lite-esque game that evokes a rather unique sense of nostalgia while still staying true to its own style. It is a very short game - for a completionist-run you won't really spend more than an hour on it unless you're going for every ending or you're not used to bullet hells, but the experience will still make your day a little lighter. The humour doesn't get old (though it helps the game is too short to run the style of humour into the dirt), and the dialogue is refreshingly lighthearted. Additional pros are that, in the ending (spoilers ahead, obviously), you aren't limited in your marriage choices to just male characters. In fact, you can marry basically anyone. I would have gladly paid £2 for a short & sweet little game like this, so the fact that on top of all these wonderful points the game is FREE? It certainly deserves all my recommendations. Give this game a try, seriously! The charm will lighten your day, even if only for a little while, and if it doesn't? You lose nothing for having given it a shot. Go have some fun and heal some people! :)

First, let's get through the negatives. Yes, the writing is mostly a joke — it resembles the movies too much, and goes nowhere interesting. The palette is pretty boring, or at least it bored me; there's too many washed out blues, reds, and purples throughout the game. The camera was jerky at times (though the initial complaints of it being too zoomed in was something I never understood). Leon is no longer funny and Helena is even worse. Some enemies reminded me too much of L4D, a game which I was not a huge fan of. Cover shooting is kind of tacked on. That's about it.
This game is still good. There's so much content here. 4 different campaigns, each with several different environments you play through. There are SO many environments in this game! There's also a ton of enemies; granted, many of them are just small variations of one another, but it's still an impressive amount overall. There's plenty of weapons, the melee system has been revamped, the inventory has been revamped... Capcom really put a lot of effort into the game. No Mercy Mercenaries is also incredible and totally blows Resident Evil 5 Mercenaries out of the water. The co-op action and content of this game more or less makes Resident Evil 5 unplayable and irrelevant now.
Too many people, mostly nostalgia-driven, played this just looking for something to complain about I think. They failed to realize all the great things it did as a result. For example, the campaign intersections — who ever brings those up? Except those were awesome and were no doubt an idea from the director Eiichiro Sasaki who also directed the Outbreak games. The intersections added a layer of immersion not seen before in games, it reminded you that other players were going through the other campaigns and thus made the story feel like it was happening in real-time. This new dimension of campaign storytelling was an ambitious improvement, apparently too ambitious because nobody even recognized how amazing it was! The combat system is also so intricately balanced and complex here, that many people end up just complaining that it's too hard; they say there isn't enough ammo in the game, or the camera is too hard to control, when these things simply weren't the case. I ranked in the top 10 in Mercenaries the first month of release prior to any camera patches, any complaints about the camera are a complete result of utter incompetence in my opinion.
Overall it's not the best Resident Evil, and it's not the best game of all time, but it was still a very good game. The hate was uncalled for. If you want to play No Mercy on PC with me feel free to hit me up, I'm down for that any day.

So I played through this game, got all of the achievements, and I'm still at a loss of what it was all about. Jazzpunk is a cartoon. There are games with cartoony graphics, some that are actually based off of cartoons, but Jazzpunk is straight-up Tex Avery. If you've never heard of the guy, you're missing out. He directed a ton of hilarious shorts back in the mid-20th century that still hold up today. His directorial style resulted in wacky, off-kilter, crass, and sometimes totally ridiculous cartoons.
There is a plot to Jazzpunk, but it's designed solely to set up as many gags as possible. Apparently you're a spy, and your mission is to infiltrate various locations and steal super-important stuff. I can't say much else because, since this is an interactive-adventure game, it'll ruin a lot of the jokes & surprises. I can give you a vague idea of what to expect though. Almost every chapter consists of an area you can explore. There are objects and citizens you can interact with, and there's some very light puzzle-solving as well. Everything is set up as part of the experience, so whatever happens you just roll with it.  It's impossible to die and there are no fail-states for your mission, so there's no sense of danger or urgency.
It's important to note that this is a very short game. Anyone should be able to get all of the achievements in less than two hours. There are plenty of secrets and things to try at least, but that's still less than four hours of game-time. If we're speaking strictly in terms of value, you don't have to look hard to find titles with more game for less money. However if you, like I, happened upon this game due to its appearance in a bundle, then I definitely recommend exploring it.

I've just finished the game at the hardest difficulty and AI was a complete disappointment, after Cevat Yerli's comments on it, "the most sophisticated AI you'll ever see in a video game." Sadly no, AI was a disaster. Cloak mode and armor mode of your nanosuit are your biggest helpers in the game, and with them, "Post-Human Warrio" difficulty was no match. Enemies and allies, all comporting strange... Crysis 3 will be an improvement on this I hope.
Scenario: Well, the story was good honestly, being compared to most FPS. Steven Spielberg's War of the Worlds and Arnold Schwarzannager's Predator are big inspirations for the writers of this game, definitely. The story takes place after 3 years of the Crysis 1 and Crysis Warhead. To be able to understand it completely, you have to pay full attention to the in-game dialogues and watch entire of the Prophet's Visions videos, which are available in unlockable section in main menu. Otherswise you'll be confused with big gaps on the fiction, therefore you may not like the story. It's like a puzzle. My only criticism here to Crytek might be the bad presentation of it. And if you don't like the science-fiction/aliens genre, this is not your game.
Crytek also appointed a science-fiction writer to write a novel, thay may help studying the story in a wider perspective. Lastly, Crysis Wikia will be enough to "veneer" your knowledge of Crysis universe, especially the page of Jacob Hargreave.
And even though the game imposes the usual alien invasion theme, Nanotechnology is an important research are in 21st century, so I kinda like it how they built the story of the nanosuit and its capabilities on it. A huge potential area to tell a story, via a game.
Gameplay: My biggest concern on the gameplay was "spawning enemies". Yeah, when you're beating the game on the hardest difficulty, spend your 30 minutes to clear a part of the map with huge effort, and after all seeing spawning enemies out of nowhere is not a nice experiment.
So FFS Crytek, drop spawning enemies from your future games.
There's no savegame function, but that's okay. My only complaint about it is the long time periods between the checkpoints. Dying after a large progression can take you back to a so early portion, which can ruin your gaming and enthusiasm.
Lastly, abouth the "Nanosuit Improvement" part... You can access this part by pressing H in-game. You're granted catalyst point by killing Cephs throughout the game, the with enough accumulation, you can buy some cools improvements. But some of these improvements are so pointless. For example, de-cloaking your invicible enemies... There were only 4 invicible enemies in the game, all of them were in the last mission, at the last part of it. Which took 1 minute for me to kill them all. Unlocking this feature took 16000 catalyst points, which was also the most expensive feature of all.
What were you thinking Crytek? Have you released the game without being finished?  With the distributor being Electronic Arts, that's a high possibility. EA is known for putting stress on the developers to release unfinished products in a pushed calendar.
Musics composed by Hans Zimmer, who's known for his works in movies like Batman Trilogy, Rain Man, Gladiator, vice versa. The Main Theme was perfect.
Graphics are alreadly critically acclaimed.
So 10 points for visuals, 10 points for sound effects and musical score.
And my overall score for Crysis 2 is 8/10 with all pros and cons summed up.
Post Script: I haven't tried the multiplayer experience, I'll give it a shot when Crysis 3 hits.
Cheers, Can

I've been playing guitar on and off for almost 20 years. After getting my dream guitar, I picked this up to get my chops up again, and I'm loving it. The style of play is similar to other karaoke style music games with the benefit that you're not just pushing plastic keys, you're actually playing guitar.  I'm a big fan of game based learning and I think Ubi has done well with this.  The game gives good feedback on areas where you need to improve and has a good number of built in tools. Multiple guitar parts are included with some songs, so you can play to your preference (lead/rhythm).  This is not a complete solution to learning guitar, but I think it's a good starter. Going back and forth between Rocksmith's version of Tab and traditional can be tough, I have to say, I prefer Rotcksmith's.  I also wish they had a tool to start to teach reading music, not just tab.  I do like that as you advance the game starts to give you chord names as you learn the fingering.
PRO: Excellent for any level of guitar player. Easy setup to get you going and matching the songs.
CON: Not enough music. Previous version songs are supposed to be compatible, but I think you have to own the previous version?  Too bad if you are on mac, don't know if the conversion will work yet without the game installed.

For a learning tool, this game is a 50/50 situation. It effectively teaches you to play, however since you don't have a teacher next to you, you can often get confused on how to play a part of a song, or potentially get a technique wrong.
This game is very effective when it comes to teaching even then though, so don't be fooled, I couldn't play ANYTHING on my bass before Rocksmith. I could only play.... about... uhm...  two notes on Wrathchild (by iron maiden) and to me, it felt REALLY difficult. But after 20-30 hours on Rocksmith, I could breeze through about 50-80 percent of the song.
150 gaming hours later and I can play just about any song on the setlist and get above at least 80-90 percent.
Being a massive Iron Maiden fan, I was pleased to see Iron Maiden DLC. I currently have 98% on Two Minutes To Midnight and I've reached one hundred percent on Run To The Hills. It feels great acomplishing a song on Rocksmith as it can be very stressful and hard trying to complete a song.
As I've mentioned earlier though, because there is no teacher to help you, it can be very frustrating trying to learn techniques. Especially harder techniques such as "Tapping" And "Slap/Pop". And if you simply can't get the technique right, the game will keep making you do it over and over without ANY further tips or advice.
It pulls you by the nose really.
The arcade games are rather dull, although some like *deep breath* SCAALEE WARRIORRS! are quite addictive if you know your scales fairly well. (I don't.. but oh well.)
Guitarcade's Score Attack is certainly worth a look, I think it's a very engaging way to improve on your songs.
The DLC offered is mostly brilliant, but if you ask me, they needed more metal classics, hell, I wouldn't mind if they added video game music! I feel they needed a wider variety in terms of genre, but eh, I have my Maiden and that's all I'll ever need.
It's definately, DEFINATELY, worth the buy if you're a music fan. Just hands down. If you get bored of the setlist, you can download custom songs online, which has certainly kept me occupied for a good 50 hours. XD
All in all, fantastic. I'm very pleased with this game.

I've been playing round-based strategy computer games for more years than I care to share.
Only very few games managed to truly impress me and make it into my personal "hall of fame."
Eador Imperium, despite all its shortcomings, is one of these rare gems.
The game is hard, even painfully hard at times. Building your kingdom is tough in the beginning of
the game. There are many building options and the starting hero is weak, so the options are limited.
But with a little patience, you will manage to build an interesting hero with a strong party.
Yet, with the exception of very high-level heros with powerful items and high-level units, the game
does not get boring, because AI opponents will attack your lands with powerful heros and will keep
you in check. Also, there is almost no way that you will reach this point where "your coffers are
always filled with gold." I know of no other kingdom management-type strategy game that does such
a good job of keeping things balanced. Once your income rises, "unfortunate random events" will
deplete your gold, and then there is also corruption and the chance of provinces rebelling against
your rule. So you have to try to counteract all these threats while building a strong army. This is quite challenging,
so I'd say this is no game for "newbies."
Also, the tactical battles can also be quite difficult, either because of the sheer strength of the enemy or because a lot of micro management is required.
Terrain also plays an important role - which can work to your advantage but at times (and depending
on the hero and units) can also work against you. What I like a lot about the AI (which is medium
strong compared with other games) is that it will tend to kill weaker units if the enemy is able to do
so. You you also have to watch out for your troops.
It's a little bit of a shame that province defenders come in "generic kits", meaning their makeup is
largely standardized; this can make gameplay tedious in an area where all guards are of the same
type.
But the overall design is amazing, there is a good dose of (sometimes dark) humor in the game,
and since you "multiclass" your hero at 10th level, even playing the same hero type over again
remains interesting.
If you loved HOMM III and similar games and are not afraid of a high level of building management,
this one is for you!!
(yes, there are issues in the areas of game stability and the music in Eador Imperium is too monotonous,
but the positive aspects greatly outweigh these problems!)

Yearning for the experience of 2000s online shooters? Want to play a game where you run around in circles in linear maps like the days of yore where you have no hit detection while a latvian kid gloats in front of a 20 year old CRT monitor over crushing you  because you have 300 ping and he needs to feel better about his chainsmoking father beating the crap out of him every evening? Want this experience enhanced by graphics that were passable in 2010 and a matchmaking system that will only work properly on a game with a much, much larger playerbase? Then look no further!
If not, then congratulations. You actually support a basic standard for gameplay from sometime in the past decade, and should probably avoid this glorified counter-strike mod. The gameplay is pretty much a bland, barebones online shooter. It is not an MMOFPS in spite of what the developers keep insisting; the matches are 6v6 and most of the time the matchmaker yields 2v2 matches with 8 bots. Said bots are a relic from a bygone era as well, being completely stupid and unable to figure out how the map works or see targets a good 90% of the time before whirling around and instantly headshotting you, only for the replay to indicate that they apparently killed you by sheer force of will *before* aiming into a brick wall six feet to your left.
The gameplay modes that the developer hype targets, various forms of CTF and KotH, are barely played, and for the most part you're just going to be taking forever to whittle down a kill counter like every other online FPS ever made. The map design is poor, and I am not talking about a lack of polish. I am talking uninteresting maps with linear design that look like they lazily copied their design/tactical principles from playing MW1 for exactly one hour. The layouts can be best described as an endless series of parallel walls that manages to seem comically huge and tiny at the same time, and on many of them it honestly feels like playing Source engine mod maps from back in the day.
Levelling/ranked/advancement are nothing more than a pointless carrot on a stick that serve as time/money sinks. While not unusual for this type of gameplay, there really is no sense of advancement, and equipment stats are an elaborate yet inconsequential detail (though buying all of the otherwise inaccessible "expert/etc." gear with real money confers enough of an advantage to keep people with more money than sense interested). You can still get on quite well at high tiers sprinting around the map with the starter sawn off shotgun and punching people to death. This is not helped by the dismal matchmaking times. Expect to wait several minutes (sometimes up to 20) before getting into a match that's mostly bots.
There is absolutely nothing special about this game or its format, which is a dangerous characteristic for an in-development/early access game. The overall design really suggests that the game will never escape the obvious halfassed pay-to-win chasm that it comfortably occupies, and that the devs wouldn't know what the hell to do with it if they ever got a better budget. 20 hours was more than enough to realise this.
As a final note, if any S.T.A.L.K.E.R. fans are drawn to this because it's a product of all that's left of that series' development team, prepare to be disappointed. There is effectively no similarity. It only bears a vague resemblance to the mediocre online modes of the series that were unknown to anyone outside of Russia at the time. Really just another piece of evidence that eastern europe has no place in the gaming industry, seeing as they can only make a good game by accident.

This game is atrocious. It is so bad, I am not sure where to even begin, so let's just start with the intro scenes. The introduction takes about an hour to get through, and that is primarily because it seizes from you your ability to control the speed you move. You can also look forward to inconsistent controls. Sometimes a melee attack will hit an enemy, sometimes not - I tested this after a checkpoint. To add to the unnecessary difficulty created by bad controls, you cannot attack the enemies that will stand up to attack you until after they do. This means that if you're supposed to walk across something that will try to grab your legs, you can't shoot it ahead of time, you literally HAVE to let it try to grab you before you can harm it.
This game is clunky, slow, frustrating, and has taken several steps backwards from previous games. If ever there was a Resident Evil game to skip over, it is this one.

Jazzpunk is a comedic game aiming to surprise and amuse you. In the world of Jazzpunk, you play an agent named Polyblank. You explore the 3D world from a first-person perspective, doing everything except the main objective first so that you don't just see a only a very tiny fraction of what's actually in the game. It may be a bit thin to some players, but it still is the kind of thing only a videogame can do, and we need more stuff like this or evolved from it. Here a line something like "generic joke" can work because the whole thing is not generic. Yes, you'll get tired of such stuff if you talk to every NPC like ya should and sometimes it has referential "humor."
Well, sadly, I do feel to mention that it's probably a four hour game for people. The FOV is unchangable and character movement continues after you release movement. Also consider the price and buy when you won't feel disappointed. Regarding achievements, they are all just for poking about the Jazzpunk world well, so I suggest ignoring them due to light spoilers on your first playthrough and looking forward to them for the second.
Jazzpunk's a type we need more of. It's a 3D world with hotspots of jokes, cleverness, and surprises. When the price can't be wrong, tune your device for squelch and jump in.

WILL IT RUN CRYSIS?
That famous catchphrase known in PC gaming. As for Crysis 2, I'll do a two-shot review as I did played the game at release and now, two years later.
1) So, at release, I would say I was totally disappointed with this game. Very consolized, lack of PC functions and worst, no DirectX 11 support. So technically speaking, the game was lackluster and underwhelming. Aside from the specs, the gameplay was also underwhelming as what made Crysis known was the more freedom of approach to the missions. In C2, it is very linear. Close to no exploration. Little to none "driving/piloting".
What was even more irritating was the dismissal of NOMAD, Crysis 1 protagonist. Apparently, he got killed "offscreen" in a Comic, right after the events of Crysis Warhead.
Release rating: 6.5 / 10
2) Now, having played the game two years later AND with the full potential of DirectX 11, thanks for the patch Crytek, I'd say the game is impressive. Granted I've got a better PC to enjoy the full high-end graphical options, I was amazed by the details as everything looked good! Gameplay speaking, sure it's not as fun as C1 but I got past my disappointment and did enjoyed the game lately!
Current rating: 8 / 10
PROS:
-Nanosuit makes you feel truly powerful (a walking TANK with the .50 cal)
-Gorgeous visuals with DX11 (post-release)
-Cat & mouse play with enemies
-Suit Upgrades
CONS:
-At release, no DX11
-Noticeable bugs
-Poor story
-No recap of the story so far... wiki recap's it better!
-No mention of Nomad and Psycho from previous Crysis & Warhead
-Streamlined controls
Currently, I do recommend this game for anyone seeking a decent action game.

VERY linear compared to the first game and much smaller environments resulting in fewer tactical options... BUT, still very fun! Much more variety in potential game-play styles than your typical action shooter. Great fun for those who like to "play" with their enemies before killing them, or just want to play their own way.
Want to play cat and mouse with your foes by using stealth to lure them into a trap before taking them out? You can. Or maybe you want to go armor mode and melee your enemies into submission without firing a shot? You can do that too! Or perhaps you just want to rip a turret right off its hinges and go guns blazing as what can only be described as being a BAMF... You decide...
The controls are flawless, giving you a great sense of weight while still feeling fast, agile and most importantly accurate with every shot. The enemies can feel like bullet sponges at times, but it's more than understandable considering they're very technologically advanced ALIENS. You rarely fight more than a handful at a time and there are plenty of ammo caches lying around, so ammo never really becomes an issue. And who am I kidding, you're a bullet sponge too, so it all works out.
The story isn't great but it does its job and gets the message across loud and clear. You are a walking technical marvel who has been chosen(by Prophet) to save the world from an alien invasion. Go do it!
Side note: If you have the rig to run it, the graphics are INSANE just like the first game for its time. The amount of polish and spit shine in this game makes it really easy to feel completely immersed in the world. The sound design is also super high quality.

The creators of Eador Masters of a Broken World, which was an epic game, bring on a new challenge. This game, while I have only scratched the surface thus far, looks very promising. Note that Eador MOABW was full of bugs when I played it after the first level, but I stayed with it (quite a long game actually) in spite of all the crashing. So far the gameplay mechanics of Imperium intrigue me. I enjoy the castle setup, they seem very proud of the number of buildings you can create. I like the versatility in that as well. Nothing so far seems to "prohibit" another building which I like, though as a trade off once you form an alliance with a demirace (you can only have one) the buildings for other demiraces provide fewer bonuses. Which means you could play without forming any alliances and that would be just as valid as forming an alliance.
Things get really complex, so I better not try to explain everything here, so I'll  say even if you played Eador MOABW  you should play through the dull tutorial. Just to get your barings. I recommend this game if you enjoy turn based strategy and like such games full of lore.

I don't thjnk the AI even plays the game at all. I highly suspect it is just given provinces every so often and obtains hgih level guards on a timer. Though I can't give this game my entire reccomendation, the negative media attention it's been given since release is way harsher than the game deserves. Nobody will try to contest that Ubisoft is a greedy company that cranks out♥♥♥♥♥♥games, but the developers of this game genuinely care about it, it's community, and the longevity of the game.
If you recall, Rainbow 6 Siege (another Ubisoft title that released in the dumpster) is alive and thriving currently with a competitive and casual community that is enjoying the game as we speak. The developers claim to be taking the exact same approach as R6S with For Honor, which genuinely gives me hope for the game's future.
So now that I've gotten that out of the way, let me talk about the game itself.
With a roster of 16 characters and counting, unique movesets on the level of traditional fighting games, mix-ups, combos, hidden tech to discover and strategies to learn, the game has an intense amount of detail in it's actual gameplay mechanics. Guarding and attacking feels natural, feinting and parrying are more advanced but still intuitive.
Animation quality is top notch alongside the graphics, and the number of unique executions on kill and emotes to spam are wild.
Minor interesting note, each character speaks their respective languages during certain attacks and animations in combat, but if you rez an ally they will speak in your selected language, where if an enemy rez's one of their own, they will still speak a foreign language. I don't know why, but I found it interesting.
NEGATIVES:
Connectivity issues, easily exploitable cheap tactics, and the general toxicity of the community.
I'm not going to be one of those people who claims there's "NO HONOR IN FOR HONOR," because I honestly don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ but there are certain aspects of it that make it less fun.
1: Ledge kills. If you wanted to engage in a swordfight and make sparks fly from your clashing steel, too bad for you because they thought that cliffside looked more enticing.
2: Unlock tech. Just as a brief information dump, pressing your left trigger on a controller will lock you on to another player so you can fight them with your full moveset. There are specific abilities that can only be used while unlocked from your opponent, and these abilities (if used correctly) can result in a literal guessing game for your opponent, where if they chose incorrectly, they will take a serious punishment for it. Unfortunately, there is literally no downside to utilizing this tactic, so people tend to spam it relentlessly.
3: Spammable openers. This isn't a huge problem, but when a player doesn't properly understand how to utilize their character, they will immediately go to the most effective opening move, which typically has little downside. Reacting to these abilities takes a large amount of game time and game knowledge, so newer players will be immediately turned off when an enemy bashes their with their shield and pokes you with a flail 20 times for a kill.
The connectivity issues are supposedly being worked out, as DEDICATED SERVERS are becoming a reality in the future.
As for the toxicity in the community, I firmly believe that it is what has contributed to For Honor's steady downward decline. From the "ugh you dishonorable prick" to the "dead game" to the instant disconnects upon losing once, the game needs fresh blood who won't throw their controller through a window when someone emote spams them.
ONE FINAL NOTE: You should get a controller and a friend if you want to play the game. They're both invaluable - one for gameplay, one for stupid strategies that will definitely help you get into the game.

I was following Fabric since early days and thanks to the developers I had the opportunity to play it before it was relased.
Fabric is an indie puzzle game that is done with limited resources and it can be noticed throughout playing. This is where the right things starts off. Instead of trying to make a massive game with incredible graphics or some other random bs that they cant achieve they knew their limitations and played around it.
They realized their bending mechanics and the awe that comes from it is the true gem which makes this game shine. It is a puzzle/platforming game which actually makes you feel smart about solving stuff. Bending mechanic is trully original and the awe of first time that you bend boxes is actually amazing. Fabric knows it's limitations, what it can do good and what it cant and it helps the game massively. Minimalist look does great, musics are well fitting to the actuall game and sense of space is given nicely throughout cubes. I doubt if this game would be that good if they went for something bigger with their limited crew.
My biggest fear was that bending mechanic eventually getting boring after a while but game constantly throws new elements to the player. Game gets harder and harder but more importantly so it feels satisfying and offers  something unique every time.
Pros:
- Puzzles are fun & satisfying.
- There are enough elements to keep player occupied.
-  Developers of the game actually listens to player feedbacks.
- Game is relatively cheap. (lasts around 10 hours, 15 if you are bad with puzzle games)
Cons:
- Story is given through logs. Which could have been implemented in game.
- Game's area changes constantly, if you are not good with getting a sense of space within videogames it may disturb you.
TLDR: If you are into puzzle games or games that makes you feel good about your smarts make sure you check this out. Fabric is a simple but incredibly smart minimalist game.

Do you want Shannon Tweed? Do you want the Hollywood glitz and glamour and excitement that must fill Shannon Tweeds daily life? Do you want Plants Vs Zombies without plants, zombies or any of those fun game mechanics? Then this is the game for you.
You begin the game with a polite message from what I assume to be Ms Tweed's assistant, Sophie, who runs you through the contols of the game and the absolute havoc that comes with controling Shannon's hectic groupie filled schedule. After a while Sophie kinda leaves you to up it, updating you after each "day" on new "tools" which can help keep the groupies at bay. These range from Money Trees (Copyright pending for Ms Tweed) to what are essentially fart bombs that of course disgust the rampaging ravenous army of Tweed hungry groupies. I can't say I've progressed far beyond the fart bombs, but I cannot wait for the moment that I do. I am literally gripped right now.
All in all, this is worth every single penny if you answered yes to any of the questions in the opening paragraph. A truly revolutionary game, with a truly insightful look into the daily life and hell of a G list celebrity. I for one cannot recommend this enough. It also has the added bonus of looking good in your library. I obviously cannot speak for everyone here, but in my Steam library, it's sitting next to such subpar titles as Sanctum 2 and Sid Meier's Civilisation 5. Having Ms Tweeds game there, in HD no less, just gives me that sense of true gamer that only comes with games of this quality.

It's games like these that make me wish Steam offered more options for reviews than just recommended and not recommended. Eador Imperium (and its predecessor) is one of my favourite games. It is a turn-based hex-style strategy game, largely focused around expanding your empire and conquering difficult battles turn after turn. There is a fairly steep learning curse and a number of mechanics that are not explained very well - be prepared to invest some time into figuring out how it all works if you want to progress through the game of the highest difficulty. However, once you do understand how things work it is very rewarding. Always feels great once you finally manage to push through the final ring (the highest difficulty neutral units on the map) and steamroll through the remains of the enemy.
This new edition adds a large array of new units, among other things, like further events. Many of these new units and heroes change the gameplay quite significantly from a strategic perspective, which really adds life to the game. This time the campaign is more directed where you are given much greater starting resources - I actually really enjoyed these as they really showcase the new units of the game and force you to adapt to different ways to play the game, for example racing against the clock (turn limit). I bought this on day one of release and have met very few bugs. I do get the occasional crash every few hours, solved with a simple reload.
I would definitely recommend this game to turn based strategy verterans. Be prepared to sink a lot of time into it.

This review is for random map mode only and not for the campaign.
Within that scope, I recommend Eador: Imperium with reservations.  I prefer to play the game on a random map with settings that effectively minimize the AI, creating a sandbox with my own goals.  I like to explore the provinces, gather my forces, build my castle and enjoy an RPG-like progression of power and difficulty.  I played Eador: Master of the Broken World this way and enjoyed it a lot, and I'm glad to say I can do the same thing in Imperium except with more units, events, buildings... basically with more everything.  So far I've played nearly 30 hours on a single game and I'm not close to trying everything I'd like to try.  I will need several more sessions to experience all the new options and strategic combinations.
So why do I recommend with reservations?  Just one reason: bugs.  A range of serious to minor bugs continue to plague the game, and whether or not they stop you in your tracks varies with your personal system and whether or not they introduce new bugs with their fixes.  To give you an example, for the first 10 hours of my game I repeatedly ran into a bug that severely hamstrung my combat performance, randomly making my units unusable while they "walked in place" during a move action.  Then, a patch later, that bug went away but I had a new bug, an access violation error that prevented me from loading my game altogether.  A subsequent patch (February 6) allowed me to play again without any major issues, though, reminding just how fun this game can be *when it works.*
Nevertheless, I've gotten enough fun out of Imperium to give the Devs my recommendation.  They need to get the bugs under control and they absolutely need to stop introducing new ones.  For now, though, I can play Imperium and I'm having a lot of fun.  If that changes due to bugs and it's not promptly fixed I will update my review.
Update: Since writing this review I've both run into another bug that slowed me down and gone through a patch that promptly eliminated it.  They finally introduced a wide-ranging fix in the game options to address the dreaded "access violation" bug that can shut down a game.  For me, at least, the bug has disappeared.  I've played for hours without any problems whatsoever.

Poly Bridge is a good game for the money, but there are a few frustrating elements. For example, if someone who has been watching YouTube videos of sandbox bridges just wants to jump in and build, they can't. Not without playing through some UNDETERMINED number of levels before Sandbox is opened up.
Developers need to clearly identify how long you have to go through the game before Sandbox mode is unlocked, OR just don't lock it in the first place.
This game needs an option to skip the super annoying tutorial.

Physics is at the center of every mystery in the universe. One of those mysteries is who in their right mind would put me in charge of bridge construction, or you? Well, in Poly Bridge that is your job and the lives of people hang in the balance. Okay, it really isn't all that dramatic but having a degree in Engineering does help. From suspension bridges, arch bridges, and beam bridges and more, you will have to balance cost, effectiveness, and sometimes hope for the best as you try to move cars, buses, and ships across multiple bridges.. What makes Poly Bridge so addictive and fun to play, is the games quality of life features. Everything is easy to nudge, undo, and tinker with. Poly Bridge is a game all about experimentation and the game gives you tools to accomplish this easily. It really reminds me of Besiege, if it was completely about bridge building. Additionally with the 60 levels planned, the game has in-game map editor. Allowing you to construct your own levels and challenges. Giving the game infinite replay value. This takes Poly Bridge to top of its genre, and with a very nice price tag attached as well. If you like physics challenges, bridge construction games. Poly Bridge is a must, if you're not a huge fan of those games but still want something fun to play, like me. There is still plenty for you to enjoy here.
