Though I can't give this game my entire reccomendation, the negative media attention it's been given since release is way harsher than the game deserves. Nobody will try to contest that Ubisoft is a greedy company that cranks out♥♥♥♥♥♥games, but the developers of this game genuinely care about it, it's community, and the longevity of the game.
If you recall, Rainbow 6 Siege (another Ubisoft title that released in the dumpster) is alive and thriving currently with a competitive and casual community that is enjoying the game as we speak. The developers claim to be taking the exact same approach as R6S with For Honor, which genuinely gives me hope for the game's future.
So now that I've gotten that out of the way, let me talk about the game itself.
With a roster of 16 characters and counting, unique movesets on the level of traditional fighting games, mix-ups, combos, hidden tech to discover and strategies to learn, the game has an intense amount of detail in it's actual gameplay mechanics. Guarding and attacking feels natural, feinting and parrying are more advanced but still intuitive.
Animation quality is top notch alongside the graphics, and the number of unique executions on kill and emotes to spam are wild.
Minor interesting note, each character speaks their respective languages during certain attacks and animations in combat, but if you rez an ally they will speak in your selected language, where if an enemy rez's one of their own, they will still speak a foreign language. I don't know why, but I found it interesting.
NEGATIVES:
Connectivity issues, easily exploitable cheap tactics, and the general toxicity of the community.
I'm not going to be one of those people who claims there's "NO HONOR IN FOR HONOR," because I honestly don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ but there are certain aspects of it that make it less fun.
1: Ledge kills. If you wanted to engage in a swordfight and make sparks fly from your clashing steel, too bad for you because they thought that cliffside looked more enticing.
2: Unlock tech. Just as a brief information dump, pressing your left trigger on a controller will lock you on to another player so you can fight them with your full moveset. There are specific abilities that can only be used while unlocked from your opponent, and these abilities (if used correctly) can result in a literal guessing game for your opponent, where if they chose incorrectly, they will take a serious punishment for it. Unfortunately, there is literally no downside to utilizing this tactic, so people tend to spam it relentlessly.
3: Spammable openers. This isn't a huge problem, but when a player doesn't properly understand how to utilize their character, they will immediately go to the most effective opening move, which typically has little downside. Reacting to these abilities takes a large amount of game time and game knowledge, so newer players will be immediately turned off when an enemy bashes their with their shield and pokes you with a flail 20 times for a kill.
The connectivity issues are supposedly being worked out, as DEDICATED SERVERS are becoming a reality in the future.
As for the toxicity in the community, I firmly believe that it is what has contributed to For Honor's steady downward decline. From the "ugh you dishonorable prick" to the "dead game" to the instant disconnects upon losing once, the game needs fresh blood who won't throw their controller through a window when someone emote spams them.
ONE FINAL NOTE: You should get a controller and a friend if you want to play the game. They're both invaluable - one for gameplay, one for stupid strategies that will definitely help you get into the game.

Ember is an enjoyable 20+ hour Baldur's Gate lite WRPG with good looking environments and a focus on real time combat. For $2.49, you get a lot of exploration, crafting and looting -- but even for its base price of $9.99, it's still not a regrettable deal.

ember is not a AAA title. let's get that out of the way first. it's not a neverwinter, nor is it a baldur's gate or icewind dale or the likes. every now and then, especially when 'fast traveling' it does crash on me, although to be fair, not a very frequent issue, and heartache could easily be prevented by saving before you do one. it also feels bit rough round the edges, like the clunky way of trying to use healing potions on your party members, and to have your crafting recipes tied to your journal instead of the crafting tables, etc. well, crafting in general is quite simplistic too for that matter. but they're all minor annoyances rather than deal breaking things.in short, it's far for the perfect RPG one could play.
but all that being said, it IS a rather good game. sure combat probably isnt that intricate, and sure the story could be better and more compelling (although it isnt too bad; it's still fairly decent), but ember makes it work well enough. the graphics are quite nice, and the voice acting isnt too bad either. the world is big enough to keep me occupied, exploring and looking for hidden stuff. the story and side quests are interesting enough to keep me going, to find out what would happen. all in all, ember is a fun little package.
for an indie studio, for such a price, ember is quite a steal. you can tell they've put in quite a bit of passion and effort into the game. i kind of feel like ... ember would be to neverwinter, like torchlight was to diablo. it's good, but it's never going to be remotely the same experience, because it's also different. but if you have an rpg craving, ember would do well to sate it, and at a very good price too.

This is a solid RPG all-around and the fact that it is $10 USD retail is just astounding. Between the obvious effort that went into a mostly glitch-free game and the fact I've seen a Dev in the forum pretty regularly, compels me to give the game some of my highest praise.
Is it the best story or gameplay ever? No, but it is above average and --better still-- it is very well balanced, which I find is not too common with this genre. The world/environs is the best thing about the game in my opinion.
It's on the easy and simplistic side as far as character building and much of the combat,  so a good recommendation for newer CRPGers. Unlike many RPGs though there is crafting, which is what I spent a lot of time on -- harvesting mats, anyway.
A typical run-through on the game is probably closer to 30 hours, with completionists enjoying a longer game.
Probably the best thing about the game is the graphics -- especially as you progress in the world. I found the environment very immersive. The humor and lore is pretty decent and the overall plot isn't bad, just not special -- like most games tend to be.
TL;DR  Even if the game is RPG-lite the devs deserve support as good (old-schoolish/crpg) games produced at such value pricing (or any pricing) is rare nowadays.

I had many doubts going in. It was a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥show rating wise when it came out for consoles, and I made sure I avoided it. So when it popped in a steam sale recently, I thought what have I got to lose, and I have a PC that can handle it. And I'm very glad I did.
The positives first:  RE6 is  a good looking game. If your machine can handle it, crank up the graphics settings. Rain glistens off the characters as it falls, hair and clothes rustle in the breeze, and of particular note, the enemies are truly vile and horrifically disgusting, and I mean that a high complement. The spider-like enemies in particular always made me lean back from my monitor whenever they showed up, from their creepy scamper to the thick hairs growing off their bodies.
There's an over-arching story broken into 4 campaigns, with the occasional crossover with the other protagonists at certain points. The individual campaigns play very much like a greatest hits package of previous RE games styles. Leon’s campaign is like a retelling of RE4, from the cathedral setting down to the Ganado-like enemies. Chris's campaign is more like RE5, heavy on the action and broad daylight set pieces in a urban/military environments, and Jake's campaign is more like RE3 as him and Sherry are chased by the Nemesis equivalent UsterNakk (sp?). The last campaign of Ada Wong weaves its way through the previous 3 three explaining her presence in each, along with her own motivations. Each campaign has 5 chapters that take ~1 hour complete, so 5 one hour chapters per campaign x 4 campaigns is a pretty hefty 20hrs of action content. It’s all playable co-op too, and the AI holds its own. It also can't die, so you don't have to baby sit if you are playing solo (like I did). There’s certainly not a lack of things to take on. The story took lot of flack when it came out, but frankly, resident evils' plots have always been pretty ludicrous. At the end of the day, you are there primarily there to blow away zombies and all manner of disgusting bio-freaks, which the game serves up in droves. What probably threw people off is that the story doesn't unfold linearly and jumps all over the place as you complete each campaign. You can pick each campaign chapter and there are lists online of an order in which to play the chapters to get the story as is unfolds chronologically, but frankly i think that's unnecessary as it’s not that complex. It can suffer from pacing issues but you are thrown in some pretty large scale set pieces at least once per chapter so the slower parts are basically quiet before some zombie♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan. Plenty of difficulty levels depending on the level of masochistic pleasure you desire. Overall, lots of replay value.
Once you learn the controls (an issue which I’ll touch upon later) You will realize they have made some much needed (and appreciated by me) changes to how the game plays. Characters are no longer tanks, turning laboriously left and right. There are standing dodges, back, forward and side rolls, and a first for me, laying prone is actually a useful and viable strategy (it recovers stamina very quickly). All the moves are very well animated too. Also, there is now a dedicated melee button, which is long overdue, and makes it easier when you run out of ammo and are surrounded. Its balanced by each melee attack consuming stamina, and when you use it all you have an exhaustion period during which you can't melee at all. The new additions truly shine in mercenaries mode, which arguably stole the show for me. The now standard score attack kill zombies for time mode is surprisingly addictive. the new melee and movement options really benefit the fast paced gameplay, and you will find yourself getting hype off of some John woo acrobatics that you engage in, pulling off a satisfying headshot, then physically countering an enemy trying to cheap shot you, and finishing them off  with a stylish quick shot. Very, very satisfying and just-one-more-round inducing (also I did them all solo, Co-op would be an even bigger blast as it does get hectic). Score an A rank or higher and you'll unlock a pretty funky alternate costume for that specific character, along with a remixed weapons loadout. Another benefit I didn't realize was that Capcom and valve did a PC exclusive left 4 dead 2 crossover with the characters of L4D2 appearing in mercenaries mode. Not only are the characters fully voiced, but their levels throw absolutely insane numbers of monsters at you at once. There are some multiplayer options, but these can easily be avoided, as the active online community is long dead and you can save a couple of bucks by not opting to purchase them with the rest of the game.
Of course there is the other side of all this positivity. RE6's biggest issue is how poorly it conveys necessary information. The game tells you how to move and shoot, but that's about it. Nowhere, not even in an in game resource of some kind does it explain how to dodge, or other critical actions like quick shots and character specific quick shot combos. These is particularly baffling as several of the characters have character specific moves, like Jake's hand to hand combat and Leon/Helena's crowd control shooting maneuvers, which come in extremely handy. Fortunately there is an excellent ultimate survival guide on the steam forums which details all these things, but without that I doubt i would have stuck around for even a third of the game (which i'm sure many people didn't, which is a shame). Another valid complaint is that the default camera is much to close to the player. Makes for great screenshots, but also allows monsters to sneak up on you and get a cheap shot from behind in. The fix for this is adjusting a slider, but that option is obtusely buried in the game's title screen settings, Easily fixable, but again, i wouldn't know that unless I googled the issue. The last irritant i had was that the game suffers from the dreaded Bosses-that die-but-not-really syndrome. You fight and put down so mighty impressive creatures, only to quickly realize that you'll fight the same creature again in another similar 10 mins later, except slightly remixed (the second time in a confined space instead of an arena for example). It robs the encounters of any real weight, as you never feel like you accomplished anything, as they are back lickedy split minutes later with no sense of damage that they supposedly received.
But overall, I was very pleasantly surprised by how fun the game is. The campaigns chapters’ each have a how-can-they-top-the-last-encounter.feel, and you are guaranteed some sort of final epic boss encounter for each one. I would run through them again with a friend who was willing, but I'm glad I at least finished them each solo. The real draw will be mercenaries mode.

The game feels very "hands off" in terms of explicit instruction, which I think fits the atmosphere and the pace of the game quite well. But the concepts aren't introduced slowly and individually enough for a dope like me to understand what's going on.
So, for other people like me, here's the relevant part of the email response I got from the wonderful dev to explain the basic mechanics of the game:
There are four major elements and four child elements.
This is the list of major elements (symbol used in the game tiles) - corresponding child element - movement when stepped on
Fire (flame) - thunder - up
Water (drop) - lake - down
Earth (tree) - mountain - down
Heaven (cloud) - wind - up
When you step on an element it will trigger all tiles of that element plus all tiles of its child element.
Example : stepping on fire will trigger all fire tiles plus all thunder tiles. But stepping on thunder will only trigger thunder.
When stepped on, a tile will move according to its symbol movement. The tiles that are triggered will move in the opposite direction.
If a symbol is upside down it means the movement of that tile will be the opposite of what would be expected.
I'm lovin' it. Would love to get more games like this to play and review.

(An early review, partially played offline, so much in-game time has not been recorded. Hopefully a more complete review will follow soon.)
A Game of Changes……where to begin. How about 2,500 years ago? The I Ching, or Book of Changes is one of the most influential texts in the history of the world, studied by countless millions to this day. As such it's a natural to be the basis for a quite simple (but sometimes quite complex), interesting and generally relaxing modern game. (Please, bear with a brief but necessary history, then this reviewer will try to relate that history to an understanding of this fairly simple (HA!) game. I assure the reader, the game is more interesting and fun than this part of the review. It won’t hurt much, I promise.) In brief, the I Ching is a sort of system for understanding the world surrounding all mankind, and even a form of fortunetelling based in a very computer-familiar binary system. There are hexagrams (or groups of six lines) in the I Ching, each of the six being either a complete or a divided/broken line (essentially either a “zero” or “one”), so there are 64 I Ching hexagrams in all (2 to the 6th power.) Each I Ching hexagram has a name, and information attributed to it that may be of specific importance to the individual (or gamer) doing the research at that time and place. This is mentioned because these hexagrams will appear regularly throughout this game, as will the chart of all 64.
A Game of Changes (AGOC) is more than one thing. As far as Steam, it’s substantially a puzzle game, growing in complexity as the gamer progresses. The protagonist finds himself (the character is a bearded “he”) in a landscape to be traversed, and then exited once an I CHING hexagram has been created by chance or choice, based on the path taken. The field is made of pillars, many displaying symbols which can be utilized to raise or lower OTHER pillars for access. As mentioned, travel requires the player to choose an I Ching hexagram to help determine where his journey will next take him. Once achieved, the exit gate will open. The next destination……?
The I Ching allows users to throw straws as a method of divination (or fortunetelling) and AGOC allows the same by permitting either chance or conscious decision to choose his journey for him. As such, AGOC is, in addition to a puzzle game, a method of looking at life with the goal of a greater understanding of the HOWs and WHYs. How all 64 hexagrams/landscapes come together in one greater puzzle has yet to be determined by this player. Just as in life, there is little handholding in AGOC.
A Game of Changes has such lovely music and endearing graphics, and the game play is so intuitive and simple, I think that rage is pretty much out of the question. Any time danger is near (such as falling to one’s death), an exclamation mark shows above the player. But if life still goes awry, pressing the backspace key will return you to your prior safe point (usually. Since sometimes the result is a “death loop” each short landscape can easily be restarted with little lost.) AGOC can be played with the mouse and keyboard, but this reviewer really doubts you’ll want to. Movement can require multiple keys, and sometimes sequential movements need be done rather (but not overly) quickly. Considering that camera movement likely will need to be controlled at the same time, the mouse/keyboard can be pretty awkward to use in conjunction with the sometimes limiting camera angles. FORTUNATELY, a gamepad-type controller can be used for great simplification. Unfortunately, nothing this player saw on any screen indicates this option. Had I not seen the controller reference on the Store Page, I might have given up on this interesting game for that reason alone. Also, screen instructions are specific to mouse/KB, with no instructions as to rebinding, or how the controller usage may compare to the keyboard keys (which might be a very handy feature for the immediate future. Hint, hint.) It may be necessary to experiment a bit. Or like this player did, just give up and use KB keys when in doubt.
A Game of Changes may come in at a price point about double that of the average Steam puzzle game, but please consider it as something more. AGOC may actually provide fun AND a chance for personal growth. If you have had any interest in eastern philosophies, you may wish to treat yourself to something a little special, in which case the few dollars extra really won’t matter. As such, perhaps a niche market, but a very special niche indeed.

Pros

Cons

Indepth:
- Fun gameplay
The idea behind the game is great - original. Mice going for cheese with the help of a shaman (sometimes). However, sometimes people can be a bit too reliant, the shaman can be a jerk and just get everybody killed or worse, do nothing.
- Not TOO  buggy
I think the game is pretty polished bug-wise, but theres always a bit of a spazz here and there with the levels. This is dismissable, as it IS an MMO.
- Likable graphics
The choice of a manga-esque artstyle is an odd choice, but doesn't ruin the game and, me personally, I enjoy the style. But it's usually just a nitpick. The graphics are smooth and nice.
- Unpolished concepts
What I mean by unpolished concepts is that people will try to overtake eachother. For example, there are some levels in the game where there are two shamans, who have to guide mice to their respective mouseholes in order to get points. I have seen countless times one Shaman who's quicker than the other use a pushing object to kill the other Shaman. Heck, this almost happened to me a few times.
- The community is♥♥♥♥♥♥
I think you've seen this in many other reviews, and it's honestly kinda true. There are many good
people in the Transformice world but as told above the teamwork in this game is at fault wherever you go. It usually has to do with what I said above, Shamans killing other Shamans for experience, or just not giving a flying meow and killing everybody.

I remember Shannon Tweed from when she was on an episode of Married with Children. Now two decades later, she's in her own game. It is a tower defense game. The all female groupies start at the right and walk to the left. If they reach Shannon, its game over man. Game over. To defend her, you place water guns and money trees on the grid. Everything you place costs money. The groupies never leave their lane or have any strategy, just as your water guns can only shoot in the same lane. When the groupies get to one of your objects, they'll damage it until it disappears.
The major problem with Shannon Tweed's Attack of the Groupies is the simple fact that it is mindlessly simple. In fact, halfway through the wave, I can sit back and just let the game play itself. To top that off, the levels are exactly the same. Each of the 6 levels has 10 levels. Yeah you heard that right. Anyway,  level after level is exactly the same. After every 10 levels, the background will change. There is no sort of change in terrain. No swimming pools, roofs or dark of night. Its all the same. For completing each level, the game rewards you with either a new enemy, a new item in your arsenal or removing a barricade to make things tougher. Every so often you're rewarded with an album full of real life photos of Shannon, Gene Simmons and their family. The album layout really needed some sort of next / previous or 1 of 10 indicator so people don't just see 1 photo per album and click back.
Your arsenal has many objects, but the only two useful ones are the money tree and squirt gun. Before a level begins, you'll pick 7 things from your arsenal to use in the following level. When you start a level, a giant money sack will fall. When you click on it you get $50. They fall in random places. Once you have $100 you can place a money tree. With the money tree down it will generate two levels of money when you click on them to harvest the cash. The first level is $25, the second is $50. There's no need to let the money bloom. It could have been $60 when a tree is fully bloomed, but whatever. The cash grows often, so often they could have made a combo game out of it. Click on X number of trees in a second and get a bonus.
When you place a squirt gun, it can get upgraded after a waiting period. The upgrades cost cash and each one can get upgraded twice. These are the only two that you'll ever need. At least through the first 30 levels. To upgrade a gun, you need to pause the game by clicking the upgrade icon then click the object, then click the upgrade. I should just be able to click the object without clicking the upgrade button. A spacebar pause would have been nice, any key support would have been nice. There are other frills like bodyguards that stand there and block groupies. Gum that slows them down, a stink bomb that does damage, goo guns that slow down groupies and so on. The goo guns can get upgraded, but why buy them when the upgraded squirt guns decimate everything?
The enemies might look different, but they're all the same. At least the ones I found 30 levels into the game. They have different amounts of health and minor abilities. Red dress women can charm bodyguards to slip right by. Drunk groupies have higher health. Goth screamers do a wave of damage to your objects. Stilt walkers can merely walk over your objects. The new enemies are too few and far between.
On the first level, you only have one line to worry about. That's to get your feet wet. Then it opens up to three lanes. After a few more levels, its four lanes. Before you know it at level 20 you'll have 6 lanes open! If the game is too hardcore for you, there's an easy mode. You don't even have to upgrade your squirt guns, they'll take out everything.
On the surface, it has good looking cartoon graphics. It has Shannon saying lines like 'That wasn't hard... uh' and 'she'll climb over a glass wall to see you.' Some of the character art on the Steam store page isn't even in the game. The screenshots of the game are photoshopped. The lighting looks better on the Steam page than in the game. Its a pretty low resolution game. Not just that but the animation in the game is a little off. Groupies move faster than they walk if that makes sense. So their feet are sliding instead of walking.
Even if the 60 levels weren't draining enough, playing the same thing over and over with no variety, the music loop is awful. Notably awful. I usually don't bring up music, but single loop is grading. Hearing a few second loop over three hours straight.
Avoid this game. Its the same thing over and over, every level. So easy I don't even need to play the game halfway through the level, because I'm too busy scoring 4 touchdowns in a single game!

Well, I spent a few hours just messing around with this game, slowly but surely working my way up from a small ship with a relatively effective yet basic starting blaster to a vanguard-class ship with a couple of the stronger heavy weapons in the game, and I think I can make a decent first impressions review of this game after looking through the a couple reviews of fellow players.
I think the biggest obstacle to overcome right out of the gate is getting used to the controls.  Sure, the tutorial does help cover a good portion of it, but it still takes some time to adapt to the way the ships move.  After that...  it really just came down to finding the best ways to progress and work your way up.  Whether it be starting out with mining, attacking a couple of the weaker enemy platforms in the starting system, or perhaps landing on the closest planet and carefully picking off the enemy ships (and depending on how you play, stay near the trade stations on those first planets for a little extra protection if needed), there are a number of ways that the player could pick from to progress and upgrade their ships over time.
The exploration and combat, while admittedly somewhat clunky, doesn't get to the point where it seems downright irritating, either.  Granted, you could be going at full speed in your ship and get a notice that an object is rapidly closing on your ship and before you have time to effectively react, that object smacks into your ship and does a small portion of hull damage, but that's about it in terms of nitpicks and that could admittedly be adjusted some in the future so players could better react to it, but that's just my opinion.
AI...  while for the most part decent when it comes to the open space areas, there are some areas where that could use tweaking as well (specifically how the AI interacts with planets).  Example being that some AI ships, when in a planet's field of influence, seem to derp about and have trouble navigating to attack you if they were hostile, or in some cases, they just derp about.   I did have a rather silly experience seeing that big vendor ship tumbling about on the planet I was on when I was playing and it almost seemed like it was trying to roll onto me or find a way to get me inside his docking bay and otherwise he was just floating about a little wildly near the edge of the planet's gravity zone.  I'm sure these issues would be addressed in time, yet it was still kinda funny to see.
Now, it may sound like I am criticizing the game a little bit for it's little bugs and a slightly rough learning curve for first-time players, but once one can get past learning the controls and giving it a little bit for the various elements of the game to sink in, I can see that there is a lot of enjoyment to be had here in a budding game such as this.  I am aware that it is rather lacking in content (being just two systems and very little to do once you get to the "endgame", per se), but that's kind of expected with a game that is still so young in development.  There is a -lot- of potential within this game that has yet to be unleashed, and for what the game has so far, it leaves a lot to look forward to as well when the game is developed further.  Perhaps we'll see more in the future like more planet types, ships, weapons, and even new types of content to keep the player engaged such as missions, trade routes, multiplayer...  maybe even going as far as making your own outposts and doing things like research, fleet construction, and more?
Right now, though...  I can honestly say that Destination Sol is a really fun game that deserves some attention and play time.  It may be a little lacking in content now, but what it has already is addictive and fun once you get a feel for things, and I really look forward to seeing how this game will grow in the future.

The commets here are too harsh.  This is a good game for anyone who enjoys serious turn-based tactics and strategy.  Hopefully with ongoing support and updates/patches from the developers it will only get better.
As someone who played the daylights out of Eador Genesis (but skipped MoTBW), I am enjoying Imperium and I'm sure my time played will be steadily increasing from the 16 hours I have now.  I have not experienced any crashes and once I got the hang of the interface the pace has been about right.
If you have never played any of the earlier Eador games, I can see how Imperium could be daunting especially if you start with the campaign, which for some inexplicable reason kicks right off with a level 10 hero and a moderately developed home province.  For beginners you might be better off just starting with a random small map against a single enemy or two playing on the easiest difficulty level.  This will give you a chance to learn the game's mechanics without being thrust in the middle of an immediately challenging situation.
If you put in the time, I think you will come to truly appreciate the depth of the Eador game system on so many levels.  It can be unforgiving if you make poor choices (this is a good thing in my book), but it is very satisfying when you improve your play.  The tactical battles are top notch and the variety of heroes, units, buildings, skills, equipment, etc. incredibly rich.  If you are into strategic turn-based gaming, you really can't do much better.

Also, people scream and shout that the game is unbalanced, but it's often exageratted by a ton because people are frustrated. Some heros can have some pretty crazy attacks and chain that are mastered by very skilled players, but there isn't a meta hero to play. All of the characters are different, and none of them complete dominate the battlefield. I've seen every one of the dogs have their day, and other times they just get absolutely destroyed. The games balance isn't nearly perfect, but it isn't as awful as they say.
All around this is an EXTREMELY unique game. There aren't really any others like it. Its combat system is pretty unique and functional. Even the some of the combos are pretty creative. The characters are pretty varied and have their own personal appearance. Along with that, they can be customized to your personal liking in several ways.
tldr; The game itself is very creative and I'd definitely reccomend it. It's just that the game comes with some kinks and isuses that are being fixed and taken care of by the devs.

VERSION 2.0 Review:
Slender The Arrival has certainly had shifts in quality between updates, and I am pleased to say that v2.0 is literally perfect. First off, the new levels are TERRIFYING. And I mean Amnesia terrifying, Homestead and Memories (the two new levels) are very memorable and are a great addition to the game. The Arrival looked amazing upon release, and yet v2.0 makes it look even better. There are better textures and models in some areas, and Genesis now looks fantastic rather than being a carbon copy of The Eight Pages with some of The Arrival's entities. The biggest flaw to S:TA before v2.0 was the gameplay; it was ridden by bugs and problems such as the overly frustrating mine level, terrible interaction physics, and the simply god awful fire sequence. Everything has been fixed in 2.0. The interaction is now smooth and comfortable, the mine level's main NPC (the source of the frustration) has been perfected, and the fire sequence is now an intense but fair climax.
Some gamers may be turned off by the ten dollar price tag for a 3 hour game, but guys, come on. A group of inexperienced indie developers worked their asses off for this and they deserve the money. Not to mention, this is one of the horror greats in gaming - I liked it almost as much as the Amnesia games. This is also the first game by Blue Isle Studios, and for an indie game group's first game this is amazing.
Overall it's an amazing game with a great story. Give it a go.

This is one of those games for which I'm EXTREMELY glad to see a sequel coming because Princess Remedy is made of charm. Now, I won't say this game is perfect. It's not especially in depth and the combat system was maybe a little ~too~ simple, but for a game that was put together in four days (for charity, I might add), it's pretty freakin' good.
Basically, imagine if a multi-directional shooter like Berzerk or Robotron 2084 was given an overworld. That's this game in a nutshell. The first thing you're going to notice is that this game looks like something released on the ZX Spectrum or the Amstrad CPC in the 80's, and considering you only have the directional keys and "action button" to work with, that's not a bad description of how it plays. In all honesty, the idea of that had me a bit wary at first, even in spite of the already mostly positive reviews it was getting. Don't get me wrong, I love retro and retro-styled games, but the simplicity of Princess Remedy put me off a little at first.
But of course the game was free, so I figured "why not?"
I'm happy to say that the simplicity ends up working in its favor. While yes, I wish the combat system had a few more options, the game plays very smoothly even with a single button. And the graphics, while basic, are well-crafted and fun to look at (especially the titular character's portrait- she is just TOO cute).
Basically, this is a game that could have gone very wrong, but exceeded my expectations. So I'll be buying the sequel when it comes out, because I'm all for seeing more of Princess Remedy's adventures.

Not much to say except this is bar none the best guitar&bass  sim/trainer out there right now. While true beginners may struggle with this a bit as it doesnt seem to teach good finger to fret/string placement pratices and discipline, novices who have had basic training from real life instructors should be able to just jump right in and learn songs with minimal issue.

Having taught myself the guitar a number of years ago and, frankly, not being very good at it, I have been looking for a learning tool that is both fun and functional. Rocksmith 2014 is it!!!
I say this without any hessitation, mainly because I have played for 8 hours and have already nearly nailed two full songs, Boston's Peace of Mind and Iron Maiden's The Trooper.
Rocksmith has many advantages to traditional learning. Firstly, you can hear the track without messing with remote controls. Second, the Riff Repeater allows you to customise your learning experience. You can adjust the difficulty (thus lowering the number of notes and the complexity of cords) whilst you get the song and the rhythm in your head. This is especially useful if you are starting out and learning your way around the guitar fretboard. You can also adjust the speed. This has been the most useful tool for me. I want to play the songs on 100% difficulty and having the ability to play at a low speed whilst learning and using the mastery mode to dynamically increase the speed when you nail a section is simply awesome.
If you have played guitar before, it takes a bit of time to get used to the Guitar Band style visual layout, but, after you have, you will be rocking out in no time at all.
If you are getting this on a steam sale, buy the original Rocksmith and the Song Import Tool. This way you get all the tracks from the original Rocksmith as well.
I haven't mentioned many of the features in this game, but, trust me, they are all fantastic. Just don't forget to by the Real Tone Cable from Amazon or another decent retailer. You cannot play the game without it.
Entertainment and education in one package

This is an first person adventure that plays with any preconceptions the player has.
Your protagonist is a secret agent called Polyblank that gets sent on various proposterous missions, like extracting an artificial kidney from a cowboy.

Jazzpunk is a unique game with a style all its own that feels like a surrealistic 1950s retro spy meets Ren and Stimpy cartoon silliness. You play in a first person perspective, interacting with several things, exploring rich, colorful, living, breathing surrealistic areas. The surrealistic art style blends with the humor really well. The only controls are jump and action buttons with left stick to move, and right stick to look around or keyboard controls to do the same things. You can get items and switch between them. There are plenty of mini games that feel more like diversions to keep you engaged. Its parodies of other games and media, yet it feels distinctly like its own product.
You work for a spy agency that sends you to far away locales with serious objectives, things like infiltrate a USSR building, follow a cowboy in Japan to get his mechanical kidney, infiltrate a criminal's lavish retro penthouse and you'll even be sent on a Polynesian vacation. There are spies, madmen, robots, crazy bums and women around every corner.
The big feature here for me is the interactivity and exploration. You can interact with boxes, newspaper machines, spray pigeon perfume on NPCs to see pigeons carry them away, drink mouthwash only to discover its chlorine, use a master baster on a turkey, freeze a frozen meal in a microwave, scribble lipstick on your face, collect spiders in a jar to throw them at people, break every vase in a shop trying to swat flies. It all feels so interesting and engaging to do what I want to in this crazy world. While NPCs are faceless box people (or robots) with circle heads, NPCs say several things, most of which are hilarious and I don't usually like comedy in games. The eccentric off the wall comedy and parody really hit the mark for me, when most comedy games feel forced.
Jazzpunk parodies several games like Frogger, Wave Race in a fountain of gravy, mini golf with pool cues, virtual tennis, Wedding Quake against a bride, groom and priest, a zombie pizza game, a high score game where you play a cat ripping things to shreds, a game of Twister, finding prizes with a metal detector and so much more. It all kept me playing, even if it all was just easy fun.
It is definitely worth a playthrough, I found myself taking far too many screen shots at the crazy things I'd see. Things in the background, men in cullender hats with wheeled pigs on the background and my radio tooth on the floor. Its never in your face, its all just there for you to find it.
There is no death in the game, even if you plunge off of the fourth floor of your Polynesian hideaway, you still bounce on the ground. With that being said, you can still fail the mini games. Frogger took quite a beating and I lost a lot in Wedding Quake before I realized the rose rocket launcher was win. It is an easy game, again, the point is to explore, interact and laugh.
Is it worth the $15? Maybe and I'm surprised to say that, even if its only 2 or 3 hours to complete. The ending came pretty abruptly and even the credits have their own flare to them. I can imagine its not for everyone and I never thought it would be for me. I am shocked at how much enjoyment I got from Jazzpunk and I might have to play through it again.

My problem with this game is the listed key features (and the numerous crash to desktop bugs).
Here they are:
1.  "Classic-style RPG with 30+ hours of epic adventure"
I finished this with 100% completion in 18 hours.  I'm not sure where the other 12 would have come from, since I did every quest in the game (as far as I can tell).
2.  "Epic storytelling filled with fascinating characters, lore, adventure, and humor"
This one is pretty subjective, isn't it? The humor is the same laugh at fantasy tropes from older titles.  I didn't find the characters fascinating or memorable.
3.  "Over 70 quests with diverse gameplay enabling players to choose their path"
So the only choice that I think they were offering was whether or not you wanted to kill the person with the thing you wanted or go do a quest for them.  There was only one quest in the game with a truly distinct pair of paths that I can recall.  This may also be where the 30 hours from feature 1 came from, if they assumed you started the game over to get the other achievement.
4.  "Engaging party-based real-time combat system with tactical pause"
Each character gets 3 skills.  Basically, you mostly spam them at enemies.  If you play on hard, your probably using a bedroll after every combat to recover your energy.
5.  "Over 65 combat skills for the player to use in customized battle party strategy"
These skills are mostly just broken down into heavy single damage, light single damage with status effect, light area damage, healing, and teleport.  It doesn't really feel like you are using 65 different skills.
6.  "Encounter hundreds of NPCs with their own tales to tell"
They gave one line dialogues to a whole lot of NPC's to make this one count.
7. "In-depth crafting system, from baking bread to forging magic weapons"
What does in-depth mean in this context?  The most diverse is cooking, but the recipes just have different ingredients with repeating effects.  Everything else is the exact same formula on repeat.  So for instance, if you want any top tier piece of equipment, it is mithril ingot, ember essence, sandsilk, and the base material for that object (wood and lacquer for staves, wood and bowstring for bows, etc.).  Best of all, it doesn't matter if it makes no sense for it to include sandsilk in it (for instance, plate armor), or include mithril in it (for instance robes).  They all use the same formula.  Potions are the same.  Herb of any kind + medium bottle = potion.
8.   "A seamless world with over 20 handcrafted environments and dark dungeons that are fully interactive and feature movable objects, weather changes and day / night cycles:
What does "handcrafted" mean?  When I see coasts, mountains, and other borders, it looks like a cut and paste job.  Everything is square or based on squares.  The weather does change though, not that it has any impact on the game.  Night and day only have an impact on one quest, and many NPC's sleep at night.
9.  "Adventure with different companions with their own backstory quests"
What do they think backstory quests mean?  They habe backstories, but from what I can tell, it makes no difference to them joining your party.  There are three companions, one for each class.  That is it.  After you have them, you don't really interact with them.
Overall, I was disappointed it didn't live up to what it claimed to be.  It also makes itself boring by making you run across large areas over and over again.  There is fast travel, but it only helps so much.  I don't think it was worth the price I paid for it on sale.

Ember is a contrived action-RPG that takes all the staples from similar games and wraps it up in a nice little $10 price tag.  For those of us who need loot to grab and goblins to slay between AAA titles, it's a great value.  The world is nicely crafted and the story keeps up a good enough pace to stow off boredom.  The combat is repetitive, in that you'll face the same groups of 4 to 5 enemies with your same powers and use the same strategies, but the implementation is original with its click-and-drag activations that make it different than the "click the button" affair of most A-RPGs.
The crafting system appears deep, but it's really useless since the stat gains aren't enough to justify spending time at the blacksmith's forge trying out recipes.  The loot drops are also mostly pointless, since enemies always drop crude weapons that are beneath your level unless it's a boss.  The ability to add different powers to different equipment acquired later in the game is fun, though.  You can really make a guy the way you want him to be by changing his armor's embedded power.
The voice acting and dialogue is also pretty solid.  You won't be falling out of your chair, but it's enough to care about your followers.  All in all, it's well worth the 10 bucks you'll spend.

Premise: Stranded on a remote planet the player must find the items needed to fix their transmitter to call for help by searching the planetary grid.
A minimalistic "survival" game of the strategy kind.  No shooting, though.  Just straight methodical strategy like in the game Battleship (Board game for those who have never heard of it.) A little luck and some logic is needed plus fast thinking for those 3 second math problems while crafting.  Easy to understand, easy to play.  Not a very long game, but is easily replayable due to random generation of materials, items and bombs in every new game.
8 achievements and trading cards for those interested.  Pricing about average for an indie game.

As the other negative reviews state, the game is largely dependent on luck in the very beginning. Once you neutralize that (and you can reduce the chance of failure to very nearly 0%, unless you are further unlucky or mismanage resources), the game has 0 difficulty or meaningful interaction, and you just grind out the remainder of the game.
You are required to click markers, which takes several seconds of waiting (you can spend resources to save some time, but that takes them away from something more useful) and solve some multiplication QTEs which very rarely require actual calculation: if you multiply 65 by 67, is the answer 118, 134, or 4355? The first two are obviously too small, so the answer is obvious. The majority of the QTEs are this obvious, and those that aren't are often simple enough for you to solve it quickly. On top of that, there is no penalty for failure other than having to try again.
Aside from determining the single-minded 'optimal' strategy for game completion, the only penalty for failure is taking more of your time to gather and manage resources. If the game had an ambiance of survival or being stranded, it might be at least immersive for an hour or so, but the game is only an image of the planet and some menus with no descriptive text other than describing electrical components. I can't recommend the game in this state.

I have certain "phases" that I go through on the internet. I find something that I think is interesting, I obsess about it for a few months, then find another interesting thing, etc. Currently, the phase for me right now is Slender Man. For the past few months, I have gone through all of Marble Hornets, all of DarkHarvest00 and all of TribeTwelve (in that order). I plan to binge on EverymanHYBRID next.
My Point is, I wanted an interactive version of these stories. Not just "Find x amount of pages," no. I wanted a Slender Man game with a story. And this game gave me exactly that.
If your not that into the Slender Man/Slender Man Mythos, then the story for this game might be confusing. Very confusing. I have seen many people say that the story is bad, that it's one of the low parts of the game. I disagree. I love the story behind it, as it's vague and only creates more questions. That's what a Slender Man based story should do- it should make you think. It should stick with you, long after you finish the game/show/book.
Now, I'm going to stop blabbering about the story, and actually give a review:
First off, the graphics. From what I've seen, the graphics are great. The way the sun falls though the trees, the leaves flowing through the breeze- it's wonderful. And the Slender Man himself has much more detail than in "Slender: The Eight Pages." He doesn't look like he has an egg for a head, which is a plus. He looks creepy and just that feeling of something that almost looks human, but doesn't. The graphics on lower settings look crappy though, but thats to be expected.
Next is audio/sound effects. Great as well. The game has a great soundtrack, which really gives you that feeling of dread and isolation, but at the right moments. There are even parts of the game where you can hear crunching leaves, as if someone- or something- is following you. It adds to the game's atmosphere a whole bunch, which is very important for a horror game. The audio distortion (that occurs when Slender Man is nearby) is scary and is much better than just static.
Next is Gameplay. This part of the game was sort of a let down. Pretty much all throughout the game, all your doing is "collecting x amount of pages" or "turning on x amount of generators." It gets boring and repetitive, and sometimes annoying. I've rage quit multiple times because of this. Hopefully it is worked on in the next patch, which will add 2 more levels.
And finally, Atmosphere. As said before, the audio and visuals really add to the atmosphere. You hear the eerie squeaking of violins play, as you run around in an abandoned mine, hearing the footsteps and strange coughing-like noises of someone behind you. You walk through an abandoned house, doors left open, strange scribbling on the walls. The radio is left on, and all you hear is a song filled with static echo throughout the house. This game can be terrifying, even if you are collecting pages.
All in all, I find Slender: The Arrival to be a good game with flaws; the game could be longer. But still, I recommend this game to any fan of the Slender Man Mythos.

I understand that I have played this for less than half an hour at the time that I am writing this. But, in that 25 minutes of play time that I have sunk into it, I already have plenty of gripes with this game. First off, I am not a fam of the art style. I understand that they were going for something out of the normal pixel graphics indie game loop with something looking commorore/NES-esque graphical style, but it just does not work for me. Second, the difficulty spike in the beginning of the game is too much too fast. It doesn't take long to get used to, but it's so sudden I had a hard time getting used to it. But, with those problems, the game still has an unmatchable charm that is very difficult to find in most games nowadays. The music is some of the best I have heard in a long time, up there with games like Mega Man and NieR in my opinion. The gameplay is very enjoyable, combining a sort of action-rpg and bullet hell style that has plenty of problems, but is still a ton of fun to play with. The humour in this game is done very well, using plenty of references, puns, and portmanteaus to drive home the point that Ludosity wanted to make a funny game without being crude and offensive. Finally, the characters. Play for yourself to see what I mean by that. All in all, Princess Remedy is a fun little game that definitely deserves to be given a try.

It does what BrainPipe does - more calming and contemplative than trippy and maddening (as in going insane) -  a tower defense rather'n a... runner(? BrainPipe's not a(n endless) runner, per se - you're an eyeball moving down a tunnel avoiding obstacles - but yeah).
I appreciate what Particula is going for, aye.
It seems a bit too simplistic, but what's there could be argued (if you're really into casual strategy (pardon the paradox) or the atmosphere) to be worth the asking price of $10; plus there's multiplayer, unsure how well it works.
You are protecting a mind (human head) from bad emotions and harmful concepts:
Rage, Hate, Shame, Confusion, Cheat, etc.
When you are defeated, you are prompted that "Negativity Emerged!"
Whether you're playing as... some sort of deity (for simplicity's sake), trying to protect your human charge, or simply a manifestation of your own mind, projected outward from within to witness the evil what is on the warpath from within, spurred by your surroundings - go ahead and roll one, hit your bro up and strike up a conversation, with Particula going on in the background, rather than sitting idle otherwise or actually focusing on something.
EDIT: I forgot to mention that your (")base(") can take 9 hits; there are orbs floating above the head that disappear when an enemy successfully breaches it. The Trading Cards cite these as "Life." So. When Negativity emerges, we die... not far from the truth.
How the hell'd we wind up like this?
Why weren't we able...
You've 9 towers to pick from; 3 different types with 3 different strengths each:
Ice, Fire, Toxic; can spend either 700, 5000 or 15000 Energy towards them.
Once you place a tower, you can click on it to find these options:
Info, Upgrade, Skill, Delete, Close.
Skill just gives furthe Info.
When Upgrading, you can increase Damage by either 2 or 10, or the Speed with which the tower attacks by 0.1 seconds (max of 10 upgrades in Speed).
When done with a tower, you must Close that menu 'fore opening another one; you can't just click on a different tower with that first menu still open.
There is XP to earn; Level cap is 10.
It seems progressing increases the amount of Energy you start a map with.
There are 3 maps, with 5 difficulties.
My opening statements refute the Store Page Description of Particula "bring[ing] you a new perspective in gaming, helping you to concentrate..." but we both agree it's a good way to clear your mind.
I recommend this game to those who like the vibe / message, like casual strategy / tower defense, like living like it was your last day. Because tomorrow was too late. And I want a diam(ond) back. 'Cause Pimplecrack sucks.
But Particula doesn't... neither does it excel.

Not bad.  Kids are calling this the "scariest game evar", although since I'm over 30 I would disagree.  Truthfully, once you understand all the baddie's patterns, it's simple to avoid them.  It is a bit unnerving to see Slendy silently watching you from a distance, but if you've played any "Half-Life" games, you'll know what that's like (thanks, G-Man!  Slendy even resembles the G-Man a bit, now that I think about it..)
Anyway, the game's "scare" factor is all jump-scares, which to me is a bit of a cop-out: of COURSE you're going to jump when the ambient soundtrack abruptly blasts in your earphones whenever Slendy appears.  Just to experiment, I turned the sound all the way off in my headphones and the game was 85% less scary: the tension seems to come from its soundtrack.
It's mostly a hunter-survival game with collectable elements, very similar to "Sir, You Are Being Hunted", only without a sense of humor.  Still, I enjoyed the game, it's short and entertaining and I bought it on sale for cheap.  Fun to play with a beer after a long day at work and the kids are in bed.  It's not the "scariest video game evar", though; no, for me, that would be "Shadow Man", a pc game I only play in the daytime, preferably when I'm not alone in the house.  (Sadly, I can't tell you why because I only own it on retail so I can't review it on Steam.)
Short version: Slender's short and entertaining (but not for the kiddies.) Grab it on sale only if you aren't rattled by somewat repetitive jump-scares.

A peaceful and fairly simplistic tower defense game that has an interesting theme. I bought this game for $.50 with a 90% OFF coupon. If you enjoy TD games and are able to get it for that price definitely buy it.
PROS:
-Cheap. $5.00 or in my case $.50
-Calming. The music and theme of blasting away the negative things in your life really helps me chill.
-Steam Badge/Trading Cards.
-Multiplayer. I never tried it but it says that it is for 3 player co-op. Just an added bonus in my opinion.
-Ease. Despite the bare bones "tutorial" that they give I was able to figure out all the controls almost right away.
-Replay Value. I got a couple hours of enjoyment from it even though I don't usually play TD games. For TD lovers there are three maps and multiple (5 I think?) difficulties that could lead to many more hours of playtime.
CONS:
-Very Simplistic. Gameplay wise, it is like most other TD games, only having 9 types of towers that each have upgrade capabilities for speed and damage.
-Clumsy Controls. I found a few controls like switching between towers to be slightly annoying but it affected gameplay very little.
NOTES:
-It lacks a good tutorial. Shouldn't matter much due to the ease of use.
-Recommended for people that would like something to take the edge off a long day.
-I would not recommend it for people that are looking for a fast-paced game with a rockin' soundtrack.

Unlike the tidal wave of minimalistic, retro puzzle/platformers that have flooded the indie gaming scene, Thomas Was Alone takes the time to make this simple world and it's simple characters mean something more than an excuse for a video game, as it tells an interesting little story of AIs gone rougue, discovering the nature of the human world, and venturing forth to escape from their digital prison. The Stanley Parable-esque narration gives Thomas and the gang a surprising amount of personality for who are essentially just an assemblage of colored squares and rectangles, and there is definetly a laugh or two to be had from their verbal antics, but as far as the gameplay is concerned, Thomas Was Alone does little to differentiate itself from the crowd. There are plenty of other games that have done better platforming and better storytelling, but very few have managed to combine these elements in such a unique way. This alone is enough to give the game a significant advantage over most other minimalist indie platformers, but if all you care for is gameplay, then you'll still have fun 3-4 hours of puzzle/platforming goodness, even if you've already done it a hundred times before in other games.

I'm all for doing something a bit different within the concept of a 'game'. What Jazzpunk provides is an on-rails 'experience' telling a somewhat surreal story laced with puns and references to hard-boiled detective fiction and gaming staples and offering up a few puzzles to solve on the way.
Whilst never exactly actively bad it does suffer from being overly drawn out in places and the general pacing feels a little disjointed. The puzzles seem to actually get less difficult as the story progresses, perhaps this was a intentional 'thing' but if so the point of it was lost on me.
If you've played games long enough to anticipate some of the usual game design language (the items hidden in the bind corner, if the game points you left have a quick look to the right, pull the lever that appears to do nothing etc) then don't bother chasing after the intriguing possibilities in Jazzpunk. There a lot of hidings to nothing to waste your time on for no reward.

I've been using RS2014 for 5 days now. I've been "casually" playing on an acoustic for about the last year or so, and learned some basic (very basic) techniques, chords, and a few parts to some songs.
RS does get you practicing and does well with motivating you to do so. But, if I hadn't hadn't a few lessons and watched a few other videos, I probably would be struggling. I think that someone that was completely new to guitar would be best suited getting an acoustic and watching some videos on youtube, because there are several basics that you need keep in mind anytime that you practice and I'm not sure RS does a great job of focusing on those (for example: fingering with the very tip of your finger - you may think you're doing it, but you're probably not). In other words, a person brand new to guitar may pick up some bad habits.
With all this said, I think RS works very well with a couple of things - teaching you to navigate the fretboard and finding your strings without looking. Above all, it does have one big advatage over in-person lessons (at least for me), and that is that you don't feel like you're being scrutinized the whole time, so you have more fun and you just keep trying and you're not afraid to suck. As long as you can self-police and realize that just because you "scored 100%", that doesn't necessarily mean you are perfect, I think this is a good teaching tool.
One final thought. Learning on an electric guitar is fine, but if you do start with an acoustic, you'll have a better foundation. Because the strings are harder to press down, and there's less forgivness when sounding out notes, if you make a mistake on an acoustic, it really shows.

Originally this game was incredibly promising. It was like a multiplayer Fallout 3, with safe zones, mutant monsters, free-for-all multiplayer, factions, crafting, quests and open world exploration in post-apocalyptic city ruins. But the developer became greedy and lazy with the introduction of microtransactions becoming a higher priority than the game itself. Between Beta and this game's current state (~3 years) there has been almost no change to the gameplay or environment. Microtransactions were removed, screwing over everyone who bought into them. For a while nobody could play the game because the developers servers were offline. The direction the game took was so bad that the version that is now available is the version from just when Beta ended. All of the bad decisions made by the developers killed off the game's community of over 15,000 players. The game is void of purpose, story and content, not to mention players. Realistically this game is a prime example of what NOT to do with your steam game.
>Pretty excellent graphics.
>Relatively rich environment to explore.
>Challenging survival.
>Now offers single player mode.
>Removed microtransactions.
Cons:
>Void of meaning, the game is not rewarding to play long term and presents no lasting goals or objectives.
>Game is abandoned/left as-is by the developer in an incomplete state
>When you die you lose everything, which is only made unbearable by the fact you can level up
>Multiplayer is mostly dead
>Limited number of enemies makes the game boring after a short while
>Lack of items to pick up
>No player community
>Does not support 4K reslutions
>DX9 only
>No steam achievements

To all those who did not play Eador MotBW: Don't buy Imperium, buy MotBW.
You will be back for more. It's the only game I played more than civilization.
To all those who did play and love Eador MotBW: you know what you'll be getting. But I would like to add that after playing the game I understand why they did not just make this a DLC.
I edited (and mostly deleted) my early access review. In my opinion this game is not as good as its predecessor. But still quite a lot better than the competition - including good old giants like Heroes of Might and Magic (HOMM). That's right. It comes highly recommended.
When compared to MotBW, Eador Imperium shifts more towards HOMM, meaning there's campaigns now, including heroes and background stories which develop throughout the campaign. It's actually done pretty much ok. But that still doesn't make this a good idea. That's because the campaigns replace the more sandbox orientation of the original MotBW. And I prefer the original. Another reason why I prefer the original is becasuse the battle maps are smaller in MotBW. Resulting in a frantic, overwhelming pace. Imperium is slower, much more relaxed (and thus less interesting).
When compared to HOMM, Imperium borrowed all the right elements and improved upon those you didn't realise they could be so much better. The strategic play and exploration is much more intergrated in the tactical (battle) game. Where in HOMM the strategic layer offered mostly just flavour, but no real challenge, in Eador you will have to play strategically or you will be unable to keep up on the higher difficulty levels. And yes, Eador (both games) are more difficult. Another difference: where in HOMM you manage huge stacks of units, in Eador you will manage inividual units. These units level and receive rewards - you will really not want your experienced units to die on lower difficulty and on higher difficulty you can simply not afford it.
Just after release the game was buggy. The Snowbird studio went through a turbulent period and the Eador fans were collectively holding their breaths. When I write this review the game is much improved and stable.
So. Yeah, the game comes highly recommended.

Now the good: the levels, although linear, let you face your enemies in big open spaces, arenas, allowing different approaches to combat and letting you use the suit powers for maximum fun. The pacing is great and the battles are intense, the design of the arenas where you face your enemies is varied, making the battles play differently even though you're facing the same few enemy types during the entire game. The graphics when maxed out are amazing. Despite the flaws, I truly recommend Crysis 2. It's one of the best FPS of the last couple of years and truly worth playing if you're looking for action.

I gave this a go for about 2 hours, within this time I played 4 rounds...
The game is too slowly paced and it is just frustratingly clunky to behold.
The premise is excellent, its friday the 13th! how can you go wrong?
You start off literally not knowing what to do except the instinct to run and hide. Now until you eventually get a turn to be Jason how are you to know that Jason can basically use abilities to highlight where you are hiding, spawn in any location, throw knifes at you, if you die first you could just be waiting 15 mins watching people eventually get slaughtered.
Or in one case for me the police were called and the last remaining counsellor made it to the bridge, but decided just to be a troll and just ran circles around jason for 5 mins until they were eventually slaughtered..
I finally got a turn as Jason, and I realised then you can use abilities! These abilities are basically a buggy mess. You can move quickly like a ghost to catch your victims, you can use like a predator sight to highlights the counsellors hiding places and the counsellors themselves. You can warp to anywhere on the map and more.
The trouble is, say you are chasing someone - even you the killer has stamina that runs out, I ended up slowly chasing someone around a sofa for about 5 minutes and basically killed one person and everyone else got away.
The rest of the time I spent waiting for a lobby to fill, to play a proper round without trolls, the whole game so far is just slow paced as it is without all of this lobby waiting etc.
The graphics are something that could have been on the wii, the overall sound designworks but not really well. They could have had the sound of jasons footprints etc get closer and closer.
I feel this would be a better game if it had a single player sort of tutorial with bots or something to get you into it, but the slow pace and lobby waiting will really put you off especially when you dont really know where the fuel cannister is or anything really to help you win you have to watch others and copy what they do to find out.
Even if you do that you could literally just be playing the whole game only to find that you are playing with an idiot who is just locking himself in to get jason to chase them around a couch.
Some strategies people use like hide in a house (which there is no point as jason can use sight to see what house you are in)  then when you are jason and hunt them down they go out of a window, and then its this boring cat and mouse game of regenerate stamina, wait, run, dodge, then eventually get killed.
But when you are jason you can reach to grab them and you just catch air every time and they run so far away you stamina runs out, you can warp as much as you want but if you play with someone then who has clocked like 50+ hours just trolling jason - for the first few hours you will find this game just slow paced, frustrating and wish there was a single player mode to enjoy.
Overall I don't see this game getting any better tbh, not unless you pay for it. Im surprised they allowed the Friday 13th brand to be associated with this because it's so slow it's not fun. If anyone has played something like Resident Evil 7 where you have the father chase after you - that is very well done, a first person Friday 13th would have been a much better option because seeing your counsellor character just trip when sprinting, the old ps2 animations and just overall tank-like controls of it just make it seem cheap and I feel a first person mode would be more enjoyable.
I dunno maybe it would be better to have no context sensetive actions like "hide under bed" etc, it would be better if you just could get creative in hiding, like being prone to the ground and hiding under a bench, or in thick grass etc. You just know as soon as you are in a house, the person playing as jason will use sight to find the house you are in and where in that house you are hiding, there is no point to hiding at all it just makes the game even slower!
At the moment unless you have watched strategies on youtube and all of that there is little room for you to play it your own way, at least without just a 15 minute drawn out "chase me chase me" troll fest.

I usually don't write reviews, but I wanted to put some words in.
I had a lot of fun with this game.  Reminded me of Divinity style games, very rich in rpg, story, etc.  The pros for this game are very much associated with most of these types of games; they did this well.
Some additional cons which I felt are noteworthy, are regarding the skill setup.  I liked, though sometimes felt frustrated with, how skills were laid out.  Basically, your skills are “added” to your items via a rune system.  There are certain skills which only work on certain items such as  helms, body armor, and weapons.  Any base class (str, int, or dex) can use them, but the skills are more affective with higher stats.  This was kind of cool in that I could put certain runes on my characters, and customize them…unfortunately, any class could use any rune.  I didn’t find this character defining…in fact, I could just switch out runes whenever I wanted.
Where they are lacking, in my opinion, are the following.
30 hours to complete the game.  I love these games; I hate to end my adventure so soon.  Granted, I didn’t technically “complete” the game, but basically, I finished the game by killing the final boss and making an ultimate decision, only to get a crash/runtime error.  I wasn’t willing to repeat the final fight just for some achievements.
Party makeup: basically, you have access to melee character (your starting companion), a mage character, and a ranged character.  It works out in that you can have at least 1 of each of the three main types, but really is sort of bland.  I started as tank/melee, and my first party member was more melee than anything, I turned him into a range…only to find a better range later.  In the entire gameplay, I only found 3 party members, and one end game addition which is not really relevant.
They didn't exploit the side kick...Anyone play Planetscape: Torment?  This is how the sidekick should have been used.  I felt that this addition was non-value added, but highly valuable if done right.
Crafting system: I love the ability to craft really cool stuff, and this game had a ton of recipes and ingredients to work with, unfortunately for me, the items I had access too were the same or far better than what you could craft…this was especially true with access to recipes.  Granted, I probably could have googled Ember recipes and had access to really good gear earlier, but is that really the intent?  There were a ton of alchemical ingredients available, but I didn’t find recipes for.  I’m sure I could have spent time experimenting, but with a 30 or so hour total game time playthrough, it really wasn’t setup to do this.
My recommendations would include:
Somehow balancing content for lengthening the game time/playtime so folks don’t just burn through the main story and finish the game in under 30 hours.  There is content available, which seems like it would be fun, but the main questline doesn’t really use it and therefore, it can be bypassed. I love to succeed in a game, but I hate when I get engaged only to have it end an hour later.
Make crafting more meaningful.  Put recipes in game early on and not at the same tier as drops/chest finds.  You have put effort into putting crafting in the game, but at the same time have put the same items in vendor inventory; I can just grind a little cash and buy the items vs, trying to figure out the recipe, and then grind the same mobs for materials…for the same items.  I’d recommend making the crafting versions much better than the bought/dropped version.  Additionally, throw in some unique stuff, for those who want to put in the time to find/use crafting.
Make player party characters a bit diverse; for me, they felt limited to str, int, or dex based characters.  I really could have started the game with any position, tank, mage (healer), range, and then tweaked the first two added party members to fit the three roles.  In the end I ended up with a tank, mage like, and archer character, all which had the ability to heal.  One character had plate, one had cloth, and one had leather.  One focused on strength, one on intelligence, and one on dex.  This may have been my inability to hybrid, but with the weapon stat restrictions and the skill bonuses based on stats, I felt that anything other than focusing on these three base classes, was just inefficient. I would have loved to see some diversity here.
I loved the game; I really had fun.  I wish I had an opportunity to play more of it, learn more about the lore, or engage more in the characters…but now I’m looking for a new game.

Modern puzzle platformers have changed. Some use mind-bending puzzles, beautiful visuals, or an overly complicated story to try and turn themselves into more than just boring puzzle games. In reality, all that you need to make a good puzzle platformer is a basic story and interesting mechanics. Thomas Was Alone gets these two elements exactly right. I didn't expect there to be much of a story about the protagonist quadilaterals and was surprised at how engaging the narration style actually was. The puzzles are a joy to play through because the minamalist visual style and beautiful music make it a relaxed, fun experience. TWA doesn't force you to land dozens of unforgiving jumps or solve puzzles under time pressure. The puzzles are well-balanced: not too hard, but requiring some thought. Some will dismiss TWA as too easy, but it's a welcome and appreciated break.

Jazzpunk is a game I received from a friend some time ago now, it is a game I really wanted to play and experience, upon viewing some footage of it, I write a review now after some time has passed, because I feel it is important to wait a good amount of time after playing / completing a game, to assess whether it's a game that you can find within your heart to always return to, something that is rare in many modern titles.
Jazzpunk is not one of those games, if you see how many hours I have on the game it is 3.2 hours, and this is more or less how long it will take you to complete the game 100% and unlock all achievements, this is a very short game, something I've been keen to avoid as of recently, you will be able to complete this game in roughly 2 hours while still experiencing everything the game has to offer, and the game levels do pack in a ton of things to see and I dedicated the time within each level to exploring every single area, every single pixel to get the most out of the game. Perhaps if I didn't spend so much time the first play through doing this, I may have considered revisiting the games areas to find new things, but even if that were the case, you're still not going to get more than a few hours worth of entertainment from this game.
This is the main reason why I cannot recommend this game and my reasons are bias, I grew up with the majority of online games being the free flash based games, in which just as much effort was put into making games that could keep you entertained for a few hours, and have huge replayability, and these were uploaded for free to many free flash gaming hubs, for people to enjoy. I feel as if this way of experiencing games online is shifting, as many indie developers make these kinds of games and sell them for $10 or more rather than making them available to everyone. This game in some respects is an exception, it is extremely well made and thought out, and I would definitely pay money to play a game such as this, but is it worth the full retail price of £11? No, definitely not (although that might be a subjective viewpoint). This is one of those games that you really have to get on a sale when it's down to £4 or something that reflects it's price better. What I expect from a game that costs more than £10 is something that will keep me entertained for roughly 20 hours +, something which a lot of indie games fail to provide unfotunately.
If a lot more time has been put into expanding this game into many more levels, to bring it up to the quality we expect from a good video game, and what those who grew up with gaming have come to expect, then certainly this game could be huge, instead it simply leaves memories in my mind for a few weeks and then it sits gathering dust in my steam library as i fail to ever find a reason to replay it again. For all these reasons I cannot recommend it at it's current price.
I will however go on to say that this is definately a game you should play at some point, if you can pick it up for cheap, for it is a really entertaining and quirky game which rewards you exploring and trying things you wouldn't normally do in video games, if you're a fan of exploring games and trying to unlock everything and see everything, this game is packed full of all those kinds of easter eggs, mini-games and many cultural references that will keep you entertained and hold your attention for a whole playthrough, it is a game that is not very hard at all either, and is all round a fun experience playing it. Some may find some of it's humour a little too over the top, but I feel that there's something in this game that everyone can enjoy.
There is not much to say beyond that, the game levels are very interesting and vibrant, the crazy story adds some sense of progression to exploring the mad levels, as well as the achievements which convince you to fully explore and enjoy the game, all round it is a great game and I just wish it could have been longer, adding atleast 8 hours worth of gameplay, rather than the 2-3 hours that it provides.
Will I play it again? I highly doubt it, maybe in the distant future.
Did I enjoy it? Very much so.
Would I recommend it? Not at it's current price, but get it on sale and you won't regret it.
