Since Transformice is Free to Play, give it a try anyways. the game is about as small as the first Doom game in terms of file size.
This game is almost painfully adorable. It has you as a mouse collecting cheese, often with help from a shaman you can add to the environment to make safer passages over pits for the non-powerful mice.
The objective is to get the cheese to the mousehole, unless you're the shaman, then it's mostly to help the other mice get to your mousehole.
As you collect cheese you can buy cosmetic items which have no effect on the gameplay. There's hundreds of levels I think (There's map #888, so I assume there's maps 1-887 since... that makes sense) so tons of content, plus tons of ways to complete specific maps aswell.
There are collectibles in the game still (which are supposedly short-term, but I feel they should simply be reskinned as it adds a small depth than usual to the social elements of the game) which can get you relic items. For getting every relic item, you can redeem sets of them for specific rewards like titles.
As you play the game you will unlock titles which mark your progress as a mouse. There are easily gained titles (Such as 1 cheese gained and first time getting the cheese in the mousehole first) and then there's stupid-hard ones to gain (which are mostly all just about experience in the game and literal experience) such as Divine shaman and any achievement in steam gives a title in the game for the same things also.
Ofcourse the game has a currency aside from cheese, which are strawberries that can buy cosmetics for the head, eyes, neck, face, entire body (Sadly there's no armor-related cosmetics, like a suit of cheese but there are recolor skins) and others.
Also this game could give you diabetes if adorable things could give you diabetes.
I'd rate it at a 7/10. For a simple, free to play game, there's plenty here to keep you entertained and occupied for days' worth of time. Even if not, the game requires 60 MBs which is absurdly small for a game in today's steam market.
It is indeed Stupid-good fun and is so simple anyone could really get the hang of how the game works after a few hours of playing.
Plus the average game lasts for 5 minutes at most so it's great for at-work play if you wanna sneak a game play during break. The game also takes a few moments to load, and even less time to exit.
Con: You do need to log in everytime and there's no real "Remember Me" option, but that's the only real flaw the game has for it's simplicity.
Pros:
- Tons of Content, all unlockable without spending a cent.
- Game is entirely skill-based, there is no luck concerned in terms of success unlike almost any game released lately.
- Gameplay is simple, but has specific aspects that ca make it hard to master. Once you do master it though, you can win regardless of who you are usually.
- The only place for luck is in the selection of the map you will play next, and (i think) in the selection of who will be the next Shaman(s).
- Simplistic, but it's very much fun.
- Uber cute and adorable.

Satanist is another one of those "Where do I go? What do I do? What am I looking for? ARGH I CAN'T SEE!!!" brand of 'horror' games. You know, the type that preys on your total lack of peripheral vision thanks to the sole light source being a tunnel-illumination flashlight, while sending you all over hell and creation to find something that you haven't the first clue what it could be? Yeah, that's pretty much Satanist wrapped up in one paragraph; but wait, there's more!
Actually, there isn't. There are no sounds in this game, save for some faint footsteps, one single drop of blood (yes), and a loud jumpscare noise. There's no background music, not even droning ambiance, no voice overs, no squeaky door opening sounds, nothing. Nada. Zilch. This title isn't low budget, it's no budget. You get the same repeating textures, the same door and object models, pretty much everything looks exactly the same; a feature that makes it hard as hell to tell where you have and haven't been to yet.
So, what is Satanist exactly? Well, you roam around until you find two batteries for your flashlight, and then keep going through a maze of corridors. Since there's no prompt when you're able to pick something up, you might find the first key on the body in the toilet by accident or you just may spend an hour or two searching for it; without it, you'll simply never progress. Ever. Then it's a wild goose chase for keys thereafter. Eventually, some serial killer "satanist" is going to chase you, and since there are LITERALLY ALMOST NO SOUNDS EVER IN THIS GAME you'll never have any idea that he's behind you until you die. Then you'll die, die, and die again until you discover the keycode (089693) on some dead dude's arm. You'll die more on your way to enter the keycode. Then
because that's the end.
There, I just saved you $1.09 CAD and hours of your time. I'd also rip on this title for having spelling errors and terrible grammar, but it's obvious the developer's first language isn't English. I'm pretty close to whistleblowing Dmitry as a scam developer, because he uses multiple publisher/developer names to produce the same crappy FPSCreator titles under similar yet slightly different names; recently, some of them have changed. He never issues any updates, and his games are almost always broken beyond repair. Satanist at least runs, but that's hardly any consolation prize.

Clunky UI. Clunky combat. Clunky skill system. Clunky writing.
I desperately wanted to like the game, but the comparisons to Baldur's Gate or even Neverwinter Nights do Ember no favors at all. Many of the big beautiful areas feel essentially empty of life. The story is not exactly compelling. The books scattered throughout the game are a nice touch for elaborating on the background of the world, but they're also clearly all written by the same person, even though the in-game authors are supposed to be different people. Similarly, the various characters all have the same cadence and manner of speaking, the same text "voice." None of them are particularly memorable. Questing is very much the same old standard CRPG style, nothing new ("Go here, go there, do this, kill the thing, talk to that guy" etc).
Many of the mechanics seemed like attempts to "reinvent the wheel," so to speak:
Movement uses an awkward click and drag system that I've seen in no other game. Giving a new order to your main character cancels previous orders for the rest of the party, including movement holds, so setting up ambushes or tactical formations is rather finicky.
Skills are initially dependent upon finding equipment imbued with the skills you want, but later you can apply desired skills via runes - I'm still not clear on what exactly this skill system brings to the game other than vague frustration in early levels as you struggle to find items with essential skills, followed by irrelevance once you have the ability to create exactly your desired skill setup via runes.
The crafting system is.. well, there's a lot of choice and let's just say that more is not always more, especially when many of the options are virtually useless. The crafting UI is also, bluntly put, terrible, forcing the player to swap back and forth between separate windows to check which recipe they want to make, briefly memorize the recipe ingredients, then automatically close the recipe window in order to return to the actual crafting window to move the ingredients into the pane and begin crafting.
In short, the game feels like the developers were so set on creating unique mechanics that they forgot to ask themselves whether the various systems were actually working together as a cohesive whole, and unfortunately the story is generic enough that it can't elevate the game beyond mediocre at best. To their credit however, the developers appear to be making an effort to consider player reactions and requests, tweaking systems to be more user-friendly where possible. As these improvements trickle in, Ember may become fun instead of frustrating, but for the moment I still can’t recommend it.

Every developer starts somewhere. Whether that be coding in a basement, messing with a game engine, making ROM hacks... Every great developer had to deal with humble beginnings, because that is the nature of learning a craft. Destination Sol is clearly an early effort on the part of its developer. It is an unapologetically simple game, one that does not try to advertise itself as more than it is. That is commendable, and putting it out there not just on steam but as freeware took courage. But even acknowledging its humble origins, Destination Sol is merely adequate.
Travel is simple. Combat is simple. Progression is simple. Destination Sol's various mechanics are simple, and there's nothing wrong with that exactly. Not every game needs to scale or scope of Skyrim. But ultimately, the game's mechanics, like the game itself, are only inoffensive. They are not designed around any major mistakes. They do not feel particularly rewarding. They simply are.
I'm not recommending this game because regardless of origin, it does not leave any lasting impression. I do hope to see more from this developer in the future, and see how their techniques in game design evolve. I would like nothing more than to see, somewhere down the road, a game by them that blows me away. I hope they continue to persevere at game design and grow to greater heights. Until then, best of luck.

This game is almost painfully adorable. It has you as a mouse collecting cheese, often with help from a shaman you can add to the environment to make safer passages over pits for the non-powerful mice.
The objective is to get the cheese to the mousehole, unless you're the shaman, then it's mostly to help the other mice get to your mousehole.
As you collect cheese you can buy cosmetic items which have no effect on the gameplay. There's hundreds of levels I think (There's map #888, so I assume there's maps 1-887 since... that makes sense) so tons of content, plus tons of ways to complete specific maps aswell.
There are collectibles in the game still (which are supposedly short-term, but I feel they should simply be reskinned as it adds a small depth than usual to the social elements of the game) which can get you relic items. For getting every relic item, you can redeem sets of them for specific rewards like titles.
As you play the game you will unlock titles which mark your progress as a mouse. There are easily gained titles (Such as 1 cheese gained and first time getting the cheese in the mousehole first) and then there's stupid-hard ones to gain (which are mostly all just about experience in the game and literal experience) such as Divine shaman and any achievement in steam gives a title in the game for the same things also.
Ofcourse the game has a currency aside from cheese, which are strawberries that can buy cosmetics for the head, eyes, neck, face, entire body (Sadly there's no armor-related cosmetics, like a suit of cheese but there are recolor skins) and others.
Also this game could give you diabetes if adorable things could give you diabetes.
I'd rate it at a 7/10. For a simple, free to play game, there's plenty here to keep you entertained and occupied for days' worth of time. Even if not, the game requires 60 MBs which is absurdly small for a game in today's steam market.
It is indeed Stupid-good fun and is so simple anyone could really get the hang of how the game works after a few hours of playing.
Plus the average game lasts for 5 minutes at most so it's great for at-work play if you wanna sneak a game play during break. The game also takes a few moments to load, and even less time to exit.
Con: You do need to log in everytime and there's no real "Remember Me" option, but that's the only real flaw the game has for it's simplicity.
Pros:
- Tons of Content, all unlockable without spending a cent.
- Game is entirely skill-based, there is no luck concerned in terms of success unlike almost any game released lately.
- Gameplay is simple, but has specific aspects that ca make it hard to master. Once you do master it though, you can win regardless of who you are usually.
- The only place for luck is in the selection of the map you will play next, and (i think) in the selection of who will be the next Shaman(s).
- Simplistic, but it's very much fun.
- Uber cute and adorable.

I've been a die hard fan of the Resident Evil franchise since I played the first game on my first-gen Playstation back in the '90s. This game, RE6, is visually amazing. The intricately detailed environments are astounding and just what most would expect from a Resident Evil game. Unfortunately, the good news ends there. What I originally liked about Resident Evil games (especially RE1 through RE3) was the fact that the game involved doing things beyond shooting zombies and creatures. You had to solve puzzles and think things through. You had to hold items in your inventory and form up plans on how to get past the next barrier. I find it sad to see this element hollowed out and all but gone from these current games. I mean, come on: punch in the 3 numbers  to open the proper door? Find the 3 keys in a maze with regenerating critters constantly chasing you? This has all been done and we've played through games like that already. Don't make it boring! There is so much focus on pure action now, and I think the game is ruined by this. Don't get me wrong- I love action, but when its nonstop it gets tired and predictable. And boring. Because now its just like most other "hurry up and shoot it quick" games out there.
So while devoted fans might enjoy this game that looks and sounds fantastic, the story and gameplay make this just another 3rd person shooter. I hope Capcom can get back on track with this franchise.

Resident Evil has changed a lot over the years and the changes are not why I would not recommend this game.  The negative review comes from the fact that the game has a lot of flaws in my opinion.  I would really like to point out the things I like about the game first.  RE6 has great co-op features including the ability to play as monsters.  There are multiple characters that you play through and there are multiple story lines because of that.  This gives the game a lot of replayability and variety.  The story paths are split up into pairs of characters played alone or co-op, except for one story that is single player, and the story lines cross over each other allowing up to four player co-op at times.  Right now I bet you're saying, "WTF!!!! This game sounds awesome, why the negative recommendation?".  Well, that's because the save points are terrible making huge parts the story being replayed if you quit.  Another bad point is the fact that there is no way to kick a partner which can leave you stuck between quitting and replaying huge amounts of the story or being trapped with complete jerks at times.  Now I think this game will appeal to a lot of people too.  It is basically a third person corridor shooter so fans of that genre will most likely enjoy this game.  I just find the constant switch flipping and running back and forth in corridors a bit tedious.  RE6 is one of those games that is really on the border of being enjoyable for me but the drawbacks just slightly outweighed the assets.

After having sunk almost 100 hours into RE6 I believe I can adequately review it. Starting with the Campaign it follows the multiple characters but still interlinked approach. Now while this allows for a fun and involved overarching narrative on the rare occasions that levels are reused it can come off as a bit cheap, however not game breaking. It is also vital to understand that this is not survival horror, the pace is too frantic and ammo and supplies are too plentiful to ever leave the player in a position of vulnerability.
The plot is quite simplistic and hinges on one rather baffling event, no spoilers but it involves somebody wanting sex, I did not make that up though more detail is provided in game. Thus a GI Joe Esq. villains plots their megalomaniacal destruction of the ENTIRE WORLD with Bioterrorism.... a standard RE plot in other words.  This does however allowed for varied enemy types with your classic Zombies and the somewhat controversial J’avo, lambasted by some as’ Zombies with guns’ or ‘just an excuse for fire fights’.  However in a universe where bio weapons are common place the J’avo do not feel out of place, rather the logical conclusion of weaponised viruses. The spontaneous and often grotesque mutations are also a lot of fun and add some quirks to the run and gun shooting that marks RE6. The Resident Evil A/B team is trotted out including Chris Redfield, Ada Wong, Leon Kennedy and a returning Sherry Birkin. Joining them are some new faces Jake Muller, Helena Harper and Piers Nivans. However the lack of Jill Valentine and Claire Redfield is quite an egregious oversight in this supposed celebration of the Resident Evil franchise. While the change of pace may rub some players the wrong way, Chris’s campaign especially owing to its Gears of War gunplay and speed there are nice counter balances; Sherry’s and Leon’s being more methodical and tense and Ada’s relying mostly on stealth and her natural acrobatics to overcome puzzles and combat situations. One criticism that must be raised however is the endemic QTE’s that have been a blight on the series for quite some time, this along with the annoying habit of multi stage returning boss fights can cause the game to feel a drag at times.
While the dialogue can be somewhat stilted and melodramatic in some places the execution is done surprisingly well with solid voice acting and interesting dynamics between the characters in each campaign, two characters are required for the Co-op sections, however it’s normally either opening a duel locked door or boosting a character to a higher area. Thankfully single player is fully supported and the AI is competent enough to carry out the tasks given too it.
The Online modes are particularly fun especially the Mercenaries mode which is fast paced and frantic, providing a chance for every character in the game to stretch their legs and get to play with their arsenal of weapons. With the unlockable costumes raging from the comedic, Leon’s Pirate attire, to the risqué, Sherry in a schoolgirl uniform three sizes too small.  All of which provide an interesting challenge and a quite addictive rush to beat a high score and unlock more maps in which to play. Other modes include Predator, Survivor, Siege and Onslaught all of which are competitive multiplayer and can be played, online, split screen or LAN. My personal recommendation is Predator in which one player takes control of the Ustanak (A Behemoth Bio Weapon) and is pitted against a team of agents both trying to lay the smack down on each other.
RE6 also sports some quite stunning visuals; a compliment to the level of graphical optimisation for a console port. These include scalable FOV, adjustable Texture, Screen and Shadow quality, Vsync and audio options. On a side note the OST is quite impressive with a nice fusion of different styles and beats of music. In all it comes off as quite a good port, much better then RE5 but still with some odd keyboard mappings and mouse speed issues. Overall I would recommend RE6 to both fans and new comers to the franchise, however new comers may be baffled by some plot or character elements but plenty of online recaps and the availability of both RE4 and 5 on PC should alleviate this. The change in pace from survival horror and creeping terror to the run and gun action started in 5 and arguably in 6 may be the biggest turn off to those wanting a true horror experience and I agree this is the wrong game for that but to those wanting a competently paced and in some cases unintentionally hilarious action game then RE6 is worth your money and time.

Of course, Ubi took a solid start (and it was a start, not a finished product) and F'd it with every upd - wait, nvm; this game barely EVER updates. When you combine this aching feeling of being at a disadvantage due to OP paid characters, and the increasing toxicity of the player community, it just makes for a bitter experience every time you play, even if you do happen to win a few rounds. And even when that happens, you still didn't do it with "honor"; you're name will be besmirched with dishonor and blasphemy. It sounds funny now, but gets old, really fast.

10/10.
For its intended purpose, I have found it to be fantastic. As a beginner guitar player, I went from knowing only a few basic chords to confidently playing through entire songs in just a few hours thanks to the interactive learning style that Rocksmith offers. Learn songs in increments, repeat particular riffs to hone in on elusive sounds, play around with authentic tones used by real artists to write your own songs. Great.

I have attempted to learn to play guitar since I was 13. Every time I've tried, I've made a certain amount of progress and then never been able to master the skill I wanted to go further. While Rocksmith is not a complete learning tool, it is a lot of fun and it has helped me understand skills I didn't have before, or at least make them more fun to practice! The mini arcade games really make the game fun and help expand skills. There is a wide variety of songs, and though the scoring isn't 100% accurate (you can fake it to make it seem like you hit something you didn't and sometimes you'll genuinely hit something and it won't count it), it will definitely help you get some licks under your fingers on your favorite songs.
I was worried that I'd get dependent on their color string model and still struggle with tab reading, but the arcade games actually helped improve my tab reading by making me stronger at hitting the right string/fret combo without looking.
Will it make you the next Hendrix? No way. But if you want to have some fun and learn to play at the same time, this is definitely a great tool.

Wether you are looking to pick a string for the first time or want to get back into play guitar, this is the game you want to go for.

you can easily pick up a guitar and RockSmith guides you though the song- slowly at first with not many frets to play but then, as you practise RockSmith adds more notes and riffs to play- slowly building up a song.
is another thing I like about this game, it allows you to practise slides, fret finger placement and more through use of old arcade style games.
Really worth picking up for a guitarist or someone who wants to learn.

"Thomas Was Alone is a game about rectangles."
What can one do with a rectangle? Well, jump. And have social issues. But mostly jump, of course.
Starting out as a Unity project, it was eventually blown out of proportions. And rightfully so!
Here are my thoughts about the game.
-wise, Thomas Was Alone is a very minimalistic game, but still maintaining its own identity.
It's almost like taking a platformer and keeping it to the bare minimum. On top of that, some modern lighting effects change it completely and make it surpisingly appealing.
I really liked how the game looked, actually, and found it a very nice way of making a game look great without having to focus too much on expensive effects, models and animation.
As a Unity game, it has what one can expect regarding options. Resolution options, audio sliders are there, and then also some presets for graphics. It's not a very intensive game, but it's good that they're there for older PCs.
I didn't really have any problems running this game, no bugs, no frustrating interface, nothing. It's good when that happens.
is an interesting part of this game. David Housden, the composer, decided to add a twist to the layered way of dynamically playing music in video-games. What he's done instead, is to separate each instrument and each melody, and have them play out randomly throughout the levels. This way, you'll rarely hear exactly the same sequence each time you play.
The argument can be made that, musically, it may be worse. I can agree, but, in this case, the music is there more as a way to strengthen the atmosphere than to be played your MP3. And it actually fits the visual style, with an abstract and simple design.
In my opinion, both the music and the sound effects complemented the game perfectly, I really enjoyed it!
So, what's
like?
Thomas Was Alone is a platformer, with light puzzle elements.
Each rectangle has a purpose in the game, each with their advantages and disadvantages. The objective is to reach the end of each level by combining everyone's strengths.
It's pretty straightforward, actually.
While there isn't really anything that will blow your mind regarding mechanics by themselves, it's still an enjoyable game to play.
The
is pretty straightforward. The levels don't pose much of a threat, making for a more relaxed experience. One commendation, though, is the amount of variety. There are 10 worlds, each with 10 levels. In each world there are new characters, with new mechanics and interactions, keeping it constantly fresh.
And it's done in a way not to overwhelm the player with rectangles, which is good.
There's more to it than one would expect from a game about rectangles, actually!
Now, gameplay by itself doesn't make this game good. It would actually be a rather bland title just from a gameplay standpoint. Even coupled with the visual style and the music, it's not quite there yet.
What's left, then?
Well, the whole game is narrated. The narration, done by Danny Wallace, is mostly about the inner social struggles of each rectangle.
AH! How could that ever work?!
Well, it just does. Each rectangle has a very unique personality, directly linked to its shape (well, some are bigger, fatter, more athletic, etc.). Each character has essentially one main trait, which is actually enough to give them depth (but, but, it's a 2D game...), in the way they work together, and see each other.
As the game progresses, the problems between them may or may not be overcome by the sheer power of cooperation.
In most situations, I think these characters, if humanoid, would be seen as very bland stereotypes and taken as a negative. Somehow, by using a single shape to characterize a character, isolating one trait doesn't seem as negative. It's a different perspective, so that's cool!
This may have all been rather accidental (i.e. not the point of the game when it started), but the fact is that everything works torwards the same objective. And, while the mechanics may not be very unique, when coupled with the actual personality of each rectangle, it all seems to create a very coherent and unique experience, in which you can't really draw the line between the world/story and the game itself.
And that's something that many games struggle to do. In Thomas Was Alone, the story and world is told through the gameplay, through the characters, and through short narration in each level.
It doesn't take that much resource-wise, surprisingly, but it may be very hard to achieve well (take Type:Rider, for instance).
All in all, Thomas Was Alone was certainly a unique experience.
It also manages to draw from a very common pool of emotions, so just about anyone can enjoy it. It's a charming and relaxing game, with a great amount of character. And rectangles. That's also a thing, here.
One issue I have with it is the achievements. There isn't much of a point to them. Maybe it's just a way of having witty one-liners thrown around (?). Slender: The Arrival is the follow-up to the popular freeware horror game, Slender: Eight Pages, being made by the people responsible for making Slender so popular (Mark J. Hadley, creator of Slender: Eight Pages, and the Marble Hornets team who made a series of Slender-themed YouTube videos). It's not just another Slender clone though, it goes for a more cinematic approach to gaming, and not as in fixed cutscenes or QTEs, but in providing an interactive cinematic horror experience.
The stories pretty simple. You are going to check in on a friend who lives deep in the forest who hasn't been responding to calls, texts, or emails for the last few days. Turns out, there's evil that lurks in these woods... Now can you escape?
Slender: The Arrival is probably the closest you'll get to playing a found-footage horror film in game form, at least yet. The way everything is told through the gameplay's lens, the 'folk-story' tone the game goes with the legend, the execution of how Slender and the events that transpire work, feels very much in-line with a found-footage horror film, except you are the driver and the one tasked with capturing it all and surviving.
In that regard, Slender: The Arrival is a very cool experience. It has some good build-up, atmosphere, and escalates the situation while still retaining a more down-to-earth feeling. All through gameplay, you experience a series of events and have to respond to them.
The basic Slender gameplay is still there... Collect different items and avoid the big tall man in the suit, but there's more to it here, and this is often where the split in opinion on this game begins.
The game is rather short, and honestly you probably spend more time just exploring places in-between the game's 'main' stages than you do actually playing the core Slender gameplay.This mainly involves going around locations, like a forest trail or a house, and opening doors to get to the next story location.
Slender: The Arrival is split into nine 'stages', five of them in the story, one as a secret hidden level, two of them were added post-patch to make a hidden new miniature story, and one as a bonus stage. Beating the story should take 2-4 hours the first time (the five main stages), and consist of two stages with you actually collecting items, two scenarios with you avoiding Slender via other means 'cinematically',  and most of these stages as well as one stage entirely having 'build-up' situations where nothing actually happens, but it builds-up to the next main gameplay scenario.
The length and the cinematic direction the game takes will turn some people off, but on my part it actually made me enjoy the game more. It legitimately feels like a playable found-footage horror film, and has charm and atmosphere in its design and oppressive stages. I found myself enjoying it during its short course.
I even got scared a few times, something the original Eight Pages and many Slender clones don't do to me. Scariness is subjective, but a feat I must mention as I don't actually find the character of Slender to be scary in general.
This said, I found myself more terrified by Slender's 'unidentified' masked assistant than Slender himself. She's a stalker who appears in a specific stage in the game, and her sounds, appearance, animations, and the environment you encounter her in legitimately made me afraid of her for a time.
However, for all of this 'cinematic charm' I'm spouting about, the game maybe alienated its main audience in some ways, as part of the charm of the original Slender game was with its minimalistic atmospheric gameplay and dreary feeling without need for story, explanation, and just throws you right in. This is a very different experience and very different game, and these changes completely alters the audience the game is designed for... And unfortunately, with a character who's been popularized like Slender, it can mean the game's audience is potentially very small, as some have come to ridicule or dislike his popularity and character, and those that like him may not like the way the game is designed differently and more aimed as a playable cinematic horror game.
I feel fond of it though, and it happens to be my favorite Slender-based game for the very reason of how its different. I find it to be enjoyable to play, and to experience, and craft an interesting world and scenario that was immersive to go through.
This all said, the best parts of the game maybe came out of the optional content. The 'bonus stage I mentioned is simply a recreation of the original Eight Pages game you can play outside of the main story, but a lot prettier. The game has difficulty levels and randomized features through all of its stages which is interesting. There are a variety of secrets and Easter eggs in the game, including a hidden ending.
The two post-patch stages based around a village and a farm take criticism from the game and made really moody set-pieces that add extra elements to the story, though finding them is a bit tricky as they require specific actions during the game's main story.
And for me, the absolute best part of the game was the secret level. I don't want to spoil it here, but at least for me, it was definitely the creepiest part of the whole game, but a shame most probably wouldn't find it without looking it up... It's pretty well hidden.
Slender The Arrival isn't for everybody and ditches the minimalist direction for something more akin to a game version of a found-footage horror film, but during its short duration it delivers an interesting different take on both Slender and cinematic horror games. I'd say worth a trip for those who think the idea of playing a found-footage horror film sounds appealing.

Honestly, this game is pretty cool... at first.  Then you go to a planet.  If you never had to fight things down near a planet, this game would be great.
But here's the big problem: if you are on a planet there is gravity.  Your guns are on one side of your ship, your engines are on the other side of your ship.  Enemies can shoot in any direction, you can only shoot "forward".  So... what happens when there is an enemy below you?  You have to aim your ship down.  "Then how do you not run into the ground?"  You don't not run into the ground.  You run into the ground!  "But you said engines were only on one side of your ship.  How do you back up?"  You don't.  You die to the easiest enemy in the game because you are stuck with your nose in the ground. "That doesn't sound very fun." It's really not. If they just didn't include the planets this would be 100% thumbs up.  But the inclusion of planets and gravity in a top down game ruins everything about this game.  Really disappointed.

Princess Remedy in a World of Hurt is one of the nicest little games I've played this year.
As the titular Saturnian Princess, a recent graduate of healing school, you must descend to the tortured Hurtland below in order to heal the land's prince, who has somehow saddled himself with every illness in existence... And maybe fix up the rest of Hurtland along the way.
Gameplay is very simple, and only directional buttons and an action button are required. You simply enter various towns and caves from the overworld, and talk to sick-looking NPCs. To cure them, you must clear a small top-down shooter minigame, launching bandages at personifications of various ailments. (Unfortunately, you can only fire in the direction you are facing, but I suppose this can be attributed to style.)
Each minigame you clear and person you heal will earn you another hit point, and various other upgrades like shot power and regeneration can be found in chests throughout the world. You'll need them, as the germs and creatures you fight will get progressively stronger. Don't worry, though- If you fail a heal-fight, you can try again with no penalty.
The game has some amusing visuals and a lot of funny dialogue- most of the people you heal are grappling with some sort of silly condition, like a ghost who's scared of himself and a centaur who is worried because he believes he is real. (This is reminiscient of other games from the same folks, such as Ittle Dew- the protagonists of which make a cameo in this game.)
Finally, the heavily retro graphics may look off-putting at first, but I got used to them quickly and soon enjoyed the old-fashioned feel. I also found them to be much more colorful and identifiable than I was expecting- definitely more so than the majority of the old stuff they take inspiration from.
Overall, Princess Remedy is a quick jaunt that is absolutely worth an hour or so of your time. My only complaint is that it's free-to-play, so I can't have it permanently associated with my account.

The, “are video-games art?” debate has to-date been hampered by one glaring issue. Every video-game people point to as a great example that they ARE art is, more or less, the same. Somebody who doesn't think video-games are art, and doesn't think Journey, Flower, and its' ilk are evidence to the contrary is probably not going to be swayed by examples of other games that are very similar to Journey and Flower. I really like those games, for the record.
Enter Jazzpunk. This game is, at the core, an art game. The entire point of it is to explore the world, find interesting hidden stuff, and progress a very basic plot that takes you to new areas and new hidden stuff. Most things you interact with have no point, other than to tell a joke or show you a weird thing. The difference between this game and those other 'art' games is mostly one of tone, but it is different enough that I think people who hate Flower could easily love this. It removes the pretension from art games and grounds the genre in weird, cyber-cold-war trappings. It's genuinely hilarious. It, quite frankly, has grown up. Flower is the type of interactive art that a poetry major straight out of college would dream up. Jazzpunk, on the other hand, feels like it was made by some dude in his thirties who likes wrestling, eighties action movies, and Johnny Mnemonic. It has meat, and substance, and an actual identity that's all its' own. It has, quite literally, changed the game. From now on when I want to show a non-gamer an artsy-fartsy type interactive experience, it probably won't be Flower or Journey, as much as I like those games. It'll be Jazzpunk.

After having sunk almost 100 hours into RE6 I believe I can adequately review it. Starting with the Campaign it follows the multiple characters but still interlinked approach. Now while this allows for a fun and involved overarching narrative on the rare occasions that levels are reused it can come off as a bit cheap, however not game breaking. It is also vital to understand that this is not survival horror, the pace is too frantic and ammo and supplies are too plentiful to ever leave the player in a position of vulnerability.
The plot is quite simplistic and hinges on one rather baffling event, no spoilers but it involves somebody wanting sex, I did not make that up though more detail is provided in game. Thus a GI Joe Esq. villains plots their megalomaniacal destruction of the ENTIRE WORLD with Bioterrorism.... a standard RE plot in other words.  This does however allowed for varied enemy types with your classic Zombies and the somewhat controversial J’avo, lambasted by some as’ Zombies with guns’ or ‘just an excuse for fire fights’.  However in a universe where bio weapons are common place the J’avo do not feel out of place, rather the logical conclusion of weaponised viruses. The spontaneous and often grotesque mutations are also a lot of fun and add some quirks to the run and gun shooting that marks RE6. The Resident Evil A/B team is trotted out including Chris Redfield, Ada Wong, Leon Kennedy and a returning Sherry Birkin. Joining them are some new faces Jake Muller, Helena Harper and Piers Nivans. However the lack of Jill Valentine and Claire Redfield is quite an egregious oversight in this supposed celebration of the Resident Evil franchise. While the change of pace may rub some players the wrong way, Chris’s campaign especially owing to its Gears of War gunplay and speed there are nice counter balances; Sherry’s and Leon’s being more methodical and tense and Ada’s relying mostly on stealth and her natural acrobatics to overcome puzzles and combat situations. One criticism that must be raised however is the endemic QTE’s that have been a blight on the series for quite some time, this along with the annoying habit of multi stage returning boss fights can cause the game to feel a drag at times.
While the dialogue can be somewhat stilted and melodramatic in some places the execution is done surprisingly well with solid voice acting and interesting dynamics between the characters in each campaign, two characters are required for the Co-op sections, however it’s normally either opening a duel locked door or boosting a character to a higher area. Thankfully single player is fully supported and the AI is competent enough to carry out the tasks given too it.
The Online modes are particularly fun especially the Mercenaries mode which is fast paced and frantic, providing a chance for every character in the game to stretch their legs and get to play with their arsenal of weapons. With the unlockable costumes raging from the comedic, Leon’s Pirate attire, to the risqué, Sherry in a schoolgirl uniform three sizes too small.  All of which provide an interesting challenge and a quite addictive rush to beat a high score and unlock more maps in which to play. Other modes include Predator, Survivor, Siege and Onslaught all of which are competitive multiplayer and can be played, online, split screen or LAN. My personal recommendation is Predator in which one player takes control of the Ustanak (A Behemoth Bio Weapon) and is pitted against a team of agents both trying to lay the smack down on each other.
RE6 also sports some quite stunning visuals; a compliment to the level of graphical optimisation for a console port. These include scalable FOV, adjustable Texture, Screen and Shadow quality, Vsync and audio options. On a side note the OST is quite impressive with a nice fusion of different styles and beats of music. In all it comes off as quite a good port, much better then RE5 but still with some odd keyboard mappings and mouse speed issues. Overall I would recommend RE6 to both fans and new comers to the franchise, however new comers may be baffled by some plot or character elements but plenty of online recaps and the availability of both RE4 and 5 on PC should alleviate this. The change in pace from survival horror and creeping terror to the run and gun action started in 5 and arguably in 6 may be the biggest turn off to those wanting a true horror experience and I agree this is the wrong game for that but to those wanting a competently paced and in some cases unintentionally hilarious action game then RE6 is worth your money and time.

There are 4 campaigns in the game, each played with different pairs of characters. All the campigns are intertwined with each other, showing each pair's journey through the main storyline. There is a LOT of gameplay here if you want to experience it all. Each campaign seems to play differently as well. It's a pretty great setup. Leon's campaign reminded me of Resident Evil 2, while Jake's campaign reminded me of Resident Evil 5.
This game feels janky and unpolished a lot of the time. The dialogue is lacking and unimpressive. The graphics are mediocre, primarily from low texture quality and repetitive use of objects, textures and the like. Elements in many levels just feel all the same, with just the geometry changing. Some areas look visually impressive, but it's rare and short-lived. The controls and camera are ridiculous at times, but that's always how the Resident Evil franchise has been. Luckily, there are a lot of custom deaths when you fail quick time events, and they never get old.
The level of quality varies GREATLY throughout the game... the beginning of Leon's campaign is just awful, stereotypical, and poorly executed. It gets better later on, though. Jake's campaign felt more consistent and solid, while also being less over-the-top.
Despite all the bad, the game is actually fun COOPERATIVELY. I wouldn't recommend playing this game if you're by yourself, since relying on the AI is not fun, and you can share the ridiculousness of the game with a friend. It's like watching a bad movie and making fun of it... it ends up being fun. I highly prefer Resident Evil 5, as it's better in every single way, but if you're looking for another Resident Evil game, there's a lot of content here.

Slender: The Eight Pages, is the scariest game I have ever played. The gameplay is simple, deiliberately repetitive, and frightening. Slender: The Arrival, is a very scary game - but not as scary. That is how to describe Slender: The Arrival in a nutshell for fans of the original game. For those unfamiliar with the horror masterpiece that is Slender: The Eight Pages, I will explain. Slender: The Eight Pages, drops you into the middle of the woods, in a disturbingly eerie nighttime filled with fog, bushes, and worst of all: undescribable darkness. Your goal is to look for 8 pages. As you collect each page however, you find that you are slowly pursued by a strange and creepy stalker, known only as, The Slender Man. The game recieved universal praise for it's minimalist horror elements, sound design, and ambition. The game was released in June of 2012 as a free game. However, after more than 2,000,000 downloads were reported of the sleeper hit, a sequel from the original developers immediately began production. It was no later than March of 2013 that Slender: The Arrival was released - a highly anticipated "sequel" to Slender, only this time, for pay. No one knew exactly what to expect, so when Slender: The Arrival only recieved lukewarm reception from it's many hungry fans, I personally was disappointed. I with-held from playing the game for a long while, until I saw it was available on Steam, and decided to give it a try. I'll say though, that despite Slender: The Arrival being well worth your time, there still is much disappointment to be had. The story this time around focuses on Lauren, a young lady visiting her friend Kate in order to help her clear out and sell an old house in the woods belonging to her now deceased Mother. Once Lauren arrives at the home though, after a mild car collision, Kate is nowhere to be found. As Lauren investigates, she realizes that Kate may have been kidnapped by a supernatural entity. Soon, Lauren realizes that she too is being stalked, and must work her way through the forest to a mysterious radio tower. Once again, the sound design is superb, and the gameplay is simple, but effective. However, the element that took me most by surprise was just how beautifully rendered the settings were. After completing a tough challenge that requires difficult work and replays over and over again, there's nothing more rewarding than a pleasent stride through the great outdoors, even if they are being occupied by The Slender Man. The biggest problem with the game is, unfortunately, it's length. Though Slender: The Eight Pages is obviously a very short game, it makes up for it in the difficulty. I personally have never beat Slender, but I still try. The problem in this games design is the fact that it's only made out of 6 short stages, but each is made to be extremely difficult, and take a trial and error process. In addition, the story feels lacking as well. Though written by the superb Marble Hornets team, the story still feels anti-climactic, and unfinished, giving us hints of a much larger puzzle, but only revealing limited pieces. In the end though, the gameplay is scary, and fun, and I suppose that's all that matters. Recommended.

This is an Early Access Review so you should take what I say here with a large grain of salt.
The number 1 thing you will notice about this game is, upon booting, it will ask you to define your joystick keys. Maybe I should have taken this as a hint that the controls were going to be difficult without one although I'm not sure what they are thinking with the control scheme anyways. Moving forward takes ages and feels like you're trying to wade waist-deep in mud. It takes a full 5 seconds for the ship to reach the top of the screen. Also if you let go of forward, you fly at mach 2 to the bottom of the screen which makes moving around in a bullet-hell shooter a complete nightmare. There is a "Hover" button, but you have to hold it down and if you're firing, each bullet sends you backwards a little bit. Maybe in the beginning default control scheme I should have picked something there. But the problem is that I didn't want to scroll through and understand and research 30 undefined joystick buttons.
Also, as far as I could tell, there is no way to close the game or exit other than Ctrl+Alt+Delete. Clearly there's some much needed work on the controls.
Gameplay seems alright, there doesn't seem to be much of a curve, it feels like they started me at what would be considered level 100 of Nomltest. There is a "Boss Rap" which I thought was hilarious (Lyrically and because it comes out of NOWHERE). But then there's another rap during the credits and I got the creeping feeling that maybe they weren't being ironic.
There's also weapons, and these wierd "pools" that seem to imply they are power ups. But they didn't work. You can hold a button and they go away, but otherwise don't appear to have an affect on gameplay.
Weapons are sparse, when you get one, it is fun to use. I like that I'm able to see inside the ship when the spread gun is picked up. Oddly enough the ship can do a spin around and fire, which is incredibly useful, but it only does that when  you get hit and you have a GIGANTIC health bar. Maybe they want you to get hit a bunch and make it less about dodging and more about mitigating your damage.
I'm going to keep checking out this game as it develops further because I have a soft spot for the genre and I think this could turn out pretty good. If it does, awesome! I can always update my review.

One of the best things about being a gamer is that every once in a while, a game comes around and completely catches you off guard in the best way possible, delivering a surprise that you always remember. Jazzpunk has done this to me.
It's a short game (only took me about 2 and a half hours to play through), but there is more creativity, humor, and pure absurdity packed into this brief experience than most much longer games can conjure in their entire playthroughs. In fact, I'm not even sure how to describe this game, and I get the feeling that trying to do so will only sell it short. I can say, though, that this is probably the first game that has ever manged to pull me out of my zone of familiarity so far, yet was still able to remain engaging beginning to end, consistently make me laugh, regularly make me question if I just saw what I thought I saw, and cause me to think about the game and its world when I was away from my PC.
For the first time in quite some time, I was genuinely disappointed to see the ending credits of a video game. I wanted to exist in the world of Jazzpunk for a much longer period of time. There are still so many mysteries to unravel, so many characters to meet, and so many places to visit. The game's length is its only weakness. Otherwise, this was one of the most purely enjoyable and memorable video games I've played in quite some time. Easily one of the best of 2014.

I'm going to cover the important points of this game but keep it brief. Now I've played a TON of arpg's, crpg's and...rpg's in my life but this is a bit of an odd one.
At first glance, something doesn't quite add up, you look at the price, look at it's popularity and yet notice that the reviews are very positive from users amounting to....well not even in the 1k area.
Here's the thing...hardly anyone knows about this game. I was a bit flummoxed when I saw this pop up on the new release list thinking of how I could have missed something that looks like it appeals to me. Because of the "oh so cheap" price, I got it straight away, I mean why not? What's another game in my 200+ backlog?
After playing for about an hour, I was thinking about how great the game looked and how it felt like a mix of a number of RPG's. It's probably better to say that this is much like any isometric RPG with elements from Neverwinter nights, Dungeon siege or Sacred. In fact, my first hour felt like I was honest to goodness playing Divine divinity with different rules!
Some cracks start to show after that hour, particularly with graphics, this isn't a hi-fi game, the budget wasn't spent on next gen looks but they do however manage to look great and it has it's moments, just in a not so big budget AAA game type of way. The game doesn't seem to miss a beat on 1080p with full settings. One cool thing though is how they've managed to squeese in a day/night cycle and some weather effects. What would have been nice is some dynamic and character shadows also.
Character progression is different to games of this type. You still level up your four mainstay stats of any RPG, strength, vitality, intelligence and Dexterity but you don't have skills per level. You are granted skills depending on what type of weapon or armor you use. E.G, you pick up weapons with skills attatched to them....A staff might have abilities suited to magic using, or in my case I've chosen to play close combat, therefore some of the weapons I've come across have double attacks or area attack abilities attatched to them. Helmets, armor, rings and amulets have abilities attatched to them, some have healing and some have physical or offense.
Many crafting options. I'm actually surprised, they could have left any sort of crafting out entirely but it's darn nice to have this in there! There more I played, the more little surprises I got as I progressed...."oh, i can use alchemy!?"...."this game has smithing!?" Attatching runes is in here too. The more new stuff I found, the higher my opinion of this game increased.
I was initially going to say that the game is light on story and lore but it's actually not. Well it's not as heavy as Warcraft or Dragon age story wise but it's got some very interesting and engaging backstory.
The negative points though....There isn't any sort of bookmark settings for the world map. You can't mark an area for further exploration and because the map is so big, you have trouble finding your way around and going back to areas you found earlier.
No food during battles! This one is annoying! Seems the only way to replenish your health during battle is through a healing spell or two, which relies on mana and therefore potions, or health potions. With the ability to cook food within the games crafting, it's made almost usless because at the critical times you're just about dead, you've got a full sack of food you just cooked earlier and can't use it. I will admit though, the higher quality foods manage to give you buffs and give you a good health fix before battles. (Update: 1.043 has allowed higher level crafted food to restore some mana also, making it a little more usefull.....still, no food during battle..)
I suppose this works both ways, it's exhilarating when you forgot to get back to full health, then all of the sudden you get ambushed, only to win the battle with one character left and a small amount of life. Some of the battles can be quite touch and go.
You can't have a massive party with tons of abilities. Just remember, the gear each character wears is limited to the abilty on that individual equipment. In a way, it keeps things going and light on gameplay. If you're playing this game, it's something you want to do for a short while, otherwise it gets monotonous.
Overall, it's a damn nice little package for such a small amount of chump change, especially on sale! I doubt very much you'd waste your money.

Is a contemporary, traditional RPG, nothing muddled about it.
The openworld showcased consists of streamlined versions of classic tropes, such as dwarf mines, prison level, cemetery etc. Geo political in nature, the story reminds us that it is never time to stop being aware of our natural resources.
Graphics are low poly but pleasant. Music is quite good and atmospheric utilizing some flats in places that fantasy music in general wouldn't, overall this lends itself to the off and on comedic nature of the story, but often it misses when first listening, but still resembles quality backbone to the world. We are gratuitously rewarded at the climax of our story in both sound and visuals.
Beautiful transition between night and day, you will hardly notice the effect take place as it does so naturally and realistically, experience twilight set in or the light come into play. The sunshine radiates an ember-like aura upon any location, while the darkest of nights folds over to an entirely different looking environment.
Story is genuinely heroic in nature and making our ressurected hero again part of the world, objective to the theme.  The main antagonist holds too much power over our hero and personality wise, for the story, our hero's complete opposite- Lightbringer vs. Darkbringer. As the story progresses we can see just how simple the villain is by his decreasing power over our hero as our hero becomes more residual into the world. It really came off that this was the type of villain who would explain his evil plans directly to our hero and arrogantly laugh as he teleports away somewhere in full confidence of his success. Here is where the story shines by exemplifying faith in the good will of the player to continue the adventure, for things are not what they seem to be. Although most if not all plot holes are filled, it is only barely, the stunning conclusion guarantees the sense of accomplishment in general for this world, a world we were only privy to glimpse and then leave possibly never to return.
A true to heart RPG, for those who have played them before, we know what it takes to finish including repetitive battling and it is real time and pausable. Ember is solid and not the fathomly deep experience that seems expected, that evaporates the further along we go. Enemies respawn while exploring and there are no collectables. Crafting can be a clever yet totally voluntary involvement , gear needs no repair and the sidequests can be counted on one hand, this is still a remarkable game. Good ingame books too.

It's probably a mixed sign that the game becomes 'challenging' and 'good' about two or three hours in.  For those who are unfamiliar with the puzzle genre, the game introduces you to each of the controls step by step, introducing each character slowly and gradually.  However, what makes this become more than just a test of timing and a minimalistic platformer is the narration.  Thomas is just a rectangle, but when the narrator tells you this story he becomes more than that.
Now, there's the old motto of writing known as "show, don't tell," and based on that motto this game fails miserably.  And yet, as a player might watch those little blocks explode into tiny pieces after the fifth time you've attempted a level, the narration was Sincere enough to let this player care about the blocks.  Just a little.  The music is excellent and really maintains the mood, and the later levels are entertaining enough to keep you glued to the screen.  Thomas Was Alone is a game that requires the patience to sit through the whole thing, but when you do it's definitely worthwhile.

Thomas Was Alone is a wonderfully done minamalist "adventure" puzzle game narrated by (name escapes me) a voice many might remember from other games (I think he is in other games). While the overall game is relatively short, just 3 hours (4 if you want the collectables), you'll nonetheless have a wonderous time enjoying this game to its fullest.
The game consists of you playing the role of a bunch of quadrilaterals (henceforth called shapes for easier reading) helping each other get through numerous puzzles and obstacles, normally impossible on their own, to reach the portals. Each individual shape has it's own unique characteristics that make it useful for certain situations. More importantly, they each have a personality voiced by the narrator. Each shape's personality also matches with their physical characteristics, furthering their personification. Thanks to this narrator, the entire world the shapes traverse is given life and meaning, and draws you into each level, wondering what is going to happen next.
One thing that isn't done with the narrator that I felt was missing, was the narrating of each shapes' responses and reactions to the introduction to a new shape. While later in the game you'll realize that there isn't much point to this due to all the shapes, you'll feel that it is distinctively missing in the earlier levels.
The controls are quite simple, consisting of nothing but left, right, jump and your shape selection. The game appears to have full controller support, though I don't have access to one so I cannot confirm this. On the keyboard you have two methods of selecting the shapes. The numbers for each individual shape (shown on the bottom right in numerical order) or the q and e keys for next and previous.
The games major flaw, that appears especially on later levels when you have 5+ shapes, is that the numbers aren't responsive. To select a shape with the numbers you have to press the button numerous times or hold it down, taking you out of the game. Furthering this frustration is the shape legend on the bottom right. This legend shows each shape that is available for you to select on that level in numerical order. However, due to the colours, it is frequently hard to tell shapes in the legend apart, ending up in you pressing a number for a shape you don't want (Note: This legend is practically useless to the colourblind). Also, this legend changes all the time, so the shape that may be number one may end up be number three on a later level, never letting you memorize a single key binding for each shape.
I want to mention that the un-responsiveness may have been done on purpose, as to eliminate the player's ability to exploit any jumping glitches or bugs that may become present when stacking shapes. So if you think that you need to do some really weird jumping shenanigans to get through the level, then you're doing it wrong.
Let's look at the level design. Not noticeable at first, but the level design is clearly one of this game's strong points. The main method of getting smaller shapes up to higher areas is by stacking each shape and building a staircase. But when you get more and more shapes, you'll start to realize that each ledge was painstackingly measured out to require specific shapes to get up to the higher points of the level. Also important to note is that you will never get "stuck" and have to restart from having pushed to far with one shape. There is always a method of bringing a certain shape back to the origin, or at least to where they are necessary. If at later levels you find that you can't bring one of the larger shapes back to help the smaller shapes, then you don't actually need that larger shape to complete the level.
I'm proud and happy to say that there are NO glitches, NO bugs. Everything runs smoothly and flawlessly, just like a good completed game should.
Not putting too much about the ending, let's just say I'm disappointed in it. Even as short as it was and there isn't much one could have done, 2 monitors would have been a much better idea.
The game is certainly not a challenge, as most of the levels you can get through without failing once. This is a game that is meant to be enjoyed, meant to be seen as fun.
Pros:
- Enticing narrative
- Tonnes of levels
- Very polished
- Collectables
- Very little frustration
- Lots of fun
Cons:
- Keyboard shape selection not responsive
- Lackluster ending
- Frequently wanting a bit "more" from the narrative
Controls 7/10
Controller people might have better luck than keyboarders.
Entertainment 10/10
This is a game that is meant to be enjoyed, and you'll enjoy it to its fullest.

Simple, but interactive and keeps you entertained.

I like the concept of destroying negative thoughts, but the game is not worth more than 24 cents to a dollar, in my opinion. Fine to get if it's on sale or in a bundle. The game is a very simplistic tower defense game. Ice towers slow the negative thoughts, fire towers burn (damage over time), and  arcane towers slow (less than ice) and poison (less damage than fire). The negative thoughts come in various sizes; the bigger it is, the more HP it has. As you defeat the negative thoughts, you get energy (the currency of the game) which allows you to upgrade towers and destroy negative thoughts more quickly and effectively. The game is easy but repetitive. Multiplayer games often take a while to play unless you're playing with friends, mostly because everyone else is playing with their friends. In short, try it out if you have friends, you have nothing to do, and it's on sale.

Crysis 2 is epic. It is easy to get lost amongst the sheer scale of the seph-torn cityscapes of Manhattan, a city breathing with life due to the technically impressive CryEngine 2. That's right, the graphics are spectacular, with a great attention to detail, and cater to a range of builds. Other than the jaw-dropping, mouth-watering visuals, the combat in this game is excellently paced, challenging and genuinely fun. There is a large variety to weapons and suit upgrades, accommodating for a great many number of playstyles. The soundtrack does very well to harmonise with the constant action, in particular the main theme, composed with grandeur by Hans Zimmer. The story is fairly straightforward, with a foreseeable arc, although it does have its fair share of surprises.
Tl;dr Crysis 2 (Maximum Edition) is an excellent first-person action game, with beautiful visuals, varied gameplay and a really enjoyable campaign.

Crysis 2 is an entirely different game. I’m stunned that this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ studio could produce such a jewel after all these turds.
The setting (new york), the soundtrack (hans zimmer), the suit (more energy, smarter features and can be customized), the parkour (!!!) - everything is better. It's an audiovisual delight, controls like a boss and there were more levels that I desperately wan't to replay than I can even remember.

Crysis 2 starts the same as Crysis 1 finished; muddled, confused and frustrating. It very often leaves you fighting for your life, without any clear idea as to what you are actually supposed to be doing. This is a fault that plagues the game at a number of different points.
The game doesn't give that sense of freedom that was in 1, feeling much more constrained and scripted; much most like a console game, which of course it is.
One thing I really dislike is the inability to save whenever you like. All you get is checkpoint saves. This means that a particularly tough section you may have to play and listen to all the commentary again and again and again...!
Having said all that, it's still a very enjoyable game. It gathers pace as you play it, so stick at it for a while. It's a definite "must have" even though I still prefer Crysis 1.

A few words about Ember - a well-made,old-school inspired RPG.
The story starts when your hero is being raised from the dead as a member of an ancient group of guardians known as Lightbringers. They are protectors of flame-like beings known as Embers. The peace in the world was broken after Lightbringers were confronted by Darkbringers. So now you have to regain your memory, regain your power, and save the world...
Captivating story, cool detailed locations, lots of loot to collect,spells and skills to master,expansive crafting system with lots of recipes to discover and craft.
Well balanced battle system employs a real-time combat system with  “tactical pauses”, you have a handful of characters to control at the same time.
I enjoyed playing Ember, it's not groundbreaking but well put together package of all the things we love in an RPG. Hope you'll enjoy it too.

Pros: Overall, the gameplay is smooth and feels very polished even for an early access game.  Graphics remind me a bit of the past (Good thing! If you ever wanted proof that Ubisoft does not know what it's doing, For Honor would be it.
What it's supposed to be: A fast-paced, visceral combat game where players beat each other with a class that appeals to them, with loads of customisation and different game modes that hopefully have something for everybody.
What it actually is: A corpse, rotting in the corner after poor balancing choices, implementing said modes in the worst possible ways, all the while commiting slow, painful suicide trough micro-transactions, bad performance and bad decisions in general.
But let's start from the top. The game uses peer-to-peer. So get ready for frequent desyncs if not outright disconnects. And yes this can happen right at the end of a 20 minute dominion-match, robbing you of all progress and EXP you would've gotten at the end. It doesnt make the game unplayable, it's just frequent enough to be annoying. Particularly if you're playing with friends, because they can not rejoin.
Then the game modes:
Dominion: A 4vs4 Zergfest of the highest order, it's about capturing control points. made infinitely worse by the fact that many of your Orders (Daylie Quests) will require you to enter the mode and often get Executions and/or a high point value. Both of which can be nigh impossible due to the fact that everyone just gangs up on each other constantly. What Ubi should've done is make the Map's big enough to discourage zerging too hard, as your team wouldnt be able to hold all 3 points on the map. This would make it more viable to plit up at least a little. But the Maps are fairly small, particularly if your gear ups your Speed. So 9 out of 10 Dominion Matches will consist of 3-4 people forming a gank squadron and mercilessly zerging anyone to death that dares defend.
Elimination: Another 4vs4 Zergfest, but this time without points to capture and no NPC Soldiers to farm. The IDEA is that people fight 4 seperate duels on different parts of the Map, and then home in on each other as they finish their fights. In reality however, some will finish their duels fast, mostly due to the godawful matchmaking, and then run around on the Map collecting every buff they can see. Meanwhile you just finished up your fight, and are then faced by that one player that now has basically all his stats doubled. Or of course there's plenty of "runners" who wont fight at all until they either got all the buffs, or they just run off to 2vs1 one of the other fights going on.
Skirmish: 4vs4 Zergfest. Works as intended, as it's actually SUPPOSED to be a Zergfest.
Brawl and Duel: 2vs2 and 1vs1 respectively. These are fine, from my perspective. In Duels at least you're guaranteed to not be blindsided. And I had a mostly good experience with Brawls, where people will usually either go for the straight up 2vs2 right away, which is manageable in most cases, or actually wait until a fights' finished before they start attacking.
So you got 3 Modes where everyone zergs or at least tries to give themselves the most unfair advantage possible. And while I do think people that employ those tactics are scummy, you cant blame it all on them. It's the Designers fault for not giving any sort of motivation to actually fight "honorably" in the first place. Elimination could've been easily fixed by locking the seperate fights off, or at least remove the stupid Buffs from it. After the first 4 people die in their respective fights, put the surviving 4 into a new arena for a 2vs2. THAT would have been interesting at least. Dominion, again, would need bigger maps or a higher benefit for actually defending a point. Since none of that is in place, a lot of players will gravitate towards the easiest method of victory. And that simply is playing like an absolute scumbag.
Then we have Ledging and Hazards, such as spikes. Getting thrown into one of these is an instant kill. That WOULD be fine, if the game didnt insist on putting them EVERYWHERE and also promote their use with mechanics. A successful parry GUARANTEES a throw, meaning instant death. Some classes also heavily rely on displacement and using a lot of Guard Breaks (Throws). So if you actually dont wanna get cheap shots, both players have to be careful about positioning and often not use half their kit. And again, while I think it's cheap, I cant blame players too much for taking advantage. It's the game that makes it so attractive in the first place.
This also leads into a major bugbear when we look at the Meta. Playing on the Offense is barely if at all worth it. Again, parries will guarantee a throw, or a load of other mean things depending on what youre fighting. Missed Guard Breaks also guarantee a counter-gb. And even your fast, light attacks can very easily be parried, once you got the timing down. This leads to most players playing a very reactionary game. Watch some high-level play on Youtube. It consists mostly of people staring at each other until one of them gets tired, attacks, and then gets countered.
Beyond that, appearantly Ubi knew that ganging up would be a problem. So theres "Revenge Mode". It's a bar that fills up, quickly if you are being attacked by multiple people. Activating it will supply a temporary health, damage and defense boost, also knocking anyone back that tried to hit you as you activated it. It CAN be enough for someone to even the odds. But it has a whole set of issues on its own. On the "Unfair for the attackers" side, blocking people you are not focusing on is laughably easy, since you only have to raise your guard in the direction their attacking from. You can also parry all side attacks. And since Revenge makes you unstopabble for a brief amount of time, parries like that can be fatal. The Meter also rises very fast if even 2 people are attacking the same target. So there is a high chance of them getting Revenge right away once more, after the first one runs out.
On the other hand, the addition of the Centurion and the Shinobi as classes rendered the mode basically moot. Both of them have kicks, punches and other displacements, that will stagger you for half a century. Plenty of time for all attackers to get one heavy attack in to kill you instantly. And even if they're not around, there are plenty of attacks that floor or stagger you, while 4 people are happily beating the crap out of you.
In short, again Ubi didnt give this any thought at all.
So with all of this terribleness in place, are there redeeming factors? Well, the Single Players is... Serviceable. It's a row of missions where you play different characters (But not all of them), while a story plays out. It's okay. The Characters in the game look cool and the customization is nice. Altough this is a Ubisoft game, so ofc they try to cram micro transactions down your throat and it takes ages to unlock everything, even for one class.
The Classes are varied and you would have plenty to try out. If the game itself wasnt 90% annoyance with 10% enjoyment.
The game is also basically dead at this point, at least on PC. The two modes you can still decently find a game in are Dominion and Duel. And even those are declining.
So finally: Give this one a great big skip, until they massively reduce the price. And even then I'd prolly advice against it. The game is basically dead on PC at this point. I payed 60 bucks for this thing. i'd say its maybe worth 20 or 30.

I had this game in closed beta, open beta, and the full game. I have to say, closed beta was the most fun I had with it, and I'll tell you why:
In closed beta, I went in expecting nothing, the only thing I saw about this game was the cinematic trailer, a friend sent me the key, so I went in not even knowing what kind of game it was going to be. It was fun as ♥♥♥♥. The gameplay was steller, the graphics were outstanding, and everyone was on the same level of skill, you had the occasional guy who would muck everyone else in the game, but it wasn't a huge deal, we grew and developed skill together. Sure, there was connectivity issues and sure it was pretty unbalanced, but I expected this, after all it was a closed beta. I thought it would be fixed.
In comes open beta, which generally seemed pretty much the same as the closed beta, but with more people. With that, in come the die hards. People who seemed to play the game non stop, stats were reset after the closed beta, these people were already at level 20, when most of the people I saw again in closed beta were only level 10 or 15 on their highest character.
The worst was when the game was released, the issues still not being solved. Still peer to peer, still unbalanced, still crappy matchmaking, the only difference being the addition of three characters and a campaign. I didn't play until a week after release, because I didn't have my computer. I was grouped with people who were an extremely higher level than me. I get smashed every single game and can't find anyone my skill level to fight. Not only that, I also get disconnected 60% of my games because of connection issues.
I know I haven't played this game in a while, but I haven't heard of anything about this game that would perhaps change my mind. I wish I could refund it, 80$ for a peer to peer connection game with a lackluster story and no skill matchmaking? Come on.
Don't buy this game.
