It plays a bit like Diablo 3, has bits and pieces of numerous games in it, and yet Ember seems to be just original enough to be an interesting game thus far. I'm hoping for more story and lore than has been presented as of yet, but I'd recommend this to those looking for something to play until the next AAA game comes along.

Ember is an old school RPG which looks to pay homage to games like Baldur’s gate. Does it light up the genre or leaves a permanent darkness in the gamers’ minds, let’s find out:
Ember tells the story which is ruled by darkness and you are a lightbringer who is resurrected by a traveller who happened to get stuck in the crossfire of a bandits and giant spiders battle. After being resurrected, it is your job to ensure that the light returns to this world. Honestly, the story seemed throwaway to me. There are some particular exciting missions but the overarching concept seemed to fall flat at times. But as they say, it is the journey that matters, not the destination. Ember presents a world that is beautiful to look at and has plenty of stuff to do. It is not particularly open ended but still does a good job of diversifying its environments. Initially, you have forgotten all your powers so you have to gain the memories, the powers of being a lightbringer back. Just as you step out of the first dungeon in which you were trapped in, you will see that the whole world has gone to hell. There is not one place left in your journey that has not been devastated by swarm of goblins, spiders and various other creatures. Speaking of which, Ember has its fair share of variety of enemies which challenge you enough that you should never let down your guard. You are able to control one party member at a time and the others will follow him. Signal to attack one enemy and they will auto attack another after the first one is dead. The tutorial levels do just enough that you learn most of the basics of the game to survive the journey of becoming a lightbringer. What disappointed me was the lack of loot found in many of the levels. Picture this, you take down a tough group of enemies and there is a shiny looking chest just behind their dead bodies, you would normally like to find some serious loot but that is not present here. This makes the sense of achievement slightly less. The story also is around 30 hours in length and there are minor side quests which pop up while you are completing the main quest. None of the side missions feel important or like they have any weight in them. There is very little character development throughout the story which might disappoint some RPG fans. The combat is fairly simple with you being able to pause in the middle of the fight so you can queue up various attacks of the party members and organize everything. The UI itself though is really clunky and clutters up the screen way too much. Another minor annoyance is the difficulty of the game. The game is pretty difficult on the normal difficulty, but at times the difficulty levels seemed to spike up randomly. Try playing it on hard and it will be like a miniature version of Dark souls, with you dying every two battles you fight. Overall, Ember has  a solid gameplay mixture which lacks some minor things but can be looked over in favour of the things that are done better.
Ember looks beautiful for a 10$ game. It has a very diversified world and it shows in each of the locations. From the heat struck deserts to the cold snowlands, everything looks wonderful. It does help that nearly each place you visit has been destroyed, so ashes fly in the air and creates a wonderful environment. It creates a sense of suspense every time you are visiting a new area. The characters models look good from far and the enemy designs are fairly generic. When someone uses magic attacks and it all starts popping up on the screen, it takes away some of the dreariness I mentioned earlier. Overall, Ember packs a very solid Visual punch.
Ember features a solid soundtrack which helps in establishing the environments. The main soundtrack itself is pretty solid and the random tunes that pop up in between remain pretty well balanced throughout. The Voice Acting is limited but done well for the most part. There is a solid crunch every time you walk on the grass and the enemy sounds are also done pretty well. Overall, the sound design for Ember is very solid.
Ember is a solid RPG which has a surprising amount of content and quality for a price as low as 10$. Add a surprising amount of polish applied to the game and that makes it a superb game. The story is clichéd but done well enough to keep you invested and there is a lot of diversity available in the world to keep you hooked in exploring. If you’re looking for a fun RPG with a solid combat system and a shockingly cheap price, you can’t go wrong with Ember.

Game structure:
This game has similar graphics style as the "King's Bounty" series, but in an open action rpg setting. The whole game follows a relatively easy pattern in terms of equipment with some unique gear. You will most likely not go above level 30 here -most of your power and all skills are dependent on your gear, which is limited by your current level and oftentimes a specific stat (up to level 20). Enemy levels depend on which area you are exploring, and many can be circumvented. There are many satiric references to known movies and games, and some dialogues are made with the intention of being funny. I found many of them to be more awkward than anything else, but that is a matter of taste.
My game:
I only played it through once on Normal setting. Up until I ran out of things to buy and build the game was rather enjoyable. The story is very linear with quests you have to do and a number of side quests, although you may choose to solve them in different ways. In my opinion the character variability was rather limited. I liked the extensive foraging and looting possibilities. I feel like there is not much replayability; You can explore all equipment and skills with your other companions. But for $7 it was still quite okay.
Do I recommend it? Not if you have high demands on rpg games. But if you just want to play something with old-fashioned rpg vibes it is quite adequate.

'Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising' is a schmup/shooter that is still in Early Access, however while it is a complete game with 25 levels and 5 end bosses the developer is busy working on alot more levels and more end bosses. The game will be on sell until Dec. 1, 2015 for $1.99.
GAMEPLAY: Your typical schmup with gameplay that is already tight. You can play as a Single Player or Co-Op. While optimised for a control pad (I'm using my Logitech Xbox 360 controller in X Mode) it also works with a keyboard. There are power-ups, and you can link two ships, but you only get one life. You die. You dead. Each enemy target is worth 1 point, but enemy hits to your ship will deduct 10 points from your score. So shoot well. Dodge well. Live long (and prosper).
GRAPHICS: They are quite stunning, with several settings and resolutions to choose from. After I took several screenshots the developer contacted me to try a different setting and resolution. I have captured several screens at various settings and resolutions.
SOUND: Not as stunning as the graphics, but acceptable. As for the songs they are a matter of personal taste.
ACHIEVEMENTS & TRADING CARDS: 34 Achievements just went live, of which I have earned 2*. I only downloaded this game today so give me a break that I haven't earned more. The developer told me that more Achievements and some Trading Cards will be added as more levels and bosses are added. But so far I've only heard of 1 person beating the 25 levels and 5 bosses (one boss after each group of 5 levels) in 'Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising' as it stands.
EXTRAS:  There is a DLC game called 'Galagan's Island: Metagalactic Monstrosities' which requires the first game to be purchased and installed. In this DLC game you play as the 5 bosses. This DLC is FREE with the purchase of 'Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising OST,' which replaced some of the song tracks of the original version. However the songs swapped out are included as bonus tracks. Currently you must own the original version to buy this version. The OST version is currently on sell for $1.49 until Dec. 1. 2015. So that's two versions of the same game, plus the bonus game 'Galagan's Island: Metagalactic Monstrosities' for a total of less than $3.50. A bargin.
RECENT UPDATES INCLUDE (Developer):
*In response to player feedback, we've turned down the "floatiness" of the player ship movement to tighten up the player's controls and emphasize the bullet-dodging slow motion mechanics of the game.
*Updated controls screen to reflect the hold-to-fire change and added a message to the screen that the game was designed with gamepad in mind and that it is recommended input method.
*Adjusted UI responsiveness.
*Adjusted position of the "Back" option on the Volume Control Slider.
*Added solid black backgrounds behind the Pause and Options UI menus.
*New soundtrack. The songs switched out will stay on the OST as Bonus Tracks.
I bought everything. So $3.50 for two great games and two music options.

25 Levels of chaotic shooting and trying not to die. And it's fun!
You have powerups like shield and triple fire that make it easier to blast aliens.
Everything is very fluid and well-optimised which makes the game very enjoyable.
Game features a local co-op so you can play with a friend, or a cat, or you can be two players at once if you don't have any friends
Cool retro style with modern effects. Lots of explosions and other similiar effects commonly seen in today's games. Enemies are pretty generic for a bullet-hell game, various blobs and space octopuses, but that's okay.
Most sound effects don't stand out that much so there's not much to say about them. But the music is awesome! An interesting blend of many genres like electronica, jazz and even hip-hop. If you're planning on buying the game,I encourage you to also buy a soundtrack, If you enjoy at least 2 of these genres.
Kinda weird. You must hold hover if you don't want to be at the very bottom of the screen.
When you hold hover your ship also steers slower, so it's really hard to dodge a barrage of projectiles when you're in the middle of the screen. The flip ship works only when you have the double ship powerup. If you don't have it on levels when enemies spawn behind your back, then you must wait till they break the formation and follow you, which can take a while.
Overall, nothing ground-breaking, but simply an enjoyable indie game that features an awesome soundtrack and doesn't cost a fortune. Give it a try, it can surprise you.

The game is fun at times, once you get everything working. However, it's very difficult to set up the interface correctly so that the guitar works relyably. For example, you need to set a specific bit rate for recording, which the game never tells you to do. Also, I own 4 guitars, but the game will only recognize all 6 strings on only 1 of those (and it's not my Epiphone either). You will have to move your pickups around so that the low E string will work more than it does not, and gimp your guitar so that it souds poorly outside of the game, and then there will still be circumstances that it will drop notes on the low E string.
These issues are not my biggest complaint. Once you get these things working reasonably well, the game is very fun to play. However, the biggest issue I have with the game is how many tunings the game has. There are at least 5 different tunings in the game, which means that if you want to play more than 4 songs, you will need to change your guitar tuning (unless you miraculously own 5 guitars that all work with the game) nearly every other song you play. It's not just a matter of inconvenience; of slowing down gameplay, if you own a decent guitar, you are going to wear the tuning pegs down so fast that you will have to replace them after done playing this game, if not, you're guitar will slide out of tune very easily. So, your choice will be to either "try" to play the game with a junk guitar (for which the game is far more likely to not recognize notes played) or trash a decent guitar playing a game.
I would have recommended the game if they stuck to 2, or maybe 3 tunings, but 5+ tunings is rediculous and harmful to any guitar used to play this, and I appreciate my guitars far more than any trend game experience.

Ember is in a few words ..... A very simple old school rpg. Nothing flashy with Above average graphix. Gear determines the style - class you play. Stats and charactor level deside what type of gear you can equip and amp damage for the gear. Exploration and crafting will net you rewards on the better - best armor and weapons. Each level of gear has 2 or three variants in quality from ragged to fine with a few named variations pieces from time to time. Like most rpg's in this day and time the few boss fights don't always drop the prize gear. Side quest  and the finding of said quest are very important to finding some of the prize gear in this game. My chosen way to play the Bringer was caster and I enjoyed the play : But the games chosen Named weapon for a bringer is a tanking 1 handed sword if you find the quest. I just gave the sword to my follower. Your group consists of 2 at first, you and a follower. Then later adding in 1 more follower. Later on you have to choose which 2 of 3 you want in the group. You get a melee follower first , then a casting mage next and then a archer thief next. All classes have (direct, area and target area) healing, hard hitting damage, aoe's, dots and stuns on gear. Neet thing is if you have a great piece of gear and hate the rune on it, for a few bucks just change the rune to whatever suits your play style. If you find the guy to buy them from. Combat is pause setup simular to Dragon Age. Crafting is very simple consisting of formulas to learn or discover if you just happen to combine the correct mats by trial and error. Hope this helps in discribing the game well enough for those interested in buying Ember. It is a very nice game to relax and play. Well worth the $10 price tag and even better $8 till Nov. 18th. Enjoy!!!!

This is more of a first-impression review of the early access of the game, so the review won't go very into depth on the game, and it is more than likely that various things will change over the course of development.
Galagan's Island would probably be best described as a psychedelic arcade-style SHMUP. Though it may not strictly adhere to pixel art (at least, outside of the sprites), the influence of old arcade shooters like Galaga is evident in both its gameplay and its art style. It brings to the table its own unique blend of art & music, and deviates slightly from the typical elements that you see in many SHMUPs.
Whether or not it plays as well the old classics is not the question here. Though it is as SHMUP as it can get, instant death is not a thing here, though the raining bullets is usually more than enough to cover for it. The controls are simple and quick to learn, and though the movement speed might not be as rapid as I'd like, I feel that it helps compliment the lack of one-shot kills (a.k.a the use of a health system) for you. There are also a few additional elements, such as your ship gravitating towards the bottom, an overheat system for your weapon and so on. If you want a hellish or traditional SHMUP/bullet hell, I'd advise going back to Galaga, Raiden or even Touhou. However, I advise giving this a chance, rather than judge before you've tried it out (and it's $4.99 USD, which is close to the price of takeaway).
The art direction in this is interesting. Personally, I feel that the overall quality could do with some more work, especially with the GUI. I also feel that there are some stylistic inconsistencies with the sprites, background and effects, without bringing the UI into it.
, I am willing to forgive much (at least everything except the UI, that needs more work guys) for the psychedelic experience that's brought out from the art. From the particles to the sprites and down to the enemy patterns, it's best described as
and something I recommend more than taking LSD (additionally because it's probably cheaper to be hooked on this than on LSD). The theme that's brought out is certainly unique, and an experience that's also bolstered by...
I highly praise the music in this game in particular. Though it varies quite a bit (from a chiptune menu theme to a funky, funky tune), it brings out life to the gameplay, to say the least. This, along with the artwork, pushes the experience that the designer of the game wants to bring out (which is to give you the joy of smoking pot without having to find a dealer, it seems). The OST is wonderfully composed (at least, imo), and would be nice to be released as a pack on its own as well.
I don't like giving a rating system (since my track record indicates I rarely give below 7/10 anyways), so I'll just say this: Buy this game, and try it out. It's an experience worth having (and you have steam refund if you think I'm a dirty liar, so just buy it already).

Not a bad game! This game is a great and free way to waste a few minutes playing rounds of a pretty fun shooter. The game runs into trouble for a few reasons however.
1. I guarantee it will almost certainly never, ever, have the open world survival aspect everyone wanted and was told they would get early on.
2. The game tries to appeal to S.T.A.L.K.E.R players, but its not hardcore in the slightest and the only homages to stalker are in the maps and anomolies and the russian theme. It doesnt play like stalker at all.
These two combined mean a free game that Is not bad gets terrible reviews because it was sold as the open world stalker game we always dreamed of and instead, its more of a Call of duty game set to a stalker theme. While i do sympathize with the players who are still waiting for a big beautiful open world stalker game, I do not see this game as a failure. Its damn good fun when you can get into a match, has tons of firearms (and ive never felt that the pay to get weapons were severely unfair, i played just fine against them with free toys) and the armor system means you can really customize up your character. Be a juggernaut, using heavy armor to tank damage, or a ninja, speeding all around and nabbing objectives while the enemy are still hoofing it to the zone, or a jedi,  using the anomolies around the map to whip enemy players with your magical powers. You can really get creative with playstyles in this game. It only took me a couple of days to rank up one of the 4 factions to level 3 (you rank them via ingame missions similar to assignments in other games, and each group is levelled on its own, unlocking higher tiered toys each time). And to make sure all is fair, your equipment at each tier determines who you face. as soon as you equip tier 4 guns, you play against tier 4 players even if all your other gear is tier 1 or 2 or 3.
with all the customization and guns and toys for me to enjoy, i find it very, very hard to hate survarium. Its damn well free, for one, and for two while i despise CoD games, i have no qualms about enjoying a game with similar game modes set to the theme of the great STALKER games. (And while i compare it to CoD in terms of game modes and play, it is not nearly as watered down or repetetive or ridiculous as call of duty).
Is this the multiplayer open world stalker game we all wanted? no. Will it ever be? probably not. Is it a fun tactical first person shooter with tons of guns and armor choices that can be fun as hell still? yes it is.
Oh, and its free.

PROS:
-The best looking Slender game to date
-Written by the cast of Marble Hornets, the most popular and longest-running Slenderman ARG.
-Includes more characters and a large overarching story that is slowly told through the collectibles found in-game.
-Devs have a unique sense of humor.
-Fantastic atmosphere.
-Includes an HD remake of the original game and a secret level.
CONS:
-Glitches everywhere: The Chaser can grab you from five feet away (while stunned), and falling out of the level warrants an insta-death and Slendy breaking the fourth wall, removing the immersion of the game.
-The game's secret level includes "dialouge" between the player and Slenderman, but there is no voice acting. It's all words on the screen.
-The player switches between two or three different characters throughout the course of the entire game. You don't really know which one you're playing unless you've paid attention (especially in the secret level).
-The Chaser's identity is not revealed until the end of the game, and the identity of the monster that kidnaps you (Charlie Matheson Jr. from the posters) is not revealed ever.
-The Chaser is not a threatening enemy, if you know what you're doing. She's just tedious and annoying.
-The Hardcore Ending is a complete rip-off.
-The flashlight and key in the prologue are in different places in the beginning of the game every time. Sometimes, I couldn't find one or the other.
BOTTOM LINE:
The game has it's flaws, but is all around an acceptable horror game, and I would reccomend this to anyone who enjoys a good atmospheric horror. The game legitamately scared me at a few points and has a fantastic story written by Marble Hornets, it just underdelivers in the presentation.

I received this game for free because I worked on it, and played it all through development. Some would say that means I'm less objective. But there's no such thing as a subjective opinion; we all come in with our expectations and preferences, whether we helped create the game or not.
The project was exciting for me because it brings modern technological capabilities while hearkening back to the gameplay that made the older CRPGs great...such as the early Ultimas -- and many other (less famous) CRPG series and one-offs. They were much easier to get into and play than today's übercomplex RPGs, but that didn't make them any less engaging. By avoiding the spreadsheet-worthy elements, you get into the game quickly and stay there. (Nothing wrong with skill trees and the like, for those who want that degree of control.)
The resemblance to those older games is purposeful and carried off beautifully. The world and backstory (which was
my area of work on the game!) is so vast and thoroughly developed, and fits together so well, that it's a thrill to see how it all comes together at the end.  The graphics (again, I'm not praising my own work here) just sparkle and surprise constantly. The combat system took some getting used to for me, but then again, almost every new game makes that same demand.
As long as you understand, before you buy, where this game fits in the realm of CRPGs, you'll see that it
than does justice to its inspiration.

Ember is what I would call an RPG lite. This in no way makes it inferior to "deeper" RPGs - just different. And the main reason I call it "lite" is that the character development is far less involved than it is with other RPGs. There are no skills or skill trees for you to choose from but rather your skills are provided solely by the equipment you wear. This is a different approach and one I've not seen too many times before but it works passably. The problem is that whilst it gives you a fair bit of leaway in how you develop characters it also makes them all a bit generic as there are no specific differences to the character classes of your companions other than that some items requirements are tied to their BASE stats and, if you are developing sensibly, you will not see a warrior running around with a wand. You do, of course, level up and distribute attribute points at 2 per level and these go into the accepted core areas of vitality dexterity strength and..um...whatever they called the magic one. Unlike your companion characters you - or your main character - is/are completely generic leaving you free to push these stats in whichever direction you choose making you very flexible.
The production values in this game are nothing short of fantastic at its price point. Voice acting is good, music is atmospheric, and graphics do their job up to a pretty decent standard. Quests are (at least in the first few hours of play) deliberately quite sparse so that you will not level too quickly and run all over every enemy you run into. Do not be fooled by the start in the Barrows as later you will require some thought as to how and when you attack and careful management of restoratives and resting. This makes the difficulty setting just about right on all levels where easy means easy normal means normal and hard means hard. Quests are interesting rather than the "go here kill 5 spiders come back" variety and can be absorbing and contribute to the main storyline. Which brings us to that main storyline. It is perfectly paced and develops nicely as you go on. There are tomes scattered throughout giving background lore and sometimes just an entertaining read - all are competently written and worth your time.
Ember, on balance, lacks the character development depth that a few hardcore RPGers will expect. DESPITE this, very few will be put off by it and will enjoy diving into an absorbing game with a good story at a ridiculously low price. Furthermore, it fills a niche for those who are not experienced RPG players or may be put off by detailed stat management. I would go so far as to say that this is the best value starting price of a game I have seen in a very long time. Don't wait for the sales for this one because it is worth more than every penny/cent of its cost.
Definitely worth 10$.. and you can even get it on sale for less. Lots of skills, lots of quests, plenty of locations, party based combat system. Check it out, NOW!

- Scripts are repeated if your character dies (the level resets) [which can be annoying]

Though it's still Early Access, Poly Bridge offers a fun and unique enough experience to make up for the bugs. And yes, there are quite a few bugs. Here's a nice pros/cons list to look at:
The gameplay is very fun, and I love the fact that there is no single "correct" solution. This game not only
creativity, but it actually
creativity because there are no guidelines at all, just some materials that you can use and a budget you can't go over. Overall, I would say that Poly Bridge is definitely a game that's worth supporting, and it's one to look out for once it gets fully released. As an Early Access game, I recommend it with a warning that you will be dealing with some bugs and glitches, mostly in the sandbox mode (level creator). The gameplay is very fun and extremely addicting, and there are already quite a few player-made maps available on the Steam workshop that add to the fun. The level creator itself is fairly easy to use, but the bugs make it very difficult to actually make a complete level. To be honest, I've spent most of my time in-game fighting with the level creator because it's just so damn fun to use, but it frequently locks up and I have to restart the game, and sometimes it won't save the level I'm working on. So if you can deal with a few bugs and want to support a really fun game, go ahead and grab it, but if you want a fully polished game with no glitches, skip the Early Access and wait until it's fully released.
PS - the one thing that drew me to this game the most is the integrated .gif creator. After every level, you have the option of sharing a .gif replay, which is a ton of fun. The only problem with the .gif creator is that it has an undisclosed time limit on your replays, so it will frequently cut off the early section of the replay. To fix that, just hit "try again" and then finish the level on a higher speed.

Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising is an arcade shooter with the old-school feel of Galaga, and the new-school feel of a current-gen arcade title. While I usually avoid early access games, this one has broken that chain, as the updates that evolve it have consistently made it better and better. It is visually appealing, putting both retro and modern visual elements onto the same screen, with a color pallet that contrasts extremely well. The controls are simple to learn, and when combined with the fresh yet classic feel of the gameplay mechanics, allow for an experience that appeals to both a seasoned veteran and a beginning gamer. The soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal, with a track list that features constantly changing genres while maintaining a hint of retro throughout. Support for the game is excellent, and the developers are highly involved in the gaming community. In short, on my usual 5-point scale of rating games based on Concept, Appearance, Controls, Mechanics, and Sound I would have to give Galagan’s Island: Reprymian Rising a 5/5. This is an overall excellent game; it is well-constructed, appealing, and entertaining.

Resident Evil 6 is a tired franchise that attempts to please all, gain all, but achieves neither.  Sure it sold over 5 million, but it was 2 million short of its expected sales, and over half the players were far from pleased.  So what game is this?  Is this a survivor horror?  A third person shooter?  A Call of Duty or Gears of War (the irony!) wannabe?  It's clear that Capcom couldn't decide between wanting to please long time Resident Evil fans, such as myself, or if they wanted the big figures that all the other "AAA" titles have been shooting for, and failing for the most part.
As for how I feel, it's a conflicted relationship.  On one hand, I knew what I was getting myself into and I welcomed it, only out of interest that Capcom would try to stretch the boundaries of what Resident Evil was comfortable at, but then again, I found myself disappointed by the storyline and how they had basically shoe-horned some elements in, like the "family", Helena (though I really dig her suit~), and how Chris' campaign is more or less a generic military shooter for the first half (it DOES get better though, but it's easily the worse of the four).  Leon's campaign brings the zombies back, but you are so impowered, there is hardly any tension during gameplay.  Not bad though.  Jake's campaign was a lot of fun, and it's nice to see the siblings of two antagonists work together, to sort of fix the sins of their fathers, so to speak.  The best campaign is Ada's, because it's single player.  No co-op partner.  Just breath in the atmosphere, actually do some puzzles (brain dead simple, but hey, there are puzzles), and not have to have someone talking all the time with you.  Sure, her campaign does have a co-op option, but thankfully it is completely optional.  I wouldn't mind if the whole game just focused on Ada where it's single player, with co-op strictly as an option, not a full integration of the main game.
Anyway, game play wise, it is definitely the most controllable and technical Resident Evil to date, but it seems to be meant for a third person shooter, and NOT a survivor horror game.  Graphics looks great, music's fine, yadayada, oh and the PC version is the best version, bar none.  While Resident Evil 4 and 5's PC ports weren't very good, 6 is that definitive PC Resident Evil experience... just minus the Resident Evil we grew up with.  Times had changed, but not for the better... Oh well, at least we got a badass PC version that controls amazingly well.
I can only recommend this for hardcore Resident Evil fans.  New comers may want to trend onto Resident Evil Revelations or 4 or any of the earlier games instead, but then again, that is if you can adapt to the tank controls.  So old-school tank controls with awkward camera angles, or great controls at the expense of the Resident Evil name and experience.  Pick your poison.  :P  Either way, if you must play Resident Evil 6, the PC version is the way to go, so THAT I recommend.

It's a very pretty game, no arguments there, but there are a lot of issues that unfortunately bog it down, and nice art is not enough to save it.
Firstly, the technical bugs.  After a while of playing the game starts to hang. Either it flat out doesn't react to you clicking on things, or it does the action but the cursor then remains in the "wait" stage so you're unable to click on anything else.  While both of these can be resolved by exiting the game completely and reloading, I shouldn't have to do this just to play a game. This has been going on for a while, checking the discussions, but it seems that it's not going to be fixed, and for that, it gets a mark down.
The next thing is the fact that the devs are well aware that there is a bug involving one of the orbs and rather than fixing the bug they just changed the achievement so you don't need that orb. Again, lazy developer not fixing bugs.
And finally, the puzzles.  I love point and click games, I have plenty in my library that I enjoy playing, but this is not one of them. Some of the puzzles are nigh impossible unless you know what you're doing, which means that on your first playthrough you're going to struggle like hell.  This is made worse by the game not even explaining anything, expecting you to infer it from the cartoon bubbles "talking" to some characters produces.  While I think that not having dialogue in the game is an interesting design choice and it could work, here it just adds to the frustration.
Lastly; not all the interactable icons change your cursor, so good luck clicking on EVERYTHING to see if you can interact with it. Pixel hunts are the bane of any point and click player and here it's especially bad.

This game is a real mixed bag. I love it most of the time but often despise it, fortunately for this review I'm currently loving the state of the game! The devs have really stepped up things, we've had two updates this month adding a new jason and map as well as a small halloween update with fun costumes and kills along with balancing fixes, and over all the game is just a lot better for it. Another note worthy thing is that ever since the dev released their 'dlc roadmap' almost every promise on it has been fulfilled and I'm feeling treally optimistic about the future of this game. You see the reason this game was such a mess originally was because Gun and Ilfonic weren't thinking with their heads but rather their raging money boners when they saw the opportunity to release the game on ps4 and xbox and the console and pc launch was in no surprise a complete disaster and buggy mess with server issues as well as game breaking glitches making the game almost completely unplayable. Many months later and it seems the devs are finally on their feet again and I can confirm this game for $20 on sale, is definitely worth it (not at full price with its current lack of content but maybe when singleplayer releases). Overall am very satisifed with my purchase and the direction of the game.
Now onto the actual game and I won't ramble on too much but some great things about it are:
- Kane Hodder (Jason in part 7-10, my favourite Jason!) does the mocap for Jason in this game and its bloody fantastic and beautiful.
- The counsellors in this game all have their own unique playstyles and personalities such as LaChappa (the nerd sterotype who is good at repairing things quickly however is a huge wuss and can't run fast) or Chad (the private school pretty boy, complete wuss but boy can he run and get some good hits on Jason!).
- The screen accuracy of Jason and the environments are a ode to the old movies and if you're a Jason fan you'll really appreciate the attention to detail here, I aboslute love what they've done with the maps and Jason.
- The game while somewhat lucked based (if you're looking for a more competitive game like this I recommend Dead by daylight) is really fun and great with friends, with multiple objectives such as calling the police, repairing the 2 or4 seater cars or escaping by boat, it'll always feel rewarding when you escape.
- Its really fun to play as Jason and killing counsellors in cinematic and brutal ways always feels rewarding.
- The music is very reminiscent of the films and is done by Harry Manfredini the original composer, its great!
- I love the feeling of team work when I come together with randoms or friends to complete objectives, it feels very rewarding.
-  All the dlc is free and the only paid dlc is completely comestic and doesn't affect gameplay, this is the way it should always be done IMO, props to Gun for that.
- talking about comsetic DLC, the already released ones are fantasic and very entertaining as well as being reasonably priced at $2-3 USD,  I love fooling around with the dance animations, the swim suits were a nice addition and the halloween costumes are straight up hilarious (I love sexy cop Kenny!!) I will admit however the kill animation dlc is a bit over priced for only 3 part 4 kills but they are some of the best kills in the game.
- The game visually looks fantasic and has a great atmosphere
A quick few griples and suggestion for updates, some just my opinion and some are serious problems:
- All counsellor have practically the same voice lines except Tommy Jarvis (the hero character who gets randomly picked when a player dies in the game) and it gets repetitive (OH MY GOD IS THAT A DED BODY I CAN'T LOOK) and also this to me is a giant missed opportunity for the devs because honestly the counsellors are more interesting than most of the characters in the movies and I think if they give the counsellors unique voice lines it  would give them more depth. For example 'My Father will be hearing about this!' for Chad or even LaChappa saying 'Oh I think I wet myself' or 'Be gone demon! I am a level 100 mage!!!' for when he hits Jason or something like that, I know a bit ridiculous but you get the point.
- Another thing is I want bios for the counsellors!! I wanna know about their back stories and relationships with each other, I hope that isn't too much to ask for here but Dbd does it and it just adds way more to the characters.

Great game that has lessons and games to teach you about the guitar and techniques, plus the ability to play along with music. The best part is that when you play along with the songs it helps guide you by starting off simple and increasing the difficulty by adding notes as you get better. Even if you start to really struggle it will go back a notch so you aren't left frustrated and left feeling like you never will learn. You can also repeat a riff, adjusting the speed and difficulty so you can learn sections of the music.
I've been wanting to learn to play the guitar for years now, and it was difficult trying to learn from books and music I'd find on the internet by myself. The interactive nature of this makes it so much more fun to play along with your favorite songs and see your progress as you improve, as well as have goals you can strive for.
Adding additional songs costs money, but they are constantly adding new music and this allows you to pick and choose which songs you want to learn instead of being force-fed certain songs.
This is great for beginners just looking to learn to play the guitar and have fun doing it.

You will have trouble with this game, almost everyone has trouble setting up this game. My personal problem was in calibrating my guitar; the game always thought it was too quiet and, to compensate, it always increased the gain/volume which introduced static/noise which prevented me from advancing past the calibration screen (tldr: feedback loop prevented set up).
Uplay forums are filled with people who've had issues with everything from sound-card, to tuning, to buzzing, to my above gain/volume problems. It's also necessary that you own the "real tone cable," which costs about $30CAD. Buying a lot of DLC isn't completely necessary as (with a little online research) you can acquire some custom dlc. This will be beneficial for anyone who isn't too interested in the mainly rock/metal dlc that is currently offered through official channels.
Outside of all the above problems I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants to learn guitar. This is a great educational game. Well worth all my troubles/headaches (configuration, tuning, calibration), and hidden costs (cables, dlc, etc). It is far cheaper then hiring a tutor to conduct private lessons. It is designed well: always encouraging the student, offering help, scaling difficulty on performance, etc. Well worth your time, money, and efforts.

At first glance, this game may not appear to be worth it.  "A game about squares and rectangles, how good could that be," you might think.  Let me tell you, it is definitely worth it.  You get connected to the characters, even though they are rectangles and squares.  It has a nice story and interesting ending that leaves you pondering on what's next.  Thomas Was Alone is definitely worth a buy and you will enjoy/love the journey of Thomas and the "gang".

Absoluely wonderful narration, but unfortunately, that's all this game has going for it.
Collision detection is finicky: moving platforms are very difficult to deal with, depending on their direction of movement. You cannot consistently jump off of a platform moving vertically, and will get stuck, in a jittery manner, if pressed against the side of a platform moving horizontally. Characters tend to slide off of one another when you attempt to stack them, and that stacking is a core mechanic of the game. This is a damning problem.
I found it slightly nauseating in later, larger levels, when the camera had to sweep across large distances whenever I cycled characters, but this I cannot promise that others will experience this difficulty.
More on the level of inconvenience, the levels sometimes provide no means to backtrack individual characters. That leads to a great deal of frustration if some portion of your team completes the level before another character becomes intractably stuck, forcing you to restart the level in its entirety. A separate, very small complaint is that navigating the game's menu is tied to slow animations. This would be a lesser sin, except that you only need interface with that menu when forced to restart the level, so that your frustrations pile on top of one another.
Thomas Was Alone has good ideas! The properties of the characters are interesting, and the final levels that utilize them differently are worthy of further developement. As said at the start, the narration is beautiful. The gameplay, unfortunately, does not match.
VERDICT: Watch a Let's Play or find the audio somewhere.

Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising is a fun and unique indie game. It's a more modern take on Galaga and other arcade space shooters of the 70s and 80s.
And it's the most fun shoot 'em up of its kind, and a must-buy on Steam! Why?
1. Visuals
The game's graphics are pretty awesome. The backgrounds are well-done and look quite realistic for the game's theme. It also scrolls as you move across the screen, which is a nice touch. The player and enemy graphics are represented by pixel art, which makes them easy to recognize from the background. Visual effects, such as the shield the player can acquire and the destructive bomb attack are great to look at. Each enemy also has a unique explosion(s) when destroyed, most of which are eye-catching and colorful displays of enemy destruction. The game manages to make destroying enemies visually satisfying.
2. Gameplay
What's a game without gameplay? Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising also has great gameplay that's very easy to pick up, but certainly difficult to master. You can move left or right, toggle auto-fire and fly vertically into the air. You have a couple powerups to help you destroy those pesky aliens like the shield, triple shot, super beam and the destructive bomb.
There are many other things about the game you have to learn, like the HUD. The red meter on the right of the screen is your overheat meter. The overheat meter fills up the more you fire, and if you fill it up all the way you'll be unable to shoot until it's depleted back to 0. Luckily the game will make a sound when you approach the danger zone, so it's not too difficult to keep from overheating.
The meter on the left side of the screen is your triple shot meter. Once you get the triple shot powerup this meter will be full and as you fire it'll deplete. Pretty self-explanatory. There's one more behind the score display, which I believe is the powerup meter. It fills up as you destroy enemies, and portions of it are consumed when powerups appear from destroyed asteroids.
And then there's the enemies themselves! Every level has their own unique enemy formations. Namco's Galaga series can't even hold a candle to this game's enemy formations, as you have enemies forming different shapes like roses, fish, butterflies and treasure chests;they even make synchronized movements! The game has enemies and bullets coming from nearly every corner of the screen, forcing you to use the flying ability to avoid them or lose lives. And even though you have tons of them, every extra life is precious in this game as you won't get any more.
At first I hit the game over screen on level 10. With a little more practice I managed to get further. In order to survive in Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising, you have to pay attention and stay focused as there's many hints each level gives you to beat it without much taking too much damage. In this game, you'll be doing as much dodging and observing as you'll be shooting.
3. Music
I love the game's music. Every screen in the game has a unique music track. The type of music used within is unique to indie games, as I don't hear too many jazz tracks in other games. This game manages to be an aural experience on its own. While most triple A games have memorable soundtracks, few indie games have unforgettable music in them. The soundtrack to Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising joins the ranks of those that stay in your mind long after the game is over. The sounds of old video games, combined with jazzy harmonies and sophisticated urban grooves make each track oddly catchy and infectious.
4. Final Remarks
With 25 levels of hand-crafted and challenging gameplay, great music and visuals that are easy on the eyes, Galagan's Island: Reprymian Rising is well worth the purchase price even in Early Access. One should try the free demo, then buy this game immediately

This game is like the great movie
. Capcom despirately wanted to lose money on this game, so they can finally write off the franchise. So they got there top designers team ready, and man, they did succeed.
The whole game has that great lackluster-epic feeling, that is so hard to get exactly right: They really did some nice innovations: During most boss fights you can just go smash some random boxes and search for some extra 9-mm bullets. When you smashed all boxes in the area you can check if the boss fight is still going on. Sometimes you are lucky and a cutscene start where the boss fight is moved to a new area. Otherwise it is best to start to shoot some bullets.
The art design is also very special. Nobody else can make a grey house, an grey outdoor level in a grey American village, grey corridors, a grey catherdral, grey walls, a grey dungeon, grey rooms ,and a grey US city all look so much allike. It all has that same special RE6 feel. It is very consistant, and it is probably a shoutout to
.
From Star Trek they have borrowed the red-shirt principle. If in a cutscene a person wearing a helmet is talking to you you know he will die soon. So please never wear a helmet.
They also included many game mechanics that people really like to write about on the internets. So it got the briljant keymashing, instant-kill QTE. The game is very dark (illuminance not atmosphere) so you can save on your electric bill. It also has an erretic difficulty curve, so you are always on your toes.
And as a spoiler, here are my final 15 minutes I had with the game: ....In the end I got to the invisible wurm boss, had a really long, drawn-out and boring fight and then there was a chase sequence where you are attacked by a helicopter and you have to jump from boat to boat, sounds like fun but wasn't.  The controls are just as bad or even slightly worse than for RE5. So I just uninstalled the game instead. I think that is the only way to win at this game.
In conclusion, maybe if the women wore skimpier clothes I could have enjoyed the game a bit more.

You will have trouble with this game, almost everyone has trouble setting up this game. My personal problem was in calibrating my guitar; the game always thought it was too quiet and, to compensate, it always increased the gain/volume which introduced static/noise which prevented me from advancing past the calibration screen (tldr: feedback loop prevented set up).
Uplay forums are filled with people who've had issues with everything from sound-card, to tuning, to buzzing, to my above gain/volume problems. It's also necessary that you own the "real tone cable," which costs about $30CAD. Buying a lot of DLC isn't completely necessary as (with a little online research) you can acquire some custom dlc. This will be beneficial for anyone who isn't too interested in the mainly rock/metal dlc that is currently offered through official channels.
Outside of all the above problems I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants to learn guitar. This is a great educational game. Well worth all my troubles/headaches (configuration, tuning, calibration), and hidden costs (cables, dlc, etc). It is far cheaper then hiring a tutor to conduct private lessons. It is designed well: always encouraging the student, offering help, scaling difficulty on performance, etc. Well worth your time, money, and efforts.

Maybe once a day I might have a hold up but that would be caused by someone leaving/joining DURRING a match, which happens rarely. If you have NAT set to OPEN you most likely will not have connection issues based on my experiance and others ive seen that have good connection. . I didn't have any idea what to expect when I started it up, but I was instantly won over by its charming sense of humor. The game itself isn't bad either. It's designed very much in the spirit of old Spectrum computer games, but it has enough modern sensibilities to appeal to all kinds of gamers.
It'd be enough to simply have a game, where you blast away the pain troubling the inhabitants of Hurtland, but PRIAWOH goes the extra mile by having proper mechanics. Yep, the developer actually cared enough about their free game to have a proper hit-box for the heroine, so that she doesn't take a bunch of damage, just by kinda sorta brushing up against an enemy. A lot of games that cost money, and require way more of our limited time, don't even get this most important aspect right.
When the game is over, you get to decide who Princess Remedy marries. There are over 60 possible candidates, and they all have an amusing comment at the end. Sometimes it's the little touches that matter most, They remind me that buried deep under miles of ocean, rocks, and lava; I have something that could pass for a heart.
I guess the only replay-value is in trying to beat your best time, but it's no big deal. This is a game you play through once and retain nothing but pleasant memories about it. Maybe you'll tell your friends about it and share the love.

I want to write an honest reweiw of Nether, wich projects how I experienced the game.
I bought it a while back, don't remember when. I started it up and entered the world. I had only a knife. I fought long and hard for survival but I died several times. After a while I had gathered alot of guns. And I mean ALOT. My whole storage was full of different ones. Some I had crafted, some I had traded and some I had found. Now that is when the fun started. Knowing that I could take out a gun and, even if I died, i would have another one I started doing daring stuff. Teamed up with equally good players. Had alot of fun. I still remember this game as a fun, immersiveand beautiful. I had a great time.
Then came the dark times.
The games development was taken over by some other studio that I don't remember the name of. They implemented a system that allowed players to pay real money for in-game gold. Basicly you had to pay to have fun. I still played tho. With my armory of guns I continoued to have fun for a while. Heck I even paid a bit myself. But after a while everyone had better gear than me and I was killed over and over and over again. Me, not wanting to use alot of money on a game that I'd already bought, played less and less and less. Untill I played nothing at all. Started playing other similar games. (out of which Miscreated is the best one, which I recommend). The game is uninstalled to clear space and about a year later I think back to the good old days playing Nether. I think "Maybe I should check it out again. Maybe it's changed". So I research and it turns out. Phosphor (the original developers) are back working on Nether. They remove the in-game purchases, and everything was looking brighter. I download and launch. The game runs♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can't even tell you how bad it runs. At the lowest settings it was unplayable. I was trying with the same computer that could run medium to high without problems a year and a half ago. I don't know what happened but I'll say this: If you don't have a good PC you should not buy this game. Not in the state that it's in. My PC specs are Ok. I have a ASUS GeForce GTX 660 ti which, as I mentioned: Ran the game at medium to high before.
To sum it up: I'll give the game a 7/10... one and a half year ago.

I’ve already completed Crysis 2 on PS3, both online and offline. But now that I have it on Steam, I can get the “full” experience.
The Cry Engine 3 delivers a very high standard in terms of visual quality. Even the gameplay is varied and has options regarding how you want to play. The real let down in Crysis 2 is the lack of enemy types. You’re either fighting C.E.L.L. grunts or Alien Seph grunts and there’s not much difference between them. I was really hoping for some seriously diverse enemy types.
I also found the game too easy. There are only a few points that you’re forced into fighting enemies. The rest of the time you can just cloak through the game with no sweat on “Post Human Warrior” difficulty lol. There are elements of greatness throughout Crysis 2, but when I was expecting the best of the best, this was a bittersweet experience.
An interesting game, but a let down if you’re expecting a bigger and better sequel to Crysis.

This game is beautiful.  The way 3d rendered and hand drawn mix together is something to be noted.  The plot is almost missing, and what is there I think is lost in translation to english.  There are many gems to this game.  The diary notes are really great, and the idea of adding hidden object finding to an "adventure" game should be done more.  The bad things about this game are there right from the beginning.  There isn't a tutorial, and by the time you figure out what you should be doing, you are halfway through the game.  The puzzles are comunicated through thought bubble drawings that can be terribly confusing.  I loved Dropsy for this feature, but this game does a horrible job of it.  You never know what you are really doing, and when you can't get somethign to work, you can't be sure its not a bug in the game, which there are many.  The music I really want to like, but somehow just adds to my annoyance of the game. There is NO fast travel.  Looking for missed things or figuring out a multi room puzzel is maddenly time consuming.  I managed to finish the game, but mostly just to be done with it. The game had little parts that I could appreciate, but I spent most of the time frustrated and/or annoyed.  I can't say I hate the game, and I really wanted to like it. Its just such a wierd situation.  In some ways its almost a great game, that just needs a few things ironed out.  In otherways its too far gone, and should have been scrapped and never released. Either way I can't recommend buying it.  If you already have the game or got it for close to free, then use a guide for the first few rooms, to serve as a tutorial, and try not to get too frustrated.
I would watch for future projects from this developer, their next project might be better.
One good thing that stands out is the gamepad support.  It is pretty neat that they added point and click as well as character movement control.  Sadly, it doesn't work very well and its hard enough to solve the terrible puzzles, without second guessing if the gamepad button does what I think It does.  There is a situation where the click button no longer is the "use" button is some cases and it gets really confusing.  I do want to give them credit though for being innovative. the gamepad support is almost good.
*edit* I forgot to mention one of the most frustrating parts, you have to turn off the hints HUD element to actually find and click things you need to in game. How bad is that? Cute little fairy-tale point-and-click with lots of character and atmosphere, plagued by lackluster design, time-wasting mechanics, and a few bugs. Definitely worth a playthrough for its charm and worth the 10 bucks for the soundtrack alone.
[Story]
In this game you play a disenfranchised teenage girl who gets shrunk down to bug size and teleported into a magical world ruled by an evil spider (although we only really have the game's word for it).
[Puzzles/game design]
The puzzles are pretty much self-contained in each room and most of them can be figured out with some logic. The ones that can't be figured out by logic can be either figured out with some patient trial-and-error, or by using the pretty well designed hint system. The puzzles are pretty straightforward and fairly simple, but they are more logical and less dumb than those of, for instance, Deponia, or Broken Age. There are some unnecessarily long animations and walking sequences that cannot be skipped and sometimes have to be repeated as part of a puzzle. This felt very much like padding and is the game's worst sin.
[Bugs]
The game is plagued by the occasional bug, for instance Violett sometimes simply won't enter a door you click on or interact with an object. This can be solved by a simple save and quit. I was able to play the game from beginning to end without much of a hitch, load-times are fast. I didn't mind it and since the game is clearly on an indy budget it can be forgiven.
[Art design and atmosphere]
The main appeal of this game is its charm. It feels like a somewhat dark fairy-tale with a good dose of humor. The art-pieces are very compelling, varied, and invoke a sense of wonder. It is well drawn and animated. The world is densely populated with a variety of cute and amusing creatures. For instance, there are a hookah smoking caterpillar and a tuxedo wearing cockroach. Throughout the world are strewn pages of "uncle's bestiary" which make for a compelling read and I found myself going out of my way to find and read them all, even though I usually don't have the patience to read anything, especially not when playing a game. Some puzzles feel a little like a Rube-Goldberg machine, adding to the charm.
[Sound]
The star of the show is the soundtrack, which is absolutely magical. The sound design (done by the composer of the music as well) is strong and really helps solidify the already charming atmosphere created by the visual art pieces and animations.
[Bottom line]
The game gets way more flack than it deserves. The puzzles are more logical and less mindless than those of the average point-and-click adventure. The bugs are obnoxious but not game-breaking as are the sometimes overlong animations. It has more charm and more refined humor than most point-and-clicks out there and you will be listening to the soundtrack non-stop for days. I might replay this game from the start just to take in the atmosphere again.

Pros:
-Challenging (it is hard to back up perfectly with a trailer)
-Lots of challenges that are somewhat intense and makes you more aware

Cons:

I am not a fan of tower defense or even strategy games, in general. I got this game on a bundle, and I was glad I got it, though, as the game has a characteristic that is not usually related to tower defense games: it's a relaxing game, a game about keeping it cool while fighting balls of energy that symbolize all the things that can ruin our lives.
The game lacks a tutorial (only has a brief screen explanating the keys required to play. There is no story mode, only different scenarios and in-game achievements, most of them being related to playing the game once in a higher difficulty level. The music is soothing, and the sound effects are really nice and fit the game really well.
Gameplay consists of creating units to defend your mind from the negative forces, and you can upgrade these units using the game's currency, that is, the energy you get by destroying the negative forces. There is no explanation of the advantages of each unit, but a basic rule to play the game is be to keep removing old units as soon as possible and adding better ones, until you only have the best units. Then you need to upgrade the units to be faster (up to 2s between shots) and deal more damage (not sure if there is a limit to the damage per shot for each unit), and these upgrades also cost energy.
I have not been able to play in multiplayer, as the game found no servers at the time. I will update this review if I'm able to play with someone, in the future, but the game page tells me up to three people can play at a time, and it is also possible to chat with other players, even if you are playing alone (I don't know why this is an option).
To sum up, I do recommend the game, but I must warn you that you will not have much to do in it, unless you really want to get all the in-game achievements or just need a game to play when you need to relax for some time. However, due to the lack of story, I can only recommend it if you get it in a really good sale or in a bundle (I believe a game should be reviewed as worth playing regardless of the price, as Steam has countless sales and indie games appear in countless bundles).

Copied from someone else's review: ★★★☆☆
This game's not exactly bad, but it's no...well, game-changer, either. Altogether, it's a relatively competent entry into the genre of top-down space sims. That's the thing though. It's only "competent". Space physics and planetary gravities work. Weapons and secondaries work. Everything WORKS...but it doesn't work spectacularly. Steering with the mouse and a single button is awkward, though anyone familiar with the genre will quickly get the hang of reverse-thrusting to brake and pointing where they need to go with a series of quick taps to manuver. However, fighting gravity with the need to periodically aim up into space to keep aloft in atmosphere doesn't feel natural, particularly when enemy ships circle the planet so much more gracefully. Steering isn't so well controlled or natural that you won't end up crashing into things and losing health. Then there's the weapons. Firing with the mouse wouldn't be so bad, but it doesn't compensate for your momentum, so you actually have to learn to aim AWAY from your target to hit them. The starting blaster, which has infinite ammo, is more powerful than the limited ammo guns you can get for defeating hostile ships. The starting ship is just outright BETTER than the higher class ship you can swap to, which can't equip any guns at all unless you buy an expensive weapon for it, still needs ammo, and doesn't even seem to do as much damage, since the impressive number on said gun is divided among a spray of rapid-fire shots that mostly miss the target. Meanwhile the ship itself is a bigger target, and even with more armour than the basic ship, I found myself limping away with my tail between my legs from fights that the first ship could win with nary a scratch.
All of which begs the question, why on Earth would I recommend this game?
Well, it may be flawed in many ways, but it isn't broken. In fact, it actually IS fun. True, those of us used to the tight controls and depth of something like, say, the Escape Velocity series may find Destination Sol lacking, but it has a unique charm and design of its own. The gravity well environments, while taking some getting used to, offer a new dynamic to the game. For all I may gripe about the upgraded ship not being as good, I find myself genuinely interested in practicing with that beginner ship, and seeing just how tough of opponents, what lofty challenges, I can face in it. It's not a game I'd play for hours on end, but it's a game I'd spend a few minutes on again and again. At the low, low cost of free (at the time I am writing this, at least), it may not offer the best experience out there, but there's no real reason not to give it a little of your time.

Slender: The Arrival could have been something great. With a much larger dev team than the original Slender: The Eight Pages, and a story written by the creators of the wonderful Marble Hornets YouTube series, you'd think it would be pretty awesome. But unfortunately, while the graphics may be very beautiful, and while the atmosphere may at first feel very foreboding and creepy, the actual scares aren't very, well, scary. The Slender Man isn't a threat, he's an annoyance. To overcome him, you simply have to look away from him, and keep your distance. As long as you adhere to those two rules, there is NO WAY you can fail. And The Chaser isn't any better. All you have to do is simply shine your flashlight at The Chaser repeatedly to stun her, and then run away. These two characters aren't enemies, they're pests. The only things standing between you and your goal in a horror game are the antagonists. The point of a horror game is to be scary. When you can avoid your antagonists so easily, it makes the game not scary. And when your horror game isn't scary, that mean's you have completely failed. Not only are the scares lackluster, but so is the gameplay and story. The missions consist of finding eight items or activating six generators while avoiding the Slender Man or Chaser (which, like I said before, isn't very difficult), or simply walking from point A to point B. The objectives are very repetetive, and combined with the lack of tension aside from a few cheap jump scares, the missions are boring and not very fun. Slender's story fails as well because everything feels very pointless. Why is your character trying to find eight pages? Why doesn't she just turn around and leave? Why are we supposed to believe that a radio tower is a safe place aside from the fact that the game just tells us that it's safe? All of these questions (and more) are never answered. The writers of the story (Troy Wagner, Tim Sutton, and Joseph Delage) said that the development team warped and manipulated their original story which, if true, might explain the poor narrative quality. Combine the lack of scares, shallow story, repetetive gameplay with the short time it takes to complete the game (45 minutes-1 hour), and you have one huge letdown of a game.
So far I stink at this game but I plan on playing until I get more pages so I can experience more of the game. Also totally not scary... >.>

Destination Sol 的想法本身没有任何问题
在一个广泛的星域中探索与收集、“采矿”、贸易与猎杀太空海盗。 从一艘不起眼的民用飞船开始不断成长。平心而论Destination Sol有着一款优秀太空游戏的所有元素，但是非常遗憾的是诸多的瑕疵使得我难以进行下去。因此这里仅提供简评，我会尽可能的在这之后完善这款游戏的评测。
+ 简单易上手，出色的系统策划在游戏早期并没有加入过于冗余的功能。这对于一款太空游戏来说是至关重要的。
+ 船体插件改装，武器护盾与装甲，该有的都有。
+ 足够的探索内容，从太空到星球表面，从中立到海盗势力。
- 糟糕的操纵感。设计者将物理定律应用进游戏想要呈现出太空游戏的真实感，但是却变成了玩家进行游戏的最大阻碍。这会让玩家在游戏中感到眩晕，挫折以及失去方向感
- 完全开放的设计缺乏适当引导，游戏线杂乱无章。Destination Sol可能是一款沙盘游戏，但是目前的状态并不如意，让人很容易就放弃这款游戏，
- 劣质的音效。与画面气氛相比Destination Sol的音效显得有些可笑。
- 谈起AI设计，这款游戏的目前状态还是简单的脚本，不具有任何的策略性。
如果可以中评我会给予中评，但目前并不推荐。至少在对“飞行感”做出感动之前我不会推荐这款游戏。

When I started Rocksmith, I played zero guitar.  I could do some air guitar, but that's it.  After sixty some hours, I can play some riffs, and play along to some songs, both bass and electric guitar.  I'm not a musician, but I'm learning and I'm having fun.
It's not a substitute for a professional music instructor.  But, it's surprisingly good.  There are technique games for learning chords, slides, bends, etc.  There are a good number of songs included in the game, and they continue to add DLC for a wide variety of tastes and challenges.
Will I ever be a guitar god?  Clearly not.  But it's pretty cool to play something you recognize, and to start learning to play things beyond the songs.
The one major downside to the game is that it does not play nice with sound cards.  I had to pull mine out and use onboard sound.  Not ideal, but solved lag and distortion issues.
This game won't make you a pro at guitar or bass, don't go into it thinking that. That said, its fun for practice.

Thomas Was Alone is one of the most interesting - and wonderful - games that I have played in a while.
This game definitely has one of the better videogame stories out there. The characters, despite looking like simple squares and rectangles, are some of the most charming ones that I have ever come across in any video game, and by the end you start to really feel for them. These characters, along with the great writing and energetic narration, go a long way into making the memorable story moments work as well as they do. I did feel that the story expanded in scope a bit too much by the end, but the plot doesn't really make any wrong steps throughout the approximately four-hour adventure.
The gameplay is also done very well, with level design that ranges from being basic toward the beginning, challenging toward the end, and being filled with wonderful little touches that I dare not wish to spoil for anyone.  Switching between characters is quick and easy, and the controls work well. The minimalist design works wonders for the game, and the soundtrack fits the atmosphere of the game perfectly.
Overall, Thomas Was Alone is a fun little game that is very much worth a playthrough (or maybe two). Definiitely worth a look, by all means.

For being a puzzle platformer about an intrepid band of seven quadrilaterals, I have never cared so much about a bunch of colored blocks in a black world. It's a platformer with a heavy puzzle solving element, and the narration (same voice as Wheatley in Portal 2 and Shawn in Assassin's Creed) lends the final element: plot.
The game progresses from Thomas, Chris, and John, quadrilaterals of different sizes with different jumping capabilities, to Claire, a square that can survive in toxic pools, to Sarah, a mystical little rectangle who performs double jumps, to Lara, who bounces others higher, to James, and introverted and quite inverted green rectangle that falls upwards. Chaos ensues as they stumble through the world, pursued by an ominous pixel cloud. Puzzles appear. An amazing game is born.
It's worth every penny. And right now, it happens to be only a dollar on Humble Bundle.

In terms of gameplay mechanics you won't see anything new in TWA. It's a platformer that plays with jumping mechanics, shape and multiple characters (as in Trine, Lost Vikings etc). Not new obviously doesn't mean not good, and that is particularly true in this case. The level design is mostly very well done and explore the mechanics extremely well, and it's always introducing new elements. Some levels combine different skilled characters and create even more possibilities. It's a nice gameplay from beginning to the end, if a bit short. Some levels occasionally felt cheap but these are the exception.
But that's not really the star of the game. If this developer had written a children's book with these characters and story I truly believe it would sell just as well as the game did. The characters are extremely easy to understand and relate to while still being deep and interesting. I think that is a real achivement.
Most people are impressed by the fact that the visuals are minimalistic and that supposedly can't support a good story. As a major RPG geek who has played the best isometric RPGs this world has to offer including Planescape:Torment, Baldur's gate, Arcanum, Fallout 1 & 2, Diablo and a S*it ton of others i would say that Ember could hold a flame to the great ones in terms of combat, graphics, story, music, and atmosphere the only thing i was kinda nit-picky about is how sparse the writing is.
In the game Planescape: torment for example each NPC you meet there are big branching dialogue trees and you almost feel like you are talking to a real person and you will spend at least 5 mins with each character you encounter in that game but in ember you can finish dialogue with most NPCs you meet in a little over a minute sometimes even less it is almost like reading one of those children's books were each page you can read in like 15 seconds that is sort of how the dialogue trees are in this game.
But this game was a really fun experience and if you play on the hardest setting like i did you will get quite a few more hours of playtime than you were expecting i was pleasantly surprised how many hours i played it but i think that is due to playing on the hardest setting and i kept restarting encounters to conserve potions. but overall this game is without a doubt worth the 9 dollars asking price.

if the developers ever make a Ember 2 ( i doubt they will because of what happened at the end of the game) or even if they create a new IP i would just ask them to spend more time on the dialogue so that you feel like what you say has an impact and so you can feel better connected to the game world.
other than the simple storybook writing i would definitely recommend this game to any isometric RPG fan especially to people who are new to isometric RPGs this game will give you a good first impression of iso-rpgs and you won't feel as overwhelmed if you want to move on to a more advanced one.

I think this is a great game. Not amazing, but great. Even better if you have a friend or few.
There are some very obvious bugs in this game, but unless you are deep into PVP, they don't really cause that much of an issue.
Nether has two types of leveling up. You have each individual character leveling, and account leveling. When you die, you lose your character. But it isn't a total restart. Because over time your account will level up which helps you out especially when starting a new character. Even a slight boost helps. Also you have your storage which you keep through your characters. So if you can get back to a safezone, you can gear back up with some of your extra loot.
The enemies are interesting. This isn't some boring zombie/mutant apocalpyse stuff. The Nether creatures warp around, are attracted by sound, and can sometimes be difficult you aren't familiar with how they work. When your first jump into this game they can be somewhat terrifying. Especially as you encounter bigger, or even flying variants. I'll never forget the first time I encountered this one that high glowing red eyes and acted like a sort of serveyor. If you were caught in it's sights it would let out a loud wail, and every nether, big or small, would come running at you. In large groups these Nether are a real challenge. However, If you have a melee weapon, you can quietly take out small numbers of these nether without attracting too much more attention.
Some bugs that can majorly effect the pvp scene mostly come in the form of clipping errors. Many objects in the world have no collision meaning you can walk right through them. These objects incluede statues, building floors, rarely a brick wall, and even falling under the map at times. If you know where these bugs and objects are, you can have a major advantage in PVP as you can take out players who won't be able to see your, even if looking right at you. I find myself playing PVE servers a lot mostly because I'm killed in cheap ways by people exploiting these bugs and taking me out from places I can't see them. I won't lie, I've hidden inside a statue to avoid a few players before, but it's just broken, and really needs to be fixed.
There is a crafting system where you can create ammo, items, and weapons. Some of these items are very useful, and others... aren't worth the materials. I found myself early on trying to build my way up to be able to get the ingredients for a weapon. But by the time I could kill the enemies i needed, I had better gear. But there are still some great items to craft and it does come in handy for when you need a certain gun, but dont have the money for it in the market.
There is so much more to this game, but you should experience it for yourself. Its worth the price. (the new price, not the old price xD) I highly reccomend this game. Though I feel it could use just a bit more content. I'm hoping more of the map opens up, and maybe some new guns or special ammo types get introduced.

This game is pretty darn fun, especially with friends, but the amount of bugs in this game is overwhelming. I know more Early Access survival games that have less bugs than this game. The bugs don't make it unplayable, but...they do decrease the realism of the game. By bugs, I mean things such as phasing through rocks, tables and such. Whenever you pull out a sword, the sound you make when you chamber a gun is made. Although there are many bugs, this game is still fun. I would definetely recommend it.
