If all you're looking for is an FPS Mutiplayer shooter set within a Nuclear Post-Apocalyptic enviornment, you may get some fun out of Survarium. If you're expecting this game to be the next STALKER, then you're going to be disappointed, to say the least. While Survarium is heavily inspired by the STALKER series, I wouldn't go as far to say that it is a spirtual succcessor. It should be noted that this is NOT a STALKER game despite being promised as such but rather a Multiplayer Shooter with STALKER-esque traits (at least for now).
Most of the negativity comes from the fact that Survarium was more or less supposed to be a spirtual successor to STALKER and the promise of PvE (which is currently in development) as well a various problems which have now been rectified and are no longer an issue. While it is disappointing that the former never came to fruition, I still implore both casuals and STALKER fans to give it a try. It's also worth noting that the game's first PvE Mission was released yesterday (July 24th, 2017) which is a step in the right direction but still has a long ways to go.
Enviorments, equipment, maps and music are on point and immersive making you feel like you're living in a decaying world ravaged by radiation with some impressive visuals for a Free to Play game. It's no Crysis or Metro but a lot better than I initially thought. Performance and optimization is very well done. Had no issues hitting a solid 60fps at all times even on Ultra settings.
Combat is reminiscent of Call of Duty (and that's not a bad thing) with equipment tiers. Gun-play is fluid and responsive (though could be improved) and weapons never feel over-powered with maybe the exception of Sniper Rifles. Then again, equipment plays a significant role in the game. Best way to describe it is that weapons feel...lethal...if that makes sense. Even a pistol, if used correctly with overall good aim, can do some major damage to your opponent(s). Matches are fast-paced, yet tactical and the in-game timer never overstays its welcome usually resulting in semi-brief yet satisfying matches.
There are 4 different classes/factions to choose from and each can be tailored depending on your play style:
* Black Market
* The Fringe Settlers
* The Renaissance Army
* Scavengers
Game Modes include:
* Battery Retrieval ( Capture the Flag)
* Research (King of the Hill)
* Team Deathmatch
* Artifact Hunt (Capture the Flag with loot)
* Free Play Mode - PvE (in development)
Pros:
* Free to Play
* Impressive Visuals
* Great optimization
* Game stability has greatly improved with crashes being a rare occurance.
* Immersive enviorments and music.
* Great gameplay/gun mechanics
* Game is protected by Battle-Eye Anti-Cheat software
* Decent player base
* Skill Trees
Cons:
* Absence of promised PvE (with the exception of the first mission)
* Painfully slow development
* Grindy
* Little varitey in game modes and features
* Pay to Win model (though it's hardly an issue, at least from my experince)
* Bots are poorly coded
Overall, it's a good free to play mutliplayer game. It's far from being perfect and even further from being a STALKER game but if you're looking for a decent PvP game with a Post-Apocalyptic theme attached to it, then I would defitenly recommed giving it a try. If you can get past Survarium's flaws, then you might get some enjoyment out of it. I put over 50 hours into this game and it's no where nearly as bad a most claim it to be as. Flawed but fun.

While it generally is quite a fun game to play, and is quite a good time waster, there are some things that put me off from really reccomending this game to people.
Here are my points,
1. After clearing out pirate activity on planets (At least, I assume the skull and crossbones mean pirate activity), there isn't much else of a goal to work towards. Sure, you can buy the biggest ship and get the best guns you can find, but, that's more of a means of getting somewhere, not a goal in itself.
2. Clearing out pirate activity. Now this may sound strange when you look back on point 1, but read on.
It's never really clear how you wipe out the pirates, but when you do it, you have no idea how or why the dangerzones have disappeared on the map. The only in-game goal in Destination Sol is basically clearing this out, but it seems so easy to do that it just seems that if I buy a bigger ship, they just disappear straight away.
3. Unclear main menu. There is hardly something in the way of options, you get just a few buttons for a set few resolutions, windowed or fullscreen, and sound volume from off to very high. While I am aware that this is a free game, there should've been put a little bit more thought into the options menu regardless.
4. Performance. While the game runs very smoothly on my low-end PC, there is one big glaring issue I have.
-It randomly freezes up my entire computer, thus having me hard-reset the thing-
I am unsure if this is the case for other people, but if it is, there need to be some patches made to fix this.
My suggestions would be to add clear objectives and goals to work towards, adding missions, making it clear how to fulfill those missions and objectives and when you have fulfilled them. Make the menu a little more clear, perhaps with some sliders, for example, for the sound volume, and patching the game so that it doesn't freeze up computers at random.
Minor nitpick: I have also run into some planet-related glitches. When tackling turrets on various planets, I often find myself warped into the terrain, unable to escape, thus having to exit the game and start a new one with my previous ship, or respawning (Which takes away some of your resources (Ammo, cash). Again, this is something that could be easily fixed.
All in all, I did find this an enjoyable game, but the lack of goals, some glitches and PC-Freezing make it less fun than it could have been.

There isn't much of a story, everything that can go wrong, goes wrong; and every time something goes wrong, you have to battle more people. TLDR; Ember is a simplified, modest CRPG that plays out more akin to it's ARPG brethren Path of Exile, Diablo, or Titan Quest rather than something like Baldur's Gate, albeit with more freedom and less linear objectives.
I can't say this was exactly what I'd hoped it would be; that being a product with depth similiar to Pillars of Eternity, Baldur's Gate, etc. but it does hold tightly to the themes and feel of those games. For 10$, you really can't go wrong.
It does have its own charm, and while I consider it a very watered down version of the aforementioned CRPGs, it does have 'hardcore' adventuring: outcomes of choices aren't known and there are hidden quests and treasure. The world is fairly sparsely populated for looking as large as it does, but yet is very compact (very mobile-esque) It's mechanics, systems, and gameplay are above average but it seems very bare bones/casual.
Combat is easy, you have 4 stats, and you don't get too many abilities to handle at the same time. My only problems with combat stem from the lack of tactile fluidity to it, sometimes the clicking and or dragging results in mistakes I didn't intend where I wish I had an option of using keybinds/quickbars instead.
The dialog is simple and to the point, only the first part of the NPCs dialog is usually voice acted and the rest is text to read, that's fine, but there is not much exposition, and stuff to learn from or engage with the people of Ember. Most NPCs exhibit this type of behavior, with little tricklings of non-marked quests you can receive if you do your due diligence. THE BOOKS however contain tons of information and little niblets I'd expect the NPCs to have. I'd much rather listen to an NPC tell me a story about a Dragon Hunter than read a book about it, but I digress; what it does, it does better than average, but it still lacks a lot. It does in a lot of ways feel unfinished when you compare it to other releases but that may be where my bias and disapointment comes from and It may not be warranted.
Items are plentiful, and customization IS varied, however within an hour of play you'll fill your 90 slot inventory up 2 times with all the loot you find, most of it being green quality or better. It's nice, but it makes it feel very unimportant, unimpactful and tedious to receive loot rather than rewarding. Although upgrades do take a little bit to come around, but still, with inventory management being intuitive albeit lacking advanced features it can be quite tedious to check through 50 peices of gear and match them to your characters every time you want to sift through that stuff for an upgrade. I've honestly ended up selling every item regardless just because I couldn't be bothered checking after playing for a few hours straight.
Inventory management seems to be a large part of adventuring in Ember, and the extra bags you get are quite a pain to use. If you for example put crafting materials in them, every time you loot one of those crafting materials they won't automatically stack into the bag, you have to do it manually.
These are only a few of the things I find missing from an otherwise fabulous game. I do have hope however that Development may get around to fixing these problems, and furthering quality of life and depth of features and life to Ember but I really would have appreciated a lot of this stuff on release as it's really taking away from my enjoyment dealing with tedium.

It's not terribly long, perhaps about 4-5 days of 2-3 hour play intervals, but it's a lot of fun, and absolutely worth the excellent price. Now knowing what it was like, I'd have even paid $19.99 for it.
So naturally, as a smaller, cheaper game, you're not going to get the character creation, infinite array of spells, or super-customization of the larger aforementioned games, but you will get a compelling story, and smaller degrees of each of those things.
In Ember, there are 3 primary stats, STR, INT, and DEX, and a two weapon types affected by each. You're equipment determines your skills, of which you can have three equipped at a time -- and there aboure about 35+ skills to choose from, each of which can be useful in different situations. Healing in this game is very important, and everyone can do it, as there technically are no classes. It may sound slightly underwhelming vs what you are compared to, however, seeing as how games like Divinity and Pillars take YEARS to make, this is a phenomenal game to play while you wait. Trust me.

Gameplay duration is likely on the shorter side for RPGs, but for somebody like me who is busy, that works.  The combat is a little bit slower than Diablo, but not too much. *sigh* Ember...
If any game ever needed a neutral review, it is this one. Since my thoughts go into the negative though, Ill give it a thumbs down.
Let's start with the good points.
The game's story is actually serviceable though told in a way more dramatic fashion than needed. There is not really any danger for anyone until the very end of the game, but as I said, the story is alright. The artstyle of the game is also nice and every enviroment seems vastly different than the last - variety is always good in an RPG. The voice acting, if it is there, is alright and enjoyable to listen to.
That was it. Now the bad points.
Inventory Management and the UI in general are needlessly clunky. Want to use a healing potion for anyone other than yourself? Open the character menu, click until you are at the character you want, go to the consumables tab in your inventory, scroll all the way down to the healing potion, then use it. There are hotkeys but those are only for your own character. Why? In general, inventory management is just horrible.
The bedroll system is nice in theory but makes absolutely zero difference in gameplay. The general idea is that resting in the game gives you an EXP boost that is larger the longer you went since resting the last time. Aside from the fact that you never know when you will get how large of an EXP boost, it is useless because the majority of EXP comes from quests, not killing monsters.
The crafting in this game is absolutely worthless - the devs say its a "necessity" on the hardest difficulty, which is a blatant lie considering the hardest difficulty will make you die from simple wolves before even reaching the first crafting station with nothing you can do because of the awful combat. On Normal and Easy, crafting is completely neglectible since crafted items only give slight boosts over bought items of the same level - boosts that are ultimately not making a difference.
Combat is clunky - this isn't Dragon-Age type combat, even if you can pause. There is no need to move around in combat ever (and on hard you will die even with moving around) except for two reasons - an enemy attacks anyone else than your tank, in which case all you need is to move the character being attacked two feet away and the enemy will turn back to your tank or one of three aoe spells hits. Navigating in combat is annoying anyway since you can't directly control your party members - you can only give them commands by dragging and dropping them. Another system way more clunky than it sounds and way more annoying than needed. Why can't we just directly control a party member?
The skill system in this game is also a joke - whoever came up with the idea of tying skills to EQUIPMENT and not an actual skilltree should not be developing games. Oh, you found a new piece of equipment that has way better stats but a worse skill? Well, sucks for you, since skills are really all that matters and stat increases only matter slightly.
EDIT: I was made aware there are runes you can buy and put in equipment to alter skills, so essentially you can swap out a skill of a piece of equipment. That makes the equipment system a lot more servicable, though the game never actually tells you what runes are for and that they even exist - another design flaw but at least you can switch out skills.
That being said, on levelup you can put two points in 4 generic stats - Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Vitality - and every stat increase only barely makes a difference in damage or health, which is again why skills on equipment matter most. A completely asinine system. Can't understand it.
As a verdict, as the game stands now, it is not worth anyones time especially for the price. This isn't CRPG-lite. It is a clunky, seemingly unfinished mess that evokes frustration and only has few saving graces - but a good artstyle, okay voice acting and okay story can't save awful combat, an awful skill system, an awful UI and many small annoyances that pile up. I enjoyed the game sometimes but then the annoyances came back - pick it up at 50 or 75 % off.

A gleam of monomaniacal determination in her eye, the zaftig Princess Remedy descends upon Hurtland to deliver its denizens from their various ills.  Delving with mad joy into the pain-filled microcosmos of each, she pounds their sicknesses (everything from broken-heartedness to death to not enough spider legs) into submission with a never-ending barrage of divine pharmaceuticals -- the speed at which she nimbly flits about these painscapes proving to every awestruck eye that those pleasantly plump thighs house thews of spring steel.  One is struck with an even deeper admiration for Princess Remedy when, quest completed, she stands revealed to all as a pansexual; what singularity of purpose must have driven her onward when every man, woman, centaur, zombie, rock and tree beckoned her ever-burning loins to amorous dalliance!
Why is this game free?  I'm not the only gamer who would have gladly paid for admission into this world so deftly wired-together from the phosphorescent bones ransacked from a ZX Spectrum graveyard.  I demand that Ludosity provide me a sequel, and have the decency to ask me money for it this time!

Resident Evil 6 is not a survival horror game. Period. It's a top notch third-person shooter involving zombies, monsters, and biological weapons. I'll be the first to admit, RE6 is lacking big time as far as the "throw back" factor is concerned. However, I appreciate what they're doing here. I personally love the whole lay-on-your-back-and-frantically-shoot-enemies feature. I also like that I can actually melee instead of swipe the air in front of me with a knife hoping to make contact. I agree that having to wait for the zombies to move before I can shoot them is lame, and I had a bit of a struggle adapting to the assault rifle zombie (though he really just holds down the trigger in sporadic bursts that go all over, mostly hitting the ground). The J'Avo are NOT zombies. They are bio-weapons, superhumans if you will. They sometimes transform into other creatures. This I can accept. I had to adapt to RE6's gameplay. I do things like turn on a high difficulty and pace myself. Do I HAVE to walk down that hall with my gun drawn? Well, no. But I do because that creates more tension and I can take in the atmosphere more.
I was skeptical at first about Wesker's son Jake. It seemed pretty cliche and silly to me. Then I remembered that the entire story of all of them is. Again, this is not to say I don't like all the others, I love them. But honestly, the dialogue and voice acting has always been pretty bad. That's just one of the things that I fell in love with back then (along with tank controls!). Jake's story even has a Nemsis theme throughout, but that still isn't enough for some folks. Also, by the time I got to the second chapter of Leon's campaign (three hours in) there was some extensive puzzle solving. However, they do baby you through them via pop ups and quest markers. My solution? Turn off the HUD. It clears the screen up and makes the game more approachable. I don't feel like I shouldn't have to do that, rather I appreciate the option to do so.
It's things like these that I think offend some old school RE fans. I guarantee the last time 90% of the people complaining about the new gameplay mechanics played RE1, 2, or 3 was at least 3 years ago when they got upset about RE5, if not longer. The point I'm trying to make to you, the potential buyer, is that Resident Evil has changed. Not for better, not for worse. It's just different. If you're hoping for a survival horror experience, it won't be found here. If you're expecting an RE revival, forget about it. But if you're interested in a quality, A-list third-person game with some horror elements, a lot of gore, and a plethora of fight-for-your-life situations (which typically involve ACTION, regardless of the game) then go pick up a copy.
What eventually drove me to write this is going back and reading reviews of RE1 and 2. The complaints for those games are:
1. The camera
2. The aiming
3. The pacing (too slow)
4. The controls (move like a tank)
5. The "stupid" puzzles
6. Not enough ammo
7. Can't move and shoot
Now the complaints for RE6:
1. The camera
2. The aiming
3. The pacing (too fast)
4. The controls (move like an action hero)
5. The lack of puzzles
6. Too much ammo
7. Moving and shooting is lame
8. Zombies body parts fall off and can't shoot them in the same area anymore (someone actually complained about this)

Solid action horror game!  For hardcore fans of the old school Resident Evil formula, this game may be off-putting.  Faster paced than RE4 and 5, but less emphasis on the survival part.  Hence, action horror as opposed to survical horror.  I chalk this up to "Call-of-Duty-itis"-- many developers are borrowing elements of this formula though.  The unlockables are fun to wittle down though, giving the game replay value.  The first campaign is over all the best, with the second campaign suffering the most as far as been there, done that design -= looks at call of Duty =- Top notch art-design.  Third person perspective is a little awkward but you get the hang of it after a while.  The PC Left 4 Dead 2 characters are a nice exclusive.  Cooperative multiplayer is a welcome site, and there is also a mode to play as the bad guys in campaign mode against other real players (much like L4d).

Is this what I want Resident Evil to be? No. It strays too far from being scary and it should try next game to be more of a survival horror title.
That being said, do I like the game? Absolutely, I love it. It's action through and through, but to me it's well-made and offers a great blend of types of action game. There are slower-paced action pieces, high-octane chases, some cover-based gunplay peppered in here and there, and lots of close quarters combat.
People complain that it was a QTE fest, and in some parts of the game I completely agree. There are far too many QTE setpieces that try to build off the intense Leon/Krauser scene from Resident Evil 4. Overall it wasn't too bad, but there were definitely problem spots that need to be excised from the next installment.
In short: Do not expect horror. It is an action game. However, it's a GOOD action game and I recommend it.

The first thing you should do when considering this game as a purchase, is ignore a lot of publisher reviews, such as Metacritic, IGN, Gamespot etc. After logging 4 hours into the game, I have to ask, why all the hate on this game? Granted that RE6 took a huge turn in comparison of each Resident evil game prior to this one, I still marvel at the gameplay of this installment. In RE6 you get 4 different campaigns, all supporting both local co-op and online co-op, so instantly there's a plus if you have any friends or family who want to play with you. Also, the game isn't the most graphically demanding game on the market, it's actually optimized surprisingly well. Probably my biggest problem though is that it takes away a lot of exploration from the game. On the majority of all chapters, you're limited to a rather linear path with next to no diversions or detour routes. While this wasn't exactly game breaking, it did take away a little bit of the experience. This being said, the atmosphere is built beautifully. With the soundtrack and sfx to set the mood, it's hard not to get immersed in the experience. In addition, RE6 takes a lot of elements from the installment that came before, there's a lot more action in RE6 than you would expect. Although the horror isn't quite there anymore, for anyone who loves zombies, anyone who loved RE5, I could not recommend this game any more.

Played in a windowed facsimile of an 8-bit Gameboy screen, dots are unceremoniously tossed out onto the play field for you to click on, every dot clicked then explodes into a shower of more dots for you to click on... and on, and on, and on, ad nauseam, until you either get bored of the mind-numbing nothingness, or whither away into old age and die. There's no actual goal to aim for and your score is completely meaningless not counting for anything. Maybe it would if the game actually worked as intended, but it soon becomes clear that such a notion is just a pipe dream.
There's an upgrade system for pick-ups, and unlockable palettes to apply different colours to the screen, but from the very start all upgrades are already purchased and all palettes are freely selectable. It's hard to tell whether this is all down to sheer ineptitude of programing, or if it's all part of the plan and a poor joke that none of us are finding funny... Coz it's all pointless, you see? A-huh. The same potential cack-handedness/poor sense of humour extends to the achievements, too, as they'll either all unlock in fairly quick succession, partially unlock with the remaining ones broken, or in some cases just not trigger at all. It's a real tour de force of what de f*ck.
I'll admit there is something ever so slightly satisfying about grabbing a couple of power ups and seeing the explosive chain reactions that ensue and how these different elements interact with each other, but it's a very brief joy that's all the more tainted by the fact that the game can ultimately do nothing good with it.
This really feels more like some kind of student project than a fully fledged game, and it's not hard to see why it's now free after initially costing money. But even with that price tag, other than out of some kind of morbid curiosity for its poor quality, or to serve as an easy distraction, I really don't know why anyone would want to bother with this one. Still, I guess its music is kinda decent?

Recommended: There really isn't any reason not to play this.  This is one of the finest examples of the puzzle-platformer genre out there, if not the best, and it earns that status very honestly: high production values, an absolutely stellar narration, and a great puzzle-platform experience.
The inclusion of Thomas Was Alone in the current Humble Bundle sale has given me a chance to revisit and review a game that's very close to my heart indeed.  If I ever were to make a list of my top ten games of all time or some such contrivance, I have little doubt Thomas Was Alone would be on there.  Highly placed as well, one speculates.
For those not already acquainted with the game, Thomas Was Alone is a puzzle platformer by independent game developer Mike Bithell.  At the time of its release, it came seemingly out of nowhere, mostly unannounced and without any major backing.  When people discovered it, however, it became something of a phenomenon.  Indeed "something of a phenomenon" doesn't seem to do it justice.  While SteamCharts is no scientific tool, if there is any truth to its numbers at all, Thomas was Alone is among one of the more successful games on Steam.  Coming from a handful of talents and a single developer, that is noteworthy indeed.
Thomas Was Alone is a game that leaves a reviewer in something of a quandary.  It's a hard game to review, not because it's difficult to play, it actually hits quite a sweet spot in that regard, challenging the player but not overmuch, nor because it is buggy, because I have gone trying to find bugs and have not had any success.  It's a hard game for someone like me to review because quite frankly, the chief reason to play it is the overarching story delivered by some of the best narration I've heard used in a video game.
Stripped of that element, Thomas Was Alone would simply be a quirky, fun little puzzle platformer that you'd play through once or twice and enjoy, and leave it at that.  The narration, delivered in spectacular form by Danny Wallace (of Assassin's Creed fame), presents the story of the game in brilliant form, and if there's one thing that I have heard repeated again and again by critics, gamers, and otherwise those playing the game, be they platformer fans or not, is that they wanted to continue the game just to get that next bit of story, that incremental soundbye glimpse into the world of our quadrilateral protagonists - and antagonists!
Indeed, as some who follow my reviews know, I'm not "big" on platformers.  There's a few I enjoy, but even those ones I was terrible at, because the arthritis I suffer through and deal with on a daily basis makes it a genre that I suffer through.  There's some games that are good to the point I happily suffer them because they're just good games.  Then there's the one, that platformer I wouldn't even say I suffer through, and that is Thomas Was Alone.  The story does that for me, as it does for many others.
What Thomas Was Alone does as well, however, is a masterful job at placing the emphasis on the puzzles rather than the platforming.  Platforming in and of itself is well-trodden ground, and there isn't much new to be done with it, I feel, but the puzzles of Thomas Was Alone are where it differentiates itself in that regard.  They're really clever puzzles too - the kind of puzzles that especially towards the end do a very masterful job of being both simple and devious, requiring using the mechanics at hand without them feeling shoe-horned in or otherwise clumsy.  The mechanics evolve with the story, and vice versa, as the tale of our brave little dots unfolds.
And just the language I use hints at the powerful narrative been woven with Thomas Was Alone.  The characterisation delivered through that narration is something that sticks with you, both for how well the narration is delivered and the quality of the writing.  How the characters are established doesn't end there though - the design of each of the characters and their corresponding abilities reinforces how they are portrayed.  I have yet to see someone who plays the game that doesn't end up having a favourite.
Thomas Was Alone, on so many levels, is a very thoughtful game.  It evokes a lot of emotional response, and it does that out of a careful thought to the design and presentation of the game.  From the music which is melodious and very well-composed, to the narration, to the meticulous way in which every element has been put together, Thomas Was Alone  achieves everything it set out to do - and perhaps much, much more.
At the end of it all, Thomas Was Alone is the story of dear Thomas.  He was alone, but perhaps you might keep him company a while.

I pre-ordered Slender: The Arrival last year after enjoying Slender: The 8 Pages. As with every game there is good and bad, however mostly bad for this game.
First of all the good:
The game has a very good horror atmosphere and you are likely to get scared at several points throughout the game. The story was well thought out and when it's sunny in the game, the area does look beautiful. For an indie game the graphics are well done, even on the lowest settings. Also Slender isn't your only enemy too. The music also has variaty too, which is something you don't see much in games. This is where the good ends.
The bad:
As you can see on the "popular user-defined tags" one of them is "Walking Simulator". This describes the game pretty well in my opinion. The game also heavily relies on jump scares, which gets repetitive and you just expect it after a while. The only level which actually scared me was level 3-however you soon become aware of the tactics used by the proxy in this level (I won't reveal much more about this NPC as it will spoil the game's twist which I thought was great!). The game is also INCREDIBLY short. LIke most people, I completed it in a little over an hour on Normal mode (keep in mind I am TERRIBLE at games) however when I decided to play through the game for a second time shortly after activating the product on steam instead I did notice they added in a little extra which was great, however it didn't really do much to increase the game's length. The levels are reptitive, it's always collect or do 8 ect. ect..
Overall I suggest only buying it on sale (like it is as of me writing this review- it's £1.74 right now) as it's great for a night in with friends and I do regulary make guests at my house play it and it also comes with achievments, steam trading cards and occational contests (the recent one being the Easter Egg contest) however the original price I paid to pre-order this game (which was £20 I think? Can't remember) wasn't enough, even with all the extras.
Would I buy the sequel? Yes, but only if the price is reasonable and there is variaty. However Slender: The Arrival is a poor game with very little replay value and you'd probably find yourself quiting about half way through.

Jazzpunk is...well it's...umm...hmm...
Sitting here having finished the game, I haven't the least bit of an idea how I'm supposed to describe the bloody insanity that is Jazzpunk. I could say it's a psychedelic love letter to obscure references; an outrageous consolidation of ridiculous moments and hilarious dialog, brought to life with a bizarre art style and deadpan delivery. But what is Jazzpunk really? Well I guess it's all of these things and so much more; an barrage of creativity held together by forces beyond our understanding. It's insane and absurd, and I love it so much.
Set in an alternate history Cold War era Japan, you take on the role of Polyblank: espionage extraordinaire, who has been contracted to obtain confidential information from a top secret soviet headquarters. Utilizing prescription medicine and his many skills, from being able to speak to inanimate boxes to throwing popcorn on fellow theatergoers, he's the obvious man for the job and perhaps the only sane person left in this world (assuming he even is).
From the opening moments (which are absolutely brilliant, I might add) Jazzpunk pulls you by the throat down its rabbit hole of computer puns, pigeon degaussing, stick people, and Hunter S. Thompson. It's a mad, mad world that revels in its own absurdity and pulls it off with a consistency and potency that defies reason, but proves nonetheless hilarious and even nostalgic, pulling and referencing things I thought I'd forgotten so many years ago.
Jazzpunk exists in a vacuum of its own insanity; a colossus monument to the sheer power of imagination, and perhaps the closest thing to a videogame cult classic I've ever seen. I have no doubts that there will be people that "just don't get it", find it too simple a game, or otherwise fail to appreciate its genius and that's fine. It isn't a game for everyone, but for those that harbor a love for technology jokes, deadpan humor, and the plain bizarre, Jazzpunk's surreal brilliance is hard to miss.

Survarium is a free to play, S.T.A.L.K.E.R esq multiplayer shooter with an mmo character building twist, It plays out like most shooters but you can join factions and gain reputation to buy better armour and weapons which you can gear towards your favourite playstyle, There are also small objects around the map called anomalies, these anomalies can provide bonuses throughout the game such as a speed or armour boost.
Pros:
- Interesting spin on the generic shooter
- Lots of different weaponry and armour to unlock
- Has multiplayer squad support with a variety of orignial game modes
- Pays hommage to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R art style which I think translates well to a multipler shooter
- Runs very well on lower end machines
Cons:
- There are pay-to-unlock guns and gear, which can give a slight advantage over free players
- Small community, which often means you will have supplimentary bots in your game
- Bots are coded very lazily, they do not disguise it very well
All in all, I would give this game a 3.5/5, Survarium is a great Free to play game that offers some interesting game modes, style of play and progression system which makes it a great game for the budget gamer, it can be very fun with friends and the progression system is fun, however the lack of players and infrequent updates from the developers can lead to a bit of a slow development process. But for a free game, this is definitely a good game to enjoy both solo and with friends.

is 2D Space Arcade Shooter. Explore a hostile corner of the galaxy, fighting off pirates and enemy crafts, mining asteroids and upgrading your ship and equipment.
: You get to explore asteroid fields, giant space mazes and caves, you can land on planets in orbit, whose gravity effect is neatly realized: as you approach, the screen rotates to the incoming gravity force, pulling you in as you bomb enemy towers or land of ports. Such ports, as well as port-ships flying about, allow you to land to sell off salvage and buy better ships and equipment. Worm-holes allow you to speed your way across the map from/to fixed locations, although planetary objects locations will depend on their rotation around their star. Enemies, asteroids and debris seem to always re-spawn, making sure you never run out of things to do.
: Every time you load the game up, you can continue with the same ship, equipment and money, but the game always regenerate a new sector, so there is no sense of accomplishment or progression. The graphics are retro, which just isn't my thing: I got to play games back when such graphics were the best that they got, but a nostalgia trip into "retro" graphics and vintage-tech sound effects shouldn't be a thing in my opinion.

Guns, zombies, plots to destroy the world, monsters the size of a small house and more.. Resident Evil 6 delivers on multiple fronts.. sure, the game may be flawed and have it's share of issues but at the end of the day, it's still fun, entertaining, has a ton of content and it even looks nice too.

With Resident Evil 4, a video game series once known for survival horror and tank controls turned into a third person shooter with tank controls. Resident Evil 6 follows this direction even more consequently than previous installments. There's plenty to shoot, ammo is no longer scarce (true for every campaign save for Chris', for some reason), the characters are more agile than ever before and apart from Ada's campaign, every segment can be played cooperatively. Horror is only present in form of the various body horror moments, the monsters and the gore, of course. Little has changed in terms of mechanics and unless you were expecting survival horror to return, RE6 couldn't be better. In theory.
Unfortunately, the game is just littered with bad design decisions. For instance, the dreaded button mashing sequences have returned - with a vengeance. While they have been relatively few in-between before, in RE6 you stumble over them every few steps. Every time you think the game finally lets you play, it snatches control away from you in favor of another chase sequence. And even though the characters are as agile as they can get in a Resident Evil game, the zombies can now leap 4 meters (if you're American, convert it) and every time they get hold of you, you will engage in yet another QTE square dance.
In a series that has been known for zombies, you fight relatively few of those. For the most part, enemies consist of gun-toting humanoid mutants, placing RE6 even closer to a run-of-the-mill third person shooter. In addition to that, the railroading is insane, the setpieces are not as varied or interesting as they could be and the story, while absolutely ridiculous, takes itself way too seriously. If I didn't know better, I'd say RE6 is a parody of current-gen game design.
There are four campaigns in total, which offer different play styles: Leon's campaign is the closest to the more traditional RE games and the only one featuring zombies, Chris' campaign is a full-on third person shooter, Jake's campaign plays like a hybrid of both and Ada's campaign focuses on what Capcom perceives as stealth. RE6 tries to have its cake and eat it, but ends up doing nothing right. As a result, the game feels weirdly unfocused and makes it evident that Capcom doesn't know where to take the series.
Despite its glaring flaws, I can't bring myself to hate the game since the mechanics are rock-solid. The gunplay feels satisfying since zombies react properly to hits: A shot to the chest will throw them back or make them stagger; a shot to the leg will make them fall over, giving you enough time to line up additional shots or go for a melee finisher. Capcom even integrated a gore engine, which is always a nice touch in a game featuring the walking dead. RE6 is at its strongest when it's just pitting you against a horde of zombies and at its weakest when it's going for cinematic action. Unfortunately, moments like the latter are way too present. It almost seems like Capcom doesn't have any confidence in the game holding its own with all those other fancy third person shooters around.
There is a good game sleeping in here, mostly in the shape of the Mercenaries mode, which I enjoyed more than all four campaigns combined. Popping heads and body slamming zombies all day - this is what RE6 could have been: pure genocidal fun. It only takes a lot of digging to get there. If you like action games and have a high tolerance for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, check out RE6, but don't blame me if you want to fire it into the sun. In case you were expecting a return to the old days of survival horror: Don't even bother. Personally, I don't really care what you do with an established series as long as you do it right.
I for one am looking forward to Resident Evil Kart.

Crysis is one of those franchises that I wonder what ever happened to it. Sure, the first installment was well known because of its lush detail and that ultra settings for computers at the time would send them into a meltdown and even today is used for benchmarking computer builds. Crysis 2 happened and somwhere the developers were told to either optimize their game or somehow tone down the detail because this game does not have the same reputation as its predecessor. There is also a Crysis 3, which was sold on Origin because reasons, and from then on the developers decided to go the free2play route for other games.
I'll put it bluntly. Crysis 2 is more or less Call of Duty set in the future. New York City gets overrun first by some evil biotech firm that has armed mercs and then an alien invasion happens. Gameplay is what you expect; just shoot the bad guy. I get it that shooting the bad guy is the point of FPSes but most good FPSes stand out because they have something going for them; be it the storyline, an open world environment (which Crysis 1 apparently had), or something. Sure, it is easy to make a game with great graphics; there aren't any big name games out there that do have terrible graphics, but ultimately it doesn't do much for the game. Here, the gameplay is linear and repetitive. Any time you see an ammo or grenade cache means that you are going to face some sort of enemy. Rarely are there instances where enemies keep spawning indefinitely, and thus you can pick off enemies and then go about your merry way. Also, I have not noticed much of a difficulty spike between "recruit" and "soldier" settings. If anything, enemies on "soldier" difficulty have a bump in HP, but other than that there is no difference in AI. I get that most people prefer to play on hard because of the challenge, but there really isn't one. Hard just means your bullets go through faster. In addition, I did not see any third difficulty setting. Maybe I missed it at the beginning; who knows.
One plus side that the game has are the graphics. For a 2011 title this is still a great looking game. However, there was no real immersion in the game. Compare that to Deus Ex: HR, also a 2011 title, which had much better immersion and the graphics were just as stunning. I get that immersion differes from person to person, but graphicswise this game just did not have that punch that I would've expected from a big name title, let alone a Crysis game.
Major spoiler alert incoming, but it needs to be discussed. There's no getting around it; the ending of the game SUCKS. It's probably the dumbest thing I have seen in any video game (though granted I did not play Mass Effect 3). At the end of the game you have to go to Central Park, because apparently that's where the aliens are based. Great! This means you have to fight some sort of final boss, right? Well no; the enemies are just basic aliens you've come across, including the more paladin-like big aliens that take forever to kill. So, just pick off those aliens, destroy the control modules (which you had to do torwards the middle of the game; why the devs decided to repeat what you have done is beyond me), and then go to the spire. Then you face 4 cloaking aliens. This part I found ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because A: they have ♥♥♥♥♥onnes of HP, B: they cloak, and C: they hit pretty damn hard. Now what I am guessing the game wants you to do is use the KVolt guns provided at the end to stun and then kill the aliens, using your thermal vision to target them. However, since they hit hard, using that and your armor buff means you're going to be wasting energy. Ultimately, the best thing to do is find the aliens, stun them, and then melee them to death. There really isn't any other way that I can think of. It's just dumb, really. Now once that is all done you can go into the spire. Great! Does that mean there's a boss? No; just a series of quick time events (which the game loves) and then a cutscene with Prophet, who supposedly killed himself in the beginning of the game. Do you fight Prophet? No...the next scene shows the aliens eradicated from New York and then a happy ending with you waking up in Central Park and getting a call from someone spurring the events of Crysis 3. That's it. No final boss, no decisions, nothing. It's linear gameplay at its worst, and the ending was anticlimactic as anything I have ever seen.
I know this game can be bought on Origin, but don't bother, really. This isn't a bad game by any stretch of the imagination. There were a few features I did like about it, such as managing your nanosuit as well as your weapon attachments, but other than that, there was nothing. Save your money, honestly.
♥♥♥♥ing good game is all I can say. 7.5/10 - Only worth it if on sale, otherwise check your budget.

If Resident Evil 5 was any indication of where the series was heading, Resident Evil 6 ran miles in the opposite direction of it's survival horror roots... but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. It's still a solid action game with impressive visuals and a very noticeable triple A budget. The game is by no means a cakewalk. It's challenging and you can still run into ammo problems like classic Resident Evil and unlike modern shooters where you'll practically trip and fall over ammunition at every corner. The game challanges you to fight smart.
The game has a solid amount of content featuring 4 interwoven campaigns featuring familiar faces and an all new set of characters. Each campaign will last you several hours and each has a somewhat different flavour. One campaign has a more classic survival horror approach with minimal ammo and tight and dark corridors while other campaigns have you out in sprawling war torn cities being constantly chased by a seemingly immortal enemy.
Story wise, Resident Evil does live up to it's roots. It's got all the charm and cheese of absolute B grade horror movies complete with cheesy lines and ham fisted acting and delivery. It doesn't go too far to absolutely ruin the "dark and brooding" nature of the game but it does constantly remind you that perhaps they're trying a little bit too hard to include dark humour but the implementation is quite horrid and the timing tends to be way off.
In addition to a meaty single player, you can play the campaign co-op online or even split screen. There are even modes where you can join someone's campaign as the enemy. The Mercenaries also makes a return and you can tackle it solo or co-op online.
In short, it may not be the "best" Resident Evil in terms of it's adhering to it's classic roots, but it certainly is the "best" Resident Evil for hours of exciting action filled gunplay.

There's nothing like a good bridge building simulator to awaken the civil engineer inside of me. It's one of the few genres that allows me to be creative, giving the freedom to eschew the more obvious solution and allowing my mind to come up with something truly innovative. Polybridge, from the developers at Dry Cactus, takes a lighthearted approach to a sometimes sterile genre, tasking the player with building crossings for a variety of different vehicles from a limited selection of construction tools.
The game kicks off with a handy tutorial, detailing the various building parts, from standard wood beams and iron girders, to the more exotic suspension cables and hydraulic pistons. Each mission has its own budget and set of tools that you must use so, while there is a degree of freedom to be had, you won't be building that multistory crossing with hydraulic lifts over a ten foot gap!
Initially, you'll be tasked with building  crossings for mopeds and family cars - simple stuff, like transporting vehicles from point "A" to point "B". From there on, things become a little trickier. You'll need to account for the weight of multiple vehicles at the same time, meaning you better have enough support beams in place to take the extra load - lest your bridge flop into the ocean like a soggy pancake. Ingeniously, Dry Cactus has included coloured indicators to show which parts of your bridge are most stressed by the load, making it easier to go back to the drawing board for a quick redesign.
Levels play out a bit like a puzzle, and it's up to you as Chief Engineer to decide which structure suits the level best. The game may gently prod you in its own direction, but you are free to go off on your own. For example, some levels may require you to build bridges that will allow boats to pass through - naturally your mind will instantly go to the hydraulic pistons, and while they offer a functional solution, you can just as easily bypass them by building a bridge that is a little higher up than the boats below.  This wonderful sense of freedom is Polybridge's best asset, and I suspect the developer's know this.
Also included in the game is a robust set of tools for controlling every aspect of your own levels and, better yet, you can share them with the community, so you are unlikely to run out of challenges any time soon.
Although the few crashes and glitches I encountered during my time with game did dampen the fun a little, especially when I was working on a new design, they weren't enough to deter me. Thanks to its cute polygonal scenery, sedate music and open gameplay Polybridge is sure to build a bridge to your heart.

UPDATE AFTER 100 HOURS IN GAME.....
OK, so we are changing our review of Rocksmith 2014 to a thumbs up.  I now have 100 hours in this game.  I sometimes do exercises and cord drills while watching TV but not as much lately.  So why am I changing my review?  Well, although I feel that I am not musically gifted I now know that I can play and this is really growing on me.  I can actually play songs, hear what I am playing and am actually getting better at them without even using Rift Repeater.  I have more fun playing every song on lead and rhythm over and over and naturally progress.  Now Rocksmith will never let you rest so you have to be patient and know that if you nailed that song the last time then it will be harder this time.
I can now say that I am very happy to be doing something really fun like playing a guitar rather than just playing some other game that takes you nowhere – I still do love unwinding with Defense Grid 2 and watching people playing Rocksmith on Twitch.
As for errors: Once in a while a song by Foreigner and another song lose their tone but that is it.  The broken string thing never happened again.  As for the Xbox – Have not went back to that as I loving it on Steam with no issues.  For the bass – I am so busy with both guitar modes that I have yet to have time to get to that.  As for not hitting notes when you do – Try not to retune a lot and when you do tune again once you enter a song and you should be fine.
So lately rather than logging out and feeling like a failure or know understanding my progress I now able to improve on practically everything that I play.  There are a couple of songs where I just need to dive into the Rift Repeater to move them forward.  Right now though I am just playing everything in both guitar modes and having fun.  In a few months from now I will probably start attacking songs one at a time and finishing them up.
As for this being a computer game it could have some really easy improvements in functions and graphics but it does do what you want it to do.  So after 100 hours I can really see some improvement, can learn new things on my own, am having more fun and suggest this game for you to try.  Still faithfully doing 1 hour each night (even if I am in the mood or not  LOL).
FIRST REVIEW.....
If you REALLY have a passion to learn the guitar or bass then get this for sure.  If you want to play a game and learn guitar then pass.  For computer gammers the graphics are just horrible in the learning games.  There are no slow modes in the games so you spend more time restarting the games rather than playing them.  Every time the game tunes me from E standard to E sharp my little E string breaks - Lost 2 now.  DRM so watch that.  The people that you see ripping it up on Twitch have all played for years and just use Rocksmith to see what to play on a PC rather than on paper.  This game will not teach you to read music but only Rocksmith string colors.  Rocksmith also seems to favor speed over slowly developing good habits.  This is probably because the game is geared to hard rock, metal and alternative music.
Now, I am probably not a natural at this and am a total beginner.  Am I getting better? - No clue really.  After 40 hours still cannot play Mary Had a Little Lamb yet.  I can play partials of many songs though - That said I have yet to attack any one song and have played everything once on lead and rythm.  Even when I do good on a song run I play it again to relive that experience and they throw more at you - You really never get a chance to just relax and repeat things.
I play some pretty intense computer/console games and always have fun - I seem to log out of Rocksmith a lot feeling like a failure despite getting good progress in most things.  I have even logged out flustrated a few times.  Each night I play the games until I beat any 2 of my high scores then off to songs.  Lessons are horrible for me as I have to practice just to do one - Well the first few are easy but after that they are just way to fast.  Session mode is really cool if you can already play but if you are like me then you are just making noise even though they tell you what notes to play.  Game has some weird issues at times like the path tells me to go into session mode and tune my guitar using the tools - I do that but never seem to get the progress.  I have two hung progress goals so I quit doing those.
I first bought the game for Xbox One thinking that this would be a cool living room game but that was a total failure - Freezes/hangs and is practically unplayable.  The PC version from Steam is much better with only minor issues.  No matter how good you play you will see everyone on Twitch rebooting the game after an hour of play.
I have tested the bass and guitar.  My guitar is a Mexican Fender Stratocaster and I seem to like it but cannot tell you what is the best one for me or you.  So for me Rocksmith did show me that I can learn the guitar but I doubt that it will be my end game.  I have found some passion and play 1 to 2 hours each night.  I am also afriad that I am doing things wrong that I will have to unlearn later.  I might look into lessons later but will continue to test this out.
Oh, one more thing: A note to play comes down to you put #1 finger on it and play it only to find out that that you are about to play some notes in the other direction so you need to shift.  Why not just show you the range that is coming down?  I will keep at this game and see where I am at a month from now but I am already worried because I cannot seem to feel good despite getting better.
Good luck to you all with this game....

Shockingly, this one does exactly what it says on the box.   I'm astonished to report that the guitar cable actually works, and the level of accuracy in the interface is frankly pretty amazing.  This is the software I spent my teenage years, my 20's, and most of my 30's dreaming of.  I've played guitar for about 25 years, but never got beyond playing rhythm parts (chords and a little light noodling).  I've always wanted to melt someones face off playing lead but tablature makes me want to tear my own arms off.  Now, that future is within my grasp.  I'm very happy: practicing the guitar, at my own pace, with master tracks from a few excellent bands (though unfortunately, also a whole raft of mediocre ones).  Thankfully there's DLC, and while the available library is a mix of great and not great- there is certainly something for everyone, as well as the ability to use tools to create custom tracks.  The mini-games are fun for breaks and warm-ups, but will likely grow tiresome quickly.  The real selling point here is the progressive difficulty with which you're able to learn songs.  You start off playing only a handful of single notes on a song, and on every successive (successful) playthrough, you level up and are given more notes to try on your next pass.   The difficulty ramp seems pretty gradual, but I've no doubt there's frustration to be had, and you definitely need to commit to this if you want to get the most out of it.  Overall, VERY, VERY happy so far.

I don't have dozens of hours into Ember, but I can say that for those who want a game with quests, loot, a bit of crafting, straight forward combat, an interesting story and some light hearted humor delivered in a package that made Ultima great, then this will satisfy. For those who want elaborate combat, a massive skill tree and have the need to Min/Max, this isn't the game you're looking for.
Ember is a straightforward adventure game that points you in a direction and let's you decide on how and when to get there. You can take your time to explore the area and pick up side quests along the way. Those encounters give you a simple decision tree that may lead to more information, a reward or perhaps put you in the middle of combat. In essence, you can choose the aggressive or sympathetic track. There are markers to point you towards quests and danger and a journal to show which tasks you need to complete and where you need to go.
Additionally, Ember uses four attributes to define your character, Strength, Dexterity, Intellect and Vitality. The weapon you wield defines your attack. For example, your weapon will have +2 to this, +1 to that, -1 to something else. You have decide if that makes you better or worse. There is no "build".
Personally, I really like the way Ember plays. It's simple and doesn't get bogged down with the aforementioned Min/Max idea. You're not trying to find the perfect build or reach some level so you can unlock some specific skill. It's about exploring, swinging and looting. Again, think of Ultima from days gone by or the original Diablo.
And I'm not sure why people have an issue with the UI or movement. And you don't need to drag to get somewhere. Just click in front of your character and he will go to where you clicked. In combat, click on the creature you want to attack. To use a special skill, click it's icon next to your health and mana. I find the UI to simple and haven't had a problem. Personally, I'm glad the camera doesn't tilt or move around, it doesn't need to. It's a top down view and it works fine in my opinion.
For people who don't appreciate the combat and skills, keep in mind, this is the old school way of doing things. Ultima, Wizardy and others only had 3 stats, Str, Int, Dex. And combat wasn't tied to any sort of skill tree. You could use any weapon and your effectiveness was based on the three stats. Str was melee. Int was magic. Dex was ranged. It was simple, but that was the beauty and fun of it. Ember captures all the greatness and ease of that.
Is the game simple? Yes.
Is the game fun? Yes.
Is it worth the $10? Yes.

A pretty Baldur's Gate clone, simplified for mobile devices.  Dungeons and critters look great on the PC and it's hard to beat the price (though it's still $3 cheaper on iDevices).  It's fun to play IMO.
As a mobile game in disguise, it's weak on depth and polish by PC game standards.  For example, the interface is clunky and you have a fixed camera view, which means clicking that gold coin on the ground can be annoying when someone is standing next to it.  Character advancement is minimal (two stat points per level, with skills and most of your stat points coming from your gear).  Customization is also minimal; you can't even pick a gender or face.  But the story and maps are decent, and managing red health and blue mana makes for some interesting tactical choices.  You can craft stuff and learn recipes, there are tons of books, and a variety of enemies and items.  Things that are annoying in other games are well-simplified here for fun:  inventory management is non-annoying, and food is non-combat healing not "arrrgh I am losing health from hunger."

I pre-ordered Slender: The Arrival last year after enjoying Slender: The 8 Pages. As with every game there is good and bad, however mostly bad for this game.
First of all the good:
The game has a very good horror atmosphere and you are likely to get scared at several points throughout the game. The story was well thought out and when it's sunny in the game, the area does look beautiful. For an indie game the graphics are well done, even on the lowest settings. Also Slender isn't your only enemy too. The music also has variaty too, which is something you don't see much in games. This is where the good ends.
The bad:
As you can see on the "popular user-defined tags" one of them is "Walking Simulator". This describes the game pretty well in my opinion. The game also heavily relies on jump scares, which gets repetitive and you just expect it after a while. The only level which actually scared me was level 3-however you soon become aware of the tactics used by the proxy in this level (I won't reveal much more about this NPC as it will spoil the game's twist which I thought was great!). The game is also INCREDIBLY short. LIke most people, I completed it in a little over an hour on Normal mode (keep in mind I am TERRIBLE at games) however when I decided to play through the game for a second time shortly after activating the product on steam instead I did notice they added in a little extra which was great, however it didn't really do much to increase the game's length. The levels are reptitive, it's always collect or do 8 ect. ect..
Overall I suggest only buying it on sale (like it is as of me writing this review- it's £1.74 right now) as it's great for a night in with friends and I do regulary make guests at my house play it and it also comes with achievments, steam trading cards and occational contests (the recent one being the Easter Egg contest) however the original price I paid to pre-order this game (which was £20 I think? Can't remember) wasn't enough, even with all the extras.
Would I buy the sequel? Yes, but only if the price is reasonable and there is variaty. However Slender: The Arrival is a poor game with very little replay value and you'd probably find yourself quiting about half way through.

This game is a pretty good sequel to the Eight Pages, which everyone knows and loves. In this game, you play alongside a decent, albeit short, story of Slender's torment. Gameplay is solid, and there are two levels that are pretty similar to the first game (excluding the remake level at the end). There are other filler story chapters, but chapters 2 and 3 really stand out amongst the rest of them. Although Slender is definitely more aggressive (you'll more than likely see him more often this time around) and there are new enemies, I've found the progression to be much easier. Now, that being said, I'm sure thats for story purposes, so you can finish the game, but even the remake level we got all 8 pages on the first try without seeing Slender even once. This game is definitely interesting and chapter 3 definitely caught us off guard the first time around, but for pure entertainment purposes, the first game is superior. All that said, my largest gripe with this game is that most of the story has to be obtained by easily missable and ignorable collectables. There is almost no story if you don't find and interact with the various collectables throughout the game. If you love the Slender lore this is a decent buy, but otherwise if you are just playing for the Eight Page level, stick to the first. 7/10

Despite the concise nature of this video game, the art direction, technological homages, music, sounds, and humor make this game more than worth your attention, time, and money. There's so many homages and references to cyberpunk literature and film, old school video games, synthesizers, pre-PC computing, etc. Personally, this game wrapped everything I love about life and crapped it out into this tasty morsel of joy. As for the art direction, I felt like I took a handful of random hallucinogens and left my reality for a good few hours. This game was the closest to any drug trip I've ever been on and let me tell you, that's a hard feet to master. GTA V had some amazing drug trip scenes, but with Jazzpunk, I felt like I was tripping the entire time!
I just hope the devs make some more games in this style or even add some more levels! Thank you for this experience!

Violett is a delightful point and click game, though partially also a
, containing engaging puzzles, colorful and creative landscapes, and a memorable soundtrack. It's a bit of a blend between Coraline and Alice in Wonderland; you fall into this world of intelligent, sophisticated insects and tiny mammals, and are working towards freeing them from tyranny, and yourself from being tinier then a mouse.
What I
about this game was easily the
and the
. The maps were colorful, a creative mix of exotic flavors and household objects, and the mini game of finding all of the hidden objects (there's an achievement involved with that) helps you explore and appreciate it a little more thoroughly. The music...it's charming, and cute, and gets stuck in your head easily. I'm a fool for a neat artstyle, and both the powers you use in the game, and the style of the game, reminded me a bit of Psychonauts. While the plot isn't directly spelled out for you, journal pages and direct observation provide the bulk of the simple, age-old story.
, the game was decently smooth. It was always clear where you could go, the pathing was very fluid, and the animations never glitched or did anything unpredictable. There was no mad clicking, and whenever it required anything different then clicking, a helpful icon would appear at the bottom of the screen telling the player to drag the mouse in a certain direction.
There are a couple of known
at the time this review was made, though they didn't retract from the game. One is an unclickable orb, which does not prevent the achievement from granting, and the other is around an area called the Labyrinth, where the game crashes while saving. It saves successfully, and autosaves frequently, so you won't lose any progress, but might need to restart in that area a couple of times. While yes, it's not perfect, it hardly bothered me and was the last time I saw a glitch in the game, in that early area.
The major topic of the
...The one every fears and has a great deal of conflict on, whether puzzles are understandable and readable, or if they are counter-intuitive and too hard. To my perspective, Violett is not difficult to understand. There's visual cues in every level, detailing what you should be focusing on. In every level, there's either interaction with NPCs who directly tell you what they require from you, or a visible problem that you must correct to proceed. A couple of the early levels are actually the toughest, involving long puzzles with back and forth steps required, and items from different areas necessary to complete puzzles from previous areas. The game actually gets progressively easier and more intuitive, which I wasn't expecting, the puzzles later on being far more isolated within their given screens or pathway forks.
Over all calls? This game is worth playing for it's creative atmosphere and decent puzzles. It has a couple of issues, but the puzzles follow the logic of the story, and at no point did I ever hit a wall. New content and glitch fixes have been added recently, so it clearly gets attention from it's developers.
((Ways to improve the game? More visual cues, looking at the reviews. Maybe unique sounds for when the screens are complete, or all the orbs are gone from a screen, or a puzzle mechanic is finished. The newly added content was maybe even a little better then the original content, and didn't feel forced or shoehorned in.))

On the surface For Honor looks like a fast and fun fighting game. While there are some things the game does well, the core of the experience is lacking.
Pros
- Good Graphics
- Good Sound Design
- Interesting Setting
Cons
- You are rewarded in Combat for letting your opponent strike first ( Essentially, if you have two players of equal skill, the one who attacks first is at a disadvantage, this leads to duels often becoming staring matches )
- Terrible "War of the Factions" system.
The game was hyped up to have this awesome continuous war between the three factions. What a joke that is. Your choice at the beginning of the game between Knights, Vikings, and Samurai has little more effect than what your icon will look like and what part of the map you "Deploy War Assets" to. What are war assets you ask? They are the way by which the "War of the Factions" is carried out. Whenever you play a game, you receive war assets depending on how you did, which you then deploy on the world map. That's it. There is no actual fighting between the different factions. Nine times out of ten, your team will be composed of people from the different factions as well. This is fine for casual play, but this game could've done much better with a proper War of the Factions mode. Whereby your faction choice actually mattered, as you battled alongside your faction mates and progressed in the world map.
The campaing was very dissapoited. Other than that the game is pretty good.

I am loving this game, and especially the potential for what it can be.

The atmosphere, graphics, sound, are all spot-on.  The ship customization is fun, you can customize each of your weapons to look and act how you want them to.  Space battles with other ships are so trek'y!  I love it.
Right now, you can dock and walk around space stations, customize ship, characters, weapons, scan sectors to find planets and life and other ships, warp to them and pick up missions to complete.  You can orbit distant planets around alien suns (and the orbit mechanic is pretty neat!), form an away team and transport down to explore each planet.
The atmosphere again, is so much fun.  There are little "cut scenes" or chapter-intro scenes, that feel like straight out of an episode of sci-fi tv.  Multiple game modes, training simulations, etc.  I'm loving it!
Lots of things aren't obvious at first (you have to go left off the screen to get in your ship from the space station) , I was lost quite a bit at first, but there's some documentation and things that helped me through.
Again, early access so there are bugs and incomplete areas, but I'm loving what's already here, tons.  Dev's still releasing updates and is very responsive to questions and suggestions, which is pretty cool to see.
Here's to looking forward to the future for Big Odyssey!

I've been playing guitar since I was a teenager (I shall not tell you how many years ago that was, my age shall remain secret) and played pretty much all Guitar Hero games. It was a dream to have something like this. So yes, of course I'd recommend Rocksmith 2014, but... yes there is a but. And this is the reason why I wouldn't recommend it.
This is not a game! It needs to be gamified. This is more about learning how to play songs, almost a very advanced tab software. Rocksmith was more gamified compared to Rocksmith 2014.
Oh and yes I do know about those little games but that's not the type of gamification I'm talking about. For instance, all songs are unlocked in this game and you "learn a song", where in Guitar Hero you unlocked new songs by trying play the current unlocked ones better. This game doesn't give you any incentive for playing a song better.
It was awesome to buy the Iron Maiden DLC and play for a bit, but compared to fun GH Metalica or GH Legends of Rock provided, oh boy, this is more like doing a homework than playing a game.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to learn to play guitar or bass, or also to anyone who already plays but wants a fun way to practice. The best way to advance your skill as a guitarist is to play constantly. Practice, practice, practice - With this game, you can practice all the fun licks while playing a game on Steam. What's not to like?
There are a couple issues that I run into though with my guitar - it's an older Ibanez RG100, and the hardware isn't as good as it once was. I think with the lower quality/older pickups and instrument cable jack, my guitar sometimes has issues playing clear enough for the game to pick up. Often times when I try to play around the 9th-14th fret on the D string, it will tell me I miss the note when I know I'm hitting it. That's really my only issue, and it only occurs if you have an older guitar. Simple fix is to upgrade the hardware if you have the cash, or better yet: Buy a new guitar!
When all is said and done, like I said at the beginning: If you want to play guitar, or if you want a fun way to practice then you should definitely buy this game. Hit songs, weekly dlc, and fun mini games really sell the game for me. I have this game on PS3 and PC both with a ton of hours between the two. It's easily worth $60.

I have played Euro Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2) before i bought Scania Truck Driving Simulator (STS). So i got to compare both games. I bought STS on sale which was very cheap or almost free.
The main differences from ETS2:
1. STS has no money or economy system - you do not do any business or management. You just earn points or skills which cannot be used to upgrade or buy anything, you just unlock the next level.
2. STS is purely a driving school or driving tests.
3. The map is small (just one city, not the whole Europe like ETS2).
Similar things to ETS2:
1. The graphic and sound quality is very close, hard to tell the difference.
2. Same truck model as in ETS2 (in STS you have only one truck to play that is Scania R)
Things that STS is better than ETS2:
1. The vanilla truck physics of STS is better than ETS2 vanilla. (the cabin movement and the suspension is more realistic)
2. Sound of the truck.
My verdict:
In general, every ETS2 player should play STS before playing ETS2 because it's like going to a driving school to practice and get a license before you can drive a truck across Europe. STS will make you a good truck driver before you head out to ETS2.
But if you are like me, having played ETS2 before, then you probably don't need STS. If you still buy it anyway, you probably will not play it anymore after a few hours, unless you want to go back to retrain yourself. It's not something you will play for hundreds or thousands of hours like ETS2.
In STS you can also do cargo delivery mode, but you are stuck in one city only, and the companies are very close to each other. It will take only 5 - 10 minutes real life time to complete one delivery. You just drive within the city limits most of the time.
It's a very good game but the scope is too small that it should have been part of ETS2 or expansion pack rather than a standalone game.
Buy it if any of the following is your case:
1. You have never played ETS2 before.
2. It's very cheap for you. (maybe on sale)
3. You have played ETS2 before but you wish to retrain or get a proper training.

On the surface For Honor looks like a fast and fun fighting game. While there are some things the game does well, the core of the experience is lacking.
Pros
- Good Graphics
- Good Sound Design
- Interesting Setting
Cons
- You are rewarded in Combat for letting your opponent strike first ( Essentially, if you have two players of equal skill, the one who attacks first is at a disadvantage, this leads to duels often becoming staring matches )
- Terrible "War of the Factions" system.
The game was hyped up to have this awesome continuous war between the three factions. What a joke that is. Your choice at the beginning of the game between Knights, Vikings, and Samurai has little more effect than what your icon will look like and what part of the map you "Deploy War Assets" to. What are war assets you ask? They are the way by which the "War of the Factions" is carried out. Whenever you play a game, you receive war assets depending on how you did, which you then deploy on the world map. That's it. There is no actual fighting between the different factions. Nine times out of ten, your team will be composed of people from the different factions as well. This is fine for casual play, but this game could've done much better with a proper War of the Factions mode. Whereby your faction choice actually mattered, as you battled alongside your faction mates and progressed in the world map.
