If you like games that state the obvious such as you cannot use this item here or you need another part to complete this task, then this game is NOT for you. This game does not hold your hand.
VO’s:
There are no VO's so to speak. If you can akin their speech to "SIM" talk, that's what you get here. They kind of chitter or chirp you could say. The basic story is about a teenage girl who is defiant to her parents, doesn't listen, you know the usual. Her and her parents have moved to this old house and while her parent are fighting she goes up to her room. She finds something that shrinks her to insect size and is now on a quest to get back to her parents while along the way helping the friendly little bugs and insects that reside within the walls of the house and outside. If you help them then they will in turn help you.
HINTS:
There is a hint system, but not in the typical sense. This game does not use words to give hints but rather pictures. There is a circle in the bottom right hand corner of the screen that is quartered and numbered I, II, III, and IV. If you are unsure of what to do you can click on each section which gives you pictures of what to do next. Hovering over certain items will give you pictures as to what to do with that area. It's not easy as sometimes the clues don't always point out that you have to do something else in order to accomplish that task even when you use the hints in the bottom right.
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are cute. They are bright, charming and very imaginative. Makes you think of what it would actually be like if bugs did live like this.
SOUNDS:
The music and sounds are cute. It's not over bearing and doesn't drive you insane. Of course you can adjust it in options.
GAMEPLAY:
This is a point and click adventure. Shoes will show up if you can travel to a certain spot. A door shows up when you can travel to another area. A hand shows up if you want to move something, which you click and hold then drag to the desired spot, or if you can slide a door open for instance. A speech bubble, with pictures of what one wants, will show up over characters you can interact with. These are your quests. You have a backpack that is in the upper right hand corner of the screen where your collectibles and usable objects are stored. You hover the mouse over it and click and drag the object to where it needs to go. You collect little green, blue and celadon orbs, which I think help with upgrading your powers. You also collect diary entries on the different species that are in the game. In the beginning you get the telekinesis power from a fairy. This is something you will use quite often. Some areas require you to dress a certain way in order to continue on to the next area. It seems hard but once you get used to the gameplay, you start figuring out what makes sense for each area. I never used the hints. You just have to put some thought into it, even if it doesn’t make sense. These are bugs we’re talking about here.
There is no choice for hard or easy that I saw. You can change the controls to touch or swipe. As an example, in the beginning you have to swing a cage back and forth and I found it easier to use the touch rather than swipe. I couldn’t get my mouse to swipe well. I recommend using a plug in mouse rather than the built in laptop mouse for this game. But to each their own.
PUZZLES:
The puzzles are pretty easy. In the beginning for example you have to swing a cage back and forth to hit another cage next to you to get your telekinesis power, then you use that power to move things around so that you can get free from the cage. In the next area you have to distract something in order to get past it. In other areas you have to find objects that will complete something that can help you move from one side to the other or you may have to move ladders in a certain way in order to climb something. In another puzzle you have to divert water a certain way in order to acquire an object to use for another part of the area. Once you understand the mechanics, the games starts going faster.
OVERALL:
This game is not for everyone. I loved it because it was different and I don’t like my hand being held. I liked the idea that they used pictures for what to do instead of words. I’m usually the type of person that doesn’t go with everyone else. So try it out first and this game may surprise you

hate to write a negative review, but here it goes:
An interesting idea, but very unpolished. Time will tell if it'll end up better later in development.
Pros:
-an interesting idea; a Star Trek inspired, procedurally generated RPG
-the space battles have some potential to them
-this game is still early-early access, so who knows?
Cons:
-"procedurally generated" means different planet backrounds and aliens with different features and slightly different skills
-the size of the pixels make objects and letters difficult to identify sometimes

I recommend this to those who like space exploration / adventure games like the classic Starflight, and aren't turned off by lo-fi retro-style graphics.  I'm a big fan of Starflight and I see its influence strongly in Tiny Trek.
True to its name, Tiny Trek captures the essence of a certain "Trek" TV series and similar space adventure concepts in a very compact format.  The retro feel of the graphics is very charming (scanlines are optional by the way) - think Atari 2600 era and early 80's PC / Commodore 64 graphics.  The music and sound is in a retro chip style (also reminiscent of C-64 tech), and nicely done.  The graphics and sound create a very nice nostalgic atmosphere which hits the feel of early 80's technology perfectly.
Right now it is definitely Early Access and this means there are plenty of bugs and missing content.  Some features are not fully functional yet.  It also needs some better documentation on how things work.  The good news is that the developer is one of the most attentive and open to feedback developers I've ever seen.  He has welcomed our feature suggestions and design ideas, implemented fixes very quickly and overall is very communicative.  His passion for this project is very clear.  If you buy the game and find things you don't like about it - give him a chance to address the issues you have before slamming the game in a review.  Given his responsiveness, I'm pretty confident this game is going to turn into something great.

A fairly fun bridge building sim that makes failing almost as fun as succeeding. Some bugs but overall a good stable game.
The current early access version does feature the majority of the campaign mode. In the campaign you go through different landscapes known as worlds. Each world has several levels that increase in difficultly and complexity as you go along. The also has a sandbox mode where you can create your own levels, play them and export them online for others to play as well as playing other peoples yourself.
The premise behind each level in the game is simple, build a stable enough bridge over the water to allow a variety of vehicles to get across using the whatever building resources your given and remaining under budget. It’s a simple concept that in execution becomes a lot more difficult as you progress. Difficulty progression is key in a puzzle based game and Poly Bridge does it quite well.
There’s plenty of content to get into in the early access build, Poly Bridge is a well-built little game that would also be good for kids. It’s the kind of game that hints at what games could potentially do for education, in this case maths and engineering. One very gimmicky feature of the game is the ability to save replays of your epic bridge failures or wins as sharable GIFS that you can send direct to your social media. The game gives you the space to have plenty of creative flair but is fairly limited in terms of scope at this point however the developers are planning on expanding the game further with more content.
If you’re interested in the game you’ll get your monies worth in early access and since there will be no price difference between this version and the full launch version it’s a case of picking it up when you want.

Holy crap this game is crazy... and I love this game because of it...
ONE: I'm a huge fan of the entire Slenderman fandom.
TWO: this game has some really great jump-scares simply because of its masterfully blended combination of cheap horror elements (a beautiful but creepy atmosphere mixed with building tension, startling sounds and disturbing surprises)
THREE: It creates a pretty good level of paranoia within the player and raises your blood pressure and anxiety to the point where you're like, "Why the heck am I getting so worked up about this game?!" *slenderman then pops out of nowhere with a freakishly loud noise* "Oh holy f***, THAT's why!"
FOUR: It has randomly generated maps and locations of pages/generators which makes each game session slightly different then the next, either making it more challenging and/or annoying, or if you're lucky, it might be nice and give you an easy-going freebee game (rarely though).
FIVE: it's a GREAT game to play with friends (hooking up your laptop to a big screen TV and having all your friends sitting in a dark room, taking turns and freaking out... hehe, good stuff)
SIX: it's much more involved than Eight Pages and so if you loved that one then you MUST get this one.
SEVEN: them jump-scares... wow they catch you so off guard... (even when you tell yourself "it's gonna happen soon..." Slender never fails to make your heart stop for a second... which may or may not be accompanied by a scream or constipated facial expression and noise. <in my case, I 'effed up my knee with my desk>) Plus he does it randomly and differently in each game!! I mean, there's an achievement for getting insta-killed for crap's sake!!
EIGHT: Slender's slightly new look and his new friends are fun, annoying and freaky to mess with and run from.
and NINE:  UPDATE ALERT!! They updated the game and now it's a helluva lot harder and they added three more chapters and a secret level!  What gets better than that!! (certainly not the Chaser AND Slendy chasing you all in one level... right? and yes that♥♥♥♥♥♥happens and it hard as f**k to beat now without freakin' dying.)
So yeah, I probably have other reasons but I cant think of them right now.  I highly recommend this game to anyone who finds what I mentioned above appealing to their gaming standards.  Now of course, the game itself is pretty short and if you don't like horror games that rely simply on jump-scares to get your blood pumping then don't get this.  Also, this sequel game also tried to incorporate a story in it and to my standards I think the developers did a pretty decent job.  I'm not one of those gamers who gets all worked up about the overall plot and story of games simply because I'm more of an "in the moment" type.  Despite this, the game story does make sense (you have to really pay attention to all the in game clues and hints to figure out the "origin" story of Slender, it's like a really complicated mystery almost) and it helps the gameplay move along, but of course, there are some flaws (gaps almost- but since the update, that now seems to be because they left room to add things) so if you're a picky eater about that then this isn't the game for you. Now for everyone else who still isn't sure, just check out YouTube... you can get a pretty good idea of what the game is like just from watching well-known gaming YouTubers posting their gameplay and reactions on their channels (...plus half of them are really funny to watch).

This game came out of no where - I randomly saw it when browsing the new releases for the week, and although the developers say they've been working on it for 10 years, I'd never heard of it before. This game deserves to be talked about because it really is a solid little indie game. In my opinion it's priced extremely cheaply for a game with a 30 hour campaign, although it's worth noting there's no replayability.
The story is well written and entertaining, with great characters and decent voice acting - it's linear, but there are side quests and extra explorable areas. I love loot, I like picking up items, and I like crafting. This game has those things in oodles. Okay, maybe I don't need to pick up my thirteenth empty bucket or carry around 50 green apples but I like that there are so many interactables, so many things to pick up and a ridiculous amount of crafting.
The world looks great - beautiful graphics with a stark contrast between the light, magic feel of the surface and the dark foreboding dungeons. The music and sound effects, with a decent amount of voice work are all atmospheric.
The combat is a little weird. It's real time pause combat, with skills that are attached to items rather than a character sheet. You do need to pause and organise things a lot and the combat isn't the most responsive or intuitive, but it is interesting and has depth and variety. I messed around with the settings a bit - you can change between easy, normal and hard. On easy you will probably never need to pause and can make this a very hack and slash action RPG, on normal I only need to pause on a couple of boss fights, and later (10 hours+) into the campaign. On hard I needed to pause a lot. I tried hard on a couple of boss fights and despite 10 reloads could not kill them so would have needed to redo all my equipment - definitely a challenge. You can create quite a diverse party (only 3 maximum though) and change them on the go if you carry around multiple equipment sets.  I reported an achievement bug on the forums and the developer fixed it and responded quickly which was extremely nice to see.
It's not really comparable in depth or epic feel to Divinity: Original Sin or the old school RPGs such as Baldur's Gate, as it is a fairly small and simplified game for the genre, but priced well to reflect this. I personally enjoyed it more than Pillars of Eternity, despite the more simplistic style. Those who enjoy action or party based RPGs will definitely enjoy this one as long as you don't mind it being light on the character sheet customisation, and heavier on the action.

Pointless is a stupid clicker game, one which is - as the name says - pointless.
You click on a dot, which then blows up into a whole bunch of other dots, which you click on, and then they blow up, and so on it goes.
After a while the dots go away, but then more dots come along.
You get to click on the dots with "weapons", which are meant to be lasers, bombs, etc., but which are no more than pixelated items which blow up even more dots. They don't look like weapons, but that doesn't really matter; after all, the game is pointless.
Pointless is a good example of truth in advertising. The game's advertising blurb says that "Pointless is a game about destroying Dots". The various reviews of the game on Steam confirm that fact.
If you expect anything more from this game other than clicking on dots, then you're missing the point (ha ha, pun intended).
The only useful thing about this game is that Stat Junkies can get 100% of the achievements in under 20 minutes.
The only other reasons that I can think of for playing the game is if you want to get a high ranking on the global leaderboard, are after some Steam cards, you find the game relaxing in some sort of fashion, or you are just looking to kill some time (and some dots).
Basically, the game is rubbish; but the developers have made that obvious right from the start, so kudos to them for being honest (hence the positive review - the game delivers on what it promises).
If you buy this game to get some amazing entertainment, you need your head read.
However, if you are looking to get an easy 100% achievement game, then this is the game for you.
If you buy it on that basis (preferably when it's on special, or if you have a coupon for it), then you can't go wrong.

I had pretty good idea of what to expect when I started playing Orwell, but I was surprised time and time again about the absolutely amazing writing and the whole premise of the game. I started my first playthrough in the evening and it gripped me so much that I couldn't stop playing until I had finished the game some time around 3 a.m.
While the game doesn't offer a lot of choices, most of these actually do matter and then fold out in a logical way. Contrary to telltale games, choices have an actual emotional impact on the player, which is something I haven't seen often in videogaming.
Everyone even remotely interested in storytelling and the workings of society should have played this to completion at least once. Especially people who think they have nothing to hide and don't see an issue with the paradigm of security above all. This game does actually successfully deliver a very disturbing perspective.

TL/DR: YES if you want to test yourself and grow your skill in a competitive environment. NO otherwise.
So a disclaimer: I'm coming from Dark Souls 2 pvp, this is the stick which I measure For Honor against as opposed to more traditional fighting games.
I love the idea of For Honor, melee combat within a medieval setting where you don't shoot fireballs or Uzis at each other and time to kill is measured in succesful mind games and mixups as opposed to miliseconds as with shooters.
DS2's fashion souls game is more robust, the weapon/playstyle variety is wider in that game than in For Honor where variety is dictated by your hero class and how you implement it. While on the surface For Honor seems like a more limited experience the depth of the gameplay is where it shines brighter than my former love... and the netcode. For every single criticism that I am willing to place on Ubisoft's head I will give them full points for the netcode, hit registration is hardly ever an issue due to the peer to peer connection and when the game does start to lose it's centre from time to time the consequences are rarely unmanageable.
The game design sings when it comes to choosing between parries, feints, chained attacks, guard breaks and the directional inputs for attacks and blocks. We have all the tools to deal with problems in a variety of ways and the charcater pool's inherent bonuses to each will determine what best suits either your playstyle or what you are most comfortable with.
Where For Honor has laid a _solid_ foundation of mechanics, the balance across the hero classes is where the game starts show some wrinkles. Certain classes are better able to deal with the general hero pool far more effectively than others making these go-to options within the 1 v 1 arenas. The inability to see what your enemy plans to play or is considering at the time makes it advantageous to stick with these all rounders and thus limits the amount of variety one can reasonably expect to encounter leading to a stale experience over a longer pvp session. Especially within the ranked arenas where wins have much more value to individual pvp'ers.
The gear stats have relatively little concern for me personally as outside of getting orders completed for the associated steel/xp they don't hold much interest personally, but Ubi made some wise decisions in revamping the system. Particularly in regards to limiting a hero's ability to abuse revenge.
I believe that your opinion of For Honor is going to be based largely on what you want out of it. When looking for a test of skill vs a single other opponent this is a fantastic investment of time and the satisfaction you will get out of watching people go from absolutely destroying you to helping a younger player understand where they are going wrong because you used to do make similar mistakes is palpable. Then comes the ultimate joy in finding a like minded individual where the match could honestly go either way and you feel as though you've met your match and for _once_ the matchmaking did something right. This is why I play For Honor, it does this better than any game I've played before. In 1 v 1's I'd argue that while there is room for discussion and argument with this satement, I honestly believe that when all is said and done: Skill matters most.
If I were after more from the 2 v 2 and 4 v 4 game modes I'd be harder pressed to recommend this game, but that's not why I'm here. So for my sake and the people like me I highly recommend the experience.

And for all the people shouting "Dead Game", it's getting really annoying. It's a fighting game. Fighting games have small player bases. At the time of writing this, it's 2 AM. For Honor has 1,144 players online at this moment, while Street Fighter V has 1,048, and Mortal Kombat X has 516.
If you don't beleive me on the whole "Fighting games have small playerbases" thing, then look at the Tekken 7  steam charts. For all the hype it had, it's lost almost 40% of the players it had one month ago.
Fighting games don't keep people's attention.

The game is prominently psychedelic and surreal, and the art style is suits the weird shifts accordingly. My only complaint is that the game is very short, aside from the small sequences in between, minigames, and easter eggs, there's only 5 or so missions. So i suggest getting it when it's on sale. Well, I feel like if I gave this game a negative review, I'd be a massive d***, since it was made for the purpose of raising money to fight Ebola. But, at least the game is actually good, so it makes giving it a thumbs up easy for me.
Princess Remedy followed Princess Remedy as she goes to Hurtland and heals everyone living in it. The story is pretty repetitive, as you just walk around, talk to a monster, fight the virus, then talk to them again. There are plenty of exploration options though, as there are some pretty decently-laid secrets (but some are just flat-out obvious). The gameplay is honestly what kept me playing for so long. It's basically like the fight against Mettaton in Undertale, where in you dodge random sh**, while shooting said sh**. It does start out simple, but as you continue the viruses you fight get harder and harder... except for the boss. He was surpsingly easy. Really, really easy. But the gameplay is still enjoyable. For a game made by so few people, it sounds well and looks fine (almost like Link's Awakening if it were made for Atari).
Again, the graphics aren't perfect. There's very little actual animation in the world of Hurtland, the process of talking to people to find out a punch line after beating their virus gets old after a while. But the exploration and combat are incredibly satisfying to fully delve into. Princess Remedy isn't perfect, but it is fun and it's an enjoyable way to kill an hour or so.

Love this game with a passion. It had a story. It had love. It was simple, something most of our modern social, gaming, and movie industry doesnt understand. Its the little things that make me happy, and after finishing Thomas was Alone, I couldnt be any more satisfied.

If there’s anything that Thomas Was Alone proves, is that you can make characters you relate to and root for out of anybody – even if they’re just… blocks. Of different colors. And it’s also really interesting how their personalities are related to their abilities.
Chris is short and he can’t jump high, so he has developed sort of an inferiority complex, for example. John is a very tall block that runs fast and jumps really high, and he’s somewhat of an attention ♥♥♥♥♥ and show-off, requiring the audience of other… blocks. And they develop their personalities throughout the game! It’s amazing. And the narration is awesome.
Not to mention that the level and puzzle design is really quite smart, and there are times where it requires a very clever use of said blocks’ abilities. Thomas Was Alone is really short, though. You can beat it in around 3 hours? But it’s a very enjoyable and engaging experience, I really liked the game and would recommend you to check it out.

I liked this game quite a bit.
For reference, I bought all of the Baldur's Gate / Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights 1/2, etc. when they came out and played them a lot, but only ever finished NWN 1. I get bored of all the micro-managing of 4 or (ugh) 6 party memebers.
So if you like all the micro-management, you may not like this. For me, it was about the perfect level of managing. The closest comparison I can think of is probably NWN 1, but even that's not all that close.
I do wish it had more equipment slots (6), and some of the maps were tedious to get around in because of maze-like buildings or mountains blocking your path. It did crash a few times but I never lost any progress.
The interface took some getting used to, but it was fine once I did.
I finished it on normal in 21 hours. I did not go down most of the optional branches in dungeons or do any crafting other than health and energy potions.

I'll be honest, the game is lacking in quite a few regards. The UI is confusing to newcommers, the graphics aren't anything special, the story is something you've seen before and the combat gets tedious. Ember is not the next big RPG release and thinking it is will only hurt your reception of the game when you do play it. However, what it
is a fun little title that delivers what it has in a charming package of silly fun. It's almost Divinity Original Sin lite in that regard. It looks to capture the spirit of the game if not the quality. And that's fine considering such a reasonable price. You'll be dissappointed if you're expecting some complex, engaging and unique title, but if all you're looking for is a solid, charming new RPG to play for cheap then this is the game for you.

Poly Bridge is awesome! The design is cute and very simple but building bridges can get extremely complicated. The physics of the game is on point and every single part you build affects it. If you decide to put 2 wooden parts under a 30 degree angle and the road under a 20 degree angle while using half of the max length of the parts, you will end up with a completely different thing in case you decide to put a slightly longer wood or road part.

Resident Evil 5 was a nice surprise for me early in the gen. Playing local co-op with my brothers was something that was insanely fun, though playing any game in co-op can sometimes mask the issues with an average or worse game. While RE5 was not a small game, the direct chapter progression was enjoyable; you could play the game in smaller chunks and never feel committed to exceedingly long play sessions. However, RE6 just feels comparatively massive, with some chapters taking 90 minutes or more to complete on first go though. This result in there being a sort of invisible deterrent to actually starting up the game for me, knowing that I might not see my first results screen for a significant period of time.
The gameplay is largely improved, with a more modern TPS-like combat system along with some deeper close range abilities and quick fire mechanics that allow for slightly more interesting ways to survive the zombie hoards. The game remains highly cinematic and enjoyable and the voice acting is generally top notch. However, the game itself just seems very soulless. I don’t care for any of the characters, I feel nothing when someone dies (regardless of importance), and having so many branching story arches means that not enough time is really spent getting to know any one person or understanding any one situation. There’s a point in the game where a bio-nuke of sort hits a city and another where a playable character effectively condemns himself and yet there just simply no sense of weight to the situations at all. Another shortcoming is a  prevalent use of instant fail QTEs or QTE like sections where you have to do something such as run a particular direction in a particular manner in a particular amount of time or be instantly offed because the game demands it. I had significantly more deaths of this variety than that of dying by making mistakes in combat or such. The game remains, however, to be a stupidly entertaining blockbuster kind of experience, especially if you are able to play the game in co-op.

Resident Evil 6 is a fantastic game, if you come into it with the right expectations.
If you expect survival horror in the vein Resident Evil is known for, you'll be sorely disappointed. Ammo is plentiful, there are no jump scares, and the majority of the combat is fast and quick, not slow and threatening. While the plot measures up to Resident Evil 6 standards of being stupidly, hilariously bad and awesome, and the tone is ominous, this game does not stick to the roots in the gameplay. It's action horror, not survival horror.
I cannot and will not hold that against the game though, because the new system is so solid. It's quick, responsive, lets the player easily keep pace with the action going on around them, and has a cover system that feels more fluid than a lot of other 3rd person shooters. The melee combat works well enough, the enemies are varied and always pose a challenge, and all of this works together with one of the more fluid co-op experiences I've ever seen.
Don't expect many people online to just drop in with you, as the PC version isn't the most well-populated Co-op place. That's not a problem though, because the game's partner AI is both invulnerable, and hyper-competent. You'll have no trouble getting through the game. And it's a good port too; better graphics (even better if you want to slap ENB or SweetFX on), and  all the quicktime events indicate the actual keys you bound, not just "HIT ATTACK? OH GOD WHAT DID I BIND ATTACK TO".
If you're a fan of Resident Evil and won't mind a fast-paced shooter version of it, buy this now. If you see this game on sale for 20 bucks and want to know if it's worth it, it is. You'll easily get 15-20 hours of good single player out of it, plus the multiplayer modes.

I remember clearly sitting with my dad looking at games to try, and we tried the demo for Orwell... I was blown away, what a brilliant idea for a game.
The story is amazing, the mechanics are intuative and easy to figure out, I got totally swept away by this game, and the message it has.
A good bit of replay value as you aren't able to get all information in just one run, and it pays off to look for it.

Although it has its flaws (a few times I was frustrated that some data chunks were "contradictory" although they could both be true, or that some information appeared only after I spent a minute agonizing over which similar data chunk is least incorrect), this is a very finely crafted portrait of surveillance and its moral implications. Even as someone pro-privacy and personal freedom, I found myself thinking "This is justifiable since it's for the good and safety of innocents".
Then the ending cutscene I got was about 30s long, yet somehow I'm still recovering.

Now, when I went into Orwell, I was fairly certain of what I would be getting out of my experience. An interesting little narrative set in an Orwellian-universe where you help figure out who perpetrated a terrorist attack. In a way, that's exactly what I got. But, looking back on my time with the game, I'm struck by how utterly wrong I was. Orwell exceeds all expectations and leaves me itching to either give the game another go, or threaten the developers at knife point to let me play Season 2, which the game helpfully reminded me to add to my wishlist before exiting the program.
I'm sure there's some connection that can be made to the game monitoring me in that last sentence, but I'll let it slide because Orwell deserves all the levity I can grant it.
Addressing the actual game instead of gushing all over my laptop and nearby furniture, it plays out as a sort of Point-and-Click adventure game where websites, conversations, and remote connections act as different areas, and datablocks act as items. The real twist is that, once you collect a new piece of information, there is no undo button. Your supervisor can only see what you let him see, and you can't take any information back if you realize you made a bad call or acted too hastily. And the game makes you live with it. After making a particularly blatant error, I fell back into bad habbits and attempted to quit the game and allow myself another go from whatever autosave the game keeps.
Unfortunately for my inner gaming sins, Orwell knows exactly where you left off, as the exit screen likes to remind you. If you mess up, you've messed up permanently on that file. Wanna redo? Looks like you're starting over.
This knowledge that everything you do will have intentional and unintentional consequences makes this the most tense and nerve wracking narrative experience i've played in quite some time. This is especially apparent in the final act, which I won't be spoiling because everyone needs to experience the game's final twists and turns for themselves.
As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. And, while I love the eavesdropping system, it can be somewhat tiresome to watch a conversation playout when you're dead set into 'Network Super Sleuth' mode and have to wait for dialogue to end before resuming the hunt.
But all of those are nitpicks. The game is fantastic, and it makes me long for more games with this style of narrative/gameplay interaction. While I won't be playing through until I thoroughly forget some of the game's twists, rest assured I will be delving back into the world of The Party in the future.

I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic.
Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right.
The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive.
The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware.
In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination.
Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent.
P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :
- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

This game is a lot of fun! I played the demo first to get a sense of the game, and believe me, the demo is just the beginning!
You play as an investigator who rakes through people's social media. phones, computers and news articles, taking lots of little snippits of information like their names, associates, attitudes about the government and issues, and report them to your higher ups in the government. It's up to you what to include or leave out (though some facts MUST be included to advance the plot). So you can show the social media post that's vaguely threatening toward the government or the one where the person is calling for reason and rejects hasty or violent behavior. How that person is treated under interrogation or at their arrest is up to you. As the name of the game implies, this is an Orwellian kind of nation, where "the greater good" means giving up some liberties in order for security, to the extreme. Choices matter, like informing the authorities where a person is going to be, whether they're armed. After I got one person killed, I started playing really close to the vest, not revealing information unless the story progression required it.
The story: It's interesting! There's a lot going on, never knowing who is behind the terrorist attack you've been called in to investigate. Some of the characters you end up investigating don't play into the story later (which is a waste), but the conflicting stories and attitudes keeps you guessing. There is a mechanic that lets you decide between two conflicting pieces of information, and it really puts doubt into you.
There's a little bit of replay value in that your choices matter, but a lot of those choices just end up with you just not arresting someone, or affecting the ending. There was one opportunity you have to prevent another terrorist attack, and I was really excited to try and parse through all the information but it turned out you never had enough info to begin with and just came down to a 50/50 guess. I guessed wrong, and people died. It doesn't seem fair, because the answer is obvious after you find out what is going on, but the game didn't allow you to investigate the person actually responsible BEFORE the event, so it really is just an uneducated guess. Missed opportunity for gameplay, in my opinion. You should get rewarded for scouring every document, not punished just because you weren't given the information.
Overall, though, Orwell is a fun experience. It raises a lot of highly topical issues about safety vs. security, about big data and surveillance and all that stuff. This isn't a dystopian future far removed from our reality. I can see this happening right here, right now. And that's why you should play this game.

I've had Euro Truck for a couple of years now. I bought American Truck when it came out in February. This went on sale in June, so I picked it up, just for fun. Then, I went to school in August to get my CDL (in the USA). There's 3 parts to CDL training, the classroom, the range, and the road. In some ways this game has been effectively replaces, though I think it still it has a good place if you want a realistic truck driing simulator. That place is in the challenges. The challenges here will push your ability to drive the truck to the limit, a limit which seems nearly impossible to reach even if you have played Euro Truck Simulator for a while, because Euro Truck is not nearly as challenging as this. You need to know how to drive the truck masterfully here, and if learning to masterfully drive a truck appeals to you, this is a game worth getting,

One major note forward - this game is even less playable by generic "boredom banisher" than Euro Truck Sim. Stab and steer, while trying not to catch anything with your long and awkward container... Not the closest description of the fun I can reckon.
With that said, the game is alright - in terms of visuals, controls, and, more of all - physics and challenges. If you were ever wandering how's that feels like to drive something as big as that - it's just second best after trying the real wheel. And much more safe all along.
What is really good after you'll manage the basics - is about variety of conditions to overcome. And even if you're doing good - there's always a chart with top-scores of points and best time to beat, and it is there the line when you're understanding how casual you are... Neverending challenge to be an average, almost the same as in CS:GO and similar shooters... Only miles harder.
So - my mark is 6.5/10, but if I were the trucker, I'd vouch for 8.5/10, I guess.

All in all the game plays somewhat similar to Blizzard's "The Lost Viking", in the idea that you have to maneuver several characters around a level and work them in tandem to reach the same goal. Wonderful game design, but once you start having 4+ characters on each screen the simple tab-through system becomes extremely clunky and messes with the flow of the game. Also started to lose focus on which block the narrator was talking about once there were a larger number of characters, since they were just block it became difficult for me to keep track of each one and their name.
Switching out on various levels and not forcing you to use each block on every level was also a nice design and allows for varying levels of difficulty. That being said, due to the games length or lack thereof there was a lot of missed potential. All in all I'd give it a 4/5! Definite must buy if you get the chance and just want to relax for a little while!

My first thought upon launching this game was 'wow, that looks cool!"  The game is designed to look like a gameboy screen, complete with a matching backdrop.  It's a very nice looking game in that regard, but there didn't turn out to be a lot more to it than that, sadly.
The game itself involves clicking dots, pixels on the screen of the aforementioned gameboy (styled 'gamegal').  The dots disappear quite quickly, but clicking them spawns more dots.  The idea is to keep going without running out of dots.  Power-ups appear at regular intervals, all of which help you by creating lots more dots in different ways.  There are two problems with this; firstly, it is very easy to keep going pretty much indefinitely, because the power-ups spawn just often enough to always save you when you are low on dots.  You'd have to be very unlucky to actually run out.  Secondly, there is no endpoint in sight, save for the steam achievements and unlockable palette swaps.  However, I have only played the game once.  The palettes were all unlocked within a few minutes, and half an hour of relentless and eventually painful clicking, I had all of the achievements too.  I quit the game after hitting 100,000 points, because my hand hurt and there was seemingly nothing more to aim for anyway.
Even as cheap as it is, I can't recommend this one.  I can put it in my 'completed' pile after a single play.  There is no replay value, no real goal, no difficulty curve and it might give you RSI.  Should probably be free.

Pointless is a clicker game that takes it's name quite literally. The "point" of Pointless is to click the dots to create more dots to earn points and unlock new skins, though there really isn't much point beyond that. There are some powerups you can use as well, but they also can easily work to start lagging out the game. In fact, the game starts to lag out fairly easily considering how simplistic it is.
Considering there are far better free "clicker" games out there, I cannot recommend Pointless at all. The fact that this is going for $1 just makes me question "Why?", and if I hadn't gotten this in a bundle I likely would have just completely passed it up. Save your money and play a free clicker game instead.

Poly Bridge is awesome! The design is cute and very simple but building bridges can get extremely complicated. The physics of the game is on point and every single part you build affects it. If you decide to put 2 wooden parts under a 30 degree angle and the road under a 20 degree angle while using half of the max length of the parts, you will end up with a completely different thing in case you decide to put a slightly longer wood or road part.
Building a functional bridge is easy at start, you can probably finish the first 10 bridges of the campaign in 20 minutes but then it gets insane, there are a few bridges that will take you literally hours to figure out. One wrong cable connection, a tiny mistake of placing a wood part can ruin your entire bridge and make you go insane.
The first 2 worlds too me 6 hours the first time and 2 hours the second time to complete. The game now has a third world too that I still haven't checked out.
It also has Sandbox where you can build your own bridges and share them on Steam workshop. It is still a bit buggy but hey, sandbox didn't exist a week ago so in 2 months I bet we will have a billion community created bridges in a very good sandbox mode!
You can also automatically share your bridge wins and fails over Twitter which is pretty cool too!

Resident Evil 6 takes more steps away from it horror survival roots and pushes itself further into the third person action genre. With the removal of many survival aspects and a much greater focus action is a disappointment to many of the original fans of the series however Resident Evil 6 ___. The over the top action makes it difficult to take the game seriously but provides plenty of excitement through all four campaigns.
As the new C-virus runs rampant through Estonia, China and America the player battles through four separate campaigns to discover and stop the source between the new attacks. Each campaign provides its own focus, such as the more traditional zombie killing experience to Chris Redfield’s much more combat focused campaign. The four separate campaigns provide plenty of variation throughout the game however when characters between each story meet you will soon find yourself having to repeat the same fights. Though the intention of these events was simply to provide interaction between the main characters having to repeat them between separate campaigns can feel like tedious padding. With plenty of boss fights and approximately five to six hours in each campaign there is plenty of varied gameplay to be had.
With the Resident Evil games frequently trying to add greater events then the previous one, the 6th is no exception, as soon events turn from dramatic to just ridiculous to try to top the last death defying stunt. With a serious attitude you can soon lose interest and find it difficult to enjoy as each event because more comical then the last, however if you simply accept the lunacy of the situations and simply enjoy the action then there is plenty of fun to be had. Without spoiling a simple example of this is how persistent some of the bosses continue to be through the entire game. After watching many victory cut scenes where your enemy suffers fatal damage, only to have them appear again one hour later then those taking the game seriously will soon become irritated and lose interest.
The basic and minimalistic HUD is unobtrusive yet concise in displaying information which only appears in combat situations, allowing unobstructed views of the environment around you as well as the many cinematic scripted events you will encounter. Fixed camera angles in many areas serve to compliment this design even more, ensuring your gaze is never pulled away from the action. The use of fixed cameras can be a source of much frustration, especially during chase sequences. Many situations will have your character fleeing from one of many monstrosity’s behind you, as the fixed camera ensures you see the path of destruction behind you, you simply can’t see where you are going at all as you just blindly run towards the camera. In some situations the camera will jump to a new perspective or rotate suddenly changing the direction all of the movement keys, often resulting in you walking accidentally towards the enemy as you try to get your bearings again.
With a heavy focus on cooperative gameplay I soon expected to be dying each time my partner messed up, yet this was not the case. As the game will harshly punish you for the smallest mistake, you will soon become dependent on your co-op partner to pick up the pieces and get you back on your feet. Finding a balance between individual responsibility and cooperative gameplay can prove difficult for many games, often either being overly dependent on your teammate to a point where you can feel unjustly punished each time your partner makes a mistake. The other side where players simply don’t interact at all, making it feel like you’re simply playing a single player game with another gun at your side. Resident Evil 6 manages to seamlessly find the middle ground between the two, making co-op great fun through 3 of the campaigns, with one of the four being focused for single player gameplay. When playing single player, your AI partner will behave a little odd at times but it always manages to stay close and get the job done, making single player a perfectly viable choice if co-op isn’t your personal choice.
The game frequently changes direction from action to short periods of stealth based gameplay, chase sequences and the occasional vehicle sections in an attempt to keep things fresh. Despite the fact that these can be fun, especially as they break from the standard gameplay they also feel unfinished and misplaced. You will find yourself frequently with little direction during these, becoming confused as it can occasionally turn into a scene of trail and error after each death. I found myself trying to escape avalanche on a snow ski, only to frequently die at many corners because I picked the wrong side to approach the corner, to which I would find a bottomless pit right in front of me with no possible time to react.
Resident Evil 6 accepts the flaws in its design, while improving the strengths that it has. Yes the storyline is painful, and filled with so many plot holes that finding possible answers would be harmful to ones mental health, but I found it easy to just completely switch off to this as I waited for the next adrenaline fueling moment. Why is the building around me exploding? Why doesn’t the boss simply crush me instead? Why is this base filled with lava? If the answer “because it’s fun” is answer enough for you, you will find plenty of excitement in this game.
Pros:
Over the top action and strategic elements blend well to create smooth flowing combat
Many unique multistage boss designs
Co-op finds the middle ground between looking after yourself and your partner
Over 16 hours long
Many scripted cinematic scenes
Each campaign has slightly different gameplay from the others
Cons:
A barely functional storyline is just to tie events together
Practicality sometimes suffers for cinematic scenes
Some areas lack direction for players, often leading to trail and error
Some clear signs of a port, such as a the options menu presentation

Ember is a fantastic RPG game. If you liked Pillars of Eternity but don't want to deal with complicated RPG stuff like that game had, this game is definitely for you.

In any case, the gameplay of the game is fantastic, basic point-click-character attacks said mob you clicked on. The walking (running) around is nice as you get from place to place quickly enough so it's not a bore. The combat is pretty decent as well, as you get skills from equipping magical items ("Hide Jacket of Teleport, etc) and this gives you skills to use in the game.

Sound: Not attached to Windows Sound Mixer like all applications and software are supposed to be. 7/10. Music is GREAT though once you window the game and get it to connect to the mixer and lower the volume.

Basically, the game is not caught by the windows sound mixer and if you lower the volume in the game it does essentially nothing. So I had to do my first recording with the music BLARING in my headphones and I couldn't even watch the intro cutscene because the WOOSHES in the cutscene were WAY too loud, but I got the gist of the background story more or less.
General Other Stuff: None that I can think of really. It's got your basic pause mechanic as well for ordering your party around like Dragon Age as well which really comes in handy if you need to get your ranged characters away from monsters. Uhm... Ember is a fantasy RPG adventure where you play as a Lightbringer, and you have been resurrected to save the embers, and hold back the darkness.
When I first started playing, I had expected a more hack and slash type of game, but I found that combat was a lot more tactical than I had expected it to be, and I found it a bit difficult at first. The combat happens in real time, but you can pause time to plan out your attacks. It took me a while to get used to. It took me a while to get used to combat, and I am so glad that they included options to turn on auto-pauses in combat that give you time to react without instantly dying.
At first, I was turned off by the combat in Ember since it wasn’t what I had expected the combat to be like, but it really grew on me, and wound up being the most enjoyable part. There are several things I would have liked to change about the game, and it’s by no means perfect. The game is priced appropriately for its content though, and it’s a decent pick-up despite its annoyances.

A game that is easy to play, yet hard to master, A game that is both cute, funny, and interesting to play. A game that manage to please both casual and hardcore players. What kind of beautiful magic created Transformice ?
I don't know how they did it, but i sure know it's a success. You get sucked in by the cute mice with tiny hats and funny animaitons. You enjoy running along whatever contraption the Shaman manages to make, and grab the cheese. Then you start getting interested in some advanced mechanics like wall jumping. And you start to get greedy, you try to get the cheese first and become competitive. Finally, after a few rounds, you discover the whole new realm of shamaning, and understand how much complexity there is in that.
The game is 100% free (the only stuff you can buy with actual money are cosmetic items), so you have no excuse to not try it. And i dare you to not find something you like in it. Maybe you're gonna enjoy being a part of group of cute little mice that dance, and laugh and sometimes cry after an horrible jump into a bottomless pit. Maybe you're gonna enjoy the brain burning aspect of being the shaman and solving maps to help your fellow mice get their precious cheese. Maybe you're gonna get competitive, and strive for 1st place everytime, by taking insane risks to scalp a fraction of a second in your completion time.
Really, Transformice is the best game to play with group of people with different video game knowledge. Everyone can find something in it.

Despite this, I am still going to recommend this game. While the most popular game mode, dominion and sometimes other 4v4 modes, are very unstable, the game itself is fun. I recommend patience. For a point-and-click adventure, you're either going to enjoy this game or you're going to hate it. The initial premise evokes strong deja-vu of Coraline almost to the point of feeling like a blatent ripoff. You play Violett, a goth girl who moves into an old house and finds herself lost in a strange world - complete with a spider antagonist. This is where the simularities end however... as well as the depth of story. Simply put, if you're someone who prefers a heaping dose of narrative and gets annoyed when things are left vague, this game isn't for you. If you don't mind a game that gives you the breadcrumbs and encourages your own interpretations, you'll find an adventure reminiscent of Alice in Wonderland or The Neverending Story.
Each scenery you'll encounter is incredibly imaginitive, from opera singing frogs who can control the weather with their voice, to haunted teapots that torment their owners. The puzzles can be frustrating, but for the most part are never truly illogical. At least, they're generally as logical as a Wonderland-esque world ruled by the phrase "we're all mad here" is capable of being. The overall aesthetic is unique and (I felt) fascinating. The soundtrack is alright and comes with the game automatically.
And now the bad side. First off, the controls can more often than not be frustrating to deal with, especially if you're moving between several rooms at once. I also encountered some bugs. For example, one achievement failed to pop because one of the criteria glitched and I was forced to start a new game to complete it. Another bug involved ants that forced me to exit and enter the area several times to correct. The "boss fight" at the end is also a complete joke.
Bottom line, I would say the game is worth looking into if you're a fan of the aforementioned stories, but due to the potential problems with bugs I can't recommend paying full price. Get it during a sale.

Orwell is a short but engaging story about an investigator (that's you) being given incredible power to peer into the information of anyone you want. This idea does not seem far-fetched at all. In fact, despite its rather in-your-face name, Orwell presents a world that is quite believable. There really is nothing here that is overly dystopian or fantastic. Rather, the world in Orwell is just our own world, with surveillance taken a few notches up.
The game isn't perfect. The interface sure could use some work. I often found myself having to go through the same emails, chats, etc. until I found the link or "data chunk" it wanted. As such, it was a let down on its initial promise, and felt much more pre-determined than I hoped. There are a few choices here and there, but they don't feel like they matter much. In the end, things will go as they go, and there is little reason not to submit every data chunk.
All that said, Orwell is a good game, and well worth the time to play. It's not long - I did it in a single session. Hoping the sequel adds a bit more choice and complexity. But in a world where these type of games tend to go a bit too far in dystopian future, Orwell is very welcome, because it feels much closer to reality.  It clearly has a point to make, but it is generally not heavy-handed. Its most important trait is that it places you in the role of the investigator. You might find the level of access you have to be unnerving. But you feel like you're the good guy. In that way, it's both humanizing to the agents who pore through our data, and showing how no human should have that power.
Pick Orwell up. It'll be a few hours well spent.

I was really surprised by this beautifully designed (and beautiful looking) game that was both interesting and thought-provoking (no pun intended).
In a world where we give our information up free of charge (this review included) it is increasingly obvious that the very information can be a) sold to the highest bidder and b) used against us. Whether in the name of 'security' or 'commercial ease' this game is a timely reminder that Big Brother is here.
George Orwell could only imagine the world we are now living in but he totally called it. 'Smart' devices that spy on us. Data miners and browsers that remember our every word. Governments that trump up charges to fit a political narrative (and I'm not just talking about 'dictatorships' but democracies too).
Edward Snowdon proved a long time ago that technology, which we've all fallen in love with, has the power this game speaks so clearly about. Playing it really did give me chills as an Investigator for Orwell. I tried occasionally to do the 'right' thing and to out-manoeuvre the system, with pretty horrific consequences. That really added to the realism, as all information viewed out of context can be used to mean almost anything and fit any agenda required.
I really enjoyed this game and I’ll definitely be running back through it again in the hope of outwitting The Man. I’m also seriously excited there’s going to be a sequel, which I can’t wait to play. This was some excellent work by the devs and a real pleasure to play!

I was trying to figure out the point of Pointless yesterday. "Pointless" is literally pointless, which shouldn't come off as a great surprise as the game is called "Pointless". Yet, one could argue that the point of Pointless is to click on points, which means that Pointless isn't pointless after all, firstly because if it has a purpose, it has a point, and because there will always be points on the screen, which the whole point of the game is to click on. That makes Pointless have a point (it's a pointless point, but a point nevertheless), which means that Pointless can be pointless and have a point at the same time. Yet, that'd be a pretty pointless conclusion, because trying to understand the point of that is pointless to the average human being. So the point of the game must be something else.
Either way, here are a few more points about the game:
I was going to write some more points about the game here, but the more I write, the more pointless the game becomes. So let me tell you exactly how my pointless gameplay experience was instead.
I downloaded Pointless late at night and decided to play it to see if it would be worth it. That's easily the most pointless decision I have ever made. The game starts off alright, it's a bit hard to hit the points initially, but over time, I got a bit more used to it. I realized that this game has achievements for some pointless reason, and I got more and more interested in the game. After about five minutes, I had clicked on 10,000 points, and that's when this pointless game started going downhill. Nothing happened for a while after that, and I no longer saw the point in playing much longer. So, I opened Steam again and looked for whatever the next pointless achievement would be. Clicking 100,000 points. I was all broken down. It was utterly pointless. Yet, I kept playing for some pointless reason, and after some unknown amount of time, I got some pointless card in my inventory. "Great, the most pointless card I've ever gotten," I thought, figuring I could probably sell it on the Community Market, because I don't want to keep this pointless card in my inventory.
After 20 minutes, I started contemplating the meaning of life and the universe, and wondered why I had installed this pointless game in the first place. I would have been better off just leaving it in my library for some pointless reason than to set aside a few pointless megabytes for this game. Either way, I was going to reach that pointless 100,000 achievement at some point, so I kept playing, pointlessly.
40 minutes in, and the point counter was approaching 90,000. Finally, I thought, an end to this pointless game! As I reached 100,000 and got the last pointless achievement, I didn't hesitate to quit the game. Finally, I'm released from the pointless captivity of this pointless game! It was the greatest relief ever. I have officially *survived* Pointless. I should be proud of myself, but I'm not sure what the point of that would be.
To sum it up, this game is pointless. It does make a good point of killing your mouse, and thanks to this game, I now know what lurks within Room 101 from George Orwell's "1984". The torture chamber is literally playing "Pointless" to 1,000,000 points. No wonder why everyone was so desperate to avoid the pointless room. This game is pointless. There's no point in playing it. Overall rating: 1/10. Would not point my eyes at again.

Also started to lose focus on which block the narrator was talking about once there were a larger number of characters, since they were just block it became difficult for me to keep track of each one and their name.
Switching out on various levels and not forcing you to use each block on every level was also a nice design and allows for varying levels of difficulty. That being said, due to the games length or lack thereof there was a lot of missed potential. All in all I'd give it a 4/5! Definite must buy if you get the chance and just want to relax for a little while!

text: Good game for any guitarists out there, whether you're a beginner or an expert. Though kind of disappointed that it doesn't go in depth regarding Music Theory. Fun game all in all, especially the little mini games.

A game like "Rocksmith" is truly a difficult thing to review. There are so many different concepts to music and to how people want to evolve their talent that no one opinion will do justice to this game. It functions and provides a great distraction to rote training, but it honestly is not the best tool around.
For starters, "Rocksmith 2014" does not have the best tutorial around. I guess with the rise of the YouTube era, everything is taught to you by a quick video. You are then tasked with plucking strings and holding frets without any knowledge of why. The game neglects to go farther into music theory, as well. I suppose a quick lesson on tremolos will do, but that honestly isn't going to elevate your skills farther.
The next musical sin comes from the explanation of notes. If you play bass, you might as well skip this game. The game constantly badgers you to check the note book, but then only includes that option for lead guitar. Even then, there is no further elaboration on how to properly place your fingers or what the root of each note stems from.
There are no detailed looks into intervals, timing, self-tuning or note patterns. You simply are told to place your finger on fret 5 and play it on the first string. It would be nice to know that is an A Note, but I suppose that little detail is irrelevant.
If your only interest in music is learning how to play a very select assortment of songs, then sure; "Rocksmith 2014" will allow you to play those songs. You will more than likely sound sloppy and have no form, but man can you rock out to 'You Really Got Me'.
In the end, I haven't spent eons with the game. The only reason I got it was because I figured it would be a good supplement to my regular music lessons. It hasn't failed in getting me more interested in playing, but it definitely has held me back from growing as a musician.
I suppose this game is really only intended for those who are bored with their instrument or want to augment their playing into a really standard and unskilled manner. You will be better served calling up a good teacher and getting yourself taught the basics of music theory.
5/10

I purchased RS2014 just wanting it to be a "game" like Rockband or Guitar Hero.
I didn't have a real interest in learning to actually play the guitar (I've tried numerous times in the past and given up), all I wanted from this was something I could casually play, but with a bit more challenge/reward than the "plastic guitar" games.
It started off exactly how I was expecting - just playing a single note every now and then, but as you improve and play the notes its' giving you well the game will adjust and add more into the mix. Before too long you'll be given chords, double-stops, legato techniques, and plenty of other new bits to play.
The way the difficulty works is good, it won't give you something to play that's way over your head (too often), but keeps you improving at a good rate.
In the few weeks I've been playing, I've progressed a lot further with my skills than I have in all my previous attemps to learn guitar without Rocksmith. I'm interested in learning to play again, and this makes it a great way to do it.
Pros:
* Very cost-effective way to learn (if you already own a guitar).
* Being able to have your skills quantified (Mastery percentage, song accuracy, scores etc) and improving is great motivation to see your progress and keep playing.
* Makes practicing fun!
Cons:
* Music choice is decent, but could do with a lot more songs. New songs are released every week though.
* There's no option to see the music to play in Tab format.
Overall, I highly recommend it, it's a lot of fun and you learn something while you play.

Rocksmith 2014 is not only for beginners who want to learn how to play, but also for fairly experienced players who wants to improve their skills or simply take advantage of the many tools in-game.
There are several modes:
''Learn A Song'' which allows you to play along to one of the songs that are included in the game or can be bought as a DLC. It might be remind you a bit about games like Guitar Hero. The difficulty adapts after how good you are, and get harder and harder as you learn more and more.
''Session Mode'' gives you a virtual band to play with! You can customize and choose your scales, tempo, groove, atmosphere (club, studio, arena) and what instruments that is in your band. Or you can load up a stock one, like ''Electric Blues'' or ''Psychedelic Rock'' all after what music you intend to play.
There are also a whole catalouge of lessons that learns you everything from playing chords and the basic scales (and even how to hold your guitar, lel), through harmonics, hammer-on's and pull-off's, to the master classes.
Also there are arcade style mini-games that let's you train on your tecnhicques. Temple of Bends, Scale Warrior and Harmonic Heist are some examples.
Along with that you get some very useful tools. The tuner which allows you not only to standardize your tuning, but also change into different tunings based on the song you are playing. So it might be smart to plan ahead so you aren't stuck too long in the tuner. Also you get ''Tone Editor'' which allows you to change your effects, pedals and amps. Coolest product placement ever with Eden, Orange and Marshall. Every song that you play also have an ''authentic tone'' that loads up when you start the song. If for example the solo and the riff has different tones in a song it changes automatically. You can also load up these in Tone Editor so you can play with it in Session Mode.
The included songs ranges from hits like ''My Generation'' and ''We Are The Champions'' to songs from underated indie bands that no one has ever heard of. Try to play every song, you might find something you like. If you have the original Rocksmith you can import them with updated tabs or you can buy it if you didn't own it previosly.
Looking at the large amount of DLC, it's easy to think of this as another ''DLC: The Game'' but it isn't. New songs are released to this game constantly, but the artists need to be paid. So you have to pay for the license.
If a song you like hasn't been released however, you can download custom songs for free using some modding tools. They might be faulty however since they are made by sparetime modders.

There are some things to remember though: This is not Rock Band or Guitar Hero. You might and should have fun while playing this game, but remember it's an educational game. This means that you can't expect to learn the songs by playing it over and over again. You have to go deeper and use the ''Riff Repeater''. Riff Repeater allows you to slow down certain sections of a song and play it at any speed you want, again and again until you get it.
Also this is a TOOL not some kind of potion that magically transforms you into Jimmy Page. The challenge to take the skills you learn in the game into the real world might be tough. Sometimes you will find yourself cutting shortcuts just to hit the notes, which makes things even worse (espescially when soloing). If you really want to learn, you are gonna have to use other means too.
In short: It is a great game if you want to learn the basics of guitar/bass, improve your skills or just have some fun. Use it with caution and don't rely solely on it if you want to learn guitar properly. Great songs, good tabs and useful tools. It's worth buying for every aspiring or aspired guitar player out there.

Of course, the game is just released and the fight balance needs some minor tweaking, as permanent stun and silence let you kill anyone quite easily. Fight combos is so good invention for such games. I know Divinity has similar, but I found Ember’s one more attractive.
Crafting is probably quite useless in the game, especially when you have a “resting option” to fully recover health and energy. Proper crafting menu, where you have a list of the crafting items with ingredients auto-assigned from inventory with button “craft”, would make it worth to craft. So far I am not ready to waste hours looking through inventory for the necessary ingredients. I have made only one piece of armor and forgot about it.
I definitely see the devs used fighting system similar to the WoW, such as fight combos,skills and attributes, but that was apparently a missing thing in isometric rpg fights. Implementing side menu with auto-filling slots for potions, food etc without need to go inventory, would make the gameplay more pleasant. And I would get a need to use them:)
Pros: nice plot, fighting system, no bugs found so far, quick loading.
Cons: basically no character development with exception of four attributes (strength, dexterity, vitality and intelligence) flashback from Diablo 1:) Needs more hardcore by removing of the resting option and making potion and food crafting process simpler, as well as consuming food and potions. Right now without resting option I don’t see any good way to restore energy after fight, as drinks restore ~1 energy out of 100 roughly and crafting of energy potions become available quite late after beginning of the game. Minor fights tweaking, limitation of silence and stun uses, auto cast of skills (I want mage just spamming fireballs most of the time).

For Honor is the game I have been looking for.
-At first, I was put off by the other reviewers saying that peer to peer connection is♥♥♥♥♥♥and that if the owner quits, you lose your rewards for that match, but I found that it has been fixed. So far, I haven't come across any connection bugs and I have never once not been given my rewards after a match. If the owner quits, another player will become the owner, and the game goes on just as it did up until that point.
-I consider that most of the negative reviews came from before Ubi fixed this, and another part comes from salty people that have been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by the imbalance. It is true, the potential of some characters of being played in a tournament is low, but in normal play, everything is ok. Every character can beat every character, it is up to the player's wish to improve. The ability to adapt to your opponet's playstile is crucial, so your strategy won't work all the time.  A victory against a challenging player will be the most satisfactory thing you will ever feel.
-The community is nice, I have found very few players who give up and start flaming after getting their♥♥♥♥♥handled to them.
-Matchmaking doesn't take long at all. So far, the longest was 2 min for both 1v1 and Dominion
Overall, For Honor is a game for those who don't give up and are always looking forward to a new challenge to overcome.  The game doesn't have an obvious goal, so besides the faction war, being the best is the only objective.
A few tips for those of you who are interested in this game: the first thing to do is to learn your desired class' combos, then  beat the bots on the level 1, 2 and 3 difficulty and complete the campaign. By completing the campaign, you will become familiar with most of the classes, and by beating the bots you will have a handle on the basics. Oh, and also, don't be disheartened when you lose to someone with hundreds more hours of playtime.

Something about the graphics style and music made me nostalgic about my childhood. Gave the game a shot and figured out all there is to the game in just a few minutes. Your task is to heal the king from his sadness, however on your way you encounter lots of people / otherwise that need helping - with sometimes funny comments. Once you choose to help you end up in a rather small environment with your character shooting "vitality" towards all the nasty enemies.
Think of it as Binding of Isaac without having to fire, and without the ability to aim where you shoot. And that last is the part that didn't quite appeal to me at first. I got quite used to running around and simultaneously shoot in different directions altogether, that it felt quite frustrating at first. However ignoring this, it allowed me to enjoy the rest of the otherwise short game.
Considering it's cheap price tag - erhh, free I definitely recommend this game. Would have even bought it!
TL;DR - Install it, play it for five minutes. If you like it, keep going through the journey - there isn't much else to it, and it's quite short anyway - if you didn't like the first few minutes then don't bother going through with it. I guess it's either a hit or miss, however I found it really entertaining.
