Violett is a point and click adventure game. It's story is told through your actions as violett, and the game's imagery(mostly without words, the diary pages being the exception). This is a really cool concept, letting the player discover the story through the gameplay and not the other way around. However even with the games very pleasant artwork, and smooth animations The game struggles.
The puzzles are very unintuitive, and the game carries very little direction for the player to follow. Most of the time spent in the game is wandering aimlessly around trying to figure out what to do next. A puzzle's hardness should not be defined by it's lack of clarity, in an attempt to elongate game time. Most point and click games have some amount of vagueness to them, but this one kind of takes it to a new level. There is a pretty generous hint system in the game, but you shouldn't NEED that hint system to progress.
Other than walking around and solving some puzzles you have the ability to collect colored orbs, which is less optional then the game lets on. These little orbs are power for your abilities that you will need to fight the final boss. So if you spent the game ignoring them and ou get to the end, you'll find yourself having to do a lot of backtracking to tediously comb over completed areas. It can be a bit fun looking for the little trap doors, or moving objects to find them, but several of them are behind immovable scenery and are effectively invisible. Meaning unless you get lucky clicking around, or pick up a guide you won't find them. There is also no real way to know if you've found all the orbs in one area, making the whole thing a bit difficult for no real reason.
My last big gripe against the game are the glitches. The controls aren't great, so sometimes you end up getting stuck in one spot and are unable to leave that spot (I got stuck in the library next to the weather book, and a few other places where my icons just dissapeared, looking for orbs).I immediately went to quit the game without realizing that even though I had saved in another slot, it would continue to auto save over my manual save, leaving me trapped on the book case unable to do anything. I had to start over. It was partially my fault for not being more careful, but if you're going to force players to re-search areas having glitches like that are pretty annoying.
On the positive side I found the art very pleasing, And the diary pages' snippets of inhabitant lore very cool. Those two elements very clearly had a lot of hard work and love put into them.
Overall, I don't recommend the game, because pretty art, and tidbits of interesting lore don't make up for the gameplay it lacked.
TLDR;
Pros: nice artwork, some cool world lore.
Cons: unintuitive puzzles and gameplay, lots of wandering around aimlessly, Hard-to-find-for-no-reason orbs, lots of backtracking to pad the game, glitches that may cause you to restart entirely.

It is unfortunate, but this game looks much better on the store than in actual movement.
While the scenery and character design are first rate, 3d modeling and animation leaves plenty to be desired, perhaps the developers should have tried doing the entire thing in 2d since their ilustrator were clearly very talented.
The biggest problem this game has is the lack of narrative. While I can apreciate their attempt to tell a story with no actual dialogue, they werent thorough enough to give me any idea what the hell was going on after the game's intro. I was unable to understand Violett as a character or feel any sort of empathy for her.
In the beggining of the game, it was pretty much impossible to get trough the puzzles without hints, as the first few "rooms" you are presented with make no sense whatsoever, it's like trying to logic your way out of a fever dream.
Also, navigating an Escher maze to get trough the first 4 or so rooms? HATED IT SO MUCH MY BLOOD BOILS AT THE MEMORY.
So, uh, no, if you are a fan of pont and click adventures, look elsewere. This is a great graphical piece anchored down by terrible writting and design.

The game is beautiful. But the logic behind the puzzles" is illogical.  Everything is difficult, simply because the solutions are so far from any classic point n click logic, that it's very frustrating.  For example, there is a puzzle which involves water and pipes.  Violett must activate valves to flow water.  But nowhere is there an indication where the source comes from to know which valve does what. Narrowing down what I thought would be the source pipe, turning valves in certain directions doesn't match with other combinations.  I had give in and use a guide.
In a nutshell, this game is impossible without a walkthrough.
Story progression is messy and lazy. Off the start, we have no idea why Violett is in her "Wonderland".  I almost thought I missed a cutscene.  Violett meets all these characters which have no personality, and somehow as the player, you're supposed to want to solve their convoluted problems. But you don't know why they want help or have any interest.  You just want to get the puzzle done to see more of the game.  Then there's the completely pointless hidden object mechanic.  You can locate hidden orbs throughout the game - which I'm sure do nothing except give you an achievement - no idea.
Oh yes, there's the hint system.  The pathetic hint system - which is a puzzle itself trying to figure what the hand-drawn sketch mean exactly is more frustrating than rewarding.  And it's timed.  You'll find yourself clicking the hint button numerous times, just to get a long enough view of what the picture is supposed to represent.
Such a promising notion - a game with gorgeous visuals and abysmal logic design.  As a fan of Monkey Island, Torrin's Passage, King's Quest, Grim Fandango, Toonstruck, Day of the Tentacle, etc, Violett simply sucks.
The major basic reason Violett fails as a game, is that you puzzles are neither interesting or rewarding. You just want to see get them over with to "see" more of the game.
I couldn't finish the game.  Sadly, this game has multiple bugs.  I came to a part called "Clock Tree" or "Tree Clock", I can't remember. But the game broke.  Violett is supposed to get 3 corks from a black ant.  But the ant and cork have disappeared from the game.  Numerous people have reported this same glitch, and supposedly a game patch came out before I purchased the game to fix this.  Well, it's still broken.  And since the game uses auto-save, apparently the only fix for me to restart the game.  Well, that's not going to happen.  I hope this review helps you avoid this broken game.

The number of times I suspected a joke, had it happen and felt smart just about equals the number of times I suspected nothing and laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off in surprise, and that's excellent.

90’s cartoons + film noir + 90’s video game references.
So there I was browsing the steam store at the beginning of the summer sale, hundreds of games on sale, with crazy deals, like 60-80% off some great games, from great game makers. Plenty of tried and true games for me to buy, from franchises that probably wouldn’t disappoint, but I was looking for something new, something interesting, something I hadn’t played before, and by golley did I find it. So just what is jazzpunk, you say? Well the short answer would be that it’s a walking sim, but the long answer would be a trippy, windy road, full of some of the most distinct hummer I’ve ever seen in a game.

The game opens up by dumping you off of a luggage conveyer belt, into a sweeping montage of abstract imagery, full of Japanese symbols, air planes, and radio waves. It looks like something that could have been taken from the intro of an old western movie, if the motif were jazz, and not the Wild West. When it’s over, you get tossed in something that looks like a 50’ds-60’ds office space, crossed with a train station, and yes you can immediately start talking to boxes that are lying around.
A couple of minutes later and boom you’re in the full swing of the games plot, working as a secret agent  for the “Director”, and his “Secretary”. Right when you sit down on the whoopee cushion, to talk to your new boss, little white cartoonish lines come out of his eyes directing you towards you’re first mission objective, which is to raid some kind of Russian compound. Rite from the get go, you can get a good idea of what this games all about. Then you take you’re happy pills and go off into crazy land. This kind cartoonish hummer is bursting forth from almost every inch of the game. And that’s defiantly its strongest point, unlike most other walking sims this game won’t ever leave you board, whether you’re talking to insane hobos, hipster pies, that where sunglasses, and smok cigarettes, or talking to sexy female robots, there is always some business to poke your nose into. The game is also full of crazy side quests that you can get from talking to said persons such as; destroying clay pots in a fly shop, helping a frog cross the freeway to get his startreck data visor, catching huge spiders in a glass jar, in some Japanese themed restaurant, just to throw them on the cook’s face, who hates spiders.
This game is full of WTF moments that will have you smiling, and laughing out loud, as it pulls out gage after gage, most of which can be traced back to classic Ren and Stimpy cartoon's, and video game hummer. I even remember thinking halfway through the game “Ok, when are they going to start playing The Thieving Magpie theme?” and sure enough, there it was in the final level. But it’s really more than a one trick pony as far as the type of gages the game pulls off. Some of them are dialog based, some teleport you into areas where you are fighting cars, street fighter style in first person, and others are things like pulling an ice alarm, that’s located right next the proper fire alarm. Ice alarm, “for what reason”, one might ask one’s self? Why, for the same reason the hallway right next to it has a caution "greased up floor" sign on it. “Well that doesn’t make any sense.” you might say, however to that I would say, “Nothing in this game makes sense.”, but it's still a blast.
If you’re into shooting pigeon’s with crazy magnet guns taking their guts, and spraying "essence of pigeon" on other people, while other pigeons flock to them, to carry them off into the sky, then you will probably have fun with this game. Perhaps I write this review in vain, as it’s difficult to put into words what this game exactly is, but it’s defiantly worth playing. The only complaint I have is that it’s pretty short, if it had 2-3 more missions it would have been perfect. 9/10

I have seen the changes of Resident Evil series as Capcom is trying to preserve the franchise. RE6 applied most contents from RE4 and 5 with separated campaigns. The scale of story is bigger which is not just about viruses as the game will bring a player to taste the diversity of gameplay and atmosphere. The cut scenes and voice acting are done very well beside from heroic dialogues. The gameplay is improved version of RE5. I’m glad that character can shoot in motion, player control is more fluid and more additional movement; sliding, crawling, rolling. Plus with improved melee combat to fill the taste of hitting them up, but limit the over usage by using combat gauge which is a good solution.
However, RE6 hardly preserves its horror and intense as original RE, but it fails in implementation. Most of horror moments are based on quick-time events rather than survive from zombie hordes. It has, but the game throws player just into small area with enough ammo pile. Yes, it gives intense gameplay but it can frustrate a player at the same time with annoying enemy’s attack patterns or 1-hit kill enemy. Force player to perform non-sense action or dying from delay incapacitated animation (I prefer old button mashing to recover). Beside from bad design of game world, my biggest disappointment is too much QTE and the way they ported the input into PC. The fast switching of QTE pattern can kill player at every moments. Moreover, the camera issues during escape scenes always confuse player and force player to move in opposed direction and get killed. I understand the game want to show terror moment, but this is bad implementation. For the interfaces, I like its design, but the usage is less fluid and I miss original inventory.
Overall, I won’t say RE6 is terrible game; the story and variety of gameplay are interesting including improved Co-op mode like campaign, mercenaries mode are really fun. Agent hunt is also fun and feel like old L4D versus mode (beside from terrible spawn points and zombie delay animation). I feel like RE6 is bit dull product. The campaign setup and based combat are solid, but it still can’t fill the gap between action and horror as the original RE. I have to agree that this is RE we love and hate and I have high hope they will have the right direction in RE7.

After playing this game so much, I know exactly why it has failed. For starters, people need context in-game with survival horror - for example, DayZ tells you 'the zombie apocalypse broke out' and 'Miscreated' tells you that mutants broke out from a military lab, but 'Nether' refuses to do any of this. All that we know, at least from what we kind find walking around in the world, is that society collapsed and a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monsters now roam freely.
Gameplay is pretty simple, combat is decent, and the atmosphere is okay, but the community is incredibly small at best, which really hurts the way the game lasts. With all active players on all servers counted together across a five day time span, I counted around 200 players total at any given time - and while 200 is a lot, it pails in comparison to the hundreds-of-thousands of DayZ players keeping it alive. Without a proper fanbase or community actively participating in this game for long periods of time, I unfortunately can't recommend it.
All of that said, I'd give this game a solid 5.5/10. While it's not a bad game in itself, without an active community I still can't recommend it to others.

I wish I had bought this game sooner!
Hands down the deepest and most intricate melee combat I've seen in any game. It manages to be tactical, but still fast paced and smooth. The world is also beautiful, and the fighting styles for each character/weapon type are all very unique.
I think I know why this game has gotten so many negative reviews lately, so I want to break that down in this review.
Slashers have high skill ceilings and steep learning curves. Dark Messiah Might & Magic Multiplayer, Pirates Vikings and Knights II, War of the Roses, Age of Chivalry, the thing these games all have in common is that an experienced player could reliably deflect the attacks of an inexperienced player.
When most people are used to shooters, where being good still doesn't mean you can stop bullets, this can be a very frustrating change of pace for some people. Top that off with the fact that For Honor has a character progression system. You level up and get new skills and better equipment, etc. For people familiar with games where there is armor and swords, getting better armor and swords and leveling up is pretty standard. But not everyone is used to that.
And where the negative reviews really come in, is that they've basically added a way to exchange dollars for experience and currency. Now, for people who play MMOs, the concept of a subscription offering premium membership, or using an in game store to purchase boosters, this isn't all that crazy. But for people who don't, top that off with the fact that more skilled players are easily defeating them, and thats where all the frustration comes in. So people cry pay to win, not realizing how important it is to parry and dodge and play defensively and tactically in these types of games. They rush in and slash away and get cut down by veterans and teamwork, but blame equipment.
If you enjoy deep melee combat, I strongly urge you to buy this game. (The melee is even better than The Witcher 3, its that good) - personally I think its worth it even at full price, because it is quite simply the best in the genre at this time.
I give it 9/10. -1 because the single player story options are short, basic, and linear. They're fun because the combat is so good, but I'd love to actually take my own character out exploring, and do SP or Co-Op pve content. Hopefully in the future this is something they'll add.
Its Ubisoft, so they certainly have the funds and manpower to add innovative new content like that.

When the original Slender hit, it brought with it a new type of survival horror. Instead of several enemies, or a focus on fighting said enemies, you are simply hunted and helpless as you frantically search for ten notes as Slenderman becomes aggressively interested in you. He would initially stand from a pretty good distance, and decrease his range during teleports depending on how far you got into collecting notes, and when you completed the task, your "yes!" victory is short lived as you are given a full on jump scare at the last minute...the very same one during a Game Over.
Slender: The Arrival, as short as it is, manages to bring the addicting fun and fear from the original concept into a much fuller, and slightly longer game. This is the first indie horror game I've followed from its beta stage well into its alpha, and final release on Steam and was an interesting thing to watch as it was tweaked, given additional material, and for me personally, it was well worth the wait since it was given one final "punch" for the ending, and gives reason for people to play through this again if they've played any previous version.
This game is not for everyone. Not all of the scares or tone will work on everyone, and a majority don't enjoy playing pure survival horror games. If you liked The Last of Us, but hated the classic Resident Evil/Silent Hill games, then this isn't your kind of gaming experience.

Update #2: Alright, almost all my issues with the game have been resolved. The game was patched to be more like the console version, so doors and windows can be opened and closed with a single click, so there's no need to grab them and move them manually. It's much easier to recommend this game now. Everyone needs to play it.
Update: I changed my recommendation to Positive. The game has it's flaws, which I originally seemed to be focused on, but I still find myself drawn to this game. I replayed it again recently, and the flaws were not as big a deal as they were the first couple times I played it. The random spawning of Slender Man is still a problem (I had him spawn on top of me a couple times in Chapter 4), but it's just how the game is. As for the doors and windows, I found there really is not any reason to rush to close them in Chapter 3. You rush to them but if you take your time and are precise with your movements, it is much easier to close them (although the doors sometimes still don't want to behave). So overall, the game is actually pretty good if you don't focus on the flaws like I was. It's a good horror game, and still scares me after multiple playthroughs, just keep in mind that things happen randomly and that has a chance to spoil the atmosphere, but there is no guarantee it will or will not.
Original: This game sounded good when I heard about it, since I love a good horror game. It had potential, but ultimately just could not live up to what it made itself out to be. It had a few good jump scares, especially in Chapter 1, when you're running through a dark park, looking for 8 pages to pick up. Turning a corner and having the Slenderman right in my face was enough to make me jump and almost accidently throw my mouse across the room (as I brought my hand up when I jumped, mouse still grasped). Running through the house in Chapter 3, trying to frantically close doors and windows was also a great method for keeping the player on edge.
These positives also proved to lead to the game's negatives, however. In Chapter 1 and 2, the forest and mine levels, Slenderman (and the Proxy in the mines) can teleport anywhere they please, including right in your path, forcing you to find another way around. This started to become a problem, as the closer you get to completing each chapter, the more frequently they spawn. On both chapters, when I was close to finishing, I ended up constantly running in circles because the enemies kept spawning in my way. I would run toward my objective, and something would spawn in my way, so I would try to circle around the other way, and the same thing would happen. After a while, the fear factor is taken away, and you just start to get frustrated. Both times I ended up having to trick the enemies into spawning elsewhere so I could beeline to the objective and be done. It was just annoying.
Then there's Chapter 3, where you rush to close doors and windows (I won't say why, to not give away any plot). The first time I did it, I was frantic, trying to rush to everything to make sure it was closed. The game uses a mechanic where you have to grab a door and window and manually close it by using it and moving it so that it closes. It sounds good, and realistic, in theory, but it does not work well. Sometimes I would grab the door, and try to close it, and instead she would open it, or it would only close partway. I would spend so much time trying to get a door closed that I would end up failing the chapter and having to retry that part. After multiple failures, it was just frustrating. But then it's also too random on that level. I failed the level several times after having closed 7/8 of the doors and windows. The time I finished the level, I was only at 5/8. That just leads to irritation. Oh, and Chapter 4 mostly abandons the horror it tried to rely through the rest of the game. Ultimately, the game is too random and annoying to be recommended, which is disappointing since it started out with great potential.

Don't let the red thumb discourage you, I really enjoyed this game.
-The art styles are amazing, except for Violett herself, which leads me to believe that they threw her in a point-and-click-adventure game that they were already working on. Seriously, her walk animation looks really silly on some of the paths that they make her take. This is also shown by orbs that are hidden in each scene that don't give the "clickable" mouse when you hover over them, which is the general basis of their replayability: to find all these orbs.
-The music is also well done; it had quite the catchy main theme and enough tracks to have a different song for each area.
-The puzzles not making any sense actually makes sense in the context of the game, as you are a young girl lost in a fantacy world where things really shouldn't make sense. This however, like stated by many of these other reviews, does not create a healthy game environment as a lot of the time you are just clicking objects randomly until the pieces start to "fit" together. To be honest, I only flew right through the first puzzle only because I watched a gameplay demo before playing, however, I was quite tied up on the next room and it took me nearly an hour to figure it out. The only reason I didn't stop there is because I'm a little biased towards it for its resemblence of Coraline, which I absolutely loved.
-The thing I hated most about this game was the minimalistic gameplay, which is expected in a point-and-click adventure game, but this one was even more so. There were only a handful of mini-game puzzles and a couple times where you were timed on your actions, but outside of that, a lot of the time it's just you watching Cor... Violett walk across the screen to where you clicked only to watch her shake her head in shame. But even this didn't come close to how frustrating the end was. It looked like they had created an entire mini-game based around you actually fighting the main antagonist in the game (which really can't be called that because you don't really know it's the antagonist unless you read the flavor-text diary pages) but cut it out last minute and decided to turn it into a "cutscene" by having (spoiler) Violett defeat it in ONE throw of a fireball. JUST ONE ATTACK DEFEATS IT, AND YOU DIDN'T EVEN GET TO DO IT! It was the biggest let down I have ever experienced in a game before, the devs laughing like, "oh you wanted to do this? Too bad!". I'm probably exagurating this too much, as they probably just didn't have the time/will to script the battle scene, which is sad because it looked really fun.
-I didn't run into any glitches that the other reviewers mention, however, there was a point where it seemed like it when she was on a ladder. Other than that, the game ran through it's scenes pretty well.
TL;DR: Great art, seems like it was supposed to be a different game, terrible ending, hard to get into, great for any Coraline/Alice in Wonderland fan if they're persistant.

I just finished playing this game earlier today, I really enjoyed it. I've seen quite a few complaints about the monsters in this game being too hard to navigate. They can certainly be a challenge, but they do have a pattern.
After nearly eight hours in this game, my biggest gripes are more likely to be the puzzles and the invisible stamina restriction. I have a mild love/hate relationship with the puzzles. On one hand, they're unique and always keep me guessing. On the other hand, some of them seem a bit too abstract. Like I would get a piece of code and knew it needed to go somewhere, but didn't have the slightest idea what to do with it. Because of this, I'm ashamed to admit considering I recently just bought it, I used a walkthrough for some of the puzzles. Though the "walkthrough" was more of a guy playing through the entire game, so...
As for the stamina restriction, looking at the game you probably wouldn't see too many reasons to run in it. And technically you'd be right. But the slow pace of the character can become agonizing on longer parts of the game. You have enough stamina to run from monsters long enough to reach the next door, assuming you're not so close that they can insta-kill you. But I advise you not to get into situations where you need to run from a monster. That's how you accidentally get sandwiched by two monsters. :( There are some nice mechanics in various parts of the game to help you scope out an area a bit before walking out into the open. Or decent places to hide, assuming the monster is not hot on your trails. Otherwise, the end in my opinion, would have been a bit more enjoyable if I could just run from one spot to the next.
Those negatives aside, I loved playing this game. It had just enough horror to pique my taste for horror games/movies, while at the same time not being so over the top that I needed to play only during the day in a well lit room. :D And yes, I am a bit of a chicken, but I can't keep myself from playing these types of games sometimes.
As for the technical aspect, the game ran fine for me. I didn't experience any bugs, glitches, or crashes. Everything seemed to be in order. Threads in the community hub made it clear that there may be a glitch here or there, but they seemed to have figured things out.
I must admit, my expectation of indie games is somewhat low, especially when it comes to the visuals. But this game had a consistent look, that exceeded expectations and didn't seem too chaotic. With the only downside being that it's rather easy to miss notes hidden around some of the game.
So to reiterate, I do recommend this game. But it would probably suit individuals that enjoyed the Cat Lady more than it would the average steam user. As this game also deals with the theme of suicide.

A lengthy game that's split into 4 campaigns; length is around 24 hours in total. There's also some multiplayer modes, but no one plays them. The mercenaries mode is as fun as before, and there are 9 characters to pick from, 16 if you count the alternate costumes. As for the campaigns:
Leon: Touted as the best campaign, it's the lengthiest and the 'main' one, since more of the plotline is revealed. Overall decent, some chapters are better than others. Chapter 1 is linear as♥♥♥♥♥♥and a missed opportunity, while chapter 4 and 5 is  the game's crowning achievement.
Chris: zombies with guns; turns into a bland third person shooter in chapter 2; gets good again in the following chapter. Overall the weakest campaign because it tries to be a generic third person shooter.

Slender: The arrival is a horror game made on the Unity engine that plays around with the Slenderman myth.  If you haven't heard of Slenderman, you must have slept under a rock for a couple of years, since this baddy has been around for a while.
The game starts you off as Lauren, a normal, teen-age girl who goes to visit a friend of hers who happens to be in the middle of the woods (Who would've thought).  But, there's a certain, horrifying exception to this friendly greeting.  Slenderman wants to join the party.  Kate, your friend, has gone missing for a while, and as you uncover her secret, you regret every thought about her.
For the most part, the game is pretty terrifying.  If you've ever played a Slender game before, you'll get the basics pretty quickly, but some of the scares will probably be less effective towards you.  There are seven levels in total, including an easter egg level that messes with your head, with two more levels to be added at a later date.  Along with the similar controls, you'll find the gameplay to be also very similar to the other Slender games, which is disappointing.  I was hoping that they would add something new or have a new mechanic that's nececessary to play, but most of the levels are usually, "Collect 8 Pages", or "Close all windows and doors".  It detracts from the experience, but still keeps you on the edge of your seat at all times.
Slenderman isn't the only creature that is present.  Characters such as proxies, Slenderman's slaves who were previous victims of the Slenderman, are present in some levels.  Oh, and one thing to point out.  This and Marble Hornets are NOT connected in any way!  People are confusing characters with Masky and Hoody from the youtube channel.  Even though the writers of Marble Hornets are working on this, the stories aren't tied.  Just wanted to get that out.
Overall, the game is a terrifying game with some replay value as the scares are always randomized and even sometimes likes to break the fourth wall.
+ Vewy Scawey
+ Some Replay Value
+ New levels Added Occasionally
- Repetitive Gameplay
8/10: Highly Recommended

Slender: The Arrival is a first person adventure game. You are only equipped with a flashlight. You have to explore various locations and search for clues to your friend's whereabouts, while avoiding an unspeakable fate at the hands of Slender man himself. On your way you can pick up various papers that give you background information on the story, or clues.
There are no problems with controls and everything feels very smooth. The game itself is too short, it takes around 1 hour to finish.
The graphics are good, you will not be disappointed. Slender Man himself looks awesome, in my opinion this is the best Slender Man model of every Slender game. Everything else in the game, from the trees, to the rocks and so on looks pretty well, no complaints here.
The music is great, it really adds to the experience. You can hear that slow thumping in the background from the original Slender game when you pick up that first page in one of the levels. The sound effects are also good, sometimes you will hear the sounds of footsteps from someone or something other than you in the forest close by, or you will hear the Owls hooting at night, and other various forest sounds.
I can recommend Slender: The Arrival to people who wants a good fun scare or a nice horror game and of course all fans of the original Slender Man game. Fans of the original Slender will be happy to know that the original game is remade in one of the levels.

A tragic tale of poor 14 year old Mike left at home to fend for himself as his parents decided to leave him behind as they travel to Mexico. Little Mike is not alone however, as the neighborhood creeper girl Francisca insists on playing a terrifying game of hide-and-seek with him each and every night.
As I load up the first night, I can see that Mike is clearly in distress as he stomps around the house in his Megatron boots which make enough noise to wake up everyone in a 10 mile radius. The poor boy has also left out not only the milk, but orange juice as well. The sudden shock of his parents straight up ditching him has caused trauma to a degree so great that he's forgotten to put these basic necessities back into the fridge. As I jounrey further into the house, I continue to see things that are clearly not right here. Poor Mike doesn't even have a bedroom of his own, which further raises the question....if his parents can afford not only a trip to Mexico, but 4 4k HD cameras for him to play with, why couldn't they afford a bedroom for him?
Picking up the present left by the girl starts this terrifying life-or-death game of hide and seek, to which Mike only has one clear option, the closet. He jumps inside, shuts the doors, and closes his eyes. This stumps Francisca as she wanders all over the house, but never thinks once to open the closet Mike is in. This game goes on for 7 days, and on each day, Mike choses the same closet over and over, and by great delight, he triumphs over Francisca who is officially the worst hide and seek player in history, no wonder no one wanted to play with her.
In conclusion, Francisca is a game with a great Slenderman-ish idea, but poor execution. The girl's AI is laughable at best and the 4 cameras you're given to "track her" are completely useless, as she can just seemingly teleport wherever she wants in the house. So please, save your dollar on another game. My biggest regret is going over the 2 hour limit, so I can't refund it myself.

Its actually not bad, a fun combination of Third person shooting and platforming. Its an especially good game for kids or teens who want play shoothers but arent allowed or dont want to play M-rated games, but i can also recommend it to just about anybody. the difficulty is quite scalable making it challenging enough for pro`s yet can be simple enough for kids and you can also challenge yourself as a player by speedrunning, ignoring ammo-upgrades, etc.
I have to commend this game for how it handles its license, it doesnt follow the original storyline, you dont get any awkward zoo scene or other unnecessarily cheesy scenes(maybe a few, but not nearly as many as the movie had). the game cuts right to the good part, fighting deadly robotic appliances and you get some neat guns and an electro whip to do it with. the people who made this game knows that film is different from video games and there`s a really healthy dose of fast, fluid gameplay. mouse control works as you`d expect it too from a TPS, gamepad integration is decent. i dont think the controls are the best they can be and you do notice that PC was not the target platform, but its completely playable.
graphically, it looks decent enough. textures are kind of small, environments are sterile and fairly basic. appliances lok decent though and special effects are pretty good. it also supports 4K resolution through downsampling or Nvidia`s Dynamic Super Resolution and the game is fairly easy to run 4K@60fps. there`s no graphics options for PC other than resolution so shame about that.
the price is a little high, but if you can get behind that and want to play a fun, fresh shooter-platformer hybrid with high focus on gameplay. G-force doesnt dissapoint, its fairly long too at about 10 hours or so

If you are a bit skeptical about a game that can match notes you play on a real guitar to a programmed map of said notes in a game I wouldn't blame you at all; however, this game does it pretty well.  Now, there are some small holes that show up from time to time, like how sometimes you can get away with strumming 8 notes for every 10 and still hit every note, or how the game has trouble detecting the lower notes (usually on lower tunings) on your guitar and tells you its too quiet even though the volume knob is maxed out.  BUT you can immediately forgive all of that when it actually works as a learning tool.
I didn't think the game would really improve my guitar skills (which were average at best) but I thought it would still be a nice distraction for awhile.  Was I wrong...so wrong.  If you don't have problems buying the previous version and some dlc (there are some really good songs, but sadly most of the ones you might want are dlc $3 a song) you will find plenty of variety to keep you interested.  Also, while the game does start out slow, it ramps up the difficulty quite nicely at a pace that never really gets uncomfortable.  You will be challenged to do things you might never have been comfortable doing before, like hammer-ons and string skipping at a decent pace, but will rarely feel overwhelmed (note i said rarely, it has happened a couple times).  I was finding myself getting better every day being able to play faster and more precise, slowly mastering songs I liked to play and challenging myself to play songs outside of my comfort zone (genre wise).
In conclusion, it is a lot of fun and is very effective at making you a better guitarist.  My only advice would be to not let yourself get frustrated if you find yourself having trouble playing at times when the game decides to push the difficulty up a bit.  If you push, you will master it and become better.  Also, don't try to exploit things you might discover to make it easier.  That kind of ruins the point.

Fabulous game - I had never played guitar before, and because of this game (and its not nearly as good predecessor) now I do.  If you've never played before, you'll only be asked to play one note every once in a great while, and when you're consistently successful at playing that note, another note or two will be added. Keep getting it right, and eventually you're playing the actual song.  That said, you can adjust the 'difficulty' (how close what you're playing is to the actual song) whenever you like, and there's a phenomenal practice tool at your fingertips known as the 'Riff Repeater'. Simply press a key, and you are set to repeat a section of the song (or if you choose all sections, the entire song at once). For the practice you can set difficulty , speed, whether those will increase on success, what defines success (perfect, up to 1 mistake, etc.). how many times you have to get it right for one of those to increase, etc.
Also includes an excellent selection of interactive 'lessons' - teaching segments with exercises to reinforce what you've learned.  These start at how to hold your pick, and go up through things like 2-handed tapping. There are also some 'Guitarcade' games, which are skill-building exercises packaged as mini games. While these start to feel repetitive pretty quickly, they'll be entertaining for a while.
Lastly, every single week they release 3 to 5 new songs as DLC, from classical favorites that they've adapted themselves (the 'Bachsmith' pack), to Iron Maiden, Cake, Maroon 5, or Albert King. Pretty much everyone will find something they'll really enjoy.
I love the game, but on a pretty decent Mac some things can be buggy. Either way, it's one of the best video games ever.

Resident Evil 6 is hard to recommend but it is just as hard not to. At its best, RE6 is a weird, ambitious and drop-dead gorgeous game. At its worst, it is a mess that tries to be everything to all people at once. It is instantly obvious just how much effort went into making this game. The attention to details borders on maniacal, with each character even having a different UI. There is an incredible amount of content, with four distinct campaigns clocking at about 25 hours in total. In addition to that, there are various multiplayer modes, such as Mercenaries, and the entire game can be played in co-op.  Resident Evil 6 also features a number of inventive mechanics and some of the best animations I've ever seen. Nevertheless, it is definitely not beginner-friendly due to a lack of meaningful tutorials and explanations: needless to say, the game is more of a brawler than a cover shooter, despite all evidence to the contrary. Ultimately, Resident Evil 6 is a game of ideas, it's just a shame that a lot of them are terrible. Still, there's a good game in here somewhere and you certainly can't fault Capcom for a lack of scope or ambition. Given the poor reception, I don't think there will ever be another game like RE6 but the PC edition is the definitive version of the game, thanks to additional features such as the L4D2 crossover. Give it a shot!

Resident Evil 6 is the current latest numbered-entry in the long-running action-game series from Capcom. RE series (Resident Evil) has been evolving & moving further away from its survival-horror roots and more so into action-game territory with each entry - and in many people's opinions, this has been ringing more & more true with every entry since RE4. Regardless of what you may think of the changes in direction, there's one question still lingering: as a game, whatever it may be, is RE6 actually any good?
To answer the above question, one must also ask this: what does one actually want out a Resident Evil game? Do you want that Resident Evil 4 & 5 level of awesome action-packed gameplay and style? Leon's campaign certainly delivers this - and I think is the best overall campaign in the game; especially in the gameplay department. Leon's campaign is nothing short of awesome. Are you looking for an action-packed shooter-game w/ that "bro-feel" w/ lots of soldiers (that are AI) often surrounding you and often comes across feeling like Call of Duty and Gears of War games often does? RE6 has that - and it has its own twist on that, since you do have Resident Evil elements (i.e. Inventory and can combine items); well, Chris Redfield's campaign delivers this.
What else would you like in a Resident Evil game? Do you want a more hand-to-hand & melee-based, more-acrobatic, more stealthy experience, and some driving element with some of the well-known Resident Evil elements? Jake's campaign certainly delivers this. Would you like a more single-player style campaign (if you play it w/out another player) that has similar elements to Jake's campaign, but also actually has some puzzle elements like other survival-horror games do? Ada's campaign delivers this. Not only that, but Ada's campaign has the actual best story in the game - delivering more elements of story-telling; big twists and reveals; and filling-in many of the gaps that were left lingering from the other 3 stories.
Do you like all of these types of games? Then, certainly, this game's definitely for you. Then, the "sums of its parts" factor will certainly speak to you, as it delivers all of these gameplay experience and does them all very well. Because each campaign often feels so different and so focused on different gameplay elements and styles - RE6, in a sense, often feels like 4 different Resident Evil games rolled into one entire ridiculously huge package.
All of these campaigns, they can be played with Co-Op, if you like. All of these options can be set, when you load-up a saved game or start-up a brand new game. Each character has a partner with them, where the partner can be played by the game's AI (for all you offline and/or solo gamers) or even be played by another player online (for all you Co-Op gamers). Ada's campaign is the exception - as that is a solo-campaign by herself and without an AI partner if played solo (as it was originally built) - but it can be a Co-Op experience if you want to play online with a partner.
(SIDE NOTE: The option to make Ada's campaign an additional Co-Op experience was added later by the dev's). In an interesting twist on things - when playing online, gamers can play a monster in certain parts of the game and invade other player's actual game at certain times.
One of the best & worst things this game has going for it and against it is its overlapping story & intersecting elements. You might run through an area again entirely that you did in another campaign - and it might not be much different; or you might do a different actual one part of the map in one campaign, but then a different part of the map - and it feels totally different, until they intersect somewhere, if they actually intersect. Chris's campaign does the same exact certain boss fight a few times (which is overly repetitive); and then we run into this same exact boss fight with Jake. The problem here is - you pretty much play this same boss fight the same exact way every time, whether you're doing Jake's campaign or Chris's campaign.
Now in another campaign, you might do the same boss fight - but you're doing it as a different character with a different element and role to it, making it another kind of awesome. For example - in Leon's campaign, you do a boss fight on the ground like you normally would in a typical action game and shoot it on-foot, even though other characters are there and have a different role; while in Ada's campaign, you do this boss fight totally in a helicopter, shooting the enemy & firing missiles. You can always skip cut-scenes, which is a plus, if you don't want to see the same cut-scenes when any of the overlapping of the 4 stories take place. It's unfortunate that if you did a boss-fight on one campaign already, there's no option just can't skip that same boss-fight in another campaign - especially if the roles for the characters aren't too much different and you don't want to go through the repetition. It's when your character has a completely different role and element entirely, that you actually will really want to do the boss fight.
The graphics in this game are pretty good, for the most part. While the character models and especially the monsters are all excellent-looking, all loaded with detail galore and plenty of excellent art direction; it's the in-game textures for the objects in-game areas that can be of low-quality, when up-close. While game-areas and environments its art direction often do look great, it's the details within them that can vary. Thankfully, RE6 is not in a case like a Bioshock game would be in - where the signs, posters, and anything that's on them is important and need to be seen and read at its best quality, all so you can gather more detail and information about the game's story, lore, and get immersed in its game-world.
Most of the story-telling is told via cut-scenes and while playing in-game - and there certainly is plenty of this. While each story itself on its own is actually good - it's b/c of the overlapping of its stories, which makes this great. A lot of things that may not add-up entirely in one campaign, this can only be realized only from playing a different campaign entirely. Ada's campaign ties together a lot of the story elements, filling in most of the gaps and blanks that might've been lingering and left-over from the other 3 campaigns. Once a chapter is unlocked and finished, gamers can jump to any Chapter and even replay them. You are graded for how you perform in each campaign - so fans of this game and perfectionists might want to replay the game and certain chapters just for those reasons alone. If that isn't enough, the game has an experience system where players can upgrade specific skills for each character and actually roll all of that into New-Game+ Mode.
After 33 hours of gameplay and taking on its 4 different campaigns - where two of them are at least good and try something different for a RE game (Jake's campaign & Chris's campaign); one campaign is absolutely an fantastic campaign especially for its gameplay (Leon's campaign); and one campaign that is a stand-out just for telling the best story of the bunch and giving us the most clarity (Ada's campaign) - this game is an absolute flawed-gem of an action game. If it wasn't for some of the repetitive boss-fights & certain areas that couldn't be skipped when tackling another campaign (b/c you feel like you've done some of this before), this game would be absolute masterpiece. The "sum of its parts" factor in many ways are often what makes this game as great as it is - but in a few other ways, that also can be one of its few minor flaws. Resident Evil 6 is experimental, ambitious, grand, epic, and ridiculously huge in scope - and because of this, it might not always deliver the best Resident Evil experience, but it most of the time will deliver such an experience.
Final Grade = B

Unreal Estate caught my eye because of the tags and price. I love board and card games and hoped that this game would be a good addition to my Steam collection. For the price, I'm happy with the purchase.
Each player is trying to build fairy tale style buildings for their city. They do this by pairing building cards they picked up from the center of the board with other buildings in the scrap pile. The points are determined by the point value of the cards, the amount of cards the player is pairing, and the number of similar cards stacked in the scrap pile. Whomever has the most points at the end of the round wins. Specialty cards can be drawn and played to help players accumulate points throughout each round.
Unreal Estate can be played with two to four people. You can play with AI.
Pros:
- Simple mouse controls.
- Easy to play once you understand the rules and scoring.
- Rounds are quick.
- Specialty cards are randomized each round, so there is some variety.
- Single player AI are some-what challenging but not impossible to beat.
- Screen is easy to look at throughout play.
- Cards are easy to read.
- Audio is pleasant but easily to turn off if you like listening to other things while you play games.
- Rulebook is always accessible before and during gameplay.
- Works well on computers that aren't powerful.
Cons:
- No tutorial.
- No local multiplayer.
- Because few people know about the game, online multiplayer with strangers is impossible.
- Not enough variety to maintain one's attention for long periods of time.
- There is a specialty card that gives you points for all the cards in the scrap pile. Good card. But if you're playing with AI and an AI goes after the card is played, the point counter will cover the card that the AI is playing. It's a momentary cover-up, but it's still a cover-up none-the-less.
For $2.99, Unreal Estate is a great buy for card game fans. Even if there were no changes made to the game, I could recommend it to people looking for an easy card game to play with others, even AI.
If there are any significant updates to the game, I will update my review.

Overall a fun card game I find myself playing when I don't have a lot of time, but I want to do something fun. It is easy to learn and fun to play. For the asking price, this game is well worth it if you enjoy card games.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 was like a trucker business sim, with long stretches of road and jobs to take on and get paid so you can buy/upgrade trucks or start your own business.  Picking up trailers or delivering them was always really easy, so it wasn't challenging enough to be interesting and the long stretches of road were populated enough with details to be somewhat convincing, but it gets old after a while.  The real star of Euro Truck Simulator 2 was the fantastic traffic AI and dealing with traffic respectfully throughout your travels.  A great game for what it is.
Scania Truck Driving Simulator is made by the same company, but this time it focuses on everything about truck driving that is technical.  There are truck driving license tests, there are championship truck driving competition challenges (exact copies of real life events) which require extreme precision and there are short refined stretches of dangerous drives to attempt more like natural obstacle tracks.
I ate a lot of penalties for minor collisions, but some of the challenges were tricky just to finish at all due to very particular trailer angling requirements around certain bends.  You're forced to understand what each mirror is for and gain an appreciation for them, putting them to regular use.  Through-out the game, you come to understand some of the strategies necessary to accomodate for the semitrailer.
While it has all those challenge modes, it also has a couple freeroam modes similar to a large city in ETS2 that have trailer missions to pick up and medals to collect if you can find them.  Certainly the most casual of the modes, it does not have ETS2's lengthy 30 minute drive requirements and instead focuses more on quick pickup and deliveries with technical driving aspects.
If trucks don't interest you this probably won't change that, but if you care a little bit then you are likely to come out of it feeling elucidated in respect to trucking.

Scania Truck Driving Simulator (STDS), plain and simple: Do you need help handling your truck? STDS is a game dedicated to helping improve your understanding of truck and trailer handling. If that doesn't interest you, well, I can't make you stay. The rest of the review will be about the gameplay, so buckle up. Or get ready for a nap.
Most of you here must've played Euro Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2) to even be remotely interested in this. Don't be ashamed, this game was mostly forgotten when Euro Truck Simulator 2 came out. Why buy this when ETS2 is obviously newer and better? However, it will be on sale until 15th July, 2014, so if you play Euro Truck Simulator 2, you won't regret buying this.
First, the gameplay. The gameplay varies from simple driving tutorials to driving on dangerous mountain roads. The game gives you thorough practice on the art of trailer reversing, so if you're struggling with that in Euro Truck Simulator 2 (especially multiplayer mod!) then I will recommend this game for you. But do not think you are playing ETS2. Play the game, how you would any other new game. Expect a new game. Obvious, but true.
The handling of the truck (Scania R-series) is different to that in ETS2. The truck feels heavy, underpowered. In fact it might be. But the game isn't about power, or speed. It is about precision and agility, or sometimes even pure luck. Speed is not a big factor in the game. It is perfect if you need to learn about how your trailer behaves on and off the road, whether you try to turn a tight corner or reverse into a loading dock.
That was for comparison to ETS2. Now, onto the game itself. I will recommend you go from top to bottom of the menu list, after adjusting the options.
Driving Licence gives you basic tutorial lessons on truck driving. If you are new to trucking games, this will be a quick introduction, and it can be challenging. If you are confident with your driving skills (looking at you, ETS2 players), play this section regardless. While ETS2 focuses more on freeroaming and company-building, STDS focuses on handling and precision driving (not necessarily at speeds), and the two games are different based on those values.
Driver Competition would be next in line after you finish Driving Licence. You are entered into a competition where you must complete tasks in a showground, while getting around lots of obstacles and without collisions. It will test what you learned previously, and it will also test your patience to the max. Of course, if you're not a perfectionist, things can be a bit less annoying for you.
Dangerous Drives feature a range of locations with real-world challenges, from natural disasters to manmade ones. There are a few hours of content in the section, again, depending on whether you want to perfect every challenge or not.
Freeform Driving is self explanatory, you can deliver cargo in a freeroaming, exploring manner, although the area is not quite as big as other open-world trucking games in the SCS family. It is not the game's primary focus.
Time Reaction Test is also self explanatory, in this section you can test your reaction times. How quickly can you step on the brake pedal when the unexpected occurs?
Overall, the game is a content-rich tutorial into the world of trucking. If you are unfamiliar with how trailers behave when you travel in reverse, or to get a feel of the size of trucks (believe me, you'd be surprised at how much space you actually have), or just plain driving for the fun (and thrill of it!), then I recommend this game for you.

Not a large sandbox world for free roaming like Euro Truck Simulator 2, but in this game the sandbox plays second fiddle to challenges and hazardous courses, and they ARE good. It would be nice to have it all in one game, but if you like ETS2 a lot, you will enjoy Scania Truck Simulator too. I compare it to ETS2 a lot, and for good reason, the games are similar and attract similar gamers except Scania has little mainstream appeal in comparison.
Pros
- hazardous roads are good areas that are really missing from a game like ETS2.
- driving school and competition challenges are well done. Some are very difficult!
- graphics are as good if not better than ETS2. Some people miss the fact that Scania is actually an older game
- the game world is smaller but it is detailed (makes ETS2 look generic in comparison)
- bonus content (actual competition photos and videos are good stuff)
- there is still a sandbox mode to free-roam in, though...
Cons
- smaller and inferior sandbox compared to ETS2 (not bad, but ETS2 is just that good)
- driving physics feel inferior to ETS2
[EDIT] - After playing more i find slippery roads and mud to be better than i first thought, so overall physics are quite good.
- fewer customisation options (can't set brake sensitivity, disable speed limiter, "pretty up" your truck)
- game engine lacks some touches (water splash for ex.) Though i played with the relatively crappy Intel HD4000 IGP, so take that into consideration.
Overall i'd recommend the game. It won't dissapoint, but it wont blow your mind either. A solid "niche" game worth picking up if you're into realistic driving sims.

When I first saw this game on Kongregate, it was something of an odd ball. Just make up some name, jump in, and the servers would connect you with a couple dozen other players going through the same dozen maps to collect cheese and bring it to the hole. Simple. I first thought of it as some odd sociology expiriment, as almost all the maps at the time seemed to be testing the players. Half of them allowed players to go very quickly through it, but doing so would jeporadize the other mice. I didn't expect it to last a year, and yet in the year 2015, it stands.
So what's changed since then? Well, the community makes maps, of which there are now thousands of unique ones. Shamen have been given more interesting puzzles to work with, combined with skill trees to make interesting possibilities, along with Hard and Divine mode. Mod support is in, shown through the wide variety of rooms you can join. If you want to hone your skills as a normal mouse, Bootcamp will whip you into shape. If you want to be able to survive troll shamen, Survivor can show you the tricks to that. Music allows for users to submit Youtube videos to be watched by all the occupants, and there's more yet. Tribes are a thing, if you want to have friends collaborate for fun. The cosmetics channel true TF2 spirit by allowing you to alter the appearance of your mouse with a long line of items that all can be bought with in-game cheese. Events are brought about every holiday of the year, adding some new aspect to the game. Emotes became a thing, so you no longer need to pretend to sit or cry, because you can actually sit and cry.
And you know what? It doesn't seem to be stopping. It just keeps going, showing true devotion to the style of having a simple, fun game. Just by playing as a mouse, getting some nice, tasty cheese.

This used to be a negative review but due to upcoming changes and the devs finally trying to break the turtle meta i've decided to change it.
The game is gorgeous. Animations are fantastic, the maps look great and the character models are stellar.
Each season they are adding new maps and the most recent maps i spent a good 20 minutes in a bot game just exploring them. They are truly fantastic.
The combat system is intuitive and despite the turtle meta that grew it still is a brilliant system that feels great to use.
Each character is unique with different classes fufilling different niches and the variety between each character inside each class means using a different character than your main feels new and fresh every time.
Balancing is rather chaotic. The gap between the bottom tier characters and the top tier ones is incredibly vast. Hopefully now that that the defensive meta changes are coming characters will be buffed and nerfed to a reasonable level. Bear in mind it has been a long wait to see these changes and may take even longer to balance characters properly, understandably.
Customization is ok. The variety for weapons is amazing, armour not so much. Don't get me wrong the armour models are ace but there's not enough variety between the early tier sets and the late tier. Mostly it's the same models with spikes or studs added.
Character emblems and colouring is a basic yet elegant system but being tied to the rep system feels like an arbritrary reward with not much impact on how your character looks.
Disconnections are apparently quite common. I've never experienced one myself but a decent enough amount of people on reddit have stated they have so I feel i should put this in as a warning. I should also mention the devs have stated they will be implementing dedicated servers to improve stability in the long run.
Honestly I really enjoy this game. It has it's problems, there is no denying that but I truly believe it's a game worth playing. Heck my hours speak for themselves.
Hopefully going forward the issues that are present continue to improve and the game gets the care and attention it deserves.
The devs really do care about the game. Their weekly livestream proves that.
They're cautious and each big update that truly goes towards improving the game feels agonizingly slow, but I have no doubt that they will continue to work on the issues that the game has.

Francisca is one of the very few "dollar" horror games that've cropped up on Steam, being released in late July 2016 by publisher/developer BiscuitPlay. For such a low price, it's hard for a horror fiend such as myself to resist checking it out. The basic story is that you play as a 14 year old kid named Mike, whose parents have gone to Mexico for a week. Prior to this, Mike has been hearing strange noises around his new home.
The gameplay is rather basic, you have four cameras on tripods that you set up around your house and then observe their feed through your tablet. Once you answer the knock at the front door and grab the present, Francisca is unleashed. She screams and begins sporadically popping in and out of rooms. The ultimate goal is to avoid her entirely to survive the night, which is about five minutes. When she is close to you,your fear meter rises and if your fear meter reaches 100, it's game over. Oh, and when you're too far away... the meter goes up as well, so don't think you can cheat and stay outside of the house the whole time. It's a ridiculous concept.
Now, this game is an obvious rip-off of Five Night's at Freddy's; honestly, Steam, I thought we were over this garbage cropping up around the place... I guess not. There is a tiny, smidgen of difference, since instead of sitting in a stagnant spot you can actually move around. Overall, Francisca is a very boring experience and a poor excuse for a "horror" game. There is no horror, there's not even a lame jumpscare, and Francisca herself doesn't even look remotely scary; quite honestly, I laughed the first time I saw her and her block bobble-head.
Did I mention that this game is brought to you by Unity: Personal Edition? Yeah, that's right, so expect AWFUL optimization. I have an i7 6700k + GTX 1080 rig, this game dipped into the 20 FPS for me; to put that in perspective, I can run The Witcher 3 at all max settings and still maintain 100+ FPS at all times. This is absolutely unacceptable, even for a dollar, show some pride in your work.
I won't even comment on the terrible English translations in the game. Too long, didn't read? Francisca is a mostly Five Night's at Freddy's clone with minor additives that still manages to have incredibly boring gameplay. It doesn't deserve to be classified as a "horror" game since there are simply no horror elements included. The game has terrible optimization, and sees sub-30 FPS on THE current highest end graphics card. There are so many better games that you can get for a dollar, like Blood and Bacon. Avoid this completely and don't pay for someone's awful Year One project, you won't regret your decision. I honestly have no idea how this game has gotten 80+ positive reviews so far.

A true review by one who has faced the NETHER.
I steered clear of this game for along time. The pictures looked cool, The idea sounded fun, but other reviews kept me from getting it. Then I saw that the developers had changed and I went under recent reviews, saw alot of thumbs up, saw the game was 5 bucks and said time to try it.
How the game works: You start the game and must deliever a package,..about 3 in all for the tutorial. These packages are randomly throughout the safe zones (a place where you cannot kill or be killed by other players, monster etc) Delievering packages earns you expeirence and money. The XP is used to make your character stamina, strength, stealth, etc higher. The money is used to purchase guns, ammo, gear, backpacks, etc. Its basically grinding to make your character stronger. Like some kind of world of warcraft game these safezones have NPC shop keepers, who never move or say anything. Once you have what you need, guns and things of the sort ( you can essentially carry 1 ranged weapon, 1 side arm, and 1 melee weapon) you go off to kill other players and monsters of the world. WARNING: If you die, you lose it ALL. I mean EVERYTHING..your character was level 30 and you could run fast and far, not anymore..level 1. Cant run for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and have lost all you worked for.
The NETHER
They are something not of this world, they sound great, there seems to be about 5 or 6 different types, and they teleport around while you shoot at them. You have your flyers, bosses, screaming one that charge right at you, some spit, goliaths that look like the Hulk, Wierd zombie ones that explode and arent fast. There is a variety. Safezones can become under attack by hordes of them if the anti nether devices in the safezone fail. (they are electronic thingamajigs that prevent the Nether from being able to come into the area) It will require teamwork in order to get the safezones back up and running. There are Nether surges where they become more frequent in certian areas. Some areas of the map have them all over the place and they never stop comming. No matter how many you kill. Other parts of the map, you may not see them at all, or will see them randomly. If they hit you, it can be devasting, you get around 1,000hp and a single hit can bring you down 300 to 400hp. So get smacked 2 or 3 times and your done. However guns are very effective often requiring 1 to 5 shots to kill them.
LOOT
You can find loot in the world, just like any other survival game, If something has loot in it like a car, it blinks and it shiney, I do not like they way they did the loot, Im use to actually hunting for items, checking under beds etc, and at first it was a turn off, and it felt odd, but after you get an hour or so under your belt, you just get use to it. And it doesnt matter as much anymore, Im sure they will change it later on in the alpha. Loot can be sold at traders for pennies on the dollar. Hunger system is 1 system, so rather you drink water, or eat canned food it all goes toward the same thing. There are alot of different helmets but as far as your body, it cant be changed much. The small amount of body customization will be done at the character menu not in game. Also at the moment whatever you get (like a new helmet or mask) you must log out and then log back in for it show up on your chracter.
MAP
When you first look at it and are new it looks huge. However alot of it isnt accessible at the moment. And so it slowly shrinks as you figure it out and increase speed and stamina to cover distances quicker. The city is done really well. I praise the visuals. Small things like grass overgrown on the roads, abandoned cars parked in traffic jams for miles. Giant skyscrapers that you can get to the top of. Its the small things..going into a room and seeing 2 dead bodies on the ground clinging to one another showing their finals moments spent on earth holding each other in comfort. Its a great atmosphere, black smoke billowing from building that can be seen for miles. Downed resue choppers still burning. Police barricades no longer in service. Its all there, its all really cool. I praise the draw distance, something that I cannot say for a game like H1z1. There is a city area, its decent sized, bigger then any city in any other game including arma/dayz. But as I said the map itself is smaller. The other area would be right outside the city, some kind of marshes, or lowlands. Its not as interesting to me, but its a change of pace and still not bad. Ambulances have lights still flashing, and some signs still flicker like at gas stations etc.
Mechanics
Gun play is suprisingly good. Its smooth, its solid, and it feels out of place because I am use to crappy gun play like h1z1. ( I like h1z1 btw) shooting is actually fun and you feel as if you have full control. Another interesting concept is tribes. You can join a tribe, there is around 10 tribes. This gives you allies in the form of your fellow pvp killers. There is a PVE mode aswell, I recommend starting there until you udnerstand the game. There is enough in it to make it worth while without getting bored right off the bat becuase the NETHER can be fun to fight. There are buildings that you can capture, and take from other tribes. If you do this, the surrounding area becomes your territory. The benifit of this, is you get extra rewards. Example...find 30 bucks in your territory and get an extra 15 dollars intop of it as a bonus. Find 30 bucks in an unfriendly territory and you only get 30 bucks. There are random world events that take place such as Nether surges, bosses, and ofcourse safezones being attacked. At whichpoint you can enter the safzone guns ablazing. Something you are robbed of when it isnt under attack. There are vehicles in the game, But I know nothing of them I didnt even see or hear one til hour 10 of gameplay when I heard the roar of an engine looked out a window and some dude rolled by in a buggy or something. So, apparently there is a way to get a car.
FINAL THOUGHTS
For 5 bucks...snatch this game up!!!!!!!! Micro transactions and alot of the things listed in the negative reviews when the other developer had it are GONE. And I quote the new developer (who was the original developers and sold it then saw the abomination there game had become and took it back) "we got rid of that microtransaction ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" I like when somebody refers to it in such a way. I never played or owned it during the bad times, so I dont know what was going on with the game then, But I hope this review makes it to the top, to negate the other reviews that were accurate at the time and good reviews but are now no longer relevant. The story is told via a narrator who recites both what the characters are saying and thinking, much like listening to an audio novel. The approach works well, and serves to anthromorphize characteristics onto what would otherwise be blank slates.
The game is short, and relatively easy - it can be beaten in around 3 hours with nothing additional left to see. That being said, it's a thoroughly enjoyable experience, and I think pretty much anyone would be able to have some fun playing it.

This is a line quoted in the game, and is a line that aptly describes the dilemma faced by you, as a player, within the near-dystopian society of
. You are observing people's curated online profiles for meaningful information. You can never truly understand the motivations of someone by looking at their Timeline™ profile or through their indirect account of events after the fact. Time is ticking forwards, however, and with a looming public threat, theres no choice but for you to decide for yourself what the truth is.
is a well-crafted investigative thriller about your job as a newly assigned investigator for a government surveillance system known as Orwell. This system allows you free access to bank accounts, emails, text messages, personal contacts, location history and the like, on the condition that these have been referenced in previously accessed data. This results in a thorough perusal of a network of people and their online interactions in order to unravel a terrorist threat.
The gameplay might not be for everyone as its storytelling consists of reading other peoples text messages and Facebook posts, but trust me, it is a lot more fun than it sounds. The music is an area that is lacking, as if you've played
crime thriller game, you've pretty much heard the main soundtrack already, although the thunderous track that plays upon discovering a major lead does an amazing job at adding to the "
" factor of a huge reveal. The interesting premise is complemented by a charming presentation and gripping pacing that keeps you both tense and hungry for more. I found myself leaning forward in my seat in both anticipation and fear of what I might find out next.
I dare not say more lest I ruin the intricacies of the story, but it does leave you questioning your own morality regardless of the choices you make. The story itself does not set out to chart unexplored territory -with its themes of the moral ambiguity of government surveillance, and the nuances of truth in social media- but if you are someone who can appreciate a uniquely deft approach to storytelling, then
is an amazing buy.

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it.
The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.
The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.
Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

I don't think I met one puzzle that I felt was completely stupid, just lots that were a little too complicated or where I had been right but clicking slightly off. The achievements are bugged; the wardrobe one doesn't trigger no matter how many times I change, and other people have lots of trouble getting a particular puzzle's achievement. The full journal one actually triggers BEFORE I get all the pages, as soon as I get the last page, in fact. (I went back and found more that I'd missed.) The graphics are fantastically pretty.
But, that's about all I can wholehearedly endorse about Violett.  The best puzzle-adventure games use subtle signalling to show the user what's possible and have a sort of internal logic and consistency.  Violett is not really one of these games.  There were a number of really nice "Oh hey, this situation reminds me of this thing I saw a couple rooms back maybe I can use that oh look it worked" bits, but maybe 20% of the time what you were required to do made no sense at all and it just degenerated into "click random things on the screen until something changes."  Especially the parts where there are several on/off switches strewn about the screen and you get to guess which ones should be set which way.
They probably knew this sort of thing happened, which is why they put in the hinting system.  Unfortunately, even if you take the hint for what you're supposed to do there's still no guarantee that you can actually do it: the controls are often fidgety and difficult to get to work with a mouse, something that was especially frustrating in the later parts of the game where you had to actually time actions properly.  I'm guessing the controls were actually designed for a tablet of some sort.
The first part of the game is by far the most irritating, due to needing to getting used to the controls and on account of the illustration-based explanation style.  Probably they did that in order to avoid needing translation, but sometimes the explanatory illustrations are as mysterious as much of the rest of the game.
Speaking of translation, they clearly didn't get anyone native to look at their English.  Fortunately it's all flavor text so you can ignore it.
All that said--it's not actually
, so pick it up if it's on sale or something.  Just expect to spend the first 30 minutes cursing.
General disclaimer:  I don't generally play casual point-and-click games, which
account for some of the controls difficulties.  I do like and play puzzle solving games.
