I love this game.  I've been playing guitar since I was 14 and have found this to be a great tool to learn some new songs.
you play guitar

Firstly - unlike a lot of reviewers, I have not had any experience playing guitar before.  Seems people get much more benefit if they have already have lessons / experience, and use Rocksmith to hone / improve skills.
At this point I really don't know if I would recommend it or not (stupid Steam forcing one or the other).... Im still slogging through it, but I think the whole game is just schitzophrenic - trying to be a game and a teacher, and getting neither right.
IF YOU HAVE AN ACOUSTIC GUITAR - DO NOT BOTHER.... THE GAME IS NEARLY UNPLAYABLE!!!!!!  Feedback problems, poor pickup of chords and notes, constant re-tuning means this game SUCKS.  YOU NEED HEADPHONES .... Dont bother trying an acoustic without them.
The game needs a "Getting Started" guide or some sort of walk through to help people work out how to best use the software.  When you start the game up you just randomly pick from a menu of stuff to do with some guitar picks to try and suggest what areas you should work on.  NOTHING in the way of guidance beyond that.
Getting set up was a BIG hassle (and it still isnt 100% or even 90%) with my acoustic guitar with a piezo pickup .... Lag issues and getting my guitar to even work with it was a pain, but once that was sorted, it started out being a fun way to learn.  I tried the lessons, which quickly became frustrating because the software wont always pick up notes correctly, and the lag means I had to adjust when to strum.  The "suggested" lessons are all over the place in order... going from some basic stuff straight to slides and stuff, before even teaching a single chord, scale, or even picking any string other than bottom E.  In other words, the "difficulty" ordering of the software is TERRIBLY inconsistent.  Once you do get some basics right, it jumps in difficulty to something stupidly hard (compared to the last run through) with symbols that arent explained, progressions that you arent prepared for, to name a few issues.
The songs are the same.  Sure - each song says what lessons you should have covered, but even with that done, their suggested difficulty path was all over the place, adding in symbols that just arent covered.  As a song's difficulty ramps up, it does so in ridiculous amounts, and it doesnt adjust well to the problems you may be having until you suffer through the song, then it starts to figure what strings and notes you have trouble with.
The arcade games SUCK.  They obviously spent too much time on the "arcade" aspect of making them look like 8bit games with a lot of unnecessary, unskipable screens, and not enough on note detection, learning aspects, and difficulty streamlining.  When it says my bottom E string is in tune, the games will consistently miss detect a fret and tell me Im on the wrong one.  I had to DE TUNE the string lower than the true note in order to make it half playable.  Then once you bomb out of a game, you have to put up with screens you cant skip through before you are able to start the game again.  You spend more time in those screens than actually playing.
Overall I can see some potential in the idea, but they have a lot of room for improvement.  If you think this program will teach you to play from scratch, then be prepared for a long, slow, frustrating experience as you jump from area to area trying to figure out what you are supposed to be doing, and in what order.
Once you start getting used to the game, search around for stuff, click on things, it starts to become clearer as to how it works.  A very different approach to what friends have suggested in the past for learning guitar (learning chords, tabs, etc).  I definitely wouldnt say better though.
Pros:
+ um.... it sorta teaches you to play guitar
+ gives you something to do when you are really bored
+ a fair list of songs (see the Cons)
Cons:
- PITA to set up, especially with an acoustic.  You have to keep the game volume right down, or use headphones cause the body of the guitar picks up sound from the speakers
- Lag issues / timing is off
- Note detection sucks (at least with my acoustic) and is hit and miss, meaning lessons are hard(er) to complete
- No "How to Get Started" guide or tour
- Most songs are crap and not popular, which makes playing them much harder if you dont know them at all (I had to buy a couple I knew just so I had something familiar to work with, and funny enough, I do much better with them)
- The lessons are terrible and just repeat over and over, except maybe to slow down the speed, they give you no guidance as to what you are doing wrong beyone the basics (wrong fret / string)
- The lessons are all over the shop - why the HELL would beginner lessons be looking to do bends, slides, hammers, etc when they cant even play all the strings and pick the right frets properly

I really enjoyed Seasons After Fall. It's biggest strength is it's aesthetic. It's a relaxing experience, the stakes aren't that high, the puzzles are laid back. The picturesque art and the original orchestral music are amazing - they really do a great job of capturing the feel of each season. The sound engineering is also excellent, which is sometimes underappreciated.
Gameplay-wise, I think the game never becomes dull or too long, it introduces new concepts and gameplay mechanics constantly all the way to the end. There are no tight platforming required, so I don't get the criticism about floaty or not tight enough controls. For me it felt good enough. 100% isn't hard to get either, it just needs a little more exploration.
Story is kind of nonexistent, they put more emphasis on world building and characters. You can learn even more about them by completing 4 bonus objectives (which is needed for true ending, so keep an eye out for those)
Only disadvantage I can come up with is that there are some puzzles which take too long: either because of labyrinth-like map (bactracking, getting lost), or just simply missing some hints. Only 2 locations were like this for me.

I hate giving this game a thumbs down, since it is clear that it's heart is at the right place, and the premise, graphics and gameplay bare more than a passing resemblance to one of the greatest pc horror games of the last decade - "The cat lady", but after a promising start the game takes a head-first plunge. "Silence of the sleep" is an adventure game at it's core, and no matter how many "spooky" instant-death inducing fog monsters you throw at the player, you can't change the fact that the core gameplay is all about solving puzzles. Sure, instant death is no stranger to adventure games, but you know who else is no stranger to them? game saving.
Yes. This game commits the most atrocious sin commitable in an adventure game - sparse save points and instant deaths. You see, this mechanic, which works well in action oriented survival horror games is perfectly plausible, but not in an adventure game. It's a terrible decision to force the players to solve puzzles they already solved just because they ran into a fog monster and died. Solving puzzles is a one time affair, it's fun when you figure it out, tedious when you have to do it a second time, and game-deletion reason when you are forced to do it a third time. There's no logical way to explain this poor game design choice, other than trying to artificially prolong the experience, because unlike action oriented games, where encoutering enemies again and again raises the player's skill level, here it just raises their furiosity level.  I'm sorry, but unless the developer somehow decides to add a save button, I can't recommend it at all.

Jazzpunk was born from an alternate reality in which Leslie Nielsen did not die and instead became an adventure game designer. Quirky, bizarre, disorienting, and hilarious from the opening cutscene to the final fade to black, Jazzpunk has to be seen to be believed. Most of the obstacles are simple to overcome and the game can be finished in a single sitting, but it's all about the journey in Jazzpunk. Walking around, poking everything just to see what happens, and then rubbing your eyes in disbelief when you see the results.
It's an experience that I was sad to see end, but it's brief stay on my computer screen made it's impact all the more potent.
If you have no qualms about spending money on a short interactive comedy then definitely pick up Jazzpunk. It'll provide fourth degree burns all over your face.

Slender the arrival is a horrible game. Almost everything in this game pisses me off to no end, and made me angry that I wasted 10 bucks on this awful "horror" game.
THE GOOD
There are a few good things about this game. One is the graphics. The graphics, while unimpressive in the lower settings, looks GREAT in the higher settings. The best parts of the game were walking around in the lit areas, exploring the forest at your own pase, as slender does not appear in these sections. It is a shame that they are very short. The last thing I like is the is the very first level in kate's house. You start out in the sunset, walking to an abandoned house as the sun slowly goes down. Once you get in the house, it's pitch black. You then find a flashlight, and can explore the house as much as you like. One of the rooms is locked and once opened, causes a great scare involving the slender man watching you explore the room outside from the window. Its a very creepy opening and makes a great first impression. Shame the other levels were not like this...
THE BAD
Here's the fun part. Lets start out with it the biggest flaw that will ruin every horror game. IT IS NOT SCARY AT ALL.all the game consists of are cheap, and I mean CHEAP jumps scares that did not startle me at all. Now let me explain something: Jump scares can be well made. If the game uses the features and mechanics found in the game to make the jump scare, it can be done extremely well. Great examples are: Resident Evil 1-4, Outlast, and SCP containment breach. This game however, does not do that and goes for the cheap jump scares found in most♥♥♥♥♥♥horror movies like Insidious and the new Paranormal Activity movies. Another thing I hate is the gameplay.  I could explain it to you but ill just summarize the games objectives for you. In the second level, guess what you have to do? Get 8 pages. In the third level, guess what you have to do? Turn on 6 generators in a large map. In the fourth level, guess what's next? YOU HAVE TO CLOSE 8 DOORS AND WINDOWS!!! Its just the same task over and over and got boring very quick. now lets talk about difficulty. This game is hard. But not the good kind of hard that tests your skills or anything, Im talking about INSANELY cheap deaths. There are times were a character who is not slender man (whom I cannot say the name of as that would be spoilers) chases after you and jumps on you, leaving you limping for a few seconds. But sometimes out of the blue, SHE WILL KILL YOU WHEN SHE JUMPS ON YOU! There's nothing that tells you "Hey, your going to die if you get attacked again" and  also, you do not have a certain amount of times you can be attacked, believe me, I tested it. The same applys for the slenderman himself. Sometimes he will appear and give you a chance to escape, or sometimes he will say "♥♥♥♥ it" and insta-kill you. This is extremely frustrating in the final level where he appears right in front of you, making you either barley come out alive, or escape, but to then be insta-killed by his damn tentacles. Finally, the game is very short. wanna know EXACTLY how long it took me to beat this game? 58 MINUTES. Sure, my recorded hours say 2, but that is only because I spent a hour testing the games settings to see which would run best on my laptop. While I was happy as this experience was over very fast, its bad for the people who somehow enjoy it, as there game will be over in a flash.
THE VERDICT
This game is honestly, the worst horror game I have ever played. Don't even buy it on sale, unless you somehow get it for free, or get it gifted from a friend,it is not worth a penny. 2.5/10 AVOID AT ALL COST!

SOMA has a beautiful setting where I haven't seen many other horror games go, underwater. The underwater theme provides a niche scare factor, therefore providing a scare factor for only certain people. I personally am extremely scared of the ocean and deep, empty waters. SOMA, in addition to the setting, provides an absolutely stunning storyline, I would gladly play this game multiple times just to experience the heart-breaking, yet wonderful story again. Additionally to the main story, there are various audio-logs from dead people, dead robots, and recordings from past intercom announcements, these audio-logs provide additional details to the storyline. Although released over 2 years ago, SOMA provides a better experience than even some modern titles such as Outlast 2 (but that's just my opinion). SOMA, although being this beautiful game that I just described does have its moments where improvement is needed, such as jumping into certain corners can cause you to clip into the wall and see the entire map, the monsters' AIs could need a slight rework, staying completely silent and still relatively far away from the monster doesn't work all the time. Overall, if I could give a rating out of ten, I would give SOMA a 9.5/10, probably the best horror game that I've ever and will ever play.

Friday the 13th is a survival horror game. You play either as Jason the murdering monster, or one of Jason's would-be victims.
The game is online-only with approximately 5 different randomly chosen maps to play on.  Each map has exactly the same gameplay elements:
-search cabins
-find weapons, gas, car battery, keys, phonebox fuse, etc
-escape using a vehicle, police aid, or wait out the full 20 minutes to win (or murder everyone if you're Jason)
Yeah, it gets redundant after about 3 plays though.
Overall, the game is "okay."  The graphics are good, the controls are slightly below average, and the fun-factor is good.  The teamwork factor is fun, and the game definitely has a great creepy-horror-movie atmosphere, which can be thrilling!
The problem is, the game is buggy, glitchy, crashy, etc.  I have played around 12 games, and 4 of them crashed.  For you math wizards, that's a failure rate of 33%.  Sometimes the game will just freeze and crash.  Sometimes you'll be in a game and suddenly it will kick out all of the players, returning them to the main menu with no experience points being recorded.  Sometimes the game glitches.  Let me give you an example:  my very first and only time being Jason, the game started up, I took one step, and poof - my Jason character plummetted through the map, falling for a few seconds until suddenly the game-ending screen appeared, displaying: "0/6 camp counsellors killed"  What? WTF happened?
Naturally, I tried to get a refund because the game is broken in its current state.  A game that only functions properly 66% of the time is unacceptable in 2017.  Unfortunately, Steam denied my refund request because I have more than 2 hours of gameplay time accumulated - which is BS considering 90% of that accumulate time was spent waiting in lobies or trying to recover from crashes.  The actual amount of time I've spent actually playing the game is probably ~60 minutes.
So now I have 2 choices.
1) call my credit card company and get a refund through them - and yes VISA does not play around with broken software nonsense... but then I have to wonder what will Steam do?  Will they freeze my account?
2) suck up the $40 loss and move on to a game that doesn't break 33% of the time
Regardless of my decision, one thing is certain: I CAN NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME IN ITS CURRENT STATE.

It's a nice little experience, although I'm surprised that it's quite so acclaimed as it is.
It's a very light puzzle platformer. You play as a series of squares or rectangles, each of which has a different colour, a different size, different jumping heights, and some have bonus abilities like double jumping or floating in water. You traverse levels by switching between characters and stacking them up to use their abilities appropriately to get through the levels. When you get to the end, each square has a box they need to be in to go to the next level. There are 100 levels. The pacing is good, there's always new stuff, levels only take a minute or a minute and a half. None of the levels really have any challenge, it's generally immediately apparent what you have to do and there's only really one mechanic that actually presents any challenge in executing what you need to do (one block type has reverse gravity and you have to sort of lasso a falling block on top of a falling upward block so they sort of meet in the middle and float off each other). Some levels have a single collectible.
It took me apparently 2.9 hours total, but that includes doubling back and getting a few missed collectibles. It's very pretty because it's just made of primitives. The music is really really nice.
I guess the main thing that the game does that's unique is that it has voiceover narration that provides an inner monologue for the blocks, who all have personalities. This is pretty nice, very well written, and cheeky, and it's cool to think of coloured blocks as human-like characters, but ultimately the "plot" is unclear--something about hacking the gibsons to free the information mainframe or whatever--and most of the personalities don't really go anywhere or lead to payoff. One very cool thing is that as the voiceover speaks, there are subtitles that appear next to the character you're playing as... but as you move, the subtitles waterfall so that you always see them on screen... so if you're at the right of the screen you might see the subtitles on one line to the left, but if you run to the left and there's less space, it sort of squishes into five or six lines. It can't really be described, it's like the effect that happens if you resize your browser window horizontally and text wraps, but applied to cool effect.
So all in all, I'd say it's well worth the 3 hours and cute and I'm looking forward to what the dev does next, but it doesn't really stick with me, even now and it's not super substantial. Mild recommendation.

This little game may not seem like much at first glance -- very minimalistic character design and simple graphics don't usually impress a lot of people -- and yep, it's a "yet another" platformer.
Yet the game is well entertaining for what it looks like. The graphics even though simple create good-looking environments with not-so-basic lighting effects and pixel graphics. The story has a simple premise to it, but the narration is quite long and full of humour and references to popular memes - it accompanies the player throughout each level, revealing bits and pieces of the story every couple steps. The narrator's voice fits well too - a clear smooth voice that doesn't get annoying or boring and just feels right.
Gameplay in Thomas was Alone is simple as well, the aim of each level is to get all characters from their starting positions to their respective exit portals. This is made somewhat more challenging by the tricky level design and the fact that every character has different movement abilities or skills. Completing levels requires "cooperation" between the different characters, a little clever thinking, and
of switching between characters.
Nevertheless, the game is still quite easy overall and doesn't take too long to finish, approx. 3 hours on average. At $10/L6 the game may seem a bit pricey for a mere 3 hours, but it's well worth picking up at the nearest sale. I quite enjoyed the overall experience and can certainly recommend it to anyone looking for a short, enjoyable adventure.
Edit: It's worth adding the game is fully controller-compatible, and actually plays very well using a controller.

Violett is a little girl tumbling into a fantastic adventure where she shrinked to the size of a bug. While the main aim is to find back home to her parent's house, she needs to solve lots of puzzles with many crosslinks. The graphics are nice and cute, the music is interesting like some film score.  She can only walk - in the beginning. Through her journey, she will find many balls/orbs in three different colors and three special glowing orbs that gives her special powers (jump, psychokineses and defense shield). The normal balls will fill the energy levels for all three powers.
She has to go to the same scenes several times to completely solve all puzzles and many orbs are hidden very well (sometimes they are invisible hidden). If you are stuck, you can get help with the icon circle in the lower right. If she speaks with animals, you only here some strange queeks with some words and speech bubbles explaining the required item in sketches.
The very first scene, where she is trapped in a cage, can only be played once - all other scenes can be visited again. There is an autosave feature but you might want to save your game already right in this first scene (in case you want to get all achievements by finding all orbs). You can also save your current game in new save slots, if you like. Unfortunately, the game "froze" a few times, i.e. Violett wasn't able to move anymore, everything else continued on the screen. But saving and restarting solved these issues.
<SPOILER ON>
The very last scene is some kind of boss fight with the spider queen but I wasn't able to move Violett as I liked to. I somehow made it but this was just try and error and some luck. Too bad as an end for this nice puzzle adventure.

Scania is a great compliment to ETS2.  It provides a sizable amount of Challenge Stages, broken up into a variety of disciplines.  Those familiar with Gran Turismo's Licence Tests will be familiar with these routines.  They're challenging and rewarding, demanding that you learn the finer nuances of skilled truck driving.
My personal highlight would be the various obstacle courses, titled Dangerous Drives.  You're given a point to point stretch where you have to navigate tight passages over a great number of environments, high-mountain switchbacks, flooded cityscapes, etc.  25 completely unique environments with fresh assets to test your skills under pressure.
Game comes complete with online Leaderboards (watch top replays too) as well as a nice bonus photo/video gallery covering the real-world annual Scania driving test completions.
Just remember, this is not ETS2.  It's its own beast with its own set of unique charms.  It's polished as heck just like ETS2 and even shares the same engine.  But that's where the similarities end.  Totally worth it to Driving Simulation fans and a complete no-brainer for those who follow and enjoy SCS Software.
Highly recommended.
Note: Review based on pre-Steam retail copy.

Amazing!
For those who know and played Euro Truck Simulator 2: This is the same developer, so the "basics" in physics and gameplay are  similar (Controls and graphics seem to be much better as far as I can tell).
The game itself is different. There is a freeride/delivery-mode as you might know it from ETS2, but it is smaller and, as far as I can see now, less complex (still much fun to play). The ´amazingness´ (Is that a word?) of this game comes from the many modes and missions. Drive along a messed-up road, a mountain pass, or a flooded area (...).  This game seems to be the "middle" between ETS2 and 3, to show off what is planned for #3 and what this engine can do.
So, in short:
+better graphics
+better controls
+runs much more smooth than ETS2
+exciting (!) roads: building sites, narrow bits and tricky obstacles of all kind
+brilliant missions
+online top-lists encourage competition and motivate to play every mission a thousand times
+very well playable with keyboard, pad or wheel
+not an easy game at all, but not frustrating->If you screw up a mission, you will go out with 0 points unable to compete with anyone online, but you will never get stuck in a mission, forced to do it a million times in order to be able to go to the next one
+++Devs seem to actually read forums and watch videos about their game and listen to the players
-the AI has some minor glitches: nothing game-breaking, more funny
Conclusion: If you liked ETS2, you will love this game even more. It has everything that people wanted in ETS2.
If you have never played ETS and you like to drive trucks in every kind of situation, then this game is something for you.
Recommended .... totally!
Edit: Game seems to crash when doing Alt+Tab, at least for me. Solution: Window mode (which means fullscreen + task bar) or use OpenGL.
Edit²: I found out that this game was released BEFORE ETS2 (Thank you, comments section!). Seems like the fancy graphics have tricked me into some wrong thoughts. ;)

Orwell belongs in that catagory of indie games which mostly go under the radar due to looking somewhat innocuous and modest, but turn out to be absolutely fantastical and mind blowing upon investigation.
I loved it. It was well written, engaging and interestingly presented. It's full of choice and consequence and has a strong narrative reflecting the ongoing modern debate regarding the paradox of our unlimited freedom of information in the digital age and how that could be used (maliciously or otherwise) to inhibit our personal freedom.
Check it out!

I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go.
Orwell is
going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try.
It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.
The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself.
Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime.
I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.
Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

While not a substitute for a *good* teacher, it is a much better option than many crappy teachers, and most guitar teachers are pretty crappy. While I haven't gotten to "hero" yet, I've gone from Zero, to well, having callouses and being able to improvise over scales in a mere 30-something hours of practice with the app.
The way I've been explaining this game to my friends is, think Guitar Hero but make it an educational game with a real guitar. Individual phrases are simplified and you level them up individually from each other, and instead of "failing" you if you miss too many notes the game tries to keep you at a level to where you're on your toes.
One thing I really appreciate about this game is that it's teaching me actual songs I can relate to. I sat down the other day to practice a prhase from one of the Radiohead songs, realized it's in the same key as the primary Salsa riff, the Game of Thrones theme, the Legend of Zelda theme and the Super Mario Castle music, and had a lot of fun going between them all. After the succes of the original Rocksmith title, Rocksmith 2014 edition takes most of the first games promblems a fuses them into something that works. Such promblems in the original game as the tuning issue, where for example, you played a song in E Standard Tuning and the next song you played was in the same tuneing, you would have to tune agian. Ultimatly re-tuneing for the same tuning is ponitless and time consuming. If you pause during any song in RockSmith 2014 a little tuner will pop-up down the bottom of your screen, useful if you happen to become slightly out of tuneing. Riff Repeater has improved massively. Riff Reapeater in Rocksmith(Originial) was an option from the menu and you could only play a certain riff, where as in Rocksmith 2014 edition, you can riff reapeat any riffs you want. The 'Learn a Song' is probably where you want to spend most of your time in Rocksmith 2014, but if you get bored of that or your feeling a little competive, try Score Attack! Score Attack allows you to play any song on an 'Easy' 'Medium' or 'Hard' option and the aim is to not hit 3 strikes, it's a '3 strikes and your out!' sort of deal. If you competle all riffs with a gold mark you will recive a gold pick and if you do this on hard mode, you unlock 'Master Mode'. 'Master Mode' is a mode where RockSmith removes your notes or chords symbols and you have to master the song to play it, Score Attack sets a nice goal to get no matter what stage you are at in your chosen song. There is all a little secret in Score Attack.. if you play all the phases perfectly (green squares) you will recevie a 'Platnium Pick' to show off to everyone you are a master of that song! 'Non-Stop Play' is another mode in RockSmith 2014, 'Non-Stop Play' lets you pick an amount of time you are willing to play for, and make a playlist of songs if you choose, then you proceed to play all thoose songs, quite a nice little touch. 'Session Mode' is a mode where you can get your friends to join you in game and play random tunes together, let the good times roll! 'Multiplayer' is the mode where you can go head-to-head with your mates, or you and your mates each have a part. Lead Guitar. Rhytum Guitar, Bass Guitar and ummmm... Vocals. Rocksmith 2014 also comes packaged with a new 'GuitarCade' like the one from the first game, but with diffrent games. RockSmith 2014 aslo inclueds many, many, many lessons if you are new to Guitar and Bass.

Peer-To-Peer (P2P) connection is not the devil everyone on the internet says it is. P2P is used in all fighting games such as Tekken for example because it offers less latency when compared to dedicated servers. However they still could have opted for a P2P-Server hybrid system that would be more stable without sacrificing latency. Even GTA is using peer-to-peer. When you're finished loading GTA Online then the matchmaking servers leave you on your own; you stay connected with other players via P2P and you can fit almost 30 people in one lobby without it crashing. P2P is not bad. Badly made P2P is bad.
Not going to lie I do get disconnected from time to time but not really frequently. The state of the connection is not even close to what it was on launch, now it's a lot more stable, provided that the host doesn't have McDonald's Internet on a potato router.
About the character balance I must say that every character can be beaten by every character in a 1v1 scenario. As long you know what you are doing you can win. People who say that "X" character is broken simply:
a) Are new to the game
b) Haven't played for months and came back with the mindset that they still remember how to play the game like they used to
c) Haven't devoted enough time to master their characters and learn all the moves and combos he can offer
d) Do not think but just spam light attacks and eventually get parried and destroyed
e) (Most Important) Cannot observe and understand their opponent's playstyle. They also lack the ability to identify the weekness(es) of their opponents and exploit them
f) Refuse or are unable to spend much time with the game and when they get matched with people who have devoted a lot of time to the game, they get rekt
g) Are too agressive with characters that should be played patiently, waiting for the opponent to make the first move or the other way around.
h) All of the above.

There are parts of this game that are not that scary. Then there are parts that are absolutely horrifying. One in particular is the "Into the Abyss" level. I can take Slender popping out unexpectedly and giving me a jump while I look for pages, but there is something about being chased by a masked psycho on foot through dark hallways while hearing their footsteps and breathing, especially when you don't see them yet, that terrifies me down to my core. I've only been able to complete that level once, but I get the urge to shut the game off each time I re-enter those mines. I hear the steps and that breathing, and I lose all composure I had. That right there is the sign of a great horror game. Slender: The Arrival is short, but what is there is wonderfully presented and paced, with some fantastic visuals and chilling atmosphere. With free DLC on the way, Slender: The Arrival is looking to become one of the best indie horror games in years. For fans of the original Slender: The Eight Pages and the Slenderman's Shadow series, it is a must play.

Slender: The Arrival is a simple, yet terrifying experience. Despite an unclear story, and a slightly irritating middle section, its really a fun experience. Ultimately its our anticipation that delivers our frights. The easter egg hunt-like gameplay never gets old, as on multiple stages, your objectives are placed throughout the maps at random, and your enemies movements have no logic or pattern. There just really scary. Slender himself is a pretty creepy guy. Peering around trees and waiting behind corners, he's more of a trapper than a hunter. But then there's the proxy. The proxy shows up halfway through the game and stalks you through out an abandoned mine, and without giving anything away, he's short, fast, and kind of annoying. When being stalked by Slender, running in the opposite direction usually solves the immediate issue. But the proxy is not so easily gotton rid of. Tasked with turning on a series of generators in a maze of mine tunnels, the proxy attacks head on. One may turn and face their opponate, as he charges straight at you, and narrow their flash light beam, momentarily blinding him, giving you window to run and hide. But it doesnt really work. Doing this only buys you seconds and the proxy is quick. And if you dont have enough corners to duck around, he proceeds to tackle you to the ground and throttle you, all the while you curse at your screen in anger. But the ability to see past this minor nuesance, will reward you with better scares in the latter part of the game. The Steam ending is particularly horrifying. So check out Slender: The Arrival, and keep a change of shorts nearby.

This is not a good game. (Quick video at end of overview)
seems like a very quick, very cheap attempt at the “walk around a small location and try to survive” genre. Unlike other games of its ilk, such as
and
, which have some sort of polish and gameplay, this has neither. The game runs in Unity Personal (because of course), and its window is named “Pet_Project”. Hopefully this was thrown together quickly as part of some school program.
You play as a fourteen year old who has footsteps that sounds like he’s wearing heavy duty combat boots. Your parents have gone to Mexico, and you’re alone in the house. You decide to open a random present sitting on your porch, because obviously, which, also obviously, unleashes the ghost girl.
Your goal is to survive seven nights by managing your fear meter, which seems to constantly go up but never actually drop on its own. The popup at the beginning that tells you how to play states that the farther she is from you, the more your fear goes up, which seems backwards. Shouldn’t you be more calm if she’s nowhere near you? Either way, since your fear skyrockets and it’s almost instant game over when she’s near you, it’s a bit confusing. You can close your eyes to lower your fear, and the game conveniently tells you that doing this will stop you from being able to see AND hear her. I’m pretty sure if I close my eyes, or even cover them with a blindfold, I’ll still be able to hear. Not sure what the developer was going for here.
Setting up cameras and switching to their feeds to see where she is, and to try to avoid her, is an interesting but flawed mechanic. Your fear continues to rise, even though you know where she is in relation to you. Also, if you stand in front of a camera and switch to the feed, you’re invisible. There is nothing that shows up on the tablet. Perhaps there’s an ending where it turns out you’re a vampire. Would that explain how you suddenly lose your hearing when you can’t see?
You may look at the screenshots and think the game looks pretty good for being one dollar, and you’d be right. It looks decent. However, it’s very choppy. Did you watch the trailer? That’s not the video that’s choppy, that’s the game. On a high-end system, it chugs along, and if you choose to bring out your tablet, it chugs even more. Downstairs in the kitchen, with the tablet open, looking through the camera also set up in the kitchen, Fraps showed me single-digit FPS. That’s just poor.
is not a good game. If you’re a badge collector, you can’t really go wrong for the price, but otherwise, avoid it. There are many other games that will offer you far more value and enjoyment.

You play as Simon Jarrett, a store owner with a couple of bumps to his noggin from an unfortunate car accident that cost his would-be-girlfriend's life. Simon goes to the doctor for treatment, but instead gets sent from the doctor's office to another place altogether. Pathos-II, the remains of mankind's last hope. Unfortunately for Simon, he finds out the hard way what happened to Pathos-II, step by step.
From the beginning to end, I found next to no faults in the game's mechanics and story-setting. However, I really wish dealing with the enemies wasn't such a chore. I didn't feel a thing when dealing with them, I just saw them as things to distract.
I'd give this an 8/10. Boring enemies, No replay value, but an interesting story to make up for it.

A catchy narrator, a midly interesting story and puzzles that are so easy that could make Portal 2's main story looks like a proper puzzle game. That's all that you will find in this pretentious "game" about some running A.I.'s trying to earn their freedom by stacking one on each other while some guy with britsh accent talk about the feelings of our characters, beautifully represented as squares and rectangles with different habilities.
The idea is interesting: Several characters with different habilities (length of jump, being able to float, etc) that must be all controlled by the player in order to navigate the levels. There are the proper ingredients to create a really cool enviroment for puzzle solving but everything falls apart as the developers were way more interested in telling the story behind those "characters" than in creating an actual, proper, challenging, game. There is no real game in Thomas Was Alone, Is just one jump after other while the narrator keep talking about characters until the end. There are no twits, no "damn, how could I get up there" moments. Just press button, move right, end of level, narrator talking you into the next level.
If you are looking for some puzzle challenge, don't even think about it. If you want to write a review about how artistic gaming can be, this could be your title.

So Thomas is alone, whats a lone sqaure/rectangle to do?  Well he needs to go find some friends and not be alone anymore.
Honestly the story was rather interesting.  The narrative is by far the cutest thing ever, and really added personality to the fact you are legit playing as different colored rectangle doodads.  I will say about 3/4 through though it really dragged and felt a bit like filler, trying desperately to make the game longer then the 4-6 hours it is.
While cute and somewhat fitting, this isn't a graphics intensive game.  Environments are delegated to black platforms with fancy ambient looking particle effects in the background and the shiny "water".  The characters you control are rather straight forward too, and not all that detailed.  Some might like the simplistic design, others will wish for something more.
All you do is jump, move left or right and switch between your current posse.  They are very solid though it can get tedious if you have the whole crew in one level to have to manually cycle through each one to get to the character you wish and just hope they added individual keys for each character.
To be honest, most of the game is just you listening to the narrative and sliding your block over to the exit.  The puzzles you do come across are extremely simple, and only had issues with at most 2 out of the entire game.  I honestly felt they could've pushed the boundaries with certain puzzle elements like they attempted to in one stage where you had a death wall closing in on you and you had to switch back and forth between characters trying to get them to safety (though admittedly it was nightmarish due to the cycling problem as mentioned above).
Given the fact I haven't played this game in a good long time, I don't remember the music too well outside the narrater and the "glump" sounds your block makes on jumping.  Perhaps the music wasn't as stellar or my memory is terrible we'll never know.
I could recommend this to younger children, but for people above the age of 10 this is definitely not challenging enough of a puzzle game to warrant a purchase.  It's cute, and who knows maybe get it on sale just for the narrative, but don't expect much more out of it.

Much of the game's charm comes from the narrator, who carries the dialogue and plot perfectly. To reference an incredibly obscure movie, this narrator constantly reminded me of the narrator from the movie Milo and Otis. The game will take you around four hours to play through, which is perfect for an afternoon break from the millions of shooters available. If you like your games to have more story than explosions, and are looking for something different and unique, then this is the game for you.

There are a few tricky parts, but so far I love this game!

If you are a fan of classic point-and-click adventure games, then Violett will satisfy.  It's a traditional game with a simple structure and puzzles that are challenging without being overly frustrating.  In an era of revitalizations of classic genres and reboots of the great titles of yesterday, Violett is a combination of modern art design, and genre-traditional gamepay.  The little touches in level design and the way the story is silently told make this another entry in the recent trend of games that has been creating artistic statement in the narrative by embedding the story in the gameplay.  Violett is a lovely new entry in a series of titles that are taking gaming into a new more artistically-mature direction alongside games like Limbo, Braid and, more recently, Gone Home and The Stanley Parable.

Frustration Simulator 2015.
First of all, it controls terribly. I can never aim my ship where I want to, like a hitman that had one too many beers before his assignment, which is really painful because you can only move in the direction you are aiming. If you are trying to shoot asteroids (more on that later), you need to try to aim perfectly towards it while shooting. If there is an enemy, you will automagically lock on, which is nice. But you need to accelerate to dodge there attacks, which is bad because, when you stop accelerating, you still keep moving like a mouse in the middle of a ring of ice, and I get that this is a "space sim" and all, but when I'm in the middle of a space battle and I can't get to my target, it becomes a hassle because I have to try to turn around and prepare for another fly-by to dodge and get another hit or two. The enemies are standing still, by the way. And since space is such a barren wastleland, not only are the battles not interesting, but sometimes you lose track of where the enemy you were fight was.
But don't worry, there are planet scenarios, too. Except there are issues with that, too. First, it has the same momentum issue on the planets, except it drags you down to the surface (obviously). The issue with this is that you don't slow down on your left and right movement because you aren't sure if the big red button is ACTIVATE GRAVITY SIMULATORS or SELF-DESTRUCT, and if you do, I couldn't notice any until I hit the ground, which, more often than not, will do at least a little damage to you. And this becomes a huge problem with the randomly generated terrain. It also makes manuevability during battles a pain, as you attempt to target one enemy, and try to dodge it at the same time gets utterly painful against enemies with fully automatic weapons. Sometimes my aim would spaz out on planets because apperantly the drunk hitman was just waken up by a swat team and is still suffering from his hangover , which remember, you can only move in the direction that you are aiming, which would lead to my death because I can't escape a sticky situation like I normally can.
There are a few progression aspects, but getting new ships, weapons, and more ammo requires money. How do you get money? Grinding, of course! You could grind off of the previously mentioned space enemies, or you can get money from asteriods! Shooting asteriods, for similar reasons as enemies, is a pain, with much less payout, but since these don't shoot at you, it's less risky. What will you spend money on? Well, there are only a few types of weapons, only a couple per ammo type, and a good shield helps a lot, but the real key to success is getting tons of repair kits. Low on health? Stand still for a couple seconds and you're good to go! They really seem overpowered. Although, I guess you need them to carry Team member 2 "Bad controls" on their bare back for a chance at survival.
While I was reading the reviews for this game, wondering what others said, I found one person complaining about how they were mislead into thinking they were going into a game with RPG elements. The developer responding to this, saying, and I quote...
"We are sorry if "RPG" tag was misleading for you.
Actually this game has some RPG elements. It's not full featured RPG, but you can customize your ship with different equipment, grab and trade loot and you free to choose where to go and what to do in open world, therefore it marked with RPG tag."
I don't believe these elements are stricting for RPG's. Customization and trading are both apart of Team Fortress 2, and the open world aspect is apart of Minecraft, two games I don't think anybody considers RPG's. And if they do, they are probably the drunk hitman. The point is, when I think RPG's, I think leveling up your character and their stats! I think party members! And quests! 3 things that Destination Sol has none of. Sure, it has mercenaries that you can hire, which is kinda like a party system, but that's not a permanent member of your team as far as I can tell. And that's only scratching the surface of possible RPG elements that the game missed out on that, let's be honest here, could have actually worked well.
Finally, is there anything redeeming I could find out of this experience? Actually, a better way to put it would be "any enjoyment I could squeeze out by getting a dough roller and rolling back and forth for a nearly an hour", but the answer is "a little bit". The progression, while limited, looks like it has potential, and if the traction issue while flying is fixed, let go any direction while facing anywhere, as well as some aiming fixes, this looks like it could have been much better and actually pretty fun. Around each planet there is a teleporation device with a small fee, which, while the cutscene are overly long, like a makeout scene in a movie that your date is making you watch that you just want to end, is very useful.
Overall, while some things smaller things in the game (like a suprising small world issue that I didn't address) rubbed salt in the wound, it was the terrible controls that opened the wound in the first place and poked a couple of razor blades in for good measure. If all my complaints with the controls were fixed, I would try it again, and I can see myself giving it a much better review. Interesting concept, gives you the chance to be a cog in the machine of an orwellian surveillance state. Which I found to be a very enjoyable experience. Throw in the added bonus that the issues raised are very relevant right now, and you've got a solid game indeed.

As the term "Orwellian" has made its way into colloquial language - and has, alas, become more widespread in its use as of late - choosing this name alone builds up quite a lot of expectations, and I found those of mine fulfilled. I rever 1984 as one of the greatest books of the 20th century, and in our turbulent days, examining the topic of state-ordered surveillance, it has never lost its edge. While I wouldn't call this game a spiritual successor of the book, it splendidly represents the ideas of Orwell, and even has a few clever references to him sprinkled here and there.
Without spoiling too much of the story, you are a hired investigator examining the online records and phone calls of certain suspicious subjects. What is surprising that in a game about surveillance and suppression, you are given a surprising amount of choice: Whenever conflicting informations emerge, you have to make a choice which one to forward to your superior, and thus influencing their view on the subjects, making them appear as law-abiding citizens or subversive terrorists. This may decide over their life and death, and those of many innocents.
As you close in on the center of a supposed cell of rebellion, you are even presented with a choice concerning your own fate: Will you persevere your original task and rout the suspects, or will you rise against your superiors and the blatant injustice of the system? It all depends on your ability to copy and paste text snippets.
A creepy look into what could be the future very soon. Great game.

I don't recommend this game as it is, though with a caveat. The game is wonderful and the makers deserve to be rewarded with their efforts with people buying the game, but as a player... I cannot recommend it. Sadly this game falls in that trap of having no reason to be a game instead of an animation.
The story was small but interesting, and the atmospheric experience, music and artwork are wonderful, but the experience of actually PLAYING the game sours the fun in the end.
Personally, I got to a certain point near the end and got so bored of the soul-crushing tedium and repetetion that I gave up and watched a playthrough of the last parts instead. Again, this is subjective, because I'm not much into puzzles or platforming, and I'm very glad the game exists at all, but the experience I had while playing it was miserable.
The music is very engaging but a lot of the time I wish to hear more of it and less ambience.
The puzzles feel very unsatisfying and simultaneously like an awful lot of busy work; prepare to be frustrated with being forced to guess locations and go places without a map, a limitation that feels shoved in to extend playing time, along with puzzles that could be solved much faster if you didnt have to repeatedly navigate circling and rotating platforms. Jumping onto the same ones over and over again to solve a puzzle you already know the answer to and simply have to get around to finish off, leading to the feel of more and more busywork simply to extend the play time of the game.
Another choice I don't agree with is that there are animated sequences to be found, and they can possibly be missed. The problem with this is that if you do not go and find or search for them, you are essentially missing out on a main part of the slightly sparse at times story. So while these are "optional", if you don't spend more time on the busywork of finding them to extend the gameplay, you're missing out on what is simply the main part of the game : the story.
In review I feel like the story, art, music, animation, are all wonderful, but I would have been much less frustrated or bored if they were in the format of an animation or short movie rather then having busywork placed inbetween it. That said, the only reason I kept playing was because I wanted to find out the rest or what happened next! While it feels like the story is stretched thin over tactics to extend play length, it was captivating, endearing and atmospheric enough to juuust about hook me through the parts I didn't personally enjoy.
Areas repeat too often for me. This feels like another "busywork" tactic of streeeetching the game out to squeeze in as much playtime as it can, no matter the cost. I appreciate the idea, if felt as if you were going back to right wrongs, fix what had been broken or view places again with more experience of the world (storywise). But.. From my own cynical view it made the game feel as though stretched very thinly and each revisted area had confusing layouts due to them being created for previous puzzles within the area, which weren't necessary or made the new puzzles more convoluted, especially without a map, which was obviously intended as (again) more busywork and pointless running around to extend playtime. A feeling compounded by the way the fox moves and controls in a very ponderous manner, also adding to the  stretching of game content with artificial difficulty.
Last but not least, the ending did not, to me, feel like a real ending. Leaving me with questions or just generally unsatisfied with the lack of a finite or particularly detailed pronouncement of what was going on and what the end result was.
TL;DR Would be better as an animation but you should still consider buying it to support such a wonderful creation and atmospheric piece of art.
As an actual game, there are however better things to spend your money on, especially for this price.
If the cost doesnt bother you, get it or wait for a sale perhaps, but be prepared to probably just watch someone else play it on youtube so you can skip all of the... actual gameplay...

As other negative reviews mention, the gameplay just isnt there. The art is beautiful, the way the different handdrawn enviroments change when you flip seasons is stunning, but the gameplay is severly lackluster. It becomes really anti-climatic considering how much time and effort must have been put into the graphics.
So what is wrong with the gameplay?
Well, its really, really boring. The idea and concept of changing seasons to interact with different objects is brilliant but the way its implementated is really poor. When you see mushrooms you change to fall. When you see water you change to winter or spring depending on whether you want it frozen or not, and its always EXTREMELY obvious which one it should be. The puzzles therefore are non-existant and it becomes more of a chore to change to the season that matches the current object infront of you, cause there is never any question of which one it is.
The controls are very clunky. The animation of the fox makes him/her seem very fast and nimble, but the way the fox handles is a whole different story. Mr. Fox feels sluggish, heavy and clumsy. The controls just doesnt respond the way you want to or expect it to. As a pretty experienced gamer I missed very easy jumps more than once, and I really wish I could blame myself cause the game is beautiful, but I cant. The controls are really bad and the hitboxes of the platforms doesnt always match the graphics of the platforms. One particular jump I missed like 3-4 times cause the fox kept falling through the end of the branch before I had pressed the jumpbutton.
There are alot more details of the gameplay that makes it even worse. The way you have to chase the crabs, cause for some reason they have the same movement speed as the fox, so you have to run behind them untill they hit a wall in order to make them run the other direction.
The fact that you ALWAYS backtrack EVERYTHING. I only played for 1 hour (got winter, fall and spring back to the shrine) and I had to backtrack every single level in its entirety.
The lack of a map when the levels have a very confusing layout and everything looks the same. Normally when I play games I like to check every corner and feel like I have a deep grasp on what I just went through, but here I had to give up on that playstyle and just mash my way in the direction that seemed to be forward.
I wish I could say that it atleast have a good story, but that failed to get me immeresed aswell. The game kinda throws you into the story without explaining anything, which is fine and alot of games does that, but the way its set up doesnt make you interested even one tiny bit. I dont know if Im trying to save anything, if Im on a self-fulfilling path, if there is any conflict, nothing. I dont know the purpose of my character or the world its set in and Im not curious to find it out. You seek out the "guardians" to collect "fragments" and you really have no clue why youre doing that and the game fails to make you wanna find out more.
The game is visually stunning and has a look that no other game has. But thats all there is to it. This review may seem unnecessarily harsh, but its really frustrating to go from the trailer into the actual game. You can tell a bunch of work went into this, but the endproduct just doesnt match the amount of ambition or work at all. Its really sad, but I cant recommend this game to anyone at all. Maybe children, like 6-7 year olds, but in that case there are better platforms on the market that suits that agegroup.
And to all of you out there comparing this to Ori And The Blind Forest: I dont think we can be friends. Ori is one of the best 2D platforms released in the recent years, this game isnt even worth a playthrough.

Peer-To-Peer (P2P) connection is not the devil everyone on the internet says it is. P2P is used in all fighting games such as Tekken for example because it offers less latency when compared to dedicated servers. However they still could have opted for a P2P-Server hybrid system that would be more stable without sacrificing latency. Even GTA is using peer-to-peer. When you're finished loading GTA Online then the matchmaking servers leave you on your own; you stay connected with other players via P2P and you can fit almost 30 people in one lobby without it crashing. P2P is not bad. Badly made P2P is bad.
Not going to lie I do get disconnected from time to time but not really frequently. The state of the connection is not even close to what it was on launch, now it's a lot more stable, provided that the host doesn't have McDonald's Internet on a potato router.
About the character balance I must say that every character can be beaten by every character in a 1v1 scenario. As long you know what you are doing you can win. People who say that "X" character is broken simply:

c) Haven't devoted enough time to master their characters and learn all the moves and combos he can offer

f) Refuse or are unable to spend much time with the game and when they get matched with people who have devoted a lot of time to the game, they get rekt
g) Are too agressive with characters that should be played patiently, waiting for the opponent to make the first move or the other way around.
h) All of the above.

SOMA is a short game when compared against the usual AAA titles published today by the likes of Ubisoft or EA. It is also an incredibly simple game: there is no map, no inventory, no journal or another means of tracking what you've done or need to do, or where to go. There are no sidequests and no busy work; just the main campaign that strings you along through the story in a relatively linear fashion with a few easy puzzles to solve here and there. There are enemies scattered throughout the world, but no means for fighting them.
Despite all of these elements that make SOMA rather unconventional, it still bests many AAA titles published by enormous and foolhardy global conglomerates.
Why?
Because SOMA is not about getting from point A to point B while killing as many enemies as you can, or racking up points through some arcane mechanism, or living a second life in a virtual city. SOMA is, on the contrary, a deep meditation on what it means to be human, a work of art akin to some of the finest works produced by the likes of Arthur C. Clarke and Isaac Asimov. It has a phenomenal story that encourages you to examine yourself philosophically, and at the conclusion, leaves you in a state of awe. "Play" SOMA not as a game for amusement, but rather as a clear lens through which the powerful relationship between man and machine (increasingly important these days when you take into consideration where our world is going with respect to artificial intelligence) can be explored and dissected.
All that being said, this game is not for everyone, but if you're the kind of person like me who prefers to have their mind probed instead of fed repetitive garbage, you will enjoy SOMA.

You run around, pick up or turn on things, and try not to die. Funny thing about that, though. Running wears you out pretty fast, or something - I don't know. It's hard to say. You'll be trying to run away from something, and then you're not running fast anymore, and then OH GOD IT'S ON MY FACE. Retry. Retry. Retry. Since key objects are - in most cases - randomly generated around each level, all you can really do is hope they spawn close enough so that you can activate them before whatever thing is after you tries to kill you. Sound like Outlast? It's a lot like Outlast. Except you can't hide from things, and as far as I can tell, turning off your flashlight doesn't dissuade them from running over and clawing your face. Fun! Except not. Also, about that story: you are someone, apparently, wearing a hoodie and recording everything, because found footage, or whatever. And it seems you're trying to find your friend, or something, who apparently is a nut case and likes to draw with chalk on every surface for hours at a time in big scribbly letters. While on the surface an extension and expansion of the original 'Slender: The Eight Pages' sounded like it could make for a good horror game the actul game didn't quite live up to the impact created by it's predacessor.
To keep it brief, there two major problems I had, they are as follows:
1- Repetition: A problem I frequently have with games like Amnesia who's approach to horror is making you have no recourse to threats but to run away is that they end up feeling mind-numbingly repetitive after a while, outstaying their welcome and killing any sense of suspension and horror that might have been previously present (case in point, Outlast), Slender unfortuneately does this by the fact that the majority of the game can quite callously be summurised as 'doing The Eight Pages agaiin and again with some window dressing', by the third time they give you an objective that is 'collect X amount of Y while evading Slender/other entity' it does beg the question of could they not think of another challange that could keep the player in the area long enough to make Slenderman a credible threat? (In fact, it was encountering Chapter 'Genesis' which so far has basically just been the Eight Pages level copy-pasted that spurred me to write this review)
2- Slenderman himself: I know what people find scarey is subjective and one person's horror is another's comedy but it's very hard to be frightened by Slenderman abducting me and assaulting me with bad picture quality when he's done it over 50 times, the saying 'familiarity breeds contempt' comes into play here and this ties into my previous point about repetition. Dying instantly due to a shadowy figure snatching you from the aether and dragging you to parts unknown never to be seen again is terrifying, having it happen to you ad nauseam just makes the experience tedious since it translates what should be a frightening experience ("Oh my God, he's going to get me! Please don't hurt me!") into something more akin to frustration ("Great, I have to do this all over again, I give up"), the forest fire level (not a spoiler if it's in the achievements) epitomises this concept and was a point where I just gave up on the game for a while because of how annoying and tedious it was becoming.
Overall, if you loved the Eight Pages or the Slenderman mythos in general (particularly Marble Hornets) then you will love this game and will enjoy it greatly for those reasons, if not or if you're unsure then this game's repetitive gameplay and design will probably turn it into a seemingly long and pointless struggle with little payoff (with the exception of one or two levels which deviate from the Eight Pages formula and are all the better for it, the reccording on the VCR being a prime example of this).
It could be fun but it's hard to give an overall reccomendation.

I bought this game because it looked like a gorgeous point and click adventure game that I could play when I wanted something that was a little more relaxed than some of my other games. What I got was 3 hours of frustration that got me no where.
There is no direction. Occasionally little thought bubbles pop up to help you, but if you miss them they won't pop back up. If you get stuck too long there are supposed to be hints...but usually they were either completely unhelpful, or it was an action that you couldn't do just yet, or I'd miss it all together because if you're not paying attention you won't notice the faint sparkle that indicates your target. There are also sheets of with notes about some of the characters you seem to run into...but they fail to include any information on how to get past them.
Then, when you finally think you've figured it out, the actions don't always work, or they require you just clicking repeatedly until they do what they should. I had only made it as far as the second room when attempting to control a buzzing fly drove me nearly insane with clicking.
You collect little stones but have no idea why. There's a little animation that appears in the corner sometimes indicating I should move my mouse side to side? I think? But I have no idea why. I'm not sure if it's a hint or what. Having no idea why seemed to be the theme generally.
On top of all this, the game was glitchy and had to be restarted a couple of times because all my actions froze, which I know was an issue with my friend playing as well.
I love a good challenge, but randomly clicking all over a screen hoping something will happen is just frustrating and left me wanting my money back.

Edit: After the new hint update, I tried giving it another shot, and it made the game much more playable. I would say it's about 50/50 whether I can recommend this game or not. If you enjoy classic style point and click adventure games, this one may strike a chord with you. However, it's also very frustrating and generally incredibly vague on what you need to do next. There's really no story associated with the game, and the only dialogue is in pictures and garbled voices, so there's no Monkey Island or Day of the Tentacle style quips to keep you entertained, and no real cohesion between levels other than you're very small and in a sort of fantasy insect world.
Overall, there have been times when I've enjoyed this game, and times that I've been so frustrated that I turned it off and went and did something else. And unfortunately, the latter has been more prevalent. The graphics in the game are cool, I really like the concepts that the designers came up with. The music is very well done, but it gets a little obnoxious playing on repeat if you get stuck on a certain level for a long time. For the most part it fits in well with the game, though.
I've really enjoyed the design of some of the puzzles, like the cupboard with numbered drawers and the Mole Man water puzzle. However, a lot of the puzzles don't really seem like they're things that make you think, just things that make you click on a lot of different things or give up and use a hint. The elevator with the arrows, for example. I figured out the left and right part easily enough, but I never would have gotten the specific solution if I hadn't used a hint. And there are a lot of puzzles like this, unfortunately. With the updated hint system though, while it hurts my pride to admit defeat, I can still use a hint and get past it instead of being stuck and not being able to play the game any more.
My only compaint about the hints is that if I'm 90% through a level when I get stuck, if I haven't used any hints up to that point, it makes you use the hints in order. I have to use 4 hints just to get help with where I'm currently at. It would be nice if it would keep track of your level progress and grey out or skip hints that no longer apply to you.

PROS:
+ Fascinating mechanics. Being able to change the seasons set up some beautiful puzzles and some very tricky situations.
+ Lovely music. I never quite got the hang of which music matched which season, but I loved all the music.
+ Gorgeous graphics. Absolutely beautiful game.
+ Inviting story. Kept me playing right to the end to figure out what would happen.
CONS:
- Occasionally poor level design. The solution to some puzzles was just a bit of thought. Other puzzles required random luck or a perverse drive to see EVERYTHING in the level. I had to go to a walkthrough for a couple of places.
- Too much running and switching to get where I wanted to go. The levels are pretty big, and a lot of time you have to switch between several seasons to advance through the level, even after you've completed it. The little portal-things alleviated this to some extent, but not enough, IMO.
CONCLUSION: Beautiful game with some little problems. Would certainly recommend it to anyone looking for a light play!
FINAL RATING: 5/7

I read the recent Steam store reviews for this game, which brought up several cons against it. I decided to play after consideration, and did not regret it at all!
I describe Seasons after Fall as a puzzle exploration game. The main mechanic is the ability to change seasons, which in turn affects your environment and allows progression to new or hidden areas. The story started out slow, but around a third into the game,
(spoiler-free) which really hooked me in and I played long sittings just to find out what happens next. I'd call that a success of the writing!
Seasons after Fall is a platformer game, and as I mentioned it's heavy on exploration and environmental puzzles to progress. The platforming is fairly simple, and I really liked the level design that was clearly made to not waste time if you made a basic mistake. Hence, I would say this game isn't for people only looking for a platforming challenge.
I highly enjoyed the seasons mechanic, and the art style made it a real pleasure to interact with different seasons. The environment changes dynamically and you use different traits of the seasons to help you progress in areas. The puzzle difficulty wasn't super difficult, but entertaining enough to keep my attention. I'd say wanting to find more about the story motivated me with the puzzles, and less so wanting to be pushed to the limits by a challenge.
From what I gathered from previous reviews, people had complaints of the following:
I personally didn't encounter these, but the developers have detailed instructions on the forum as to how to fix a save file if things go wrong. However, I did encounter several bugs, for example changing to a season but not triggering a certain corresponding environmental change. Switching to another season and back, or reentering an area fixed it every time for me.
: Reviews were saying the soundtrack, while lovely, appeared infrequently and most of the game was quiet. I agree with this, and had to turn on my own music at times to fill in the silence. When the tracks did come on they were
, but I wouldn't have minded if they'd looped many more times at least.
: I noticed some mentions of the platforming being floaty or unresponsive. I personally didn't notice these issues.
There was quite a bit of backtracking (but each time with fresh mechanics so not annoying repetitive), and while I understand the exploration aspect might have been enhanced without a map, my memory failed me several times and I spent way too long trying to find something I'd seen before. There are some great player-drawn maps in the guide section that I checked out, and I'd recommend you do so too if you are getting frustrated.
I enjoyed Seasons after Fall for the most part. The best parts for me were the artwork, atmosphere, and story. The platforming and puzzle difficulty was suitable for an exploration heavy game, and not really used as an intense challenge. I really enjoyed finding out what happened to the forest and the characters, and while I don't fully understand the ending, kudos to any game that motivates me to play long sittings just to get to the bottom of things!
I'd recommend you play this if you already own it, or if you get on a 40%+ sale.

How can a game so beautiful and with such an interesting premise be so flawed? Where to start?
The controls - sluggish, laggy...The fox moves like a tank, frequently you miss platforms because of bad collision, etc., which for a platformer, even with not so challenging levels is just bad design.
The levels - samie and boring... The stylish graphics cannot save a level desing that is boring and confusing. You have more or less four "zones", one for each season. But other than hues and light changes of scenary they are the same. You also have to backtrack so much between these levels, that it's just mind bogling. I wished there was a second world or something but nope, that's it - just four zones that open up a bit and that's it. Metroidvania design is no excuse for lazy design.
No map - yeah yea indie, atmospheric, adventure, bla bla bla...I want my map - it's not the 80s and I should not memorize/draw maps on paper so I do not get lost. I do not play every day and having to remember where I left the game is no fun because the developers decided to be artsy
The seasons power - yeah why did they implement it like that - you have to stop what you are doing, stop your character mid walk, jump, etc. to choose a power? What the hell - couldn't the devs just map each of the four seasons to the four face buttons? Now you have one "bark" button and one "select seasons" button and when you need to change seasons, especially later in the game you end up having to pause, switch, pause, switch, pause, switch, it stops the tempo and makes the game even more slugish and annoying...
Lag, so much lag - even with the stopped v-sinc there is still lag and I have a gforce 970, come on I played doom on High, but this game lags....
Oh, and yeah you see the cute bear that's on the poster on the page, on everything? Yeah you will see him move for 30 sec, after that he is just talk to you after the middle of the game and that's it. They relly wanted to go on the Orie hype train with this one.
The game is not worth the 15 euro price, wait for it on sale with at least 50% discount.

Dont give too much (or anything) about the reviews complainaing "i didn´t make it through chapter 2". Listen to those who made it through the game. It´s (more or less) easily possible.
- Indeed clunky controls!!
- Sometimes "interactables" are hard to find, because they do not really stand out from the background. (kind of a disadvantage of the artystyle)
- Crashes sometimes ... for reasons. But usually takes not mroe than one minute after save points to get there again and it usually doesn´t freeze again and again at thes epoints. So still playable
- Where´s my picture?! ;)
- Great sound: The music, as well as the atmosphere, as well as sound as an important part of the gameplay itself. It´s really great, enjoyable and supports the story/gameplay really well.
- Visual design is pretty unique, though somewhat simple. A mixture of realistic movements and comic-like animations.
- Great atmosphere in sound, visuals and dialogue.
- Pretty dark and implicitly violent. (Sometimes also explicitly, like the "cutscene" ;)
- Nice mix of adventure-like story progression and horror parts. So you can breath through and relax a bit in the "story parts" while the other sometimes make your heart bump.
- Interesting and somewhat catching storyline.
- Keep an eye on the background.
- Save if u can
- Don´t forget that flashlight is on F ;)
Besides the mentioned control issues it´s a pretty decent and throughout playable game. Like with many adventure games you will sometimes have to check a playthrough if u gets tucked (but see "hints").
The atmosphere is really great in all aspects. The music is really fits the story and the overall melancholic mood that goes through the whole game. The combination of adventure like parts (find item A  use it at  spot/bring it to person B) are well combined with the more horror oriented, fast paced parts.
So some horror fans may call  the patterns/movement of the "thing" h(a)unting you too simple and easy. Adventure fans may call the "puzzles" (which really aren´t THAT much puzzling) too simple. I like the balance of both.
After all it´s a very story heavy game, which starts giving hints on the (possible) outcome of the story from the very beginning, so that you are interested and inclined to guess and wanting to know how the story will finally end.
And actually i missed a part of the conclusion that was indicated pretty strongly throughout the game (
).
The "it´s a one-man-job"-argument shouldn´t be an excuse for flaws of the game, but it is really a great work for basically one guy doing such a creative and well rounded game.
If you are a fan of horror and adventure and still doubting whether to get this game or not, just wait for a 66-75% discount or a bundle containing it. Then you probably won´t make a mistake. I got this game in a bundle and remembered latewr, that this was one of the reasons i bought the bundle in the first place. And i can say it was worth it
Concidering the control issues and minor bugs/crashes, but relatively low base price i´d give it

The more annoying part about it is that 99% of the stuff in the environment is just filler/eye candy and there is no reason to touch it. If you are in the mood for this type of interactive adventure story with very few puzzles and no fighting, it is probably better than a lot of other games.
