Okay, now for the serious part:
"F2P" aspect: Possibly the best "free to play" game in steam! No strings atached, no microtransactions, no P2W b*llsh*t... It's just a game, for free, for ever!
Graphics: Pretty good, there are some flaws here and there (the planet cores look horrible!) and I wasn't able to set my resolution (not a big deal really). I really like the artstyle, and it does a great job on setting the mood and giving everything a nice, grim-dark-ish touch that sinks in very well with the game!
Story: Non-existant. Still a better love story than Twilight.
Controls: Great! There are lots of people complaining about how "stressful" or some♥♥♥♥♥♥the controls are, but those people probably haven't played any games of this genre.
Gameplay: Really fun and rewarding, challenging but fair and not overly difficult if you know where to go, and who to shoot. The light RPG elements really help give the game some depth, but some more mechanics like leveling, upgrading... etc, could make this game even better!!  My only complaint with the gameplay is that the different ships feel too similar, so I ended up sticking with the strongest one.
Sound: A bit lacking, some ambient music and more consistent sound effects (they seem to dissapear and reapear at will) would do much good.
UI (user interface): Good enough, though it could be much better. A "character" or "status" window would be pretty useful, so you can tell what weapon slots does your ship have (I've accidentally bought weapons that didn't fit in my slots) and a bunch of other useful info.
Overall, a really nice game, very fun and well polished. It has a lot of potential and room for improvement, and seeing as the dev seems to be a pretty nice guy who actually listens to the community, I see this game becoming better and better as time goes by. Give it a try, it's free and if you like space shooters, this game will definitely have you playing for hours!

Seasons after Fall is an artistic delight but an interactive bore. Rich, hand-painted visuals and a gorgeous string quartet soundtrack tantalized my senses and drew me in. Regrettably, the game's simple platforming and uninteresting puzzles failed to retain my attention. Most of my time was spent coming across an inactive object (like a limp giant mushroom) and changing to the appropriate season so that I could interact with it (Autumn, in the case of mushrooms). This repetition of seeing a visual prompt and responding with the correct season never made me feel clever, which in my mind is a death knell for a puzzle platformer with no combat.
After two hours of play I was ready to call it quits for good. Steam global achievement statistics show a similar drop off that isn't as evident in reviews. 81% of players unlock the first achievement which only takes a handful of minutes to acquire. Half of those players, 40.2%, make it to about the one hour mark which loosely lines up with unlocking the third season, Spring. 27.2% make it to where I stopped, seemingly around the halfway point in the game. 17.8% hit the next milestone and only 10.1% finish the game. For comparison, 27.6% of players finished Ori and the Blind Forest, and that game is roughly twice as long.
Younger audiences and adults looking for a beautiful and peaceful world to explore that doesn't require much mental strain may enjoy this game. I cannot recommend this to the average gamer though.
There are a limited number of things you can do in Seasons after Fall. You can move left and right, jump, bark and change seasons. This simplicity doesn't have to be a bad thing. However, due to platforming controls not feeling quite tight enough and the already mentioned uninspired puzzle design, it wasn't satisfying to control this cute little fox.
Clearer directions or a map with a destination marker would have been welcome at times. The game has a bad habit of showing a brief cutscene of the spot where it wants you to go but doesn't give adequate indication of where it is in relation to you. One nitpick of silly game design comes each time you unlock the ability to change to a new season. In this moment the forest spirit you play as is pulled out of the fox that you possess. Afterward you are forced to find the fox again but they are placed seemingly randomly somewhere off screen to the left or right. Having to guess which way is frustrating enough but for the life of me I don't know why they make you do this to begin with rather than include repossessing the fox in the cutscene.
I also ran into one bug several times. There are vines that extend during summer that refused to do so on first attempt. I ran to them, changed season and watched it light up as if it were going to unwind but it would not. Even if I ran several paces away and came back it refused to budge. I played through this game on Origin and recently received the game through steam via a Humble Monthly Bundle; so I felt it was time to put my thoughts on the game out there. I'm someone who is very aware of the constant privacy invasions of our internet connected lives, and how we are losing ground constantly. One of my favorite books is 1984 by George Orwell, so the name of this game was the first thing to pique my interest before I knew what it was about. Without any major spoilers, you play as an employee of a Big Brother-like watch system over the people in your country at the beginning of its implementation. You spend the game looking at a computer OS style UI where you scan through documents, web pages, and other online material to profile people for this "all-seeing" system.

The most interesting thing about this game is how well it presents all the different types of dangers (as well as pros if you look for them) with surveillance systems like the United States NSA stuff that has come out over the past years. It does such a good job at it because you aren't just looking at leaked documents about the system, but you ARE the system. Which means you make mistakes (or not) which leads to incorrect profiles and taking things out of context, which  endangers everyone.
Orwell is by far the best way to have someone that doesn't understand why national surveillance is bad for its citizens, truly understand all the intricacies and nuances of such a complex issue. I highly reccomend everyone play through this game. I honestly wish everyone had to play through this game so that misinformation and ignorance surrounding this issue would be minimized and we could all work together for the benefit of society as a whole. Play this game, and get someone else to play it; you won't be disappointed!

Transformice is a cute little game, with hours of your time to be wasted.
I've only started playing this a few months ago, and i've noticed the lack of educated Shamans, so ill list some controls that are basically need-to-know towards the bottom, and ill link their website's tutorials.
The goal of this game?
Getting cheese. It's pretty much the currency, and is used to buy aesthetic items like hats, skins, clothes, and building block re-skins for the shaman. The only problem i have with this, is that a lot of things cost thousands upon thousands of cheese, which can be quite a grind.
Unlike a lot of 'F2P' games, the only thing that spending money does, is get you the before-mentioned aesthetic items, and plays no factor in whether you'll be good or not.
Sometimes you get cheese, sometimes you completely miss a jump and fall to your doom. That's the cruel reality of Transformice.
There are a few game modes, and levels with different mechanics (Like Soul-Mate levels [which you'll learn to hate]), but the premise of the game never really changes. You're collecting cheese to level up, and buy shiny things.
Oh, and speaking of leveling up, lets talk about the shamans skill tree. There's 3 categories to work your way up in, one focuses on saving the poor mice that have fallen or gotten stuck, while another focuses on making sure YOU stay alive. The last is completely mechanic based, making anvils weigh more, or giving you a larger radius to place things.
Gaining skill points is fairly quick, but leveling your shaman is another story as it counts how many mice you have saved and how quickly you can save them all.
Now, im gunna talk about the controls, since so many people spawn as shaman and say "wut duh eh duh?"
Now you'd probably notice, when you're shaman, that there is a box in your GUI that has several items and symbols. "What could this mean?!", you may ask if you're not witty enough to realise, those are the objects and whatnots that you can spawn within a blue circle around yourself (not all require being in the circle to be used).
Most of the time, there is going to be a gap in between you/the mice and the cheese/the goal. You might already be guessing that you'll need to make a bridge with the objects at your disposal, but dont know how to make them connect.
I will teach you, young padawan.
I WILL TEACH YOU THE CONTROLS THAT SO MANY MICE BEFORE YOU HAVE FAILED TO COMPREHEND!
C – Yellow Anchor – This anchor needs to be attached to another item and make this item unable to rotate. (Basic bridge/structure building tool.)
B – Red Anchor – This anchor can be directly attached to the map or to any other item, but it can only be selected with a plank. Items are limited to a single red anchor and can’t be attached to any item that has a red anchor. Its main function is to rotate, and that’s not all! Red anchors have an other nice function: they can be placed on a dynamic item in order to prevent them to move! (This is probably one of the most useful tools because it can prevent things from moving or spinning, if you know how to use it.)
V – Blue Anchor – This anchor needs to be attached to another item. It hinges the item. (press multiple times to change where it hinges)
N and J – Blue Motorized Anchors – These anchors are to be attached to another item. They share the same properties with the blue anchor but the difference resides in the fact they can rotate automatically thanks to their motor. (Not used a lot, from what i've seen, but can still have its uses. J spins counterclockwise N spin clockwise)
Spacebar - Ghost Blocks - Ghost Blocks are easily recognizable thanks to their transparency and blue shade. >mice can go through them but items can’t< (Mainly used to set an 'anchor' so that your structures dont slide around when mice are running about them.)
I hope my review swayed some minds to join the cheese-race, and helped some aspiring shamans to nudge their mice along. My name in-game is stinkyviking, and if you're truly grateful and want to give back for the totally free and google-able information, then when you create an account you can use my name as a referal, doing this lets me exploit your cheese collecting by getting 1 for every ten you get, which can add up quickly over time. So go ahead, and invite your friends too.

This game definitely needs some work. The P2P matchmaking system is extremely unreliable, and it's been unacceptly common that I disconnect from a game (and lose any experience, in-game currency and gear I would've gotten otherwise). On top of that, there seems to be a bug that crashes the game at the very end of a match, just before the end cutscene and the final scoreboard: again, robbing you of any in-game goodies you earned during that game. It's just a hearty kick in the balls when you work so hard to complete an order (basically contracts such as, "get a killstreak of 8 without dying") and then to see the game freeze right after you acheive your goal. And the devs don't seem to care so much about these issues.
Now, with that being said I think the combat system works pretty well. Sure, there are mechanics which can be abused, such as environmental hazards, unblockable attacks, "vortex" combos, and kill-stealing is something that will happen to you quite often. But on the whole I think the game has some incredible cinematic moments. The combos are satisfying as hell when you do them correctly and when you get an execution the world somehow seems all-right again. And emote spamming is still funny as hell to me, though some people can do without it. You can also customize pretty much anything about your heroes, which makes the game that much more addicting because some of the gear/executions look incredible, and it gets more unique as you progress your characters. This all pertains to multiplayer, by the way. There is a singleplayer, but it's pretty forgettable. The story is weak, the characters are weak, and you can beat it in the better part of an afternoon. But it's a good way to get accustomed to the game if you've never played, and it gives you in-game gear for completing the story at certain difficulties.
Overall, I really don't think this game is worth the full $60. Like many others, I felt cheated, because what we saw as a promising intense medieval fighter in the beta soon proved to be an unfinished game rushed out of development when it was released. It's just not well-optimized and Ubisoft has a lot of work to do before they can honestly sell this game for full retail price. Anyway I've said enough. Buy it when they reduce the price or add dedicated servers.

An odd, surreal, colorful world, the first thing you'll notice about this game is just how creatively bizarre it is. It's strangely familiar with many of its elements and homages, and yet when it mixes them all up you still feel a breath of creativeness shine through. If you enjoyed things like old 60's cartoons or shows with their campiness, and love tongue in cheek humour, this is a great game for that. It also reminded me a bit of the Venture Bros., with the tone of everything satirizing and poking fun at the "cartoons of yesteryear".
The humour and art direction are indeed the strongest points to this game. If you're looking for a plot, however, I would say this doesn't really have much of one, aside from glimpses of the world they live in. The writing is at its strongest with humour, which is what the game 100% is.
Unfortunately, the game is very short, at most 2 hours, and not much replay value unless you like to experience it again after a long time or 100% the game. I recommend it solely off of the fact that it is an extremely funny game, but I would not pick it up for its full price of $15. Pick it up for when it's under $5, preferably around $3. It is well worth that price in broken sides and laughs alone.

Okay... there's one very good point I will give this game, and that that it's absolutely gorgeous and imaginative. A true piece of art. If you're looking for an abstract painting (you'll recognise its inspiration, such as MC Esher), but that you can interact with a little, than you've found something you'll like. Otherwise I have many grippes with this game. After less than an hour it was too annoying and I couldn't keep playing.
First off, the interaction system is wayyy too clunky. I much prefer the good ol' verb-based system : push, pull, take, talk, etc. Here you have to actually pull stuff by making very specific motion with your mouse. And because of this, it took me the longest time to get out of the cage at the beginning. After clicking furiously all around the screen, after having poked and pulled at the paperclip to no effect I was about to give up already. Then I just went crazy on it, moving my mouse all around, and it finally fell. My only thought was : ARE YOUR SERIOUS?
So yeah, this isn't nearly as intuitive nor as charming as Monkey Island, unfortunatly. The few characters there are only speak with speech bubbles and gibberish. This would be fine if their message was interesting, but they are only boring. Yes, the characters are pretty much untinteresting at best, shallow and blank at worst. Even the main character is weird and uncharacterised. He/she never speaks, you don't really know anything about him/her except that his/her parents moved in a new house and she is pulled into this miniature dimension. It would of added a lot to have given him/her an actual voice, so he/she could give his/her thoughts about the strange world he/she got into.
The puzzles themselves seem very contrived and strange, which follows the style of the world. I guess I'm just not smart enough, but I honestly couldn't solve most of them. The problem being, I didn't even know what the problems were most of the time. One room I solved out of pure luck, distracting an evil teapot with a fly I randomly captured in a bottle. Half the time I just looked, scratching my head, trying to understand what I was looking at. If the character could at least of given me a hint or something to identify what I needed to do it would of helped. Unfortunatly, after seeing all the strange rooms and not making any progress, I decided to stop playing. Now you might decipher the cryptic solutions to these rooms, connected by a kind of MC Escher maze, but I wasn't enjoying it so I couldn't be bothered. The last straw was a room where a firework kept firing in an endless loop of ear-destroying pain, while I got posed by a piece-swapping puzzle to this noise. NO THANKS. I'M OUT.
So yeah. Very pretty game, but mechanically too frustrating. If you're the type, like me, to enjoy artsy visuals, than I recommend this. Otherwise, if you want a well put together point n' click game, look elsewhere. Unless its on sale for very cheap. If you want a number, I'll give it a 6.5, 5 points for excellent visuals plus 1.5 for playability. It just couldn't pull me in (pun intented).

Full video review: at
If you love point and clicks go buy this game now, if you're on the fence read on.
Violett is the usual Point and Click affair, there’s a puzzle and you have to solve it. You might have some inventory items and you may need to backtrack every so often in order to get all the pieces. All that stuff is in Violett, if you're a fan of something like the Monkey Island series you'll feel right at home here. Violett differentiates itself through its mysterious nature
Violett is a world where nothing seems to make sense and there’s a lack of cohesion between levels, and that’s a good thing. It represents how crazy this world Violett is in and keeps things fresh and non-repetitive.
There’s no comprehensible language, as such you learn everything about the world visually and through interactions with other characters. They do have speech bubbles but they’re filled with various pictures/drawings and from that you have to solve the puzzles.
While this helps the narrative of Violett and brings a sense of mystery and wonder, it’s also where a large portion of the frustrations come from. Sometimes objectives are unclear and you’ll spend more time trying to work out what the objective is rather than trying to solve the puzzle. Violett does its best to alleviate this issue but it doesn’t always succeed.
Violett features a really nice soundtrack, though they feel more like compositions than BGM. It comes free with the game so you may as well give it a listen! The songs for the most part are well choreographed with the background images.
The scenery is of a high standard and there’s enough going on that you can spend a large amount of time just taking it all in. In saying that Violett does seem to stand out very harshly in some of the environments and while it can be said this is to show how she’s out of place, it sometimes ruins these amazing backdrops. This isn’t always the case though and is only something you notice in the more simplistic levels.

I'll write this game from the standpoint of a beginner (Starter's Pack).
First off, I went into the game, don't know wtf was going on. Situations helped with controls, but in multiplayer, strategy changes, an exponential learning curve kicks off.
However, by rank 10 you should have sufficient knowledge of the game and what's going on; enough to kill.
This game is mostly (if not, purely) based on experience. Knowing the maps, the operators, camera locations, and using the surroundings to complete the mission. Using what you have to make do with the current situation.
Starter's Pack is a bit of a grind. 12 hours for base operators, 24 hours for DLC operators. Quite an intense grind. But if you're just in it for the fun and the thrill then Starter's Pack would suffice.
Here's the best thing about this game. People say it's all about skill, but to me teamwork and "opportunity" has its fair share in this game. Just because you're at a low rank, killing a rank 100 doesn't necessarily mean it's skill or that you're better than a rank 100 (newbs brag about that all the time). Sometimes, You were given the opportunity to kill and you took it. Similarly, a rank 100 who killed you doesn't necessarily mean you suck, maybe you just didn't know he was coming from behind.
But sometimes; to kill, you need a little bit of skill ;)
TL;DR
Improvise. Adapt. Overcome.

This game was really colourful and the artwork was nicely done for every season, which had it's own way of shaping the gameplay into a platformer where could make new platforms appear. Also the classical music in the background makes it even more peaceful and adventorous. The story is quite mysterious and in the beginning you are just trying to go from season to season and acquire the ability to control it. It's exciting to explore the levels and try out the ability to change seasons at first, but you kinda lack an antagonist/villain, which without spoiling to much gets made up for later on in the storyline.
I completed it in one playthrough and will say it was both fun and annoying sometimes. The thing that annoyed me was the missing direction you were given. Although i understand that an adventure where you're forced to follow a certain path can be a bit predictable or like the opposite of free and exploring, on the other hand this openworld makes you sometimes just running around without knowing where you're supposed to go, in terms of progressing the story. (An arrow where to go maybe or just more hints from the speaker would have been nice). And at that point i just used my intuition to guess where, but it was frustrating when you wasted time running around and go back to find you just missed an entrance to a new place. Besides that there was a puzzle in one place that was pretty difficult compared to the platformer gameplay of the rest of the game, here some hints (or maybe just the ability to ask an NPC for it) would have been good, cause i was stuck here and also a friend of mine was and he thought they were a bit weird too. It's like that math revelation moment on them, where you just think oh.. So that was the solution, but meanwhile figuring it out you didn't have fun trying. That's just my opinion, maybe you like that kind of challenge. Also i felt like i got delayed by having to wait for platforms for me to complete the puzzle, so if you fail a couple of times the wait time is not great.
To conclude I think this is a very visually beautiful game accompanied by adventorous music, the gameplay is alright, sometimes annoying and with an interesting mechanic that changes your surroundings, same level just different conditions. I think the ending is cool too.
If you want a platformer with bossbattles and fighting this probably ain't one for you, but if you like to explore and do a couple of puzzles on the way, I think you will have a good experience. :)

Don't get me wrong, this is a fun game, but boy is it horribly made. There are no graphics options (can't even change the default (720p), nor is there a tutorial anywhere in sight. I'm not sure which is worse, but the lack of a tutorial is inexcusable as there's a bit of a learning curve to actually play the game (as there is a huge difference from Don Bradman Cricket 14). If you plug in a controller after you've launched the game, you have to close and re-open the game all over again. The mouse cursor is also constantly spinning, and doesn't disappear even when a controller is plugged in. You can move it to one side, but why is it spinning (and why doesn't go transparent for that matter) in the first place?
There's constant crashes and hangs, which just continues to show the game has been badly ported or supported. This is in stark contrast to Don Bradman Cricket 14, which really shines on the PC.
Versus Mode doesn't even work properly (or at least it didn't at the time I wrote this). Sure, you can choose to play two players, but once you get into the game, it's just player one against the CPU.
I'm a massive Big Ant fan, so I'm not sure what they were thinking on this one, though I have a bit of confidence they'll patch a lot of these issues that really shouldn't be issues.
Just as well the price point is lower than on consoles, because it would be unforgivable otherwise. This has clearly been rushed, when it had no reason to be. For a game that was announced in 2012, it's an immense disappointment. Therefore, at the moment, I just cannot recommend this.

4 Months before this games release, my good friend wouldn't shut up about how excited he was for it to come out. Whenever an alpha, tech test, or beta would come out he'd convince me and everyone else in our numerous friend circles to download it and play it.
At first, I was skeptical about the game, as he told me it was being published by ubisoft, and their track record (in my opinion) has never been above decent. But, once I played it for the first time I was completely enthralled by the combat system and the number of characters to pick from and how different they all were from eachother. After that first alpha was over, I was just as excited for the full game to be released as my friend was, and it soon became the main topic of all our conversations.
A few more tech tests and betas later, the final beta comes out and its final day is 2 days before the full game was to be released. Now, up until this point I had forgiven the frame drops and numerous disconnection issues that occurred throughout my time of playing the game, because those are to be expected in alphas, tech tests and betas. But, the question occurred to me: 'How will they be able to fix these game breaking connection problems within 2 days?' 2 days later, I got my answer. The numerous betas weren't meant for testing, they were simply marketing gimmicks in order to ensure more pre orders.
Instead of allowing Ubisoft Montreal, Ubisoft Quebec, Ubisoft Toronto, and Blue Byte to make the best possible version of this game they could, they decided to give them a lower budget than they needed, forcing them to take shortcuts that hinder the experience Jason Vandenberghe originally intended to create.
Instead of letting the matches play out based on player's skill level, Ubisoft forced in a gear score system that boost your attacks, just to ensure more people would spend money on micro transactions in order to get high level gear (A.K.A. pay to win). This system, while being intended to lure more players in, only deters new players and experienced players from trying new characters.
Instead of focusing on balancing characters and many problems that were present in the game since day 1 of release, Ubisoft forced the developers to rush the development of 2 new characters, in an attempt to ressurrect their already dying player base.
I WANT to tell you that I recommend this game. I WANT to tell you to buy it, but while Ubisoft continues to make these poor decisions, I refuse to do so. Maybe when new characters come out and as they continue to patch the game, I'll come back to this review and change my mind entirely, but, frankly, I don't see that happening.

Well, I just got done with Violett and I must say there's a lot that's both good and bad.
The Good:
Overall, I found the experience charming. The art is excellent, most (but not all) of the puzzles are challenging but not impossible, and I liked the hidden item collection. The Machinarium-style pictograms were a good choice, making localization a breeze.  Music was great too, and I appreciate the OST coming with the Steam release sale.
The Not So Good:
The hint system is TERRIBLE!  Totally tells you nothing you need to know. Plus, some of the puzzles aren't tremendously intuitive, and when you suddenly need to start backtracking after a series of self-contained rooms it's unexpected.  The hidden item aspect, which I do like, actually makes no sense in terms of mana since you never use it. I haven't tried, but I expect you can finish the game quite handily without picking up a single bit of mana throughout which makes it pointless except to gain an achievement.  Finally, there's the rather inexplicable ending scene which I suspect was intended to be interactive but somehow plays automatically.  Makes no sense in context, since you haven't seen or heard about this character from the beginning, so it's quite confounding.
I should make special mention of the story, or rather the lack thereof. At the beginning, we are given a pretty bare-bones setup. Unhappy girl, taken to big house, finds amulet and gets sucked into another world.  And...that's pretty much all you get.  Other than a glimpse at the beginning of the game and a diary entry that you can easily miss out on, the player has NO CLUE who the villain at the end is. Even then, there's no indication if they're the one who brought you into this world. You also aren't given any idea what this place is, or how it's related to you. There's one reference that the diary belonged to your uncle, but that's the sole mention of him, so again we're lost.
Finally, there are the bugs. I only had to restart the game from the beginning once (from the library) but others have had to do it multiple times. I also ran into a couple of graphical glitches towards the end. Better quality control should have been done before this was released onto Steam, for sure.
Overall:
Despite all that, I'd still recommend the game although you might need to look in the community for hints. It is undeniably charming, and that's a large part of it for me. I just wish there were a more engaging story to go with it.

I quickly snapped up Violett and eagerly jumped into the game once it installed. I have to admit feeling a little lost at the beginning as there is no spoon feeding. You are plunged straight into an environment that encourages you to explore. I normally enjoy these sort of games but I find Violett frustrates me more than entertains me. I'm a good portion of my way in and I no longer have the satisfaction of solving a puzzle or the excitement of a new location.
Graphically it is interesting and the imaginative game world, inspired by Alice in Wonderland, certainly adds a new dimension. Music is okay and helps set the atmosphere. But something is missing, something just doesn't quite gel.
Most of the puzzles do make sense in their own, sometime surreal, way although I do find myself randomly clicking on things without a sense of direction when I'm stuck. Other times I've missed important clues that blended a little too well with the background or solved something by accident without really knowing what I did. A few puzzles were simple enough to solve but tedious to execute and my only satisfaction in completing them was I didn't have to do it again.
Maybe part of what is missing, for me at least, is some sort of feedback mechanism. I feel detached from what is going on in the game. I can only make sense of the various scenes by what I see with my eyes. Violett does not attempt to enrich that with any further explanation, for example items that are picked up cannot be examined closer nor do they have labels. I've come across a few things that I have no idea what they are let alone what to use them for. Violett is also a little helpless when trying something that isn't valid. Just a shrug with little indication (in most cases) as to why it is not valid. It reminds me of those old school Text Adventures that had the default response "I can't do that". I'm never sure if it's because it is impossible in the game or I haven't satisfied all the prerequisites.
It must be noted that the controls are simplistic but unfortunately a tad clunky. They feel as they've been designed with a touch device in mind. I'm playing with a keyboard and mouse so that may be why.
I can't not recommend this game as it certainly does have merit, it's reasonably executed and it has generated a lot of eager discussion and favourable comments in the forum, but for me I don't think I have the will to progress much further. If you enjoy puzzle based games then you may get something out of Violett but mileage will vary.

Ah, Rocksmith. such a brilliant game, with one big flaw.
Don't get me wrong, I love the concept, and (to the most part) its execution. However there is a niggle which I, as a musican, can't stand.
I'll start with the negative, as it is indeed, only one negative. The sheer fact that the game never tells you what notes you're playing or are supposed to play. It's all well and good knowing that you need to play the 5th fret on the A string, but you are never told that 5th fret A is a D and can be played on the open D string. This can make some songs a LOT easier to play.
Segwaying slightly; during the session mode and certain guitarcade games, you are able to choose what scale you are playing in, this is all well and good but again, you are never told what notes constitue the scales, only the frets. I can foresee a fairly large number of amateur musicians thinking they can play guitar/bass but not knowing what they are actually doing.
Rant over. Now onto the good stuff
and there's a lot of it.
I absolutley adore the concept of a guitar hero-esque game where you use an actual guitar/bass and Rocksmith does it exceptionally, the roar of the crowd whilst shredding through the solo to the Trooper is just brilliant (or so I imagine it would be, if I actually played guitar and not just bass)
The session mode is a glorious addition too, being able to stick a band together, or just jam with a drum kit, is so much fun. I just wish you could do it in other tunings.
and the final thing I shall discuss, the guitarcade. honestly one of my favorite things about the game, learning various techniques in a game-like environment is just genius.
All in all, I thoroughly enjoy playing Rocksmith, I just hope they add a Red Hot Chili Peppers song pack at some point.

To sum up how I feel about this: "Why is this free?". I don't have much experience with free games, except for android apps which are riddled with ads (which this is obviously not). I can only assume this author wants to put their work out there and get people to play it, I dunno. I'm really happy I did try it. Though, when I first saw it, it did connect with me. I saw it on the store page, thought "This looks neat" then watched the trailer and thought "this looks like what I've been waiting for". I say that because I'm the type to have a game (usually big name and/or great reviewed game) to play; I also want a simple mindless game to help break up the play through of that other game. This game is more than that though, its what you make of it. Nothing you NEED to master to play the game, easy to learn and you get better and enjoy it more thoroughly as you master it. This is asteroids physics, which I've not played a game similar yet on steam personally, I did see someone mention SPAZ, which I should check out at again.
So, you start in the basic ship, spend some time mining (by shooting asteroids... feels like punching trees but funner because of physics) to gain enough money to buy upgrades and better ships to fit better weapons. There is no direction in the game and a very minimalistic tutorial, but it feels genuinely like this was meant on purpose, kind of an exploration aspect, you learn the game by playing (which is fine). This isnt some rpg (apparently it does claim it is...), it is like "See how far you can get". This would be AWESOME and worth like 30 bucks if it were more refined and had more content. You'll find yourself saying "OH *this* should be added!" all the time.
It doesn't seem like there is any end game, but it is mesmerizing to say the least and is definitely worth the one second DL time and $0. I spent my whole evening playing it and bothered to leave a review.
A couple tips: stick with your original blaster with unlimited ammo until you feel confident with the combat, the starting trade ship sells the ship your in already for 200 and the game will let you throw money away buying the ship you already own. Other than that, just jump in and F around!
TL;DR: It's worth your time, not just because it's free

A cute and short little game with an amazing artstyle and even better soundtrack. It's not particularly hard or challenging (apart from one point near the end where I nearly tore my hair out in frustration before eventually consulting a guide), but I don't think it's trying to be.
The animations are fluid and watching the world and your character move around is a lot of fun! I also took way too many screenshots of the scenery, because it's pretty like woah.
I was a little wary going into the game, because another reviewer mentioned the slow animation speed when solving puzzles, but I never found that to be an issue. It comes down to personal taste, probably, but there really aren't that many puzzles where the game makes you sit around until it's done showing your correct solution, so if you're unsure about getting the game because of this - don't be.
Changing seasons was a bit tiring until I realized you can also quick-dial them (right-stick on the Xbox controller I was using), after which it never bothered me again.
There is some backtracking if you want to get all the achievements and didn't look out for them from the start. The puzzles are easy, but a few of them become a little tedious if you pass through an area several times because you forgot something.
There's no map and while I did get lost a couple of times in the beginning, I never felt the need for one.
The controls were tight for the most part of the game and in some areas, I went wild with jumping around while changing seasons to see if there were any hidden paths that could only be accessed by doing crazy fountain height shenanigans.
There were a handful of times, however, when my character didn't jump as I told it to and I had to redo some puzzles because of that, but I honestly can't say if that was the game or my controller having a mind of its own. Given how the levels are designed, you don't get thrown back a lot if you mess up a jump, though.
Seasons after Fall is probably not a game for everyone. If you want something cute and relaxing that lets you sit back and simply enjoy a nice looking game with wonderful music, great voice acting and season changing gimmicks, you should definitely give this game a try! Given its short runtime, you might want to wait for a sale, though.

It's hard to say that either Orwell's story or its interface is earth-shattering in any way, but put together they create an experience that's enough to keep you always running after what's around the next corner. As on-the-nose as it may be to call your game on state surveillance "Orwell", the narrative inside is more restrained and explores accurate and disturbing tactics used by state spies. You get the sense that the "choice" in the story is often somewhat an illusion, but maybe that's the point. It's a game that empowers you by letting you crawl inside peoples' PCs and phones while teaching you about privacy invasion and only once it's put you through the preset experiences it thinks are necessary does it let you decide what to do about this spy apparatus.

I don't think anything could have prepared me for Orwell.
Playing the role of a law enforcement agent, researching a potential terrorist cell through the social media and communications of its members, the simple browser-styled interface makes it easy to lose yourself in the characters, their interactions and the over-arching story which often hits close-to-home in 2017.
Overall, a really relaxing play and an interesting look at real-life issues surrounding privacy, social media and free speech.

This game was surprisingly effective. I went in expecting some heavy-handed story based purely on the title, but apart from some suspension of disbelief problems I really enjoyed the game. The UI was a masterpiece, the story interesting enough, but it's the characters where Orwell really shines. Each and every one of them felt believable and real, and I, at least, ended up rather moved by some of the characters and their motivations.
What I thought was especially interesting was how they're written to be very open to interpetation and to your preconception. The user-selectable portraits really help in this regard, as they each seem to represent different facets of the cast's personalities. A novel approach to interactive fiction, and I highly recommend it.

tl;dr: amazing atmosphere, wonderful soundtrack and ambience, great detalis, very creepy dungeons and monsters, wonderful story and deep reflections about humanity, consciousness and ethic choices.
The best of this game is not the stealth survival horror thing per se (while the monsters are still creepy and the scaring side is genuine, they can be easily passed once you get used to know their behaviour, so the challenge is limited), but the incredible immersion you experience while playing. Discovering what happened to this world, the backstories of the crew of Pathos II, all the creepiness in detalis inside levels (notes, photos, objects around etc.), the outstanding atmosphere around you (enriched by the wonderful ambient soundtrack by Mikko Tarmia) and above all the food-for-thought in the plot. Ethic dilemmas, heartly moral choices (euthanasia, the right to decide for the others, mors tua vita mea, having the right thing to do, having the necessary although sad thing to do, continuing living in a nightmare or not, whether a fake dream is better than crude reality etc.), solipsisms, thinking about the line dividing humanity from machine and when an artificial intelligence could be considered a person, question about who Simon really is after mind scanning and the toss-coin metaphor. Probably the best game by Frictional Games.
Buy it.

SOMA is the most recent game from Frictional Games. SOMA is down right brilliant when it comes to story, lore, and the way it tells the story. However, the horror in this game comes down to being extremely mixed, with moments of brilliantly made terror, and down right frustration.
In SOMA, you play as Simon, a normal man from Toronto Canada. On this day, you go in for a brainscan, for an injury recieved awhile ago. However, at the end you find yourself in a mysterious underwater facility filled with machines that take on human characteristics. You meet up with someone named Catherine, who explains that she's been working on a device named the ARK. Humanity is at the brink of extinction, and this device will allow people to be scanned, and put onto it to allow them to live on in an artifical world. You and Catherine then procced out to find the device. While I loved to talk more about the story, I really can't due to major spoilers. The story and lore of the game is truely top notch, and the best frictional has made, and some of the best in gaming.
Frictional is well known for horror, and to some extent gameplay, with their previous series, Amnesia and Penumbra. However, where SOMA creates a fantastic story, the game is an extremely mixed bag on the horror and gameplay. Each monster has its own set of rules, such as not looking at it, or detecting players on movement. This is fun, increased by the fact that monsters only appear once or twice, and are never repeated (except for one time), which means each area has something new. This is could be really cool, but it starts to die when you look at it. Some monsters are introduced horribly, with no explanation given. This means players must figure it out themselves, and that's fun, but SOMA makes it tedious. One end game monster detects the player based on movement, which is a cool idea, but there's no way for the player to really figure this out. Since moving by monsters is often already done crouched,  this is hard to notice, and the monster also gives no indicator that this might be how they act. I think most of the monsters in this game are fine, but simply aren't used in a good way, or one that would make sense. One final thing before the countdown, gameplay in SOMA is much more simplistic, with no inventory, players dont have to worry about management or what they carry around. Having an infinite light sources also loosens it a bit. Here is my quick thoughts on each monster (names not mentioned, numbered from first to last in game):
1. Good
2. Ok
3. Bad
4. Good
5. Bad
6. OK
7. Bad
8. Ok
9. Good
10. OK
All in all, SOMA truely is a brilliant game when it comes to story, but is a mixed bag when it comes to monsters and their encounters. In the end I would recommend the game. If you want to experience the story, there is a mode where the monsters exist but can't attack you, which is a good thing to take a look at.

Before I had ever heard of this game, I had bought a guitar years ago. I always wanted to learn, but never came through to learning how to play a song. I had once in a while picked up the guitar and strummed a few cords, just for the heck of it. Until December 2013 I heard about this new program called Rocksmith 2014, and although I've heard about the Rocksmith 2011 and I heard reviews that the 2011 edition was not accurate guitar teacher, I passed for buying the game. Since I heard about this new 2014 edition, I seemed interested on what all the fuss was about. After reading reviews and watching videos, I finally decided to buy the game. When plugging in my guitar for the first time, I was confused with scheme of the game. When I reversed of to the Learn a Song section, and played a song, I was confused with the notes and did not seem to be getting anywhere to playing the actual song. However, after playing the song for about a half-hour, the notes started to adjust to my ability as I learned the song more and more. I even used the handy riff repeater that can strengthen my skills within the notes of the song by speeding up or slowing down, and/or adjusting the difficulty. The game includes mini games if you ever get bored of Learn a Song and want to practice chords, finger picking, or just strumming the guitar. Don't worry too much about the option as I focus much with Learn a Song and the mini games. And after 8 months and 20 hours of practicing, not including off time practicing, I have learn about 10 songs fully. And the worth the price rather than paying a guitar teacher, in addition to paying the game on your own time.
-Also supports bass :P
Buy this game if you want to be a rockstar!!!!!

-Find some songs you ABSOLUTELY LOVE. That way you have something to strum along with for fun when you don't feel like doing anything 'serious'.

This game is underrated.
There is no other way to say it. The fans attacked this game right off the bat and have subsequently abandoned it.
That being said, this is not for the fans who I presume will not listen to anything I have to say. This is for the curious gamer who is looking for a fun zombie-survival-action game to play with a friend.
First and foremost, this is not a survival horror game (nor have any of the numbered REvils ever been) but an evolution of the original game concept that has been present in all the numbered games.
It is highly action oriented, designed more to get your heart racing than scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you. There are no supernatural gimmicks or creepy solos through mansions here. You are fighting a war against bio-terrorism, and you are losing.
What is perhaps most ironic about this game is that it follows the formula of the popular movies, and yet has received such heavy attacks for doing just that while actually being better than any of the movies could ever hope to be.
The characters are more memorable, developed better, and even more likeable to the point where you actually care when one of them dies. The gameplay is solid 3rd-person with the exception of camera steal happening when they want to show you a particular sequence.
One complaint I've heard is that the game makes it too easy for you. I don't know what difficulty these people have been playing on, but the game is not easy, you will die quite a bit and not simply because a quicktime event got you but because the enemies will overwhelm or overrun you.
Perhaps the most interesting thing I've found in this game is that no two characters (with the exception of the Generic Agent Man) play quite like any of the others. They all have their own unique HUDs, weapons, and even melee moves which keeps the gameplay interesting as something you have access to isn't always the same as your partner and vice versa.
The intersecting stories are handled well and if you play through the game in order it weaves a fascinating intertwining plot where you can see everything develop in each from different points of view. I even had my opinions about different characters change as I played the different campaigns and was allowed to see more into their rasons for what they do in the game.
So to sum up, this game doesn't deserve the bad ratings and poor reviews it has received. It's a solid zombie-action game with survival undertones and a solid cast of characters with a story filled with all the action cheese of the movies.
At the end of the day, you should give it a shot. It might surprise you.

Really fun and original, get that game !

I think there's probably a game here somewhere. I can't find it past the bugs and the noise however.
Industry Giant 2 is an old-school tycoon type game. Don't let the release date fool you. This game came out in 2002 and was a bit dated even back then. I can get by the graphics even if it does take a fair amount of squinting. That's not the issue.
The issue is the "quality of life" improvements that we've seen these 15 years are not reflected in the game. For instance, getting something as simple as milk from one place to another takes the following steps:
1. Build cattle farm
2. Go into cattle farm and select milk
3. Build warehouse near farm
4. Build truck depot near farm
5. Build market near destination city
6. Build warehouse near destination city, making sure it's within the market radius
7. Build truck depot near destination city, making sure it's within the warehouse radius
8. Build road to connect the farm depot with the city depot, making sure to connect the exits on both of the truck depots that are often hidden by the header over the depot (and you can't rotate the map)
9. Go to the farm depot, click to choose the type of truck, hit accept
10. Go to the next screen, tell it what you want to collect and whether it waits until it is full to run the route
11. Click on the destination depot
If you've managed to do all of this correctly - and often the game gives an error - then your little truck will pick up milk and drive it to the destination city. Then there's the fiddling with the price, quantity supplied, amount produced, etc.
*phew*  That's a bunch of steps! If that kind of micromanagement doesn't bother you then this might be your type of game. It kind of is my type as well.
But then there are the numerous bugs. There are your normal lockup/crash type issues here but sometimes the game glitches and entirely screws you over. For instance, on the very first scenario I did the following steps. For some reason the AI decided it was a good idea to have other cars use my dirt road which terminated at my truck depot. They wouldn't move and the line of AI cars kept getting bigger and bigger which prevented my trucks from reaching the depot. With no way to remove the cars, I had to restart the scenario and there wasn't any part of that which was my fauilt. That's just the game deciding to take a dump on my scenario. Then the next time through it crashed and I lost what progress I had made. This does not make Blackadar happy.
Then there are the QoL improvements that I spoke of earlier. The devs decided that bird noises were the best way to fill players' speakers and thus be prepared to here a cacophony of bird and other noises piercing your airspace. The interface is simply too small in spots and trying to see what you're doing can be difficult. You can't rotate the map and getting to certain spots or even buildings can be difficult - and this matters when you're trying to link up tracks/roads and so forth. It's an older game and there's been nothing done to bring it up to today's UI standards. Then there's the income statement which only shows per YEAR which means it's very difficult to figure out whether you've turned things around or not. Losing money and made some adjustments? Well, you're not going to be able to tell because there's no monthly income statement! That's a pretty massive oversight in a business sim.

SOMA is ultimately a brilliant game, not simply for its execution, but for the subjects it explores and the world it builds.  It makes a few minor missteps along the way, but I would consider it one of the best non-combat horror games available today, and a must-play for anybody who enjoys the horror genre or has an interest in concepts like A.I., immortality, consciousness, and what is "real".
+ Absolutely
story explored through a series of unique, immersive environments--this game could very well make you question the nature of existence, what the survival of the human species is worth, and your very conception of "living" and "self"--without being pompous or self-righteous about it
+ Each enemy posseses its own rules, and almost none of these opponents are reused needlessly; makes great use of the setting to provide a variety of unsettling creatures and characters; creates a very tangible "don't know what might be around the next corner" scenario, even 6 or 7 hours in
+ While there are startling moments, the game does not have an over-reliance on cheap horror tactics like "jump" scares; the horror aspects of the game are delivered in much more nuanced ways
+ Does not feel like a game that cut any significant corners during its development:  Its execution is very satisfying, with a substantial plot that delivers a solid 8-12 hours of gameplay without overstaying its welcome
- A few of the AI encounters can be somewhat tedious, bogging the game down in trial-and-error attempts at progression
- Given the number of times you have to evade hostiles, it might have been nice for the game to provide a greater variety of options for hiding/escaping (such as Alien: Isolation provides with hiding under furniture and inside of sufficiently large containers).  As it stands, you might be caught and killed while standing in a room with plenty of
places to hide, but no means to actually do so
- The AI never seems to approach the complexity of something like Alien: Isolation's Xenomorph

SOMA is a great game. I enjoyed playing it. However I'm going to be a contrarian and point out a few gripes I have with this game.
Now there's a lot that goes into making a game, much less a game like this with excellent visuals that you don't need a super high end video card to enjoy. The story has some good originality and is not too far fetched. I'd even argue it's plausible. That makes for the best kind of horror after all, when it could actually happen.
Now that said my most common reaction was to sigh with annoyance due to yet another power failure, or malfunction, or dealing with the unintuitive computer interfaces that are in some cases not self explanatory. Given real computer programs have the ability to hover the mouse cursor over buttons and have helpful menus or dialog boxes pop up, this isn't fun, it's just annoying.
Even for a damaged facility there are sure a lot of power failures, missing equipment that you need to hunt for, and other horror cliches like the doors that take forever to open. The worst example is late in the game when you have doors that inexplicably have eight locks that need to unlock before they open with no reason I could find as to why.
Earlier in the game is an elevator that you need to insert a control chip into, but no you can't just insert the chip after you find it. You need to update it which can be justified in the story. However the panel design is unrealistically complicated with weird locking tabs, oh, and you have a monster chasing after you so you have to do it quickly. Blatant horror cliche.
Also while the story is great and really makes you think, you get railroaded too often. SPOILERS AHEAD:
You switch from one body to another late into the game. Since you are a copy downloaded into a new body, your old copy is still alive and well. You have the option to kill them or leave them be to wake up not knowing what happened. You have no option to leave them a note explaining what happened.
Later Johan Ross wants you to poison the WAU, which for all its horrors is at least trying to do the right thing and judging by Simon's creation is getting better at it. Ross is mutated but still arguably sane and can be talked to. I would have loved to have the chance to reason with him. Something like "Stop your popping in and out and listen for a minute! Humanity is likely dead. I'm going to launch the ARK. At this point why bother killing the WAU? Why not let it continue to evolve? In time it could bring humans back in some form."
In the end these are minor gripes and most of them center around the things done to make the game artifically longer, or compromises made for the sake of development time. That said there is so much that could be done with this story. Perhaps some DLC where if you keep your copy and the WAU alive, Simon could start teaching it. Or getting Ross to help as he's an A.I. psychologist.
So overall it's a great game, but it leaves me wanting more. It feels like a tease for a much bigger story and there are some good possibilities left unexplored.

For games of 2v2 and higher it might be worse as the connection could be coming from a guy in England while you and the other players are for example somewhere in Kenya, why is this bad well the game might assign the person with the worst connection to the other players as host resulting in unplayable matches for you and the others but not for him/her.  For Honor also does not have a proper balancing system, *Example,  you are rank 1, you have no gear, no skill, nothing, your opponent on the otherhand is a ranked 30 presitge or in For Honor's case reputation 30 with max level gear, because of this we can already see the outcome of this match and its not pretty. Overall this game is not worth it. Before anyone says "he cant review because hes new" you are wrong.  I just bought this on my steam account because I loved it so much.  I have played over 200 hours on uplay.  Yes thats not a "ton" but in this game if you don't know whether or not you like it after 10 hours you are a goner lol.
So lets be realistic though.  THere are two sides and I STRONGLY agree with both.  Ill start with pros then move on to cons and then explain my final opinion.
Pros:
-Actual physical combat unlike any other game.  When I parry, it REALLY parrys.  You will NEVER see two characters bodies/weapons go through eachother.  Everything is stopped by physics.
-Procedural kills.  Now some people are going "BS" but let me explain.  I don't mean that the kills are done in different ways.  But the alignment of kills is done procedurally which saves you from seeing and BS screen glitching or having characters magically execute through objects or down slopes.  If I execute someone on the staircase and their body is tilted down the stairs, my execution matches that angle and swings down farther.  It's a small but nice detail proving how hard they worked to make combat authentic.
-Character for everyone: Yea some characters have their issues which I will address later (most have been resolved through rebalancing), but there is a character for EVERY SINGLE playstyle.  However you want to fight, there is a man/woman who fits perfectly.
-Reward for skill: Most games are a cluster F that get you killed based on being spotted first.  This game is different.  Because the game is focussed on encounters being mini battles of their own, you almost never are taken by surprise from behind and one-shotted (if you are, kudos to the person for being so sneaky and shame on you for not being aware of surroundings).  I started as a freshie and was getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked left and right.  I felt like I couldnt get a single hit on other people's combos and was dying in seconds.  I was right.  You know why? Ubisoft doesn't teach you the real tactics.  Learning to properly parry and feint makes an amazing difference.  Youtube it or you will be destroyed by EVERY SINGLE PLAYER who has more than a few hours of playtime.  Anyone serious about the game has memorized their character weaknesses, strengths, combos, and disabling strategies.  TIP: ASK SOMEONE FOR HELP.  I had two guys kicking myself and a friend around like we were school children and they kindly offered to train us.  Within an hour of training I had learned to feint and parry and was finally kicking♥♥♥♥♥again.
Good community: Some people are salty af.  This isn't true across the board though.  Everything I know about my characters I was taught by SUPER kind community members.  They created custom matches and trained me for hours without even blinking. They were happy to explain how to beat their characters and how to counter others.  This game is about knowledge.  You don't know your opponent, he will destroy you.
Cons: Steep learning curve.  Yea this is super obvious after an hour of play.  YOu need to put time into reading guides, watching videos, and asking other players for help to train you.  This game's tutorial will make you suck.  Don't count on just those skills as they only work for singleplayer.  If you go into multiplayer and only block/light/heavy you will be destroyed like the hindenburg.  Although I personally find this a pro because it means I am rewarded on skill, its something most people see as daunting hence why its in cons.
Slight character imbalance:  This was more an issue at the beginning, now it is almost entirely resolved.  By imbalance I dont mean OP characters, but I will explain my thoughts.  This game is 95% skill based, but there is that 5% you should be 100% aware of.  Don't pretend it doesnt mean much.  That 5% is your character choice.  My main is lawbringer.  He is a heavy hitter with amazing stun abilities and probably the best turtle (slow, come to me character) in the game.  BUT, there are some characters that are incredibly hard to counter with him.  Namely Shinobi the ninja and the Peacekeeper who is mean af lol.  But I still play law because I know their weaknesses and how not to let them get their attacks on me.  If they do, I will die.
Matchmaking issues: I hate to say it, but these are still consistent. Let me start with connectivity.  My connection has been fine and I never get disconnected unless someone elaves the match in which case it is simply changing host.  (it changes host in-game and just pauses it for a moment to do so, really handy!).  The issue I do have is matchmaking.  When i started I was lvl 1 (obviously) and being matched with Prestige 28, armor lvl 144 (max level armor) and getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked.
BOTTOM LINE: Buy it.  Stop getting hung up on the problems.  The problems are 95% your fault because you don't put the effort into learning characters.  If you haven't read at least 5 articles, had a personal training session and watched a video about your character, you are at fault.  This game needs to be treated like a MOBA because it is one in so many ways while not at the same time.  Skill > Everything else

As a large fan of horror games, I have a huge problem with them. Most horror games rely on the initial shock of whatever it is you're dealing with. In this case, the whatever it is you're dealing with is Slender Man. He's creepy and extremely startling. He'll scare you to death the first run through this game. Slender, or better yet the mechanics that make up Slender, rely on the unknown and the confusion that's conjured in your own head. Being lost AND hunted make for a stressful situation. And they only lay it on thicker as you continue. But after the first playthrough, you know exactly what to expect and you know exactly how Slender and his hooded companion are going to react to you and your actions. The shock wears off and you're left only a little startled every time your camera lense gets a bit of static. All of that boils down to the lack of any real replayability. Nothing is left to keep you wondering except a few collectables. If you are looking for story in this game, almost the entire narrative is found within the many collectables found in the game. The collectables and the narrative found within those collectables adds a very miniscule amount of replayability. Which brings me to my conclusion; I think this game is very worthy of its $9.99 price tag, but doesn't have much more to offer after the experience.

Let me begin by saying that I am an experienced guitarist, playing for 34 years, and therefore I am unable to provide a beginner's view of this software. If you are a beginner reading this review, please understand that I can't fully appreciate the suitability of this software to your personal needs as a new player. I hope that you will still find my review useful.
RS2014 is an interactive songbook which features fully notated guitar and bass arrangements for a great many popular songs, mainly from the past few decades. The base content is diverse, and the DLC includes a wide variety of genres and styles with the abilty to download band or theme packs or individual songs. Many songs have two guitar parts, plus bass. Not all songs have two guitar parts, but you'll find plenty to keep you busy.
The way the notation is presented may be difficult to get used to at first, especially if you are used to using TAB up until now, but you will adapt to it and find it quite intuitive. Beginners seem to have little trouble adapting where experienced players may be more....resistant :X
RS2014 is the ultimate practice tool, motivating you to pick up the instrument often and therefore practice regularly. There are lesson features and technique guides which cover many aspects of guitar playing, like hammer-ons, slides, harmonics, pull-offs, etc. Some arcade style games are included, using the guitar as the controller. These games are designed to improve your skills and muscle-memory.
A session mode includes a band that dynamically plays according to your own playing intensity. This is a useful jamming tool, and good for practicing and learning scales.
'Learn A Song' is the main part of Rocksmith, and the notation will be simplified at first, then as you improve it gets harder until you have the whole tune. At the end of each song you will get stats on the percentage of correct notes hit and your longest continuous streak. This is a fun way to learn new songs and you always have something ready to practice, just a few clicks away.
With very few acceptions, the songs are the actual recordings by original artists, so you'll be playing along to tracks that sound like they should. Additionally, your guitar tone will sound like the guitar in the recorded version, allowing you to play the song more authentically. This raises the immersion and enjoyment level as well. I don't know if the emulation is perfect, but it is certainly very good.
For added motivation you can use the leaderboards, though I don't personally, but many others do and seem to enjoy the challenge very much.
You need the Real Tone Cable to use this software. I like RS2014 so much I bought an extra cable. Check online stores. One cable is compatible with all platforms and works with guitar or bass.
There are literally thousands of hours of value to be found amongst the core content and the additional songs available as DLC. This is not a game, this is a guitar practice portal. Rocksmith is a digital interface for an interactive guitar tutorial/songbook which encourages you to practice, makes you want to play, helps you hone your techniques, and teaches you songs.
Rock on, brothers and sisters.

A haunting, visceral and occasionally frustrating journey through a shattered psyche, Silence of the Sleep is set in a stunningly realised vision of a mind coming to grips with pain, loss and grief, as well as the tormented and fractured path to realisation after personal tragedy.
Set against a dark, brooding art style and a despairing rain washed sky, a man plunges from a clifftop, asking for forgiveness. From here a strange, surreal journey through his past actions and memories plays out in a side scrolling, slow paced and intensely unnerving narrative, involving puzzle elements and avoidance combat with enemies. The man, Jacob, finds himself in one strange place after another, always somehow familiar and oddly out of place. The people he meets are cryptic and often vague about what they are doing there or how indeed they got there, and no one really seems to know what's going on.
One of the game's biggest strengths is its sense of foreboding atmosphere. Each location feels disconnected from any proper sense of reality, and the player is constantly uneasy about what could be around the next corner or hiding in the shadows. This is largely due to the incredible atmosphere the game creates through a minimilistic and strikingly unique art style and colour tone, with oppresively dark, dirty environments contrasted against gashes of bright red of blood soaked interiors. The visuals, as the essence of the world, perfectly encapture a broken, twisted and depressing place that allows the theme of the story to shine through brightly in this dark nightmare.
The sound direction and design is some of the best I've witnessed in any game. Ambient creaks and gnarls of the environment echo around the player as they navigate through the game's locations, always keeping tension just tangible enough to keep the player's wariness at a draining level. The shrills and alien cries of the grotesque, deforrmed monsters instill such dread that for the most part their presence is a terrifying and heart pounding thrill. There is a beautiful musical score throughout the journey, across many instruments and often involving the player's input. The overture haunts and bleeds as the story unravels, and fills the sky of the game like the grey, oozing rain that never stops.
Gameplay revolves primarily around exploring areas, finding items or clues to advance to the next area, talking to NPC's and avoiding the enemy monsters. There is no combat at all, and if you get too close to the enemies its Game Over. This allows for a tense hide and seek between you and the patrolling enemies as you navigate the dark hallways and hide to avoid a quick death. While this system is effective and can be genuinely skin crawling, it can get incredibly frustrating when you are trying to solve puzzles or get through an area and have to constantly stop and wait for the enemies to pass. In fact, this might be the biggest gripe I have with the game and I spent a lot of time reloading again and again with growing annoyance at some sections, as a simple task could stretch well beyond the point of tension or enjoyment.
The puzzles are fairly straightforward but fit in well with the world created. The story unravels slowly and deliberatley vaguely, never completely telling the player everything and shrouding the whole experience in a veil of uncertainty and clouded clarity. The story's tone and somewhat ambiguous nature is perfectly presented in the dark, dank and gloomy environments, and the twisted and sporadic nature of the events that occur. Jacob can rarely discern what is real or indeed what is happening, and the player is just as submerged in this confusion. The player wanders the levels in the crushing darkness, getting lost and fumbling through rooms hoping to find the next clue, just as they do with the game's narrative.
Overall, Silence of the Sleep is a beautiful, terrifying experience, not so much for the scares it imbues but more toward the brutal tone and theme of Jacob's journey. Life and death is presented as shards of glass, constantly sticking and twisting into the strange world as Jacob's memories and emotions bleed onto the screen. It's not perfect and will most likely frustrate, but as a grim walk down a very mature and despondent road, it is a marvellous, dreadful time.

This game is an absolute disaster, but let's be fair and address its admirable qualities first. Silence of the Sleep does have some very interesting sound design and visuals (even the pause menu looks impressive), and a decent story too. The concept itself was just brimming with potential. Unfortunately, the developer simply failed to capitalize on much of it, probably on account of their inexperience in making games. While it feels like a very early attempt, if we assume that was the case, it's a really good start, and I'm sure the developer will make great games once they've got some more experience under their belt.
Now, let's get into why it's not worth playing (and certainly not its pricetag!). While the game had some very interesting things going for it, it ultimately just wasn't fun to play. The first thing you'll notice about it is that it's extremely tedious at times, and it only gets worse about this as you progress. It violates a basic rule in horror, particularly in games, which dictates that no matter how terrifying your monsters are, if you're overexposed to them, the whole thing goes from scary to obnoxious very fast. I can't say that its puzzles helped with that either, as most of them are just a lot of running around and very little else (Chapter 3 is particularly guilty of this). And speaking of the weak point that is Chapter 3, all of the game's attempts at humor not only felt out of place, but also fell mostly flat. The whole thing is filled with unentertaining mini-games that completely break imersion and leave you wondering whether you bought a horror game or the Halloween edition of Wario Ware. (In all seriousness though, one of said mini-games is trying to lure a rabbit out from under a bed with a carrot.) These minigames, while not necessarily bad things in and of themselves, don't belong in the bigger picture and are reflective of one of the larger problems with the game, which is a lack of focus. It meanders in a lot of ways, wasting effort that should've been spent on making the gameplay more tolerable and the plot development smoother. Last and possibly worst of all (the thing that made me finally quit, in fact): the puzzles toward the end of the game make very little sense and rely on artificial difficulty that results from enemies that are extremely tough to avoid. Said enemies make the labyrinth environments difficult to memorize or even navigate once you have them down. On top of all this, a new and player-disabling game mechanic is introduced to make it all even more frustrating.
tl;dr: Despite its wonderful aesthetic, atmosphere, and interesting themes, I can't say I enjoyed the game itself due to its many frustrating design flaws.

Honestly I can't justify why this game got the lukewarm reception it did. A negative commonality between most critic and gamer reviews has been focused on how the game strays from being survival horror. The truth is though that Resident Evil has not fit that genre since 1999's Resident Evil 3 - Nemesis (as far as the main series is concerned). That being said critics and fans have had nearly a decade to either accept this new direction or simply walk away from the franchise.
With that said, if you're looking for an actual survival horror game you might want to look elsewhere. As a more action-oriented horror/sci-fi title however you can't really do much better than this game right here.
RE6 gives you four campaigns that each feature their own characters and story-lines (which tie into the main story arc) as well as gameplay styles that, for the most part, are different from one another. Three of the four allow the player to choose between two playable characters in singleplayer mode or allows for online co-op play. In addition, three of those campaigns will take you on average five to eight hours to complete with the final taking somewhere between two or three. Add it up and you've got a game that can take you upwards of seventeen hours to finish.
There are some issues with the game though. While each campaign has its own series of events, most of them share some common locations and you'll feel like you're playing through the same thing each time during certain areas just with a different character. Also I found that Chris' campaign lacked in some parts. Clearly his campaign is intended to be more third person shooter-based but the cover system is a little wonky (though MUCH better than the one in Operation Raccoon City) and I found myself running out of ammo way too often. Beyond these two gripes the only other negative aspect worth mentioning is that the main story can be a little confusing sometimes despite seeing it from four different perspectives. Hunting down the break-able symbols (thus unlocking info files) certainly helps but there definitely needed to be a little more clarity.
Overall RE6 is actually a pretty good game. It might have completely stripped most of things that made the franchise the definitive survival horror experience it was but if you can look past that you'll find an enjoyable experience.

You're a special agent, and you get missions to achieve. Until stuff happen and you have to save someone (I won't spoil it).
Yea, the story is pretty weird and not much clear, but it fits into the game perfectly.
The style its pretty simple and cartoonish, but really original and good looking, the settings its like a 60s spy movie, with all the prerecorded sounds you have heard in a lot of classic movies (yes, they have the Wilhelm Scream).
The humor is great. I love it. It kinda feels a little bit like a Monty Python adventure. It's all set up to take you by surprise, and it works super-well.
The gameplay itself it's pretty easy, a sort of first-person adventure game. Even tho looks easy, it's a lot of fun to play. Expecially if you have to pick a nose to open a door or stuff like these.
The music is probably the main problem. I mean, it works a lot since it all sounds like a 60s movie, but it's way too ripetitive and loud.
Also, it is pretty short. It only took me 2 hours and a half to finish it 100%. And that's a shame, I was seriously hoping to last at least around 5-6 hours. Oh well, it was all fun.
Final rating: 7.5/10
