Before I start, let me say this: I only have 28 minutes of time on this game due to a computer crash and all of the time was lost due to Steam force quitting. Okay, now for the start of this review: This was one of the most fantastic experiences in my entire gaming career. It's hilarious, spitting out cleverly worded dialog throughout the entirety of the game. There are so many things to do in the levels of the game - and that's where the game falls flat. If you just want to get through the story, it will surprise you with how quick it ends. It's about three hours long. BUT you can forget all of that - because there is TONS of extra content just beneath the surface of the game. What Jazzpunk reveals to you barely scratches the surface - there are tons of minigames that you can find and do (a great example are all of the little nooks and crannies in the Kai Tai Resort level you can find by just running around and clicking on things, which include a small little Quake minigame, first person Fruit Ninja, and a Street Fighter II car smash parody). Another thing is the art style - the cartoony feel you achieve from this game. Even on lowest graphical settings, this game looks absolutely fantastic due to the rather simple shapes and shades of the objects. The cartoony environment as well as the comedy combined with the story that seems serious in its own right is fantastic, giving you a sort of contrasting feel, but don't get me wrong - that contrast is fantastic. For every minute - no - second I was playing this game, I enjoyed it. Even on a 2009 Macbook - it runs at 60 FPS on the highest settings. Another great thing is the joystick support (which I won't delve in to). Anyway, great plot, great graphics, and especially great humour. Let me close with this - This is the best game I have ever played.

I bought this on sale and let it sit for several months unplayed.  Then when I opened it something about the UI hit me, and I didn't want to bother learning it and asked for a refund.  But they told me I had owned it long enough they wouldn't refund it (even though I had only played for 1 hour).  So fine... I decided to try it again.  And it is fun - but it borders on tedious in places.
Hints would have helped this game a lot.  Like "Hint: + and - will change game speed."  That's a big one.  Or "Hint: Just because water looks contiguous doesn't mean a boat can go through it because the graphics are buggy."  That one kind of sucks.
What would I compare this to?  It strangely reminds me of Factorio - some of the same logistics take place here, and some of the same tedium.  What is not like Factorio is the possibility of having maintenance costs that overwhelm an economy into a downward spiral.  This is a really great feature of the game.  Build a bunch of warehouses and a ton of transportation and watch the balance sheet go deeper and deeper into the red with no hope of reversal!
This is probably more accurately a precursor to Anno 2017 - although I find this more playable and engaging - maybe because has more logistical puzzles than Anno has (for example the warehouse placement can introduce interesting problems).
This is an economic sim.
In all I'm happy they refused to give me the refund.  This is not a bad game, and it was worth the effort overcoming small learning curve and UI.

A cute little game and pretty fun once you know what you're doing. Being a normal mouse is really straightforward. Get to the cheese, get to the hole. You get a little tutorial in the beginning.
What you DON'T get is a tutorial on being a Shaman mouse. And this can end badly. If you get the hand of being a mouse real quickly and get thrown into Shaman position without knowing what the heck you're doing, the pressure is on and the other mice will let you know. Instead of noticing that there's a newbie in power and trying to give you tips and guidelines, the community resorts to name calling and shaming resulting in a failed level for everyone.
There is a way to practice on your own (I typed /room Test in the chat box), but you're never explicitly told that. For a single player game it's fine to throw the player into the game not knowing what they're doing, but in one where you screw over 30 players at a time, yourself included, by not knowing what to do, it feels like a bad design choice.
That aside, once you actually do know what you're doing it's a cute, fun little time waster with a highly immature community. I like the game, and would recommend judging the game for itself rather than the community, and perhaps joining as a mature person just there for fun. It needs more of those people. And for your own sake, go to a wiki and read up on Shaman controls before playing.

As someone who doesn't really play many horror games I enjoyed this so much! Kudos to the devs for adding safe mode - it allowed me to enjoy one of the best stories I've come across in games without getting bogged down by the monsters which usually turn me off these types of games. Cheers!

So, I just finished this game and, ummm...
Well, I'll put it this way: SOMA is one of those games that you have to go into as blind as possible. I have never, in all my life had a game impact me as much as SOMA has, which may contribute to the positive outlook I have on it. So, to avoid giving away too much, I'll get right to it.
The good
+ The visuals are stylistic, filled with detail, and just generally fantastic. Definitely a step up from Frictional's previous game.
+ Each character you interact with has an amazing amount of development, including your main character.
+ Finely polished stealth mechanics
+ Absolutely incredible enemy design
+ Improved AI in the enemies, who also have different behaviors, meaning you have to use different tactics for each one
+The story of the game is, quite simply, pitch perfect. When it comes to the story, there is not a single flaw that comes to mind. From beginning to middle to end, the story has perfect pacing, writing, dialogue, characters, is absolutely sublime, and provokes many philosophical questions that actually makes the player think beyond just raw gameplay.
+ The world it takes place in is amazingly built and has one of the most interesting premises ever the further you get into it.
+While it is a horror game, it's more along the lines of having extremely intense moments (especially for someone afraid of the ocean like me), and some more "relaxed" sessions in between. However, much of the horror comes from the wide array of emotions the game put me through, namely Isolation, Powerlessness, and suspense. It is purely unsettling.
The bad
-Up until near the end, once you find out how they work, the monsters are relatively easy to escape from.
-In general, there is a noticeable lack of difficulty in the game, exept for...
-The puzzles either range from laughably easy, to annoyingly ambiguous.
-In general, it feels like they were trying to develop a walking simulator style to their story telling, but tried to separate it from that genre by including the relatively easy monster encounters and various other more intense segments. I'm not saying it's a neccesarily bad thing, but if they wanted to do it, they should hae executed it in a more challenging manner. I'm not saying make us die one million times, but rather make the struggle towards a victory more of a, I dont know, A STRUGGLE? (although SOMA's "safe mode" makes the game more focused at what it was built around)
Verdict:
There is a reason it is getting the following rating: despite some glaring issues, SOMA sets out with a very specific goal in mind. the fact that it is able to accomplish said goal in such a masterful execution, makes it, by a long shot, the finest horror game I have ever played, and a possible contender for the best game I have ever played, period. It is my new benchmark for all future horror games, and for storytelling.
Rating:
10 / 10 - An Absolute Masterpiece
Recommendation status:

Rainbow Six Seige is a mixed feelings game for me. I love it due to its simple yet tactical gameplay. Its obviously unique for its multiplayer take to it with a 5 vs 5 showdown with soon to be 4 gamemodes to play (not including terrorist hunt and its mini sort of campain called Situations). It has many operators to play as with special abilities and gadgets that aid in the game with no microtransactions to obtain them, all it cost is renown to unlock them and thats all. However there are some down sides to the game. There are countless of game breaking glitchs. To start there are some problems with the characters hitboxes to were it doesn't register any sort of damage or headshots. There are even times were someone won't load in game and it'll take them a long time to load in and start the match. Still ubisoft does notice the problems and unlike other companies they will try and make an attempt to fix and resovle the issues to make the game balanced and/or better in general. The community feels very shallow in terms of player count. However when I did make contact with other players, they were very friendly and a bit stacked (stacked = had A LOT OF GEAR). I received the top melee weapon and backpack immediately upon joining a PvE server thanks to some fellow players. I probably could've turned it down but I was not looking to invest more than a few hours into the game.
I can not recommend the game in its current state due to the lack of a community and more quantity than quality when it comes to content.
I am definitely impressed by the scale of the game. The city feels desolate and worn down. The empty subway tunnels echo your foot steps and it is an incredible experience. But those are the only moments I felt immersed in the world. The progression system is standard and doesn't bring anything new to the table but it definitely adds more filling to the gameplay.

Now here's a real curveball from the horror genre. Silence of the Sleep looks very much like another Lone Survivor-style side-scrolling horror game, and it is, for a little while. Then it turns into something very, very different, and the change is not altogether unwelcome. I'm going to have to spoil some things about how the game is laid out, because it's very hard to give a proper recommendation without speaking on the game's true structure. However, if what I tell you sounds good, spoilers shouldn't really hurt the experience.
You play as Jacob Reeves, a very sad man who opens the game by chucking himself off a cliff. However, instead of Kratosing through a pantheon, he ends up in a strange, dilapidated hotel with a man I can only assume is the bartender from The Shining. They have a nice talk, and then a shadow thing tries to find and eat Jacob. So, we're off to a pretty good spooky start, right?
The elevator out of the hotel takes Jacob to a black-tie affair in a swanky ballroom. Suddenly the game turns into an adventure game, with Jacob chatting with guests and trying to work out some odd puzzles. There's still a dreamlike veneer over everything that ties back to the hotel opening, but the tone is completely different. After the ballroom is another horror segment, and a very effective one. But after that the game launches into its longest chapter, which has almost zero horror elements throughout. It's nearly all dialog and dealing with NPCs, with hardly even any puzzles to work out.
The end takes it back to horrorland and ties it all together, but all told the game is way more adventure than horror. And that rather works to its benefit, actually. The horror segments can be clumsy and frustrating, with hiding mechanics more touchy than those in Knock Knock and the same navigation problems that plagued Lone Survivor and Claire. I will admit that the spooky bits have some very effective monsters and moments, but playing through them quickly became more tiring than the dialog-heavy parts, strangely enough. The characters of Silence of the Sleep are all well-written and fully-realized, each with goals and hangups to explore. They also make it easier to know how to move the story forward than the scurrying about darkened hallways.
All of this is presented in rich, detailed backdrops for the silhouetted characters to break out against. Silence is a very good-looking game, with some clever uses of its 2D style. The sound design is solid as well, and while the controls are a little stiff, it won't matter much outside of fleeing monsters. I'm not a big fan of this particular story archetype, but Silence of the Sleep had the presentation and the polish to keep me engaged all the way through.

After almost 300 hours of playing, here's my two cents on many of the hot topics concerning this game and my personal experience.
Connection:
-I don't disconnect as much as some others do, but as I have travelled to different places with varying qualities of internet, I did notice that the slower the connection, generally the more disconnects I experience
Balance:
-I'm not ultra-high super tier, but after getting to over rep 5 on four characters, I feel like each character does have glaring weaknesses, that can be exploited (with the exception of Warlord); However, there are some occassions in gameplay where I just go "what the hell just happened?"; 80% of the time, it's because I've forgotten how to fight a particular toon, but 20% of the time, its the things that you cant really counter consistently. However, though I dont think balance is perfect by any means, it's in a good enough place where I don't froth at the mouth at every time I die. Alot of losses can be attributed to bad reactions or timing.
Microtransactions:
-It's basically all cosemetics, so I'm not too concerned with this.
Overall, I feel like it's a recommend, with stipulations:
- Do you have an itching need to play some medieval fantasy combat?
- Are you patient enough to master timings for every attack in order to fight other characters?
- Are you willing to maybe, if you have potato connection, disconnect from every non-1v1 or 2v2 game mode?
- And finally, are you of the opinion that this game is not dead?
If anyone of these answers are no, don't buy. Maybe come back during the Winter sale and see what has gotten fixed. If your answer is yes, get this, and make sure you find a group of likeminded combat fiends and have some jolly good fun. I personally get my jimmies rustled alot by this game, but the constant progression, getting better in combat is exhilarating.
TL;DR: Not for the faint of heart, kiddies.

A short but cute game. A 2D puzzle platformer where you are a spirit who learns to control the seasons, using your powers to try and solve a mystery plaguing the forest.
The story isn't deep or elaborate, but charming enough. The voice actors are decent, and the visuals are fantastic.
Pros:
- Changing seasons to solve puzzles is a unique gameplay addition
- Each seasons is visually distinct, has its own musical score and ambient noises
- Each season provides its own unique changes to the landscape, making switching between them to solve puzzles necessary (Winter freezes water so you can walk on it, Fall makes mushrooms grow you can jump between, etc)
- A simplistic but charming art style
Cons:
- Some of the puzzles do not appropriately explain what you need to do. I had to resort to online guides for a few solutions
- Movement can be sluggish, and jumping can be tedious when trying to time jumps between platforms
- Certain aspects can be repetitive as you have to re-solve simple puzzles to go back to old areas
Over all, I think it is a cute game for those that like 2D puzzle platformers. I enjoyed it, and while I did get it on sale, I felt I got my money's worth. I cannot say if it is worth it at full price, as that's really up to personal opinion. But i found the art style beautiful and the story charming enough, and changing seasons to solve puzzles was quite a bit of fun.

This game is very reminiscent of Ori and the Blind Forest. There are some differences, for instance I only walked into my doom two times in this game.
The way the game is actually set up is much like it is in Ori. There's the background, the middle ground where your character is, and then a foreground. In Seasons After Fall, the art is much more rough and painterly in these three sections than it is in Ori. I still found it appeal and easy to look at, though I'll admit my nit-picky side found a few flaws in how things flowed, namely animation of close-up objects in cutscenes.
Onto the story. I've read the reveiws of this game and I'm not really sure why people are disappointed with the story. It is a simple story, yes, but it has a solid story nonetheless. The ending is a bit animbuous I will admit, but after some reflection it makes solid sense. Especially if you take the time to find all the 'extra' pieces in the game.
The lore is both simple and deep at the same time. I think they did okay on presenting it, they could've done better in a few parts that I think hurt the clarity of the ending, but overall there is some depth in the story if you know where to look.
The puzzles are simple. I did get stumped for a bit here and there but it wasn't to where I got so frustrated with the game and gave up at any point. I finished this game in one day. It is very relaxing and not stressful. There aren't any 'enemies' to defeat or anything like that, and there's no punishment for walking off the end of the world (like I did one or two times). If you're looking for a chill platformer to enjoy, this game will fit the bill.
I will agree that the game is short - especially for the price tag of $15. I'd definitely wait until the game goes on sale before purchasing. $7-10 is a good price range for this game, but I wouldn't pay more than that personally. However, I do think I'll probably play this game again simply because it is nice and calming, the music is nice, and it is a cute game. If you're looking for a more challenging game in this sort of niche of platformers, look at Ori and the Blind Forest.

Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. Rocksmith 2014 is much less of a game, more of a learning tool.  While there ARE mini-games designed to help your muscles memorize movement, and there is an Arcade mode with leaderboards, the meat of this game is education.  There are hours of video lessons which work side-by-side with you, changing the exercises as you struggle with them or breeze through them.  The game recommends lessons and other songs to help you build up skills you need for more difficult songs, and the "free play" Session Mode has its own lessons, which focus on music theory and composition.  This teaches players not only how to play songs, but how to improvise and write their own music.  I recommend this program for ANYONE who has an electric guitar or bass.  Just realize you must buy the cable, although you can also do two-player using two cables!

Nether somewhat recently took on a new developer, who took control of the game and removed microtransations, but even though the game is getting better it still needs a lot of work. Nether is essentially "another survival game" in the vein of DayZ, but with more varied enemies and more focus on trading and missions. But while everything looks better at a glance, the monsters are only loosely functional, and instead of doing any real animating or pathfinding for them they just make it so that most of the monsters teleport right in front of you every time they need to move, making all of the combat one big pain. It's also still fairly buggy, even retaining some bugs that seem to have existed for months despite being obvious things like flashlights being disabled entirely when the player rebinds their keys. But above all, the damning aspect of the game is that there just isn't anybody playing. The only server that I've seen regularly have more than 20 people is a PVE server, which removes the tension of meeting another player in the field and not knowing if they're friendly that makes the genre so appealing to a lot of people. The only way I could really recommend Nether is if you have a bunch of friends who can't afford much better games like Ark: Survival Evolved and have to make do with buying this for $1 on sale, because that's really all it's worth right now. This is pretty much an Early Access game disguised as a full title.

An original classic from 2007, Overlord really stood out as a creative game for its time, from what could have been basically a very not-well-known company. A basic descriptor would be: "Think Pikmin, but twisted into a evil guy, doing evil things, because he wants to rule, with power, and lustrous, lustrous gold." And there's Overlord right there for you. Of course, there are two paths to rule you can choose from, governed primarily by decision vs. decision events (and a few other things you can do involving cold-blooded murder), and, of course, what Overlord would not be complete without the ability to forge his own weaponry and armor?
In any case, this game is a fantastic classic, and I absolutely enjoyed it. It's also received other games, one being its direct sequel, another a spin-off on the Nintendo DS, and the last... Well. Honestly it's best that remains unsaid.
I'd say it's well worth the purchase if you decide to act upon it, as Overlord is an easily cherished title. Overall, this is a fantastic game, certainly better than the average survival game on steam. The world is immersive, the "nethers" feel like they're living things that want to survive just as much as you do, they just happen to see you as food. On the other hand, this doesn't take away from the fear, nethers are definitely creatures to be feared, ESPECIALLY the larger ones. Take STALKER and combine it with DAYZ and you get this.
Now onto some less positive things.
First off, I don't get what people mean by microtransactions in this game, I've simply not seen them (granted I only have 4 hours logged, but I did a lot in that time). Judging from other reviews, microtransactions existed in the past but were removed, same goes for most issues people complain about. But this game is by no means perfect.
In the time I've played this game, I've experienced crashes fairly often (when taking screenshots primarily) which the devs claim to be working on, but they've been saying that since 2014 from what I see, so it might take a bit. I've also seen glitchy hitboxes, ranging from slightly hovering over the ground to whole structures with no colision at all, that you can comically just walk straight through. Finally, as much as this isn't a personal concern for me, I know it is for a lot of other people: graphics. The visuals are decent, the lighting is really nice and what graphical quality the game does have is well used in enhancing the atmosphere, but there are moments that make you notice how old the game looks. If graphics are a concern for you, I recommend looking at some youtube gameplay, really I recommend this for many games but this one especially.
Overall, dispite its flaws, I highly recommend this game and I hope the devs keep up the good work!

This is a game that is about style over substance, and unfortunately that was just not what I was looking for.
Pros-
+Beautiful art work
+The soundtrack is great
+Decent voicework
+Some cool looking mechanics when changing seasons
Cons-
-The animations range from servicable to bad
-The movement has some delay, partially because the game wants you to see its poor animations
-The season changing mechanic feels like it's designed to waste your time/show off
-Tedious puzzles, partially because of the waste of time
This game is at its strongest when you have the narrator talking to you and guiding you and you have violins playing in the background while you enjoy the art. Unfortunately that's only half the game and the other half has tedious puzzles involving things like backtracking and confusing maze like design. Throughout the entire game I felt unsure I was going the right way unless there was narration because the levels are simulationusly linear yet open with all the paths. You could jump up all these mushrooms to get to the left side, or you could just run across the ground. Both paths end the same way but for some reason they still exist just because they can.
The worst problem with the game is the main gimmick, which is why this review is negative. I could overlook a lot of the problems, but the season changing mechanic just made me sigh in annoyance every time I had to use it. When you select to change a season it takes roughly 2-3 seconds where you float up in the air and see a neat looking wave effect change the background. This would be slightly okay if changing the seasons instantly effected the platforming elements. Let me give an example.
There's a geiser gushing water. You need to freeze it so you can jump on it and get to a ledge. So you push the winter button, you wait 3 seconds, it changes to winter, then you wait for the orb to fly to the geiser and transform it into ice. Then you jump across with the delayed platforming controls, hopefully making it on your first attempt. Then you need to raise the geiser so you can make the ice platform higher. So you push the button to turn the season to spring, you float for 3 seconds, then you wait for the orb to fly to the geiser to melt it. The geiser slowly rises and then you push the winter button and wait 3 seconds... Wait for the orb to fly to the geiser to freeze it. Then you finally jump across to the other side again hopefully making it across. Now imagine doing this same puzzle back to back for 20 minutes. It's incredibly not fun.
The season switching and effects should be instant. It's not fun to watch the same thing over and over while losing control of my character. As a side effect of this, every single platforming section in the game is literally just about being a tedious busywork puzzle. There's no timing jumps, there's no switching seasons mid jump, there's no skill involved at all besides compensating for the animation delay. At that point I'd rather the game be a straight up walking simulator.
I hope these developers make another game but polish up the gameplay. I was pretty close to giving this a positive review but I just got more and more annoyed with the game since all the new seasons just keep making me have to do more and more season changing making the game more and more about watching the fox fly in the air for 3 seconds until I just got fed up and lost interest.

From the creators of Amnesia: The Dark Descent comes an ambitious new survival horror that's fun for the whole family! In this epic retelling of the story of The Brave Little Toaster, you play as Simon, the plucky dive suit and Catherine, the quirky Radio Disney AI as they embark on a quest to find their original owners. You must solve fun, brain-busting puzzles and sneak past other grumpy appliances who never found their owners and have consequentially been driven mad with jealousy.  This game has a total play time of about thirty minutes, but a complex dialogue tree and morality system guarantee a different ending for at least the first five or six playthroughs! (And you know kids, they'll want to play or watch you play through this heart-warming adventure over and over!) The beautiful undersea city is truly breathtaking. The original cast members of Jon Lovitz as Simon and Deanna Oliver as Catherine, along with an entirely new soundtrack by David Newman really helped recapture the warm, fuzzy feeling of the 1987 classic film! So pack your bags and embark on a magical adventure to a wonderous undersea city and help the lovable Simon find his way back to the home he so fittingly deserves!

After almost 300 hours of playing, here's my two cents on many of the hot topics concerning this game and my personal experience.
Connection:
-I don't disconnect as much as some others do, but as I have travelled to different places with varying qualities of internet, I did notice that the slower the connection, generally the more disconnects I experience
Balance:
-I'm not ultra-high super tier, but after getting to over rep 5 on four characters, I feel like each character does have glaring weaknesses, that can be exploited (with the exception of Warlord); However, there are some occassions in gameplay where I just go "what the hell just happened?"; 80% of the time, it's because I've forgotten how to fight a particular toon, but 20% of the time, its the things that you cant really counter consistently. However, though I dont think balance is perfect by any means, it's in a good enough place where I don't froth at the mouth at every time I die. Alot of losses can be attributed to bad reactions or timing.
Microtransactions:
-It's basically all cosemetics, so I'm not too concerned with this.
Overall, I feel like it's a recommend, with stipulations:
- Do you have an itching need to play some medieval fantasy combat?
- Are you patient enough to master timings for every attack in order to fight other characters?
- Are you willing to maybe, if you have potato connection, disconnect from every non-1v1 or 2v2 game mode?
- And finally, are you of the opinion that this game is not dead?
If anyone of these answers are no, don't buy. Maybe come back during the Winter sale and see what has gotten fixed. If your answer is yes, get this, and make sure you find a group of likeminded combat fiends and have some jolly good fun. I personally get my jimmies rustled alot by this game, but the constant progression, getting better in combat is exhilarating.
TL;DR: Not for the faint of heart, kiddies.

For Honor has come to be one of my favorite games, despite its countless problems. Sadly, these problems have driven most of the PC player base away.This game had boundless potential, but problems are never adressed in a timely fashion and leaves the game in a poor state for extended periods of time. Balance is one of the biggest issues; with the introduction of the first two DLC characters, the centurion and shinobi, these new characters instantly rose to a tier of their own. They both had lines of play which, in certain game modes, were impossible to deal with. Centurion still presents the largest balance issue: In 4v4 gamemodes, one common strategy is to pair up with another player and work together to fight a single person to greatly increase chances of winning the fight. Normally, a skilled player can still have a fair chance of beating both attackers using the revenge comeback mechanic; fighting against two competent centurions working together is nearly impossible to win without a good deal of luck or godlike skill paired with high gearscore. When you join a 4v4 match and see that the enemy team is composed of four centurions, you have a lower chance of winning than with any other composition.

(Note: I wrote this review somewhere else on the internet shortly after Ludosity first released Princess Remedy in 2014. The new features (controller support, more difficulty modes and options) are nice quality of life additions but as far as content goes it appears to be the same as the version I have sitting on my desktop. This game is still as cute and fun as I remember it to be.)
-
Princess Remedy is one of the 6 or so games to come out of the recent Games Against Ebola game jam. The other games haven't been released to the public but fortunately for you and I, the fine folks at Ludosity have released it for free!
The game puts you in the role of the titular Princess Remedy, who has been sent on a mission from her home planet of Saturn to heal all the sick people in Hurtland! The various peoples of Hurtland have many ailments, ranging from sick burns to an actual lack of a body. What I'm getting at is that it's a Ludosity game. It's got their trademark playful writing and has some cameos from characters from a couple of their other games too.
Despite being made in less than 4 days the game has some solid gameplay. When you heal people you go inside their bodies(?) and blast their troubles away with your Saturnian healing magic. You're constantly shooting, so you only need to focus on dodging enemies and their bullets. After you heal someone you get a heart, which increases your max health in healing mode and are also used to unlock doors to other areas. There are also other upgrades you can find in the overworld that increase your damage, the number of shots you shoot, health regen and the amount of flasks (bombs) you can carry.
Oh, and at the end of the game you are given the option to literally marry anyone you've healed over the course of the game. It comes straight out of left-field but it's still a neat addition since there are about 30+ characters to choose from. That's like 30 different endings! I love everything about this game and I kinda wish they would expand this game into something longer. I'm 1000% sure they probably won't but I can dream can't I?

Super cute game, a little challenging on some of the people that you have to heal though worth it.

Do you know these games jokingly called walking simulators? Orwell is a reading simulator.
Player interaction in this game (if you can call it that) is minimal, and the tutorial never ends. Any and all interactive elements are brightly highlighted, and all they're good for is for you to drag them from the right half of the screen the the left. This then results in more interactive elements being unlocked and highlighted. Rinse and repeat.
The job you are doing is litearlly useless. The system you're working with filters all the information automatically, highlights anything relevant to the story, and doesn't need your help, at all. All you do is put the already digested information from file stack A to file stack B.
Click on highlighted text, hold mouse button. Move to the left half of the screen, release mouse button. That's it, that's the gameplay.
Since all the information gathering and filtereing is completely automated, you don't have to read a single piece of information, except maybe for the following.
Every once in a while, you have some conflicting pieces of information. The system already knows that they exist, it already knows what they conflict with, and it already has all the information (that it itself processed automatically), but for some reason you are needed to tell it which one is true. This sounds reasonable at first, but remember: The information you use to make that decision has already been fully processed by the system itself. Your involvement, again, is completely useless.
I suspect that this was only implemented to give at least some "meaningful" player interaction, other than the dragging and dropping described above.
What about the story itself? It's meh. Anti-government, anti-surveillance activist group blows up stuff and kills people. Your (literally useless) job is to use surveillance to catch them. Big Brother is the cause, and also the solution. Isn't that controversial?!
No, it's just incredibly dull. There may be some unexpected twist further down the road, but I feel no motivation to go that far.
So if you're looking for a game to actually play, pick literally anything else. A standard game of Memory has more advanced and engaging gameplay than this game here, and is also more challenging.
If you just want to read a story, open a book. I hear 1984, by George Orwell, is pretty good.
Orwell tries to combine both, and fails horribly.

Compared to Resident Evil 5... this game is not as good.  The problem boils down to trying to do WAY too many things at once.
--Compared to RE5, there's a few Dead Space esq grotesque elements, but they are extremely insonsistent in how they want to place such elements.  A few deaths are gruesome while others are laughably tame or even literally non-fatal.
--The storyline is more than aa bit disjointed due to sudden-skip and explosion-prone transitions, almost like a bad action movie.
--The combat is alright with several different variations of enemeies depending on the campaign selected, but again there is some inconsistency.   Normal zombies damage you just by grabbing you regardless of any visual violence while other enemies do not.  The bosses are basically all puzzle bosses and really quite forgettable, even the recurring ones.
--The cover mechanics are rarely useful and often clunky, and the controls are in general more than a bit unwieldy when it comes to turning.  Aiming is for the most part fine.  The camera can be nauseatingly claustrophobic when in certain indoor areas.  Adjusting the FOV helps a bit
--QTEs return, and like the cinematic ones in RE5 they dont really add at all to the enjoyment of the game nor are a meaningful part of the gameplay.  There is one egregious instance with an enemy that has an instant-kill grapple attack, but takes a several-seconds long cinematic to actually perform which the Co-Op partner is (both mechaically and thematically) pointlessly prevented from interrupting.  This happens cinematicaally too later in the game's first campaign with a one-button-or-you-die QTE.  These sorts of situaations are neither fun nor interesting for the player.  'Oh sudden QTE I missed, gruesome game over.  Mistimed it, forced to watch again.  Mistimed it, forced to watch again.  Repead until you get the timing right.'  Devs need to learn that this is not fun, challenging, or rewarding, especially when presented with a gruesome visual afterwards.  Heavy Rain does this right. with cumulative QTEs required for complete success or complete failure, as well as possible middle-road results.
--The inventory system is bad becaause you can carry too many guns and they can't be quick selected like in an FPS, you have to scroll through about 4-5 to get to the one you want.  RE5's limited inventory, while sensical for a controller, was also VERY nice as a game mechanic because it let you customize your loadout.  You could carry many items to be ready to fight, or few in expectation of collecting in the level.  You could take one gun and a lot of ammo, or many guns with less ammo each.  You could take more armor and health and less guns, all your choice with the limited inventory space.  That and you would never get ammo for a gun type you weren't carrying.
--Items in the world are instanced so co-op ammo or health management is not as interesting.  As opposed to sharing found health items to your partner to hold and use, healing yourself while near them miraculously heals them too.
--There is an added versus mode where players can enter the games of people playing campaign mode, and take the role of the enemies to kill the hero characters, but there really isn't much point to this except as a sort of pseudo versus mode.  Luckily this is a disablable feature, which lets newer players avoid potential abuse from veterans.  I haven't tried it myself, but from what I have read there is no benefit to the hero-player aside from a slight chance of a health item drop.  It is merely for potential added difficulty.
A few other complaints but you get the idea.  There's a whole lot of things done not-that-great.  Its still an OK game to play in co-op and the production value of the game is fairly high (especially with facial animations).  It uses Steam instead of GFWL now and still runs great with no hitches or lag, and the graphics options are good too so its glad to see that it still runs well like its predecessor.  Its not awful, but a bit underwhelming.

An excellent economic management game. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.
First, I should mention that I originally played this game years ago and so I'm somewhat biased due to nostalgia. Even so, I've spent quite a few hours with it in 2016 and I think it's still a very good game.
The gameplay consists of managing production chains. You have factories that make stuff, railways (and ships and trucks and planes) that move stuff, warehouses that store stuff before it's sold, and stores that sell stuff. Cities have limited demand for each individual product, so you can't just produce lots of one of them. There are over 200 products, and typically you'll be producing several at any one time. What you can produce depends on what raw materials you have access to. (And if playing a mission, what the restrictions are. If 200+ products sounds overwhelming, playing the missions helps.) The basic raw materials are wood, oil, various ores and various farm products. Wood can only be harvested from forests, oil and ores from relevant deposits, and farms require good soil. Different plants and animals thrive in different conditions, so for example a dry map will let you grow the likes of peanuts and cotton, whereas a wet map will let you grow wheat and corn and potatoes and tomatoes and such.
The challenge mostly lies in choosing what to invest in. Once a production chain is set up, it's rare to not make a profit, but the size of that profit can vary greatly. Setting up production chains is usually quite expensive, so if you make bad choices at the start, you'll likely end up not making enough money to invest in anything else, and thus fail the mission or fall behind in endless play.
The second challenge is transportation. It's possible to avoid building any, as warehouses have a short range in which they transfer goods automatically. This is one of the major strategic decisions you'll face - do you go for a less profitable chain entirely built close to the customers, thus skipping transports, or do you go for a more profitable chain that requires transportation? What type of transportation to use is also an important consideration.
One of the main strong points of the game is how consistently a chain works once set up. You don't really have to micromanage, other than occasionally adding production capacity to account for increased demand due to cities growing larger over time. This means you can focus on actually growing your business while the existing parts of it work fine without constant oversight. There are 2 semi-exceptions. First, there are variations in climate that can increase or decrease agricultural production for a few years. You should account for this by having some surplus warehouse capacity, so excess production from good harvests can cover insufficient production from bad harvests. Second, some products get replaced as technology marches on, so you'll have to adjust or replace chains as necessary when that happens. For example, deep freezers lose their popularity once refrigerators are invented.
There's actually a third semi-exception. The amount of available ores and oil is finite, and the mines and oil wells don't cover the entire deposit, so you'll need to demolish and rebuild them every once in a while to cover a different part of the deposit, then finally move them to a new deposit once the first runs out, which also requires replacing infrastructure. And if you manage to exhaust ALL the deposits, that's it, no more of that raw material. In practice, this won't be much of a problem in actual gameplay unless you go for very long games in endless mode, but I still found it annoying enough to mod it out.
And speaking of modding, quite a lot can be modded. You'll need the file "Industry Giant 2\config\Config.gen". Make a backup, open it with Notepad, copy everything inside and paste it in a blank excel sheet. This lets you actually see what the different values do. When you figure out what you want to change, open Config.gen with Notepad again and find the values there. Credit goes to Turel97 for teaching me this.
Two issues I have with the game that I modded out are the extremely short coverage area of shops, which means it can take a ridiculously large amount of them to cover a large city (and there are many different types of shops!), and the negative effects industries have on city growth. The latter is nonsensical, as industries provide jobs, and nobody moves to a city with sky high unemployment. So I modded all the non-polluting industries to give postive, not negative growth, and decreased the growth bonus of shops to compensate, as it was overly high by default.
In conclusion, this game achieves something of a holy grail of economic games - it lets you set up production chains that require minimal micromanagement, and what few frustrating issues it has can easily be modded away. Add to that a map editor and enough content already in the game to keep you interested for many dozens of hours and you get one of the best economic management games ever created.

Industry Giant II
Fancy Bytes & Reactor
United Independent Entertainment
Economic Simulator
Industry Giant II was initially released in 2002 but found its way onto Steam in 2015. And it is a fortunate thing too, since it’s still one of the most complex (even if the graphics themselves are aged) industrial simulations for PC. Everything from the gathering of raw materials, processing them into finished products and supplying them to their intended retail outlets, is very well simulated within this game. Where it lacks in eye candy, it makes up for in the gameplay mechanics and especially the ever shifting economy. The cities on the maps develop at an equal pace to your (hopefully) successful business plans and the means of transportation for the goods you produce are also nicely represented through many age appropriate choices. You have a well designed campaign featuring a scaling challenge which serves as a great tutorial at the same time, for the open-ended levels you will enjoy the most. This title’s educational value is beyond a shadow of doubt.

A friend gave this game to me. I'll admit, the screenshots didn't impress me much. I love a good lo-fi game as much as any other greying nerd with an RF modulator permanently switched to GAME attached to the antenna screws of a tired old cathode-ray-tube television, sure, but at first, I thought the lo-fi-ness was the entire gimmick. There's a fine line between homage and pandering to nostalgia, and there are certainly a lot of games on the market today that are trying to cash in on the "less is more" visual style without any "more" to shore up all the "less." I feared Thomas Was Alone might be one more such game.
Oh man, was I ever wrong.
This game is a series of relatively straightforward jumping puzzles. As time goes on, you acquire additional "characters," all rather plain quadrilaterals with slightly different dimensions and capabilities, and you use them, in varying combinations, to arrive at the 'endspot' for each level, for each participating character on the level. You jump a lot. You learn the map, and you plan which characters to bring where, in what order, to surmount the many obstacles along the way. In this respect, the game is acceptable but hardly exciting. The physics are pleasant, the many characters all behaving a bit differently, and you soon acquire a "phrasebook" of tricks to navigate the world of these quadrilateral protagonists. There's nothing wrong with the game's implementation of these puzzles, but there's nothing uniquely right about it, either.
Oh no. Where Thomas shines is in the spectacular narration. No, really. Trust me. What makes this game is the narrator's monologue that begins every level.
I'm not kidding. Why are you staring at me like that? I'm serious.
Thomas Was Alone gives personality to its many rectangular (squares are also rectangles!) players with subtle nuances of their differing physics. You get a real sense of them as characters in space, with mass, with energy, with...dare I say it, posture and "body language." But it's the narrator telling their story, divulging their innermost thoughts, hopes and dreams, that transforms the game from a simple lo-fi puzzle with Atari 2600-style visuals into a rich and detailed narrative that rewards the player for completing the next puzzle by adding additional meaning to the events being played. Rectangle people meet, form opinions of one another. There's fondness, smugness, jealousy, hope, fear...even a romance. Over time, you even discover who and what these characters are, and why the game is represented in the way it is...but this, my friends, is far too deep into the realm of spoilers to divulge here.
It's a beautiful story, told as a narrative extension of a puzzle game. The story is captivating and engaging, and by the end, you will care about those silly little rectangles, and the journey they undertake, with your assistance.
I have enough trouble caring about human beings I meet in the world; I didn't think I had "love and cheer for rectangles" in me. Thomas Was Alone, however, made this greying nerd's gaming basement a little bit dustier. Dust. *sniffle* Yeah, that's my story and I'm sticking to it. Dust.
Every now and then, someone tries something this crazy, and it works. This is one of those. If you're comfortable with lo-fi jumping puzzles, the story you'll unfold by playing them is a thing of real beauty.
May look a simple game, but it's fun to play and a even better story, that gives a new live to the game, impossible to capture in a screenshot. It's also a game that kids (and adults) enjoy to play.

SEASONS AFTER FALL
PUBLISHER – Focus Home Interactive
DEVELOPER – Swing Swing Submarine
GENRE – Adventure/puzzle/Metroidvania
THE BASICS:
SAF is a 2-D puzzle-platformer game with just a pinch of Metroidvania. You play as a “seed” spirit which, for much of the game, possesses a fox in order to accomplish its goals – namely, gaining control of the ability to alter the seasons at will, and using the results in order to solve puzzles. There are no enemies, you don't have to worry about dying; this may or may not be your cup of tea – but, in the end, this is a good thing. It gives you time to just sit back and take in the gorgeous scenery and hand-painted art style, while you resist the urge to smash your controller against the wall because you missed that one tiny little bug hanging from the bottom of a mushroom which is critical to clearing the current obstacle.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
Your character is voiceless – which, for once, makes perfect sense – save for the little yips and barks which you use to control other wayward spirits that you will come across from time to time. Instead, the downtime is filled with frequent running commentary from your caretaker of sorts – an unseen voice which gently nudges you along the path to your destination (without simply spelling out exactly what to do), comments upon random bits of the environment, and gives you warnings about the entities upon whose domains you are intruding.
The first chunk of the game has you gaining the powers of the seasons in order to gain access to new areas, Metroidvania style. Winter causes water (including small geysers) to abruptly freeze, allowing you access to higher areas and making it easier to cross large bodies of water. Spring brings with it torrential rains, raising the water level – which you can then freeze by shifting to winter...etc. Fall causes huge mushrooms to open up to use as platforms. Summer brings everything back to normal. Some plants are only useful during certain seasons, and they all change in obvious ways to help sell the changes. All of this is key to the puzzles, which are mostly ways around obstacles, or to gain access to higher ledges.
The game does break down a bit once you do have all four seasonal powers, however, as it shifts to pure puzzles with even less hand-holding than before. You end up traversing new bits of mostly the same general areas – which, while they look amazing, tend to wear after a while. The voiceovers do change, which is nice, as the plot gets a welcome does of thickener. There isn't much story to speak of, save for the charming narrator's breathless excitement as she encourages you to keep on going and gather the needed powers.
CONTROLS:
Native support for keyboard and controllers (XBONE wired unit here, no problems at all). Move, jump, and bark are the basic commands; once you unlock the ability to manually change the seasons, you do so by holding a shoulder button and selecting the new season via the d-pad.
GRAPHICS:
Beautiful backgrounds and characters done in a hand-painted style. Each season looks distinct – Winter has snow falling constantly, spring is rainy, fall is full of oranges and reds and yellows, while summer is bright and green.
SOUND:
Great music – much of it ambient. Solid voice acting; charming narrator.
OVERALL:
A wonderful, enjoyable game that even makes for a fine screensaver if you just wanna relax and take the scenery in. You can do much worse for the price. Highly recommended.
Never too easy, never really all that hard – the challenge level is just right, and is a unicorn of sorts: It's a non-violent game that isn't insultingly simple. It is enjoyable for all ages, without feeling insipid. When it comes down to it, ¾ of the puzzle aspect is simply knowing when to switch seasons, and which one to switch to. There is no penalty to choosing wrong, save for having to maybe backtrack a bit or run around to get back to your original position, if you should fall.

This game is art.  Quite literally; the cutscenes look like oil paintings, and the game itself continues the painting look.  It's not a long game or very complex, and no real fail state, but it's got more gameplay than a walking simulator.

I'm just going to start by saying I enjoyed every second of this game, from the art and music to solving the little puzzles to get to the new areas. Througout my 7-ish hours of gameplay, there was only one part that I got stuck on which luckily let me brute force through. Otherwise this was a very calm and relaxing experience where I got to play my favorite creature, a cute and cuddly fox.
The art is very well done and the music is charming. While not a long game, it is a nice break among all the super explosions, gunfire, and zombies that were riddling the steam store. I got this after watching a Twitch Streamer, Dendroth, play it for a couple hours.
If you love simple puzzles and/or platforming, definitely give this a try. There's nothing too stressful about it and can be a nice thing to play if you don't have much time in a day. Along with that, I really enjoyed the story for being differnt. Not unique or innovative, but just something that really makes you put down the controller and think, "oh hey, that's kind of familiar" without spoiling too much.
Each season is really conveyed well and you'll probably be spending a lot of time hopping around as your little buddy just taking in the scenery.

For Honor recipe: mix equal parts Tekken and Mount and Blade, and add a dash of MOBA on the top.
I had really high hopes for this game.  As a Mount & Blade and War of the Roses veteran, I was excited to see if a big name dev could address some of the issues that kept those games from really being huge.  And some of the concepts were promissing - the fighter game style target locking in For Honor sounded like a good idea to deal with the control issues of the other games, and the character classes with set combos and identities seemed like a good way to encourage teamwork and keep matches interesting.
Unfortunately, that also ends up taking the already high skill ceiling of M&B up even higher.  In total, there are probably hundreds of moves between all the heros.  Some things can be reacted to if your reflexes are sharp enough, but once you figure in delay for lag (♥♥♥♥ing peer-to-peer), there are dozens of situations where you need to try to guess what opponent is going to do, and pre-emptively counter it.  A lot of the most popular chars have a way to counter your counter.  At first it sounds like a interesting mind game, where you have to outsmart your opponent.  In reality, for fights between evenly skilled players) it just turn into a $60 coin toss simulator.
On top of that, the tutorial covers only the most basic of these interactions, forcing players to try to learn the counters from meticulously studying the opponents that beat them to try to find the hidden counterplay paterns, or watch dozens of hours of high teir streams hoping the streamer points out and explains the interactions well.  Even if you have 100% game knowledge, you're still going to lose an obsurd number of fights due to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ connections and stability preventing your (situationally perfect) inputs from registering.
TL;DR, if the devs abandon the♥♥♥♥♥♥peer-to-peer system, tone down the insane number of (undocumented) differences in the interactions between heros, and fix the glitches they've been "working on" since day one, I would love to come back to this game.  Sadly right now, that seems very unlikely.

Absolutely loving this game! <3 I love it so much that I'll critique it without including a single spoiler because I want you all to play it for yourself as blind as I did. It's wonderful. - The art style is quite unique which is a nice thing to see in any game, but if I had to liken it to another game it would be "The Cat Lady" which makes it all the more terrifying. It's simplistic at first glance, but there are some WONDERFUL details if you just look - hooking your attention and sucking you in just enough to scare you when it wants to. - There is a perfect amount of making you commit to awful choices, puzzle solving, plot development, and showing just enough to scare you without being in your face - and I'm only through the prologue and a bit of chapter 1 as I write this. - The music and sound effects are superbly horrific - reminds me of David Firth's style (Salad fingers, Spoilsbury Toast Boy, Dog of Man). Personally I couldn't ask for more on this front. - Despite being a horror game, I laughed out loud a couple of times due to little things in the dialogue which is a nice touch. The dialogue itself is quite good and it may seem text heavy for some but I didn't find it overly wordy enough to ruin the game for me. I think the balance is fairly good. - I like the fact the text dialogue isn't read out-loud by a voice actor, that can sometimes ruin perfectly excellent games and it makes you feel quite isolated even from the people you speak to. ATMOSPHERE - Colours and minor details are so important to determining the importance of objects and characters and what sort of person they are. I love this feature. It really immerses you. - The scary parts of this game are beautifully crafted and there are some great mechanics involved. - Amazing story thickening so far and I can see so many threads crossing and coming together. So wonderful. Hats off to Jesse Makkonen - Note, I'd not recommend this game to those who are easily frustrated and take stuff at face value. You need to figure stuff out for yourself. I'm sure someone has done a walk-through but if you're a puzzle solver you're going to love this. I have a playlist for this game on youtube if anyone wants a "Let's Play" of this beautiful game by a sweary northern girl.

Nether has got to be my game of the year. To start, it has a superbly refreshing and original premise. This is a first person shooter, and you are a lone survivor in a post-apocalyptic ruin of modern Earth in which you must sneak and shoot your way past hordes of mutant-looking monsters and possibly hostile players. I cannot think of any game that has done this before Nether. And a game like this on steam early access of all places; who'd have thought? This game is pushing the boundaries of what games can be. But there's more. The way that this scenario is brought to life in the realistic and heart-pounding gameplay is expertly realized. You are given only a kitchen knife to start. That's ALL. You have to put in the most challenging and rewarding effort while casually stumbling over dozens of katanas, fresh, unopened bags of Doritos, and useless parts of good weapons. The scavenging mechanic in this game is so true to life and fun to constantly collect with after you die and lose everything because of a hacking unfriendly player. There is a diverse and balanced weapons list. Should I use this crowbar that does 290 damage as my melee weapon? Or perhaps this machete that does 375 damage? The possibilities are ENDLESS.
It should also be noted that this game has an extremely helpful and in-depth wiki site that is there for you should you ever need to know some stats. That's where I learned how much damage all the weapons do. So refer to it often if you want to be on the top of your game. The current owners of this game are taking every step to keep everything up to date and constantly supporting the player base. They are always available and respond quickly. They're really creating a growing and thriving community with Nether. Nether is the great campfire upon which we all gather and politely socialize.
I also like how the game doesn't let you close the game by clicking the red x button on the game's window. Instead you have the pleasure of pressing i to open your inventory, choosing exit, waiting for the disconnect timer to reach zero, then from the main menu selecting exit a second time and selecting the desktop button to leave. You see, even when you sadly must stop playing Nether, it's like a roller coaster of fun and merriment as you quit the game. Brilliant. And by the way, if you're one of those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that uses alt+tab to leave the window, then you're scum and deserve to be punished. How could you possibly have the sheer effrontery to subvert to elegant game exiting sequence? The developers did this for YOU. They didn't have to do that, but they did. And they did it because deep down, they love us all. And when you alt+tab, you're spitting in the face of that love. So don't. Not even once.
You should always be aware of your enemies. The Nether can all teleport at will, making your attempts at escaping with your little remaining health and stamina worthless. Escape is for the weak, and retreat provides no tactical advantage whatsoever. The programmers of Nether have taken great pains to make the AI as smart and deadly as any real wild predator. No joke, these people actually went all over Indonesia studying Bengal tigers to make the enemies in this game come to life. I almost believe they have a mind of their own. When the singularity finally occurs and machines become self-aware, the programmers at Phosphor Games will be there to usher in that new age. But that's another story, let us carry on.
Here's the thing. Get ready for it. My absolute favorite thing of all about this game is the environment. Goodness gracious me, the amount of attention to detail and care that the designers put into crafting this breathtaking world has me floored. The high quality textures and huge variety of models and other assets makes me feel like I'm really wandering around a ravaged urban wasteland with a scarcity of resources. You would not believe all of my immersive interactions with these NPCs. The animations are the best part by far. Speaking of immersive, there's nothing I look forward to more than getting stuck in a body of water and slowly dying because of the tactically placed glitches strewn about in just about all of them. I just never know when a new threat will emerge. True horror genius. And when you're making treks back and forth safe zones stretched kilometers apart to deliver boxes that all fit snugly in your precious inventory space, you might get lonely. Which is why you can bring the box with the red blinking light that makes a happy little beeping sound all the way across the map. Who needs weapons out when the calming melodic beeping box fills your ears with a playful and entertaining bop en route to your far away destination?
I give this game a one hundred out of ten. I couldn't think of a single negative thing to say about this game if I tried. A modern MASTERPIEC.﻿

It's a flawed game, a bit inferior to RE 5, but still a fun game, definetly better than other AAA games like Tomb Raider, that somehow get all the praise from the media...

Brilliant platformer. Controls are great, for what they are (literally just move and jump) - may be a little tighter with a controller but keyboard works great too. Each of the individual 'characters' are unique and they feel different enough to be justified as a separate character and not just a clone of an exisiting one. Minor puzzling elements, mostly to work out how to use the 2-to-9 different characters you are controlling in order to get them all to their exit portals - and there are very few places where you can actually get stuck and have to restart the level; there is usually a way to backtrack (or, you just die and respawn).
The narration is very much a defining feature, and is a driving force in wanting to continue (to the point of completing all 100 levels in one sitting). It is delivered by a fantastic narrator, in chunks of about 2 bits of narration per level, and it is all interesting and often genuinely funny. It has a feel of Bastion to it, without outright copying it or being obvious about its inspiration.
It is not a difficult game, and can be beaten in around 3 hours (including finding all the achievement mcguffins, which aren't hard to find and collect). It is no harder than a standard 2D Mario game, really. Certainly no Super Meat Boy.
If you like platformers, this is a must buy. If you do not like platformers, you may not get as much enjoyment from this but I still suggest picking it up (maybe in a sale) and giving it a play - the narration and story may hook you in to finish it.

I bought Rocksmith when I had 5 days experience of playing guitar, so I was a complete beginner. To cut a long story short, 6 months down the line I can actually call myself a guitar player, but there are other factors which you may be interested in. Rocksmith is a great way to convert from playing guitar hero to a real set of strings, and the UI was one hell of a way to go about it. It's easy to understand and ushers you on your journey from pleb to rock god, so what about the game itself?
Well, if I am to be completely and utterly honest, all Rocksmith has done is teach me a few techniques, and how to play certain songs, sure it makes it more fun and attempts to immerse you in the song you're trying to master, but to be blunt, it is just music tablature, but with a more 'arcade' feel to it, and then of course there's a few minigames to try keep you from getting bored.
The cons? The song list seems particularly limited, which reduces the lifespan of the game. The only way around this is by 2 ways, 1) You purchase the DLC, which I personally believe is rather expensive, I'd prefer to see them go down to about £1.50 per track, but hey, you're learning an entire song right? So on that ground I'm not complaining too much. 2) Use custom DLC, which basically lets you import whatever song you wish into the game, provided the community has made the track for it. This is modding the game of course, and because it's ubisoft, it's probably against their terms, but it didn't stop me. Besides the song list, after using rocksmith for quite a while you begin to discover that all you are doing is learning songs, not so much guitar, so don't expect to be learning musical theory on this game.
Definitely not a subsitute for a real guitar teacher, but something that might assist a guitar student. If you just want to learn songs then this is for you, but don't disregard youtube or normal music tablature (which is mostly free). After 6 months, I find more use in the cable so I can use guitar rig instead of rocksmith.

Seasons after Fall is a very beautiful but also a very tedious experience. The first two hours of the game I was so bored of running back and forth between places that I was actually thinking of refunding the game. But as I am not a quitter I decided to keep going. (Pros, Cons and TLDR at the end of the review.)
The idea of changing seasons and using different elements is wonderful and fun, but most of the time you're just changing seasons to get from point A to point B. The "puzzles" the game gives you are so easy that even a baby could do them. I dont know if you can even call them puzzles.
The game is very casual and doesnt require a lot of thinking (or at all). And the same could be said about the plot; I just didnt know what was going on or why you were doing the things that you were. You're just thrown into a forest with no explanations other than a girls voice asking you do things for her and that's about it. The end was very anticlimatic and left me with even more questions than answers. The feeling at the end was "What the ♥♥♥♥? Why?" so the end left a bit of a bad taste in my mouth. The funniest thing about the end was that some of the cutscenes in the middle of the game were twice as long as what the ending was!
SPOILER:
+ The graphics and art style are amazingly beautiful
+ The sounds are simple and fit well (see Cons for music)
+ Original idea with changing the seasons was fun
+ Voice acting is splendid and fitting
+ Personally did not encounter any bugs or glitches (this shouldnt even be considered a Pro these days)
+ Getting 100% of the achievements was rewarding even though most of them required running around aimlessly for 15 minutes (expect the ♥♥♥♥ing bird achievement, I admit I had to google that one)
- No feeling in the game, you dont get any connection to the fox, the Seed or the Guardian(s)
- For myself the game was NOT athmospheric
- No map, running around in circles for 10 minutes at a time gets boring really fast
- Music = a string quartet playing a "song" from 30 seconds to a few minutes long and only on special parts of the game
- No real ambient music/sounds
- Run there for 5 minutes, take X, run back, give X, run there for 5 minutes, take X, run back, give X...
- Controls were a bit wobbly and strange compared to other platformers I've played
- The end was one of the most anticlimatic endings I have ever seen
- Definetly not worth 15 euros

This game is, first of all, gorgeous. Musically and artistically it was a joy to experience. Just running and hopping around as the little fox was generally cute and enjoyable. This can not be overstated, because this is where this game shines radiantly.
Unfortunately, beyond that, there is simply not much to say about Seasons After Fall.
The story was pretty simple, and to be clear, not in itself bad at all, although I did find that I did not feel any particular connection to the events taking place or a sense of what was at stake. This is hammered in by an ending that just sort of limps into the credit roll.
Game design and programming is the major failing here. Several times, I ran into bugs in which the little fox would get stuck and I would be forced to reload the game in order to proceed as intended. Another time the game acknowleged me as having completed a puzzle that I had not done yet. These kinds of flaws cropped up infrequently, but just enough in this scale game to be frustrating.
This game could benefit from a map or something to tell you roughly where to go, just because sometimes events will be shown to be happening nearby, but not whether it's to your left or right, and the backgrounds and the environments, beautiful as they are, are not diverse enough to make clear where something is happening.
If you are looking for a game every bit as beautiful as Seasons After Fall, but surpasses it in every other way, I would recommend you play Ori and the Blind Forest instead.

This game worked perfectly for me and to quickly point out the main reasons why people could like or dislike it, here I go:
- Story is quite brief.
- It doesn't bother with advanced visuals and sophisticated soundtrack.
- You will have to read stuff to play it.
- The premises are absolutely nothing new to the world of conspiracy theories.
Now in a little more detail and opinion:
The game doesn't take too much time to complete and although in the end it really doesn't matter what you choose (duh) it still might keep you wondering what could go differently. Because it does offer more than one chance to actually affect the progress.
Still, the game might feel like it's taking a while because at some points you may find yourself struggling to find that one crucial piece that's needed to go forward, at others - you will get overwhelmed by the amount of choice. Not that it's bad, but if you're not really patient you might get actually bored.
The game really doesn't bother to give you some superb visuals and sounds. But the fact is it doesn't really need those. I don't even know if the voice-over of some parts of the game would be appropriate or not. But "Orwell" does have a distinct style to it which actually brings some of it's own atmosphere along without a claim to be something very special.
What is special though is an attempt to create an intertwined character development (not for you personally, sorry) that can keep you willing to go on and complete the whole story.
Well, this game is 90% text. Please read it, please read it carefully and not just because the game plot demands it but because every piece of information in this game can be actually useful later on or right now or maybe a couple of minutes before you made that decision you now regret.
This game is called "Orwell" for an obvious reason. It doesn't even need an explanation. Like the setting? Fancy the idea of total government (or other type of) control? Or maybe you're completely against it? Well, in any case, the game gives some food for thought if you haven't yet though about this topic that much or explores those scenarios you might've already seen somewhere, but this time with you behind the wheel... or rather exactly not behind the wheel (duh).
This is not the best game of all ages, but I believe its creators brought exactly what they've wanted to bring into it. Which means "Orwell" serves its purpose perfectly.
I would recommend it for anyone who likes smart and level entertainment and doesn't mind spending some time exploring the world of text rather than beautifully rendered landscapes.

TLDR: "I am suffering from a severe case of death." 10/10 Like undertale but with less talking and more healing.
In all seriousness I love this game and knew it was coming before all of you. How?
I played the 48 Hour jam version (which i believe didn't have the difficulty settings), and immediately, with my 5 hours in game maker pro went "I'm going to port this."
Welp, i'm sorry whoever was in charge that day, because i, of course, never came through (because porting from GM7, to GMS is the hardest thing you will ever do.) He did end up telling me they were thinking about putting it on Steam themselves, though.
In case you are wondering, i got to after the intro cutscene, before the game refused to work.
Anyway, review time:
Story: You play as princess remedy, helping cure diseases so you can become queen, and to find a suitable prince. Armed with magic bandaids and
healing flasks, you must heal everyone in the World of Hurt. Very simple plot, but it does the job.
Gameplay:  This is an Action RPG/Cute em up with no leveling or random encounters. Instead, you walk into the villiage or special area (Marked by a discolorment in the terrain), talk to people, animals, or random out of place stuff like flowers, and fight thier illnesses. after that, you get a permanent powerup. you can also find these permanent powerups in chests. I wasn't too sure what I was expecting when I began to play Silence of the Sleep.  What could a 2D horror game really provide?  The story, atmosphere, and scares were top-notch, as well as all of the graphical and audio work. Any fan of horror, or just a good story needs to play this game.  Sure the controls were wonky at times, and resulted in me experiencing a few unnecessary deaths...but these small shortcomings did little to ruin the amazing experience that Jesse has provided.  A year and a half of work well spent!

tl;dr: a game with an amazing atmosphere, made dull by mediocre gameplay.
Silence of the Sleep is a lush game, filled with beautiful scenes and a musical score that sits between unsettling and mournful. At first the game allows you to explore the world without danger. However, the mysterious atmosphere creates plenty of tension. I was genuinely enjoying taking in each location, and teasing out each puzzles.
Then the game introduced monsters that kill you in one hit.
Tension turned to frustration. I'd be in the middle of a puzzle, and every half a minute a monster would spook on up to me, and I'd just have to hide behind some boxes. Over and over and over. It was like the game was actively discouraging me from progressing.
Monsters worked in games like Silent Hill because you had plenty of options for how you wanted to deal with them. They also wouldn't interrupt you in the middle of a puzzle, if you'd cleared out the room. There were rules in that world which allowed enemies to coexist with the more exploratory nature of Silent Hill.
But the 2D world of Silence of the Sleep removes many of these options. The monster gameplay becomes a dull 'run the opposite way' goose chase, until you find some boxes to hide within, or hit a dead end and start over. It's incredibly restrictive.
I really wanted to like this game, but it just reminded me of better horrors. Hopefully the developer's next game, the Human Gallery, plays to its strengths, rather than introducing needless elements.

I always seemed to be on the wrong side of them.  That however is a very small issue in the overall scheme of things.

I have just JUST finished Silence of the Sleep (SotS). Overall, I can recommend SotS with a score of a 7/10 as it has been lovingly creafted through hard work and dedication with a deep story and beautiful art direction, however, it's on the shorter side clocking in at 6 hours on my first playthrough. This is how business simulations / management games should be: Lot's of stuff to do, to create, many choices what stuff you want to produce. Micromanagement is also a big deal in this game. If you ever wanted to create your own business while experience freedom of choice in finally doing it, you're gonna love this game.
Industry Giant 2 on Steam is a HD version of the classic game made in the early 2000s. It works perfectly fine on Win7 and I guess it does also on Win8 and above.
The game itself contains several campaigns with different difficulties and also a tutorial of how to play the game. Of course there is still a sandbox-mode without any goals where you can just run your enterprise. You start between 1900 and newer dates and can experience everything that comes with it: technologic advantages and possibilities. For example if you start in 1900 most of your business might be farming and stuff, while in the 50's you can produce sunmilk, boats, vendingmachines, bottles and other stuff.
The only thing I really dislike is the fact that you can't switch to the optionsmenü during the game. If you press ESC the game will end while creating an automatic savefile and will then show you the mainmenu where you can change your graphic and audio options. This can be annoying sometimes.
The price itself for such an old game is pretty high, despite the unique high quality it has for a business simulation game if you compare it with newer ones (which do not exist, sadly). You should buy it during a sale or if it's included in the Humble Bundle or something similar.
