There are very few games that can test the very limits of what a game can be, and even make you ponder for many months in a row about the preciousness of human existence. One of these games are SOMA.
Through the dark and claustrophobic corridors of underwater research facilities and the tense yet superb atmospheres of the Atlantic ocean, SOMA stands as one of the best story-based games ever told in my opinion. The rich world building, character progressions, narrative and plot, existential themes and overall depth (excuse the pun) of the content overshadow most of the games in the mediocrity-based business today.
In a world where videogames are steadily indoctrinating violence and decreasing our moral compasses, SOMA challenges the player’s conscience with the consequences of their actions with complex choices and situations. For this reason I think SOMA is one of the most important games of our generation. A core theme of SOMA is hope. Even though the surface of the earth has been annihilated by an asteroid’s fatal impact, the game surrounds the human struggle for survival in the midst of an almost impossibly antagonistic set of odds. All of these are very brave themes for a video game to embark on.
A great standout for me was the relationship between the main characters, Simon Garrett and Catherine Chun. The writers have done their very best at achieving a level of realism in dialogue, equally matching games such as Bioshock Infinite and The Last of Us, and even outshining most movies in my opinion. Frictional Games have undertaken tremendous feats to achieve this goal with almost five years spent on writing alone. The organic performances of the voice actors made me feel like these characters were real people, and not just some synthetic archetypes made to thrill ten year-old boys.
Even though I agree with most of the reviewers that the game could’ve been better without the application of horror elements with the monsters, I feel Frictional has done a great job at tying them in with the theme of the game by presenting the perils of humans’ reliance on technology, even to the point of them having to preserve life and create a terrifying surrogate. The main idea of the game, being transcendental consciousness has been a long-going concept in the sci-fi community and is a worldview which I respectively disagree with, although is masterfully executed in the game’s storytelling. In the game I have often at times abhorred the horror elements of the game in terms of the monsters, and have always stood a good distance away from horror titles. I personally feel that SOMA could have been better as a stand-alone sci-fi storyline without the application of monsters.
The tension is magnificently executed, whether it be in the adversaries or in the environments. The gameplay may not be the main aspect of SOMA, but it withdraws no grandeur from the brilliant storyline.
SOMA stands as a must-play masterpiece.

SOMA has a really great story but it is told rather flat and linear - and without any twists and turns in the plot. This makes your adventure rather foreseeable and not as cool as it could be.
The puzzles are simple and there could be more, especially more challanging ones.
I'm a player who likes to explore a lot in these types of games which is sadly not very rewarding: with a few exceptions all drawers and closets contain nothing interesting and there is little additional content to explore (f. ex. more background info about the plot) except for the obvious things that stare right into your face. Worth noting that even though I took my time to explore the world, it felt kind of short (12 hours total playtime) and there is little incentive to play a second walkthrough (your decisons don't affect the ending or open up different story arcs).
Except for 2-3 encounters, the monsters are very simple to handle and I don't quite understand why the devs felt the necessity to create a more peaceful mode - but maybe it was still too challanging for console-platforms where you lack the precision of keyboard/mouse controls. So don't be afraid to play it in "normal" mode - even if you die, there are plenty of savepoints you you don't have to start a longer episode all over again.
It is a moody game for 1-2 rainy sunday afternoons and the great story puts it slighty above average (hence the thumbs up) but don't expect too much. I bought it at a high discount, so it was worth the few hours of entertainment for me, but it's clearly not worth the full price.

There are two things Rocksmith 2014 stands for.
One is that it's the most fun and probably the easiest way to learn to play guitar. You may have zero knowledge about music and musical instruments yet still play the game and get results. It will teach you everything you need to start playing and creating music - from how to attach the strap to the guitar to more advanced things like slapping or using effects pedals (available within the game).
Another thing is that even if you're already a good guitar player, you can still enjoy playing Rocksmith. There are over 50 songs of different genres and decades you can play along with. You can have a friend connect their bass guitar and join you, or you can even sing in the mic. You can also treat the game as something to beat, by mastering all the songs without any visual help from the game. You also get to experiment with the large amount of sound effects Rocksmith provides. Still not happy? Try the mini-games with leaderboards. Beat the world or just your Uplay friends at sliding, playing chords, scales and so on. And if that doesn't satisfy, the Session Mode will give you a band that can equip a variety of instruments related to many genres to create a rhythm for you or support you adjusting to the way you play.
All in all, it's a must-buy if you have an electric guitar or a bass. The amount of money invested totally pays off, even if you buy the Import tool to get the tracks from the original Rocksmith or choose to add more songs by buying separate DLCs from well-known bands like KISS, AFI, Muse or The Police (Sting).
Having a music teacher, finding a band, guitar tabs, buying amps, effects pedals or a dedicated computer program that would emulate these would require way more money and effort.

Slender: The Arrival is a horror game based on the popular (and free) Slender: The Eight Pages.  The game is relatively short (should be less than 2 hours for most people), and divided into several different chapters that each feature different gameplay.    Fans of the original will notice a substantial visual improvement, and effective use of sound.  This game understands how to execute a horror  experience- make the protagonist defenseless, and build up tension before a single encounter.
The longest chapter is a recreation of the original Slender gameplay of collecting 8 pages, with them and their corresponding landmarks randomly distributed, with each further discovery angering a hostile presence in the woods.  Simple enough, and it's absolutely chilling. Collecting the pages is reasonably guided inside a large area, but still confusing at first.
The sound and dim lighting crete a constant sense of unease, and when -something- appears, it caused a feeling of dread deep in my gut.  Even knowing that it was silly to be surprised multiple times, I'd still jump.  Twisted tree branches seen outside my flashlight often seemed like gnarled arms reaching out to me.  There's something about games like this, and the Amnesia or Penumbra series, that strike at something deep and primal in the subconscious.
Every chapter after the first and second was not as impressive, and only one of them stood out to me.  For gamers concerned about value for their dollar, this may be an issue.  The story, told mostly through found letters, is pretty incomprehensible, and although good horror never shows all its cards, there's not a lot to grab hold of here.
Personally, though, I think the quality and intensity of the experience is worth the low asking price.  A solid recommendation.

Funniest moment:

Jazzpunk presents itself as a parody of spy movies, but quickly wears out its welcome with never ending references and sight gags, most completely unrelated to the task at hand, leaving you with a thin vein of a plot to serve as a vehicle from one joke to the next.
That’s not to say all the humour is bad, but a lot is random for the sake of being random. There's no narrative hooks for many of the jokes, they just exist for the sole purpose of delivering a punchline; experience it and move on. Funnily enough, the better jokes are ones that are actually tied into the game plot, making the others feel tacked on and unnecessary filler.
There reigns the problem with the game; if you don't make an active effort to seek these jokes out, you'll miss most the content of the game (possibly without even meaning to) and probably finish the game within an hour. Even looking for them I finished at just shy of three hours, with the ending just kind of happening rather than being built up to. £9.99 for a game that feels like it was a student's spare time project seems rather hefty to me. At that price point, I'd rather just go watch a terrible blockbuster comedy, I'd probably enjoy it just as much.
The game gets split up into levels, which are small but distinct zones. Actually, scrap small, most are tiny. They look nice enough, but they're mainly just straight lines with a few offshoots if you want to go indulge in the humour, and there is no other reason to go explore. There's not much else to say about the game because, well, there's not much else to the game. There's a bunch of mini-games, though Wedding Qake repeats, which was a "ha ha, okay" the first time, a revisit of the joke was needless. You can swat flies in a vase shop, I avoided smashing the vases and killed the flies, the only effect was I now had a fly swatter, that had no influence outside that game room. I went back and smashed the vases, no effect. Sadly the gameplay part of the game seems like an inconvenience just getting in the way of the game telling its next joke.
Also, there's a Rita Repulsa gag (see power rangers circa 20 years ago). In a game released in 2014... Who's this aimed at again?
True, games like Wario Ware get by without much of a narrative, but it also just takes you immediately from one gag to the next, not leaving you to seek it out.
I do really like the aesthetics, the graphics, character design, the audio; it is actually a pleasant game to play from that point of view. It’s a shame it gets bogged down with trying to cram in as much 'humour' as possible at the expense of a more fleshed out main story arc.
This is the game equivalent of going to a forum for the sole purpose of looking at a random assortment of animated gifs; just a series of out-of-context punchlines.
I guess you might counter all this by saying it sounds like I bought a joke book and expected a novel, I guess that may be true to a certain extent. But I feel a more apt comparison is meeting a new group of people and having them telling all their in jokes and expecting you to laugh along with them without engaging in any actual conversation.
If you're just looking for humour, then honestly, Jazzpunk will deliver that, you may not like everything (I'll put myself in that camp), but the chances are you'll find something to laugh at. Just beware that most the gameplay is in service of jokes... and going and looking for more jokes... oh and there's a frogger inspired mini game.

A nice optimization game based around producing, transporting, and selling various goods.
Pros:
- Tons of industries, products, and resources. Lots of transportation options.
- Very little guessing with the products. Lots of graphs and statistics tell you exactly how much of a product will be produced and consumed at each factory/store. This really helps optimizing.
- In-game wiki describes each product, where it is made, where it is sold, and what it takes to make.
Cons:
- Graphics are outdated (early 90s sprites). This doesn't really bother me a ton, but it could bother others.
- You never miss something until it's gone: the interface is outdated. Specifically, there is no time dilation (faster/slower) or pause. There is no view rotation which can make hooking up roads/rails difficult.
- The range of their buildings should be rebalanced. I find myself constantly either kicking myself or just taking dynamite to things because they are just out of range. Often by just one or two squares.
Nitpicks:
- They skimped on their English translator. You get the gist of what they're conveying, but it is off-putting. Names aren't exact so if you look for one thing, it's often called something else (though similar enough).
- Trains need brains. Even with two rails, they often go down the same side and slow each other down.
Edit: Found on the forums that + increases speed and - decreases. "P" will pause. Still marking them down for not showing key bindings in the options or something. Who knows what other keys I'm missing?

This "game" is genious. I have never had that much fun learning an instrument before. The main reason is that you hear the actual song (which sounds great) and your own notes mostly when you play them right, although you hear your wrong notes quietly as well. Sometimes during learning, it ramps you up fast (to chords for instance) but it also recommends that you take the lesson.
Unfortunately, we currently only have a 1/2 size e-guitar, since this was a gift for my son, who at age 7 loves to play this, although he still struggles a bit with the fret board at the same time. It is amazing how quickly you can progress, although to be fair you will hit speed bumps when you need to take a moment to learn a new skill.
It makes you feel really good when the game starts hiding numbers (number of the string) and string colours from you, showing that you are really progressing. I have even found myself not needing to look at the screen in certain parts at all anymore, because I start to "get it".
Only complaint is that unfortunately custom songs are difficult to make (with dynamic aid, which you need unless you are a pro), and while there is a lot of for-purchase DLC, not all the songs that I would like to have are in that list.
If you play the guitar, this is the game for you!

Thomas Was Alone, although very short, has so much charm and heart that I almost prefer it at its 3-4 hours of playtime. From the ongoing narrative that is built upon in each level to the terrific soundtrack, TWA is a great way to spend an afternoon. Think of it like this: Let's say that you're a huge fan of flavored tea. You pick up the traditional "indie platform" flavor, brew it, and bring what seems like a flavor you've tasted over and over to your lips. However, the taste has a vibrancy and a unique kick to it. You almost wonder if you grabbed the wrong flavor of tea, but you simply shrug back with a smile on your face, the magical brew reminding you exactly why you loved that flavor in the first place. It's a wonderful addition to the platforming puzzle-solver genre, and will have you both laughing and crying. The fact that you're laughing and crying over 4-sided shapes may leave you questioning your mental state, but don't question your sanity on this one: this game is a real knock out.

I hate saying I wouldn't recommend this game, but when I really asked myself, "would I go out of my way to tell someone to buy this game on Steam or PSP/PS3?" I knew deep down I never would.  That said, this is a VERY GOOD game.  I have no gripes with it or the way it plays.  It's very polished from the movement mechanics down to every aspect of the sound design and music.  Similar to the way Bastion or Stanley Parable plays, the narration is a key part in forming the narrative of the game.  However, in this game, the narration FORMS the narrative around the mechanics.  In the way that Antichamber was a video game about video game design, training you puzzle by puzzle, Thomas Was Alone is another sort of post-modern platformer that makes sense of what platformers are... if that makes sense.  I just found myself getting bored and, upon finding out there are 100 levels total when I got about 40% of the way through the game, I decided to move on.  I appreciate this game and what it accomplishes, but I just don't personally love platformers enough to finish the whole thing or recommend it.

Seasons after Fall is very strictly a light puzzle-platformer with amazing hand-painted art and a greatly relaxing soundtrack.
I wouldn't call Seasons after Fall a particularly challenging platformer. I went in comparing it to Ori and the Blind Forest because of the general look and feel that the videos and screenshots gave me. The game is not nearly so challenging as OatBF, but whether that is a positive or negative is really up to the individual.
SaF is very strictly a platformer -- there are no enemies, and very little in the way of mind-bending puzzles. All puzzle solving is delgated to figuring out which Season needs to be active in order to progress. Considering that you can switch seasons easily with just a press of a button and a flick of your mouse/joystick, it only takes a few tries to figure it all out. There were many areas where the need to switch season was incredibly clever -- but there were also a few puzzles that I solved on accident, which doesn't give me so much a feeling of victory as a feeling of confusion and possible annoyance for future playthroughs.
Not that future playthroughs would be particularly difficult, as the game is only about 7 hours long, which may make the $15 pricetag offputting for some. I bought it on sale for about $8 and I don't feel at all cheated, and I don't think that I would if I had paid the full $15 -- as just the art itself is worth that and more.
Exploration is necessary to complete all the achievements, though most of them come along with the story and don't require much effort. So if you're one of those people that like quick runthroughs for achievement based Steam perks, this may be interesting for you.
I was not expecting it to have fully voiced scenes, and while some of the dialogue can come off as a little childish it was enjoyable and engaging overall. The story is simple, but the game is simple overall, and so everything fits neatly together.
The only negative that I can really think of is the controls. I don't know if it was because I was using a gamepad rather than the mouse/keyboard, but often I found that the jumping wasn't nearly as responsive as it needs to be. Sometimes I would definitely press the jump button only for my fox to run directly off the edge. While the game doesn't punish you for slip ups, and therefore the issue with the controls wasn't gamebreaking, it was still frustrating and added time to otherwise simple jumps that I didn't need to repeat up to three times.
So, overall, I enjoyed my time with this game and would recommend it to most people who enjoy "Walking Simulators" such as Journey, as this game has a similar feel with a few clever puzzles and platforming added in. This is not a game for anyone who prefers to be pressed or challenged, but for those of us who like to take breaks with games that don't exert any pressure, this game is a perfect way to spend a few hours.

Such a lovely little game with an interesting puzzle mechanic: change the active season for different effects on your environment (specifically, certain types of plants and mushrooms).  Beautiful music, a wonderful painterly aesthetic, with an interesting story to boot.  The controls can be a bit wonky at times, if you're used to platform games with more aerial control, but I found them easy to get used to.  Definitely an indie gem.

If I told you that I spent several hours as a fox running through a forest changing the seasons in order to grow trees, ride on air vents, grow mushrooms... and then another several hours barking at rocks to free magic jellyfish, or put fireflies into intricate patterns, or create mystical puddle portals...
You'd probably think I was doing all the drugs.
But I wasn't.
I was playing Seasons After Fall.
10/10 would go on all the drug trips with my little fox again.
In all seriousness now, this game is beautiful, adorable, sad and uplifting all at once.  The platforming is fun, though it does get challenging and confusing at times - I suck at platformers anyway.  And I'm running the game on a potato, which says a lot since it runs beautifully even on a low-end laptop.  I definitely recommend this to anyone who wants to go on a beautiful adventure - and the music!  The tone is set so well with the amazing soundtrack that brings everything to life.  I want to buy the soundtrack.
I recommend using a controller to play this if you can, it allows for more fine movements and hotswitching seasons by simply flicking the right stick.  And it rumbles when you hit the ground.
Also, play with the sound on full.
Now for the bad stuff:  There are a few bugs and glitches.  Sometimes when you jump up to a ledge the fox will simply fall through it and through the terrain into nothingness, or back to the place you just climbed from.  Also, the game tends to glitch out after an hour or two on my computer.  Still 100% recommend this game to everyone.

This is a final review after getting 100% of achievements.
TL;DR: Enchanting, but unfulfilling. Definitely worth getting on sale.
WARNING. This review contains minor spoilers. Only a couple of them though, and they're not critical, so don't fret.
Pros:
+ Simple, but majestically arranged and animated artwork
+ Gorgeous string quartet soundtrack with only a single weak spot (explained below)
+ Intriguing world
+ Wonderful voice acting
+ Carefully crafted backdrops (all map segments are fully realized in all four seasons, which is incredible!)
+ Cool season-switching method
+ Cute fox protagonist
Cons:
- Potential of the world is bearely touched
- Poor story, silly conflict, underdeveloped characters
- Terrible fast travel methods, hence...
- Backtracking, backtracking, backtracking
- The Sirocco puzzle (also knows as the cicada puzzle)
- Lack of a desperately needed minimap
- Lack of goal progress indicators
- Ending that explains nothing and doesn't feel like an ending
- Minor control issues
Let's get the obvious things out of the way. The colors and the handling of artwork are stunning. The effects are beautiful, too. Drawings themselves are nothing to write home about, but it's actually better this way, because you're not supposed to focus on stills, you're supposed to focus on movement and how different it feels in different seasons: the crunching snow, the warm breeze, the playful rain, the thick hotness. The forest is beautiful, the seasons are distinct.
Some of the sound tracks reminded me of glorious Arcanum, and not just because both games employed string quartets. However, the Seasons After Fall OST is more diverse and... more playful, I guess? It certainly firmly stands on its own. The one dip is the track that plays during one of the most annoying parts in the game—talk about convergence of missteps—the cicada puzzle. More on it further down.
The voice acting in the English version! Goodness, how I loved the Seed! Both voice actors did a great job. Bravo to them.
Now... The thing about short games (and this one is pretty short, albeit not as short as Inside or Little Nightmares) is that they rarely have depth. It just doesn't fit in the few hours of gameplay. And it's usually fine, as they're there to provide a bite-size serving of entertainment with a possible tiny philosophical punch somewhere in the middle and at the end. Seasons After Fall doesn't have any depth in any department. The seasonal mechanics are underutilized and have few instances of combinations. Navigation is both convoluted and straightforward (part of a larger problem explained in the next paragraph). Character relationships and motivations are either simplistic or nonexistent. The story and conflict are kindergarten-level. Without spoiling anything, just... don't expect too much from them.
Seasons After Fall has a problem a lot of artsy games have: attempting to bolster immersion by minimizing the UI, the developers undershoot and overshoot with explanations to the player of what they're capable of and what's expected from them. The cicada puzzle is a major example of that. My personal advice: look it up online once you get to it. It's not difficult, it's just poorly explained. This UI minimization fever leads to unnecessary inconveniences and inconsistencies. For example, if you decide to go without a minimap, you're limiting yourself to simple level layouts—otherwise a lot of your players will probably get lost and frustrated. At the same time, they can't be too simple, 'cause navigating and backtracking through them will be boring.
The inconsistency here is that you still have obvious UI elements like the season switcher, the tree markings, the flower plot counter. Yet you don't have a minimap. And by the time you've understood and memorized the arrangement of levels and don't need the minimap as much, you're in the section of the playthrough that's 80% backtracking. It's basically artificial extension of play time by means of confusion and repetition.
I may re-play the game sometime in the future, but only for the visuals and the music. And boy, are those great! Great enough to lift this game from a 4/10 to a 7/10.
P.S. For all you 100%-achievement-seekers, look up the 'A Bird' achievement beforehand. It's stupid.

I must admit that I like the game.  I bought it on sale, still I consider it was expensive for what I got.  I really enjoyed the first version of Stardrive.  It was a nice little game, nothing like a major production game, but interesting.  This second version is a very diffrent game.  According to me, they took out a few things that made the first version interesting and diffrent from similar games.  Although, not every changes are bad.
Significant changes: This second version is really a turn-based game and not a real-time strategy game.  It relies on an hex-grid strategy map, I must admit this approach is a little deceiving to me.  Although, they added a concept that was missing in the first version, the player can now really own territory outside of system's reach.  The way chosen to do so is a little weird through building weak starbases centered in the hex tile...  Another addition is the notion of command points that really limits the number of ships that the players can build.  The way that research is conducted VERY diffrent from the first version, the techs are gathered in  sub-groups of 2-3 techs and the player has to choose one tech to research and cannot research the other techs from this group later.  It forces the player to exchange techs with allies to be able to exploit the more of tech tree.  This approach, I must admit, is interesting and allows to have real racial differences.  This is really missing in CIV type games...  Ground combat and ground troops managment is uselessly more complex.  Ship combat is interesting but strategic decisions possibilities are fairly limited.
AI: As for the AI, the game is fairly hard even when playing at 'easy' difficulty.  Random events are interesting but really increase the difficulty of the game.  Pirates are a very serious treath especially at the beginning of the game since transport ships are fully automated and will not avoid them at all (they even run into them).  Therefore, pirates will chush your merchant fleet in a few turns and your planets will starve to death meaning that you will need to build a fairly large fleet to crush the pirates, to build colony ships again and, after multiple turns, to build your merchant fleet again until the next pirate attack.  I am not sure the AI players face this treath, therefore the human player is often very late expanding and researching techs.  The human player is really threatened by the AI players.  If you expand to much every other player will declare war on you.  Though, diplomacy appears better than in the first version of the game.
Bugs:  A lot of people complain about bugs...  After nearly 20 hours playing the game, I faced only one bug and it was a minor bug solved by reloading the autosaved game.  No crash or fatal errors yet.
In a few words, the game is interesting, neither good or bad... it is average.  I good way to spend a few extra bucks and hours.  *** My rating: 6.5/10 ***

This is the best way for beginners to learn guitar with its many lessons while keeping it fun at the same time - also great for intermediate to advanced guitarists looking to improve or touch up on their skills.
The mini games are also a huge plus. They are basically lessons for scales, chords, slides and bends disguised as little arcade games. What other games make you say you played a beat 'em up with your guitar while learning scales at the same time? Exactly.
Session mode is a lot of fun as well. Pick your AI band's instruments, the complexity of the jam, a genre, hell, faff around with pretty much anything, and start shredding. The band plays along with you. You'll feel like a rockstar in no time! Fantastic way of learning how to improvise as well - especially when you feel confident enough to add mini solos for the hell of it. Great feeling!
That's not to say there's a couple of (minor) cons with this game. Sometimes the game crashes when picking a song or going to riff repeater, but it happens very rarely now. Also, the note detection, especially for power chords (for me, anyway) can be a little iffy. Also the in-game tuner is a little... whack. Get yourself a chromatic tuner, go with what the game says and then retune it yourself. Don't let this deter you from an absolutely amazing experience though. These are just the small problems I personally have with the game.
All in all... worth it. So worth it.

One night, we were talking a whole awful lot about friendship and what it means. The next day, I woke up to this game in my inventory. I didn't play it until now. We don't talk or play together anymore and my like for you has faltered but Thomas Was Alone, albeit a ♥♥♥♥ing jumping game which I am terrible at, is a beautiful game with a touching meaning and I'm thankful you've given this to me. Really, I am. I just never thought jumping blocks could move me.

What makes this platformer/puzzler stand out and worth your time is the novel and interesting story which drives the experience.  The game somehow manages to get you to develop sympathy and scorn for the otherwise-generic blocks you control. Other strong points are the music, voice acting, visual aesthetic, and varied jumping mechanics and player-character properties.  I think a weak point is the difficulty level--it's pretty low. Not once did I have to think for more than 5 seconds before figuring out the puzzles.  So eventually the levels became rituals of moving the blocks around so I could get to the next level and move the story along.
What made me buy this game ultimately was that Kotaku said "The jump in Thomas Was Alone might be amongst the best ever programmed." So, as a platformer junky, I couldn't pass it up.  The jumps are indeed very good. You're quite firmly in control of the little blocks, although sometimes I felt like the acceleration late in the jump was a little too high, but that's a personal preference. My jump mechanic award goes to Super Meat Boy and Spelunky, but whatever.
All in all, this game delivers a good platform/puzzle experience with a unique and compelling story, which is very rare in this genre.

Thomas Was Alone is a minimalist puzzle platformer. You play as several rectangles/squares, each with different names and varying personalities. After a serendipitous fluke, an A.I. named Thomas is created. He decides he wants to learn about the world, and as his adventure goes on, he meets other A.I.s. When people talk about fusing narrative with gameplay, TWA is a great example of this. All of the characters abilities and (limited) appearances reflect their personalities and their motives. For some strange reason, I became emotionally invested with these simple geometric shapes. There are even some tear-jerker moments strewn throughout, which delightfully caught me by surprise. The writing (all of it narrated, reminiscent of the Stanley Parable... the mod came out before) for them is very comedic and charming, making you want to keep seeing these shapes interact and finish their goals. I would like to say more about the narrative and characters, but anything is really a spoiler, and it is better to experience it without any prior knowledge.
The presentation for the game is quite pretty actually. Like I've said, the art style is minimal, but it doesn't make the game look boring. The lighting effects look nice while the squares slide through the environment, and their pastel colors contrast the stark black obstacles and the shaded background. It shows they have life in the dead computer world they inhabit.
Along with the art style is the soundtrack. The songs consist usually of violins, piano, and a reoccuring electronic melody. It is gorgeous, and really enhances the emotional impact of the more melancholic levels. One of my favorite pieces included ascending guitar tremolo, very similar to popular post-rock sounds (Sigur Ros, Godspeed You! Black Emperor). It just heightened everything I was feeling so much, that it is one of the most memorable gaming moments I have had yet.
However, the game isn't perfect. The thing is, the game really leaves you wanting more with the characters. A narration only happens twice (I might be wrong on that, but I'm pretty sure) within a stage, so it is very limiting to how much anyone can talk. The game is quite short, taking four hours and 100 stages, leaving only (approximately) 200 bits of dialogue.
The biggest problem with the game is the puzzles. I think "puzzles" is the wrong term for what you navigate in the game. They are more akin to obstacle courses, where you have to avoid spikes or hot water, and have to use teamwork between the squares to press buttons, make jumps, and get to each shape's respective portal. These obstacle courses leave much to be desired. Sure, the ones in the game already do make the characters seem to have a better connection when they have to help each other finish a stage. If there was more challenge to finishing a stage, they would seem more dependent with each other's help, and the catharsis of completing a hard puzzle would be like a high-five moment between them.
Thomas Was Alone is an interesting gem. I found its story/characters just as interesting as bigger indies like Braid and Bastion, but it lacks in the overall gameplay department. I can see this being a staple for my future children, as it is simple enough for them to play, and has a light-hearted atmosphere with some poignantly sad moments sprinkled throughout to (hopefully) keep it memorable for them. Thomas Was Alone definitely is for me.

Chapter 1 is actually pretty good. The atmosphere and the environment is nice and it promises a decent horror adventure game. Just the controls are really clumsy, for some reason you can't turn 180° when facing the wall, you first need to turn left or right. Also the hero can run only for about 3 seconds before getting tired.
Starting with Chapter 2 you get randomly attacked by monsters insta-killing you on touch, often giving you little chance to avoid them. Yeah I know you can learn their paths and how to avoid them, but at the same time you are supposed to find your way in a labyrinth of same-looking rooms, find hidden items and solve complicated cryptic illogical puzzles. Even after an hour of playing when I knew the level pretty well, I still got regularly killed resetting my progress to the only savepoint in the level. Also it forces you to spend a lot of time just waiting for the monster to finally go away (over and over and over again). This is not scary at all, it's just annoying, frustrating and boring.
Chapter 3 is completely different but not better. The monsters are gone but so is the atmosphere. This chapter consists of a bunch of dumb fetch quests (find a lost bunny, get a toilet paper, ask everyone some question, ...) and running around trying to find out what the game wants you to do next.
Chapter 4 and the monsters are back. This time it's actually a bit better. There are two savepoints in the level, plenty of places to hide and a MAP! Finally! I realized why I had liked Amnesia so much. Unlike this game Amnesia didn't throw a monster on you every 30 seconds and it didn't kill you every 2 minutes.
Chapter 5. This one consists of a ton of cutscenes (this game has more endings than The Lord of the Rings trilogy) and pointless "walk right" sections. The biggest problem is that there is no savepoint and the cut-scenes and dialogues are not skippable! On my first playthrough the game crashed after a few minutes, returning me back to the end of Chapter 4. So after restart I had to watch the cutscenes and click through the dialogues again. Then I got to a level so dark I could barely see anything. I heard a telephone ringing but couldn't see it so I continued walking right and suddenly I got instantly killed by a monster. Back to chapter 4!! The third time I didn't miss the telephone booth but the game crashed again. BACK TO CHAPTER 4!!! Finally I was able to finish this damn game. The ending was... ok, I guess. Not very surprising, I expected something like that, but it could have been worse.
Overall: Not many games were able to make me scream on the screen like crazy. Silence of the Sleep did it several times. Both thumbs down.

When I first saw this game on Kongregate, it was something of an odd ball. Just make up some name, jump in, and the servers would connect you with a couple dozen other players going through the same dozen maps to collect cheese and bring it to the hole. Simple. I first thought of it as some odd sociology expiriment, as almost all the maps at the time seemed to be testing the players. Half of them allowed players to go very quickly through it, but doing so would jeporadize the other mice. I didn't expect it to last a year, and yet in the year 2015, it stands.
So what's changed since then? Well, the community makes maps, of which there are now thousands of unique ones. Shamen have been given more interesting puzzles to work with, combined with skill trees to make interesting possibilities, along with Hard and Divine mode. Mod support is in, shown through the wide variety of rooms you can join. If you want to hone your skills as a normal mouse, Bootcamp will whip you into shape. If you want to be able to survive troll shamen, Survivor can show you the tricks to that. Music allows for users to submit Youtube videos to be watched by all the occupants, and there's more yet. Tribes are a thing, if you want to have friends collaborate for fun. The cosmetics channel true TF2 spirit by allowing you to alter the appearance of your mouse with a long line of items that all can be bought with in-game cheese. Events are brought about every holiday of the year, adding some new aspect to the game. Emotes became a thing, so you no longer need to pretend to sit or cry, because you can actually sit and cry.
And you know what? It doesn't seem to be stopping. It just keeps going, showing true devotion to the style of having a simple, fun game. Just by playing as a mouse, getting some nice, tasty cheese.

I purchased this game for $1.00, on sale, as I had wanted to play this game for so long.
The game, at its current state, is not much at all.
The game is playable, but very buggy. You may not be able to walk over things crouched, get stuck on corners of buildings, mobs may jitter around, mobs may get stuck...etc. However, it is still playable.
The game has very little content. The map is large, but at the base level the game is: deliver a package, escort a deliverer, defend a safe zone (it's actually defend yourself until you fix the anti nether machines). Killing mobs/nethers and killing other players, I did not include as content as these are things that you do anyways.
Additionally, as the game looks very underdeveloped and there is such little content, there are not many people on. There are about 20 servers total with none of them being full most of the time.
That being said, I find Nether to be fun and really just the main thing being that it has little content. If content can be added, this game would be quite fun.
Though limited, the forms of combat and approach to exploring the cities are great. Sneaking is a real thing and you can level up your efficiency of stealth by leveling.
Each Nether/mob is different and must be combated differently. Due to this, they are actual real threats and players must not only be cautious. but smart. This offers an additional entertainment value besides player killing. This also promotes cooperation as purely pvping is not always the best.
As mentioned before, this offers entertainment based not purely on other players. You can play this game solo and still enjoy it. Such games like DayZ require you to have other players to enjoy it, as it is a garbage game. (It's not even a sandbox, it's just an environment with players).
What I would like to see:
traps
diversity of building layouts
more exploration of buildings, inside houses, different floors to buildings
more items and crafting
more variety of nethers/mobs
roof top access to buildings.

This game had it's 10th birthday this year, I only played it for the first time a few years back and have made it my yearly tradition to come back around this time of year (October - December) to replay Overlord + Raising hell. I got this game years prior in a bundle of some kind for about 90p/just over $1. After neglecting to play it for ages I finally got round to it and for that amount of money it blew my mind - even for the average price it is on here now (£3.50) it's an absolute steal.
I'll sum up every major point with a title so jump to the sections you want to know about.
The elephant in the room is what this game looks like and there's no other way to put it than "It's an old looking game" - though thats not necessarily a bad thing. There was a certain style of graphics from mid 2000-2010 that really stuck out, I'll call it the "Nostalgia aesthetic" because that's what it really is to me. It shares the same visual style as games such as Fable (2004) Everquest 2 (2004) and LOTR: Battle for Middle Earth (2006). The style wont be for everyone, but for those that grew up around these kind of visuals it's a massive blast of nostalgia welcoming you back to when games weren't buggy frame-killing messes.
This is where Overlord comes into it's own. You control your character as you would in any game, but the main mechanic here is controling minions. This game is primarily based around managing your minions to complete puzzles, kill enemies and grab treasure. You get 4 types of minions throughout the game, and several upgrades that increasue your capacity to summon more minions to destroy things with.
Along with this, your character the Overlord can also be upgraded. Through the game you will come across molds for weapons and armour that you can make, along with extra spells, health and magic upgrades in the from of totems.
Overlord is packed full of various settings and things to see. In essence it's a dungeon crawler, but hardly feels like one in a lot of places since it's very player driven. As with many games from this era there are set paths with a lot of invisible walls, but the sheer amount of set paths there are in each zone with places to explore and treasure to get is pretty amazing. The area you'll see the most will be your tower, where you can monitor your progression visually as it happens - more on that later. The zones go through all the tropes of fantasy (with a twist on every one) with the game pointing out how stereotypical things are, which brings up the next point.
There is so much typical British humour packed in I don't even know where to begin. Throughout the whole game you'll have a minion named Gnarl who gives you pointers on what to do and chimes in with random thoughts along the way when things happen. You know it's good when even the comedy stands up 10 years later, every sarcastic comment he makes accompanying what happens on screen at that point in time is perfection.
Similar to Fable again, the story isn't anything mindblowingly incredible - it's on the same level as a Bethesda game. The thing you want to focus on more here is the choice system. In Fable, the choices you make will effect your physical appearance drastically with good choices giving you blonde hair with a halo and bad choices eventually leading to your eyes going black and you growing horns.
Similarly, Overlord does this via your amour; the more evil you become your armour will progressively get spikey, turn a black-ish gray colour with a black cloak. If you decide to be good your armour will look a very bright polished silver with a red cloak.
That's not all though, it's not just you who changes. The entire tower changes too in the same ways you do. Your evil deeds will make the skies dark, the tower darker and will become just as spikey as you are. If you're good the skies will become brighter and so will the tower. You can also customise the tower with your gold, able to spend it on furnashings for your main hall, throne, torches and even the private quaters.
(For the hoarders, You also get a treasure room, similar to fable 3 where the more gold you have the more it floods the room with coins, to the point where you can't even enter it anymore.)
As with the visual style, the OST has the same feel. You can certainly tell it's an old fantasy game but that just adds to the appeal. Each zone's music is masterfully crafted by none other than Michiel van den Bos, composer of Unreal Tournament Age of Wonders and Deus Ex! I've usually taken the good choices in games, but my GOD does this soundtrack encourage the evil side of you to come out.
This is one of the best games of it's time, but overlooked by everyone including myself. It went from sitting in my library for YEARS to being played every single year. If you like good RPGs, if you like games that give you choices, if you like Fable or any of the others I listed - PLEASE give this game a shot, for a mere £3.50 there is nothing to lose.

I came back to retry this game after several months; the initial version was just unbearable, the current version is much better but is still missing... something.
So theres some production bugs with enemies, approval on blockaded planets remains at 60% yet when your own planets are blockaded they drop much further. An example of this would be blockading enemy planet with a population of 5 and still pumping out a cruiser every 2-3 turns from said planet. Vanilla Vulfar will zerg rush you, destroy a fleet with CP of 20, in two turns you will be fighting a near identical fleet, in two turns a near identical fleet... gets quite repetitive.
Diplomacy interface could use some work, looks and feels like a Total War diplomacy menu/mechanic except AI doesn't get penalized by your race for espionage but will penalize your relations for espionage actions.
Which brings us to in my opinion, the most broken mechanic in the game - espionage. Biggest peeve - its integrated into the diplomacy menu poorly. Granted you can crank out spys in 1 turn, this feels like the AI is somehow managing to spam you with ships, crank out spies and steal your tech simultaneously without getting a relations penalization. But if your spy gets caught you lose relations with that race for like 50 turns or something godawful and the kicker is these penalties stack for you as the player. Espionage acts take 250-500 espionage points, nothing wrong there, to plant a mole to steal tech is 500 points, figure each spy generates 1 point by default and while generating points must roll to not be destroyed by counterintelligence - which penalizes you, not AI relations. Then you plant 1 mole which sacrifices an offensive spy and usually gets intercepted within 10 turns. YET the AI is able to steal tech from you back to back on turns early game (pre battleships) so I'm not sure if the machinic is broken but espionage system needs a LOT of work, complete overhaul even.
I think that ground combat mechanics of the original were better, customization of troops is nice, limits are'nt but theres tricks to get around it, you can max troops on every planet except the one thats donating troops to all the others. The combat missions are a nice touch though.
Cannot customize starbases! They level like your fighters with tech research which is pretty lame.
Once you figure out the strategy of the game, its pretty much wash rinse repeat. Even with randomizing personalities or creating and assigning your own it still breaks down to cheap corvette missle spam early game, shields and DPS or spam fighters mid game and if you make it to late game (without beating the AI or getting one of the victory conditions) canopy shields and chaos cannons (i think thats what they're called - purple pieces) but you propbably wont see a late game unless you start out very isolated. If you want a challenge start next to Vulfar so they can spam you with missile cruisers right as you get a decent fleet going, by then another faction will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you for trying to steal thier tech or expanding to more than 3 systems and the Vulfar will magically get a better shield tech than you have traded to them.
I'd like to see better/more modding, I'm not a big fan of the turn base (I just use pause in the original for planning), fix espionage system, creatable starbases, blockade mechanic/production spamming by AI - theres other ways to make AI challenging than allowing it to "cheat". Not much replayability at this time. Hope to see that change.

The original StarDrive was fun and it was the first 4x strategy game I've ever played. It had some balancing problems though, and the way of moving units around felt slow and was difficult.
StarDrive 2 fixed the movement issue, but it made the bad balancing worse and introduced a lot of new bugs that make the game nearly unplayable. I would not recommend this game unless you turn off random encounters and try to be allied with all the other races, or you're willing to have the game go nowhere or set out to bully you into quitting.
I'll go through a list of the bugs and issues I encountered:
-With random encounters on, the alien forces (not the other races) will show up and ruin all of your progress, and they appear so early in the game that you don't have the technology to defend against them.
-The AI can build hundreds of ships and somehow support them all, even while in debt. They can then send these huge fleets to fight you and they will obliterate you no matter what you do.
-If you only have a space station in a planet space defense battle, the AI ships will not move to attack. The only exception is if it's the aliens mentioned before, and after they start having the ships with the canopy shields in their fleets, they destroy everything.
Those are the biggest issues I've encountered. As for what the game did right:
-Everything is turn-based similar to Civilization, and movement still takes time which is handled by the passing of each turn after issuing an order. Researching is handled by turn, building as well, and etc.
-The map's planet systems and any other area of the map is in a hex system, which makes it cleaner to look at and easier to find things (for me, at least).
-You cannot just research everything in the game.
Overall, I can't recommend the game. If the big issues of the game are fixed, then I could recommend it, but until then I cannot.

Whether or not to recommend this game is a very difficult decision to make for me.
I truly enjoyed this game. I enjoy the shipbuilding and playing around with all the components and designs and how it allowed me to try different builds. I liked how some hulls had special benefits to them, like one hull gave a bonus to armor placed in it and another one that gave a large damage boost to beam weapons, and if you didn't want those, probably due to the increase in production cost, you could stick with the bonus-less hulls. I also loved a lot of the writing, as this game is not a "serious" game. A lot of the interactions with other races and events are funny, and there are a lot of references to other media, like Stargate, Masters of Orion, Futurama, and even Ghostbusters.
However, the game is significantly unpolished and very buggy. For example, when I auto finished a space battle, if my fleet was large enough, I couldn't scroll all the way down to see if all the ships survived. At first, when I tried to see what a research topic was, the tooltip was hidden behind the research screen so I couldn't read most of it. When going to the next turn, if you were colonizing a planet and invading another, the screens would appear at the same time. All minor things, just little nuisances.
There are also a lot of bugs, some bigger problems than others. Sometimes, even when I have surplus food and freighters to move the food to starving planets, those planets still starve. I can have deep space stations next to a sector and the sector can have full influence, but I still don't gain control over it. Various bugs that I've seen on the forums that still haven't been fixed. Thankfully, most of these bugs, while they do affect certain aspects of gameplay, they are pretty much never, in my experience, game breaking, and usually pretty easy to deal with or doesn't hurt too much.
Like I said, even with those issues, I still enjoyed the game. If you have a low tolerance for bugs and general lack of polish, then I would say you should pass on this game. I would probably suggest that you try other 4X space games like Stellaris before trying this, but if you've tried most of those games or this one goes on a really good sale, I would probably say you can give it a try.

This is a final review after getting 100% of achievements.
TL;DR: Enchanting, but unfulfilling. Definitely worth getting on sale.
WARNING. This review contains minor spoilers. Only a couple of them though, and they're not critical, so don't fret.
Pros:
+ Simple, but majestically arranged and animated artwork
+ Gorgeous string quartet soundtrack with only a single weak spot (explained below)
+ Intriguing world
+ Wonderful voice acting
+ Carefully crafted backdrops (all map segments are fully realized in all four seasons, which is incredible!)
+ Cool season-switching method
+ Cute fox protagonist
Cons:
- Potential of the world is bearely touched
- Poor story, silly conflict, underdeveloped characters
- Terrible fast travel methods, hence...
- Backtracking, backtracking, backtracking
- The Sirocco puzzle (also knows as the cicada puzzle)
- Lack of a desperately needed minimap
- Lack of goal progress indicators
- Ending that explains nothing and doesn't feel like an ending
- Minor control issues
Let's get the obvious things out of the way. The colors and the handling of artwork are stunning. The effects are beautiful, too. Drawings themselves are nothing to write home about, but it's actually better this way, because you're not supposed to focus on stills, you're supposed to focus on movement and how different it feels in different seasons: the crunching snow, the warm breeze, the playful rain, the thick hotness. The forest is beautiful, the seasons are distinct.
Some of the sound tracks reminded me of glorious Arcanum, and not just because both games employed string quartets. However, the Seasons After Fall OST is more diverse and... more playful, I guess? It certainly firmly stands on its own. The one dip is the track that plays during one of the most annoying parts in the game—talk about convergence of missteps—the cicada puzzle. More on it further down.
The voice acting in the English version! Goodness, how I loved the Seed! Both voice actors did a great job. Bravo to them.
Now... The thing about short games (and this one is pretty short, albeit not as short as Inside or Little Nightmares) is that they rarely have depth. It just doesn't fit in the few hours of gameplay. And it's usually fine, as they're there to provide a bite-size serving of entertainment with a possible tiny philosophical punch somewhere in the middle and at the end. Seasons After Fall doesn't have any depth in any department. The seasonal mechanics are underutilized and have few instances of combinations. Navigation is both convoluted and straightforward (part of a larger problem explained in the next paragraph). Character relationships and motivations are either simplistic or nonexistent. The story and conflict are kindergarten-level. Without spoiling anything, just... don't expect too much from them.
Seasons After Fall has a problem a lot of artsy games have: attempting to bolster immersion by minimizing the UI, the developers undershoot and overshoot with explanations to the player of what they're capable of and what's expected from them. The cicada puzzle is a major example of that. My personal advice: look it up online once you get to it. It's not difficult, it's just poorly explained. This UI minimization fever leads to unnecessary inconveniences and inconsistencies. For example, if you decide to go without a minimap, you're limiting yourself to simple level layouts—otherwise a lot of your players will probably get lost and frustrated. At the same time, they can't be too simple, 'cause navigating and backtracking through them will be boring.
The inconsistency here is that you still have obvious UI elements like the season switcher, the tree markings, the flower plot counter. Yet you don't have a minimap. And by the time you've understood and memorized the arrangement of levels and don't need the minimap as much, you're in the section of the playthrough that's 80% backtracking. It's basically artificial extension of play time by means of confusion and repetition.
I may re-play the game sometime in the future, but only for the visuals and the music. And boy, are those great! Great enough to lift this game from a 4/10 to a 7/10.
P.S. For all you 100%-achievement-seekers, look up the 'A Bird' achievement beforehand. It's stupid.

On a lazy Sunday afternoon, I decided to go through my Steam library and play some games I haven't played yet. The first game that got me interested was "Thomas Was Alone". I've heard and read from the internet that it's a pretty awesome indie game. So then I decided to download and installed it.
After I played it, the internet was right! (again)
Who would have tought that a game this simple could touch your heart and make us feel warm inside? If you look at the game's graphics and gameplay mechanics, Thomas Was Alone is a pretty damn simple game. It is just a simple puzzle platformer with boxes with different shapes and colours as the characters that we control!
But what makes Thomas Was Alone interesting, touching, and makes us wanting more is the glorious story narration and music. Props to the narrator, Danny Wallace, for bringing such a great story narration and making the characters (boxes) feel alive. The music is gorgeus and feels right in each moment of the game. Because of this narration and music combination, I feel like I was emotionally attached with the characters, which is once again, boxes.
The only (tiny) negative I can give for this game is the level design. Halfway through the game, I feel bored with some of the levels. But the positives kept me playing.
So if you have some time to spare, try Thomas Was Alone. Worth your time.

Rocksmith 2014 is, without a doubt, the BEST way to pick up and learn guitar or bass today. I already knew how to play guitar before I ever touched Rocksmith, I even thought I was pretty decent. Since I primarily play bass I've felt that the instrument is always seen as inferior to many, so I was overjoyed to see that the game featured a fully-integrated bass "career path" and it wasn't just a slapped-on, last-minute feature. The only thing I would like to see added for bass is full support for 5 and 6-string basses; you can use them just fine it's just the tuning screen and the main gameplay sessions show a 4-string.
There's a great selection of songs from different genres to choose from and all of the DLC packs are fantastic, even the original Rocksmith DLCs are forward-compatible. Aside from learning songs and watching the technique videos and doing the exercises, there are many other things you can do: the "Guitarcade" where you play (music-themed) arcade games using your instrument, "Score Attack" for competing on the online leaderboards, and a Session mode where you can jam with AI band members to practice your skills. That's just the tip of the iceberg, so be prepared for hours upon hours of fun (and learning!).
No matter if you're a complete beginner or you consider yourself a guitar god give this game a shot, you won't be disappointed. 10/10

Around December of last year, I was looking for a good and solid method for learning guitar. I came across Rocksmith when I visited a friend. When trying it out on his PC, I got into the game immediately and it became very difficult to put my friend's guitar down. After that, I purchased the Rocksmith guitar bundle on Amazon and got it for Christmas.
Rocksmith introduced me to guitar in an incredible way. The dynamic difficulty system started off with simple notes that gradually led to chords over time. As I got the hang of chords and techniques, I became better at more difficult phrases. Fairly soon, I found myself jamming constantly on the main menu. Commençons par le commencement  -
Résumé : Vous venez d'être embauché par un service de l'Etat, afin de bosser sur leur nouveau logiciel de sécurité publique : Orwell. Ce logiciel top secret, permet de mettre sous surveillance des personnes et leurs proches. Chose utile, quand vous avez pour mission d'enquêter et de démanteler un réseau d'extrémistes, suspectés d'avoir commandité un attentat à la bombe.
Avis : Bon vous l'aurez compris, ce jeu s'inspire directement de l'œuvre de George Orwell : 1984.
C’est donc sans grande surprise que vous allez devoir vous immiscer dans la vie de personnes, les espionner, et ainsi, essayer d'en apprendre plus sur le ou les extrémiste(s) impliqué(s) dans l'attentat.
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, est une fiction interactive exclusivement en anglais.  En effet, les seules actions du joueur consistent à lire (beaucoup) de texte, pour ensuite faire des choix. Le gameplay est assez intuitif et l'on arrive vite à comprendre les différentes ficelles du jeu.
Là où le jeu gagne des points c'est, indubitablement, grâce à son scénario. Le jeu se découpe comme un livre, avec plusieurs "chapitres". Chaque donnée enregistrée et collectée apporte sa pierre à l'édifice. Petit à petit, le scénario prends de l'ampleur, et ce, jusqu'au paroxysme final.
En conclusion : Si vous êtes totalement hermétique à l'anglais ou aux fictions interactives, passez votre chemin. Sinon, vous pouvez acheter ce jeu les yeux fermés. Si Orwell est un jeu dans lequel l'histoire prime avant tout, le joueur n’est pas passif, loin de là. Le scénario vous fera hésiter, mais aussi réfléchir au travers de choix qui vous allez devoir faire.  Une chose est certaine : dans notre monde hyperconnecté d’aujourd’hui, le thème de la liberté ainsi que de la frontière entre le domaine public et le domaine privé, touche tout le monde. De ce point de vu, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" ne peut laisser personne indifférent...  :)

I wanted to love this game, but after 7 hours I decided to walk out from constantly battling the interface and the mechanics. The concept is utterly brilliant, the backstory hilarious, though within the game the humour ranges from utterly marvellous and very clever to puerile and utterly gross.
I would have put up with the bad bits a bit longer to get to more good bits. One of the major design decisions was to let the game autosave at checkpoints with no option to manually save, which means that if you fail in a boss battle (and the difficulty of those is pretty hardcore, do not be fooled by the humour, you need fast reflexes and a LOT of strategic understanding to win here) you have to go through the whole sequence that led up there again, and you have to sit through every cut scene and clever comment again.
Ah yes, the cut scenes. They're clever and seamless - so seamless, at times, that I failed to recognise when my character became responsive (since the in-game-guide is still talking and the animation still playing) and thus failed to dodge in time. Add to that that you need to run around and dodge and keep an eye on characters, but the mouse responsiveness varies, so that you're sometimes simply whizzing past the direction you want to look in and stare at a wall again, which is... not good for your health.
Before you play, you need to set up each and every key. The keybinding makes you scroll through a list of acceptable keys (the arrow keys are not on it) to choose; and a lot of the presets do not exist on a Mac keyboard or are otherwise misleading: press '`'  to do x means 'click the third mouse button' but I had to quit the game and start the launcher and scroll through the list to find THAT out because pressing the ` key did precisely nothing. Total immersion fail. (AND then I had to go through the whole scene again and do a number of tedious tasks AGAIN because see above re: autosave).
In this game, your minions will do a lot of the work for you - squeeze into places your overlordship just will not fit - and the designers have included an override for the AI's pathfinding algorithm, but this is, in itself, somewhat imprecise. The point where I decided to walk out was when - repeatedly - I tried to follow instructions to direct my minions to a certain location and failed: instead they jumped into the fray and were, predictably, killed, leaving me with not enough minions to complete the quest. Hu-bloody-ray.
There is much to like about this game, but for me, the annoyance over the mechanics outweighs the (considerable) amount of fun I've had playing.

This ruins the experince for you and the other players because now theyre playin with a bot which are easy to fight so it hurts the team you were on because they now have "dead weight" and it ruins the experince for the opponents because now they have an easy opponet that presents no challenge.
2a. Turtling- biggest problem with gameplay in For Honor  is "turtling" or in other words playing defensively and not attacking at all. The way the game is now there are about 4 heros that can make a turtle have to do something while the rest literally can not get past a turtle defense and it just becomes a staring match unless you want to lose because the way this game is setup playing aggresive is just asking to die since parrying and defending is so easy once you learn the game. If you just let attacks fly youre guarenteed to get destroyed by any player who knows what theyre doing.
2b. Hero imbalance- there are about 5 heroes on the game that are so much better than the rest that if youre not playin one of them and you are fighting one of them you are at a pretty big disadvantage if it s a similarly skilled player or better. Those 5 heros are mainly better because they can open up "turtles" and make them have to do something. Silence Of The Sleep (Not Silence Of The Lambs) made by only one man managed to create an interesting world to explore in as your main character Jacob Reeves tries to figure out why he tried to commit suicide in the first place but before I say anything good about the game I want to address the game's flaws first & it has some very annoying flaws that I just have to mention because I want this game dev to succeed.
Alright one of my main gripes about this game is in Chapter 4 with that god damn sewer level it just drives me up the wall on how tedious, mundane & boring it is because while I'm trying to solve the puzzles in the sewer I can't constantly keep hiding from monsters that move too slow it just ruins the tension for me which equals a lot of rage inducing moments when I'm backtracking a lot. This is actually one of the main cons in the game which almost gave the game it's downfall but thank god chapter 5 saved it from turning the game into a disaster because I was enjoying the game a lot & I just want to mention in Chapter 2 with the monsters in the motel as much as they only had a repeated pattern of walking they didn't move slow as hell so hopefully more of that tension in your next game & if your going to add a sewer level please add something new in the plate because backtracking isn't fun or scary. My final issue is the controls for moving your character I'm just going to be blunt I hate turning my character like a ballerina a lot in the calm sections but I didn't mind it when I'm chased by monsters because it added tension for me so that's the last con to mention but hopefully the next game won't make me twirl around like an idiot the entire game.
Now for the accomplishments the one man game dev delivered an awesome story to get addicted on (The game lasts around 10-11 hours but it depends on how good you are at puzzles because I sucked at some puzzles & sadly there is no voice acting in the game so you have to read all the text) despite the game having some common horror tropes the game manages to remain fresh with a unique animation style, great music, weird shadow monsters (I think that's where the Silent Hill influence kicks in), some cool puzzles (I'm leaving out the sewer puzzles because that level sucked) & a bunch of interesting NPCs like the mysterious bartender for example but I could just ramble on forever on what the game did right but I can't do that because there is a limit of how many words I can type so overall on a good sale or if you want to pay full price you have to check this game out.
Bonus: An official short film for the game has been made
Bonus 2: The game dev is making a new psychological horror game called The Human Gallery so keep your eyes on that game in the future
EDIT: The game dev takes feedback seriously & I respect that kind of passion

The game is very enjoyable, it has a good selection of production, sale and transport methods to begin with, a nice early game, the mid game introduces much more complicated production chains, which you can however ignore if you prefer simpler production chains. As of writing this review, I have not gotten to the late game yet.
I would also not be too quick in comparing it with OpenTTD, as some reviewers seem to do. The similarities between the games are merely that they are 2D isometric games which feature vehicles. The base game of OpenTTD focuses on transporting one of about 10 different goods with very simple production chains, this game features complex production chains and much more flexible vehicles, which allow you a much greater ability to plan efficient routes (For example a truck can transport one good one way and another the other way)
Overall I think you should try the game out. As other reviewers pointed out, there is the chance it might not run on your computer, however if that proves to be the case you can just take advantage of Steam's refund policy.

As divisive as it may be for "fans" of the franchise i must say that i had a blast with this game.
Re6 is a game that has its quirks; abrupt camera angle switches, an abundance of QTEs, dated visuals and overly ambitious yet lukewarm set pieces.
Underneath those flaws however lies a combat system so unique and well made that i'd go as far to say that it's without a doubt one of the best ones i've had the pleasure to play this gen.
If i were to keep 3-4 TPS combat systems from this gen then RE6 would definitely be included alongside the likes of Vanquish, Max Payne 3 and maybe Space Marine with its intense mix of ranged and melee.
RE6's combat is based upon awareness, precision and evasion. Each encounter requires you to know your enemy's weakpoints, be aware of your environments and use them for massive damage and finally evade and properly time your strike to deliver a counter attack.
Enemy weak point knowledge is a must as nearly all enemies can be downed with a few well placed shots. Failure in focusing on said weakpoints will find you spending mag after mag in an attempt to kill an adversary.
While chest-high cover is in the game its only purpose is to regain stamina as the game forces you to go toe to toe with enemies finishing them off with melee and exploiting invincibility frames.
Range of movement is also incredible with 4 way roll/evade, slides, 180 degree spins on the floor, quick recovery from attacks, quick attacks that stun enemies and consume stamina points,etc.
Inventory management is also the best the franchise has seen so far, allowing you to mix, match and discard items on the fly and the tablet system makes healing a breeze.
Another thing to applaud is the enemy mutation system with foes reacting on each and every hit differently, forcing you to constantly adapt to their forms and attack patterns.
In place of gun upgrades there is a perk system this time arround that lets you customize and fine tune your play style; you can focus on ranged and/or melee, opt for more in-game drops or equip perks that boost your healing capabilities and that of your allies.
The game's story is a 20+ hr long roller coaster ride through a wide gamut of emotions and the story itself can be described as a mix between Lethal Weapon, 28 days later and Maniac Cop (?!) with the everpresent (and personally always welcome) RE6 cheesiness.
There's a bit of Demon's/ Dark Souls flavor in the campaign as there are options to invade ones game as a creature and at certain points in the plot where paths entwine between characters, two pairs of players can join forces.
Mercs mode makes a welcome return alongside its frantic PC only variant: No Mercy with guest cameos from L4D characters and foes. If you also opt for the season pass there are 5 more modes each with its unique play style.
The PC version while not looking spectacular, is still way better than the console variants with many options in the menu and no frame cap for the 120+ Hz crowd.
Due to the game's idiosyncrasies i'd suggest to 1st play (classic) mercs on the very first stage (Urban Chaos), fine tune the controls and FoV to your liking (choosing laser sight aiming is STRONGLY recommended) and then proceed to familiarize yourself with the combat system until you can get at least an A grade consistently. Then go into options and turn QTE assist on. While most QTEs are not hard by any means there are a couple of them that are rage-inducing so it's better to save yourself from the mental breakdown alltogether.
Finally the game criminally forces you to go through the prologue when you fire it up for the first time, prohibiting you from even changing some gameplay options. My advice? Stick with it! It's not indicative of the in-game experience by any means and all it manages to do is to outline the game's flaws. Why did they choose to give such a bad first impression? I'd guess to set a cinematic "feel" but it fails miserably imo.
Highly recommended for TPS aficionados and action enthousiasts in general with an appetite for something exotic and distinct.

The beginning was all good and dandy, but then the bugs started creeping in. The worst was a bug that prevented creating new ship designs since all the sudden edit roster screen remained blank. Apparently the feature has been broken for at least a year without a fix. Luckily the panel started to work after awhile and game restart. So far I got some 15 hours to the game without other major bugs. Once one of my ship got stuck in limbo in interstellar space (couldn't take any orders) after I pressed "cancel orders" while the ship was moving to refit. The ship probably would have remained there forever unless I wouldn't have built listening post to that sector that somehow freed it. Some other bugs were related to graphical glitches. I have to keep the negative review up to this point since the game still feels its in beta. I read that some updates are eventually coming which might balance the game and fix some more bugs but at this point, I'd probably hold my purchases.
"Shortly" the negative and positive things:
- game has balancing issues pacing, tech and AI wise
- ship refitting is just nightmare (confusing UI, slow)
- building ships using tiny square modules is fun at the beginning but at the end, you wish you just had a list of things to put
- spacebattles are a bit meh, since there isn't much strategy you can use (pretty much you go forward and shoot). Also sfx, especially sound effects are poor
- fleet management is painful at times since your fleet can be scattered around free coordinates (not starbound). Example: you think your fleet is protecting your planet with starbase when "Antares" attacks but its not since its few pixels off the planet coordinates -> you don't get your starbase into the battle
- general lack of originality: everything is nicked from other 4x games
- ridden with bugs that probably never gets fixed
+ hey, its a decent Moo2 clone
+ ship design micromanagement is fun at the beginning (lots of options)
+ ion storm / nebula sectors are new inventions (?)
+ pixel art is good
